(سُورَةُ المائِدَةِ مَدَنِيَّةٌ وهي مِائَةٌ وعِشْرُونَ آيَةً)
Surat al-Ma'ida (the Table Spread, a chapter) is Medinan and has one hundred and twenty verses.

﷽
In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أوْفُوا بِالعُقُودِ أُحِلَّتْ لَكم بَهِيمَةُ الأنْعامِ إلّا ما يُتْلى عَلَيْكم غَيْرَ مُحِلِّي الصَّيْدِ وأنْتُمْ حُرُمٌ إنَّ اللَّهَ يَحْكُمُ ما يُرِيدُ﴾
"O you who have believed, fulfill (all) contracts. Lawful to you are the (domesticated) beasts of grazing livestock, except what is recited to you, but not while you are in a state of ihram (sacred state of pilgrimage) hunting game. Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills."

﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا تُحِلُّوا شَعائِرَ اللَّهِ ولا الشَّهْرَ الحَرامَ ولا الهَدْيَ ولا القَلائِدَ ولا آمِّينَ البَيْتَ الحَرامَ يَبْتَغُونَ فَضْلًا مِن رَبِّهِمْ ورِضْوانًا وإذا حَلَلْتُمْ فاصْطادُوا ولا يَجْرِمَنَّكم شَنَآنُ قَوْمٍ أنْ صَدُّوكم عَنِ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ أنْ تَعْتَدُوا وتَعاوَنُوا عَلى البِرِّ والتَّقْوى ولا تَعاوَنُوا عَلى الإثْمِ والعُدْوانِ واتَّقُوا اللَّهَ إنَّ اللَّهَ شَدِيدُ العِقابِ﴾ [المائدة: ٢]
"O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah, nor the sacred month, nor the offerings, nor the garlands, nor those heading to the Sacred House seeking bounty from their Lord and His good pleasure. And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt. And do not let the enmity of a people (for having barred you from the Sacred Mosque) incite you to transgress. Cooperate in righteousness and piety, and do not cooperate in sin and aggression. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment."

﴿حُرِّمَتْ عَلَيْكُمُ المَيْتَةُ والدَّمُ ولَحْمُ الخِنْزِيرِ وما أُهِلَّ لِغَيْرِ اللَّهِ بِهِ والمُنْخَنِقَةُ والمَوْقُوذَةُ والمُتَرَدِّيَةُ والنَّطِيحَةُ وما أكَلَ السَّبُعُ إلّا ما ذَكَّيْتُمْ وما ذُبِحَ عَلى النُّصُبِ وأنْ تَسْتَقْسِمُوا بِالأزْلامِ ذَلِكم فِسْقٌ اليَوْمَ يَئِسَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِن دِينِكم فَلا تَخْشَوْهم واخْشَوْنِ اليَوْمَ أكْمَلْتُ لَكم دِينَكم وأتْمَمْتُ عَلَيْكم نِعْمَتِي ورَضِيتُ لَكُمُ الإسْلامَ دِينًا فَمَنِ اضْطُرَّ في مَخْمَصَةٍ غَيْرَ مُتَجانِفٍ لِإثْمٍ فَإنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ [المائدة: ٣]
"Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, that which has been dedicated to other than Allah, the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen, the gored, and that which wild beasts have eaten, except what you have slaughtered properly; and what is sacrificed on stone altars; and (forbidden is) that you seek to know your fate by arrows. That is a transgression. Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion, so do not fear them but fear Me. Today I have perfected for you your religion, completed My favor upon you, and approved Islam as your religion. But whoever is compelled by severe hunger, without inclination to sin, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."

al-bahima (livestock): every four-legged creature on land and sea, as stated by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: In the speech of the Arabs, al-bahima is that which is rendered obscure (unclear) due to a lack of speech and understanding. End of quotation.

Whatever is of the pattern fa'il or fa'ila, whose middle radical is a guttural letter, whether a noun or an adjective, it is permissible to vowel its first letter with kasra (i), matching the vowel of its middle letter. This is the dialect of the Banu Tamim. They say ri'iy and bihima, and sa'id and sighir, and bihira and bikhil.

al-sayd (game/hunting): the verbal noun of sada, yasidu and yusadu, and it is applied to the thing hunted (al-masid). Dawud ibn 'Ali al-Isbahani said: al-sayd is that which is wild (resistant to capture), has no owner, and whose flesh is lawful to eat. It seems he was defining the legal sense of hunting.

al-qilada (garland) in the context of the offering: that with which the animal is adorned, such as a sandal, or a water-skin handle, or the bark of a tree or other things. A man of the Haram (sanctuary) would sometimes adorn his mount with bark from the trees of the Haram, and thereby he would be protected from harm.

al-amm: one who intends (a destination). amamtu al-shay' means I aimed at the thing. Jaramahu 'ala kadha means he compelled him to (something), as stated by al-Kisa'i and Tha'lab. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' said: jaramahu means he earned it, and it is said: fulan jarimat ahlihi, meaning, their earner (provider); and al-jarim is the earner. Ajrama fulan means he earned sin. Al-Kisa'i also said: jarama and ajrama both mean he earned (something other than himself). Jarama yajrimu jarman means he cut off. Al-Ramani said: this is the original meaning. So jarama (meaning compelled) is from cutting off himself from others to focus on the matter; jarama (meaning earned) is from being cut off by concentrating on earning; and jarama (meaning deserved) is because the right is cut off for it. Al-Khalil said regarding the verse "La jarama anna lahumu al-nar" (Without doubt, they will have the Fire): meaning, it is indeed deserved (haqqa).

al-shana'an: hatred, and it is one of the verbal nouns of shani'a. It is said: shani'a yashna'u shan'an and shana'anan, with the letter shin having three vowels. So these are six: shana'an, shana'a, shina', shan'a, mashna'a, mashni'a, mishni'a, shanaan, and shinaan. These are sixteen verbal nouns, and they are the most that have been preserved for the verb. Sibawayh said: every form of verbal noun that is on the pattern fa'alan, with the vowel fatha on the middle letter, does not have a transitive verb, except that some things are anomalous, like shana'an.

al-mu'awana: assistance. al-munkhaniqa: the one who holds her breath until she dies, whether her confinement is by a rope, a hand, or other than that. al-waqdh: striking something until it becomes limp and close to death. It has been said: al-mawquza is the one struck with a stick or a stone with no sharp edge, so it dies without ritual slaughter. It is said: waqadhahu al-nu'as meaning sleep overcame him, and waqadhahu al-hukm meaning the ruling calmed him.

al-taraddi: falling into a well or plunging from a mountain. It is said: radiya and taradda, meaning he perished. It is also said: ma adri ayna radiya, meaning I do not know where he went.

al-nati'a: the one gored by another, so it dies from the goring. It is on the pattern fa'ila meaning maf'ula, an adjective which functions like nouns, so it takes governing particles, and therefore the feminine marker (ha') remains in it.

al-sabu': every animal with fangs and claws, like the lion, the panther, the bear, the wolf, the fox, the hyena, and similar. It has also been applied to birds of prey; the poet said:
"And the birds of prey go out at dawn with full bellies, passing over them and not able to rise."

Some Arabs restrict al-sabu' to the lion. The vowel-less ba' (sab') is a Najdi dialect, and it is also heard with fatha; perhaps that is a dialect.

al-tadhkiya: slaughter. Tadhkiyat al-nar means lifting it up. Dhakka al-rajul and others mean he became old. The poet said:
"Over its limbs the noble mounts run, and not over its exhaustion and effort."

al-nusub: it is said it is the plural of nisab, which are stones erected around the Ka'ba. The people of the Jahiliyya would venerate them, slaughter upon them for their gods and for them, and smear them with blood, and place meat upon them in pieces for people to eat from. It has also been said that nusub is singular. Al-A'sha said:
"And the erected idol, do not approach it."

al-azlam: arrows, its singular is zalam and zulam, with the letter zay vowelled with damma or fatha; they are the arrows. When any of them wanted a journey, a raid, trade, marriage, or some matter of great importance, he would cast the arrows. On some of them was written "My Lord has forbidden me," on some "My Lord has commanded me," and some were blank. If the one commanding came out, he proceeded to his goal; if the one forbidding came out, he refrained; and if the blank came out, he repeated the casting.

al-ya's: cutting off hope. It is said yai'isa yay'asu and yay'a'su, and it is said ayisa, which is an inversion of ya'isa. The evidence of inversion is that the ruling differs from what the apparent form indicates as its cause. Do you not see that they did not change its ya' to alif because it is vowelled and the letter before it is open? So they did not say "a'sa," just as they said haba.

al-makhmasa: famine in which the stomachs become empty, that is, shrink. al-khams is the shrinking of the belly and the physique. From it comes the praise of a woman's slenderness; from it it is said khamsana, and batn khamis (a slender belly), and from it akhma as al-qadam (the arch of the foot). It is used very often for hunger and emptiness. al-A'sha said:
"You sleep in winter with your bellies full, while your neighbours, hungry, pass the night empty."

Another said:
"Eat from the bellies you have, so that you remain chaste; for your time is a time of hunger."

﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أوْفُوا بِالعُقُودِ﴾
"O you who have believed, fulfill (all) contracts."

This surah is Medinan. It was revealed when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from al-Hudaybiya; some of it was revealed during the Farewell Pilgrimage, and some during the year of the Conquest. Everything that was revealed after the Hijra in Medina, or during a journey, or in Mecca, is Medinan. They mention the virtues of this surah, and that it is called al-Ma'ida, al-'Uqud, al-Munqidha, and al-Mubat'hira. The connection of its opening to what precedes it is that when Allah mentioned their asking about kalala (inheritance of one without children or parents) and His giving them a ruling on it, He mentioned that He clarifies for them the disliked (aspect of) misguidance. So in this surah He explained many rulings which are the detail of that summary. They said: this surah contains eighteen obligations which He did not explain in any other surah, and we will explain them one by one, if Allah wills.

They mentioned that the philosopher al-Kindi was told by his companions: "O wise one, produce for us something like this Qur'an." He said: "Yes, I will produce something like part of it." So he secluded himself for many days, then came out and said: "By Allah, I cannot, and no one can match this. I opened the Mushaf and it was Surat al-Ma'ida, so I looked and it had spoken of fulfilment, forbidden breaking of contracts, made a general permission, then made an exception, then informed about His power and wisdom in two lines, and no one can bring such a thing except in pages."

The apparent meaning is that the address is to the believers of the Messenger's community. Ibn Jurayj said: they are the People of the Book. Allah commanded the believers to fulfil contracts, which is the plural of 'aqd, and it is the covenant (al-'ahd). This was said by the majority, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Qatada, al-Dahhak, and al-Suddi. Al-Zajjaj said: 'uqud is more emphatic than 'uhud, and its origin is in physical objects, then it was extended to the meanings. Al-Zamakhshari followed him and said: it is the firm covenant, compared to tying a rope and the like. Al-Hutay'a said:
"A people who, when they make a covenant for their neighbour, tighten the knot and tighten over it the strongest bond."

The apparent meaning is the general inclusion of believers, sincere and outward, and the generality of contracts in every binding which agrees with the Shari'a, whether it is Islamic or from the Jahiliyya. Furat ibn Hayyan al-'Ijli asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the alliance of the Jahiliyya, and he said: "Perhaps you are asking about the alliance of Taym Allah." He said: "Yes, O Prophet of Allah." He said: "Islam only increases it in strength." The Prophet (ﷺ) said about the alliance of al-Fudul, which he had witnessed in the house of 'Abd Allah ibn Jud'an: "I would not like to have the red camels in exchange for it, and if I were called to it in Islam, I would respond." This alliance was that the Quraysh bound themselves not to find any wronged person in Mecca, from its people or from other than its people, without standing with him until his wrong was returned, and they named that alliance the Alliance of al-Fudul.

Al-Walid ibn 'Uqba was governor of Medina, and he oppressed al-Husayn ibn 'Ali regarding some property. He said: "You will either give me my right, or I will take up my sword, then I will stand in the Mosque of the Messenger (ﷺ), then I will call for the Alliance of al-Fudul." 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr said: "If he calls me, I will take up my sword, then I will stand with him until he obtains justice from his opponent, or we all die." This reached al-Miswar ibn Makhrama and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Uthman ibn 'Abd Allah al-Taymi, and they said the same. When this reached al-Walid, he granted justice.

Included in this generality is every contract with a person, such as a pledge of safety, blood-money, marriage, sale, partnership, gift, mortgage, manumission, delegation of a slave's freedom to death, granting choice, transferring ownership, reconciliation, sharecropping, divorce, purchase, and hire; and what a person binds upon himself for Allah, the Exalted, of obedience, such as pilgrimage, fasting, seclusion (i'tikaf), night prayer, vows, and what is similar to that.

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: they are the covenants which Allah took from His servants regarding what He permitted and forbade. This statement is one with which al-Zamakhshari began, saying: they are the covenants which Allah established upon His servants and obliged them with, of the duties of religious obligation; and this is a statement which was stated in summary and then followed by detail.

Qatada said: it is the alliance which was between them in the Jahiliyya. He said: It was transmitted to us from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Fulfil the Jahiliyya covenant, and do not introduce a covenant in Islam." Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Ibn Zayd, and others said: they are whatever a person binds upon himself, of sale, marriage, or other things. Ibn Zayd also said, and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayda said: the 'uqud are five: the knot of faith, the knot of marriage, the knot of covenant, the knot of sale, and the knot of alliance. It has been said: they are the contracts of trusts, sales, and the like. Ibn Jurayj said: they are those which Allah took from the People of the Book, that they should act by what the Messenger brought them. Ibn Shihab said: I read the document which the Messenger (ﷺ) wrote for 'Amr ibn Hazm when he sent him to Najran, and at its beginning was: "This is a declaration from Allah and His Messenger: O you who have believed, fulfil the contracts," up to His saying: "Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning." It has also been said: the 'uqud here are the obligations.

﴿Permitted to you are the beasts of cattle (bahimat al-an'am)﴾. It is said: this is a detailing after a general statement. It is also said: it is a new legislative statement in which He makes clear the invalidity of forbidding the flesh of the sa'ib, the wasila, the bahira and the hami, and that it is lawful for them.

"Bahimat al-an'am" is an idafa (construction of annexation) of a thing to its genus, so it has the meaning of "min" (of), because "bahima" is more general, so it is annexed to the more specific. Thus "bahimat al-an'am" is all of them. This was said by Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, al-Rabi' and al-Hasan, and they are the eight pairs that God Most High mentioned. Ibn Qutayba said: they are camels, cattle, sheep and all wild animals. A group, among them al-Dahhak and al-Farra', said: "bahimat al-an'am" is its wild kind, such as gazelles and wild oxen and wild asses. It seems they meant what resembles the an'am and approaches it from the genus of the an'am, the beasts, in harmlessness and the lack of fangs, so it is annexed to al-an'am because of the resemblance. The discussion of the meaning of the word "al-an'am" has already passed.

Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas said: "bahimat al-an'am" is the fetuses that come out when their mothers are slaughtered, and they are eaten without dhakat (ritual slaughter). This is far-fetched. It is also said: "bahimat al-an'am" is that which grazes of the four-footed ones; and a predatory animal such as the lion, and every animal with fangs, has left the state of being ambiguous (ibham) and has come to have some clarity.

﴿Except what is recited to you﴾. This is an exception from "bahimat al-an'am". The meaning is: except what is recited to you as forbidden, such as His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3]. Al-Qurtubi said: the meaning of "yutla 'alaykum" (is recited to you) is "is read in the Qur'an and the Sunna", and from this (is the hadith): "Every carnivorous animal with fangs is forbidden." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the apparent meaning of this exception is general (mujmal), and the exception of a general statement from a detailed statement makes what remains after the exception general. However, the exegetes agreed that the intended meaning of this exception is what is mentioned after this verse, which is His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3] up to His saying: ﴿and what is slaughtered on the altars﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3]. The reasoning behind this is that His saying: ﴿Permitted to you are the beasts of cattle﴾ requires their being permitted to them in all respects. So God Most High made clear that if they are carrion, or slaughtered for other than the name of God, or strangled, or beaten to death, or fallen, or gored, or eaten by a predator, then they are forbidden. End of his words.

The place of "ma" is in the accusative by way of exception, and it is permissible to put it in the nominative as an attribute of "bahima". Ibn 'Atiyya said: some of the Kufans permitted that it be in the place of the nominative by way of substitution (badal), and that "illa" be conjunctive ('atifa), but that is not permitted according to the Basrans except after an indefinite noun or what approximates it from the nouns of genus, like your saying: "The man came, except Zayd," as if you said: "other than Zayd." End of his words.

What he related from some of the Kufans, that it is in the place of the nominative by substitution, is not valid at all, because what precedes it is affirmative. Just as it is not permitted to say: "The people stood, except Zayd," as substitution, so likewise substitution is not permitted in ﴿except what is recited to you﴾. As for "illa" being conjunctive, it is something some of the Kufans held, as Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned. His saying: "that is not permitted according to the Basrans" apparently refers to both the two aspects of the nominative, substitution and conjunction. His saying: "except after an indefinite noun" is an ambiguous exception, not known from what it is. Both aspects of the nominative cannot be an exception from it, because substitution from an affirmative statement is permitted by no one we know, neither Basran nor Kufan. As for conjunction, no Basran permits it at all; what the Basrans permit is that it be an attribute of what precedes it in a construction like this. Some of them stipulated what was mentioned, that the modified noun be indefinite or what approximates it from nouns of genus. Perhaps Ibn 'Atiyya confused substitution with attribute and did not distinguish between them in the ruling. And if we assume that what follows "illa" follows what precedes it in i'rab (grammatical case) by way of substitution, so as to make that permissible, the indefiniteness of what precedes "illa" would not be stipulated, nor would its approximating an indefinite noun from nouns of genus, because the substitute and the substituted-for may differ in definiteness and indefiniteness.

﴿Not lawful to hunt while you are in ihram﴾. Al-Jumhur read "ghayra" with the accusative, and most of those whose words we have examined, from the grammarians and exegetes, agreed that it is accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Some related the consensus on that. They differed about the owner of the state. Al-Akhfash said: it is the pronoun of the subject in "awfu" (fulfil). Al-Jumhur, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and others said: it is the pronoun in the genitive in "uhilla lakum" (permitted to you). Some said: it is the omitted subject of "uhilla", whose place is taken by the object, which is God Most High. Some said: it is the pronoun in the genitive in "alaykum" (upon you). Al-Qurtubi related from the Basrans that His saying: ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ is an exception from "bahimat al-an'am", and that His saying: ﴿not lawful to hunt﴾ is another exception from it. So the two exceptions have their meaning from "bahimat al-an'am", and in the excepted part, and the estimate is: except what is recited to you, except game, while you are in ihram. This is unlike His saying: ﴿We have been sent to a people who are criminals﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 32], as will be explained, and it is a statement excepted from what comes before it from the exception. He said: if it were so, it would be necessary to permit hunting while in ihram, because it would be excepted from the prohibited, if "except what is recited to you" were excepted from the permitted. But this view is baseless. So its meaning is: The beasts of cattle are permitted to you, not lawful to hunt while you are in ihram, except what is recited to you, other than game. End of his words.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: People have confused this place regarding the accusative of "ghayra", and have estimated fronting and postponements, and all of that is not satisfactory, because the statement, on its consistent course, is well-formed as an exception after an exception. End of his words. He too is among those who confused, as we will clarify.

As for al-Akhfash's view, it involves separating the owner of the state from the state by an interjected clause, and indeed that clause establishes rulings, and that is not permitted. It also restricts the fulfilment of contracts by the condition that those fulfilling do not make game lawful while they are in ihram, though they are commanded to fulfil contracts without any restriction. The estimate becomes: fulfil the contracts in the state of your not being those who make game lawful while in ihram, and they have been permitted the beasts of cattle themselves. If by it is meant the gazelles, wild oxen and wild asses, the meaning becomes: and these are permitted to you in the state of your not being those who make game lawful while in ihram, and this is an involved, awkward construction, and the Qur'an is too exalted for such a thing to occur in it. Had this meaning been intended for the verse, it would have come in the most eloquent and best construction. As for the view of the one who made it a state of the subject and estimated: "God permitted to you the beasts of cattle, not making game lawful for you while you are in ihram", he said as you say: "I permitted you such-and-such, not permitting it to you on Friday", it is invalid, because they have stated that the omitted subject in such a construction becomes forgotten and unmentioned, and it is not permitted for a state to occur from it. If you said: "The rain was sent down to the people, answering their supplication", when the original is "God sent down the rain answering their supplication", it would not be permitted, especially according to the view of the Kufans and those among the Basrans who agree with them, because the form of the verb in the passive voice is a form established originally, just as its form in the active voice is established originally, and it is not changed from a form built for the active. And because God's permitting the beasts of cattle becomes restricted, when by them are meant the eight pairs, to the state of His not permitting game while they are in ihram, and He has permitted them in this state and in other states.

As for what al-Qurtubi related from the Basrans, if the transmission is sound, it is to be understood in light of what we will clarify, God willing. We say: the problem in the verse arose only from their making "ghayra muhilli al-sayd" a state of those commanded to fulfil contracts, or of those for whom it is made lawful, or of the one who makes it lawful, who is God Most High, or of those upon whom it is recited. What misled them in this was that it was written "muhilli" with a yā', and they estimated that it is an active participle from "ahalla", and that it is annexed to "al-sayd", the annexation of an active participle transitive to its object, and that it is a plural from which the nūn was dropped for the annexation. Its original is: "ghayra muhillina al-sayd wa-antum hurum". Except in the view of the one who made it a state of the omitted subject, for in that case the dropping of the nūn is not estimated, but the dropping of the tanwin. The problem disappears and the meaning becomes clear only if "muhilli al-sayd" is of the type of their saying "husan al-nisa'" (the beautiful women); the meaning being "the beautiful women", and likewise this, its original being "ghayra al-sayd al-muhill" (other than the lawful game). "Muhill" is an attribute of "al-sayd", not of the people, nor of the omitted subject. And describing game as "muhill" is in two ways: one of them is that its meaning is that it entered into the lawful state (hill), as you say: "ahalla al-rajul", i.e., he entered the state of lawfulness, and "ahram" he entered the sacred state (haram). The second way is that its meaning is that it became possessed of lawfulness, i.e., lawful by God's making it lawful. That is because game is of two kinds: lawful and forbidden. "Sayd" in the language of the Arabs is not restricted to the lawful. Do you not see the saying of some of them: "He hunts hares, even foxes"? But it is restricted to it in the Sharia. The Arabs have used a figurative expression, applying "sayd" to what is not described as lawful or forbidden, as in the verse:

"A lion at 'Atharr hunts men, when the lion lies about his peers, he speaks truth."

And another said:

"Salma has taken away all your reason, so is there anything but game that her snares have caught?"

And another said:

"Mayy hunts the hearts of men, and escapes from her, Ibn 'Umar and Hajar."

The occurrence of af'ala with the two meanings mentioned above is common in the speech of the Arabs. Among the uses of af'ala to mean reaching a place and entering it are their sayings: aḥrama al-rajulu (the man entered the state of iḥram), a'raqa (he reached Iraq), ash'ama (he reached ash-Sha'm, Syria), ayman (he reached Yemen), atahama (he reached Tihama), and anjada (he reached Najd), when he reached these places and settled in them. Among the uses of af'ala to mean becoming possessed of something are their sayings: a'shabati al-ardu (the land became full of grass), abqalat (it produced fresh herbage), aghadda al-ba'iru (the camel became plump), albanati ash-shatu (the ewe gave milk), and others like them; ajraati al-kalbatu (the bitch came into heat), aṣramma al-nakhlu (the palm trees were harvested), atlati an-naqatu (the she-camel became heavy with young), aḥṣada az-zar'u (the crop was ready for harvest), ajraba ar-rajulu (the man became afflicted with scabies), and anjabati al-mar'atu (the woman bore noble children). Since it is established that game may be described as muḥill (one who has entered the state of ḥill, i.e., being outside iḥram) on either of the two meanings mentioned, namely that it has reached the ḥill or has become possessed of ḥill, it becomes clear that this is an exception from an exception, because that is not possible given the contradiction of the ruling. For the excepted item from the permitted is forbidden, and the excepted item from the forbidden is permitted. Rather, if the meaning of his words "beast of the cattle" is the cattle themselves, then it is a disjunctive (munqaṭi') exception. If the intended meaning is gazelles, wild cattle, wild asses, and the like, then it is a connected (muttaṣil) exception according to one of the two interpretations of muḥill: it excepts the game which has reached ḥill, in respect of their being in iḥram. (If you ask:) what is the benefit of the exception with the restriction of reaching ḥill, when game that is in the Ḥaram is also not lawful? (I answer:) game that is in the Ḥaram is not lawful for the one in iḥram nor for the one not in iḥram, whereas the game that is in the ḥill is lawful for the one not in iḥram. So He draws attention to the fact that if the game that is in the ḥill is forbidden to the one in iḥram, although it is lawful for others, then it is all the more fitting that game which is in the Ḥaram be forbidden to him. According to this interpretation, His words ﴿except what is recited to you﴾, if what is meant by it is what comes after it, His words ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] ... to the end of the verse, then it is a disjunctive exception, since it does not apply specifically to carrion and what is mentioned with it, but to gazelles, wild asses, wild cattle, and the like. So the meaning becomes: "But what is recited to you," that is, its prohibition, is forbidden. If the intended meaning of "beast of the cattle" is cattle and wild animals, then the two exceptions refer to the whole group in detail. So "except what is recited to you" refers to the eight pairs, and "other than those who make game lawful" refers to the wild animals, since it is not possible for the second to be an exception from the first exception. And when that is not possible, but its reference to the first is possible in some way, it is permitted. The grammarians have stated that when it is not possible to make some of the excepted items an exception from others, then all of them are exceptions from the first noun, as in your saying: "The people stood, except Zayd, except 'Amr, except Bakr." (If you ask:) what you have mentioned of this strange derivation, namely that muḥill is an attribute of the game and not an attribute of the people, nor of the omitted agent, is disturbed by the fact that it is written in the ʿUthmānic codex (rasm al-muṣḥaf) with a yā' (ي), which indicates that it is an attribute of the people; for if it were an attribute of the game, it would not be written with a yā'. And the fact that al-Farrā' and his companions stopped on it with a yā' contradicts that. (I answer:) this derivation is not disturbed, because they often wrote the rasm of the codex in ways that differ from the pronunciation, such as: bi-ayyidin with two yā's after the alif, and their writing of ulā'ika with a wāw after the alif, and their omission of an alif from it, and their writing of aṣ-ṣāliḥāt and the like with the two alifs dropped; and this is common in the orthography. As for their stopping on it with a yā', that is not permissible, because one does not stop on the mudāf (the first term of an construct phrase) without the mudāf ilayhi (the second term). They only intended by that a test, or that the breath would run out, so they stopped on the written form, just as they stopped on ﴿We shall call the guards of hell﴾ [al-'Alaq: 18] without a wāw, following the written form. Moreover, it is possible to explain its being written with a yā' and stopped upon with a yā' by saying that it comes according to the dialect of the Azd, for they stop on bi-zaydin as bi-zaydī, replacing the tanwīn with a yā'. So muḥillī was written with a yā' in accordance with stopping in this dialect. This is an explanation of an orthographic anomaly, and the rasm of the codex is not something to be analogized upon.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read (ghayru) in the nominative (marfū'). The best way to analyze it is that it is an adjective (ṣifah) of His words ﴿beast of the cattle﴾. It does not necessarily follow from describing something with ghayr that what comes after it must be similar to the described item in kind, and the separation between the adjective and the noun it qualifies by the exception does no harm. It was also analyzed as an adjective of the pronoun in yutlā (is recited). Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: "Because ﴿other than those who make game lawful﴾ is in meaning equivalent to: 'other than what is made lawful when it is game.'" End of quotation. This artifice is not needed according to our analysis, which takes muḥillī al-ṣayd (those who make game lawful) and antum ḥurum (while you are in iḥram) as a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah). Ḥurum is the plural of ḥarām. It is said: aḥrama ar-rajulu when he entered into iḥram for ḥajj or for ʿumrah, or for both; then he is muḥrim and ḥarām. And aḥrama ar-rajulu also means: he entered the Ḥaram. The poet said:

"I said to her, 'Turn back to me, for I am in iḥram, and after that I am wise'"

That is, I am one who utters the talbiyah (the invocation "Labbayka..."). His words "while you are in iḥram" may bear both meanings, since game is forbidden to one who is in the Ḥaram and to one who has entered iḥram for ḥajj or ʿumrah; this is the view of the jurists. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "'While you are in iḥram' is a circumstantial clause relating to the position of the game, as if it were said: 'We have made lawful for you some of the cattle while you refrain from hunting and are in iḥram, so that it would not be a burden upon you.'" End of quotation. We have already shown the corruption of this view, since the cattle are permitted absolutely, not restricted to this state.

﴿Indeed, Allah decrees what He wills﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "He makes lawful and makes unlawful." It was also said: "He judges concerning what He created with what He wills without restriction." This sentence came to confirm these legal rulings which differ from the familiar customs of the Arabs: the command to fulfil the contracts, the permitting of beast of the cattle, the exception from them of what is recited as forbidden absolutely both in ḥill and in Ḥaram except in necessity, the exception of game during the state of iḥram, and the implication that this is lawful for one who is not forbidden. These are five rulings, which He concluded with His words ﴿Indeed, Allah decrees what He wills﴾. So the obligation of the ruling and the legal responsibility is due to His will; there is no objection to it, and none can reverse His ruling, not what the Muʿtazilah say about observing public interests (maṣāliḥ). For this reason al-Zamakhsharī said: "Indeed, Allah decrees from among the rulings what He wills, and He knows that it is wisdom and interest." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said, pointing out what this verse contains of rulings, in these words: "This verse is one in which its eloquence and the abundance of its meanings with the fewness of its words are apparent to everyone who has insight into speech, and to whoever has even a little discernment." Then Ibn ʿAṭiyyah mentioned the report we previously cited (p-419) from al-Kindī and his companions. And in this regard I say, from a qaṣīdah I composed in praise of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, in response to the qaṣīdah of Kaʿb concerning the description of the Book of Allah, the Exalted:

"It proceeds upon the path of the Arabs; it has defeated them; it remains forever, its alteration is impossible.
Its eloquence has left the eloquent speechless, so that he has not uttered a word, and through its guidance the misguidances have perished."

﴿O you who believe, do not violate the rites of Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2]. Surayḥ, a man from Banu Ḍubay'ah, set out for Makkah to perform ḥajj, driving the hadī (sacrificial animals). In another report, he had merchandise with him. He had previously come to Madinah and spoken with the Messenger, ﷺ, and had deliberated about his Islam. The Messenger, peace be upon him, had said: "He entered with the face of a disbeliever and departed with the heels of a treacherous one." Then he passed by a herd in Madinah and drove it off. When he arrived in Makkah in the year of al-Ḥudaybiyyah, the people of the herd wanted to raid him and asked the Messenger for permission, and the verse was revealed. As-Suddī said: his name was al-Ḥuṭaym ibn Hind al-Balādī, one of Banu Ḍubay'ah, and the Messenger wanted to send some of his Companions to him, and the verse was revealed. Ibn Zayd said: it was revealed in Makkah in the year of the Conquest, when the polytheists performed ḥajj and ʿumrah. The Muslims said: "O Messenger of Allah, these are polytheists, and we will not leave them unless we raid them." Then the Qur'an was revealed.

﴿Nor those who sacrifice to the Sacred House﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2].

Ash-shaʿā'ir (the rites) is the plural of shaʿīrah or shiʿārah; that is, Allah has made known (ashʿara) that they are His limits and His obedience. So they mean the markers (maʿālim) of Allah. Its explanation has already been mentioned in ﴿Indeed, aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah are among the rites of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 158]. Al-Ḥasan said: "The religion of Allah in its entirety", meaning His laws which He set for His servants; so it is general in all His obligations, the Exalted. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "What He forbade you in the state of iḥram." He also said, together with Mujāhid: "The rites of the Ḥajj." Zayd ibn Aslam said: "The rites of the Ḥajj, and they are six: aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah, the camels (al-budn), the stoning pillars (al-jimār), al-Mash'ar al-Ḥarām, ʿArafah, and the Corner (al-Rukn)." He also said: "The forbidden things are five: the Sacred Ka'bah, the Sacred City, the Sacred Month, the Sacred Mosque, until it is made lawful." Ibn al-Kalbī said: "The majority of the Arabs did not count aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah among the rites, and Quraysh would not stand at ʿArafāt, so they were forbidden from that." It was said: "The erected markers scattered between the ḥill and the Ḥaram; they were forbidden to pass beyond them into Makkah without iḥram." Abū ʿUbaydah said: "They are the offerings, which are stabbed in their humps and garlanded." He said: "This is indicated by ﴿And the camels We have made for you among the rites of Allah﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 36]." But his view was judged weak because He conjoined with it "the offering" and "the garlands." It was said: "They are what Allah has forbidden absolutely, whether in iḥram or otherwise." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "They are what has been made to bear a sign (ushʿira), that is, made a sign and mark for the rite from the stations of the Ḥajj, the places of the stoning, the circumambulation, and the actions which are the signs of the pilgrim, by which one is recognized: from iḥram, circumambulation, running between aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah, shaving, and sacrifice." End of quotation.

﴿Nor the Sacred Month﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2]. The apparent meaning is that it is a specific singular noun known to the listeners. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is the month of the Ḥajj." ʿIkrimah and Qatādah said: "It is Dhū al-Qaʿdah, since it is the first of the sacred months." Al-Ṭabarī and others said: "It is Rajab, and it is attributed to Muḍar, because they used to forbid fighting in it and glorify it, and they would remove weapons and spear points from the lances in it." The Arabs agreed on glorifying Dhū al-Qaʿdah and Dhū al-Ḥijjah, and differed about Rajab, so Allah, the Exalted, emphasized its importance. This is the reason for singling it out by mention. It was also said: "The month is singular, defined by the definite article of genus (al-jinsiyyah), so what is meant by it is the generality of the sacred months, and they are: Dhū al-Qaʿdah, Dhū al-Ḥijjah, al-Muḥarram, and Rajab; and the meaning is: do not make lawful by fighting, raiding, or plundering." Muqātil said: "Junādah ibn ʿAwf would stand in the marketplace of ʿUkāẓ every day and say: 'Behold, I have made lawful such-and-such, and forbidden such-and-such.'"

﴿Nor the offering﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2]. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "There is no disagreement that the hadī is what is sent as an offering from the cattle to the House of Allah, and is intended as a means of drawing near to Allah; so He commanded that it not be made lawful and not be raided." End of quotation. But the disagreement among the commentators concerning it exists. It was said: "It is a name for what is sent as an offering to the House of Allah, whether a she-camel, a cow, a sheep, or charity, and the other slaughtered animals and charities." It was also said: "It is what is intended for the sake of Allah." And from this is in the ḥadīth: "Then like one who offers a hen, then like one who offers an egg," so he called these a hadī. It was also said: "The rites are the camels from the cattle, and the hadī is the cows, sheep, garments, and everything offered." It was said: "The rites are what bears the mark of the flowing of blood from its hump or by other signs, and the hadī is what is not marked, for which garlanding is sufficient." And whoever explained the rites as the rituals said: "He mentioned the hadī as an indication of its details."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 2–3 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Nor the garlands﴾. Mujahid, 'Ata' and Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: the garlands (qala'id) are what they used to hang on themselves from the trees of the Sacred Precinct (haram) so that they would be safe thereby. The believers were thus forbidden to imitate the practice of the Jahiliyya (the Age of Ignorance) and to take garlands from the trees of the Sacred Precinct. There is a hadith: "Its grass shall not be cut, and its trees shall not be felled." The majority said: the garlands are what they used to hang on themselves of the sami (a kind of tree bark or plant) when they set out for the Hajj, so that this would be a sign of pilgrimage. It was also said: or what a man of the Haram would hang on himself when he went out on some need, so that this would show that he was a man of the Haram; thus God, exalted is He, forbade making lawful those who had put on any of these. Al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas that the garlands are the garlanded offering (al-hady al-muqallad), and that an offering was only called a hady when it had not been garlanded; so it is as if he said: nor the offering that has not been garlanded, nor the garlanded one of it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is an imposition upon the wording of Ibn 'Abbas, and it is not part of his speech that the word hady is used only for what has not been garlanded. Rather, it implies that God, exalted is He, forbade the offering in general, and then mentioned the garlanded part of it as emphasis and as an intensification in alerting to the sanctity of the garlanded one. It was also said: he meant the garlands themselves, so he forbade touching the garlands of the offering, as an intensification of the prohibition against touching the offering; i.e., do not make lawful their garlands, let alone that you should untie them, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and that they should not display their adornment﴾ [al-Nur: 31], forbidding the displaying of adornment as an intensification of the prohibition against displaying its places. Al-Tabari said: its interpretation is that He forbade making lawful the sanctity of what is garlanded, whether an offering or a person, and He dispensed with mentioning the garlanded one by mentioning the garlands, since it was understood by the addressee.

﴿Nor those who make for the Sacred House, the Inviolable House﴾. 'Abd Allah and his companions recited: "wa-la ammi" (without the nun), by deletion for the idafa (construct) to "the House"; i.e., nor make lawful people intending the Sacred Mosque, who are the pilgrims and the visitors ('umrah). Al-Zamakhshari said: and the making lawful of these, i.e., that the sanctity of the rites is disregarded, and that there be placed between them and the devout those who would hinder, and that they create in the months of the Hajj what would turn people away from the Hajj, and that the offering be harmed by seizure or by preventing it from reaching its place of sacrifice.

﴿Seeking bounty from their Lord and good pleasure﴾. The majority read "yabtaghuna" with the ya', so that it is an attribute of "amminin". Al-Zamakhshari interpreted "bounty" as reward, which is the view of some. It was also said: bounty is trade and the profits in it. It was also said: increase in wealth and children; they seek the hope of increase in this. As for "good pleasure" (ridwan), they used to aim at it even if they did not attain it, and seeking a thing does not indicate its attainment. It was also said: this is a distribution among the polytheists: some of them sought trade, since they did not believe in a return, and some of them sought good pleasure by the Hajj, since some of them believed in recompense after death and that one would be raised, even though the good pleasure of God would not be attained for him, so He informed of that on the basis of his supposition. It was also said: the Muslims and the polytheists both performed the Hajj; so the seeking of bounty is from both of them, and the seeking of good pleasure is from the believers. Qatada said: it is that He sets right their livelihoods in this world and does not hasten punishment upon them in it. Some said: bounty and good pleasure in the verse have one meaning, namely God's pleasure and His bounty through mercy. God, exalted is He, forbade that one should approach a people with this description, as a glorification of them and as a disapproval of approaching the likes of them. In the prohibition against approaching them there is a winning over of the Arabs, kindness toward them, and an encouragement to come to the season; and in the season they hear the Qur'an, the proof is established against them, and their entry into faith is hoped for, as had happened.

This verse was revealed in the year of the Conquest, so whatever in it concerns a Muslim pilgrim is muhkam (established), and whatever concerns an unbeliever is mansukh (abrogated); that was abrogated after the year nine, when Abu Bakr performed the Hajj and the proclamation was made among the people with the Surat Bara'a. The saying of al-Hasan and Abu Maysara: there is no abrogated element in it, is a rejected view. Humayd ibn Qays and al-A'raj read "tabtaghuna" with the ta', as address to the believers; and the meaning according to the address is that the believers used to intend fighting them and raiding them, and to bar them from the Sacred Mosque in compliance with God's command and seeking His good pleasure, since God, exalted is He, commanded fighting the polytheists, killing them, taking their children captive, and seizing their wealth, until they believe or give the jizya (poll tax). Al-A'mash read "wa-ridwanan" with a damma on the ra', and it has preceded in Al 'Imran that this is the reading of Abu Bakr from 'Asim, wherever it occurs except in the second occurrence in this surah, where there is a difference of transmission from him.

﴿And when you have left the state of ihram, then hunt﴾. The end of His saying: ﴿lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 1] included the prohibition of hunting in the state of ihram, and the end of His saying: ﴿Do not make lawful the rites of God﴾ included the prohibition against making lawful the people of the House; so this sentence came with its ruling referring back to the first sentence, and what follows it, His saying: ﴿and let not the hatred of a people...﴾, refers back to the second sentence, and this is of eloquent excellence. Thus this sentence is not an interjection between His saying: ﴿nor those who make for the Sacred House﴾ and His saying: ﴿let not...﴾; rather it establishes a ruling and is not a confirmation that consolidates, so it would be an interjection; rather it conveys the permissibility of hunting in the state of ihram. There is no preposing or postposing here; the original structure would be: "not making lawful the game while you are in ihram; then when you have left the state of ihram, hunt." In the second verse the original structure would be: "nor those who make for the Sacred House, seeking bounty from their Lord and good pleasure, and let not...," as one of them went to it, and he took from it the story of the slaughter of the cow, saying: the way of looking at it is that one should say: ﴿And when you slew a soul﴾ [al-Baqara: 72], the verse, then one should say: ﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾ [al-Baqara: 67]. He often mentioned this preposing and postposing in the Qur'an, and the wonder about him is that he makes it part of the science of eloquence and rhetorical embellishment; and this is not permissible in our view except in the necessity of poetry, and it is among the most ugly of poetic licences, so it is fitting, rather obligatory, that the Qur'an be exonerated from it.

He said: the reason for this is that when the Companions collected the Qur'an they did not arrange it according to the order of its revelation, but arranged it according to the closeness of meanings and the harmony of wordings. What he said is not correct; rather what we believe is that the Messenger of God, ﷺ, is the one who arranged it, not the Companions, and likewise we say concerning its surahs, though some have differed in that.

The command to hunt here is a command of permission by consensus, and for this reason al-Zamakhshari said: "And when you have left the state of ihram, there is no blame upon you that you should hunt." End of quote. Since hunting is permissible, and only the state of ihram prevented it, when the preventing factor is removed it returns to its original permissibility. They spoke here about the form of the imperative when it comes after a prohibition, and about it when it comes without indicators, and what it is to be understood as, and about the actual usage of it; and that belongs to the science of the foundations of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), so it is researched there.

It was also read: "fa-idha halaltum," which is a dialect; it is said: halla min ihramihi and ahalla. Abu Waqid, al-Jarrah, Nubayh and al-Hasan ibn 'Imran read "fi-subadu" (fa-ittasadu?) with a kasra on the fa', i.e., "fisṭādū". Al-Zamakhshari said: it is said it is a substitute for the kasra of the hamza at the beginning. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a difficult reading, and among its justifications is that one observes the kasra of the alif of connection when you begin, saying "isṭādū" with a kasra on the fa', as a reminder of the original alif of connection. End of quote. In my view it is not a pure kasra, but rather of the category of pure imala (inclination), because of the supposed presence of the kasra of the hamzat al-wasl, just as they inclined the fa' in "fa-idha" because of the presence of the kasra of "idha."

﴿And let not the hatred of a people, because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, lead you to transgress﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: "yajrimannakum" means: let not carry you, it is said: "jaramani kadha 'ala bughdika," so "an ta'tadu" originally is "'ala an ta'tadu," and the preposition was deleted from it. Others said: its meaning is that of "kasaba" which is transitive to two objects, so "an ta'tadu" is in the position of the second object; i.e., your transgression upon you. It is also transitive to one object; you say "ajrama" in the sense of "kasaba," which is transitive to two; it is said in its meaning: jaramaa and ajrama. Abu 'Ali said: ajrama I know it to mean earning, in sins and misdeeds. Al-Hasan, Ibrahim, Ibn Thabit and al-Walid from Ya'qub read "yajrimankum" with a sukun on the nun, making the nun of emphasis light.

Al-Zamakhshari said: and the meaning is: let not the hatred of a people because they barred you from transgression earn you, and let it not carry you to it. End of quote. This is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of grammatical analysis, because it is impossible that the signification of "hamala" and "kasaba" be the same in one usage, owing to the difference of their requirements; so it is impossible that "an ta'tadu" be in the place of a direct object and in the place of an object after dropping the preposition.

Al-Nahwiyyan, Ibn Kathir, Hamza, Hafs and Nafi' read "shana'an" with a fatha on the nun. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read it with a sukun, and it is related from Nafi'. The more apparent reading with the fatha is that it is a verbal noun (masdar), and the coming of the masdar on the pattern fa'alan has been frequent, and they permitted that it be an adjective, and fa'alan exists among adjectives, such as their saying: "himarun qatawan," i.e., hard to travel; and "taysun 'adawan," i.e., much running; and it is not in plurality like the masdar. They said: on this basis the meaning is: let not the hatred of a people earn you. They mean by "baghid" an active participle "mubghid," because it is from "shana'a" in the sense of hatred. It is transitive, and it is not in the genitive to the object or subject, unlike when it is a masdar, for it may be in the genitive to the object, which is the more apparent, and it may be in the genitive to the subject; i.e., the hatred of a people toward you. As for the sukun, the more apparent is that it is an adjective, for it is reported: "rajulun shan'anun" and "imra'atun shan'anatun," and by analogy this is from a transitive verb. It is also reported: "shan'anun" and "shan'a," like "'atshanun" and "'atsha," and by analogy this is from an intransitive verb. A single root may produce both transitive and intransitive forms, as in: "faghara fahu" and "faghara fuwhu," meaning opened and became open. It was permitted that it be a masdar, and the coming of masdars on fa'lan with fatha on the fa' and sukun on the 'ayn is rare; they said: "lawaytuhu daynahu laiyanan." Al-Ahwas said:

"And love is nothing but what you love and desire, / even if the one with hatred blames him in it and rebukes."

Its origin is "al-shan'an," and he deleted the hamza and transferred its vowel to the consonant before it. The adjectival form on fa'lan is more frequent than the masdar, like "rahman." Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read "in saddukum" with a kasra on the hamza, as a conditional. Ibn Mas'ud's reading "in saddukum" supports this. Ibn Jarir, al-Nahhas and others denied the reading with kasra on "in," and said: the polytheists only barred the Messenger and the believers in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, and the verse was revealed in the year of the Conquest, in the year eight, while al-Hudaybiyya was in the year six; so the barring preceded the revelation of the verse, while the kasra requires that it be afterward; and because Mecca in the year of the Conquest was in the hands of the Muslims, so how could they be barred from it while it was in their hands? This denial from them of this reading is very difficult, for it is a mutawatir reading, since it is among the Seven, and its meaning with it is sound; the sense is: if a barring occurs in the future similar to that barring which took place at the time of al-Hudaybiyya, and this prohibition is a legislation for the future. It is not unanimously agreed that the revelation of this verse was in the year of the Conquest; rather al-Yazidi mentioned that it was revealed before they barred them, and on this view the conditional is clear. The rest of the Seven read "an" with a fatha on the hamza, making it an explanation of the hatred, and this is a clear reading; i.e., the hatred of a people because they barred you in the year of al-Hudaybiyya from the Sacred Mosque. "I'tida'" means retaliating against them by inflicting harm upon them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 2–3 (part 2 of 3):

﴿And help one another in righteousness and piety﴾. When He forbade transgression, He commanded mutual assistance and cooperation in good. Forbidding transgression does not necessarily entail cooperating in good, because between them there is an intermediate state, which is abstaining from both transgression and cooperation. Al-Zamakhshari explained "righteousness and piety" as pardoning and overlooking [wrongs]. He said: "It is also permissible to intend the general meaning of every righteousness and piety, which would then include pardoning." End of quote. Some said: "They have one meaning, and it was repeated for emphasis through the variation of wording." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is loose usage. The customary meaning of these two terms covers what is obligatory and what is recommended, and piety is the observance of what is obligatory. If one is put in place of the other, it is permissible." End of quote. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Righteousness is what you are commanded to do, and piety is what you are forbidden from." Sahl said: "Righteousness is faith, and piety is the Sunnah," meaning following the Sunnah.

﴿And do not help one another in sin and aggression﴾. Sin (ithm) refers to acts of disobedience, and aggression ('udwan) refers to exceeding the limits of God. This was stated by 'Ata'. It was also said: sin is disbelief and rebellion, and aggression is innovation (bid'a). It was also said: sin is the ruling that attaches to offences, and aggression is wronging people; this was stated by Ibn 'Atiyya. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Sin and aggression are retaliation and the seeking of revenge." He said: "It is also permissible to intend the general meaning of every sin and every aggression."

﴿And fear God. Indeed God is severe in punishment﴾. He commanded piety in an unrestricted form, even though He had already commanded it in the context of cooperation, to emphasise the command. Then He gave the reason: that He is severe in punishment, so He must be feared. The severity of His punishment lies in the fact that no one can bear it, and in its being everlasting, since most of worldly life comes to an end. Mujahid said: this was revealed as a prohibition against seeking [to return] to the ignorance (jahiliyya) when some of the believers wished to do so. It has been said that this concerned an ally of Abu Sufyan from the Hudhayl tribe.

﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which any name other than God's has been invoked﴾. A similar sentence was discussed previously in al-Baqara. Ibn 'Atiyya said here: "The flesh of swine implies its fat, by consensus." End of quote. This is not so, for Dawud and others disagreed about it. We discussed this in al-Baqara. Here it is mentioned later, and there earlier, for variety of expression and breadth in speech, and because the divine name (al-Jalala) occurred there as an intervening element or something like one. Here, coordinated items follow it, so it is not an intervening element nor like one. What comes in this manner in most instances requires the lengthened vowel (madd).

﴿And the strangled, the beaten, the fallen, the gored, and that which a beast of prey has eaten﴾. The meanings of these words were explained earlier in the Vocabulary section. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: the people of the jahiliyya would strangle sheep and other animals, and when they died they would eat them. Abu 'Abd Allah said: "The beaten animal (mawquda) applies only to domestic animals, not to game." Malik and other jurists said: "In hunting, the ruling for game killed by a blow is the same as the ruling for the beaten animal." This is explicit in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the mi'rad (a blunt-headed arrow): "If it strikes with its width, do not eat it, for it is beaten (waqidh)."

Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: the gored (natiha) is a sheep gored by another, so that both die, or a sheep gored by cattle or goats. Others said: the gored is the one that is struck by butting, because two sheep may butt each other and die. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Whatever dies from being crushed is gored (natih)." 'Abd Allah and Abu Maysara read: "al-mantuha" (the gored).

The intended sense of "that which a beast of prey has eaten" is what a predator has seized and eaten from. It cannot be taken literally, because what is assumed to have been eaten entirely by a predator no longer exists to be forbidden. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: "That which a beast of prey has eaten of, in part." All these were eaten by the people of the jahiliyya. Al-Hasan, al-Fayyad, Talha ibn Salman and Abu Haywa read "al-sab'" (with a sukun on the ba'), and this is reported from Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim in a non-standard reading, and from Abu 'Amr. 'Abd Allah read "wa-akilat al-sab'" (and what the beast ate). Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-akil al-sab'" (and the eaten by the beast). Both mean "what is eaten by a beast of prey." The mention of these forbidden things is a detailing of what was stated in summary in the general phrase ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 1]. Thus the item excepted from and the exception have become known.

﴿Except what you have slaughtered (dhakkaytum)﴾. 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, Ibrahim, Tawus, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd, and the majority said: it refers back to the items mentioned, that is, from "the strangled" to "what a beast of prey has eaten." So whatever in them still shows some life, by one's eye, or by striking with a foot, or moving a tail, is slaughtered (dhukkiya) and may be eaten. In general, whatever is known with certainty to still have life is slaughtered and eaten. This is the view of Malik in one opinion. The well-known position of Malik and his Medinan companions is that the slaughter (dhakat) for these items is what has not reached a lethal state and has not been determined to be unable to survive. When it reaches that state, it has the ruling of carrion.

According to these two views, the exception is connected (istithna' muttasil), but there is disagreement about the condition in which slaughter takes effect on these items. Al-Zamakhshari inclined to the well-known opinion of Malik, for he said: "Not what you have obtained the slaughter of while it convulses like one slaughtered, and its blood flows." It was also said: the exception is connected, returning to the nearest preceding item, which is "what a beast of prey has eaten," and is specific to it. The meaning is: except what you find still living from what a beast of prey has eaten, and you slaughter it, for it is lawful. It was also said: the exception is disconnected (istithna' munqati'). The sense is: "But what you slaughter from other than these is to be eaten." It seems that the one who held this view considered these attributes to have been present in what died from one of them, whether by strangling, beating, falling, goring, or being seized by a predator, and that it reached a point where it could not survive because of one of these attributes, according to the view of those who take that into account. For this reason the exception is disconnected.

The apparent view is that the exception is connected. The reason these five were specified, though they are in the ruling of carrion, and carrion was not mentioned alone, is that the Arabs believed these events upon the animal to be equivalent to slaughter, and that carrion is what dies from illness without any cause known among these causes.

The apparent sense of the words ﴿except what you have slaughtered﴾ implies that what cannot be caught in time to be slaughtered may not be eaten, such as a fetus that emerges dead from the belly of its slaughtered mother. If the exception is disconnected, the fetus falls under the general prohibition of carrion. This is the position of Abu Hanifa. The majority held that it may be eaten. The hadith from which they derived permission is an argument for Abu Hanifa, not for them: "The slaughter of the fetus is the slaughter of its mother." The meaning is by way of comparison: the slaughter of the fetus is like the slaughter of its mother. Just as the slaughter of the mother is by cutting, so too the slaughter of the fetus is by cutting. Had it been as they claim, the wording would have been "the slaughter of the mother of the fetus is its slaughter."

﴿And what is sacrificed on the altar stones (nusub)﴾. Mujahid, Qatada and others said: these are stones on which the people of the jahiliyya used to slaughter. Ibn 'Abbas said: and they would also anoint them [with blood]. Ibn Jurayj said: they were not idols, for an idol is a figure carved in an image. The Arabs used to slaughter at Mecca and sprinkle the blood on whatever came toward the House, cut the meat, and place it on the stones. When Islam came, the Muslims said: "We have more right than they to honour this House with these acts." The Messenger (ﷺ) disliked this, so ﴿and what is sacrificed on the altar stones﴾ was revealed, and ﴿Neither their flesh nor their blood reaches God﴾ [al-Hajj: 37] was revealed. End of quote.

The Arabs had stone altars (ansab) in their lands which they worshipped, and they anointed with blood the altars of Mecca, among them the stone called Sa'd. Ibn Zayd said: "What is sacrificed on the altar stones and what is invoked with a name other than God's are one thing." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "What is sacrificed on the altar stones is a part of what is invoked with a name other than God's, but it was singled out for mention after its general category because the matter was well known, the place held honour, and people held it in reverence. An idol may also be called nusub, because it is set up (yunsab)." End of quote.

The majority read "al-nusub" with two damma vowels. Talha ibn Musarrif read with a damma on the nun and a sukun on the sad. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read with two fatha vowels, and this was also reported from him in the majority reading. al-Hasan read with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the sad.

﴿And that you seek to know by the divining arrows (istiqsam bi-l-azlam)﴾. This is coordinated with what precedes it; that is, He forbade you the seeking of knowledge by the divining arrows. Istiqsam is seeking to know one's portion (qism), which is the share, or the apportioning (qasm), which is the verbal noun. Ibn Jurayj said: its meaning is that you seek to learn what has been apportioned to you by the arrows, or what has not been apportioned to you. End of quote. Mujahid said: they are the knucklebones of Persia and Rome with which they used to gamble. It was also reported from him that they were the arrows of the Arabs and the knucklebones of Persia. Sufyan and Waki' said: they are chess. It was also said: the azlam were pebbles with which they cast lots, and this is what the poet referred to in his words:

"By your life, the casters do not know by the pebbles,
nor the bird-divining augurs, what God will do."

This was reported from Ibn Jubayr. They said: the Arabs' azlam were of three kinds. The first: three arrows which each person made for himself; on one was written "do," on another "do not," and the third was blank. He put them in a bag, and when he wanted to do something he put his hand into the bag and acted according to whichever came out, whether it was the command or the prohibition. If the blank came out he cast again. The second: seven arrows (qidah) which were kept by Hubal inside the Ka'ba. On one of them was written "the blood-money (aql)" regarding diyya payments; whoever among them is to pay it, they cast with the seven, and whoever has the arrow of "aql" drawn against him must pay. On another: "Yes," on another: "No." When they wanted to do something they cast, and followed what came out. On another: "From among you," on another: "From others," on another: "Attached." When they disagreed about a person, whether he was of them or not, they cast and followed what came out. On the rest was written the rulings on water, so that when they wanted to dig for water they cast with the arrows, and wherever the lot came out, they acted on it. These seven were likewise kept by every soothsayer (kahin) among the Arab soothsayers and judges, in the manner they were kept in the Ka'ba with Hubal. The third: the arrows of gambling (maysir), which are ten. The explanation of maysir was given earlier in surah al-Baqara.

﴿That is transgression (fisq)﴾. The apparent sense is that the demonstrative refers specifically to the seeking by arrows. This was transmitted by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zamakhshari said: it refers to the seeking by arrows and to the taking of what was forbidden to them, since the meaning is: "It was forbidden to them to eat carrion, and so on and so forth." (If you say): why was the seeking by arrows, whether by a traveller or someone else, to learn the state of affairs, transgression? (I say): because it is an intrusion into the knowledge of the unseen, which God has reserved for Himself, the Knower of the unseen. He said: ﴿None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except God﴾ [al-Naml: 65]. Holding that there is a path to it and a means of deducing it is the belief. His words "My Lord commanded me, and my Lord forbade me" are a fabrication against God, the Exalted. What is claimed by the soothsayers and astrologers, that God commanded or forbade them, is of this nature, even if by "Lord" they meant an idol. It has been reported that they used to cast lots at their idols, and the matter is clear. End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding the demonstrative: this was transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas by 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, and it is the view of Ibn Jubayr. Al-Tabari said: God forbade these matters in which soothsayers and astrologers engage, because of the speech about hidden things that they involve. Others said: the reason for the prohibition of seeking by the arrows is that money is consumed by falsehood through them. When they wanted to circumcise a boy, marry, bury a dead person, or doubted a lineage, they went to Hubal with a hundred dirhams and a camel. The hundred was for the one who cast the arrows, and the camel was slaughtered and eaten. They named their companion and said to Hubal: "O our god, this is so-and-so; we want by him such-and-such; so bring forth the truth concerning him." The caster would cast, and whatever came out they acted upon. If it came out "no," they postponed the matter for their year until they brought it again another time. They ended all their affairs at whatever the arrows indicated.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 5, verses 2–3 (part 3 of 3):**

﴿Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion.﴾ The alif and lam in *al-yawm* ("today") are for a known referent (*al-'ahd*). It is the Day of 'Arafah. This is what Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said. It was the day it was revealed, after the afternoon prayer, during the Farewell Pilgrimage, on a Friday, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was at the station on his camel, and there was no polytheist at the station. It was also said that it was the day the Messenger (ﷺ) entered Makkah, eight days before the end of Ramadan in the ninth year. It was also said it was in the eighth year. His herald proclaimed safety for whoever uttered the testimony of Islam, for whoever laid down his weapons, and for whoever closed his door. Al-Zajjaj said: "He did not intend a particular day; the meaning is: now they have despaired, just as you say, 'I am old today.'" End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari followed al-Zajjaj and said: "'Today' does not refer to a specific day, but to the present time and what is connected to it and adjacent to it of past and future times, as in your saying: 'Yesterday you were young, and today you are gray-haired.' You do not mean by 'yesterday' the day before your day, nor by 'today' your day." Its like is *al-an* ("now") in his saying:

*Now that my body hair has turned white,*
*and I have gnawed with my teeth on a stump.*

End of quote.

*Those who disbelieve* are the polytheists of the Arabs. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and 'Ata' said: they despaired of your returning to their religion. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the manifestation of the affair of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, and the manifestation of his religion, requires that the despair of the disbelievers regarding returning to their religion had already occurred long before. This despair, in my view, is rather about the collapse of the affair of Islam and the corruption of its community, because this was a matter that those among the disbelievers who remained were hoping for. Do you not see the saying of the brother of Safwan ibn Umayyah on the day of Hawazin, when the Muslims were routed and he thought it a defeat: "Has magic not been nullified today?" Al-Zamakhshari said: they despaired of nullifying it and of returning to make lawful these abominations after they had been forbidden to you. It was said: they despaired of your religion, of overcoming it, because Allah fulfilled His promise of making it prevail over all religion. End of quote. Abu Ja'far recited *yaisa* without hamzah, and it is reported from Abu 'Amr.

﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me.﴾ Ibn Jubayr said: do not fear them lest they prevail over you. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: do not fear them lest they prevail over your religion. It was also said: do not fear the consequence of them. The apparent meaning is that He forbade fearing them, and that they do not fear anyone except Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you.﴾ *Al-yawm* ("today") may carry the meanings mentioned regarding His saying: "Today those who disbelieve have despaired." The majority said: its perfection is its manifestation, the comprehensiveness of the magnitude of its obligations, and its declaring things lawful and unlawful. They said: after that, a great deal of Qur'an was revealed, such as the verses on usury and the verse on *kalalah* and other matters. Rather, most of the religion was completed, as was the matter of the pilgrimage, if they performed it with no polytheist among them. Al-Zamakhshari delivered a sermon on this meaning and said: "I have settled for you the matter of your enemy, and made the upper hand yours, as kings say: 'Today our kingship is complete, and everything we wanted is complete for us,' when they have restrained those who contend with them for kingship and have reached their aims and objectives. Or: I have perfected for you what you need of teaching the lawful and unlawful, of directing you to the laws, the rules of analogy (*qiyas*) and the foundations of independent legal reasoning (*ijtihad*)." End of quote. This second view is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi; they said: the perfection of His obligations and limits, and no lawful or unlawful ruling was revealed after this verse. On this view, the meaning is: I have perfected for you the laws of your religion. Qatadah and Ibn Jubayr said: its perfection is that He removed the polytheists from the House, so no polytheist performed the pilgrimage. Al-Sha'bi said: the perfection of the religion is its might and its manifestation, and the humiliation and effacement of polytheism, not the completion of the obligations and recommended practices, because these kept being revealed until (the Prophet) died. It was also said: its perfection is the security from its abrogation (*naskh*) afterward, just as earlier laws were abrogated by it. Al-Qaffal said: the religion was never deficient at all; rather, the laws kept descending at every time, sufficient for that time. However, He, exalted is He, knew at the beginning of the mission that what is complete today is not complete tomorrow, and He would abrogate after establishment and add after absence. But at the end of the time of the mission He sent down a complete law and made its firmness lasting until the Day of Resurrection.

It is related that when this verse was revealed on the Day of the Greatest Pilgrimage, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited it, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (رضي الله عنه) wept. The Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: "What makes you weep?" He said: "What made me weep is that we were in an increase of our religion; but now that it is complete, nothing completes except that it diminishes." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "You have spoken the truth."

﴿And I have completed My favor upon you﴾, that is: in the manifestation of Islam, the perfection of the religion, the abundance of conditions, and other things encompassed by this upright religious community, up to entering Paradise and abiding in it. Al-Zamakhshari embellished the expression, saying: "By the conquest of Makkah and entering it safe and victorious, by demolishing the landmarks of the Jahiliyyah and its rites, that no polytheist performs the pilgrimage and no naked person circumambulates the House." End of quote. So his words gather the sayings of the earlier scholars. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: the completion of the favor is preventing the polytheists from the pilgrimage. al-Suddi said: it is the manifestation over the enemy. Ibn Zayd said: by guidance to Islam. Al-Zamakhshari said: "And I have completed My favor upon you by completing the matter of the religion and the laws, as if He said: 'I have completed My favor upon you by that, for there is no favor more complete than the favor of Islam.'"

﴿And I have approved Islam for you as a religion﴾, meaning: I have chosen it for you from among the religions, and informed you that it is the only approved religion: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85]; ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community﴾ [al-Anbiya': 92]. This is what al-Zamakhshari said. Ibn 'Atiyyah al-Rafdi said: this place may mean "will" (*al-irādah*), and it may be an attribute of action, an expression of Allah's manifesting it, because approval (*al-rida*) is among the attributes that are ambiguous between attributes of essence (*sifat al-dhat*) and attributes of action (*sifat al-af'al*). Allah, exalted is He, approved Islam and willed it for us, and there are things Allah wills to occur but does not approve of. Islam here is the religion in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19]. End of quote. His words indicate that if approval is among the attributes of essence, then it is an attribute distinct from will. It was also said: the meaning is: I have informed you of My approval of it as a religion for you, for He, exalted is He, has always been approving of Islam as a religion for us; so the specification of approval to that day would have no benefit if taken in its apparent sense. It was said: "I have approved of you when you worship Me with the religion I have legislated for you." It was also said: "I have approved your Islam, which you are upon today, as a complete religion until the end of time, from which nothing will be abrogated."

﴿So whoever is compelled by severe hunger, without inclining toward sin, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ This is connected to the mention of the prohibited things. "That is grave disobedience" (verse 3) emphasizes it, and what follows it, meaning the prohibition, because the prohibition of these abominations is part of the complete religion, the perfect favors, and Islam described as approved, to the exclusion of other faiths. The explanation of this sort of sentence has preceded. The recitation of Ibn Muhaysin was *famani ttarra* with the *dad* assimilated into the *ta'*. The meaning of *mutajanif* is "deviating and inclining." The majority recited *mutajanif* with an alif. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Nakha'i and Ibn Thabit recited *mutajannif* without an alif. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is more eloquent in meaning than *mutajanif*, and the form *tafa'ala* is only for imitating a thing and approaching it. Do you not see that when you say *tamayala al-ghusn* ("the branch swayed"), that implies a bending and an approach to inclination, whereas when you say *tamayyala*, the inclination is established. Likewise *tasawwana al-rajul* and *tasawwana*, and *taghafala* and *taghaffala*. End of quote. The sin here was said to be: eating beyond satiety. It was said: disobedience by travelling.
