It was said: the sin here is the forbidden, and from this is the saying of 'Umar: "We did not deviate in it toward sin, nor did we intend it while knowing it," meaning: we did not incline in it toward what is forbidden.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 2–3 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Nor the garlands﴾. Mujahid, 'Ata' and Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: the garlands (qala'id) are what they used to hang on themselves from the trees of the Sacred Precinct (haram) so that they would be safe thereby. The believers were thus forbidden to imitate the practice of the Jahiliyya (the Age of Ignorance) and to take garlands from the trees of the Sacred Precinct. There is a hadith: "Its grass shall not be cut, and its trees shall not be felled." The majority said: the garlands are what they used to hang on themselves of the sami (a kind of tree bark or plant) when they set out for the Hajj, so that this would be a sign of pilgrimage. It was also said: or what a man of the Haram would hang on himself when he went out on some need, so that this would show that he was a man of the Haram; thus God, exalted is He, forbade making lawful those who had put on any of these. Al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas that the garlands are the garlanded offering (al-hady al-muqallad), and that an offering was only called a hady when it had not been garlanded; so it is as if he said: nor the offering that has not been garlanded, nor the garlanded one of it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is an imposition upon the wording of Ibn 'Abbas, and it is not part of his speech that the word hady is used only for what has not been garlanded. Rather, it implies that God, exalted is He, forbade the offering in general, and then mentioned the garlanded part of it as emphasis and as an intensification in alerting to the sanctity of the garlanded one. It was also said: he meant the garlands themselves, so he forbade touching the garlands of the offering, as an intensification of the prohibition against touching the offering; i.e., do not make lawful their garlands, let alone that you should untie them, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and that they should not display their adornment﴾ [al-Nur: 31], forbidding the displaying of adornment as an intensification of the prohibition against displaying its places. Al-Tabari said: its interpretation is that He forbade making lawful the sanctity of what is garlanded, whether an offering or a person, and He dispensed with mentioning the garlanded one by mentioning the garlands, since it was understood by the addressee.

﴿Nor those who make for the Sacred House, the Inviolable House﴾. 'Abd Allah and his companions recited: "wa-la ammi" (without the nun), by deletion for the idafa (construct) to "the House"; i.e., nor make lawful people intending the Sacred Mosque, who are the pilgrims and the visitors ('umrah). Al-Zamakhshari said: and the making lawful of these, i.e., that the sanctity of the rites is disregarded, and that there be placed between them and the devout those who would hinder, and that they create in the months of the Hajj what would turn people away from the Hajj, and that the offering be harmed by seizure or by preventing it from reaching its place of sacrifice.

﴿Seeking bounty from their Lord and good pleasure﴾. The majority read "yabtaghuna" with the ya', so that it is an attribute of "amminin". Al-Zamakhshari interpreted "bounty" as reward, which is the view of some. It was also said: bounty is trade and the profits in it. It was also said: increase in wealth and children; they seek the hope of increase in this. As for "good pleasure" (ridwan), they used to aim at it even if they did not attain it, and seeking a thing does not indicate its attainment. It was also said: this is a distribution among the polytheists: some of them sought trade, since they did not believe in a return, and some of them sought good pleasure by the Hajj, since some of them believed in recompense after death and that one would be raised, even though the good pleasure of God would not be attained for him, so He informed of that on the basis of his supposition. It was also said: the Muslims and the polytheists both performed the Hajj; so the seeking of bounty is from both of them, and the seeking of good pleasure is from the believers. Qatada said: it is that He sets right their livelihoods in this world and does not hasten punishment upon them in it. Some said: bounty and good pleasure in the verse have one meaning, namely God's pleasure and His bounty through mercy. God, exalted is He, forbade that one should approach a people with this description, as a glorification of them and as a disapproval of approaching the likes of them. In the prohibition against approaching them there is a winning over of the Arabs, kindness toward them, and an encouragement to come to the season; and in the season they hear the Qur'an, the proof is established against them, and their entry into faith is hoped for, as had happened.

This verse was revealed in the year of the Conquest, so whatever in it concerns a Muslim pilgrim is muhkam (established), and whatever concerns an unbeliever is mansukh (abrogated); that was abrogated after the year nine, when Abu Bakr performed the Hajj and the proclamation was made among the people with the Surat Bara'a. The saying of al-Hasan and Abu Maysara: there is no abrogated element in it, is a rejected view. Humayd ibn Qays and al-A'raj read "tabtaghuna" with the ta', as address to the believers; and the meaning according to the address is that the believers used to intend fighting them and raiding them, and to bar them from the Sacred Mosque in compliance with God's command and seeking His good pleasure, since God, exalted is He, commanded fighting the polytheists, killing them, taking their children captive, and seizing their wealth, until they believe or give the jizya (poll tax). Al-A'mash read "wa-ridwanan" with a damma on the ra', and it has preceded in Al 'Imran that this is the reading of Abu Bakr from 'Asim, wherever it occurs except in the second occurrence in this surah, where there is a difference of transmission from him.

﴿And when you have left the state of ihram, then hunt﴾. The end of His saying: ﴿lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 1] included the prohibition of hunting in the state of ihram, and the end of His saying: ﴿Do not make lawful the rites of God﴾ included the prohibition against making lawful the people of the House; so this sentence came with its ruling referring back to the first sentence, and what follows it, His saying: ﴿and let not the hatred of a people...﴾, refers back to the second sentence, and this is of eloquent excellence. Thus this sentence is not an interjection between His saying: ﴿nor those who make for the Sacred House﴾ and His saying: ﴿let not...﴾; rather it establishes a ruling and is not a confirmation that consolidates, so it would be an interjection; rather it conveys the permissibility of hunting in the state of ihram. There is no preposing or postposing here; the original structure would be: "not making lawful the game while you are in ihram; then when you have left the state of ihram, hunt." In the second verse the original structure would be: "nor those who make for the Sacred House, seeking bounty from their Lord and good pleasure, and let not...," as one of them went to it, and he took from it the story of the slaughter of the cow, saying: the way of looking at it is that one should say: ﴿And when you slew a soul﴾ [al-Baqara: 72], the verse, then one should say: ﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾ [al-Baqara: 67]. He often mentioned this preposing and postposing in the Qur'an, and the wonder about him is that he makes it part of the science of eloquence and rhetorical embellishment; and this is not permissible in our view except in the necessity of poetry, and it is among the most ugly of poetic licences, so it is fitting, rather obligatory, that the Qur'an be exonerated from it.

He said: the reason for this is that when the Companions collected the Qur'an they did not arrange it according to the order of its revelation, but arranged it according to the closeness of meanings and the harmony of wordings. What he said is not correct; rather what we believe is that the Messenger of God, ﷺ, is the one who arranged it, not the Companions, and likewise we say concerning its surahs, though some have differed in that.

The command to hunt here is a command of permission by consensus, and for this reason al-Zamakhshari said: "And when you have left the state of ihram, there is no blame upon you that you should hunt." End of quote. Since hunting is permissible, and only the state of ihram prevented it, when the preventing factor is removed it returns to its original permissibility. They spoke here about the form of the imperative when it comes after a prohibition, and about it when it comes without indicators, and what it is to be understood as, and about the actual usage of it; and that belongs to the science of the foundations of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), so it is researched there.

It was also read: "fa-idha halaltum," which is a dialect; it is said: halla min ihramihi and ahalla. Abu Waqid, al-Jarrah, Nubayh and al-Hasan ibn 'Imran read "fi-subadu" (fa-ittasadu?) with a kasra on the fa', i.e., "fisṭādū". Al-Zamakhshari said: it is said it is a substitute for the kasra of the hamza at the beginning. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a difficult reading, and among its justifications is that one observes the kasra of the alif of connection when you begin, saying "isṭādū" with a kasra on the fa', as a reminder of the original alif of connection. End of quote. In my view it is not a pure kasra, but rather of the category of pure imala (inclination), because of the supposed presence of the kasra of the hamzat al-wasl, just as they inclined the fa' in "fa-idha" because of the presence of the kasra of "idha."

﴿And let not the hatred of a people, because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, lead you to transgress﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: "yajrimannakum" means: let not carry you, it is said: "jaramani kadha 'ala bughdika," so "an ta'tadu" originally is "'ala an ta'tadu," and the preposition was deleted from it. Others said: its meaning is that of "kasaba" which is transitive to two objects, so "an ta'tadu" is in the position of the second object; i.e., your transgression upon you. It is also transitive to one object; you say "ajrama" in the sense of "kasaba," which is transitive to two; it is said in its meaning: jaramaa and ajrama. Abu 'Ali said: ajrama I know it to mean earning, in sins and misdeeds. Al-Hasan, Ibrahim, Ibn Thabit and al-Walid from Ya'qub read "yajrimankum" with a sukun on the nun, making the nun of emphasis light.

Al-Zamakhshari said: and the meaning is: let not the hatred of a people because they barred you from transgression earn you, and let it not carry you to it. End of quote. This is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of grammatical analysis, because it is impossible that the signification of "hamala" and "kasaba" be the same in one usage, owing to the difference of their requirements; so it is impossible that "an ta'tadu" be in the place of a direct object and in the place of an object after dropping the preposition.

Al-Nahwiyyan, Ibn Kathir, Hamza, Hafs and Nafi' read "shana'an" with a fatha on the nun. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read it with a sukun, and it is related from Nafi'. The more apparent reading with the fatha is that it is a verbal noun (masdar), and the coming of the masdar on the pattern fa'alan has been frequent, and they permitted that it be an adjective, and fa'alan exists among adjectives, such as their saying: "himarun qatawan," i.e., hard to travel; and "taysun 'adawan," i.e., much running; and it is not in plurality like the masdar. They said: on this basis the meaning is: let not the hatred of a people earn you. They mean by "baghid" an active participle "mubghid," because it is from "shana'a" in the sense of hatred. It is transitive, and it is not in the genitive to the object or subject, unlike when it is a masdar, for it may be in the genitive to the object, which is the more apparent, and it may be in the genitive to the subject; i.e., the hatred of a people toward you. As for the sukun, the more apparent is that it is an adjective, for it is reported: "rajulun shan'anun" and "imra'atun shan'anatun," and by analogy this is from a transitive verb. It is also reported: "shan'anun" and "shan'a," like "'atshanun" and "'atsha," and by analogy this is from an intransitive verb. A single root may produce both transitive and intransitive forms, as in: "faghara fahu" and "faghara fuwhu," meaning opened and became open. It was permitted that it be a masdar, and the coming of masdars on fa'lan with fatha on the fa' and sukun on the 'ayn is rare; they said: "lawaytuhu daynahu laiyanan." Al-Ahwas said:

"And love is nothing but what you love and desire, / even if the one with hatred blames him in it and rebukes."

Its origin is "al-shan'an," and he deleted the hamza and transferred its vowel to the consonant before it. The adjectival form on fa'lan is more frequent than the masdar, like "rahman." Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read "in saddukum" with a kasra on the hamza, as a conditional. Ibn Mas'ud's reading "in saddukum" supports this. Ibn Jarir, al-Nahhas and others denied the reading with kasra on "in," and said: the polytheists only barred the Messenger and the believers in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, and the verse was revealed in the year of the Conquest, in the year eight, while al-Hudaybiyya was in the year six; so the barring preceded the revelation of the verse, while the kasra requires that it be afterward; and because Mecca in the year of the Conquest was in the hands of the Muslims, so how could they be barred from it while it was in their hands? This denial from them of this reading is very difficult, for it is a mutawatir reading, since it is among the Seven, and its meaning with it is sound; the sense is: if a barring occurs in the future similar to that barring which took place at the time of al-Hudaybiyya, and this prohibition is a legislation for the future. It is not unanimously agreed that the revelation of this verse was in the year of the Conquest; rather al-Yazidi mentioned that it was revealed before they barred them, and on this view the conditional is clear. The rest of the Seven read "an" with a fatha on the hamza, making it an explanation of the hatred, and this is a clear reading; i.e., the hatred of a people because they barred you in the year of al-Hudaybiyya from the Sacred Mosque. "I'tida'" means retaliating against them by inflicting harm upon them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 2–3 (part 2 of 3):

﴿And help one another in righteousness and piety﴾. When He forbade transgression, He commanded mutual assistance and cooperation in good. Forbidding transgression does not necessarily entail cooperating in good, because between them there is an intermediate state, which is abstaining from both transgression and cooperation. Al-Zamakhshari explained "righteousness and piety" as pardoning and overlooking [wrongs]. He said: "It is also permissible to intend the general meaning of every righteousness and piety, which would then include pardoning." End of quote. Some said: "They have one meaning, and it was repeated for emphasis through the variation of wording." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is loose usage. The customary meaning of these two terms covers what is obligatory and what is recommended, and piety is the observance of what is obligatory. If one is put in place of the other, it is permissible." End of quote. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Righteousness is what you are commanded to do, and piety is what you are forbidden from." Sahl said: "Righteousness is faith, and piety is the Sunnah," meaning following the Sunnah.

﴿And do not help one another in sin and aggression﴾. Sin (ithm) refers to acts of disobedience, and aggression ('udwan) refers to exceeding the limits of God. This was stated by 'Ata'. It was also said: sin is disbelief and rebellion, and aggression is innovation (bid'a). It was also said: sin is the ruling that attaches to offences, and aggression is wronging people; this was stated by Ibn 'Atiyya. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Sin and aggression are retaliation and the seeking of revenge." He said: "It is also permissible to intend the general meaning of every sin and every aggression."

﴿And fear God. Indeed God is severe in punishment﴾. He commanded piety in an unrestricted form, even though He had already commanded it in the context of cooperation, to emphasise the command. Then He gave the reason: that He is severe in punishment, so He must be feared. The severity of His punishment lies in the fact that no one can bear it, and in its being everlasting, since most of worldly life comes to an end. Mujahid said: this was revealed as a prohibition against seeking [to return] to the ignorance (jahiliyya) when some of the believers wished to do so. It has been said that this concerned an ally of Abu Sufyan from the Hudhayl tribe.

﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which any name other than God's has been invoked﴾. A similar sentence was discussed previously in al-Baqara. Ibn 'Atiyya said here: "The flesh of swine implies its fat, by consensus." End of quote. This is not so, for Dawud and others disagreed about it. We discussed this in al-Baqara. Here it is mentioned later, and there earlier, for variety of expression and breadth in speech, and because the divine name (al-Jalala) occurred there as an intervening element or something like one. Here, coordinated items follow it, so it is not an intervening element nor like one. What comes in this manner in most instances requires the lengthened vowel (madd).

﴿And the strangled, the beaten, the fallen, the gored, and that which a beast of prey has eaten﴾. The meanings of these words were explained earlier in the Vocabulary section. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: the people of the jahiliyya would strangle sheep and other animals, and when they died they would eat them. Abu 'Abd Allah said: "The beaten animal (mawquda) applies only to domestic animals, not to game." Malik and other jurists said: "In hunting, the ruling for game killed by a blow is the same as the ruling for the beaten animal." This is explicit in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the mi'rad (a blunt-headed arrow): "If it strikes with its width, do not eat it, for it is beaten (waqidh)."

Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: the gored (natiha) is a sheep gored by another, so that both die, or a sheep gored by cattle or goats. Others said: the gored is the one that is struck by butting, because two sheep may butt each other and die. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Whatever dies from being crushed is gored (natih)." 'Abd Allah and Abu Maysara read: "al-mantuha" (the gored).

The intended sense of "that which a beast of prey has eaten" is what a predator has seized and eaten from. It cannot be taken literally, because what is assumed to have been eaten entirely by a predator no longer exists to be forbidden. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: "That which a beast of prey has eaten of, in part." All these were eaten by the people of the jahiliyya. Al-Hasan, al-Fayyad, Talha ibn Salman and Abu Haywa read "al-sab'" (with a sukun on the ba'), and this is reported from Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim in a non-standard reading, and from Abu 'Amr. 'Abd Allah read "wa-akilat al-sab'" (and what the beast ate). Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-akil al-sab'" (and the eaten by the beast). Both mean "what is eaten by a beast of prey." The mention of these forbidden things is a detailing of what was stated in summary in the general phrase ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 1]. Thus the item excepted from and the exception have become known.

﴿Except what you have slaughtered (dhakkaytum)﴾. 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, Ibrahim, Tawus, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd, and the majority said: it refers back to the items mentioned, that is, from "the strangled" to "what a beast of prey has eaten." So whatever in them still shows some life, by one's eye, or by striking with a foot, or moving a tail, is slaughtered (dhukkiya) and may be eaten. In general, whatever is known with certainty to still have life is slaughtered and eaten. This is the view of Malik in one opinion. The well-known position of Malik and his Medinan companions is that the slaughter (dhakat) for these items is what has not reached a lethal state and has not been determined to be unable to survive. When it reaches that state, it has the ruling of carrion.

According to these two views, the exception is connected (istithna' muttasil), but there is disagreement about the condition in which slaughter takes effect on these items. Al-Zamakhshari inclined to the well-known opinion of Malik, for he said: "Not what you have obtained the slaughter of while it convulses like one slaughtered, and its blood flows." It was also said: the exception is connected, returning to the nearest preceding item, which is "what a beast of prey has eaten," and is specific to it. The meaning is: except what you find still living from what a beast of prey has eaten, and you slaughter it, for it is lawful. It was also said: the exception is disconnected (istithna' munqati'). The sense is: "But what you slaughter from other than these is to be eaten." It seems that the one who held this view considered these attributes to have been present in what died from one of them, whether by strangling, beating, falling, goring, or being seized by a predator, and that it reached a point where it could not survive because of one of these attributes, according to the view of those who take that into account. For this reason the exception is disconnected.

The apparent view is that the exception is connected. The reason these five were specified, though they are in the ruling of carrion, and carrion was not mentioned alone, is that the Arabs believed these events upon the animal to be equivalent to slaughter, and that carrion is what dies from illness without any cause known among these causes.

The apparent sense of the words ﴿except what you have slaughtered﴾ implies that what cannot be caught in time to be slaughtered may not be eaten, such as a fetus that emerges dead from the belly of its slaughtered mother. If the exception is disconnected, the fetus falls under the general prohibition of carrion. This is the position of Abu Hanifa. The majority held that it may be eaten. The hadith from which they derived permission is an argument for Abu Hanifa, not for them: "The slaughter of the fetus is the slaughter of its mother." The meaning is by way of comparison: the slaughter of the fetus is like the slaughter of its mother. Just as the slaughter of the mother is by cutting, so too the slaughter of the fetus is by cutting. Had it been as they claim, the wording would have been "the slaughter of the mother of the fetus is its slaughter."

﴿And what is sacrificed on the altar stones (nusub)﴾. Mujahid, Qatada and others said: these are stones on which the people of the jahiliyya used to slaughter. Ibn 'Abbas said: and they would also anoint them [with blood]. Ibn Jurayj said: they were not idols, for an idol is a figure carved in an image. The Arabs used to slaughter at Mecca and sprinkle the blood on whatever came toward the House, cut the meat, and place it on the stones. When Islam came, the Muslims said: "We have more right than they to honour this House with these acts." The Messenger (ﷺ) disliked this, so ﴿and what is sacrificed on the altar stones﴾ was revealed, and ﴿Neither their flesh nor their blood reaches God﴾ [al-Hajj: 37] was revealed. End of quote.

The Arabs had stone altars (ansab) in their lands which they worshipped, and they anointed with blood the altars of Mecca, among them the stone called Sa'd. Ibn Zayd said: "What is sacrificed on the altar stones and what is invoked with a name other than God's are one thing." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "What is sacrificed on the altar stones is a part of what is invoked with a name other than God's, but it was singled out for mention after its general category because the matter was well known, the place held honour, and people held it in reverence. An idol may also be called nusub, because it is set up (yunsab)." End of quote.

The majority read "al-nusub" with two damma vowels. Talha ibn Musarrif read with a damma on the nun and a sukun on the sad. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read with two fatha vowels, and this was also reported from him in the majority reading. al-Hasan read with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the sad.

﴿And that you seek to know by the divining arrows (istiqsam bi-l-azlam)﴾. This is coordinated with what precedes it; that is, He forbade you the seeking of knowledge by the divining arrows. Istiqsam is seeking to know one's portion (qism), which is the share, or the apportioning (qasm), which is the verbal noun. Ibn Jurayj said: its meaning is that you seek to learn what has been apportioned to you by the arrows, or what has not been apportioned to you. End of quote. Mujahid said: they are the knucklebones of Persia and Rome with which they used to gamble. It was also reported from him that they were the arrows of the Arabs and the knucklebones of Persia. Sufyan and Waki' said: they are chess. It was also said: the azlam were pebbles with which they cast lots, and this is what the poet referred to in his words:

"By your life, the casters do not know by the pebbles,
nor the bird-divining augurs, what God will do."

This was reported from Ibn Jubayr. They said: the Arabs' azlam were of three kinds. The first: three arrows which each person made for himself; on one was written "do," on another "do not," and the third was blank. He put them in a bag, and when he wanted to do something he put his hand into the bag and acted according to whichever came out, whether it was the command or the prohibition. If the blank came out he cast again. The second: seven arrows (qidah) which were kept by Hubal inside the Ka'ba. On one of them was written "the blood-money (aql)" regarding diyya payments; whoever among them is to pay it, they cast with the seven, and whoever has the arrow of "aql" drawn against him must pay. On another: "Yes," on another: "No." When they wanted to do something they cast, and followed what came out. On another: "From among you," on another: "From others," on another: "Attached." When they disagreed about a person, whether he was of them or not, they cast and followed what came out. On the rest was written the rulings on water, so that when they wanted to dig for water they cast with the arrows, and wherever the lot came out, they acted on it. These seven were likewise kept by every soothsayer (kahin) among the Arab soothsayers and judges, in the manner they were kept in the Ka'ba with Hubal. The third: the arrows of gambling (maysir), which are ten. The explanation of maysir was given earlier in surah al-Baqara.

﴿That is transgression (fisq)﴾. The apparent sense is that the demonstrative refers specifically to the seeking by arrows. This was transmitted by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zamakhshari said: it refers to the seeking by arrows and to the taking of what was forbidden to them, since the meaning is: "It was forbidden to them to eat carrion, and so on and so forth." (If you say): why was the seeking by arrows, whether by a traveller or someone else, to learn the state of affairs, transgression? (I say): because it is an intrusion into the knowledge of the unseen, which God has reserved for Himself, the Knower of the unseen. He said: ﴿None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except God﴾ [al-Naml: 65]. Holding that there is a path to it and a means of deducing it is the belief. His words "My Lord commanded me, and my Lord forbade me" are a fabrication against God, the Exalted. What is claimed by the soothsayers and astrologers, that God commanded or forbade them, is of this nature, even if by "Lord" they meant an idol. It has been reported that they used to cast lots at their idols, and the matter is clear. End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding the demonstrative: this was transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas by 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, and it is the view of Ibn Jubayr. Al-Tabari said: God forbade these matters in which soothsayers and astrologers engage, because of the speech about hidden things that they involve. Others said: the reason for the prohibition of seeking by the arrows is that money is consumed by falsehood through them. When they wanted to circumcise a boy, marry, bury a dead person, or doubted a lineage, they went to Hubal with a hundred dirhams and a camel. The hundred was for the one who cast the arrows, and the camel was slaughtered and eaten. They named their companion and said to Hubal: "O our god, this is so-and-so; we want by him such-and-such; so bring forth the truth concerning him." The caster would cast, and whatever came out they acted upon. If it came out "no," they postponed the matter for their year until they brought it again another time. They ended all their affairs at whatever the arrows indicated.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 5, verses 2–3 (part 3 of 3):**

﴿Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion.﴾ The alif and lam in *al-yawm* ("today") are for a known referent (*al-'ahd*). It is the Day of 'Arafah. This is what Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said. It was the day it was revealed, after the afternoon prayer, during the Farewell Pilgrimage, on a Friday, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was at the station on his camel, and there was no polytheist at the station. It was also said that it was the day the Messenger (ﷺ) entered Makkah, eight days before the end of Ramadan in the ninth year. It was also said it was in the eighth year. His herald proclaimed safety for whoever uttered the testimony of Islam, for whoever laid down his weapons, and for whoever closed his door. Al-Zajjaj said: "He did not intend a particular day; the meaning is: now they have despaired, just as you say, 'I am old today.'" End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari followed al-Zajjaj and said: "'Today' does not refer to a specific day, but to the present time and what is connected to it and adjacent to it of past and future times, as in your saying: 'Yesterday you were young, and today you are gray-haired.' You do not mean by 'yesterday' the day before your day, nor by 'today' your day." Its like is *al-an* ("now") in his saying:

*Now that my body hair has turned white,*
*and I have gnawed with my teeth on a stump.*

End of quote.

*Those who disbelieve* are the polytheists of the Arabs. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and 'Ata' said: they despaired of your returning to their religion. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the manifestation of the affair of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, and the manifestation of his religion, requires that the despair of the disbelievers regarding returning to their religion had already occurred long before. This despair, in my view, is rather about the collapse of the affair of Islam and the corruption of its community, because this was a matter that those among the disbelievers who remained were hoping for. Do you not see the saying of the brother of Safwan ibn Umayyah on the day of Hawazin, when the Muslims were routed and he thought it a defeat: "Has magic not been nullified today?" Al-Zamakhshari said: they despaired of nullifying it and of returning to make lawful these abominations after they had been forbidden to you. It was said: they despaired of your religion, of overcoming it, because Allah fulfilled His promise of making it prevail over all religion. End of quote. Abu Ja'far recited *yaisa* without hamzah, and it is reported from Abu 'Amr.

﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me.﴾ Ibn Jubayr said: do not fear them lest they prevail over you. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: do not fear them lest they prevail over your religion. It was also said: do not fear the consequence of them. The apparent meaning is that He forbade fearing them, and that they do not fear anyone except Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you.﴾ *Al-yawm* ("today") may carry the meanings mentioned regarding His saying: "Today those who disbelieve have despaired." The majority said: its perfection is its manifestation, the comprehensiveness of the magnitude of its obligations, and its declaring things lawful and unlawful. They said: after that, a great deal of Qur'an was revealed, such as the verses on usury and the verse on *kalalah* and other matters. Rather, most of the religion was completed, as was the matter of the pilgrimage, if they performed it with no polytheist among them. Al-Zamakhshari delivered a sermon on this meaning and said: "I have settled for you the matter of your enemy, and made the upper hand yours, as kings say: 'Today our kingship is complete, and everything we wanted is complete for us,' when they have restrained those who contend with them for kingship and have reached their aims and objectives. Or: I have perfected for you what you need of teaching the lawful and unlawful, of directing you to the laws, the rules of analogy (*qiyas*) and the foundations of independent legal reasoning (*ijtihad*)." End of quote. This second view is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi; they said: the perfection of His obligations and limits, and no lawful or unlawful ruling was revealed after this verse. On this view, the meaning is: I have perfected for you the laws of your religion. Qatadah and Ibn Jubayr said: its perfection is that He removed the polytheists from the House, so no polytheist performed the pilgrimage. Al-Sha'bi said: the perfection of the religion is its might and its manifestation, and the humiliation and effacement of polytheism, not the completion of the obligations and recommended practices, because these kept being revealed until (the Prophet) died. It was also said: its perfection is the security from its abrogation (*naskh*) afterward, just as earlier laws were abrogated by it. Al-Qaffal said: the religion was never deficient at all; rather, the laws kept descending at every time, sufficient for that time. However, He, exalted is He, knew at the beginning of the mission that what is complete today is not complete tomorrow, and He would abrogate after establishment and add after absence. But at the end of the time of the mission He sent down a complete law and made its firmness lasting until the Day of Resurrection.

It is related that when this verse was revealed on the Day of the Greatest Pilgrimage, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited it, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (رضي الله عنه) wept. The Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: "What makes you weep?" He said: "What made me weep is that we were in an increase of our religion; but now that it is complete, nothing completes except that it diminishes." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "You have spoken the truth."

﴿And I have completed My favor upon you﴾, that is: in the manifestation of Islam, the perfection of the religion, the abundance of conditions, and other things encompassed by this upright religious community, up to entering Paradise and abiding in it. Al-Zamakhshari embellished the expression, saying: "By the conquest of Makkah and entering it safe and victorious, by demolishing the landmarks of the Jahiliyyah and its rites, that no polytheist performs the pilgrimage and no naked person circumambulates the House." End of quote. So his words gather the sayings of the earlier scholars. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: the completion of the favor is preventing the polytheists from the pilgrimage. al-Suddi said: it is the manifestation over the enemy. Ibn Zayd said: by guidance to Islam. Al-Zamakhshari said: "And I have completed My favor upon you by completing the matter of the religion and the laws, as if He said: 'I have completed My favor upon you by that, for there is no favor more complete than the favor of Islam.'"

﴿And I have approved Islam for you as a religion﴾, meaning: I have chosen it for you from among the religions, and informed you that it is the only approved religion: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85]; ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community﴾ [al-Anbiya': 92]. This is what al-Zamakhshari said. Ibn 'Atiyyah al-Rafdi said: this place may mean "will" (*al-irādah*), and it may be an attribute of action, an expression of Allah's manifesting it, because approval (*al-rida*) is among the attributes that are ambiguous between attributes of essence (*sifat al-dhat*) and attributes of action (*sifat al-af'al*). Allah, exalted is He, approved Islam and willed it for us, and there are things Allah wills to occur but does not approve of. Islam here is the religion in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19]. End of quote. His words indicate that if approval is among the attributes of essence, then it is an attribute distinct from will. It was also said: the meaning is: I have informed you of My approval of it as a religion for you, for He, exalted is He, has always been approving of Islam as a religion for us; so the specification of approval to that day would have no benefit if taken in its apparent sense. It was said: "I have approved of you when you worship Me with the religion I have legislated for you." It was also said: "I have approved your Islam, which you are upon today, as a complete religion until the end of time, from which nothing will be abrogated."

﴿So whoever is compelled by severe hunger, without inclining toward sin, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ This is connected to the mention of the prohibited things. "That is grave disobedience" (verse 3) emphasizes it, and what follows it, meaning the prohibition, because the prohibition of these abominations is part of the complete religion, the perfect favors, and Islam described as approved, to the exclusion of other faiths. The explanation of this sort of sentence has preceded. The recitation of Ibn Muhaysin was *famani ttarra* with the *dad* assimilated into the *ta'*. The meaning of *mutajanif* is "deviating and inclining." The majority recited *mutajanif* with an alif. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Nakha'i and Ibn Thabit recited *mutajannif* without an alif. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is more eloquent in meaning than *mutajanif*, and the form *tafa'ala* is only for imitating a thing and approaching it. Do you not see that when you say *tamayala al-ghusn* ("the branch swayed"), that implies a bending and an approach to inclination, whereas when you say *tamayyala*, the inclination is established. Likewise *tasawwana al-rajul* and *tasawwana*, and *taghafala* and *taghaffala*. End of quote. The sin here was said to be: eating beyond satiety. It was said: disobedience by travelling. It was said: the sin here is the forbidden, and from this is the saying of 'Umar: "We did not deviate in it toward sin, nor did we intend it while knowing it," meaning: we did not incline in it toward what is forbidden.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 4 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: "Lawful for you are the good things, and what you have taught the trained predatory animals, training them as Allah has taught you. So eat of what they catch for you, and mention the name of Allah over it, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning."﴾ ﴿Today, the good things have been made lawful for you. The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them. And chaste women from among the believing women, and chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you, when you give them their bridal payments, seeking chastity, not committing fornication, nor taking secret lovers. And whoever disbelieves in faith, his deeds have become worthless, and he will be in the Hereafter among the losers.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5] ﴿O you who believe, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles. And if you are in a state of major impurity, purify yourselves. And if you are ill, or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it. Allah does not want to place upon you any hardship, but He wants to purify you and to complete His favor upon you, so that you may be grateful.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]

Al-jawarih (the trained predatory animals): the beasts of prey and birds that seize, such as the dog, the leopard, the panther, the eagle, the falcon, the hawk and the shahin (a type of falcon). They are so called because they usually wound what they hunt, or because they earn (gain). It is said: "a woman who has no jarih," meaning no earner (kasib). From this is the verse: ﴿And He knows what you have earned (jarahtum) by day﴾ [al-An'am: 60], meaning what you have earned (kasabtum). It is said: jaraha and ijtaraha with the meaning of "earned."

Al-mukallib, with the shaddah: the trainer of dogs and the one who sets them on game. With the lightening, it means the owner of dogs. Al-Zajjaj said: a man who is mukallib, mukallab, or kallab is an owner of dogs.

Al-ghusl (washing) in language: bringing water to the washed thing together with passing something over it, such as the hand or the like. Some said this. Others said: it is passing water over the place. From this is the statement of one of the Arabs:
"How beautiful she is, as the tears wash away her kohl"

Al-mirfaq (elbow): the joint between the wrist and the upper arm. Opening the mim and breaking the fa is the more well-known form. Al-rijl (foot) is well known, and its plural is af'ul in both the paucity and the abundance forms. Al-ka'b (ankle) is the bone that protrudes on the front of the foot where the strap of the sandal gathers. Al-haraj: narrowness. Al-haraj also means a thin she-camel, and al-haraj means a bier.

﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them﴾: the occasion of its revelation, as said by Ikrimah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b, was the question of 'Asim ibn 'Adi, Sa'id ibn Khaythamah and 'Uwaymir ibn Sa'idah: "What is lawful for us from these dogs?" At that time the Messenger had ordered their killing, and they were killed until they reached the outskirts, because of Jibril's statement, peace be upon him: "We do not enter a house in which there is a dog." In the Sahih of Abu 'Abdullah al-Hakim, with its chain back to Abu Rafi', he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered me to kill the dogs." So the people said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is lawful for us from this community which you have ordered to be killed?" So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them﴾, the verses. Ibn Jubayr said: it was revealed concerning 'Adi ibn Hatim and Zayd al-Khayl, who said: "O Messenger of Allah, we hunt with dogs and hawks, and the dogs of the family of Dir' and the family of Abu Hawriyyah take cows, donkeys, gazelles and lizards. Of that, some we reach in time to slaughter, and some are killed and we do not reach them in time to slaughter. Allah has forbidden carrion, so what is lawful for us from it?" Then it was revealed.

According to the consideration of the occasion of revelation, the answer exceeds what the question was about, because they asked about a specific kind of food and were answered with what they asked about, and with something general about food.

It is possible that all of "mada" is an interrogative and the clause is a predicate. It is possible that "ma" is interrogative and "dha" is a predicate, that is: what is it that has been made lawful for them? The clause then is a relative clause. The apparent meaning is: what has been made lawful for them of foods, because when He mentioned what He had forbidden of carrion and what was joined to it of impure things, they asked about what is lawful for them. Since the agent of "yas'alunaka" is a pronoun of the third person, He said "lahum" with the third-person pronoun. It is permissible in speech to say "mada uhilla lana" (what has been made lawful for us), just as you say: Zayd swore: "He will surely strike" and "I will surely strike." The first-person pronoun requires quoting what they said, as the phrase "la-adribanna" requires quoting the sentence sworn to.

Al-Zamakhshari said: in the question is the meaning of saying, so for this reason "ma uhilla lahum" came after it, as if it were said: "They say: what has been made lawful for them?" End of quote. He did not need what he mentioned, because it is of the category of suspension (ta'liq), like His saying: ﴿Ask them which of them will guarantee that﴾ [al-Qalam: 40]. So the interrogative clause is in the position of the second object of "yas'alunaka." They stated that the verb of asking is suspended, even if it is not one of the verbs of the heart, because it is a cause of knowledge; just as knowledge is suspended, so is its cause. Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: if it were a quotation of their speech, they would have said: "mada uhilla lahum," and it is known that this is false, because they do not say that; they say: "mada uhilla lana." Rather, the correct view is that this is not a quotation of their speech in their wording, but an explanation of the manner of the event. End of quote.

﴿Say: lawful for you are the good things﴾: since the Arabs used to forbid things among the good things, such as the bahirah, the sa'ibah, the wasilah and the ham, without permission from Allah the Exalted, He established here that what is lawful is the good things. This supports the view of al-Shafi'i that the meaning is "the pleasant things," and it weakens the view that the meaning is "the things made lawful" (al-muhallalat). His saying supports this: ﴿and He makes lawful for them the good things and forbids for them the impure things﴾ [al-A'raf: 157], such as beetles, geckos and other such things. In the language of the Arabs, "tayyib" is used for the lawful and for the pleasant, and the discussion of this has preceded in al-Baqarah. What is considered in finding something pleasant and agreeable is the people of manliness and good character, for some people find the eating of all animals agreeable. This clause came as a verbal sentence, so it is an answer to what they asked about in meaning, not in wording, because the preceding clause, which is ﴿mada uhilla lahum﴾, is a nominal sentence, and this is a verbal sentence.

﴿And what you have taught of the trained predatory animals, training them﴾: the apparent meaning of "'allamtum" differs from the apparent meaning of the new sentence "mukallibin." Al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' gave priority to the apparent wording of "mukallibin," and so they said: the jawarih are dogs specifically. Ibn 'Umar used to say: hunting is only done with dogs. He and Abu Ja'far said: what is caught by other than them, such as the falcon, the hawk and the like, is not lawful unless one reaches its slaughter and slaughters it. A group permitted the hawks, so they permitted their catch on the basis of the hadith of 'Adi ibn Hatim. The majority gave priority to the apparent meaning of ﴿what you have taught﴾, and they said: the meaning of "mukallibin" is "disciplining," "training," and "accustoming," and they generalized "jawarih" to the beasts of prey and birds, anything that accepts training. The furthest limit of training is that it is sent and it goes, it is called and it responds, it is restrained after catching and it desists, and it refrains from eating of the game. The benefit of this state, although it emphasizes "'allamtum," is that it would be dispensed with if the trainer were not one who is commanded to train, skilled in it and described by it. This state is derived from the dog, although it came as the furthest extent regarding the jawarih by way of predominance, because discipline is most often found in dogs, so it is derived from its name because of the abundance of that in its kind.

Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: it was said "mukallibin" because most of their hunting is with dogs. End of quote. It is derived from "kalab," which is ferocity. It is said: "he is kalib with such-and-such" when he is fierce with it. Al-Zamakhshari said: or because the predator is called a dog (kalb), and from this is his (peace be upon him) saying: "O Allah, set upon him a dog from Your dogs," and a lion ate him. This derivation is not valid, because the lion being a dog is a description inherent in it, whereas "taklib" is from the description of the trainer, and the jawarih are predators by themselves, not by the making of the trainer. The apparent meaning of his saying "what you have taught" is that it is addressed to the believers. If the trainer were a Jew or a Christian, al-Hasan disliked hunting with him; if he were a Magian, Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, al-Hasan, 'Ata', Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, al-Thawri and Ishaq disliked hunting with him. Malik, Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i permitted eating the game of their dogs if the hunter was a Muslim. They said: this is like his slaughter-knife. The majority hold that what a People of the Book catches is permissible. Malik said: there is no distinction between his game and his slaughtered animal. As for what a Magian catches, the majority hold that eating it is prohibited: 'Ata', Ibn Jubayr, al-Nakha'i, Malik, Abu Hanifah, al-Layth and al-Shafi'i. Abu Thawr said: there is a view that they are People of the Book, and that their game is permissible.

﴿And what you have taught﴾: the place of "ma" is nominative, on the basis that it is conjoined to "al-tayyibat," and this would be by omitting a modifier, that is: "and the hunt of what you have taught." Some estimated it as: "and the taking of what you have taught." Or it is nominative as a beginning, and "ma" is conditional, and the answer is "fa-kulu." This is better, because there is no implied element in it. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Hanafiyyah read "wa-ma 'ullimtum" in the passive voice, that is: concerning the command of the trained animals and the hunting with them. And he read "mukliban" from "akleb," and "fa''ala" and "af'ala" may share a meaning. The apparent meaning is that the black, fully black dog is included in the generality of the jawarih, and that it is permissible to eat its game; the majority hold this. The school of Ahmad and a group of the Zahiris hold that it is not permissible to eat its game, because it is commanded to be killed, and what the Law has required to be killed, its game is not lawful. Ahmad said: I know of no one who permitted it if it is black. Ibn Rahawayh also held this. Al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Nakha'i disliked hunting with it. The furthest limit of training in the dog has already been mentioned: that when commanded, it obeys, and when restrained, it desists. A group added another condition, which is that it does not eat of what it catches. As for the predatory birds, eating is not a condition for them according to the majority. Rabi'ah said: whatever responds to it is the trained one. Ibn Habib said: there is only one condition for them, which is that when commanded it obeys, because their desisting when restrained is not possible for them. The apparent meaning of His saying "what you have taught" is that training is achieved without a count being considered. Abu Hanifah did not set a number for this. Our companions said: if the dog catches and holds back three times, then training has been achieved for it. Others said: if it does that once, it has become trained.

You teach them from what Allah has taught you. That is, your teaching them does not come from yourselves. Rather, it is from the knowledge that Allah has taught you, namely that He gave you reflection and thought, by which you accepted knowledge. Likewise, the hunting animals acquire a certain perception and awareness, by which they accept being commanded and restrained. In His words, *"from what Allah has taught you,"* there is an indication and proof of the excellence and nobility of knowledge, since He mentioned it in the context of bestowing favour. The second object of *"taught"* (ʿallama) and of *"you teach them"* (tuʿallimūnahunna) is omitted. Its implied meaning is: what you have taught them of pursuing game for you, not for their own sake, is what you teach them. This indicates that the game of an animal that has not been trained is unlawful to eat, because Allah, exalted is He, permitted it only on condition of training. The evidence for this is the address in *"for you"* (ʿalaykum) in His words: *"So eat of what they catch for you,"* and an untrained animal catches only for itself. The meaning of *"from what Allah has taught you"* is: from the discipline with which Allah, exalted is He, has disciplined you, which is following His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. So when he is commanded and obeys, and when he is restrained and desists, he has learned from what Allah, exalted is He, has taught us. Al-Zamakhshari said: *"from what Allah has taught you"* refers to the words of obligation, because it is inspiration from Allah, exalted is He, and also acquired by reason. End of quote. The clause *"you teach them"* is a second circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). It may also be a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf), provided that *"mā"* in His words *"and what you have taught of the hunting animals"* is not conditional, unless it is a parenthetical insertion between the condition and its response. Al-Zamakhshari delivered a sermon here and said: There is a great benefit in it, which is that every person who takes knowledge should not take it except from its people who are most knowledgeable and most insightful in understanding it, most profound in grasping its subtleties and realities. Many a person who takes from one who is not proficient has wasted his days, and at the meeting of the masters he bites his fingertips.

*"So eat of what they catch for you."* This is a command of permission. *"Of"* (min) here is partitive; the meaning is: eat of the game that they caught for you. As for one who holds that *"min"* is superfluous, his view is weak. Its apparent meaning is that if the animal holds the game for its sender, eating it is permitted, whether or not the hunting animal ate from it. This was the view of Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, Salman al-Farisi, Abu Hurayra and Ibn Umar. It is also the view of Malik and all his companions. If a small piece remains after it has eaten, eating that remainder is permitted. Among their arguments is that killing by the animal is its slaughter (dhakāh), so what it has slaughtered is not forbidden. Abu Hurayra also said, along with Ibn Jubayr, Ata', Qatada, Ikrima, al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Thawr: what remains of what the dog has eaten, or of what any other animal has eaten, may not be eaten, because it held the game only for itself and not for its sender. Also, in the hadith of Adi: *"And if it eats, do not eat, for it has held it only for itself."* And from Ali: if the falcon eats, do not eat. Some people made a distinction between what a dog has eaten from, which they forbade, and what a falcon has eaten from, which they permitted. Among them were Ibn Abbas, al-Shaʿbi, al-Nakhaʿi, Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, Abu Jaʿfar Muhammad ibn Ali al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa and his companions, because a dog, when struck, stops, whereas a falcon is not struck. The apparent view is that if the hunting animal has drunk blood, the game is still eaten, though Sufyan al-Thawri disliked this. The apparent view is also that if it escaped from its owner and then hunted without being sent, it is not permitted to eat what it has caught. Ali and al-Awzaʿi said: if its owner had released it for the hunt, eating what it caught is permitted. Among those who forbade eating what was caught when it hunted without its owner's sending were Rabiʿa, Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafiʿi and Abu Thawr. The apparent view is that it is permitted to eat what the dog has killed with its mouth without any wound, by the generality of *"of what they hold for you."* Some said it is not permitted, because it is carrion.

*"And mention the name of Allah over it."* The apparent view is that the pronoun in *"over it"* refers to the verbal noun implied by *"eat,"* i.e., over the eating. In the hadith in Sahih Muslim: *"Mention the name of Allah and eat from what is nearest to you."* It was also said that it refers to *"what they hold"*, meaning: mention Allah's name over it when you reach its slaughter. This view is far-fetched. It was also said that it refers to *"what you have taught of the hunting animals"*, meaning: mention Allah's name over it at the time of releasing it, based on His words: *"When you release your dog and mention the name of Allah, then eat."* They differed over whether mentioning the name at release is obligatory or recommended. The preferred form is to say: "In the name of Allah, Allah is greatest." As for the view of one who claims that the sentence has inversion and that the original order is: *"Mention the name of Allah over it, and eat of what they hold for you"*, it is a view to be disregarded because of its weakness.

*"And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning."* Since the mention of what is forbidden and what is permitted of foods has preceded, He commanded taqwa, for by taqwa a person restrains himself from the unlawful. He gave as the reason for the command to taqwa that He, exalted is He, is swift in reckoning for whoever opposes what He has commanded regarding taqwa. This is a warning of the Day of Resurrection, and His reckoning of you will come swiftly, since the Day of Resurrection is near. Or "reckoning" may mean recompense, so He threatens whoever does not fear Allah with swift and near recompense. Or, because He, exalted is He, encompasses all things, He does not need to count in reckoning with the process of counting, but rather He reckons all creatures at once.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 5 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you.﴾ The purpose of repeating the permission of good things is to draw attention to the completion of the blessing in matters concerning this world, among which is the permission of good things, as He indicated with His words: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My blessing upon you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], which points to the completion of the blessing in everything that concerns the religion. Whoever claims that "today" is a single day says that it is repeated three times for emphasis, but the apparent meaning is that these are different times. It has also been said regarding the three that they are times, meaning simply a time and not a specific time. The apparent meaning is that the good things here are the good things mentioned before.

﴿And the food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you.﴾ Their food here refers to slaughtered animals (dhaba'ih), as most of the people of tafsir (exegesis) have said. They said: because what is of the kind of wheat, bread and fruit, and what does not require dhakah (ritual slaughter), is not disputed as to its lawfulness regardless of the state of any person, since it is not made unlawful in any way, whether the one who handles it is a People of the Book, a Magian, or otherwise. And the specification of it to the People of the Book would have no benefit left. And because what comes before this is about hunting and slaughtered animals, so it is better to take this verse as referring to slaughtered animals. Some people held that the meaning of "food" in His words is all of their foods. It is attributed to some people, among them some of the imams of the Zaydiyyah (Zaydis), that the food here is taken to mean what does not require dhakah, such as bread and fruit, and the Imamiyyah (Imamis) also said this. Al-Sharif al-Murtada said: marriage to a Kitabiyyah (woman of the People of the Book) is forbidden, and so are their slaughtered animals, and their food, and the food of one whose disbelief is certain. If we take "food" to mean slaughtered animals, as the majority said, then they differed regarding what is forbidden for them: is it lawful for us or unlawful? The majority held that the dhakah of a dhimmi (a non-Muslim living under Muslim protection) affects the whole animal, both what is forbidden for them of it and what is lawful, so it is permissible for us to eat it. Others held that dhakah does not take effect on what is forbidden for them, so it is not lawful for us to eat it, like pure fats. This is the apparent meaning, because of His words: ﴿And the food of those who were given the Book﴾, and what is forbidden for them is not part of their food. This disagreement exists within the school of Malik.

The apparent meaning is that their food is lawful, whether they mention the name of Allah over it or the name of someone else. This was said by 'Ata', al-Qasim ibn Bahsarah, al-Sha'bi, Rabi'ah, Makhul and al-Layth. Others held that if the Kitabi does not mention the name of Allah over the slaughtered animal and mentions something other than Allah, it is not to be eaten. This was said by Abu al-Darda', 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, and a group of the Companions. This was also said by Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Zufar and Malik. Al-Nakha'i and al-Thawri disliked eating what was slaughtered and dedicated to other than Allah. The apparent meaning of His words "those who were given the Book" is that it is specific to the Children of Israel and the Christians to whom the Torah and the Gospel were revealed, not to those among the Arabs or non-Arabs who entered their religion. So their slaughtered animals are not lawful for us, like the Christians of the tribe of Taghlib and others. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, forbade their slaughtered animals and said: "They adhered to nothing of Christianity except drinking wine." The majority, including Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Sha'bi, 'Ata', Ibn Shihab, al-Hakam, Qatadah, Hammad, Malik, Abu Hanifah and his companions, held that there is no difference between the Children of Israel, the Christians, and those among the Arabs or non-Arabs who became Jews or Christians, regarding the lawfulness of eating their slaughtered animals. The apparent meaning is that the slaughtered animal of a Magian is not lawful for us, because they are not among those who were given the Book. As for what was narrated from Malik, that he said: "They are People of the Book, and a messenger called Zoroaster was sent to them," it is not authentic. Some people permitted eating their slaughtered animals, citing the hadith: "Treat them as you would the People of the Book." Ibn al-Musayyab said: if a Muslim is sick and he orders a Magian to mention the name of Allah and slaughter, there is no harm. Abu Thawr said: and if he orders this when healthy, there is no harm. The apparent meaning is that the slaughtered animal of the Sabians is not permissible for us to eat, because they are not among those who were given the Book. Abu Hanifah differed and said: their ruling is the ruling of the People of the Book. His two companions said: they are of two kinds: one kind reads the Psalms and worships the angels, and another kind does not read any book and worships the stars; these are not among the People of the Book.

﴿And your food is lawful for them.﴾ That is, your slaughtered animals. This is a concession for the Muslims, not for the People of the Book. Since the matter requires that a thing for which dhakah was legislated for us, we should protect it from them, a concession was granted to us in this regard, lifting the hardship by way of permissiveness, so there is no harm for us in feeding them. Had the food of the believers been forbidden to them, it would not have been proper for the believers to feed them. The meaning becomes: He has made lawful for you the eating of their food, and made lawful for you to feed them from your food. Al-hill means the lawful, and in the rhyming form it is said "hadha hillun billun" (this is lawful and fine).

﴿And the chaste women from among the believing women﴾ This is conjoined to His words: ﴿And the food of those who were given the Book﴾. The meaning is: and the marriage to the chaste women from among the believing women is made lawful for you, ﴿and the chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you﴾. Ihsan (chastity, or being a protected/married woman) occurs through Islam and through marriage, and these two are not applicable here; and through freedom and through chastity. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Mujahid, Malik and a group said: ihsan here means freedom, so marriage to a slave Kitabiyyah is not permissible. A group, including Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, Abu Maysarah and Sufyan, said: ihsan here means chastity, so marriage to a slave Kitabiyyah is permissible. Some scholars forbade marriage to a woman who is not chaste under this second meaning. Al-Hasan said: if a man discovers a grave sin (fahishah) from his wife, then let him separate from her. From Mujahid: the prostitutes among the believing women and among the People of the Book are forbidden. Al-Sha'bi said: the ihsan of a Jewish or Christian woman is that she does not commit adultery and that she performs ghusl from janabah (major ritual impurity). 'Ata' said: marriage to a Kitabiyyah was permitted because the Muslim women were few at that time, but now there is abundance of them, so the need for them has ceased, and the concession regarding marrying them has ceased. There is no disagreement among the salaf (early generations) and the jurists of the cities regarding the permissibility of marrying free Kitabiyyat women, and the Companions agreed on this, except for something narrated from Ibn 'Umar: a man asked him about this, and he said: "Recite the verse of permission" — referring to this verse — "and the verse of prohibition," referring to ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221]. This has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah in His words: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221].

'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, married Na'ilah bint al-Farafisah al-Kalbiyyah while he had wives, and Talhah ibn 'Abd Allah married a Jewish woman from Syria, and Hudhayfah married a Jewish woman.

(If you say): there must be an implied word; that is: and the chaste women who were People of the Book and then embraced Islam; and He described them as "from those who were given the Book" in consideration of what they were upon, as He said: ﴿And among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 199], and He said: ﴿Among the People of the Book is an upright community﴾ [Al 'Imran: 113], then He said after that: ﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [Al 'Imran: 114]. (I say): the unrestricted use of the expression "People of the Book" refers to the Jews and the Christians, not the Muslims, nor the rest of the disbelievers, and it is not applied to a Muslim as being of the People of the Book, just as it is not applied to him as a Jew or a Christian. As for the two verses, the term was used in a restricted way with the mention of belief in them, and it is not found unrestricted in the Qur'an without a restriction except that its intended referents are the Jews and the Christians. Also, He said: ﴿And the chaste women from among the believing women﴾, which includes all believing women, among whom were polytheists or Kitabiyyat, so His words ﴿and the chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you﴾ must be taken to mean the Kitabiyyat who did not embrace Islam, otherwise its benefit would vanish, since they would already be included in His words ﴿and the chaste women from among the believing women﴾. Also, it is known from His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you﴾ that He did not mean by it the food of believers who were from the People of the Book, but rather the Jews and the Christians; so likewise this verse.

(If it is said): the prohibition of Kitabiyyat is connected to His words, exalted is He: ﴿And do not hold on to the ties of disbelieving women﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10]. (It is answered): this applies to the harbiyyah (women of a hostile state) when her husband has become a Muslim, or when a harbi's wife emigrates as a Muslim. Do you not see His words: ﴿And ask for what you spent, and let them ask for what they spent﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10]? Even if we accept it as general, it would be specified by His words: ﴿and the chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you﴾. The apparent meaning is the permissibility of marrying a harbiyyah Kitabiyyah, because she is included in the generality of: ﴿and the chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you﴾. Ibn 'Abbas restricted this generality to the dhimmiyyat (women under protection), so he permitted marrying a dhimmiyyah but not a harbiyyah, and he recited His words, exalted is He: ﴿Fight those who do not believe﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29] up to His words ﴿and they are humbled﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29]. Others among the Companions did not distinguish between harbiyyat and dhimmiyyat. As for the Christians of the tribe of Taghlib, 'Ali, Ibrahim, and Jabir ibn Zayd forbade marrying their women, while Ibn 'Abbas permitted it.

﴿When you have given them their wages﴾ That is, their mahr (bridal gifts). The scholars derived from this that a husband should not enter upon his wife except after he has offered her of the mahr that makes her lawful to him. Whoever permitted entering without offering that held that it is a binding obligation in the ruling of the one who is had. In the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿when you have given them their wages﴾, there is an indication that the slave-girls of the Kitabiyyat are not included in His words ﴿and the chaste women﴾, which strengthens that it means free women, since slave-girls are not given their wages; rather, the master is given them. Unless one permits that we consider giving to the master as giving to them. There is also an indication in it that the minimum of the bridal gift is not fixed, since He called it a wage (ajr), and wages in hiring contracts are not fixed.

﴿Chaste, not fornicators, nor those who take secret lovers﴾ The explanation of its parallel has already been given in al-Nisa'.

﴿And whoever disbelieves in faith, his deeds have become worthless, and he will be among the losers in the Hereafter.﴾ The occasion of its revelation, as narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, is that when He permitted marriage to Kitabiyyat, the women among them said: "Had Allah not been pleased with our religion and accepted our deeds, He would not have permitted the believers to marry us," and so this was revealed. Muqatil said: concerning the Muslims' chastity (ihsan) in marrying women of the People of the Book, He says: the Muslims' chastity toward them is not that which brings them out of disbelief. End.

Since He had mentioned obligations and rulings that must be upheld, He sent down what implies a threat against violating them, so that the warning against neglecting them would be emphasized. Al-Qaffal said, in substance: "Since they gained in this world the merit of marrying their women and eating their slaughtered animals, there resulted for them, in the Hereafter, a distinction whereby whoever disbelieves, his deeds are nullified." End of quote. Disbelief in faith is not conceivable. Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said: that is, "And whoever disbelieves in Allah." This metaphor is made good by the fact that He, exalted is He, is the Lord of faith and its Creator. Al-Kalbi said: "And whoever disbelieves in the testimony that there is no god but Allah," making the word of monotheism (kalimat al-tawhid) into faith. Qatada said: some Muslims said, "How can we marry their women when they are not upon our religion?" So Allah, exalted is He, sent down: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in the faith﴾; that is, in what was sent down in the Qur'an. The Qur'an was called "faith" because it is the one that contains the explanation of everything that is necessary in faith. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is whoever makes lawful what Allah has forbidden, or forbids what Allah has made lawful, then he is a disbeliever. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: whoever denies what Allah has sent down of the laws of Islam and what He has made known of the lawful and the unlawful. Al-Zamakhshari followed him in this explanation, saying: "And whoever disbelieves in the faith"; that is, in the laws of Islam, and what Allah has made lawful and unlawful. Ibn al-Jawzi said: I heard al-Hasan ibn Abi Bakr al-Naysaburi say: "Allah only permitted the women of the People of the Book because some Muslims may be attracted by their beauty, so He warned those who marry them against inclining toward their religion by His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in the faith, his deed has become void﴾." Ibn al-Sumaygʿ recited: ḥabaṭa (with a fatḥa on the bā'), ﴿and he in the Hereafter will be among the losers﴾. The nullification of his deed and his loss in the Hereafter is conditional upon dying in a state of disbelief.

﴿O you who believe, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows﴾. It was revealed concerning the incident of ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, when she lost the necklace, which led to the lack of water and to the legislation of tayammum (dry ablution). Wudu' (ablution) was impossible for them at that time. It was mentioned only as a digression leading to tayammum. This happened during the expedition of al-Muraysiʿ, which is the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq. In it there occurred the blowing of the wind, the saying of ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, ﴿If we return to Madinah﴾ (63:8), and the incident of the slander (ḥadith al-ifk). ʿAlqamah ibn al-Fagh, who was one of the Companions, said: it was revealed as a concession for the Messenger, because he did not do any action except in a state of wudu', nor would he speak to anyone or return a greeting, except after that. So Allah informed him that wudu' is required only at the time of standing up for prayer, and not for the rest of the actions. (p-434)

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is as follows. When the surah opened with the command to fulfil the covenants, and mentioned permissions and prohibitions regarding food and marriage and examined these in detail, and since food is more emphatic than marriage and was placed before it, and since these two kinds are among the bodily pleasures of this world and its important matters for a human being, and they are worldly dealings between people, it moved from them to the otherworldly dealings that are between the servant and his Lord, glorified and exalted is He. Since prayer is the best of acts of worship after faith, and prayer cannot be performed except with purity, it began with purity and the conditions of wudu', and mentioned the substitute for it when water is unavailable. Since attempting prayer is for the most part done standing, the expression came: ﴿when you rise﴾, meaning when you intend to rise to perform the prayer. The intention to rise was expressed by the act of rising, since rising results from the intention, just as they expressed the ability to act by the act itself in their saying: "The blind man does not see", meaning he is not able to see. And His saying: ﴿We shall repeat it as a promise upon Us; indeed We are ever doers﴾ (21:104), meaning: able to repeat it. And His saying: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge﴾ (16:98), meaning: when you intend to recite the Qur'an. Since the action results from ability and intention, the effect was put in the place of the cause.

It has been said that the meaning of ﴿you rise to prayer﴾ is: you intend it, because whoever turns toward something and rises to it is intending it, so the intention toward it was expressed by rising to it. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that wudu' is obligatory on everyone who rises to prayer, whether he is already in a state of purity or in a state of minor impurity. This view was held by a group including Dawud. It is also reported that this was the practice of ʿAli and ʿIkrimah. Ibn Sirin said: the caliphs used to perform wudu' for every prayer. But the majority (al-jumhur) held that there must be an omitted element in the verse, and its estimate is: ﴿when you rise to prayer in a state of minor impurity﴾, because wudu' is obligatory only on one who is in a state of impurity. This omitted element is indicated by its contrast with His saying: ﴿and if you are in a state of major impurity, then purify yourselves﴾ (5:6). It is as if it were said: if you are in a state of minor impurity (al-ḥadath al-aṣghar), then wash these limbs and wipe these two limbs; and if you are in a state of major impurity (al-ḥadath al-akbar), then wash the whole body. A group, among them al-Suddi and Zayd ibn Aslam, said: ﴿when you rise﴾ means: when you get up from your beds, meaning sleep. They said: there is inversion in the statement; meaning: when you rise to prayer from sleep, ﴿or one of you comes from the place of relief, or you have touched women﴾, meaning the minor touching (al-mulamasah al-ṣughrā), ﴿then wash your faces﴾. This interpretation is held to be one from which the Book of Allah should be exempted, and they mentioned it only seeking to include all causes of impurity in the mention. (p-434)

A group said: the address is specific even though its wording is general, and it is a concession for the Messenger, ﷺ. He was commanded to perform wudu' at every prayer, and it was hard on him, so he was commanded to use the siwak, and wudu' was lifted from him except for a state of impurity. A group said: the command to perform wudu' for every prayer is by way of recommendation (nadb), and many of the Companions used to do it seeking extra reward, among them Ibn ʿUmar. A group said: wudu' at every prayer was obligatory and then was abrogated (nasakh). It has been said: it was obligatory upon the Messenger alone, and then it was abrogated for him in the year of the Conquest. It has been said: it was obligatory upon the community, then it was abrogated for them and for him. It is not permissible that ﴿wash﴾ should be a command to those in a state of impurity as obligatory and to those in a state of purity as recommended, because the carrying of speech over two different meanings is a kind of riddling and obscurity; this was said by al-Zamakhshari.

﴿Wash your faces﴾. The face (al-wajh) is that which faces the one who looks, and its length is bounded by the place of hair growth above the forehead together with the bottom of the chin. The apparent meaning is that the beard is not included in washing the face, because it is not part of it. Likewise the two ears, in breadth, from ear to ear. Whoever holds that washing means making water reach the washed part together with passing something over it makes rubbing (dalk) obligatory, and this is the view of Malik; but the majority do not make it obligatory. The apparent meaning is that rinsing the mouth (al-madmadah) and sniffing water into the nose (al-istinshaq) are not commanded in the verse in the washing of the face, and they hold this to be sunnah.
