Mujahid said: sniffing water into the nose is half of wudu'. ʿAṭaʾ, al-Zuhri, Qatadah, Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, Ibn Abi Layla and Ishaq said: whoever leaves out rinsing the mouth and sniffing water into the nose in wudu' must repeat the prayer. Ahmad said: he must repeat if he leaves out sniffing, but he does not repeat if he leaves out rinsing the mouth. There is consensus (ijmaʿ, scholarly agreement) that it is not required to wash the inside of the eyes, except what is reported from Ibn ʿUmar, that he used to splash water into his eyes.

﴿And your hands up to the elbows﴾. The hand (al-yad) in the language extends from the tips of the fingers to the shoulder, and the washing has been limited (ghayyā) by reaching it. They differed about whether the elbows are included in the washing. The majority held that they must be included; Zufar and Dawud held that they are not obligatory. Al-Zamakhshari said: "ilā" (up to) conveys the meaning of the limit in general, and whether what follows is included in the ruling or excluded is a matter that depends on evidence. Then he mentioned an example of something that was included and excluded, and then said: and His saying ﴿up to the elbows﴾ and ﴿up to the two ankles﴾ contains no evidence for either of the two matters. End of his words. Our companions (the Shafiʿi scholars) mentioned that if what follows "ilā" is not accompanied by an indication of inclusion or exclusion, there is disagreement about it. Some held that it is included, and some held that it is not included, and this is the correct view, and most of the researchers (muḥaqqiqūn) hold it. This is because when a contextual indication accompanies it, the usage in their speech is most often that what follows is not included; so when it is bare of any indication, it must be taken according to the most common usage. Also, if you say: "I bought the place up to the tree", what follows "ilā" is the inside of the place where the purchased land ends, so the tree cannot be part of the land purchased, because a thing does not end while any part of it remains, unless one uses a figurative sense, by treating what is near the end as the end. When inclusion cannot be conceived except through a figurative usage, it must be understood as not included, because figurative meaning is not taken when the literal meaning is possible, unless there is a indication that prefers the figurative over the literal. So al-Zamakhshari's statement: "when there is no indication of inclusion or exclusion, there is no evidence for either of the two matters," contradicts the transmission of our companions, for they mentioned that the grammarians hold two views: one is inclusion, and the other is exclusion, and this is what they corrected. According to what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, one must suspend judgment, and it becomes among the ambiguous (mujmal) until what it is to be understood by is clarified from outside the speech. According to what our companions mentioned, it is among the clear (mubayyan), so it does not depend on anything external for its clarification. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the statement of this meaning should be put as follows: if what follows "ilā" is not of the same kind as what precedes it, the limit is the first thing mentioned after it; if what follows it is part of what precedes it, caution requires that the limit be the last thing mentioned after it, and for this reason the inclusion of the two elbows in washing is preferred. Both narrations are preserved from Malik. Ashhab narrated from him that the two are not included, and others narrated that the two are included. End of his words. This division was mentioned by ʿAbd al-Daʾim al-Qayrawani, who said: if what follows it is not of the same kind as what precedes it, it is included in the ruling. (p-436)

The apparent meaning is that wudu' is a condition for the validity of the prayer from this verse, because He commanded wudu' for prayer, so whoever performs it without it has left the commanded act, and leaving a commanded act deserves punishment. Also, He explained that whenever water is lacking one moves to tayammum, which indicates that it is a condition when one is able to perform it. The apparent meaning is that the first of the obligatory parts of wudu' is washing the face, and Abu Hanifah held this view. The majority said that intention (niyyah) is the first of them. Ahmad and Ishaq said: saying the basmalah (tasmiyah) at the beginning of wudu' is obligatory, and if one deliberately leaves it out, his wudu' is invalid. Some said: it is obligatory to refrain from speaking during wudu'; the majority hold that this is recommended. The apparent meaning is that what is obligatory in this command is one single time. The apparent meaning is that the whole face must be covered in washing, starting from any part of it. The apparent meaning is that it is obligatory to wash the whiteness between the sideburn and the ear; this was said by Abu Hanifah, Muhammad, and al-Shafiʿi. Abu Yusuf and others said it is not obligatory. The apparent meaning is that what is under the light (khafifah) beard is not obligatory to wash; this was said by Abu Hanifah. al-Shafiʿi said it is obligatory. And the hair that hangs down under the chin is not obligatory to wash; this was said by Abu Hanifah. Malik and al-Muzani said it is obligatory, and there are two views reported from al-Shafiʿi. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿and your hands﴾ does not require an order in washing the two hands, nor in the two feet; rather, beginning with the right over the left in both is recommended by the sunnah. Ahmad said it is obligatory. The apparent meaning is that the limit expressed by "ilā" requires that the washing end at what follows it, and it is not permitted to begin from the elbow until the water flows down to the palm; this was said by some jurists. The majority said this does not invalidate the validity of wudu'. The sunnah is that water be poured from the palm so that it flows from it to the elbow.

﴿And wipe your heads and your feet up to the ankles﴾. This is a command to wipe the head. They differed about the meaning of the preposition bāʾ (in) here. It was said: it denotes attachment (ilṣāq). Al-Zamakhshari said: what is meant is attaching the wiping to the head, and whether one wipes part of it or the whole of it, both attach the wiping to his head. End of his words. This is not as he stated: it is not that whoever wipes part of it is described as attaching the wiping to his head; rather it is described as attaching the wiping to a part of it. As for describing him as attaching the wiping to his head in the literal sense, that is not so; it is applied to him only figuratively, by calling a part by the name of the whole. It was said: the bāʾ denotes partiality (tabʿīḍ). That the bāʾ denotes partiality is denied by most of the grammarians, to the point that one of them said: "Whoever has no expertise in Arabic said: the bāʾ in such a case denotes partiality," and this is not a thing known to the people of knowledge. It was said: the bāʾ is an extra, emphasizing particle, like it in His saying ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing﴾ (22:25), ﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree﴾ (19:25), and ﴿And do not throw yourselves by your own hands into destruction﴾ (2:195), meaning deviation, the trunk, and your hands. Al-Farrāʾ said: the Arabs say "hazzahu" and "hazza bihi" (he shook it and he shook with it), "khudh al-khiṭām" and "bil-khiṭām" (take the rope and with the rope), "ḥazza raʾsahu" and "bi-raʾsihi" (he cut his head and with his head), "maddahu" and "madda bihi" (he stretched it and stretched with it). Sibawayh reported: "khashantu ṣadrahu" and "bi-ṣadrihi" (I roughened his chest and with his chest), and "masaḥtu raʾsahu" and "bi-raʾsihi" (I wiped his head and with his head), with the same meaning; and this is an explicit text on the question.

And on the basis of these understandings the scholars differed regarding wiping the head. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar that he wiped only the yafukh (the crown of the head, the top point between the forehead and the crown). It is reported from Salamah ibn al-Akwa' that he wiped the front of his head. It is reported from Ibrahim and al-Sha'bi: "Whichever parts of your head you wipe, it suffices for you." It is reported from al-Hasan: "If the woman touches only a single hair, it suffices for her." As for the jurists of the major cities, the well-known position of the school of Malik is that wiping the whole head is obligatory. The well-known position of al-Shafi'i is that the obligation is the least amount to which the name of wiping applies, and the well-known position of Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i is that the better practice is to cover the whole head. Among the strange views reported from those who argued that wiping part of the head suffices is their argument that the words of God, Exalted be He, ﴿and wipe your heads﴾ are like your saying, "I wiped my hands with the handkerchief." Just as this does not indicate the wiping of the whole hand with a part of the handkerchief, so too the verse; thus the head and the foot are instruments for wiping that hand, and the obligation in that case is not the wiping of the head and feet but the wiping of that hand with the head and feet. In that case the hand would have two obligations: first, washing all of it up to the elbow, and second, wiping its moisture with the head and feet. For those who hold the view of partial wiping, it follows that the partiality mentioned in the story of tayammum (dry ablution) in His words ﴿then wipe with your faces and your hands from it﴾ would require that one suffice with wiping part of the face and part of the hand, and no one holds this. And for those who make the ba' (the preposition "with") an instrument, this also follows, and it follows that what is commanded in tayammum is wiping the dust with a part of the face and hand.

The apparent meaning is that the command to wash and to wipe is fulfilled by one time, and repeating the washing of the washed parts three times is a sunnah (recommended practice). Abu Hanifa and Malik said it is not a sunnah. Al-Shafi'i said that the wiping should be done three times. It is reported from Anas, Ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' the same as this. It is reported from Ibn Sirin that he wiped twice. The apparent meaning of the verse is that however one wipes, it suffices. They differed regarding the better way of beginning from the front toward the back of the head and then toward the middle, in three opinions. The one established in the sound sunnah is the first, which is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and a group of the Companions and the Successors. The second is the view of al-Hasan ibn Hayy. The third is reported from Ibn 'Umar. The apparent meaning is that returning the two hands over the hair of the head is not obligatory, so wiping is accomplished without returning. Some said that it is obligatory. The apparent meaning is that wiping over a turban does not suffice, because it is not wiping of the head. Al-Awza'i, al-Thawri and Ahmad said it suffices, and that wiping suffices even with a single finger. Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said it does not suffice with less than three fingers. The apparent meaning is that if one washes the head, it does not suffice, because washing is not what is commanded; this is the view of Abu al-'Abbas ibn al-Qadi of the Shafi'is, and it is what the Zahiri school implies. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "We know of no disagreement that washing suffices instead of wiping, except what al-Shashi related to us in the lesson from Ibn al-Qadi, that it does not suffice."

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamza and Abu Bakr recited (wa-arjulikum) with the kasra (genitive) ending. This is also the recitation of Anas, Ikrimah, al-Sha'bi, al-Baqir, Qatadah, Alqamah and al-Dahhak. The apparent meaning of this reading is that the feet are included in the wiping along with the head. It is reported that wiping both feet is obligatory from Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, Ikrimah, al-Sha'bi, Abu Ja'far al-Baqir, and it is the view of the Imamiyyah (the Twelver Shi'a). The majority of jurists said: their obligation is washing. Dawud said: it is obligatory to combine wiping and washing, and this is the view of al-Nasir li-l-Haqq among the imams of the Zaydiyyah. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: one may choose between wiping and washing. Those who make washing obligatory interpret the jarr (the genitive) as a permissible lowering of the case, and this is a very weak interpretation, for it occurs only in the case of an adjective, where no confusion arises, regarding a disagreement established in the science of Arabic grammar. Or they interpret that the feet are in the genitive because of a deleted verb that takes the preposition ba'; that is: "And do with your feet the washing," the verb and the preposition being deleted, and this is an interpretation of extreme weakness. Or they interpret that the feet, among the three washed limbs, are a likely place of blameworthy excess, which is forbidden, so the feet are linked to the fourth, the wiped limb, not for wiping but to alert to the necessity of moderation in pouring water over them. It was said: "up to the two ankles," so the limit was mentioned to remove the suspicion of one who supposes that they are wiped, since wiping is not given a limit. This is the end of this interpretation, and as you see, it is in extreme patchwork and a confusion of rulings. It is reported from Abu Zayd that the Arabs call a light washing "wiping," and they say: "I wiped myself (tamassahtu) for the prayer," meaning: "I washed my limbs."

Nafi', al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Amir and Hafs recited (wa-arjulakum) with the accusative ending. They differed regarding the explanation of this reading. It was said: it is conjoined to His words ﴿your faces and your hands up to the elbows﴾ and ﴿your feet up to the ankles﴾, and in this there is a separation between two conjoined elements by a clause that is not a parenthetical insertion but establishes a ruling. Abu al-Baqa' said: "This is permissible without any disagreement." Abu al-Hasan ibn 'Usfur, mentioning the separation between the conjoined and the conjoined-to, said: "The worst form of this is with clauses," and this statement indicates that he regards the Book of God as too exalted for this explanation. This is the explanation of one who holds that the obligation for the two feet is washing. As for one who holds wiping, he makes it conjoined to the position of (bi-ru'usikum), and makes the accusative reading like the genitive reading, indicating wiping. Al-Hasan recited (wa-arjulukum) with the nominative ending, and it is a subject with a deleted predicate; that is: "wash them up to the ankles" according to the interpretation of one who washes, or "wiped up to the ankles" according to the interpretation of one who wipes. The meaning of the ankle has been mentioned before. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The view of the majority is that they are the limit of ablution by consensus, as far as I know, and I know of no one who made the limit of ablution the bone that is on the top of the foot." Others said: "The Imamiyyah and everyone who holds the obligation of wiping the ankle say it is the one on the top of the foot, so the wiping is limited by it." Ibn 'Atiyyah also said: "Ashhab related from Malik: the two ankles are the two bones that adjoin the shin and are adjacent to the heel; the ankle is not the prominence on the top of the foot. This is evident from the verse in its words about the hands ﴿up to the elbows﴾, since in each hand there is an elbow. Had it been so with the feet, it would have said 'up to the ankle-bones,' but since each foot has two ankles, they were singled out for mention." The end. There is no proof in the verse that the continuity of the acts of ablution is not a condition for its validity, since the verse admits the division in your saying: "consecutive" and "non-consecutive." This is the well-known view of Abu Hanifa and Malik; it is related from Malik and from al-Shafi'i in his old opinion that it is a condition. Nor does the verse indicate that the order of the acts is not a condition, since they are joined by the conjunction "and" (wa), and this is the view of Malik and Abu Hanifa; the view of al-Shafi'i is that it is a condition. The full evidence for these questions is mentioned in jurisprudence. The verse does not explicitly mention the ears. The view of Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, and Malik in what Ashhab and Ibn al-Qasim related from him, is that they belong to the head and are wiped. Al-Zuhri said: they belong to the face and are washed with it. Al-Shafi'i said: as for the face, they are a limb standing by itself, neither part of the face nor part of the head, and they are wiped with fresh water. It was said: what faces forward from them belongs to the face, and what faces backward belongs to the head. Upon these opinions is built whether wiping or washing is obligatory and whether that is recommended.

﴿And if you are junub (in a state of major ritual impurity), then purify yourselves﴾. When He mentioned the minor purification, He mentioned the major purification. The meaning of junub has been mentioned in ﴿nor junub, except passing through (the mosque)﴾ [an-Nisa: 43]. The apparent meaning is that the junub is commanded to perform ghusl (full bathing). 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud said: a junub never performs tayammum, but leaves the prayer until he finds water. The majority hold otherwise, that he performs tayammum, and they both returned to what the majority held. The apparent meaning is that washing, wiping and purification are only with water, because of His words ﴿and you find no water﴾, meaning for wudu' and ghusl, ﴿then perform tayammum with clean earth﴾, which indicates that there is no intermediary between water and earth, and this is the view of the majority. Al-Awza'i and al-Asamm held that wudu' and ghusl are permissible with all clean liquids. The apparent meaning is that the junub is obligated only to purify himself, without wudu'. There is no order required among the washed limbs, nor rubbing (dalk), nor rinsing of the mouth, nor sniffing water into the nose; rather, the obligation is to cover his whole body with water reaching it. Dawud and Abu Thawr said: it is obligatory to begin with wudu' before ghusl. Ishaq said: it is obligatory to begin with the upper part of the body. Malik said: rubbing is obligatory, and Muhammad ibn Marwan al-Zahiri related from him that immersion in water without rubbing suffices. Abu Hanifa, Zufar, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, al-Layth and Ahmad said: rinsing the mouth and sniffing water into the nose are obligatory in it, and Ahmad added wudu'. al-Nakha'i said: if his hair is tightly braided so that it prevents water from reaching the scalp, it is not obligatory to undo it.

The majority recited (fa-tatahharu) with the taa' and ha' both doubled and fathah, and its original form is tatahharu, in which the taa' is assimilated into the ta' (the emphatic ta'), and a hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamzah) is added. It was also read (fa-ath-hiru) with the taa' sukun and the ha' kasra, from (athhara) in the four-letter form; that is: "then purify your bodies," and the hamzah in it is for causation (transitivity).

﴿And if you are sick, or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving yourselves, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then perform tayammum with clean earth, and wipe your faces and your hands from it﴾. The explanation of this conditional sentence and its response was mentioned in an-Nisa', except that in this sentence there is the addition of (minhu, "from it"), which is intended in that one in an-Nisa'. In the word "minhu" there is an indication of conveying some of the earth to the face and hands, so it is not permissible to perform tayammum with what does not adhere to the hand, such as stone, wood, or bare sand that does not leave anything clinging to the hand so that it reaches the face. This is the view of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa and Malik said: if one strikes the earth and no dust clings to his hand, and he wipes with it, it suffices. The apparent meaning of the command to perform tayammum with earth and the command to wipe is that if someone else performs tayammum for him, or if he stands in the direction of a wind that blows dust onto his face and hands, and he passes his hand over it, or does not pass it, or if he strikes a garment and dust rises from it onto his face and hands, that this does not suffice for him. In each of these three cases there is disagreement.

﴿God does not desire to place upon you any hardship﴾, that is, any constriction; rather He has granted you concession to perform tayammum with clean earth when water is absent. The will (irada) is an attribute of His essence, and it came in the present tense in consideration of the events that arise from it, for they come connected with the removal of hardship, the existence of purification, and the completion of His favor. The discussion of a similar lam in (li-yaj'ala, "in order to make") was mentioned in His words ﴿God desires to make clear to you﴾ [an-Nisa: 26], so it is not repeated. And whoever claims that the object of "desires" is deleted and that the lam is attached to it, makes the addition of "min" (from) in the affirmed statement as for the negation at the beginning of the sentence, even though the negation does not fall on the act of hardship. Similar to this sentence is what came in the hadith: "The religion of God is ease," and "I was sent with the tolerant (samha) monotheistic faith (hanifiyya)." The word "religion" came in general terms, and what is intended is what was mentioned just before it, which is tayammum.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 6 (part 3 of 3):

﴿But He wishes to purify you﴾: i.e., with dust (tayammum) when purification with water is unavailable to you. In a hadith: "Dust is the purifier of the Muslim, even if he goes ten years without water." The majority (al-Jumhur) said: the purpose of this purification is the removal of the legal impurity (al-najasah al-hukmiyyah) resulting from the emergence of a minor ritual impurity (hadath). It was also said: the meaning is that He purifies you from the filth of sins through wudu' and tayammum, as came in Muslim: "When the Muslim servant, or the believer, performs wudu' and washes his face, every sin that he looked at with his eyes will leave his face along with the water," through to the end of the hadith. It was also said: the meaning is that He purifies you from rebelliousness against obedience. Ibn al-Musayyab recited (liyuṭhirakum) with a sukun on the ṭā' and a lightened hā'.

﴿and to complete His favour upon you﴾: i.e., and to complete His bounty upon you by His concessions (rukhas) along with His obligations ('azA'im). It was also said: the statement is connected to what the beginning of the surah indicates, namely the permissibility of good things in foods and marriages; then, after describing the manner of wudu', He said: "and complete His favour upon you"; i.e., the favour mentioned secondly, which is the favour of religion. It was also said: the clarification of the laws and their rulings, so this is an emphasis of His saying: ﴿And I have completed My favour upon you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. It was also said: by forgiving their sins. In a report: "The completion of the favour is by entering Paradise and being saved from the Fire."

﴿so that you may be thankful﴾: i.e., that you may give thanks to Him for facilitating His religion, purifying you, and completing His favour upon you.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 7:

(p-440) ﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you and His covenant with which He bound you when you said, "We hear and we obey."﴾ The address is to the believers. The favour here is Islam, and what they came to through the unity of the word (ijtima' al-kalimah) and might (al-'izzah). The covenant (al-mithaq) is what the Messenger took from them at the Pledge of al-'Aqabah, the Pledge of al-Ridwan, and every occasion of pledging. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, and a group of scholars. Mujahid said: it is what was taken from the souls (al-nasam) when they were brought forth from the back of Adam. It was also said: it is the covenant taken from them when he pledged them to hear and obey in ease and hardship, in what they like and what they dislike. It was also said: the covenant is the proofs which He set before their eyes and placed in their minds, and the miracles which He manifested in their days, until they heard and obeyed. It was also said: the covenant is each believer's acknowledgment of what he has been commanded. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the covenant which Allah took from the Children of Israel when they said, "We believe in the Torah and in everything in it," and among its contents is the good news of the Messenger ﷺ, so they were bound to acknowledge him. This view cannot hold unless the address is to the Jews, and it is far-fetched. The two views after it make the covenant metaphorical in both, and the better interpretation is to take it as the covenant of the Pledge, since it is literal in that sense, and in His saying: ﴿when you said, "We hear and we obey."﴾

﴿And fear Allah; indeed Allah is Knowing of what is in the breasts.﴾ That is: fear Allah, and do not forget His favour, and do not break His covenant. The explanation of the similar sentence has already been given in al-Nisa', so there is no need to repeat it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 8–9:

﴿O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice, and do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just﴾ The explanation of this same sentence has already been given in Surah al-Nisa', except that there it began with "bil-qist" (justice), whereas here it is delayed. This is from the expansiveness of speech and the variety of eloquence. It follows that whoever stands for Allah must be a witness in justice, and whoever stands for justice must stand for Allah. However, the one in al-Nisa' came in the context of acknowledging oneself and one's parents and relatives, so it began with "al-qist," which is justice and equality without favoritism toward oneself, parent, or relative. Here it came in the context of abandoning enmities and rancor, so it began with standing for Allah the Exalted first, because it is more restraining for the believers. Then it was followed by testimony with justice. Thus, in the context of love and favoritism, it began with what is more emphatic, which is "al-qist," and in the context of enmity and hatred, it began with standing for Allah. Each context is thus matched by what is brought to it. Also, there the discussion preceded was of disobedience (nushuz) and turning away, and His saying: ﴿And you will never be able to be just﴾ [al-Nisa': 129] and His saying: ﴿there is no blame upon them if they make settlement﴾ [al-Nisa': 128]. So mention of putting justice first was appropriate. Here the mention of enmity came later, so it was appropriate that mention of justice be adjacent to it. The construction of "yajrimannakum" with "ʿalā" is only possible if it is taken to imply the meaning of a verb that takes that preposition, and this is contrary to the original usage.

﴿Be just; that is nearer to righteousness﴾ That is, justice. He first forbade them to let grudges move them to abandon justice, then commanded them a second time for emphasis. Then he resumed and mentioned to them the reason for the command to be just, which is His saying: ﴿it is nearer to righteousness﴾, meaning: more fitting to it, or nearer, being a means of drawing closer to it. In the verse there is an alert to observing the right of the believers in justice, since the Exalted had commanded justice even with the disbelievers.

﴿And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ Since the seat of hatred is the heart, which is what drives one to abandon justice, He commanded taqwa. He used the attribute "Khabir" (Acquainted), whose meaning is "ʿAlim" (All-Knowing), but it is specific to what is subtle in perception, so it suited this attribute to alert to the inner, heart-based quality.

﴿Allah has promised those who have believed and done righteous deeds: for them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾ When the Exalted mentioned commands and prohibitions, He mentioned the promise to those who follow His commands and avoid His prohibitions. "Wa'ada" takes two objects, and the second is omitted; its estimate is "al-Jannah" (Paradise), which He has stated explicitly in other places. The clause "lahum maghfirah" (for them is forgiveness) explains that omitted object as an explanation of cause for effect, since Paradise is consequent upon forgiveness and the attainment of the reward. When the clause is explanatory, it has no place in the grammatical structure, and the speech before it is complete. Al-Zamakhshari made His saying "for them is forgiveness and a great reward" an explanation of the promise; he said: it is as if He said: He presented to them a promise, so it was said: what is His promise? He said: for them is forgiveness and a great reward. Or it may be on the presumption of a saying: He promised them and said: for them is forgiveness. Or by treating "wa'ada" in the manner of "qāla" (said), since it is a kind of speech. Or it may make "wa'ada" govern the clause which is "maghfirah," as "tarakna" governed His saying: ﴿Peace upon Noah among the worlds﴾ [al-Saffat: 79]; it is as if it was said: He promised them this statement, and when He who does not break His promise promises them, He has promised them its content of forgiveness and great reward. This statement they receive at death and on the Day of Resurrection, so they are gladdened and comforted by it, and the agonies and terrors are made light for them before they reach the dust. End. These are possible estimations, and the first of them is the most likely.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 10:

﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs — they are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾

When He mentioned what is due to those who believe, He mentioned what is due to those who disbelieve. Regarding the believers, the sentence came as a verbal sentence (jumlah fi'liyyah) containing a promise in the past tense, which is an indication of its certainty (al-wuqu'). Thus their souls yearn for what they were promised, longing for it and rejoicing throughout their lives in this true promise. Regarding the disbelievers, the sentence came as a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah), indicating the establishment of this judgment for them, and that they are companions of the Fire; so they remain in punishment permanently, since it has been decreed for them that they are the companions of the Blazing Fire (al-Jahim). It did not come in the form of a threat (wa'id), so there would have been hope for them in that.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 11:**

﴿O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you when a people determined to extend their hands against you, but He withheld their hands from you. And fear Allah. And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾ Abu Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas that it was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh, whom had already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿And do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8]. Mujahid (al-Mujahid) said the same. Al-Hasan said: Quraysh sent a man to kill the Messenger (ﷺ), but Allah informed him of that. Mujahid and Qatadah said: He (peace be upon him) went to the Jews of Banu al-Nadir seeking their help regarding a blood money (diyya), and they determined to kill him. A group of the commentators (mufassirun) said: He came to Banu Qurayzah, and with him were Abu Bakr, Umar and Ali, may Allah be pleased with them, seeking a loan of the blood money for two Muslim men whom Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri had killed by mistake, having thought them to be polytheists. They said: "Yes, O Abu al-Qasim, sit down until we feed you and lend you." So they seated him in a raised bench (suffa) and determined to kill him. Amr ibn Jahhash went to a great millstone to drop it upon him, but Allah restrained his hand, and Jibril (peace be upon him) descended and informed him, so he left. It was also said: He stopped at a place during the expedition of Dhat al-Riqa', among Banu Muharib ibn Khafsah ibn Qays ibn Ghaylan, and the people scattered among the thorny trees seeking shade under them. The Messenger (ﷺ) hung his weapon upon a tree. A Bedouin came, drew the sword of the Messenger (ﷺ), and his name was Ghawrath; it was also said: Da'thur ibn al-Harith. Then he approached him and said: "Who will protect you from me?" He said: "Allah." He said it three times. Then he said: "Do you not fear me?" He said: "No." So he sheathed the sword and was held back. In al-Bukhari: that the Prophet (ﷺ) called the people, and they gathered while he was seated with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he did not punish him. It was said: he embraced Islam. And it was said: he struck his head against the trunk of the tree until he died. And it was reported that the polytheists saw the Muslims stand up for the noon prayer (salat al-zuhr), praying together at Usfan during the expedition of Dhi Amar. When they had prayed, they regretted not having attacked them, and said: "They have a prayer after it which is more beloved to them than their fathers and their sons," and that is the afternoon prayer (salat al-asr). They determined to strike them when they stood for it, so Jibril (peace be upon him) descended with the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf). (p-442) They lengthened the discussion with other causes. The summary of what they mentioned is that Quraysh, or Banu al-Nadir, or Qurayzah, or Ghawrath, determined to kill the Messenger; or the polytheists determined to kill the Muslims; or it was revealed concerning the meaning of ﴿Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], as al-Zajjaj said; or it was after the Trench (al-Khandaq), when Allah repelled the confederates and Allah sufficed the believers in the fighting. What the verse requires is that Allah, exalted is He, reminded the believers of His favors when a people of the disbelievers, whom Allah did not specify but left unnamed, intended to harm the Muslims with evil, so Allah prevented them. Then He commanded them with piety and reliance upon Him.

It is said: "He extended his tongue against him," meaning he insulted him, and "he extended his hand against him," meaning he stretched it out to seize him. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and they extend against you their hands and their tongues with evil﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 2]. It is said: "So-and-so is open of stride (basit al-ba')," and "extending the stride" have the same meaning. And "withholding the hands" means preventing them and restraining them.

The command to piety came in the direct address form (amr muwajahah), suitable to His saying "remember." The command to rely upon Him came in the third-person form (amr ghaib), for the sake of the verse-final rhyme (fasila), and to indicate dominance, and to convey the generality of the attribute of faith, meaning: because of their belief in Allah and His Messenger, every believer is commanded to rely upon Him. And the verse began with "believers" by way of particularization, and concluded with "believers" by way of encouragement.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 12 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And God had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised from among them twelve leaders. And God said: "Indeed I am with you. If you establish the prayer, give the zakat, believe in My messengers, support them, and lend God a goodly loan, I will surely remove your evil deeds from you and surely admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow. But whoever among you disbelieves after that has certainly strayed from the right way."﴾ ﴿So, because of their breaking their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts hard. They distort words from their places and have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of. And you will not cease to discover treachery from them, except for a few of them. So pardon them and overlook. Indeed God loves the good-doers.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 13] ﴿And from those who said, "We are Christians," We took their covenant, but they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of. So We caused enmity and hatred to arise among them until the Day of Resurrection. And God will inform them of what they used to do.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 14] ﴿O People of the Scripture, Our messenger has certainly come to you, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture and pardoning much. There has certainly come to you from God a light and a clear Book.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 15] ﴿By it God guides whoever follows His pleasure to the ways of peace and brings them out of darkness into light by His permission and guides them to a straight path.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 16] ﴿They have certainly disbelieved who say, "Indeed God is the Messiah, son of Mary." Say: "Then who can prevent God at all if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother and everyone on earth entirely?" And to God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. He creates what He wills, and God is over all things competent.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 17] ﴿And the Jews and the Christians said, "We are the sons of God and His beloved." Say: "Then why does He punish you for your sins? Rather, you are but human beings of those He created. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, and to God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and to Him is the final return."﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 18] ﴿O People of the Scripture, Our messenger has certainly come to you, making clear to you after a interval between the messengers, lest you say, "There came to us no bringer of good tidings and no warner." But there has certainly come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner. And God is over all things competent.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 19] ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, remember the favor of God upon you when He appointed among you prophets and made you kings and gave you what He had not given anyone else among the worlds."﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 20] ﴿"O my people, enter the Holy Land which God has prescribed for you, and do not turn back on your heels, for you will become losers."﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 21] ﴿They said, "O Moses, indeed there are in it a people of tyrants, and we will never enter it until they leave it. But if they leave it, then we will enter."﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 22] ﴿Two men from among those who feared (God), upon whom God had bestowed favor, said, "Enter upon them through the gate, for when you have entered it, you will be victorious. And upon God rely, if you are believers."﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 23] ﴿They said, "O Moses, we will never enter it as long as they remain in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting right here."﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 24] ﴿He said, "My Lord, I have no power except over myself and my brother, so part us from the defiantly disobedient people."﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 25] ﴿He said, "It is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land. So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people."﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 26]

Naqqaba fi al-jabali wa al-ha'iti: he opened in it what had been closed. Al-tanqib (inspection, searching) is from this, and from it (comes) ﴿فَنَقَّبُوا فِي البِلَادِ﴾ [Qaf: 36] ("so they searched through the lands"). Naqaba 'ala al-qawmi yanqubu means he became a naqib, i.e., he searches into their conditions and secrets, and that is al-niqabah. Al-niqab is the great man. Al-nuqab is mange, its singular being al-nuqbah, and it is also pluralized as nuqb on the pattern of zulm, which is the analogical form. The poet said:

*Dressed in plain clothes, his fine qualities appear; he applies the tar-like ointment to the places of mange.*

That is, the mange. Al-nuqbah is trousers without legs. Al-manaqib are the virtues that appear through searching. A woman is said to be "hasanat al-nuqbah wa al-niqab," meaning beautiful. Apparently, al-naqib is on the form fa'il for intensification, like 'alim. Abu Muslim said it is in the sense of maf'ul, meaning that they chose him with knowledge from them. Al-Asamm said: he is the one looked to, the one to whom command and management are attributed.

ʿAzzara al-rajul: Yunus ibn Habib said: he praised him with good. Abu Ubaydah said: he glorified him. Al-Farra' said: he restrained him from injustice, and from it comes ta'zir, because it prevents repeating the ugly act. Al-Qatami said:

*Has Mayy not come at dawn without foolishness, reproaching, while the one who is loved benefits from ta'zir?*

That is, prevention. Another poet said in the sense of glorification:

*How many a noble man, generous among them, and a lion honored in the assembly.*

On these reports, it falls under the category of the homonym (mushtarak). Al-Zamakhshari made it from the category of the univocal (mutawati') and said: ʿazzartumuhu means you supported him and protected him from the hands of the enemy, and from it comes al-ta'zir, which is punishment and prevention from repeating corruption. This is also the view of al-Zajjaj, who said: al-ta'zir is deterrence. ʿAzzartu fulanan means I did to him what deters him from ugliness, like nakkaltu bihi. Accordingly, the interpretation of ʿazzartumuhum is "you repelled their enemies from them." End. This is not correct except if the original (meaning) in ʿazzartumuhum is: you supported with them.

Talaʿa al-shay'u means it appeared and became manifest, and iṭṭala'a is its reflexive form (ifta'ala). Gharā bi al-shay'i ghiraʾan wa ghiran means it stuck to it, and it is the glue (al-ghirā) by which it is stuck. Aghra fulanun Zaydan bi-ʿAmrin means he incited him to him, and aghraytu al-kalba bi al-ṣayd means I set the dog on the prey. Al-Nadr said: aghra baynahum means he stirred up. Muwarrij said: he incited some of them against others. Al-Zajjaj said: he attached them (to it). Al-ṣun' is work. Al-fatrah is cessation; fatara al-wahy means revelation ceased. Al-fatrah is also the stillness after movement in bodies, and it is used metaphorically for meanings. The poet said:

*Indeed, a lassitude overcomes me when I remember you.*

The ha' in it is not for the single instance; rather fatrah is a synonym of futur (lassitude). It is said: "ṭarfun fatir" when the glance is languid. Al-jabbar is fa'al from al-jabr, as if, due to his strength and force, he compels people to what they choose. Al-jabbarah is the tall palm tree that cannot be reached by hand, and the generic noun is jabbar. The poet said:

*Racing steeds of a tall tree, lush its branches, and rising above us, clusters of red unripe dates.*

Al-tih in language is bewilderment; it is said from it: taha yatihu, yatuhu, and tawwahtuhu, with the form with ta' being more common. Al-ard al-tawha' is the land in which one is not guided, and ard tih. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-tih is going in the land toward no destination. Al-asa is sorrow; it is said from it: asa ya'sa.

﴿And God had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised from among them twelve leaders.﴾ The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that He commanded mention of the covenant which God took from the believers in His saying: ﴿and His covenant with which He bound you﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 7]. Then He mentioned His promise to them. Then He commanded them to mention His favor upon them when He restrained the hands of the disbelievers from them. He reminded them of the story of the Children of Israel regarding the taking of the covenant from them, and His promise to them of the expiation of their evil deeds and their admission into Paradise. But they broke the covenant and resolved to kill the Messenger. He warned them with this story, lest they follow the way of the Children of Israel, while (the true way) is faith and monotheism. As for the raising of the leaders (nuqaba'), it is said: they were kings sent among them to establish justice, command them to good, and forbid them from evil. The naqib is the chief of the people, who is in charge of their affairs. The meaning in the verse: He enumerated for them His favors in that He sent to their enemies this number of kings, as al-Naqqash said. He said: Only five of them fulfilled (the covenant): Dawud, his son Sulayman, Talut, Hizqil and his son. Seven disbelieved, changed (the religion), and killed the prophets. Among the twelve, thirty-two tyrants emerged, each seizing kingship by the sword and acting corruptly among them. The ba'th (raising) is from the sending of armies. It was also said: it is from the sending of messengers, meaning sending them, and the nuqaba' were messengers whom God made messengers to their peoples, each prophet among them to a tribe.

It was also said: the covenant and the leaders here refer to what happened between Moses and his people in the matter of fighting the tyrants. That is, when the Children of Israel settled in Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh, God commanded them to set out for Jericho, the land of Syria, which was inhabited by disbelieving tyrants, the Canaanites. He said to them: "I have written it for you as a home and dwelling, so go out to it and fight those in it, and I am your helper." Moses was commanded to take from each tribe a naqib who would be a guarantor over his people for fulfilling what they were commanded, as a pledge upon them. He chose the nuqaba', took the covenant from the Children of Israel, and the nuqaba' took responsibility for it on their behalf. He led them, and when he approached the land of Canaan, he sent the nuqaba' to spy. They saw enormous bodies, strength, and might; they feared and returned and reported to their people, though Moses had forbidden them to report it. So they broke the covenant, except Caleb son of Jephunneh from the tribe of Judah, and Joshua son of Nun from the tribe of Ephraim son of Joseph, and both were among the nuqaba'. Muhammad ibn Habib mentioned in al-Muhabbar the names of these nuqaba' whom Moses chose in this story, in wording whose letters and vowels cannot be determined, and others mentioned them differing in most of them from what Ibn Habib mentioned, also indeterminable. They also mentioned the creation of these tyrants, the greatness of their bodies, and the size of their frames, which cannot be substantiated in any way. They said: the number of these nuqaba' corresponded to the number of the nuqaba' whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) chose from the seventy men and the two women who pledged allegiance to him at the Second 'Aqabah, and he named them the nuqaba'.

﴿And God said: "Indeed I am with you"﴾ meaning: with support and protection. In this "being with" there is an indication of the great care and aid, and of making lawful what He stipulated upon them of what comes after. The pronoun of address refers to all the Children of Israel. Al-Rabi' said: it is addressed to the nuqaba', but the first is the preponderant view, because the rulings that come after this sentence apply to all the Children of Israel.

﴿If you establish the prayer, give the zakat, believe in My messengers, support them, and lend God a goodly loan, I will surely remove your evil deeds from you and surely admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow.﴾ The lam in la'in aqamtum is the one that announces an oath, and it prepares what follows it; after the conditional particle, it must be the answer to the oath. It is possible that the oath is elided. It is also possible that la-ukaffiranna is the answer to His saying: ﴿And God had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾, and that His saying "and We raised" and the clause after it are in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), or that both are parenthetical clauses; and the answer of the conditional is elided, because the answer of the oath indicates it. Al-Zamakhshari said: This answer, meaning la-ukaffiranna, serves as the answer to both the oath and the condition together. End. This is not as he stated: la-ukaffiranna does not fill the place of both, but rather it is the answer to the oath alone, and the answer to the condition is elided, as we mentioned. Zakat here means the obligatory portion of wealth that was incumbent upon them. It was said: it is possible that the meaning is: you gave from yourselves everything that contains zakat for you, as you were recommended to do, as Ibn 'Atiyyah said. The first is the preponderant view.

﴿And believe in My messengers﴾: faith in the messengers is affirmation of everything they brought from God, exalted is He. He placed the prayer and zakat before faith to honor them, and it is known and established that no deed benefits except with faith, as Ibn 'Atiyyah said. Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: The Jews acknowledged the attainment of faith together with establishing the prayer and giving zakat, but they denied some of the messengers. So He mentioned after these two faith in all the messengers, and that salvation is not attained except by faith in all of them. End, summarized. Al-Hasan recited: bi-rusli, with a sukun on the sin, throughout the Qur'an; and ʿazzartumuhum. ʿĀṣim al-Jahdari recited: wa-ʿazartumuhum, with a light zay. In the fath (form), he recited (wa-ta'zuruhu) with a fatha on the ta', a sukun on the 'ayn, and a damma on the zay, and its verbal noun is al-ʿazr.

**"And you lend Allah a goodly loan"**: The giving of zakat (obligatory almsgiving) is in the case of the wajib (obligatory), and this lending is in the case of the mandub (recommended). He drew attention to the recommended charities by mentioning them alongside what follows from the whole, honouring them and magnifying their place in beneficence that extends to others. Al-Farra' said: "Had it come as *iqrad* (lending), it would have been correct, the noun being used here in place of the verbal noun, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So his Lord accepted her with a goodly acceptance and caused her to grow in a goodly growth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37]. He did not say *taqbil* or *inbat*." End of quotation. This lending has been explained as spending in the way of Allah, as spending on one's family, and as zakat. But this is far-fetched, because it is a repetition. He described it as "goodly" either because it is not followed by reproach or harm, or because it is given with a willing heart.

**"I will surely remove your evil deeds from you and surely admit you to gardens"**: He made the removal of evil deeds follow from these five conditions, which points to the removal of punishment, and the admission to gardens, which points to the delivery of reward.

**"Whoever of you disbelieves after that has certainly strayed from the right way"**: That is, after that covenant that was taken and that emphatic condition, he has certainly erred from the straight path. *Sawa' al-sabil* is its middle and its purpose, which leads to the right course, and it is what Allah has legislated. The singling out of disbelief by the transgression of taking the covenant, although straying from the straight path was already present before it, is because after the emphatic condition, confirmed by the true, trustworthy and mighty promise, it is more heinous and greater, since the taking of a covenant requires fulfilling it, especially after this warning. The greatness of disbelief is in proportion to the greatness of the blessing that is denied.

**[Qur'an 5:13]** *Fa-bima naqdihim mithaqahum* (So because of their breaking of their covenant). The discussion of this phrase has already been given.

*(La'annahum)*, that is: We expelled them and removed them far from mercy. This is the view of ʿAṭāʾ and al-Zajjāj. Or: We punished them by transforming them into apes and swine, as in His words: ﴿Or We will curse them as We cursed the people of the Sabbath﴾ [Qur'an 4:47], meaning: We will transform them as We transformed them. This is the view of al-Ḥasan and Muqātil. Or: We punished them by imposing the jizya (poll tax), as Ibn ʿAbbās said. Qatādah said: They broke the covenant by denying the messengers who came after Moses, by killing the prophets without right, and by neglecting the obligations.

﴿And We made their hearts hard﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: harsh and dry. It was also said: thick, not softening. It was also said: rejecting, not accepting admonition. All of these are close in meaning. The hardness (*qaswa*) of the heart is its thickness and rigidity, to the point that it is not moved by good. The majority of the Seven Readers read *qāsiyatan*, an active participle from *qasā yaqsū*. ʿAbd Allāh, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read *qasiyyatan*, without an alif and with a doubled yāʾ, which is the form *faʿīl* used for emphasis, like *shāhid* and *shahīd*. Some people said: this reading does not come from the meaning of hardness, but is like *al-qasiyyah* of dirhams, which is the coin mixed with adulteration and fraud. Likewise, the hearts were not purely faithful, but were mixed with disbelief and corruption. Abū Zubayd al-Ṭāʾī said:

*They have neighings amid the silent weapons, as the counterfeit coins cry out in the hands of the money-changers.*

Another said:

*They did nothing to me except rub off a turban, and five dirhams in which there is a counterfeit and a fake.*

Al-Fārisī said: this word is arabicized (*muʿarrabah*) and is not originally part of Arabic speech. Al-Zamakhsharī said: ʿAbd Allāh read *qasiyyatan*, meaning bad and adulterated, from their saying "a *qasiy* dirham," and it comes from *qaswa* (hardness), because pure gold and silver are soft in themselves, while the adulterated has dryness and hardness. *Al-qāsī* and *al-qāsiḥ* (with a ḥāʾ) are two words with the same implication of dryness and hardness. End of quotation. Al-Mubarrad said: the counterfeit dirham was called *qasiyy* because of its strength in the adulteration within it, and this returns to the first meaning; *al-qāsī* and *al-qāsiḥ* have one meaning. End of quotation. Al-Mubarrad's statement contradicts that of al-Fārisī, because the known view is that it is Arabic, from *qaswa*, while al-Fārisī made it an arabicized loanword that is not among Arabic's own words.

Hayṣam ibn Shaddākh read *qusiyyatan*, with a *ḍammah* on the qāf and a doubled yāʾ, like *ḥuniyy*. It was also read with a *kasrah* on the qāf, by assimilation (*itbāʿan*).

Al-Zamakhsharī said: We forsook them and withheld from them the kindnesses, until their hearts became hard; or We gave them respite and did not hasten to punish them until they became hard. End of quotation. This is in accordance with his Muʿtazilī (rationalist) school. As for the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah), they say that God created hardness in their hearts.

﴿They distort words from their places﴾. That is: they change the rulings that were hard for them. Like the verse of stoning (*rajm*), they replaced it for their leaders with *tahmīm*, which is blackening the face with charcoal. Ibn ʿAbbās and others said this meaning. They said: the distortion is by interpretation, not by changing the wording, and they had no power to change the wording, nor was it possible. Do you not see that they placed their hands upon the verse of stoning? Muqātil said: their distortion of the words (p-446) is their changing of the description of the Messenger. They removed it and wrote in its place another description, so they changed both the meaning and the wording. The correct view is that distorting words from their places is change in both wording and meaning, and whoever has looked into the Torah knows this as a fact. The discussion of this meaning has already been given. This sentence and what follows came as an explanation of the hardness of their hearts, and there is no hardness greater than fabricating against God and altering His revelation.

Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and al-Nakhaʿī read *al-kalām* with an alif. Abū Rajāʾ read *al-kilm*, with a *kasrah* on the kāf and a sukūn on the lām. The majority read *al-kalima*, with a *fatḥah* on the kāf.

﴿And they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of﴾. This also is from the hardness of their hearts and the evil of their conduct toward themselves, in that they were reminded of something, then forgot it and abandoned it. This portion is of the covenant that was taken from them. It was also said: when they changed what they changed in the Torah, they continued to recite what they had changed, so they forgot a portion of what is in the Torah. This was said by Mujāhid. It was also said: God made them forget a share of the Book because of their sins. From Ibn Masʿūd: a person may forget some knowledge because of sin, and he recited this verse. The poet said:

*I complained to Wakīʿ of my bad memory, so he pointed me to abandoning sins.*

It was also said: they abandoned their share of what they were commanded, namely faith in the Messenger and the explanation of his description.

﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them, except a few of them﴾. That is: this is their habit and their custom with you. They are following the example of their forefathers in betraying the messengers and killing the prophets. They will not cease to threaten you, to break your pacts, to support your enemies against you, and to intend to kill you, and to poison you. The word *khāʾinah* may be a verbal noun like *ʿāfiyah*, and this is supported by the reading of al-Aʿmash: *ʿalā khiyānatin*. Or it may be an active participle, with the *hāʾ* for emphasis, like *rāwiyah*; that is, *khāʾin* (a treacherous one). Or it may be an adjective for a feminine noun: a treacherous town (*qaryah khāʾinah*), or a treacherous deed (*fiʿlah khāʾinah*), or a treacherous soul (*nafs khāʾinah*). The apparent reading of the exception (*istithnāʾ*) is that it refers to persons in this sentence, and the exempted ones were ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it may also refer to actions, that is: except a few actions, so you will not discover treachery in them. It was also said: the exception refers to His words: ﴿And We made their hearts hard﴾, and what is meant by those exempted are the believers, since the hardness was removed from their hearts. But this view is far-fetched.

﴿So pardon them and overlook, for indeed God loves the doers of good﴾. Its apparent meaning is the command to pardon and overlook them all, and this is an incitement to good conduct with them and noble character. Ibn Jarīr said: it is permissible to pardon them for a betrayal they committed, so long as they did not take up war and did not refuse to pay the jizya. It was also said: the pronoun refers to those among them who believed, so do not hold them accountable for what they did earlier, and this refers back to the exempted ones. It was also said: this command was abrogated (*mansūkh*) by the verse of the sword. It was also said: it was abrogated by His words: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in God﴾ [Qur'an 9:29]. It was also said: it was abrogated by His words: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people﴾ [Qur'an 8:58]. His words "God loves the doers of good" were explained as: those who pardon people; and as: those who made their deeds good through faith; and as: the exempted ones, who did not break the covenant; and as: the ones who believed and [followed] the Prophet, peace be upon him, because he is the one commanded in the verse to overlook and pardon.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 14:

﴿And from those who say, "We are Christians," We took their covenant.﴾ It is apparent that (مِن) is connected to the verb أخَذْنا (akhadhna, "We took"), that the pronoun in مِيثاقَهم (mithaqahum, "their covenant") refers back to the relative pronoun (al-Ladhina, "those who"), and that the clause is conjoined to His saying: ﴿And Allah had already taken the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 12]. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, took from the Christians the covenant of their own selves, which is faith in Allah, His messengers, and righteous deeds. It has also been said that the pronoun in مِيثاقَهم refers to the Children of Israel, and that it is a masdar shabih (a noun resembling a verbal noun, i.e., a noun of the same form as the verbal noun); the meaning being: "And We took from the Christians a covenant like the covenant of the Children of Israel." It has also been said that ومِنَ الَّذِينَ (wa-min alladhina, "and from those who") is conjoined to His saying, "(min-hum)" in His saying: ﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 13]; that is, from the Jews, and from those who say, "We are Christians." (p-447) His saying أخَذْنا مِيثاقَهم ("We took their covenant") would then be mustaʾnafan (a new, independent clause). This has a remoteness to it, because it separates the clause and prepares the governing verb for action and then cuts it off from it without necessity.

Qatada said: The covenant was taken from the Christians just as it was taken from the People of the Torah, that they should believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), but they abandoned what they were commanded. Others said: The covenant was taken from them to act upon the Torah, and upon the books of Allah that were revealed, and His prophets and messengers.

In His saying ﴿They say, "We are Christians"﴾ there is a rebuke to them and a deterrence from what they claimed, namely that they are the helpers of the religion of Allah and of His prophets, since He made that, on their part, a mere claim and not a reality. And since the word "Christians" (al-Nasara) came without attribution to their saying it about themselves, it is of the category of a proper name (ʿalam), in which the original meaning they intended, of victory (al-nasr), is not taken into account, just as "the Jews" (al-Yahud) became a proper name in which the meaning of His saying "hudna ilayk" (we have turned to You) is not taken into account.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Why was it not said "wa-man al-Nasara" (and who are the Christians)? (I answer): Because they named themselves thus, claiming to be the helpers of Allah, and they are the ones who said to Jesus: "We are the helpers of Allah" (ʾAnsar Allah). Then they later disagreed into Nestorians (Nasturiyya), Jacobites (Yaʿqubiyya), and Melkites (Malkaniyya). End of quotation.

It has already passed in the beginning of al-Baqara that it was said they were called Nasara because they came from a village in al-Sham called Nasira. As for his saying, "They are those who said to Jesus, 'We are the helpers of Allah,'" the ones who said that were the Hawariyyun (the disciples); according to al-Zamakhshari they are unbelievers, and he has clarified this on his own view at the end of this surah, while according to others they were believers. They did not disagree among themselves; rather, those who came after them disagreed, among those who claim to follow them.

﴿So they forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of﴾. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: In the written Gospel is the command that they believe in Muhammad (ﷺ). The portion (ḥazz) is faith in him. The indefiniteness of ḥazz indicates that what is meant by it is one single portion, which is faith in the Messenger. This single portion was singled out for mention, even though they abandoned most of what Allah had commanded them, because this is the most important and the most significant.

﴿So We incited among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection﴾. The pronoun in بَيْنَهم (baynahum, "among them") refers to the Christians, as said by al-Rabiʿ. Al-Zajjaj said: The Christians are among them, and the Nestorians, the Jacobites, and the Melkites; each sect among them opposes the others. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the Jews and the Christians; that is, between the Jews and the Christians, as said by Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Suddi, for they are enemies who curse one another and declare one another unbelievers.

﴿And Allah will inform them of what they used to do﴾. This is a threat and a severe warning of the punishment of the Hereafter, since what their deeds necessitate is nothing but abiding forever in the Fire.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 15–16:

﴿O People of the Scripture, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture and pardoning much.﴾ Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: The first of this surah to be revealed were these two verses, concerning the Jews and the Christians. Then the rest of the surah was revealed at 'Arafah during the Farewell Pilgrimage. "People of the Scripture" encompasses the Jews and the Christians. It has been said: the address is to the Jews specifically, and this is supported by what Khalid al-Hadhdha narrated from Ikrimah, who said: The Jews came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asking him about stoning, so they gathered in a house. He said: "Which of you is the most knowledgeable?" They pointed to Ibn Suriya. He said: "You are the most knowledgeable?" He said: "They claim that." He said: "I adjure you by Allah, who sent down the Torah to Moses, and who raised the Mount above you, [to tell me]..." So he adjured him with the covenants that were taken from them, until he was seized with trembling, and said: "Indeed our women are beautiful, so killing increased among us, so we made it lighter: we flogged one hundred lashes, shaved the heads, and differentiated the heads by the she-camels, I think he said: the camels." He said: Then Allah revealed: ﴿O People of the Scripture, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger﴾. It has also been said: the address is to the Jews and the Christians who conceal the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), stoning and the like. Most of the cases of concealment were revealed concerning the Jews, because they were neighbors of the Messenger in his migration. By his saying "Our Messenger" is meant Muhammad (ﷺ), and it is attributed to Allah, Exalted, as an attribution of honor. In this verse there is evidence for the truth of his prophethood, because his informing them of what they conceal of their Book, while he was unlettered, who neither read nor wrote nor associated with reciters, is evidence that he is taught only by Allah, Exalted. His saying "of the Scripture" means the Torah. ﴿And pardoning much﴾: that is, of what they conceal, he does not make clear when no religious benefit calls for it, and he does not expose you by it, out of sparing you. Al-Hasan said: "And pardoning much" is what the Messenger brought of lightening what had been made strict upon them and permitting what had been forbidden to them. It has been said: He does not hold you accountable for them. This left-unmentioned matter that is not made clear is in the sense of their boasting and the like, of what does not specifically require, in the religion of Islam, exposing them by it and refuting them. The apparent reading is that the agent of "makes clear" and "pardons" refers to "Our Messenger," and it is permissible that it refers to Allah, Exalted.

﴿There has certainly come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book﴾. It has been said: it is the Qur'an; it was called a light because it uncovers the darkness of polytheism and doubt, or because it is manifest in its inimitability. It has been said: the light is the Messenger. It has been said: Islam. It has been said: the light is Moses, and the clear Book is the Torah. Had they followed it with true following, they would have believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), since it commands that and gives glad tidings of him.

﴿By it Allah guides whoever follows His good pleasure to the ways of peace﴾: that is, the pleasure of Allah; "the ways of peace" are the paths of salvation and safety from the punishment of Allah. The pronoun in "by it" apparently refers to the Book of Allah, and it may refer to the Messenger. It has been said: it may refer to Islam. It has been said: "the ways of peace" — it has been said: the religion of Islam. Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: "al-Salam" is Allah, Exalted, and "His ways" are His religion which He legislated. It has been said: the paths to Paradise. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, al-Zuhri, Salam, Humayd, and Muslim ibn Jundub read "bihi Allah" with a dammah on the ha' wherever it occurs. al-Hasan and Ibn Shihab read "subul" with the ba' sukun.

﴿And brings them out of darkness into light by His permission﴾: that is, from the darknesses of disbelief into the light of faith, by His enabling and facilitating. It has been said: the darknesses of ignorance and the light of knowledge.

﴿And guides them to a straight path﴾: it is the religion of Allah and His Oneness. It has been said: the path to Paradise. It has been said: the path of truth, and it is narrated from al-Hasan. The apparent meaning is that all these clauses are close in meaning and are repeated for emphasis, and the verb in them is ascribed to Allah, Exalted.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 15–16:

﴿O People of the Scripture, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture and pardoning much.﴾ Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: The first of this surah to be revealed were these two verses, concerning the Jews and the Christians. Then the rest of the surah was revealed at 'Arafah during the Farewell Pilgrimage. "People of the Scripture" encompasses the Jews and the Christians. It has been said: the address is to the Jews specifically, and this is supported by what Khalid al-Hadhdha narrated from Ikrimah, who said: The Jews came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asking him about stoning, so they gathered in a house. He said: "Which of you is the most knowledgeable?" They pointed to Ibn Suriya. He said: "You are the most knowledgeable?" He said: "They claim that." He said: "I adjure you by Allah, who sent down the Torah to Moses, and who raised the Mount above you, [to tell me]..." So he adjured him with the covenants that were taken from them, until he was seized with trembling, and said: "Indeed our women are beautiful, so killing increased among us, so we made it lighter: we flogged one hundred lashes, shaved the heads, and differentiated the heads by the she-camels, I think he said: the camels." He said: Then Allah revealed: ﴿O People of the Scripture, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger﴾. It has also been said: the address is to the Jews and the Christians who conceal the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), stoning and the like. Most of the cases of concealment were revealed concerning the Jews, because they were neighbors of the Messenger in his migration. By his saying "Our Messenger" is meant Muhammad (ﷺ), and it is attributed to Allah, Exalted, as an attribution of honor. In this verse there is evidence for the truth of his prophethood, because his informing them of what they conceal of their Book, while he was unlettered, who neither read nor wrote nor associated with reciters, is evidence that he is taught only by Allah, Exalted. His saying "of the Scripture" means the Torah. ﴿And pardoning much﴾: that is, of what they conceal, he does not make clear when no religious benefit calls for it, and he does not expose you by it, out of sparing you. Al-Hasan said: "And pardoning much" is what the Messenger brought of lightening what had been made strict upon them and permitting what had been forbidden to them. It has been said: He does not hold you accountable for them. This left-unmentioned matter that is not made clear is in the sense of their boasting and the like, of what does not specifically require, in the religion of Islam, exposing them by it and refuting them. The apparent reading is that the agent of "makes clear" and "pardons" refers to "Our Messenger," and it is permissible that it refers to Allah, Exalted.

﴿There has certainly come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book﴾. It has been said: it is the Qur'an; it was called a light because it uncovers the darkness of polytheism and doubt, or because it is manifest in its inimitability. It has been said: the light is the Messenger. It has been said: Islam. It has been said: the light is Moses, and the clear Book is the Torah. Had they followed it with true following, they would have believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), since it commands that and gives glad tidings of him.

﴿By it Allah guides whoever follows His good pleasure to the ways of peace﴾: that is, the pleasure of Allah; "the ways of peace" are the paths of salvation and safety from the punishment of Allah. The pronoun in "by it" apparently refers to the Book of Allah, and it may refer to the Messenger. It has been said: it may refer to Islam. It has been said: "the ways of peace" — it has been said: the religion of Islam. Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: "al-Salam" is Allah, Exalted, and "His ways" are His religion which He legislated. It has been said: the paths to Paradise. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, al-Zuhri, Salam, Humayd, and Muslim ibn Jundub read "bihi Allah" with a dammah on the ha' wherever it occurs. al-Hasan and Ibn Shihab read "subul" with the ba' sukun.

﴿And brings them out of darkness into light by His permission﴾: that is, from the darknesses of disbelief into the light of faith, by His enabling and facilitating. It has been said: the darknesses of ignorance and the light of knowledge.

﴿And guides them to a straight path﴾: it is the religion of Allah and His Oneness. It has been said: the path to Paradise. It has been said: the path of truth, and it is narrated from al-Hasan. The apparent meaning is that all these clauses are close in meaning and are repeated for emphasis, and the verb in them is ascribed to Allah, Exalted.

[p. 449] The apparent meaning of ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say: Indeed, God is the Messiah, son of Mary﴾ is that they said that God is literally the Messiah. What God relates of them contradicts that God is the Messiah, because they said "son of Mary," and whoever is the son of a woman, born from her, cannot be God, the Exalted. The exegetes differed in interpreting this verse. Some held that all of them say this statement, and they are in three sects, as was mentioned earlier, and that they agree, although their statements differ, that their worshipped one is a single substance (jawhar) with three hypostases (aqanim): the Father, the Son, and the Spirit, meaning the Life, which they call the Holy Spirit (ruh al-qudus). They also hold that the Son has always been begotten of the Father, the Father has always been the begetter of the Son, and the Spirit has always been passing between the Father and the Son. They agree that the Messiah is divinity (lahut) and humanity (nasut), meaning God and man. So when they say "the Messiah is one God," they have said "God is the Messiah." Others held that those who say this statement are an unspecified group, who say that the Word (al-kalima) united with Jesus, whether it is estimated as an essence or as an attribute. Others held that the Ya'qubiyya among the Christians are the ones who say this statement, as al-Baghawi mentioned in Ma'alim al-Tanzil.

Some exegetes said: All three of their sects, the Ya'qubiyya, the Malkaniyya, and the Nestoriyya, deny this statement. What they affirm is that Jesus is the Son of God, the Exalted, and that he is God. When they believe that he is God, it necessarily follows from that that they say he is God. End of quote. I have seen among the Christians of the lands of al-Andalus someone who was affiliated with knowledge among them, and he mentioned to me that Jesus himself is God, the Exalted. The Christians of al-Andalus are Malkiyya. I said to him: How can you say that, when it is agreed upon that Jesus used to eat and drink? He was amazed at my statement and said: If you, being one of God's creatures, are able to eat and drink, how would God not be able to do that? From this I inferred his extreme stupidity and his ignorance of the attributes of God, the Exalted.

Ibn 'Abbas held that they are the people of Najran. A group of them claimed that He is the God of the earth and God is the God of the heavens. From some of the Christians' beliefs, those who conceal disbelief under outward Islam and affiliate with the Sufis deduced the indwelling (hulul) of God, the Exalted, in beautiful forms. Among their heretics who held the doctrine of union (ittihad) and oneness (wahda) were al-Hallaj, al-Shawdhi, Ibn Ahla, Ibn al-'Arabi who resided in Damascus, and Ibn al-Farid. And the followers of these, such as Ibn Sab'in, al-Tustari his disciple, Ibn Mutarrif who resided in Murcia, al-Saffar who was killed in Granada, and Ibn al-Labbaj. And Abu al-Hasan who resided in Lorca. Among those whom we have seen being accused of this accursed doctrine is al-'Afif al-Tilimsani, and he has many poems on this subject. Also Ibn 'Ayyash al-Malaqi, the black, one-handed one, who resided in Damascus; 'Abd al-Wahid ibn al-Mu'akhkhar, who resided in Upper Egypt; al-Ayki al-'Ajami, who held the shaykhhood in the khanqah of Sa'id al-Su'ada in Cairo in the lands of Egypt; and Abu Ya'qub ibn Mubashshir, the disciple of al-Tustari, who resided in the quarter of Zuwayla. I have only listed the names of these people as advice for the religion of God, which God knows, and out of compassion for the weak Muslims, so that they may beware of them, for they are worse than the philosophers who deny God, the Exalted, and His messengers, and who say that the world is eternal and deny the resurrection. Some ignorant people who are affiliated with Sufism have become infatuated with exalting these people and claiming that they are the elite of God and His friends.

The refutation of the Christians, the Hululites, and those who hold the doctrine of oneness is part of the science of the fundamentals of religion (usul al-din). Ibn 'Atiyya said: Those who say that God is the Messiah are a sect of the Christians, and all their sects, despite the differences in their statements, grant the Messiah a share of divinity. Al-Zamakhshari said: It was said that among the Christians there were those who said this, and it was said that they did not declare it explicitly, but their doctrine leads to it, since they believed that he creates, gives life, causes death, and governs the world.

﴿Say: Who then has any power against God if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother, and everyone on earth, all of them?﴾ This is a refutation of them. The fa' in "fa-man" (then who) is for conjunction with an omitted sentence that contained their lie in their statement; the estimate is: Say: They have lied; and say: It is not as they said.

"Fa-man yamliku" (then who has power): the meaning is: then who prevents anything from the power and will of God? That is: no one prevents anything of what God wills, if He wills to destroy those whom they claimed as a god, the Messiah and his mother. In this there is evidence that he and his mother are two servants among God's servants, who cannot remove destruction from themselves, but rather the will of God, the Exalted, takes effect in them, and whatever His will takes effect in cannot be a god. He conjoined to them: ﴿and everyone on earth, all of them﴾, as the conjunction of the general with the specific, so that they are mentioned twice: once by explicit naming, and once by inclusion in the general.
