It is related that they used to travel at night and would journey the whole night, so that when they awoke in the morning they found all of them in the place where they had started. And they would travel by day, striving, until when evening came they found themselves in the place from which they had set out. Thus their travel was circling. Mujahid and others said: they would sometimes travel by day and sometimes by night, so they would reach the evening where they had been in the morning, and the morning where they had been in the evening. This was within a distance of six farsakh, and they were in a wandering with no place of rest. End of quotation.

It has been mentioned (p-459) that they were six hundred thousand fighting men. They also mentioned that the wisdom of the wandering was that when they said ﴿Indeed, we will remain seated here﴾, they were punished with sitting, so they came to be in the form of those who sit while they were travelling. Whenever they travelled for a day, by evening they were in the place where they had been in the morning.

They also mentioned that the wisdom of the period in which they wandered being forty years was that they had worshipped the calf for forty days, so the punishment was made one year for each day in the wandering.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is also possible that their wandering was by the splitting of their word and the scarcity of agreement in opinion, and that God cast disagreement among them. They knew that the land was forbidden to them for forty years, so their dwellings scattered throughout that open expanse, and they continued to move from place to place without order or unity until this period was completed, and God permitted their departure. This is a wandering that is possible and plausible according to human custom. The other [explanation], which Mujahid mentioned, is merely a breaking of custom and a wonder of God's power.

﴿So do not grieve over the defiant people﴾. The apparent meaning is that the address is from God, the Exalted, to Musa (peace be upon him). Ibn ʿAbbas said: Musa regretted his supplication against his people and grieved for them. End of quotation. So this is a consolation to Musa, peace be upon him, against grieving over what befell his people, and the reason given for his not grieving is that they are defiant people, bahut (liars), deserving of the punishment that befell them.

It was also said: the address is to Muhammad (ﷺ), and by "the defiant" is meant his contemporaries. That is: these are the deeds of their forefathers. So do not grieve, you, because of their wicked deeds with you and their rejection of you, for this is a wicked disposition inherited among them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 20–26 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, remember the favour of God upon you when He appointed prophets among you, made you kings, and gave you what He had not given to anyone among the worlds."﴾ The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that He, exalted is He, explained the rebelliousness of the ancestors of the Jews against Moses and their disobedience to him, along with his reminding them of God's blessings and his enumeration of the greatest of them. And these people who are in the presence of the Messenger are following in the path of their ancestors with Moses. The "favour of God" is meant in the generic sense. The meaning is: "Recount to them, O Muhammad, by way of informing them of the unseen (contents) of their books, so that they may verify your prophethood." This includes mention of God's favours upon them and their receiving those favours with disbelief and little obedience. He enumerated three of His favours upon them. The first: the appointing of prophets among them, and this is the greatest honour, since they are the intermediaries between God and His creation and the ones who convey His laws from God. It has been said: no nation was sent as many prophets as the Children of Israel. Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil said: the "prophets" here are the seventy whom Moses chose for the appointed time of his Lord, and they were among the best of his people. It has been said: they are those who were sent afterwards among the Children of Israel, like Moses; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi and others. According to this view, "made" (ja'ala) does not mean the literal past in actuality, since some of them had appeared at the time of Moses' address to them, and some had not yet been created but he informed that they would be among them. The second: making them kings. Its apparent meaning is a favour upon them, in that He made them kings, since He made kings from among them, for kingship is a worldly honour and dominion. So He reminded them that among them were leaders of the Hereafter and leaders of this world. Al-Suddi and others said: He made you free, those who own and are not owned, since you were servants to the Copts, and He rescued you from them, so their rescue was called kingship. Some said: He made them kings by sending down the manna and quails upon them (p-453), and by making the rock gush forth for them, and by making their clothes neither wear out nor become soiled, and growing as they grew; so they are kings because this burden was lifted from them. Qatadah said: "kings" because they were the first to employ servants and acquire slaves. Ibn 'Atiyyah and Qatadah said: He only said "and made you kings" because we used to hear that the first to serve a human being was another human being. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is weak, because the Copts used to make the Children of Israel serve them. The apparent state of the children of Adam is that some of them have subjected others to service since they multiplied and spread. End of quotation.
These three views are general to all the Children of Israel, and this is the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿and made you kings﴾. 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and a group said: whoever has a dwelling, a wife, and a servant is a king. It has been said: whoever has a dwelling into which no one may enter without permission is a king. It has been said: whoever has a wife and a servant; this was related from Ibn 'Abbas. 'Ikrimah said: whoever possesses a servant and a house among them is called a king among them. It has been said: whoever has a spacious dwelling in which there is running water. It has been said: whoever has wealth that does not require him to undertake laborious tasks and bear hardships. It has been said: they are kings through their contentment, and this is a hidden kingship. For this reason it came in the hadith: "Contentment is a treasure that never runs out." It has been said: because they possessed their own selves and protected them from disbelief and from following Pharaoh. It has been said: they possessed the desires of their own souls. Al-Tibrizi mentioned these three views in his tafsir. The third: His giving them what He had not given to anyone among the worlds. Ibn 'Abbas explained it, as related from him by Mujahid, as: the manna, the quails, the rock, and the cloud. 'Ata' related from him: the house, the wife, and the servant. It has been said: the multitude of prophets. Ibn Jarir said: no one among the people of Moses' time was given blessings like those given to them. They were singled out with the splitting of the sea for them, the sending down of the manna and quails, the bringing forth of sweet water from the rock, and the cloud being spread over them. Prophethood and kingship were never combined for one people as they were combined for them, and in those days they were the scholars of God, His beloved ones, and the supporters of His religion. End of quotation. What is meant is either the multitude of prophets or the particular features of the totality of Moses' signs. Thus the word "the worlds" is restricted to the time in which the Children of Israel existed, because the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) has been given, from the signs of Muhammad (ﷺ), more than that. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was shaded by a cloud before his mission; stones and animals spoke to him; a tree came towards him; the trunk moaned for him; water gushed from between his fingers; many people were satisfied from a small amount of food through his blessing; the moon was split for him; a staff returned as a sword; and a rock blocking the trench turned into scattered sand. Beyond these, there are his greatest signs and his mightiest miracles. This statement from Moses to the Children of Israel and his reminding them of God's favours is a preparation for their souls and an advance warning of what would befall them concerning the fight against the giants, so that their hearts might be strengthened and they might know that whoever God has favoured with these great blessings, God will not forsake, but will raise him over his enemy, elevate his station, and give him authority and dominance over them.
The address in His words "and gave you" — its apparent meaning is that it is to the Children of Israel, as we have explained, and that it is part of Moses' speech to them, and this is the view of the majority. Abu Malik and Ibn Jubayr said: it is an address to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). The speech ends at His words: ﴿and made you kings﴾; then He turned to this community. When Moses reminded his people of God's blessings, God reminded the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) of this apparent blessing, to comfort their hearts, and that He gave them what He had not given to anyone among the worlds. On this view, "the worlds" is general, for God has preferred the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) over the rest of the nations, given them what He has not given anyone among the worlds, and bestowed upon them blessings that He has not bestowed upon any nation. This is the meaning of Ibn Jarir's view, and it is his preferred opinion. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is weak. It was weakened in his view because the speech is in one continuous sequence of Moses' address to his people, and this is connected to what precedes it. But what he said is not necessarily binding, because the Qur'an came according to the rules of Arabic speech, which include shifts (al-iltifat, a change of addressee) and moving from one address to another, especially when the apparent address does not suit the one first addressed, but suits the one addressed second. Thus the apparent meaning, when taken literally, strengthens the direction of the address to the second. Ibn Muhaysin read: "yā qawmu" with a damma on the mim, and so wherever it occurs in the Qur'an (p-454). This was related from Ibn Kathir. This damma is according to the sense of the construct (idafa), like the reading of the one who read: "Qul rabbu uhkum bil-haqq" with a damma. It is one of the five permissible dialects for the vocative noun when attached to the first-person ya' (my).
﴿O my people, enter the holy land which God has prescribed for you.﴾ "The holy land" (al-muqaddasa) means the purified one. It is Jericho; this was said by al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd, and 'Ikrimah related it from Ibn 'Abbas. It has been said: it is the site of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It has been said: Iliya. Ibn Qutaybah said: I read in the supplication of Moses; he said: "O God, You have chosen," then he mentioned things, then he said: "Lord of Iliya, the Bayt al-Maqdis." Ibn al-Jawzi said: I read to Abu Mansur the linguist, who said: Iliya is Bayt al-Maqdis. Al-Farazdaq said:
"Two houses: the House of God, which we visit, and another house, elevated and honoured, in the highest part of Iliya."
It has been said: it is Mount Tur; this was related by Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Zajjaj preferred it. It has been said: Palestine, Damascus, and part of Jordan. Qatadah said: it is the Levant. Al-Kalbi said: Abraham (peace be upon him) climbed Mount Lebanon, and Gabriel said to him: "Look; whatever your sight reaches is holy, and it is an inheritance for your offspring." It has been said: what lies between the Euphrates and the Brook of Egypt ('Arish). Al-Tabari said: there is no disagreement that it is what lies between the Euphrates and the Brook of Egypt. He said: al-Udfuwi said: the people of exegesis, the historians, and the scholars of reports unanimously agreed that it is what lies between the Euphrates and the Brook of Egypt. Al-Tabari said: the reports are unanimous that Damascus is the capital of the giants. End of quotation.
"Sanctification" (al-taqdis) means purification; it has been said: from calamities. It has been said: from polytheism. It was made a dwelling and abode for the prophets, and the domination of the giants over it does not remove it from being holy. It has been said: "holy" means blessed; it was purified from drought, famine, and other things; this was said by Mujahid. It has been said: it was called holy because in it is the place where one is sanctified from sins; and from this comes the saying that a bucket is called qudus, because one performs ablution with it and purifies oneself. The meaning of "God prescribed it for you" is: He apportioned it, named it, or inscribed on the Tablet that it is for you a dwelling and an abode. Ibn Ishaq said: He granted it to you. Al-Suddi said: He commanded you to enter it, and this is an encouragement to them and a strengthening when He informed them that God has prescribed it for them. The apparent use of "prescribed" (kataba) is in the sense of obligation, as in His words: ﴿Fasting is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183] and ﴿Fighting is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216]. As for if "He prescribed it" means "inscribed it in eternity and decreed it," then the apparent wording does not need to conflict with His words: ﴿it is forbidden to them﴾. It has been said: the wording is general, and the intended meaning is particular; as if He said: it is prescribed for some of them and forbidden for others. Or this is conditional on the condition of obeying the fight, and since they did not obey, the condition did not occur. Or the prohibition was limited to forty years, and when they were over, what He had prescribed came about. As for if He prescribed it for them in the sense of commanding them to enter it, then it does not conflict with the prohibition. It was forbidden for them to enter it, and they died in the wilderness, and their sons who had not been prohibited entered with Moses. It has been said: Moses and Aaron (peace be upon them both) died in the wilderness, and only their sons went out with Hizqil. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was a gift, then He forbade it to them because of their disobedience.
﴿And do not turn back on your heels, lest you become losers.﴾ That is: do not recoil upon your heels out of fear of the tyrants, through cowardice and panic. It has been said: when the chieftains informed them of the condition of the giants, they raised their voices in weeping and said: "Would that we had died in Egypt!" and they said: "Let us appoint a leader who will lead us back to Egypt." It is possible that what is meant is: do not turn back on your heels in your religion by opposing the command of your Lord.
As for their "turning back as losers": if "turning back" is literal, namely returning to the place from which they left, then its meaning is that they will fall into humiliation after honour and deliverance from the hands of the Copts. If "turning back" is metaphorical, namely their apostasy from their religion, then its meaning is that they will lose the good of this world and the reward of the Hereafter. Whoever opposes what God has obligated upon him of struggle and opposes His command deserves to be a loser.
﴿They said, "O Moses, indeed there are in it a people of giants.﴾ That is: the chieftains whom Moses sent to examine the condition of the giants said, or their leaders said, whose custom was to be informed of secrets and consulted in matters. This statement is remote, given their reluctance to fight; that is: indeed there are in it people whom we cannot fight. It has been said: they are remnants of 'Ad (p-455). It has been said: they are of the Romans, from the sons of Esau son of Isaac. Ibn al-Sumayqa read: "They said, 'O Moses, in it is a people who are giants.'"
﴿And we will never enter it until they leave it.﴾ This is an explicit declaration of total refusal to fight the giants, and for this reason the negation was with "lan" (never). "Until they leave it" means: by someone else fighting them, or by a cause through which God makes them leave, and then they will leave.
﴿So if they leave it, then we will enter.﴾ This is a deliberate direction from them to themselves by the departure of the giants from it, since they made their entry conditional upon a possible condition. Most exegetes said: they did not doubt what God had promised them, but their recoiling from fighting was due to the weakness of nature and the cowardice that God had built into them, and no one can overcome that except the one whom God protects. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except for a few of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246]. It has been said: they said this as a way of considering it unlikely that the giants would leave it, like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Nor will they enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf: 40].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 20–26 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Two men from among those who feared (God), on whom God had bestowed His favour, said: "Enter upon them through the gate."﴾ The most well-known view among the exegetes (mufassirun) is that the two men were Yusha' ibn Nun ibn Afrathim ibn Yusuf, who was the son of Musa's sister, and Caleb ibn Yuqanna, Musa's brother-in-law through his sister Maryam daughter of Imran. It is also said that his name is Kilab, and it is said Kaluw. These two were among the chieftains (nuqaba') whom Musa had sent to investigate the condition of the giants (jababirah). They concealed what they had observed of the condition of the giants, except from Musa, but the rest of the chieftains spread that news among their tribes, and this led them to weakness and cowardice, to the point that they refused to fight. It is also said that the two men were from among the giants who believed in Musa and followed him, and God bestowed upon them faith. If the two men were Yusha' and Caleb, then the meaning of His words "who feared" is: who feared God. In that case there were with Musa people who feared God and did not care about the enemy, because their faith was sound and their hearts were steadfast, and these two were among them. Or they feared the enemy, but God bestowed upon them faith and steadfastness. Or the Children of Israel feared them, and then the pronoun in "yakhafuna" (they fear) refers to the Children of Israel, and the connecting pronoun linking the relative clause to the relative pronoun is omitted, its implied form being: "from among those whom they fear", i.e., whom the Children of Israel fear. This interpretation is supported by the recitation (qira'ah) of Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid, who read "yukhafuna" with a dammah on the ya'. This recitation admits that the two men were Yusha' and Caleb. The meaning of "yukhafuna" is: they are revered and held in awe, and their words are heeded, because of their piety and merit. It may also be from "akhafa", meaning: they frighten (the enemy) through God's commands, prohibitions, warnings and threats. In that case this is praise for them, like His words: ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts God has tested for piety﴾ [al-Hujurat: 3]. The clause ﴿on whom God had bestowed His favour﴾ is a description of the word "two men": first described by the prepositional phrase, then secondly by the clause. This follows the more common order of placing the prepositional phrase or adverbial before the clause when both are used as descriptions. It is also permitted that the clause be a circumstantial clause (hal) with "qad" implied, or a parenthetical clause (i'tiradan), in which case it has no place in the grammatical structure (i'rab). In the recitation of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud): "on whom God had bestowed His favour, woe to you, enter upon them through the gate." "The gate" means the gate of the city of the giants. The meaning is: advance to jihad and strive until you enter upon them through the gate. This indicates that Musa had camped near the city.

﴿So when you enter it, you will surely be victorious.﴾ They said this in confidence in God's promise in His words: ﴿which God has prescribed for you﴾. It is also said: (they said it) in hope of God's aid to His messengers, and this became dominant in their assumption. No people are invaded in the heart of their homes except that they are humiliated, and when they do not guard the gate of their city until it is entered, which is the most important point, then surely they will not guard what is behind the gate. According to the view that the two men were from among the giants, it is said that they told them: "The Amalekites are bodies without hearts, so do not fear them, and return to them, for you will surely overcome them," as encouragement for them to fight them.

﴿And upon God rely, if you are believers.﴾ When the two saw that the Children of Israel had disobeyed the Messenger in advancing to jihad, despite God's earlier promise to them, they doubted their faith, so they commanded them to rely upon God, for He is the refuge and the recourse in times of hardship, and they conditioned this upon faith, the attainment of which they doubted for the Children of Israel.

﴿They said: "O Musa, we will never enter it as long as they are in it.﴾ When he repeated the command to fight to them, they repeated their refusal in the emphatic manner with two negations. First they restricted the negation of entry with a temporal adverbial that is specific to the future, whose real meaning is perpetuity (ta'bid), though it may be applied to a long period of time, so it was as if they negated entry for the length of eternity. Then they returned to tying that to the continuance of the giants within it, so they replaced a limited time with a time that is apparently general in the future. Thus it is a partial substitution (badal ba'd min kull).

﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight, both of you.﴾ The apparent meaning of "going" is moving from place to place, and this indicates that they were anthropomorphists (mushabbihah). For this reason al-Hasan said: "This is disbelief in God, the Exalted." Al-Zamakhshari said: "The apparent meaning is that they said this out of contempt for God and His messengers, with little concern for them, and mockingly, and they intended their actual going, because of their ignorance, harshness and hardness of hearts, with which they worshipped the calf and asked to see God openly. The evidence for this is that their going is contrasted with their sitting." It is related that Musa and Harun fell on their faces before them, because of the severity of what had befallen them, and they (the Children of Israel) intended to stone them. For a certain reason God joined the Jews with the polytheists and placed them before them in His words: ﴿You will surely find the most hostile of people toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate partners with God﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 82]. It is also said: it is possible that they did not intend actual going, but rather, as you say, "I spoke to him, so he went to answer me," meaning the sense of intention and purpose to answer; as if they said: "I want their coming forward."

The term "Lord" here refers to God, the Exalted. Al-Naqqash reported from some exegetes that the term "Lord" here refers to Harun, because he was older than Musa and was esteemed among the Children of Israel and loved for the breadth of his character and the openness of his heart; so it was as if they said: "Go, you and your elder." This is a far-fetched interpretation which spares the Children of Israel from disbelief. "Your Lord" is conjoined to the concealed pronoun in "go", which is emphasized by the separate pronoun. This matter has already been discussed in His words: ﴿Dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 19]. We have rejected the view of those who held that it is in the nominative case by an implied verb of command, which can be expressed explicitly, so that it is a conjoining of sentences; the implied sense: "So go, and let your Lord go." Some people held that the "wa" is the "wa" of circumstance, and "your Lord" is nominative as a subject with an implied predicate. Or the clause is a supplication, the implied sense in both: "and your Lord helps you." This interpretation is invalid because of His words "and fight".

(﴿We will remain seated here.﴾) This is evidence that their dispositions had weakened, so they were unable to rise with him to fight, nor to return from where they had come; rather they remained where the dialogue between Musa and them had taken place. The "ha" in His words "hahuna" is for emphasis of address, and "huna" is an adverb of place for what is near, and the governing element in it is "qa'idun" (remaining seated). In such a construction it is permitted that the predicate be the adverbial, and what follows it be a circumstantial clause in the accusative; and that the predicate be the noun and the adverbial be a complement to it. The latter is more eloquent.

﴿He said: "My Lord, I have no control except over myself and my brother.﴾ When they disobeyed God's command and rebelled against Musa, and he heard from them what he heard of the word of disbelief and of ill manners toward God, and no one remained with him in whom he trusted except Harun, he said this. This is speech in which the speaker expresses seeking refuge in God and complaint to Him, and a tenderness of heart that draws mercy and invites aid, like the words of Ya'qub: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God﴾ [Yusuf: 86]. It is related from Ali that he used to call people from the pulpit of Kufa to fight the hypocrites, but none answered him except two men. So he sighed deeply, prayed for them both, and said: "Where are you following me in what I intend?" The apparent meaning is that "and my brother" is conjoined to "myself". It is also possible that "and my brother" is nominative as a subject with an omitted predicate, indicated by what precedes it; the sense: "and my brother has no control except over himself." In this case he has conjoined a non-emphatic sentence to an emphatic one. Or it is accusative, conjoined to the noun of "inna" (indeed): i.e., "and indeed my brother has no control except over himself"; the predicate is omitted, and the noun and predicate are conjoined to the predicate, like: "Indeed Zayd is standing, and 'Amr is staring"; i.e., "and indeed 'Amr is staring." Ibn Atiyyah and al-Zamakhshari permitted that "and my brother" be nominative, conjoined to the concealed pronoun in "amliku" (I control), and they permitted this because of the separation between them by the restricted object. But it follows from this that Musa and Harun, peace be upon them, control only Musa's own self, and this is not the intended meaning; rather the apparent meaning is that Musa controls the matter of his own self and the matter of his brother only. He also permitted that it be genitive, conjoined to the first-person ya' in "nafsi" (my self), but this is weak according to the opinion of the Basrans. It seems that in this restriction he did not trust the two men who had said: ﴿Enter upon them through the gate﴾, and he was not at ease with their steadfastness, because of what he witnessed of his people's conditions and their changing, despite long companionship. So he mentioned only the infallible prophet whose steadfastness is beyond doubt. It is said: or he said this in a manner of annoyance when he heard from them, as an explanation for one who agrees with him; or by his words "and my brother" he meant whoever agreed with him in religion, not Harun specifically. Al-Hasan read "illa nafsi wa akhi" with a fatha on the ya' in both.

﴿So separate us from the defiant people.﴾ Its apparent meaning is that he prayed that God separate them from them, by causing them to lose sight of their faces and not witness their forms, when they disobeyed Him and opposed God's command, and for this reason he alerted to the cause that necessitates the separation between them and the wicked. The obedient one does not desire the companionship of the wicked and does not prefer it, lest he be afflicted by what afflicts them through association: ﴿And beware of a trial that will not strike only those among you who have done wrong﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. (Will you destroy us for what the wrongdoers among us did? And among us are the righteous.) God accepted his supplication, so they were not with them in the wandering (tih), but He separated him from them, because the wandering was a punishment specific to the defiant and disobedient. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and others said: the meaning is: "Decide between us by a judgment that removes this disagreement and gathers the scattered." It is also said: the meaning is: separate us from them in the Hereafter, so that the station of the obedient is distinct from the station of the disobedient, wicked one. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Decide between us and them by granting us what we deserve, and them what they deserve; and it has the sense of a supplication against them. For this reason he connected to it His words: ﴿for it is forbidden to them﴾, in the manner of an explanatory connection." Ubayd ibn Umayr and Yusuf ibn Dawud read "fafriq" with a kasrah on the ra'. The rajiz (a poet of the rajaz meter) said:

"O my Lord, separate him and me,
with the most severe separation You have made between two."

Ibn al-Sumayfa read "fafarriq". The "defiant" (fasiqun) here, Ibn Abbas said: the disobedient. Ibn Zayd said: the liars. Abu Ubayd said: the disbelievers.

﴿He said: "So it is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land.﴾ That is, God the Exalted said (this), so the one who said it is implied in "said" [i.e., God said], and the pronoun in "fa-innaha" refers to the Holy Land, ﴿forbidden to them﴾; i.e., its entry and their possession of it are forbidden. The discussion has already been made regarding the coherence of His words ﴿which God has prescribed for you﴾ with His words ﴿forbidden to them﴾, and this indicates that after the forty years it will not be forbidden to them. It is related that Musa and Harun, peace be upon them, were with them in the wandering as a punishment for them and as comfort and peace for the two of them, not as punishment, just as the fire was for Ibrahim and for the angels of punishment. It is related that after the forty years Musa set out with those of the Children of Israel who remained, and Yusha' and Caleb were at the vanguard. He conquered Jericho (Arihah) and killed 'Uj ibn 'Unuq. They mentioned descriptions of 'Uj and the manner of his killing by Musa that are not authentic. Musa remained there for as long as God willed, then he died. It is said: Harun died during the wandering. Ibn Atiyyah said: there is no disagreement about this. It is related: Musa died during the wandering eight years after Harun. It is said: six and a half months. It is said: one year. God gave Yusha' prophethood after the completion of the forty years, and the Children of Israel believed him, and he informed them that God had commanded him to fight the giants, so they believed him and pledged allegiance to him. He set out among them toward Jericho and killed the giants and drove them out, and all of Syria became the Children of Israel's. In that battle the sun stood still for Yusha' for an hour until he had continued and defeated the giants. Abu Tammam alluded to the standing still of the sun for Yusha' in his poetry, and said:

"The sun was returned to us while the night was humbled,
by a sun that appeared from beyond the curtain, rising.
Its light stripped away the dye of the darkness,
and the cloak of the spotted sky was folded up for its splendour."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 20–26 (part 3 of 3):**

Wa-llahi ma adri a-ahlamu na'imin * allammat bina am kana fi al-rakbi Yushaʿu
(By God, I do not know whether it was the dreams of a sleeper that visited us, or whether Joshua was in the caravan.)

Al-zahir (the apparent meaning) is that the governing element (al-ʿamil) in the word ʾarbaʿin (forty) is muharramatun (forbidden). In that case the prohibition is limited to this period. Yatihuna (they wander) is then either a new sentence (mustaʾnafan) or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ʿalayhim (upon them).

It is also permissible that the governing element is yatihuna, meaning: they will wander in the land for this period. In this case the prohibition is not limited to this period. Rather, it is a report that they will not enter it, and that they will nevertheless wander in the land for forty years, during which those who die will die.

It is related that whoever had passed twenty years of age did not live to leave the wandering, while those under twenty did live. As if the responsible sinners did not live. Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) pointed to this, and for this reason he held that the governing element in arbaʿin is muharramatun.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is possible that the governing element in arbaʿin is an implied element indicated by the later yatihuna. End of quotation.

I do not know what led him to say that the governing element is implied, as he stated. Rather, what people have permitted in this matter is that the governing element is yatihuna itself, not an implied element explained by the words ﴿they wander in the land﴾.

The land in which they wandered, according to what has been reported, was thirty miles long and six farsakh (parasangs) wide, which is the distance between Egypt and Syria. Ibn ʿAbbas said: nine farsakh. Muqatil said: this is its width, and its length is thirty farsakh. It was also said: six farsakh in length and twelve farsakh in width, and it was said: nine farsakh.

The statements of the commentators agree that this wandering was by way of khariq al-ʿadah (breaking of the normal custom, i.e. a miracle), for it is a wonder of God's power, since it was possible for a group of intelligent people to travel a short distance of farsakh without finding their way out of it. It is related that they used to travel at night and would journey the whole night, so that when they awoke in the morning they found all of them in the place where they had started. And they would travel by day, striving, until when evening came they found themselves in the place from which they had set out. Thus their travel was circling. Mujahid and others said: they would sometimes travel by day and sometimes by night, so they would reach the evening where they had been in the morning, and the morning where they had been in the evening. This was within a distance of six farsakh, and they were in a wandering with no place of rest. End of quotation.

It has been mentioned (p-459) that they were six hundred thousand fighting men. They also mentioned that the wisdom of the wandering was that when they said ﴿Indeed, we will remain seated here﴾, they were punished with sitting, so they came to be in the form of those who sit while they were travelling. Whenever they travelled for a day, by evening they were in the place where they had been in the morning.

They also mentioned that the wisdom of the period in which they wandered being forty years was that they had worshipped the calf for forty days, so the punishment was made one year for each day in the wandering.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is also possible that their wandering was by the splitting of their word and the scarcity of agreement in opinion, and that God cast disagreement among them. They knew that the land was forbidden to them for forty years, so their dwellings scattered throughout that open expanse, and they continued to move from place to place without order or unity until this period was completed, and God permitted their departure. This is a wandering that is possible and plausible according to human custom. The other [explanation], which Mujahid mentioned, is merely a breaking of custom and a wonder of God's power.

﴿So do not grieve over the defiant people﴾. The apparent meaning is that the address is from God, the Exalted, to Musa (peace be upon him). Ibn ʿAbbas said: Musa regretted his supplication against his people and grieved for them. End of quotation. So this is a consolation to Musa, peace be upon him, against grieving over what befell his people, and the reason given for his not grieving is that they are defiant people, bahut (liars), deserving of the punishment that befell them.

It was also said: the address is to Muhammad (ﷺ), and by "the defiant" is meant his contemporaries. That is: these are the deeds of their forefathers. So do not grieve, you, because of their wicked deeds with you and their rejection of you, for this is a wicked disposition inherited among them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 20–26 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, remember the favour of God upon you when He appointed prophets among you, made you kings, and gave you what He had not given to anyone among the worlds."﴾ The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that He, exalted is He, explained the rebelliousness of the ancestors of the Jews against Moses and their disobedience to him, along with his reminding them of God's blessings and his enumeration of the greatest of them. And these people who are in the presence of the Messenger are following in the path of their ancestors with Moses. The "favour of God" is meant in the generic sense. The meaning is: "Recount to them, O Muhammad, by way of informing them of the unseen (contents) of their books, so that they may verify your prophethood." This includes mention of God's favours upon them and their receiving those favours with disbelief and little obedience. He enumerated three of His favours upon them. The first: the appointing of prophets among them, and this is the greatest honour, since they are the intermediaries between God and His creation and the ones who convey His laws from God. It has been said: no nation was sent as many prophets as the Children of Israel. Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil said: the "prophets" here are the seventy whom Moses chose for the appointed time of his Lord, and they were among the best of his people. It has been said: they are those who were sent afterwards among the Children of Israel, like Moses; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi and others. According to this view, "made" (ja'ala) does not mean the literal past in actuality, since some of them had appeared at the time of Moses' address to them, and some had not yet been created but he informed that they would be among them. The second: making them kings. Its apparent meaning is a favour upon them, in that He made them kings, since He made kings from among them, for kingship is a worldly honour and dominion. So He reminded them that among them were leaders of the Hereafter and leaders of this world. Al-Suddi and others said: He made you free, those who own and are not owned, since you were servants to the Copts, and He rescued you from them, so their rescue was called kingship. Some said: He made them kings by sending down the manna and quails upon them (p-453), and by making the rock gush forth for them, and by making their clothes neither wear out nor become soiled, and growing as they grew; so they are kings because this burden was lifted from them. Qatadah said: "kings" because they were the first to employ servants and acquire slaves. Ibn 'Atiyyah and Qatadah said: He only said "and made you kings" because we used to hear that the first to serve a human being was another human being. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is weak, because the Copts used to make the Children of Israel serve them. The apparent state of the children of Adam is that some of them have subjected others to service since they multiplied and spread. End of quotation.
These three views are general to all the Children of Israel, and this is the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿and made you kings﴾. 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and a group said: whoever has a dwelling, a wife, and a servant is a king. It has been said: whoever has a dwelling into which no one may enter without permission is a king. It has been said: whoever has a wife and a servant; this was related from Ibn 'Abbas. 'Ikrimah said: whoever possesses a servant and a house among them is called a king among them. It has been said: whoever has a spacious dwelling in which there is running water. It has been said: whoever has wealth that does not require him to undertake laborious tasks and bear hardships. It has been said: they are kings through their contentment, and this is a hidden kingship. For this reason it came in the hadith: "Contentment is a treasure that never runs out." It has been said: because they possessed their own selves and protected them from disbelief and from following Pharaoh. It has been said: they possessed the desires of their own souls. Al-Tibrizi mentioned these three views in his tafsir. The third: His giving them what He had not given to anyone among the worlds. Ibn 'Abbas explained it, as related from him by Mujahid, as: the manna, the quails, the rock, and the cloud. 'Ata' related from him: the house, the wife, and the servant. It has been said: the multitude of prophets. Ibn Jarir said: no one among the people of Moses' time was given blessings like those given to them. They were singled out with the splitting of the sea for them, the sending down of the manna and quails, the bringing forth of sweet water from the rock, and the cloud being spread over them. Prophethood and kingship were never combined for one people as they were combined for them, and in those days they were the scholars of God, His beloved ones, and the supporters of His religion. End of quotation. What is meant is either the multitude of prophets or the particular features of the totality of Moses' signs. Thus the word "the worlds" is restricted to the time in which the Children of Israel existed, because the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) has been given, from the signs of Muhammad (ﷺ), more than that. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was shaded by a cloud before his mission; stones and animals spoke to him; a tree came towards him; the trunk moaned for him; water gushed from between his fingers; many people were satisfied from a small amount of food through his blessing; the moon was split for him; a staff returned as a sword; and a rock blocking the trench turned into scattered sand. Beyond these, there are his greatest signs and his mightiest miracles. This statement from Moses to the Children of Israel and his reminding them of God's favours is a preparation for their souls and an advance warning of what would befall them concerning the fight against the giants, so that their hearts might be strengthened and they might know that whoever God has favoured with these great blessings, God will not forsake, but will raise him over his enemy, elevate his station, and give him authority and dominance over them.
The address in His words "and gave you" — its apparent meaning is that it is to the Children of Israel, as we have explained, and that it is part of Moses' speech to them, and this is the view of the majority. Abu Malik and Ibn Jubayr said: it is an address to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). The speech ends at His words: ﴿and made you kings﴾; then He turned to this community. When Moses reminded his people of God's blessings, God reminded the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) of this apparent blessing, to comfort their hearts, and that He gave them what He had not given to anyone among the worlds. On this view, "the worlds" is general, for God has preferred the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) over the rest of the nations, given them what He has not given anyone among the worlds, and bestowed upon them blessings that He has not bestowed upon any nation. This is the meaning of Ibn Jarir's view, and it is his preferred opinion. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is weak. It was weakened in his view because the speech is in one continuous sequence of Moses' address to his people, and this is connected to what precedes it. But what he said is not necessarily binding, because the Qur'an came according to the rules of Arabic speech, which include shifts (al-iltifat, a change of addressee) and moving from one address to another, especially when the apparent address does not suit the one first addressed, but suits the one addressed second. Thus the apparent meaning, when taken literally, strengthens the direction of the address to the second. Ibn Muhaysin read: "yā qawmu" with a damma on the mim, and so wherever it occurs in the Qur'an (p-454). This was related from Ibn Kathir. This damma is according to the sense of the construct (idafa), like the reading of the one who read: "Qul rabbu uhkum bil-haqq" with a damma. It is one of the five permissible dialects for the vocative noun when attached to the first-person ya' (my).
﴿O my people, enter the holy land which God has prescribed for you.﴾ "The holy land" (al-muqaddasa) means the purified one. It is Jericho; this was said by al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd, and 'Ikrimah related it from Ibn 'Abbas. It has been said: it is the site of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It has been said: Iliya. Ibn Qutaybah said: I read in the supplication of Moses; he said: "O God, You have chosen," then he mentioned things, then he said: "Lord of Iliya, the Bayt al-Maqdis." Ibn al-Jawzi said: I read to Abu Mansur the linguist, who said: Iliya is Bayt al-Maqdis. Al-Farazdaq said:
"Two houses: the House of God, which we visit, and another house, elevated and honoured, in the highest part of Iliya."
It has been said: it is Mount Tur; this was related by Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Zajjaj preferred it. It has been said: Palestine, Damascus, and part of Jordan. Qatadah said: it is the Levant. Al-Kalbi said: Abraham (peace be upon him) climbed Mount Lebanon, and Gabriel said to him: "Look; whatever your sight reaches is holy, and it is an inheritance for your offspring." It has been said: what lies between the Euphrates and the Brook of Egypt ('Arish). Al-Tabari said: there is no disagreement that it is what lies between the Euphrates and the Brook of Egypt. He said: al-Udfuwi said: the people of exegesis, the historians, and the scholars of reports unanimously agreed that it is what lies between the Euphrates and the Brook of Egypt. Al-Tabari said: the reports are unanimous that Damascus is the capital of the giants. End of quotation.
"Sanctification" (al-taqdis) means purification; it has been said: from calamities. It has been said: from polytheism. It was made a dwelling and abode for the prophets, and the domination of the giants over it does not remove it from being holy. It has been said: "holy" means blessed; it was purified from drought, famine, and other things; this was said by Mujahid. It has been said: it was called holy because in it is the place where one is sanctified from sins; and from this comes the saying that a bucket is called qudus, because one performs ablution with it and purifies oneself. The meaning of "God prescribed it for you" is: He apportioned it, named it, or inscribed on the Tablet that it is for you a dwelling and an abode. Ibn Ishaq said: He granted it to you. Al-Suddi said: He commanded you to enter it, and this is an encouragement to them and a strengthening when He informed them that God has prescribed it for them. The apparent use of "prescribed" (kataba) is in the sense of obligation, as in His words: ﴿Fasting is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183] and ﴿Fighting is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216]. As for if "He prescribed it" means "inscribed it in eternity and decreed it," then the apparent wording does not need to conflict with His words: ﴿it is forbidden to them﴾. It has been said: the wording is general, and the intended meaning is particular; as if He said: it is prescribed for some of them and forbidden for others. Or this is conditional on the condition of obeying the fight, and since they did not obey, the condition did not occur. Or the prohibition was limited to forty years, and when they were over, what He had prescribed came about. As for if He prescribed it for them in the sense of commanding them to enter it, then it does not conflict with the prohibition. It was forbidden for them to enter it, and they died in the wilderness, and their sons who had not been prohibited entered with Moses. It has been said: Moses and Aaron (peace be upon them both) died in the wilderness, and only their sons went out with Hizqil. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was a gift, then He forbade it to them because of their disobedience.
﴿And do not turn back on your heels, lest you become losers.﴾ That is: do not recoil upon your heels out of fear of the tyrants, through cowardice and panic. It has been said: when the chieftains informed them of the condition of the giants, they raised their voices in weeping and said: "Would that we had died in Egypt!" and they said: "Let us appoint a leader who will lead us back to Egypt." It is possible that what is meant is: do not turn back on your heels in your religion by opposing the command of your Lord.
As for their "turning back as losers": if "turning back" is literal, namely returning to the place from which they left, then its meaning is that they will fall into humiliation after honour and deliverance from the hands of the Copts. If "turning back" is metaphorical, namely their apostasy from their religion, then its meaning is that they will lose the good of this world and the reward of the Hereafter. Whoever opposes what God has obligated upon him of struggle and opposes His command deserves to be a loser.
﴿They said, "O Moses, indeed there are in it a people of giants.﴾ That is: the chieftains whom Moses sent to examine the condition of the giants said, or their leaders said, whose custom was to be informed of secrets and consulted in matters. This statement is remote, given their reluctance to fight; that is: indeed there are in it people whom we cannot fight. It has been said: they are remnants of 'Ad (p-455). It has been said: they are of the Romans, from the sons of Esau son of Isaac. Ibn al-Sumayqa read: "They said, 'O Moses, in it is a people who are giants.'"
﴿And we will never enter it until they leave it.﴾ This is an explicit declaration of total refusal to fight the giants, and for this reason the negation was with "lan" (never). "Until they leave it" means: by someone else fighting them, or by a cause through which God makes them leave, and then they will leave.
﴿So if they leave it, then we will enter.﴾ This is a deliberate direction from them to themselves by the departure of the giants from it, since they made their entry conditional upon a possible condition. Most exegetes said: they did not doubt what God had promised them, but their recoiling from fighting was due to the weakness of nature and the cowardice that God had built into them, and no one can overcome that except the one whom God protects. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except for a few of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246]. It has been said: they said this as a way of considering it unlikely that the giants would leave it, like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Nor will they enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf: 40].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 20–26 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Two men from among those who feared (God), on whom God had bestowed His favour, said: "Enter upon them through the gate."﴾ The most well-known view among the exegetes (mufassirun) is that the two men were Yusha' ibn Nun ibn Afrathim ibn Yusuf, who was the son of Musa's sister, and Caleb ibn Yuqanna, Musa's brother-in-law through his sister Maryam daughter of Imran. It is also said that his name is Kilab, and it is said Kaluw. These two were among the chieftains (nuqaba') whom Musa had sent to investigate the condition of the giants (jababirah). They concealed what they had observed of the condition of the giants, except from Musa, but the rest of the chieftains spread that news among their tribes, and this led them to weakness and cowardice, to the point that they refused to fight. It is also said that the two men were from among the giants who believed in Musa and followed him, and God bestowed upon them faith. If the two men were Yusha' and Caleb, then the meaning of His words "who feared" is: who feared God. In that case there were with Musa people who feared God and did not care about the enemy, because their faith was sound and their hearts were steadfast, and these two were among them. Or they feared the enemy, but God bestowed upon them faith and steadfastness. Or the Children of Israel feared them, and then the pronoun in "yakhafuna" (they fear) refers to the Children of Israel, and the connecting pronoun linking the relative clause to the relative pronoun is omitted, its implied form being: "from among those whom they fear", i.e., whom the Children of Israel fear. This interpretation is supported by the recitation (qira'ah) of Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid, who read "yukhafuna" with a dammah on the ya'. This recitation admits that the two men were Yusha' and Caleb. The meaning of "yukhafuna" is: they are revered and held in awe, and their words are heeded, because of their piety and merit. It may also be from "akhafa", meaning: they frighten (the enemy) through God's commands, prohibitions, warnings and threats. In that case this is praise for them, like His words: ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts God has tested for piety﴾ [al-Hujurat: 3]. The clause ﴿on whom God had bestowed His favour﴾ is a description of the word "two men": first described by the prepositional phrase, then secondly by the clause. This follows the more common order of placing the prepositional phrase or adverbial before the clause when both are used as descriptions. It is also permitted that the clause be a circumstantial clause (hal) with "qad" implied, or a parenthetical clause (i'tiradan), in which case it has no place in the grammatical structure (i'rab). In the recitation of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud): "on whom God had bestowed His favour, woe to you, enter upon them through the gate." "The gate" means the gate of the city of the giants. The meaning is: advance to jihad and strive until you enter upon them through the gate. This indicates that Musa had camped near the city.

﴿So when you enter it, you will surely be victorious.﴾ They said this in confidence in God's promise in His words: ﴿which God has prescribed for you﴾. It is also said: (they said it) in hope of God's aid to His messengers, and this became dominant in their assumption. No people are invaded in the heart of their homes except that they are humiliated, and when they do not guard the gate of their city until it is entered, which is the most important point, then surely they will not guard what is behind the gate. According to the view that the two men were from among the giants, it is said that they told them: "The Amalekites are bodies without hearts, so do not fear them, and return to them, for you will surely overcome them," as encouragement for them to fight them.

﴿And upon God rely, if you are believers.﴾ When the two saw that the Children of Israel had disobeyed the Messenger in advancing to jihad, despite God's earlier promise to them, they doubted their faith, so they commanded them to rely upon God, for He is the refuge and the recourse in times of hardship, and they conditioned this upon faith, the attainment of which they doubted for the Children of Israel.

﴿They said: "O Musa, we will never enter it as long as they are in it.﴾ When he repeated the command to fight to them, they repeated their refusal in the emphatic manner with two negations. First they restricted the negation of entry with a temporal adverbial that is specific to the future, whose real meaning is perpetuity (ta'bid), though it may be applied to a long period of time, so it was as if they negated entry for the length of eternity. Then they returned to tying that to the continuance of the giants within it, so they replaced a limited time with a time that is apparently general in the future. Thus it is a partial substitution (badal ba'd min kull).

﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight, both of you.﴾ The apparent meaning of "going" is moving from place to place, and this indicates that they were anthropomorphists (mushabbihah). For this reason al-Hasan said: "This is disbelief in God, the Exalted." Al-Zamakhshari said: "The apparent meaning is that they said this out of contempt for God and His messengers, with little concern for them, and mockingly, and they intended their actual going, because of their ignorance, harshness and hardness of hearts, with which they worshipped the calf and asked to see God openly. The evidence for this is that their going is contrasted with their sitting." It is related that Musa and Harun fell on their faces before them, because of the severity of what had befallen them, and they (the Children of Israel) intended to stone them. For a certain reason God joined the Jews with the polytheists and placed them before them in His words: ﴿You will surely find the most hostile of people toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate partners with God﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 82]. It is also said: it is possible that they did not intend actual going, but rather, as you say, "I spoke to him, so he went to answer me," meaning the sense of intention and purpose to answer; as if they said: "I want their coming forward."

The term "Lord" here refers to God, the Exalted. Al-Naqqash reported from some exegetes that the term "Lord" here refers to Harun, because he was older than Musa and was esteemed among the Children of Israel and loved for the breadth of his character and the openness of his heart; so it was as if they said: "Go, you and your elder." This is a far-fetched interpretation which spares the Children of Israel from disbelief. "Your Lord" is conjoined to the concealed pronoun in "go", which is emphasized by the separate pronoun. This matter has already been discussed in His words: ﴿Dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 19]. We have rejected the view of those who held that it is in the nominative case by an implied verb of command, which can be expressed explicitly, so that it is a conjoining of sentences; the implied sense: "So go, and let your Lord go." Some people held that the "wa" is the "wa" of circumstance, and "your Lord" is nominative as a subject with an implied predicate. Or the clause is a supplication, the implied sense in both: "and your Lord helps you." This interpretation is invalid because of His words "and fight".

(﴿We will remain seated here.﴾) This is evidence that their dispositions had weakened, so they were unable to rise with him to fight, nor to return from where they had come; rather they remained where the dialogue between Musa and them had taken place. The "ha" in His words "hahuna" is for emphasis of address, and "huna" is an adverb of place for what is near, and the governing element in it is "qa'idun" (remaining seated). In such a construction it is permitted that the predicate be the adverbial, and what follows it be a circumstantial clause in the accusative; and that the predicate be the noun and the adverbial be a complement to it. The latter is more eloquent.

﴿He said: "My Lord, I have no control except over myself and my brother.﴾ When they disobeyed God's command and rebelled against Musa, and he heard from them what he heard of the word of disbelief and of ill manners toward God, and no one remained with him in whom he trusted except Harun, he said this. This is speech in which the speaker expresses seeking refuge in God and complaint to Him, and a tenderness of heart that draws mercy and invites aid, like the words of Ya'qub: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God﴾ [Yusuf: 86]. It is related from Ali that he used to call people from the pulpit of Kufa to fight the hypocrites, but none answered him except two men. So he sighed deeply, prayed for them both, and said: "Where are you following me in what I intend?" The apparent meaning is that "and my brother" is conjoined to "myself". It is also possible that "and my brother" is nominative as a subject with an omitted predicate, indicated by what precedes it; the sense: "and my brother has no control except over himself." In this case he has conjoined a non-emphatic sentence to an emphatic one. Or it is accusative, conjoined to the noun of "inna" (indeed): i.e., "and indeed my brother has no control except over himself"; the predicate is omitted, and the noun and predicate are conjoined to the predicate, like: "Indeed Zayd is standing, and 'Amr is staring"; i.e., "and indeed 'Amr is staring." Ibn Atiyyah and al-Zamakhshari permitted that "and my brother" be nominative, conjoined to the concealed pronoun in "amliku" (I control), and they permitted this because of the separation between them by the restricted object. But it follows from this that Musa and Harun, peace be upon them, control only Musa's own self, and this is not the intended meaning; rather the apparent meaning is that Musa controls the matter of his own self and the matter of his brother only. He also permitted that it be genitive, conjoined to the first-person ya' in "nafsi" (my self), but this is weak according to the opinion of the Basrans. It seems that in this restriction he did not trust the two men who had said: ﴿Enter upon them through the gate﴾, and he was not at ease with their steadfastness, because of what he witnessed of his people's conditions and their changing, despite long companionship. So he mentioned only the infallible prophet whose steadfastness is beyond doubt. It is said: or he said this in a manner of annoyance when he heard from them, as an explanation for one who agrees with him; or by his words "and my brother" he meant whoever agreed with him in religion, not Harun specifically. Al-Hasan read "illa nafsi wa akhi" with a fatha on the ya' in both.

﴿So separate us from the defiant people.﴾ Its apparent meaning is that he prayed that God separate them from them, by causing them to lose sight of their faces and not witness their forms, when they disobeyed Him and opposed God's command, and for this reason he alerted to the cause that necessitates the separation between them and the wicked. The obedient one does not desire the companionship of the wicked and does not prefer it, lest he be afflicted by what afflicts them through association: ﴿And beware of a trial that will not strike only those among you who have done wrong﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. (Will you destroy us for what the wrongdoers among us did? And among us are the righteous.) God accepted his supplication, so they were not with them in the wandering (tih), but He separated him from them, because the wandering was a punishment specific to the defiant and disobedient. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and others said: the meaning is: "Decide between us by a judgment that removes this disagreement and gathers the scattered." It is also said: the meaning is: separate us from them in the Hereafter, so that the station of the obedient is distinct from the station of the disobedient, wicked one. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Decide between us and them by granting us what we deserve, and them what they deserve; and it has the sense of a supplication against them. For this reason he connected to it His words: ﴿for it is forbidden to them﴾, in the manner of an explanatory connection." Ubayd ibn Umayr and Yusuf ibn Dawud read "fafriq" with a kasrah on the ra'. The rajiz (a poet of the rajaz meter) said:

"O my Lord, separate him and me,
with the most severe separation You have made between two."

Ibn al-Sumayfa read "fafarriq". The "defiant" (fasiqun) here, Ibn Abbas said: the disobedient. Ibn Zayd said: the liars. Abu Ubayd said: the disbelievers.

﴿He said: "So it is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land.﴾ That is, God the Exalted said (this), so the one who said it is implied in "said" [i.e., God said], and the pronoun in "fa-innaha" refers to the Holy Land, ﴿forbidden to them﴾; i.e., its entry and their possession of it are forbidden. The discussion has already been made regarding the coherence of His words ﴿which God has prescribed for you﴾ with His words ﴿forbidden to them﴾, and this indicates that after the forty years it will not be forbidden to them. It is related that Musa and Harun, peace be upon them, were with them in the wandering as a punishment for them and as comfort and peace for the two of them, not as punishment, just as the fire was for Ibrahim and for the angels of punishment. It is related that after the forty years Musa set out with those of the Children of Israel who remained, and Yusha' and Caleb were at the vanguard. He conquered Jericho (Arihah) and killed 'Uj ibn 'Unuq. They mentioned descriptions of 'Uj and the manner of his killing by Musa that are not authentic. Musa remained there for as long as God willed, then he died. It is said: Harun died during the wandering. Ibn Atiyyah said: there is no disagreement about this. It is related: Musa died during the wandering eight years after Harun. It is said: six and a half months. It is said: one year. God gave Yusha' prophethood after the completion of the forty years, and the Children of Israel believed him, and he informed them that God had commanded him to fight the giants, so they believed him and pledged allegiance to him. He set out among them toward Jericho and killed the giants and drove them out, and all of Syria became the Children of Israel's. In that battle the sun stood still for Yusha' for an hour until he had continued and defeated the giants. Abu Tammam alluded to the standing still of the sun for Yusha' in his poetry, and said:

"The sun was returned to us while the night was humbled,
by a sun that appeared from beyond the curtain, rising.
Its light stripped away the dye of the darkness,
and the cloak of the spotted sky was folded up for its splendour."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 20–26 (part 3 of 3):**

Wa-llahi ma adri a-ahlamu na'imin * allammat bina am kana fi al-rakbi Yushaʿu
(By God, I do not know whether it was the dreams of a sleeper that visited us, or whether Joshua was in the caravan.)

Al-zahir (the apparent meaning) is that the governing element (al-ʿamil) in the word ʾarbaʿin (forty) is muharramatun (forbidden). In that case the prohibition is limited to this period. Yatihuna (they wander) is then either a new sentence (mustaʾnafan) or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ʿalayhim (upon them).

It is also permissible that the governing element is yatihuna, meaning: they will wander in the land for this period. In this case the prohibition is not limited to this period. Rather, it is a report that they will not enter it, and that they will nevertheless wander in the land for forty years, during which those who die will die.

It is related that whoever had passed twenty years of age did not live to leave the wandering, while those under twenty did live. As if the responsible sinners did not live. Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) pointed to this, and for this reason he held that the governing element in arbaʿin is muharramatun.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is possible that the governing element in arbaʿin is an implied element indicated by the later yatihuna. End of quotation.

I do not know what led him to say that the governing element is implied, as he stated. Rather, what people have permitted in this matter is that the governing element is yatihuna itself, not an implied element explained by the words ﴿they wander in the land﴾.

The land in which they wandered, according to what has been reported, was thirty miles long and six farsakh (parasangs) wide, which is the distance between Egypt and Syria. Ibn ʿAbbas said: nine farsakh. Muqatil said: this is its width, and its length is thirty farsakh. It was also said: six farsakh in length and twelve farsakh in width, and it was said: nine farsakh.

The statements of the commentators agree that this wandering was by way of khariq al-ʿadah (breaking of the normal custom, i.e. a miracle), for it is a wonder of God's power, since it was possible for a group of intelligent people to travel a short distance of farsakh without finding their way out of it. It is related that they used to travel at night and would journey the whole night, so that when they awoke in the morning they found all of them in the place where they had started. And they would travel by day, striving, until when evening came they found themselves in the place from which they had set out. Thus their travel was circling. Mujahid and others said: they would sometimes travel by day and sometimes by night, so they would reach the evening where they had been in the morning, and the morning where they had been in the evening. This was within a distance of six farsakh, and they were in a wandering with no place of rest. End of quotation.

It has been mentioned (p-459) that they were six hundred thousand fighting men. They also mentioned that the wisdom of the wandering was that when they said ﴿Indeed, we will remain seated here﴾, they were punished with sitting, so they came to be in the form of those who sit while they were travelling. Whenever they travelled for a day, by evening they were in the place where they had been in the morning.

They also mentioned that the wisdom of the period in which they wandered being forty years was that they had worshipped the calf for forty days, so the punishment was made one year for each day in the wandering.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is also possible that their wandering was by the splitting of their word and the scarcity of agreement in opinion, and that God cast disagreement among them. They knew that the land was forbidden to them for forty years, so their dwellings scattered throughout that open expanse, and they continued to move from place to place without order or unity until this period was completed, and God permitted their departure. This is a wandering that is possible and plausible according to human custom. The other [explanation], which Mujahid mentioned, is merely a breaking of custom and a wonder of God's power.

﴿So do not grieve over the defiant people﴾. The apparent meaning is that the address is from God, the Exalted, to Musa (peace be upon him). Ibn ʿAbbas said: Musa regretted his supplication against his people and grieved for them. End of quotation. So this is a consolation to Musa, peace be upon him, against grieving over what befell his people, and the reason given for his not grieving is that they are defiant people, bahut (liars), deserving of the punishment that befell them.

It was also said: the address is to Muhammad (ﷺ), and by "the defiant" is meant his contemporaries. That is: these are the deeds of their forefathers. So do not grieve, you, because of their wicked deeds with you and their rejection of you, for this is a wicked disposition inherited among them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 20–26 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, remember the favour of God upon you when He appointed prophets among you, made you kings, and gave you what He had not given to anyone among the worlds."﴾ The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that He, exalted is He, explained the rebelliousness of the ancestors of the Jews against Moses and their disobedience to him, along with his reminding them of God's blessings and his enumeration of the greatest of them. And these people who are in the presence of the Messenger are following in the path of their ancestors with Moses. The "favour of God" is meant in the generic sense. The meaning is: "Recount to them, O Muhammad, by way of informing them of the unseen (contents) of their books, so that they may verify your prophethood." This includes mention of God's favours upon them and their receiving those favours with disbelief and little obedience. He enumerated three of His favours upon them. The first: the appointing of prophets among them, and this is the greatest honour, since they are the intermediaries between God and His creation and the ones who convey His laws from God. It has been said: no nation was sent as many prophets as the Children of Israel. Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil said: the "prophets" here are the seventy whom Moses chose for the appointed time of his Lord, and they were among the best of his people. It has been said: they are those who were sent afterwards among the Children of Israel, like Moses; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi and others. According to this view, "made" (ja'ala) does not mean the literal past in actuality, since some of them had appeared at the time of Moses' address to them, and some had not yet been created but he informed that they would be among them. The second: making them kings. Its apparent meaning is a favour upon them, in that He made them kings, since He made kings from among them, for kingship is a worldly honour and dominion. So He reminded them that among them were leaders of the Hereafter and leaders of this world. Al-Suddi and others said: He made you free, those who own and are not owned, since you were servants to the Copts, and He rescued you from them, so their rescue was called kingship. Some said: He made them kings by sending down the manna and quails upon them (p-453), and by making the rock gush forth for them, and by making their clothes neither wear out nor become soiled, and growing as they grew; so they are kings because this burden was lifted from them. Qatadah said: "kings" because they were the first to employ servants and acquire slaves. Ibn 'Atiyyah and Qatadah said: He only said "and made you kings" because we used to hear that the first to serve a human being was another human being. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is weak, because the Copts used to make the Children of Israel serve them. The apparent state of the children of Adam is that some of them have subjected others to service since they multiplied and spread. End of quotation.
These three views are general to all the Children of Israel, and this is the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿and made you kings﴾. 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and a group said: whoever has a dwelling, a wife, and a servant is a king. It has been said: whoever has a dwelling into which no one may enter without permission is a king. It has been said: whoever has a wife and a servant; this was related from Ibn 'Abbas. 'Ikrimah said: whoever possesses a servant and a house among them is called a king among them. It has been said: whoever has a spacious dwelling in which there is running water. It has been said: whoever has wealth that does not require him to undertake laborious tasks and bear hardships. It has been said: they are kings through their contentment, and this is a hidden kingship. For this reason it came in the hadith: "Contentment is a treasure that never runs out." It has been said: because they possessed their own selves and protected them from disbelief and from following Pharaoh. It has been said: they possessed the desires of their own souls. Al-Tibrizi mentioned these three views in his tafsir. The third: His giving them what He had not given to anyone among the worlds. Ibn 'Abbas explained it, as related from him by Mujahid, as: the manna, the quails, the rock, and the cloud. 'Ata' related from him: the house, the wife, and the servant. It has been said: the multitude of prophets. Ibn Jarir said: no one among the people of Moses' time was given blessings like those given to them. They were singled out with the splitting of the sea for them, the sending down of the manna and quails, the bringing forth of sweet water from the rock, and the cloud being spread over them. Prophethood and kingship were never combined for one people as they were combined for them, and in those days they were the scholars of God, His beloved ones, and the supporters of His religion. End of quotation. What is meant is either the multitude of prophets or the particular features of the totality of Moses' signs. Thus the word "the worlds" is restricted to the time in which the Children of Israel existed, because the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) has been given, from the signs of Muhammad (ﷺ), more than that. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was shaded by a cloud before his mission; stones and animals spoke to him; a tree came towards him; the trunk moaned for him; water gushed from between his fingers; many people were satisfied from a small amount of food through his blessing; the moon was split for him; a staff returned as a sword; and a rock blocking the trench turned into scattered sand. Beyond these, there are his greatest signs and his mightiest miracles. This statement from Moses to the Children of Israel and his reminding them of God's favours is a preparation for their souls and an advance warning of what would befall them concerning the fight against the giants, so that their hearts might be strengthened and they might know that whoever God has favoured with these great blessings, God will not forsake, but will raise him over his enemy, elevate his station, and give him authority and dominance over them.
The address in His words "and gave you" — its apparent meaning is that it is to the Children of Israel, as we have explained, and that it is part of Moses' speech to them, and this is the view of the majority. Abu Malik and Ibn Jubayr said: it is an address to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). The speech ends at His words: ﴿and made you kings﴾; then He turned to this community. When Moses reminded his people of God's blessings, God reminded the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) of this apparent blessing, to comfort their hearts, and that He gave them what He had not given to anyone among the worlds. On this view, "the worlds" is general, for God has preferred the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) over the rest of the nations, given them what He has not given anyone among the worlds, and bestowed upon them blessings that He has not bestowed upon any nation. This is the meaning of Ibn Jarir's view, and it is his preferred opinion. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is weak. It was weakened in his view because the speech is in one continuous sequence of Moses' address to his people, and this is connected to what precedes it. But what he said is not necessarily binding, because the Qur'an came according to the rules of Arabic speech, which include shifts (al-iltifat, a change of addressee) and moving from one address to another, especially when the apparent address does not suit the one first addressed, but suits the one addressed second. Thus the apparent meaning, when taken literally, strengthens the direction of the address to the second. Ibn Muhaysin read: "yā qawmu" with a damma on the mim, and so wherever it occurs in the Qur'an (p-454). This was related from Ibn Kathir. This damma is according to the sense of the construct (idafa), like the reading of the one who read: "Qul rabbu uhkum bil-haqq" with a damma. It is one of the five permissible dialects for the vocative noun when attached to the first-person ya' (my).
﴿O my people, enter the holy land which God has prescribed for you.﴾ "The holy land" (al-muqaddasa) means the purified one.
