First they restricted the negation of entry with a temporal adverbial that is specific to the future, whose real meaning is perpetuity (ta'bid), though it may be applied to a long period of time, so it was as if they negated entry for the length of eternity. Then they returned to tying that to the continuance of the giants within it, so they replaced a limited time with a time that is apparently general in the future. Thus it is a partial substitution (badal ba'd min kull).

﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight, both of you.﴾ The apparent meaning of "going" is moving from place to place, and this indicates that they were anthropomorphists (mushabbihah). For this reason al-Hasan said: "This is disbelief in God, the Exalted." Al-Zamakhshari said: "The apparent meaning is that they said this out of contempt for God and His messengers, with little concern for them, and mockingly, and they intended their actual going, because of their ignorance, harshness and hardness of hearts, with which they worshipped the calf and asked to see God openly. The evidence for this is that their going is contrasted with their sitting." It is related that Musa and Harun fell on their faces before them, because of the severity of what had befallen them, and they (the Children of Israel) intended to stone them. For a certain reason God joined the Jews with the polytheists and placed them before them in His words: ﴿You will surely find the most hostile of people toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate partners with God﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 82]. It is also said: it is possible that they did not intend actual going, but rather, as you say, "I spoke to him, so he went to answer me," meaning the sense of intention and purpose to answer; as if they said: "I want their coming forward."

The term "Lord" here refers to God, the Exalted. Al-Naqqash reported from some exegetes that the term "Lord" here refers to Harun, because he was older than Musa and was esteemed among the Children of Israel and loved for the breadth of his character and the openness of his heart; so it was as if they said: "Go, you and your elder." This is a far-fetched interpretation which spares the Children of Israel from disbelief. "Your Lord" is conjoined to the concealed pronoun in "go", which is emphasized by the separate pronoun. This matter has already been discussed in His words: ﴿Dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 19]. We have rejected the view of those who held that it is in the nominative case by an implied verb of command, which can be expressed explicitly, so that it is a conjoining of sentences; the implied sense: "So go, and let your Lord go." Some people held that the "wa" is the "wa" of circumstance, and "your Lord" is nominative as a subject with an implied predicate. Or the clause is a supplication, the implied sense in both: "and your Lord helps you." This interpretation is invalid because of His words "and fight".

(﴿We will remain seated here.﴾) This is evidence that their dispositions had weakened, so they were unable to rise with him to fight, nor to return from where they had come; rather they remained where the dialogue between Musa and them had taken place. The "ha" in His words "hahuna" is for emphasis of address, and "huna" is an adverb of place for what is near, and the governing element in it is "qa'idun" (remaining seated). In such a construction it is permitted that the predicate be the adverbial, and what follows it be a circumstantial clause in the accusative; and that the predicate be the noun and the adverbial be a complement to it. The latter is more eloquent.

﴿He said: "My Lord, I have no control except over myself and my brother.﴾ When they disobeyed God's command and rebelled against Musa, and he heard from them what he heard of the word of disbelief and of ill manners toward God, and no one remained with him in whom he trusted except Harun, he said this. This is speech in which the speaker expresses seeking refuge in God and complaint to Him, and a tenderness of heart that draws mercy and invites aid, like the words of Ya'qub: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God﴾ [Yusuf: 86]. It is related from Ali that he used to call people from the pulpit of Kufa to fight the hypocrites, but none answered him except two men. So he sighed deeply, prayed for them both, and said: "Where are you following me in what I intend?" The apparent meaning is that "and my brother" is conjoined to "myself". It is also possible that "and my brother" is nominative as a subject with an omitted predicate, indicated by what precedes it; the sense: "and my brother has no control except over himself." In this case he has conjoined a non-emphatic sentence to an emphatic one. Or it is accusative, conjoined to the noun of "inna" (indeed): i.e., "and indeed my brother has no control except over himself"; the predicate is omitted, and the noun and predicate are conjoined to the predicate, like: "Indeed Zayd is standing, and 'Amr is staring"; i.e., "and indeed 'Amr is staring." Ibn Atiyyah and al-Zamakhshari permitted that "and my brother" be nominative, conjoined to the concealed pronoun in "amliku" (I control), and they permitted this because of the separation between them by the restricted object. But it follows from this that Musa and Harun, peace be upon them, control only Musa's own self, and this is not the intended meaning; rather the apparent meaning is that Musa controls the matter of his own self and the matter of his brother only. He also permitted that it be genitive, conjoined to the first-person ya' in "nafsi" (my self), but this is weak according to the opinion of the Basrans. It seems that in this restriction he did not trust the two men who had said: ﴿Enter upon them through the gate﴾, and he was not at ease with their steadfastness, because of what he witnessed of his people's conditions and their changing, despite long companionship. So he mentioned only the infallible prophet whose steadfastness is beyond doubt. It is said: or he said this in a manner of annoyance when he heard from them, as an explanation for one who agrees with him; or by his words "and my brother" he meant whoever agreed with him in religion, not Harun specifically. Al-Hasan read "illa nafsi wa akhi" with a fatha on the ya' in both.

﴿So separate us from the defiant people.﴾ Its apparent meaning is that he prayed that God separate them from them, by causing them to lose sight of their faces and not witness their forms, when they disobeyed Him and opposed God's command, and for this reason he alerted to the cause that necessitates the separation between them and the wicked. The obedient one does not desire the companionship of the wicked and does not prefer it, lest he be afflicted by what afflicts them through association: ﴿And beware of a trial that will not strike only those among you who have done wrong﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. (Will you destroy us for what the wrongdoers among us did? And among us are the righteous.) God accepted his supplication, so they were not with them in the wandering (tih), but He separated him from them, because the wandering was a punishment specific to the defiant and disobedient. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and others said: the meaning is: "Decide between us by a judgment that removes this disagreement and gathers the scattered." It is also said: the meaning is: separate us from them in the Hereafter, so that the station of the obedient is distinct from the station of the disobedient, wicked one. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Decide between us and them by granting us what we deserve, and them what they deserve; and it has the sense of a supplication against them. For this reason he connected to it His words: ﴿for it is forbidden to them﴾, in the manner of an explanatory connection." Ubayd ibn Umayr and Yusuf ibn Dawud read "fafriq" with a kasrah on the ra'. The rajiz (a poet of the rajaz meter) said:

"O my Lord, separate him and me,
with the most severe separation You have made between two."

Ibn al-Sumayfa read "fafarriq". The "defiant" (fasiqun) here, Ibn Abbas said: the disobedient. Ibn Zayd said: the liars. Abu Ubayd said: the disbelievers.

﴿He said: "So it is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land.﴾ That is, God the Exalted said (this), so the one who said it is implied in "said" [i.e., God said], and the pronoun in "fa-innaha" refers to the Holy Land, ﴿forbidden to them﴾; i.e., its entry and their possession of it are forbidden. The discussion has already been made regarding the coherence of His words ﴿which God has prescribed for you﴾ with His words ﴿forbidden to them﴾, and this indicates that after the forty years it will not be forbidden to them. It is related that Musa and Harun, peace be upon them, were with them in the wandering as a punishment for them and as comfort and peace for the two of them, not as punishment, just as the fire was for Ibrahim and for the angels of punishment. It is related that after the forty years Musa set out with those of the Children of Israel who remained, and Yusha' and Caleb were at the vanguard. He conquered Jericho (Arihah) and killed 'Uj ibn 'Unuq. They mentioned descriptions of 'Uj and the manner of his killing by Musa that are not authentic. Musa remained there for as long as God willed, then he died. It is said: Harun died during the wandering. Ibn Atiyyah said: there is no disagreement about this. It is related: Musa died during the wandering eight years after Harun. It is said: six and a half months. It is said: one year. God gave Yusha' prophethood after the completion of the forty years, and the Children of Israel believed him, and he informed them that God had commanded him to fight the giants, so they believed him and pledged allegiance to him. He set out among them toward Jericho and killed the giants and drove them out, and all of Syria became the Children of Israel's. In that battle the sun stood still for Yusha' for an hour until he had continued and defeated the giants. Abu Tammam alluded to the standing still of the sun for Yusha' in his poetry, and said:

"The sun was returned to us while the night was humbled,
by a sun that appeared from beyond the curtain, rising.
Its light stripped away the dye of the darkness,
and the cloak of the spotted sky was folded up for its splendour."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 20–26 (part 3 of 3):**

Wa-llahi ma adri a-ahlamu na'imin * allammat bina am kana fi al-rakbi Yushaʿu
(By God, I do not know whether it was the dreams of a sleeper that visited us, or whether Joshua was in the caravan.)

Al-zahir (the apparent meaning) is that the governing element (al-ʿamil) in the word ʾarbaʿin (forty) is muharramatun (forbidden). In that case the prohibition is limited to this period. Yatihuna (they wander) is then either a new sentence (mustaʾnafan) or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ʿalayhim (upon them).

It is also permissible that the governing element is yatihuna, meaning: they will wander in the land for this period. In this case the prohibition is not limited to this period. Rather, it is a report that they will not enter it, and that they will nevertheless wander in the land for forty years, during which those who die will die.

It is related that whoever had passed twenty years of age did not live to leave the wandering, while those under twenty did live. As if the responsible sinners did not live. Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) pointed to this, and for this reason he held that the governing element in arbaʿin is muharramatun.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is possible that the governing element in arbaʿin is an implied element indicated by the later yatihuna. End of quotation.

I do not know what led him to say that the governing element is implied, as he stated. Rather, what people have permitted in this matter is that the governing element is yatihuna itself, not an implied element explained by the words ﴿they wander in the land﴾.

The land in which they wandered, according to what has been reported, was thirty miles long and six farsakh (parasangs) wide, which is the distance between Egypt and Syria. Ibn ʿAbbas said: nine farsakh. Muqatil said: this is its width, and its length is thirty farsakh. It was also said: six farsakh in length and twelve farsakh in width, and it was said: nine farsakh.

The statements of the commentators agree that this wandering was by way of khariq al-ʿadah (breaking of the normal custom, i.e. a miracle), for it is a wonder of God's power, since it was possible for a group of intelligent people to travel a short distance of farsakh without finding their way out of it. It is related that they used to travel at night and would journey the whole night, so that when they awoke in the morning they found all of them in the place where they had started. And they would travel by day, striving, until when evening came they found themselves in the place from which they had set out. Thus their travel was circling. Mujahid and others said: they would sometimes travel by day and sometimes by night, so they would reach the evening where they had been in the morning, and the morning where they had been in the evening. This was within a distance of six farsakh, and they were in a wandering with no place of rest. End of quotation.

It has been mentioned (p-459) that they were six hundred thousand fighting men. They also mentioned that the wisdom of the wandering was that when they said ﴿Indeed, we will remain seated here﴾, they were punished with sitting, so they came to be in the form of those who sit while they were travelling. Whenever they travelled for a day, by evening they were in the place where they had been in the morning.

They also mentioned that the wisdom of the period in which they wandered being forty years was that they had worshipped the calf for forty days, so the punishment was made one year for each day in the wandering.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is also possible that their wandering was by the splitting of their word and the scarcity of agreement in opinion, and that God cast disagreement among them. They knew that the land was forbidden to them for forty years, so their dwellings scattered throughout that open expanse, and they continued to move from place to place without order or unity until this period was completed, and God permitted their departure. This is a wandering that is possible and plausible according to human custom. The other [explanation], which Mujahid mentioned, is merely a breaking of custom and a wonder of God's power.

﴿So do not grieve over the defiant people﴾. The apparent meaning is that the address is from God, the Exalted, to Musa (peace be upon him). Ibn ʿAbbas said: Musa regretted his supplication against his people and grieved for them. End of quotation. So this is a consolation to Musa, peace be upon him, against grieving over what befell his people, and the reason given for his not grieving is that they are defiant people, bahut (liars), deserving of the punishment that befell them.

It was also said: the address is to Muhammad (ﷺ), and by "the defiant" is meant his contemporaries. That is: these are the deeds of their forefathers. So do not grieve, you, because of their wicked deeds with you and their rejection of you, for this is a wicked disposition inherited among them.

﴿Recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam, in truth, when they each offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them but not from the other. He said, "I will surely kill you." He said, "Allah accepts only from those who are God-fearing."﴾ ﴿If you stretch your hand toward me to kill me, I will not stretch my hand toward you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, the Lord of the worlds.﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 5:27-28) ﴿Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin, and thus be among the companions of the Fire. That is the recompense of the wrongdoers.﴾ (5:29) ﴿So his soul made the killing of his brother seem appealing to him, and he killed him, and became among the losers.﴾ (5:30) ﴿Then Allah sent a crow scratching in the earth to show him how to conceal the body of his brother. He said, "Woe to me! Am I unable to be like this crow and conceal the body of my brother?" And he became among the regretful.﴾ (5:31) ﴿For this reason We decreed upon the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the earth, it is as if he had killed all of mankind; and whoever saves a life, it is as if he had saved all of mankind. Our messengers had already come to them with clear proofs, yet many of them afterward were indeed transgressors in the earth.﴾ (5:32) ﴿Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption is that they be killed or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be exiled from the land. That is a disgrace for them in this world, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.﴾ (5:33) ﴿Except for those who repent before you gain power over them. So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (5:34) ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah, seek the means of nearness to Him, and strive in His cause, that you may succeed.﴾ (5:35) ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, even if they had all that is on the earth and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves thereby from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ (5:36) ﴿They wish to come out of the Fire, but they will not emerge from it, and for them is a lasting punishment.﴾ (5:37) ﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as recompense for what they have earned, as a deterrent from Allah. And Allah is Almighty and Wise.﴾ (5:38)

Al-ghurab: a well-known bird. Its plural for small numbers is aghriba, and for large numbers ghirban. Ghurab is a generic noun (ism al-jins). Generic nouns, when they refer to their referents and are not derived from something else, are treated as such. If something in them can be derived, they are taken as derived, but this is very rare. Most often they are underived, as in turab (dust), hajar (stone), and ma' (water). Ghurab may be derived from al-ightirab (estrangement), since the Arabs regard it as a bad omen and claim that it signifies separation. Harran al-Ud said:

"As for the crow, it is the stranger, wandering far away."

Al-Shanfara said:

"A crow for estrangement from the homeland, and at al-Bad, a separation from a beloved whom one keeps company with."

Al-bahth fi al-ard means digging up the dust and stirring it. From this the Surah of Bara'ah is called Bahuth. There is a proverb: "Do not be like one who searches for the knife." Al-sawʾah means the private parts. Al-ʿajz means inability to do something. Its past tense follows the pattern fa'ala, with a fatha on the ʿayn, and this is the common dialect. Al-Kisa'i also related fa'ila with a kasra on the ʿayn. Al-nadam means regret, and one says from it: nadima yandamu. Al-salb (crucifixion) is well known, and it means striking the spine against a trunk or wall, as one says: ʿanahu, meaning he struck his eye, and kabidahu, meaning he struck his liver. Al-khilaf means opposition, and one says: a horse with a shikal of khilaf if it has the marking on its foreleg. Nafahu means he drove him away so that he departed, and it may also be used intransitively as nafa. Al-Qatami said:

"So your neighbor became a slain man and an exile."

That is, one who has been banished. Al-wasilah, al-wasilah means that by which one draws near. One says: wasala-hu and tawassala ilayhi. The term wasilah has been borrowed for that by which one draws near to Allah Most High through acts of obedience. Labid said:

"I see people not knowing the value of their affairs. Verily every intelligent person is a seeker to Allah."

Al-Tabari recited:

"When the slanderers are heedless, we return to our union, and the flirtation and the means of approach return between us."

Al-sariq is an active participle from saraqa, yasriqu, sarqan. Al-sarq and al-sariqah are nouns. So said some of them, and they sometimes say sariqa malan. Ibn Arafah said: according to the Arabs, the thief is one who comes stealthily to a place of safekeeping and takes from it what is not his.

* *

﴿Recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam, in truth, when they each offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them but not from the other.﴾ The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when Allah Most High mentioned the rebellion and disobedience of the Children of Israel against Allah's command to rise up and fight the tyrants, He mentioned the story of the two sons of Adam and the disobedience of Qabil to Allah's command. They followed in disobedience the first one who disobeyed Allah Most High. They reached, in the weakness of nature, the panic of souls, cowardice, and fear, to the point that they said to their prophet, through whose hands great miracles had appeared, and who had informed them that Allah had decreed for them the holy land: "Go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we will sit here." (5:24) Qabil went to the opposite extreme of audacity, violence, strength of soul, and disregard, by committing the greatest of matters and the gravest of sins after shirk, which is killing a soul that Allah has forbidden to kill. He became the first to establish killing, and upon him was its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection. Thus the two stories were alike in cowardice about killing and boldness in it, and in disobedience through both. Also, earlier in the verses, His saying: "When a people intended to stretch out their hands toward you" (5:11) preceded, and after it: "There has come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture" (5:15), and His saying: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved" (5:18). Then came the story of fighting the tyrants. It became clear that the reason the Children of Israel did not follow Muhammad ﷺ was envy, despite their knowledge of his truthfulness.

The story of the two sons of Adam encompassed all of these verses: stretching out the hand, informing of the unseen, the failure to benefit from nearness and its claim along with disobedience, killing, and envy. The meaning of "recite to them" is: read and relate. The pronoun in "to them" apparently refers to the Children of Israel, since they were the first ones spoken about. The proofs were established against them because of their intention to stretch out their hands against the Messenger and the believers. They were informed of what is in the obscure parts of their earlier books, which the Messenger had no connection to except through revelation, so that the proof would be established against them, since this is among the signs of prophethood. Al-naba' is the news. The two sons of Adam, according to the majority, including ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and others, are Qabil and Habil, and they were his sons from his own loins. Al-Hasan said: they were not his sons from his loins, but rather two brothers from the Children of Israel. He said: because the sacrifice was legislated only among the Children of Israel and did not exist before them. Al-Hasan was mistaken in this. It has been objected: how could burial be unknown among the Children of Israel so that one would follow the crow in it? Also, the Messenger said about him: "He was the first to establish killing," and killing had already existed among the Children of Israel before.

His saying "in truth" may be a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun in "recite," meaning accompanied by truth, which is the sincerity beyond doubt in its correctness, or it may be in the position of an adjective for a deleted verbal noun, meaning a recitation connected with truth. The governing element of "when" (idh) is "story" (naba'), meaning their account and story at that time. Al-Zamakhshari said: it may also be a substitute for "the story," meaning: recite to them the story of that time, with the omission of an annexed element. End quote. This is not permissible, because idh is only annexed to a time expression, and "naba'" is not a time.

The commentators elaborated on the reason for offering this sacrifice, and its summary is: Hawwa used to give birth to a male and a female in every pregnancy, and Adam would marry the male of one pregnancy to the female of another, and the female of this one to the male of that one, and it was not permitted for a male to marry his twin. Along with Qabil was born a beautiful sister named Iqlimia, and along with Habil was born a sister less beautiful than her named Lubudha. Qabil refused except to marry his own twin and not Habil's twin, and to violate the custom of marriage out of preference for her beauty. Qabil disputed with Habil over this. It was said: Adam commanded them to offer a sacrifice. It was also said: they offered it on their own initiative, since Adam was absent, having set out for Mecca to visit the House with the permission of his Lord. The sacrifice they offered: Qabil's was grain, since he was a farmer, and Habil's was a ram, since he was a shepherd. It was accepted from one of them, namely Habil, and not accepted from the other, namely Qabil; that is, the sacrifice was accepted and the other was not. The sign of acceptance was that a fire descending from heaven consumed the accepted sacrifice and left the rejected one. Mujahid said: the fire would consume what was rejected and lift up what was accepted to heaven. Al-Zamakhshari said: one says "qarraba sadaqatan" (he offered a charity) and "taqarraba biha" (he drew near by it), because taqarraba is the reflexive form (mutawaʿa) of qarraba. End quote. Taqarraba with charity is not the reflexive of qarraba with charity, because the subject of both verbs is the same. In a reflexive form, the subject differs: one performs an action and the other undergoes it, as in kasartuhu fa-inkasara (I broke it and it broke) and falaqtuhu fa-infalaqa (I split it and it split). "I offered charity" and "I drew near by it" are not from this pattern, so this is a gross error.

﴿He said, "I will surely kill you."﴾ This is a severe threat and warning. This statement is emphasized with an implied oath, meaning: "I will surely kill you," out of envy for the acceptance of your sacrifice and for your gaining the right to the beautiful sister who was my portion. Zayd ibn ʿAli read: la-aqtulannka with the light nun.

﴿He said, "Allah accepts only from those who are God-fearing."﴾ Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: before it there is an omitted statement, its meaning being: "Why do you kill me, when I have committed no offense and I am not at fault regarding Allah's acceptance of my sacrifice? Indeed, I fear Him, and I was on the clear path of truth. Allah accepts only from the God-fearing." Al-Zamakhshari spoke here and said: "If you ask: how was His saying, 'Allah accepts only from the God-fearing,' a response to 'I will surely kill you'?" I answer: since envy of his brother over the acceptance of his sacrifice was what drove him to threaten him with killing, he said to him: "You were brought to this only from your own self, by stripping off the garment of piety, not from me. So why do you kill me? And what is wrong with you that you do not punish yourself and do not bring it to the fear of Allah, which is the cause of acceptance?" So he answered him with a wise, concise statement comprising many meanings. In it is evidence that Allah Most High accepts no act of obedience except from a believing, God-fearing person, so how much of the deeds of most doers are rejected. ʿAmir ibn ʿAbd Allah reported that he wept when death approached him. He was asked: "What makes you weep, when you were what you were?" He said: "I hear Allah saying: 'Allah accepts only from the God-fearing.'" End of his words. It was not free of the subtle influence of Mu'tazilite doctrine, as is his habit. Understanding his speech requires these interpretations. What we proposed first is sufficient, namely: the meaning is "I will surely kill you out of envy for the acceptance of your sacrifice." So he alluded that the cause of the acceptance of the sacrifice is piety, and that he himself was not God-fearing. He alluded to this only because he had not been content with the custom of marriage that Allah Most High had established, intended its opposite, and disputed it. The result of this was that he committed the greatest of the major sins after shirk, which is killing a soul that Allah has forbidden. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The people of the Sunnah agree on the meaning of these words, that they refer to avoiding shirk. Whoever guards against it while being a monotheist, his deeds with sincere intention are accepted. ʿAdi ibn Thabit and others said: the sacrifice of this nation is the prayer. As for the view of one who claims that His saying, "Allah accepts only from the God-fearing," is not part of the speech of the one who was killed, but is rather the speech of Allah Most High to the Messenger as an interjection between the speech of the killer and the killed, with the pronoun in "he said" referring to Allah, this is not apparent.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 28:**

﴿If you extend your hand toward me to kill me, I shall not extend my hand toward you to kill you.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning is, "I will not take vengeance for myself." 'Ikrimah said: the meaning is, "I would not be the one to initiate killing you." Mujahid and al-Hasan said: "Defending oneself at that time was not permissible." 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, Ibn 'Abbas, and the majority (al-Jumhur) said: Habil was stronger than Qabil, but he refrained (taharraja) from killing. This indicates that the killer is not a disbeliever but a sinner, for if he were a disbeliever, Habil would not have scrupled about killing him. Habil submitted to him just as 'Uthman ibn 'Affan submitted. It was also said: he abandoned defending himself only because he perceived signs that his life was about to end, and he acted upon that, or because of his father's report. This is like what happened to 'Uthman, when the Messenger (ﷺ) gave him the glad tidings of Paradise in return for a trial that would befall him, "and he saw him in the night in which he was killed, in a dream, saying: 'You will break your fast with us tonight'," so he abandoned defending himself until he was killed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Lay your face down and be the servant of Allah who is killed, and do not be the servant of Allah who kills."

It was also said: Habil perceived strong indications from Qabil that he would kill him, but he was not certain of it. So he said these words to him before Qabil proceeded to the killing, to deter him from it and to censure this act. For this reason it is narrated that Qabil waited until Habil slept, then struck his head with a large stone and killed him. Ibn Jarir said: there is no evidence in the verse that the one who was killed knew of the killer's determination to kill him and then abandoned defending himself.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "(If you ask): Why did the conditional (shart) come with a verb, while the response (jaza') came with the active participle (ism al-fa'il), namely His saying: ﴿If you extend﴾ ﴿I am not one who extends﴾?" (I answer): "So that it conveys that he would not do what would earn him this vile description. For this reason he emphasized it with the emphatic bi (al-ba' al-mu'akkidah) for negation." End of quotation.

Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi cited this question and answer without attributing them to al-Zamakhshari, and it is a statement open to criticism. The reason is that His saying ﴿I am not one who extends﴾ is not the response to the conditional at all, but the answer to an omitted oath (qasam) that precedes the lam in "la-in," which signals an oath and introduces the answer (al-muwatti'ah lil-jawab), not the conditional. The response to the conditional is omitted, its meaning being indicated by the response to the oath. Had it been the response to the conditional, it would have needed the particle fa' (fa'), because when the response to a conditional is negated with "ma," a fa' is required, as in His saying: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, their argument is only that they say [...]﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 25]. Moreover, if it were also the response to the conditional, it would follow that the grammatical rule would be broken, namely that when the oath precedes the conditional, the response belongs to the oath and not to the conditional. Al-Zamakhshari himself contradicted this statement in what he said in al-Baqarah regarding His saying: ﴿And even if you brought those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qiblah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145]. He said: "They did not follow" is the response to the omitted oath, which took the place of the response to the conditional. We discussed this with him there, so refer to it there. (p-463)

﴿Indeed, I fear Allah, the Lord of the worlds.﴾ This is a statement of the reason for his refraining from extending his hand toward him to kill him, and in it is an alert that the killer does not fear Allah.

﴿Indeed, I wish that you should bear my sin and your sin, and so be among the companions of the Fire.﴾

Some scholars held that the "wish" (*irada*) here is metaphorical (*majaz*) and not a desire that loves the object of a craving. Rather, it is a choice between two evils, as the Arabs say of evil, "khiyar" (the lesser of two). The meaning is: "If you kill me, and that was predestined, then my choice is to be the wronged one, whom God will vindicate in the Hereafter."

Others held that the "wish" here is literal (*haqiqa*) and not metaphorical. It is objected: "How is it permissible for him to wish his brother's wretchedness and his punishment by the Fire?" The answer is that the recompense of the wrongdoer may rightly be willed, and if God Most High may will it, it is permissible for the servant to will it too, since he wills only what is good. This is the view of al-Zamakhshari, and in it there is a hint of Mu'tazilism (*i'tizal*). Ibn Kaysan said: the wish came after Qabil had stretched out his hand to kill, which is a repugnant act, and by this he became an unbeliever, because whoever deems lawful what God has forbidden has disbelieved, and an unbeliever wishes that evil be willed for him.

It was also said: the meaning is that when he said, "I will surely kill you," he deserved the Fire by what had already preceded in God's knowledge. A believer should will what God wills. The apparent meaning of the verse is that both of them are sinners.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada said: "He bears the sin of my killing, and your sin which you committed before killing me." The word "sin" is understood with an omitted modifier (*hadhf al-mudaf*). This is the view of the majority of the exegetes (*mufassirun*).

Al-Zajjaj said: "with the sin of my killing and your sin, because of which your offering was not accepted," and this, in meaning, returns to what precedes it.

It was also said: the meaning is "with my sin, were I to fight you and kill you, and the sin of yourself in fighting me and killing me." This is the sin that his saying, ﷺ, implies: "When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are both in the Fire." It was asked: "O Messenger of God, this is the killer, but what about the killed?" He said: "He was eager to kill his companion." Thus it is as if Habil meant: "I am not eager to kill you, so the sin that would have befallen me had I been eager to kill you, I wish you to bear it together with your sin in killing me."

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say) how can he bear the sin of his killing him, when "no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another" (al-An'am 164)? (I say) the meaning of "like my sin" is by extension in speech, as you say, "I recited the recitation of so-and-so, and wrote his writing," meaning "the like of," and this is a widespread, common extension that is hardly ever replaced by anything else. (If you say) then when Habil refrained from killing his brother, submitted, and abstained from what was forbidden in his law concerning repelling aggression, where is the sin so that his brother may bear its like, and the two sins combine upon him? (I say) it is hypothetical; he bears the like of a hypothetical sin, as if he said: "I wish you to bear the like of my sin had I stretched out my hand to you." End of quotation.

It was also said: "with my sin," which belongs specifically to me for what I have been guilty of; that is, it is taken from my evil deeds and cast upon you because of your wronging me, and you bear your sin in killing me. This is supported by the saying of the Prophet, ﷺ: "On the Day of Resurrection the wrongdoer and the wronged will be brought, and some of the good deeds of the wrongdoer will be taken and added to the good deeds of the wronged until he is compensated. If he has no good deeds, some of the evil deeds of the wronged will be taken and cast upon him."

Two aspects are summarized from his saying, "with my sin and your sin." The first: with my sin that attaches to me, that is, with the like of my sin that would attach to me on the supposition that I had killed you, and your sin that attaches to you because of my killing. The second: with my sin that attaches to you because of my killing, which he attributed to himself since it was its cause, and your sin that attaches to you before my killing. These two aspects are based on the affirmation of the metaphorical and the literal wish.

It was also said that the meaning is in negation. The estimated sense is: "I wish that you not bear my sin and your sin," like His saying, "firm mountains lest they shake with you" (al-Nahl 15), that is, lest they shake, and "lest you go astray" (al-Nisa 176), that is, lest you go astray, the "lest" having been omitted. This interpretation is a way of avoiding the attribution to his believing brother of the wish for evil. Al-Qurtubi weakened this aspect, citing the saying of the Prophet, ﷺ: "No soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Adam bears a portion of its blood, because he was the first to institute killing." By this, it is established that the sin of the killer is realized. End of quotation.

This view is not weakened by what al-Qurtubi mentioned, for the one who holds this does not hold that negating his wish for killing necessitates that killing does not occur; rather, one may not wish it and it may still occur. Al-Mawardi supported the negation interpretation and said: killing is ugly, the wish for what is ugly is ugly, and for prophets it is uglier. This interpretation is supported by the reading of whoever read (*anna uridu*, "how do I wish"), that is, "how can I wish?" Its meaning is the disapproval of the wish (p-464). For this reason some exegetes said: this interrogation is in the mode of denial, meaning "how," the hamza having been omitted because the meaning indicates it, since the wish for killing is disobedience. This was related by al-Qushayri. End of quotation.

All of this is a departure from the apparent sense of the wording without necessity. The wish has already been clarified earlier, and its occurrence here has been discussed.

It has been used as evidence, from His saying, "and so be among the companions of the Fire," that Qabil was an unbeliever, because this expression occurs in the Qur'an only regarding unbelievers. On this view, there is evidence that unbelievers are addressed with the branches of the Sharia (*furu' al-shari'a*). This argument is not strong, because the expression "companionship" is a figurative reference to remaining in the Fire for a period.

﴿That is the recompense of the wrongdoers.﴾ That is: your being among the companions of the Fire is your recompense, because you are a wrongdoer in killing me. By His saying "the wrongdoers," He draws attention to the cause that necessitates the killing, and that it is a killing by wrong and not by right. The apparent view is that this is from the speech of Habil, who draws attention to the reason so that he may be deterred. It was also said that this is from the speech of God Most High, not a report of Habil's speech, but an announcement from Him, Most High, to the Messenger, ﷺ.

﴿So his soul facilitated for him the killing of his brother, and he killed him.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: "It urged him to kill him." He also said, together with Mujahid: "It encouraged him." Qatada said: "It adorned it for him." Al-Akhfash said: "It made it lenient." Al-Mubarrad said: it is from *al-taw'* (compliance), and the Arabs say, "*ta'a lahu kadha*," meaning, "it came to him willingly." Ibn Qutayba said: "It followed him and yielded to him." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It widened it for him and made it easy for him," from *ta'a lahu al-mar'a* when the pasture expanded. These sayings are close in meaning, and the verb is from *al-taw'*, which is submission. As if killing was unreachable for him, defiant. Its origin is: "the killing of his brother submitted to him," that is, yielded to him and became easy, then it was made transitive by doubling so that the subject became the object. The meaning is that killing in itself is difficult and great for souls, but this stubborn soul, which commands evil, brought it back to him compliantly and submissively, until the one who owns this soul carried it out.

Al-Hasan, Zayd ibn Ali, al-Jarrah, al-Hasan ibn Imran and Abu Waqid read *fa-taw'athu* (فطاوعته), which is the form *fa'ala* with mutual participation (*al-ishtirak*), like *darabtu Zaydan* ("I struck Zayd"). As if the killing was summoning him, by means of envy, to the striking of Qabil, or as if the soul refused that and it was hard on it, and each of them wanted the other to obey him, until the matter intensified and the soul complied with the killing and agreed to it.

Al-Zamakhshari said there are two aspects to it: that it is among what came as *fa'ala* in the sense of *fa'ala* (*faa'ala* with the meaning of *fa'ala*), and that the meaning is that he killed his brother, as if he urged his soul to advance upon it, and it complied and did not refuse; and "*lahu*" (to him) is for the increase of connection, as in your saying, "I preserved for Zayd his wealth." End of quotation.

As for the second aspect, it agrees with what we have mentioned. As for the first aspect, Sibawayh mentioned *dha'aftu* and *di'tu* (ضاعفت وضعفت), like *na'amtu* and *ni'mtu* (ناعمت ونعمت). He said: "They came with it in the pattern of *'aqabtuhu*," and said: "*Fa'ala* may come without intending the action of two, but they built the verb on it just as they built it on *af'ala*," and he mentioned examples of it, such as *'afahu Allah* (God pardoned him). This meaning, that *fa'ala* has the meaning of *fa'ala*, was overlooked by some of our authors in morphology (*al-tasrif*), such as Ibn Usfur and Ibn Malik, though they are sufficient in gathering and mastery, for they did not mention that *fa'ala* comes with the meaning of *fa'ala*, nor *fa'ala* with the meaning of *fa'ala*.

As for his saying, "and *lahu* is for the increase of connection": he means in His saying, "so his soul facilitated for him." He means that if it had come as "so his soul facilitated the killing of his brother," it would have been a complete sentence following the usage of the Arabs, and it was only brought in this way for the increase of connection in the speech, since connection occurs without it, just as if you said, "I preserved the wealth of Zayd," it would be a complete sentence.

﴿So he killed him.﴾ God Most High informed that he killed him. The exegetes spoke about matters of how it was done, the place of his killing, and his age when he was killed, and they differed on this, but the verse does not address any of that.

(p-465) ﴿So he became among the losers.﴾ *Asbaha* means "became." Ibn Atiyya said: "Part of the time has been put in place of all of it, and the morning was singled out for this because it is the beginning of the day, the setting out toward affairs, and the seat of vigor." Among this is the saying of al-Rabi':

"I became one who does not bear weapons, nor..."

and the saying of Sa'd: "Then the Banu Sa'd became (*asbahat*) strengthening me in Islam," among other uses of the Arabs of what we have mentioned. End of quotation.

What he mentioned as the reason why *asbaha* is an expression for all of its times, since the morning was singled out because it is the beginning of the day, is not good. Do you not see that they made *ad-ha*, *zalla*, *amsa* and *bata* mean "became"? None of them is the beginning of the day. Just as these are used like *sara* (became), so *asbaha* is too, not for the reason Ibn Atiyya mentioned.

Ibn Abbas said: he lost in this world by provoking his parents and by remaining without a brother, and in the Hereafter by provoking his Lord and his going to the Fire. Al-Zajjaj said: "among the losers of good deeds." Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: "among those who lost themselves by destroying them." Mujahid said: his loss was that one of the killer's legs was bent to its thigh from that day until the Day of Resurrection, his face toward the sun wherever it turned; upon him in summer is an enclosure of fire, and upon him in winter an enclosure of ice. Al-Qurtubi said: perhaps this is his punishment for the view that he was a disobedient sinner rather than an unbeliever, so his loss would be in this world. It was also said: "among the losers" by the blackening of his face and his disbelief in deeming lawful what was forbidden, the killing of his brother, and in the Hereafter by the torment of the Fire. It is established in the hadith: "No soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Adam bears a portion of it, because he was the first to institute killing." It was related from Abdullah ibn Umar that he said: "We find that the killer son of Adam shares with the people of the Fire in a correct division of torment, and upon him is half of their torment."

﴿Then God sent a crow scratching in the earth to show him how to cover the nakedness of his brother﴾ (al-Ma'ida 31). It is related that he was the first slain on the face of the earth. When he killed him, he left him in the open, not knowing what to do with him. He feared the beasts, so he carried him in a bag on his back for a year until he decayed, and the beasts gathered around him. Then God sent two crows, and they fought, and one of them killed the other. It dug a grave for it with its beak and feet, then threw it into the pit, and said: "Woe is me! Am I incapable?" It was said: he carried him for a hundred years. It was said: he sought, on the second day, a way to conceal the killing of his brother, and did not know what to do. It was said: God sent a crow to a dead crow, and it began scratching the earth and throwing the dirt over the dead crow. It was said: God sent one crow, and it began scratching and throwing dirt over Habil. It is related that he was the first dead person to die on the face of the earth, and so he was ignorant of the custom of burial.

The apparent meaning is that it was a crow sent by God, scratching in the earth so as to show Qabil how to cover the nakedness of Habil. Qabil benefited from the crow's scratching in the earth by scratching himself in the earth, and concealing his brother in it. By "nakedness" (*sawa'a*) here it was said: the private parts (*al-'awra*). It was singled out for mention though the intention is covering the whole body, out of concern for it and because covering it is more emphatic. It was also said: all of the corpse. It was said: the whole dead body is a nakedness, and for this reason (p-466) it is shrouded in burial cloths. Ibn Atiyya said: it may be that "nakedness" means this state which offends the viewer by its totality, and it is attributed to the slain because the calamity befell him, not in order to belittle him; rather, the shame falls on the killer, who is the one who brought the nakedness. End of quotation.

*Sawa'a* means disgrace, because of its ugliness. The poet said:

Alas, my people, for this monstrous disgrace!

That is, for a great scandal. Some have said that, if it is authentically reported that one crow killed another crow, or that the crow was dead, then the pronoun (damir, pronoun) in *akhihi* ("his brother") may refer back to the crow. That is, *liyuriya Qabil* ("so that He might show Qabil") how the crow covers the *sawʼah* ("private parts") of its brother, the dead crow, so that he would learn from it, by means of the tool, how Qabil should cover the *sawʼah* of Habil. This view is far-fetched, because a crow has no *sawʼah* that would be visible. The more apparent sense is that *al-iraʼah* ("showing") here is from *jaʻlihi yara* ("making him see"), that is, to make him perceive. The phrase ﴿لِيُرِيَهُ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 31] ("so that He might show him") is linked to the second object (*mafʻul thani*, second object) by the clause containing the interrogative, which occupies the place of the second object. *Kayfa* ("how") is governed by *yuwari* ("covers"), and *liyurihi* is connected to *yabhathu* ("searching"). It is also permissible for it to be connected to the statement ﴿فَبَعَثَ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 31] ("then He sent"). The pronoun of the subject in ﴿لِيُرِيَهُ﴾ most apparently refers back to Allah, the Exalted, because showing in its literal sense (*haqiqah*, literal meaning) is from Allah, since the crow has no intention or purpose of showing. It is also permissible for it to refer back to the crow, meaning that the crow showed him, that is, taught him, since the crow was the cause of his learning, so he is figuratively treated as having intended to teach him (*majaz*, metaphor). It appears that the wisdom in this messenger being a crow rather than any other animal or bird is that it is regarded as a bad omen in separation and estrangement, and this suits this story. It has also been said that ﴿فَبَعَثَ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 31] is an omitted clause whose meaning is understood from context, and its estimated form is: "So he was ignorant of how to cover it, then He sent [a crow]."

Al-Hasan, Zayd ibn Ali, al-Jarrah, al-Hasan ibn Imran and Abu Waqid read *fa-taw'athu* (فطاوعته), which is the form *fa'ala* with mutual participation (*al-ishtirak*), like *darabtu Zaydan* ("I struck Zayd"). As if the killing was summoning him, by means of envy, to the striking of Qabil, or as if the soul refused that and it was hard on it, and each of them wanted the other to obey him, until the matter intensified and the soul complied with the killing and agreed to it.

Al-Zamakhshari said there are two aspects to it: that it is among what came as *fa'ala* in the sense of *fa'ala* (*faa'ala* with the meaning of *fa'ala*), and that the meaning is that he killed his brother, as if he urged his soul to advance upon it, and it complied and did not refuse; and "*lahu*" (to him) is for the increase of connection, as in your saying, "I preserved for Zayd his wealth." End of quotation.

As for the second aspect, it agrees with what we have mentioned. As for the first aspect, Sibawayh mentioned *dha'aftu* and *di'tu* (ضاعفت وضعفت), like *na'amtu* and *ni'mtu* (ناعمت ونعمت). He said: "They came with it in the pattern of *'aqabtuhu*," and said: "*Fa'ala* may come without intending the action of two, but they built the verb on it just as they built it on *af'ala*," and he mentioned examples of it, such as *'afahu Allah* (God pardoned him). This meaning, that *fa'ala* has the meaning of *fa'ala*, was overlooked by some of our authors in morphology (*al-tasrif*), such as Ibn Usfur and Ibn Malik, though they are sufficient in gathering and mastery, for they did not mention that *fa'ala* comes with the meaning of *fa'ala*, nor *fa'ala* with the meaning of *fa'ala*.

As for his saying, "and *lahu* is for the increase of connection": he means in His saying, "so his soul facilitated for him." He means that if it had come as "so his soul facilitated the killing of his brother," it would have been a complete sentence following the usage of the Arabs, and it was only brought in this way for the increase of connection in the speech, since connection occurs without it, just as if you said, "I preserved the wealth of Zayd," it would be a complete sentence.

﴿So he killed him.﴾ God Most High informed that he killed him. The exegetes spoke about matters of how it was done, the place of his killing, and his age when he was killed, and they differed on this, but the verse does not address any of that.

(p-465) ﴿So he became among the losers.﴾ *Asbaha* means "became." Ibn Atiyya said: "Part of the time has been put in place of all of it, and the morning was singled out for this because it is the beginning of the day, the setting out toward affairs, and the seat of vigor." Among this is the saying of al-Rabi':

"I became one who does not bear weapons, nor..."

and the saying of Sa'd: "Then the Banu Sa'd became (*asbahat*) strengthening me in Islam," among other uses of the Arabs of what we have mentioned. End of quotation.

What he mentioned as the reason why *asbaha* is an expression for all of its times, since the morning was singled out because it is the beginning of the day, is not good. Do you not see that they made *ad-ha*, *zalla*, *amsa* and *bata* mean "became"? None of them is the beginning of the day. Just as these are used like *sara* (became), so *asbaha* is too, not for the reason Ibn Atiyya mentioned.

Ibn Abbas said: he lost in this world by provoking his parents and by remaining without a brother, and in the Hereafter by provoking his Lord and his going to the Fire. Al-Zajjaj said: "among the losers of good deeds." Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: "among those who lost themselves by destroying them." Mujahid said: his loss was that one of the killer's legs was bent to its thigh from that day until the Day of Resurrection, his face toward the sun wherever it turned; upon him in summer is an enclosure of fire, and upon him in winter an enclosure of ice. Al-Qurtubi said: perhaps this is his punishment for the view that he was a disobedient sinner rather than an unbeliever, so his loss would be in this world. It was also said: "among the losers" by the blackening of his face and his disbelief in deeming lawful what was forbidden, the killing of his brother, and in the Hereafter by the torment of the Fire. It is established in the hadith: "No soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Adam bears a portion of it, because he was the first to institute killing." It was related from Abdullah ibn Umar that he said: "We find that the killer son of Adam shares with the people of the Fire in a correct division of torment, and upon him is half of their torment."

﴿Then God sent a crow scratching in the earth to show him how to cover the nakedness of his brother﴾ (al-Ma'ida 31). It is related that he was the first slain on the face of the earth. When he killed him, he left him in the open, not knowing what to do with him. He feared the beasts, so he carried him in a bag on his back for a year until he decayed, and the beasts gathered around him. Then God sent two crows, and they fought, and one of them killed the other. It dug a grave for it with its beak and feet, then threw it into the pit, and said: "Woe is me! Am I incapable?" It was said: he carried him for a hundred years. It was said: he sought, on the second day, a way to conceal the killing of his brother, and did not know what to do. It was said: God sent a crow to a dead crow, and it began scratching the earth and throwing the dirt over the dead crow. It was said: God sent one crow, and it began scratching and throwing dirt over Habil. It is related that he was the first dead person to die on the face of the earth, and so he was ignorant of the custom of burial.

The apparent meaning is that it was a crow sent by God, scratching in the earth so as to show Qabil how to cover the nakedness of Habil. Qabil benefited from the crow's scratching in the earth by scratching himself in the earth, and concealing his brother in it. By "nakedness" (*sawa'a*) here it was said: the private parts (*al-'awra*). It was singled out for mention though the intention is covering the whole body, out of concern for it and because covering it is more emphatic. It was also said: all of the corpse. It was said: the whole dead body is a nakedness, and for this reason (p-466) it is shrouded in burial cloths. Ibn Atiyya said: it may be that "nakedness" means this state which offends the viewer by its totality, and it is attributed to the slain because the calamity befell him, not in order to belittle him; rather, the shame falls on the killer, who is the one who brought the nakedness. End of quotation.

*Sawa'a* means disgrace, because of its ugliness. The poet said:

Alas, my people, for this monstrous disgrace!

That is, for a great scandal. Some have said that, if it is authentically reported that one crow killed another crow, or that the crow was dead, then the pronoun (damir, pronoun) in *akhihi* ("his brother") may refer back to the crow. That is, *liyuriya Qabil* ("so that He might show Qabil") how the crow covers the *sawʼah* ("private parts") of its brother, the dead crow, so that he would learn from it, by means of the tool, how Qabil should cover the *sawʼah* of Habil. This view is far-fetched, because a crow has no *sawʼah* that would be visible. The more apparent sense is that *al-iraʼah* ("showing") here is from *jaʻlihi yara* ("making him see"), that is, to make him perceive. The phrase ﴿لِيُرِيَهُ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 31] ("so that He might show him") is linked to the second object (*mafʻul thani*, second object) by the clause containing the interrogative, which occupies the place of the second object. *Kayfa* ("how") is governed by *yuwari* ("covers"), and *liyurihi* is connected to *yabhathu* ("searching"). It is also permissible for it to be connected to the statement ﴿فَبَعَثَ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 31] ("then He sent"). The pronoun of the subject in ﴿لِيُرِيَهُ﴾ most apparently refers back to Allah, the Exalted, because showing in its literal sense (*haqiqah*, literal meaning) is from Allah, since the crow has no intention or purpose of showing. It is also permissible for it to refer back to the crow, meaning that the crow showed him, that is, taught him, since the crow was the cause of his learning, so he is figuratively treated as having intended to teach him (*majaz*, metaphor). It appears that the wisdom in this messenger being a crow rather than any other animal or bird is that it is regarded as a bad omen in separation and estrangement, and this suits this story. It has also been said that ﴿فَبَعَثَ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 31] is an omitted clause whose meaning is understood from context, and its estimated form is: "So he was ignorant of how to cover it, then He sent [a crow]."

﴿He said, "Woe is me! Am I unable to be like this crow and hide my brother's corpse?"﴾ He regarded his own understanding and reason as too deficient, in his ignorance, to know what to do with his brother, until he was taught by a bird that has no reason, though he himself possessed reason, with thought, sight and judgment built into him. The meaning of this interrogative is a rebuke to himself and a lament: "I am not unable to be like this crow." In this there is a belittling of himself and a demeaning of his own status through his words "like this crow." The basic use of the vocative (al-nida', calling out) is for one who has reason, but it may also be used, metaphorically, for what has no reason, as in their saying, "O wonder!" and "O regret!" The intent is to express amazement, as if he were saying, "Look at this wonder and this regret." The meaning is: "Pay heed to this destruction." Its interpretation is: "This is your time, so be present."

The majority of readers recite ﴿yā-waylatā﴾ with an alif after the tā', which replaces the first-person pronoun ya' (my). The original form is *yā waylatī* with the ya'. This is the reading of al-Hasan. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr pronounced the alif of *waylatā* with imala (a vowel shift toward i, the "inclination" of the alif). The majority read ﴿a'jaztu﴾ with a fatha on the jim [p. 467]. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, Fayyad, Talha and Sulayman read it with a kasra, which is an irregular dialect form. The kasra is well known only in their saying *ajizat al-mar'atu* ("the woman's buttocks became large," from *'ajiz*, meaning the hindquarters).

The majority read ﴿fa-uwāriya﴾ with a fatha on the ya', in coordination with his words ﴿an akūna﴾. It is as if he said, "Am I unable to hide my brother's nakedness?" Al-Zamakhshari said: *fa-uwāriya*, with the fatha, is in answer to the interrogative. This is a gross error, because the fa' that comes as an answer to an interrogative forms a conditional structure from the interrogative sentence, and the answer is a condition and its consequence. Here you say, "Will you visit me so that I may honour you?" The meaning is: "If you visit me, I will honour you." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So have we any intercessors that they may intercede for us?﴾ [al-A'raf: 53], meaning: "If there were intercessors for us, they would intercede." If you were to say here, "If I am unable to be like this crow, I will hide my brother's nakedness," it would not be sound, because hiding the corpse does not follow from his inability to be like the crow.

Talha ibn Musarrif and al-Fayyad ibn Ghazwan read ﴿fa-uwāri﴾ with a sukun on the ya'. The best interpretation of this is as a resumption (qat', an independent clause), meaning: "So I hide my brother's nakedness," and then *uwāri* is in the nominative. Al-Zamakhshari said: It was also read with the sukun, as "so I hide," or as a sukun in the place of the accusative for lightness. The meaning is that he dropped the vowel, which is the fatha, for lightness, finding it heavy on the weak letter. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is a dialect in which vowels succeed one another. The end. It should not be taken as an accusative, because the accusative of such a word is marked by the appearance of the fatha. The fatha is not felt as heavy so that it should be dropped for lightness, as al-Zamakhshari suggested, and this is not a dialect as Ibn 'Atiyya claimed, nor is the justification of successive vowels valid, because vowels have not succeeded one another here. According to the grammarians, the accusative with the dropping of the fatha is permissible only in poetic necessity. Therefore the recitation should not be understood in this way when it can be understood in a sound way, and that way exists, namely the resumption: "So I hide."

Al-Zuhri read *sawata akhī* ("the nakedness of my brother") by dropping the hamza and transferring its vowel to the waw. It is not permissible to change the waw into an alif, because it is vowelled and the letter before it is open, since the vowel is incidental, as in *samawal* and *ja'awal*. Abu Hafs read *sawwata* by changing the hamza into a waw and assimilating the waw into it, as they say of *shay'* the form *shayy*, and of *say'a* the form *sayya*. The poet said:

*And if they see an evil, they hasten to it with joy at me, and they do not know of any good they have buried.*

﴿So he became of the regretful﴾. Before this there is an omitted clause, whose sense is: "So he hid his brother's nakedness." The apparent meaning is that his regret was over the killing of his brother, because of what befell him of disobedience and of displeasing his parents, and because he was given the news that he was among the companions of the Fire. This indicates that he was disobedient, not an unbeliever. It has been said: his regret did not benefit him, because regret being a repentance is specific to this community. It has been said: he was regretful over carrying the corpse. It has been said: he was regretful out of fear of disgrace. Al-Zamakhshari said: He was regretful over killing him, when he was tired of carrying him, perplexed about his affair, and it became clear to him from his own weakness and his being taught by the crow, and from the blackening of his colour and his father's wrath, but he did not regret with the regret of those who repent. The end. The scholars differed concerning Qabil: was he an unbeliever or a disobedient one? There is a hadith: "God struck for you the two sons of Adam as an example, so take the good of it and leave its evil." The commentators also recounted wonders that happened upon the killing of Habil: the trembling of the earth for seven days, the earth drinking his blood, the trees weeping, the change of food, the sourness of fruits, the bitterness of water, the earth becoming dusty, and Qabil's flight with his sister Iqlimiya to Aden in the land of Yemen, his worship of fire, and his sons' absorption in making instruments of amusement, drinking wine, fornication and abominations, until God drowned them in the flood. God knows best the soundness of all this. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is related that Adam remained a hundred years after his killing without laughing, and that he lamented him with poetry, but this is a pure lie, and poetry is only a forged and corrupted composition. It is established that the prophets are protected from poetry. Maymun ibn Mihran related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Whoever says that Adam composed poetry is a liar, and he has attributed to Adam what does not befit prophethood, because Muhammad and all the prophets, upon them be peace, are alike in being free from poetry. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it fitting for him﴾ [Ya-Sin: 69]. Rather, he used to lament over him, and he was the first martyr on the face of the earth, and he described his grief over him in prose resembling an elegy. Generations then transmitted it and preserved his words, until it reached Ya'rub ibn Qahtan, who was the first to write in Arabic, and he versified it, saying:

*The lands have changed, and those upon them, so the face of the earth is dusty and ugly.*

After this verse he mentioned six more verses, and that Iblis answered him in metre and rhyme with five verses. Al-Zamakhshari's remark that the poem is *malhun* (ungrammatical or faulty in its metre) refers to a verse which is the second:

*Every thing of colour and taste has changed, and the brightness of the beautiful face has diminished.*

He relates it as *bashashata al-wajhi al-malīh* with the vowel of *iqwā'* (a metrical fault of vowel-rhyme), and it is also reported with the accusative *bashāshatin* without tanwin and the nominative *al-wajhu al-malīh*. It is not ungrammatical. They have explained it by the dropping of the tanwin from *bashāshatin*, its accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and the dropping of the tanwin because of the meeting of the alif and lam has indeed occurred in their speech. It was read: ﴿Ahad﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1], ﴿Allahu al-samad﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 2], and it was related: *wa-la dhākira Allāh* ("and not one who remembers God"), with the tanwin dropped.

﴿Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, other than in retribution for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had killed all of mankind; and whoever gives life to one, it is as if he had given life to all of mankind.﴾ The majority hold that ﴿because of that﴾ is connected to "We prescribed." Some said it is connected to "of those who regret," meaning he regretted because of what had happened. It is said: "ajala al-amr ajalan wa ājilan" when one commits the matter alone, by himself. Zuhayr said:

"And a household in a tent, good, with discord among them; they fought over a hasty matter, and I am the one who bears its consequence."

That is, its perpetrator. Ibn ʿAtiyyah attributed this line to a different context, but it is in the Diwan of Zuhayr. The meaning is: because of that. When you say, "I did that because of you," you mean that you committed it and brought it about. Its meaning is the same as "min jarrāka" (from your offense), that is, from your misdeed. ﴿That﴾ refers to the killing: "from committing that killing, We prescribed for the Children of Israel." "Min" here denotes the starting point, meaning the beginning of the prescribing, and it arose because of the killing. The word "ajl" (cause) is preceded by "min," and the lam is also used with it, as the object of purpose (al-maf'ul lahu, the object indicating the reason for an action) is permitted to drop the preposition and let the verb reach it, under its conditions. It is said: "fa'altu dhālika min ajlika wa li-ajlika," and the hamzah may be pronounced with a fatha or a kasra. Ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ recited with kasra, with its omission, and with transferring its vowel to the preceding consonant, just as Warsh recited with its omission, with fatha, and with transferring the vowel to the nun.

The meaning of ﴿We prescribed﴾ is that it was prescribed by Our command in books revealed to them, containing the obligation of that. The Children of Israel were singled out for mention, although there were nations before them for which the killing of a soul was forbidden and for which retaliation applied. This is because, as it is related, they were the first nation upon whom the threat concerning the killing of a soul was revealed, and the severity of the matter upon them corresponded to their tyranny and their shedding of blood. It is also to show their blameworthiness, in that this was prescribed for them, and yet they do not refrain and do not understand. Rather, they intended to kill the Prophet (ﷺ) unjustly.

The meaning of ﴿other than for a soul﴾ is: other than for killing a soul, so that he deserves to be killed. God has forbidden the soul of a believer except through one of the causes that make killing obligatory. His saying ﴿or corruption﴾ is conjoined to "soul," meaning "or other than for corruption." Corruption has been said to be associating partners with God. It has also been said to be highway robbery, cutting down trees, killing animals except out of necessity, burning crops and what is similar to that, and this is the corruption referred to after this verse. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "The comparison has not been clarified to either extreme of these sayings. What I say is that the comparison between the killer of one soul and the killer of all does not apply in every respect, but the resemblance may arise from three aspects. The first: retaliation, for it is one [in both cases]. The second: the threat, for God has promised the killer of a soul abiding in the Fire, and that is the utmost punishment. If we consider it, he may leave the Fire after that because of monotheism; likewise the killer of all, if that were to happen. The third: the violation of sanctity, for one soul in this respect and all souls are equal, and the violator in one is regarded in the same way as the violator of all. An example of that is two men who swore by two trees that they would not eat any of their fruit, so one of them ate one fruit from (p-469) his tree, and the other ate all the fruit of his two trees; both of them have thus become equal in breaking the oath." End of quotation.

Another said: "It has been said the resemblance is in sin, meaning that he bears the sin of one who kills all of mankind," as said by al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj. It has also been said that the comparison is in the punishment, meaning that he will burn in the Fire for killing one Muslim just as if he had killed all mankind, as said by Mujahid and ʿAtaʾ. This view requires examination, because punishment is lightened or intensified according to the crimes. It has also been said that the comparison is in terms of retaliation (qisas), as said by Ibn Zayd, and this has already been mentioned. It has been said that the comparison is in terms of condemning the ugliness of the act, meaning that all people should help the guardian of the slain man until they exact retaliation from the killer, just as if he had killed all of their guardians. This was mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Yaʿla. This ruling was specific to the Children of Israel, made severe for them just as it was made severe for them regarding the killing of their own selves, as said by some scholars. Others said: this applies to them and to others as well. Sulayman ibn ʿAli said: "I said to al-Hasan, 'O Abu Saʿid, is it for us as it was for the Children of Israel?' He said, 'Yes, by Him besides whom there is no god, the blood of the Children of Israel was not more honoured before God than our blood.'"

It has been said regarding His saying ﴿and whoever gives life to one﴾ that it means he rescues it from destruction. ʿAbdullah, al-Hasan and Mujahid said: that is, from drowning, burning, or destruction. It has been said: whoever supports a prophet or a just imam, since his benefit returns to all people. It has been said: whoever abstains from killing a soul that is forbidden, it is as if he has given life to mankind by withholding his harm from them. It has been said: whoever deters from killing a soul and forbids it. It has been said: whoever helps in carrying out retaliation, because He said: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 179]. Al-Hasan said: "The greatest form of giving life to it is that He gives it life from its disbelief, and its proof is: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light﴾ [al-Anʿam: 122]." End of quotation. The giving of life here is a metaphor, because giving life in the literal sense belongs to God Most High. The meaning is rather: whoever seeks to preserve it and does not destroy it. A similar metaphor is the saying of the one who argued with Ibrahim: "I give life." He named abstention "giving life."

﴿And certainly Our messengers came to them with clear proofs; then, after that, many of them are indeed extravagant in the land.﴾ God Most High informs that excess and corruption were among them despite the coming of the messengers with clear proofs from God. The requirement of the coming of God's messengers with clear evidence was that no excess should proceed from them, and excess is going beyond the limit. They contradicted this requirement. The governing element in "after" (baʿda) and what is connected to it, "in the land," is the predicate of "inna" (indeed). The lam of commencement did not prevent the governing of that, even though it precedes, because its entry upon the predicate is not essential. The demonstrative "that" refers to the coming of the messengers with clear proofs. "The land" means: wherever they settled, they were extravagant. The apparent meaning of excess is that it is not restricted. It has been said that ﴿extravagant﴾ means killing without right, like His saying: ﴿so let him not commit excess in killing﴾ [al-Isra': 33]. It has been said that it is their demand for equality of lineage, so that one person is killed in retaliation for a group of their killers.

﴿Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption is that they be killed, or crucified, or that their hands and feet be cut off on opposite sides, or that they be banished from the land﴾. Anas ibn Malik, Jarir ibn Abd Allah, Abd Allah ibn Umar, Ibn Jubayr and Urwah said: it was revealed concerning the people of ʿUkl and ʿUrayna, and their story is well known. Ibn ʿAbbas said, as related by ʿIkrimah from him: it was revealed concerning the polytheists, and this was also the view of al-Hasan and ʿAtaʾ. Ibn ʿAbbas said in another narration, and so did al-Dahhak: it was revealed concerning a people of the People of the Book who had a covenant with the Messenger, but they broke it and spread corruption in the religion. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the people of Abu Burdah Hilal ibn ʿAmir, who killed a group of the Banu Kinanah who passed by them intending to embrace Islam, and seized their property. There was a truce (muwada‘ah) between the Messenger (ﷺ) and Abu Burdah that he would not assist against him and would not stir up anyone who came to him as a Muslim, but his people did this while he was not present. The majority hold that this verse is neither abrogating (nasikhah) nor abrogated (mansukhah) [naskh: abrogation, the cancelling of a ruling by a later revelation]. It was also said that it abrogated what the Prophet (ﷺ) did to the ʿUrayniyyin of mutilation, and that the ruling was confined to these prescribed penalties.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is evident. When the previous verse mentioned the gravity of the sin of killing a soul without a soul having been slain or corruption on the earth, it followed it with an explanation of what corruption on the earth is that requires killing, since some forms of corruption on the earth do not require killing. There is no disagreement among the scholars that the ruling of this verse applies to Muslim muharibun (those who wage hirabah, armed highway robbery). The school of Malik and a group hold that the muharib is one who takes up weapons against people in a city or in the open country, so as to terrify them regarding their lives and property, without a grudge, enmity or a personal motive. The school of Abu Hanifah and a group hold that the muharibun are highway robbers outside the city; as for within the city, he is liable to the prescribed penalty for whatever he committed of killing, theft, usurpation and the like. The minimum of hirabah is terrorizing the road, then taking property together with terrorizing, then combining terrorizing, taking property and killing. The waging of war against Allah Most High is not possible, so it is understood as an elided construction; that is, "those who wage war against the allies of Allah and His Messenger." Otherwise it would follow that the waging war against Allah and His Messenger would combine the literal and the figurative sense. When this is taken as an elided construction, or as an interpretation by a shared common meaning, the difficulty is removed. The statement of Ibn ʿAbbas that hirabah here means shirk (polytheism), and the statement of Urwah that it means apostasy (irtidad), are not sound according to the majority, and the majority has cited what refutes their statements.

In His saying ﴿wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾ there is severe emphasis on the matter of hirabah. The phrase ﴿strive upon the earth in corruption﴾ may mean that it is their waging war itself, or they attribute corruption to the waging of war. The word ﴿corruption﴾ (fasadan) is in the accusative either as a object of purpose (maf‘ul lahu), or as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), or as a verbal noun derived from the sense of "strive upon the earth," meaning "they cause corruption"; since striving for corruption is made into corruption itself, the meaning is "causing corruption." The apparent sense of the four punishments is that the imam has the choice to apply whichever of them he wishes to the muharib, whatever rank among the ranks we have mentioned the muharib is in. This was the view of al-Nakhaʿi, al-Hasan in one narration, Ibn al-Musayyab, Mujahid and ʿAtaʾ, and it is the school of Malik and a group. Malik said: I prefer that the one who did not kill be dealt with by the lightest punishment, especially if he was not known for great evil; but if he killed, then he must be killed.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Mijlaz, Qatadah, al-Hasan also, and a group said: for each rank of hirabah there is a corresponding rank of punishment.
