Whoever kills is killed; whoever takes property without killing is subject to cutting off from opposite sides; whoever only terrorizes is subject to banishment; and whoever combines them is killed and crucified. Those who hold this order disagreed. Abu Hanifah, Muhammad, al-Shafiʿi and a group, and it is related from Malik, said: he is crucified alive and stabbed until he dies. A group said: he is killed and then crucified, as a deterrent to others; this is the view of al-Shafiʿi. Killing is either by striking the neck with the sword; it was also said: by striking with the sword, or by stabbing with a spear or a dagger. Equivalence (mukafa'ah) with the one he killed is not a condition for killing him. Al-Shafiʿi said: equivalence is taken into account in it as in retaliation (qisas). The duration of crucifixion: a day or three days, or until its pus flows, or for the period in which his crucifixion becomes evident. As for cutting: the right hand is cut from the wrist, and the left foot from the joint. It is related from ʿAli that the cutting is from the fingers, leaving the palm, and from half the foot, leaving the heel. This is contrary to the apparent sense, because the fingers are not called a hand, and half the foot is not called a foot. Malik said: little or much property is the same, so the muharib is cut off if he takes it. The people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) and al-Shafiʿi said: he is not cut off unless he takes what a thief is cut off for. As for banishment, al-Suddi said: it is that he be pursued forever with horses and foot soldiers until he is seized, and then the prescribed punishment of Allah is applied to him and he is expelled from the abode of Islam. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Anas that banishment means he is pursued; this is related from al-Layth and Malik, except that Malik said: no Muslim should be compelled to enter the abode of polytheism. Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas, al-Zuhri and al-Dahhak said: banishment is from the abode of Islam to the abode of polytheism. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz and a group said: he is banished from one city to another distant place. Abu al-Zinad said: banishment in earlier times was to Dahlak and Nasiʿ, which are among the farthest parts of Yemen. Al-Zamakhshari said: Dahlak is at the farthest end of Tihamah, and Nasiʿ is in the lands of Abyssinia. Abu Hanifah said: banishment means imprisonment, which is removing him from the earth. The poet said, saying this while he was imprisoned:

We went out from the world, and we were of its people, so we are not among the dead in it nor among the living.
When the jailer came to us one day on some errand, we were astonished and said: this one has come from the world.
And the dream pleases us; it occupies our talk, and when we rise in the morning, talk is of the dream.

The apparent sense is that his banishment from the land is his removal from the land in which he waged war, if the alif and lam (in "al-ard") denote a known land, so he is banished from that place of activity; and if they denote the genus, then he is continually pursued and harassed, fleeing in fear, until he reaches a place outside the domain of Islam. The explicit view of Malik is that if he is a dangerous person he is exiled and imprisoned wherever he is exiled.

The emphasis in ﴿that they be killed, or crucified, or that they be cut off﴾ is the reading of the majority; it denotes multiplicity in relation to those upon whom the act falls. The lightening (takhfif) of all three is the reading of al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin.

﴿That is for them a disgrace in this world﴾: that is, that penalty of cutting, killing, crucifixion and banishment. Here khizy means humiliation, abasement and disgrace. Khizy also means shame, and it is used here to express public disgrace, since shame is its cause; a person is exposed and so feels shame.

﴿And for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾: its apparent sense is that the sin of hirabah differs from other sins, since in it punishment in this world and punishment in the Hereafter are combined, as an aggravation of the sin of hirabah. This is contrary to the apparent sense of his saying, peace and blessings be upon him, in the hadith of ʿUbadah: "Whoever suffers something of that and is punished for it in this world, it is expiation for him." It may be that this is according to distribution: the disgrace is in this world if he is punished, and the punishment is in the Hereafter if he is spared punishment in this world, so the sin of hirabah falls under the same rule as other sins. This threat, like others, is conditional upon Allah's will; He may forgive this sin. But in the threat there is a fear for the one threatened, lest the threat be carried out.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 34:

﴿Except for those who repent before you have power over them. So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ Its apparent meaning is that it is an exception from those who are punished with the punishment of the highway robber (qati' al-tariq). So if they repent before they are captured, what was incurred because of hirabah (armed robbery/brigandage) falls away from them. This was the action of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, toward Harithah ibn Badr al-Urani, for he had been a muharib (armed robber), then he repented before he was overpowered, so he (Ali) wrote for him a public document (kitaban mansuran) dropping from him the claims concerning property and blood.

They said: The imam has no authority over this except as he has over the rest of the Muslims. So if he is claimed for blood, it is examined and retaliation (qisas) is carried out against him upon the demand of the guardian of the victim. If he is claimed for property, then the school of Malik, al-Shafi'i and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) hold: what is found in his possession of another's property is taken, and he is required to pay the value of what he consumed (istahlaka). And a group of the Companions and the Successors said: he is not required to pay for what he consumed, and what is found in his possession is taken in its own form (bi-'aynihi).

Al-Tabari narrated from Urwah: that the repentance of a muharib is not accepted; but if he fled to the enemy and then came to us repentant, I would not see any punishment upon him. Al-Tabari said: "I do not know whether he meant that he apostatized or not." Al-Awza'i said something similar, except that he said: if he joined the abode of war and apostatized from Islam, or remained upon it, and then came to us repentant before we had power over him, his repentance is accepted.

(p-472) The connection of this verse to what precedes it: when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the punishment of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth to cause corruption, namely the four penalties and the great punishment prepared for them in the Hereafter, He commanded the believers to fear Allah and to seek nearness to Him, for that is what delivers one from warring and from the punishment prepared for those who wage war. Since the verse was revealed concerning the 'Uraniyyin and the Kalbiyyin, or concerning the Jews of the People of the Book, or concerning the polytheists, as the scholars differ on the occasion of revelation, and all of these strove upon the earth to cause corruption, He specified jihad, although it falls under seeking the means (al-wasilah), because through it the earth is set right, through it the religion is sustained, and the Shari'ah is preserved. Thus it is distinct from the matter of warring, since jihad is a permitted form of fighting, and through jihad the warring aggressors are repelled. Also, there is in it an alert that the strength and valour possessed by the fighter must be confined to jihad in the way of Allah, exalted is He, and that he must not put that courage, which Allah has bestowed upon him, to fighting in disobedience to Allah, exalted is He. As for whether the wasilah is the act of nearness that one should seek by it, or the need, or obedience, or Paradise, or its highest rank, these are the views of the exegetes. He mentioned the hope of success (al-falah) on the condition that what He had previously commanded, namely fear of Allah, seeking the means, and jihad in His way, is realised. Al-falah (success) is a comprehensive term for deliverance from what is disliked and attainment of what is hoped for.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 36:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve—if they had all that is on the earth and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves thereby from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them.﴾ When He guided the believers to the foundations of good and the keys of happiness, and mentioned their success in the Hereafter and what they attained of prosperity, He explained the condition of the disbelievers, the outcome of their disbelief, and the punishment prepared for them. The clause consisting of "law" (if/even if) and its answer is in the position of the predicate (khabar) of inna. The meaning of "what is on the earth" is: all kinds of wealth by which one might ransom himself. "And the like of it" is conjoined to the subject of inna. The lam of purpose (lam kay) is connected to what the predicate of inna is connected to, namely "lahum" (for them). The meaning: if what is on the earth and the like of it with it were established as their possession, so that they might make it a ransom for themselves, it would not be accepted. This is by way of illustration (tamthil), and of the necessity of punishment for them, and that there is no way for them to be saved from it.

In a hadith: "It will be said to the disbeliever: Tell me, if you had the fill of the earth in gold, would you ransom yourself with it? He will say: Yes. It will be said to him: You were asked for something easier than that." 

He made the pronoun in "bihi" (with it) singular, although two things preceded it—the conjoined and the conjunct, namely "what is on the earth" and "the like of it with it." This is either because their co-occurrence is presupposed, so they are treated as one thing, as in the saying: "A day and a night passed over me," or because the pronoun is treated like a demonstrative, as if he had said: "to ransom themselves with that."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible for the waw in ﴿wa-mithlahu﴾ to mean 'with' (ma'a), so that the referent is singular." (If you say): "Then in what is the object of 'with' (maf'ul ma'ahu) put in the accusative?" (I say): "By the verb that law implies, because 'law' establishes that they have what is on the earth." End of quote.

The pronoun is singular only because the rule for what precedes the object of 'with' regarding predicate, circumstantial clause, and the return of a pronoun that comes later is the same as for what comes first: you say "the water and the plank levelled," just as you say "the water levelled and the plank..." 

Al-Akhfash permitted in this case that the item be given the rule of the conjunct, so that you say: "the water with the plank became level (dual)," but Ibn Kaysan forbade this.

Al-Zamakhshari's statement that the waw in ﴿wa-mithlahu﴾ means "with" is not valid, because the sense would become "with its like with it"; that is, "with the like of what is on the earth, with what is on the earth," if you make the pronoun in "ma'ahu" refer to "mithlahu"; i.e., "with its like, with that like," so the meaning would be "with two like things." Expressing this meaning with that phrasing is clumsy, since the proper construction for that meaning would be "with its two likes."

As for al-Zamakhshari's statement "If you say..." through the end of the question, this question need not be raised, because we have already shown the corruption of taking the waw as the waw of "with." And even granting it, this is his reasoning based on the view that "anna" after "law" is in the position of the subject (raf' 'ala al-fa'iliyya), so the sense would be: "If the existence of what is on the earth together with its like were established for them, so that they might ransom themselves with it," and the pronoun would refer only to "ma." This is his deduction from the view of al-Mubarrad that "anna" after "law" is in the position of the subject, and that view is weaker. Sibawayh's view is that "anna" after "law" is in the position of the inchoative (nominative as subject of a nominal sentence).

Nothing in al-Zamakhshari's statements in this book or his other works shows that he was acquainted with Sibawayh's view on this question. And on the basis of al-Mubarrad's view, "wa-mithlahu" cannot validly be an object of 'with', with the governing element being the verb mentioned—"thabata" (was established)—through the mediation of the waw, because of the presence of the word "ma'ahu" mentioned earlier. And even if that is dropped, it is not valid, because "thabata" does not govern "ma" to which the pronoun refers; rather it governs a verbal noun formed from "anna" and what follows it, namely "kawn" (existence), since the sense is: "If the existence of what is on the earth entirely were established for them, and its like with it, so that they might ransom themselves with it," and the pronoun refers to what is other than the existence. So the agent of the subject is not the same as the governor of the object of 'with', for if it were, it would follow that the establishment accompanies the like; the meaning would be "on the existence of what is on the earth accompanied by the like," not "on the establishment of that accompanied by the like." This is somewhat obscure, and its clarification is this: when you say "The standing of Zayd and 'Amr pleases me," whether you make 'Amr an object of 'with' governed by "pleases me," it follows that 'Amr did not stand, and that the standing together with him pleased you; but if you make the standing the governor of it, then 'Amr is standing, and the pleasing has attached itself to the standing accompanying the standing of 'Amr.

(If you say): "Why not make 'wa-mithlahu ma'ahu' an object of 'with', governed by the same governor as 'lahum', since that is the sense intended?" (I say): This is not valid, for the reason we have mentioned, namely the presence of "ma'ahu" in the sentence; and even if it is dropped, it is not valid, because they have stated explicitly that your saying "this is yours and your father's" is disallowed in the preferred usage. Sibawayh said: "As for 'this is yours and your father's,' it is ugly, because he has not mentioned a verb nor a particle containing the sense of a verb, so that it is as if he had spoken with a verb." Sibawayh thus made clear that the demonstrative and the prepositional particle implying the sense of 'being established' do not govern the object of 'with'; and if either of them could make the object of 'with' accusative, one would be free to attribute the governing to the demonstrative or to the prepositional particle. Some grammarians have permitted the adverbial phrase and the prepositional particle to govern the object of 'with'; on this view, if the sentence lacked the words "ma'ahu," it would be permissible for "wa-mithlahu" to be an object of 'with', its governor being the same governor as "lahum."

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read: "ma tuqubbila," in the passive voice. Yazid ibn Qutayb read: "ma taqabbala," in the active voice; i.e., "what Allah accepted from them." In the speech there is an omitted clause, the sense being: "and they expended it and ransomed themselves with it, so it would not be accepted from them," since the non-acceptance does not follow from the existence of what is on the earth and its like with it; it follows only from expending that or ransoming oneself with it.

﴿And for them is a painful punishment.﴾ This threat is for whoever dies in disbelief, and the verse of Al 'Imran clarifies it: ﴿And they die while they are disbelievers—never will there be accepted from any of them…﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91]. This clause may be conjoined to the predicate of ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾, and it may be conjoined to ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ itself. Some have also permitted that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), but this is not strong.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 37–38 (part 1 of 3):

﴿They wish to come out of the Fire﴾. That is, they hope, or they desire, or they are about to, or they ask. These are close in meaning, and wishing is possible on their part, so it should not be taken out of its apparent sense. Al-Hasan said: When the Fire seethes with them, they flee from its violence, and at that point they wish to come out and hope for it. This is His saying: ﴿They wish to come out of the Fire﴾. It was said to Jabir ibn Abd Allah: "You, companions of Muhammad, say that a people will come out of the Fire, while Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and they will not come out of it﴾." Jabir replied: "This is only about the disbelievers specifically." Al-Tabari related from Nafi' ibn al-Azraq the Kharijite that he said to Ibn Abbas: "O you who are blind in sight, O you who are blind in heart, do you claim that a people will come out of the Fire when Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿and they will not come out of it﴾?" Ibn Abbas said to him: "Read what comes before it. This verse is about the disbelievers." Al-Zamakhshari said: As for what is related from Ikrimah, that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq said to Ibn Abbas, and he mentioned the account, then said: This is among what the Mujbira (the determinists, a group who deny human choice) fabricated, and it is not the first of their lies and inventions. It is enough to show its falsehood that it has Ibn al-Azraq confronting the cousin of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while he was in the midst of his supporters from Quraysh and his helpers from the Banu Abd al-Muttalib, and he was the scholar and sea of this community and its interpreter, with an address that no one among the people of this world would dare to use toward his like, and by its being traced back to Ikrimah, these are two clear proofs that the report is a fabrication beyond doubt. End of quote. He is in his usual manner and foolishness in abusing the people of the Sunnah, and his doctrine is that whoever enters the Fire does not come out of it.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿أنْ يَخْرُجُوا﴾ (an yakhrujū), in the active voice, and ﴿وما هم بِخارِجِينَ مِنها﴾ fits with this. Al-Nakha'i, Ibn Watthab, and Abu Waqid read ﴿أنْ يُخْرَجُوا﴾ (an yukhrajū), in the passive voice.

﴿And theirs is a lasting punishment﴾, that is, one that is perpetual and will not be changed.

﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands﴾. Al-Sa'ib said: It was revealed concerning Ta'mah ibn Ubayriq, and its story has passed in Surat al-Nisa'.

Its connection to what precedes it: when He mentioned the punishment of those who wage war (al-muharibun) with penalties that include cutting off hands and feet on opposite sides, and then commanded that one be cautious lest a person fall into any part of hirabah (armed robbery or brigandage), and then mentioned the state of the disbelievers, He mentioned the ruling on theft, because in it is the cutting of hands according to the Qur'an, and of feet according to the Sunnah, as will be mentioned. It is also a form of hirabah in meaning, because it involves seeking corruption, except that the one is done openly with force and power, while theft is done secretly and covertly. The apparent meaning is that cutting is obligatory for the mere name of theft, and this is the apparent sense of the text. If one steals an egg, his hand is cut off; if one steals a camel, his right hand is cut off; if one steals anything at all, little or much, his hand is cut off. This view was held by a group of the Companions and of the Successors, among them al-Hasan, and it is the doctrine of the Khawarij (an early sect) and of Dawud (al-Zahiri).

Dawud and those who agree with him said: The hand is not cut for stealing a single grain or a single date, but only for the least thing that is called property, and at the least thing that shows stinginess and niggardliness. It was said: The threshold (nisab) at which the hand is cut is ten dirhams or more, or its value in other goods. This was related from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Amr Ayman al-Habashi, Abu Ja'far, Ata', and Ibrahim, and it is the view of al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Zufar, and Muhammad (al-Shaybani). It was said: a quarter of a dinar or more. This was related from Umar, Uthman, Ali, Aisha, and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, and it is the view of al-Awza'i, al-Layth, al-Shafi'i, and Abu Thawr. It was said: five dirhams, and this is the view of Anas, Urwa, Sulayman ibn Yasar, and al-Zuhri. It was said: four dirhams, and this is related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Abu Hurayra. It was said: three dirhams, and this is the view of Ibn Umar. Malik, Ishaq, and Ahmad also said this, except that if the theft is of gold, the hand is not cut unless it is a quarter of a dinar. It was said: one dirham or more, and Uthman al-Battі held this. Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr cut a hand for one dirham. The theft for which the hand is cut has conditions mentioned in jurisprudence (fiqh).

The majority read ﴿والسّارِقُ والسّارِقَةُ﴾ (wa-l-sāriqu wa-l-sāriqatu) with the nominative (raf'). Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud) read ﴿والسّارِقُونَ والسّارِقاتُ فاقْطَعُوا أيْمانَهم﴾, "And the male thieves and the female thieves, cut off their right hands." Al-Khaffaf said: I found in the codex of Ubayy: "wa-l-suruqu wa-l-suruqatu," with a doubled sin vowelled with a damma in both, as Abu Amr vocalized it. Ibn Atiyya said: It seems that this is a scribal error by the one who vocalized it, because the reading of the community, when the word al-sariq is written without an alif, agrees with this in the script.

The nominative in ﴿والسّارِقُ والسّارِقَةُ﴾ is as a subject (mubtada', the topic of the sentence), and the predicate (khabar) is omitted. The estimate is: "What is recited to you" or "What has been made obligatory upon you" is the ruling on the male thief and the female thief. Sibawayh does not permit the predicate to be ﴿فاقْطَعُوا﴾, because the particle "fa" (fa') enters only into the predicate of a topic that is a relative construction (ism mawsul, a relative noun such as "the one who") joined to an adverb of place or time or to a prepositional phrase, that is, a clause suitable to follow a conditional particle. The relative here is "al" (the definite article used as a relative), and its complement is an active participle or passive participle, and according to Sibawayh the "fa" does not enter the predicate of such a construction. A group of the Basran grammarians permitted it, meaning that ﴿والسّارِقُ والسّارِقَةُ﴾ is the topic and the predicate is the imperative clause. They treated "al" and its complement as if it were the relative mentioned, because its meaning is general: that is, "the one who stole and the one who stole (feminine)." Since Sibawayh's view is that this is not permitted, he interpreted it by supposing an omitted predicate, so that his interpretation becomes: "In what is made obligatory upon you is the ruling on the male thief and the female thief," a clause whose apparent form would be independent, but the intended point is in His saying ﴿fa-qtaʿū (so cut off)﴾. The "fa" was brought as a linking particle for the second clause, so the first clause clarifies the ruling that was vague in the first clause.

Isa ibn Umar and Ibn Abi Abla read ﴿والسّارِقَ والسّارِقَةَ﴾ with the accusative (nasb) through what is called ishtighal (a construction in which the verb is occupied with a pronoun referring back to the noun). Sibawayh said: The preferred form in the speech of the Arabs is the accusative, as you say: "Zayd, strike him." But the common readers insisted on the nominative, meaning the majority of the readers. Since most of the readers are on the nominative, Sibawayh interpreted it in a way that is valid, namely that he made it a topic with an omitted predicate, because if he made it a topic and the predicate were ﴿fa-qtaʿū﴾, that would be a construction contrary to the usage of the Arabs, and the "fa" would enter the predicate of "al," which he does not permit.

Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Umar, known as Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, son of the preacher of al-Ray, presumed to criticize Sibawayh and attributed to him what he did not say. He said: What Sibawayh held is not valid, and several points show its corruption. The first: he criticized a reading transmitted by mass transmission (mutawatir) from the Messenger, and from the leading scholars of the community, and that is clearly false. (I say:) This is an invention against Sibawayh and a lack of understanding of him. Sibawayh did not criticize the reading in the nominative. Rather, he gave it the interpretation mentioned, and he made clear that the issue is not one of ishtighal built on the permissibility of making the noun a topic in it and the imperative clause being its predicate, nor of leaving the noun in the accusative. For if it were of that kind, the accusative would be preferable, as it is in "Zayd, strike him," according to what is established in the speech of the Arabs. So the fact that the majority of readers turned to the nominative is evidence that they did not make the nominative here a topic whose predicate is the imperative verb, because that is not permitted on account of the "fa." Therefore his statement "The common people insisted on the nominative" strengthens his interpretation and weakens the accusative as ishtighal in the presence of the "fa." For the accusative as ishtighal, preferred over the topic in such a structure, is not permitted, unless it is permissible for the noun to be a topic whose predicate is the verb that explains the governing element in the ishtighal, and here that is not permitted on account of the "fa" that enters the predicate. So the accusative should not be permitted. Thus the meaning of Sibawayh's speech supports the nominative as stated, so how could he be one who criticizes the nominative? Sibawayh also said: It is good and correct: "Abd Allah, strike him," when it is built on an implied or stated topic. As for the stated one, your saying: "This is Zayd, strike him." And if you wish, you do not state "this." It works in the same way when stated, as in your saying: "The crescent, by Allah, look at it," as if you said: "This is the crescent," then you brought the imperative. Among that is the verse of the poet:

"And a speaker said: 'Khawlan, marry their young women,' and the nobility of the two tribes is empty, just as it is."

Thus it was heard from the Arabs reciting it. End of quote. If Sibawayh says: "It is good and correct: Abd Allah, strike him," how could he be a critic of the nominative, when he says that it is good and correct? Rather, he allowed it on the basis that the nominative noun is a topic whose predicate is omitted, as he interpreted it in "the male thief and the female thief," or the predicate of an omitted topic, as in his saying: "The crescent, by Allah, look at it."

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: "If you say" — meaning Sibawayh — "I do not say that the reading with the nominative (raf') is impermissible, but I say that the reading with the accusative (nasb) is preferable," then we say to him: this is also poor, because preferring a reading that only ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read over the reading of the Messenger and of the entire community in the time of the Companions and the Successors is an abhorrent and rejected matter.

(I [Abu Hayyan] say): This objection was not raised by Sibawayh, nor is he one who would raise it. How could he say it, when he has already preferred the reading with the nominative, as we have made clear! Moreover, his statement, "because preferring a reading that only ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read over the reading of the Messenger and of the entire community in the time of the Companions and the Successors," is a disparagement and gives the false impression that ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read it on his own authority. That is not so. Rather, his reading is grounded in (p-478) the Companions and in the Messenger (ﷺ), so his reading is also the reading of the Messenger (ﷺ). And his statement, "and the entire community," this generalization is not valid, because ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, Ibrahim ibn Abi ʿAbla, those who agreed with them, and their teachers from whom they took this reading, are all part of the community.

Sibawayh said: "Some people have read: 'and the male thief and the female thief, and the adulteress and the adulterer,'" thereby informing us that it is the reading of some people. His statement "the entire community" is not a valid generalization.

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: The second of the aspects that indicate the corruption of Sibawayh's view: if the reading with the accusative were preferable, it would necessarily follow that among the readers there would be someone who read ﴿وَاللَّذَانِ يَأْتِيَانِهَا مِنكُمْ فَآذُوهُمَا﴾ [an-Nisa: 16] with the accusative. Since no reader is found to have read it that way, we know that this view is invalid.

(I say): Sibawayh did not claim that the accusative reading is preferable, so this objection does not apply to him. Rather, Sibawayh said: "Some people have read 'and the male thief and the female thief, and the adulteress and the adulterer,'" and it is, in Arabic, as I have mentioned to you, of considerable strength; but the general body of readers refused anything but the nominative reading. What Sibawayh means by "of strength" is: if it were stripped of the fa' (fa' al-jaza'/particle of consequence) that is presumed to enter upon the predicate of a nominative subject beginning a sentence, with the imperative clause as its predicate. But the general body of readers, i.e., the majority of readers, refused anything but the nominative, because of the reason for the entry of the fa', since it is not valid for the imperative clause to be the predicate of this subject. Thus, when the fa' entered, the majority preferred the nominative. For this reason, when Sibawayh mentioned the preference for the accusative in the imperative and prohibitive, he did not illustrate it with the fa' but with it stripped of it. Sibawayh said: "That is (p-479) your saying: Zayd, strike him; ʿAmr, pass by him; Khalid, strike his father; Zayd, buy him a garment." Then he said: "In the imperative and prohibitive, the verb may be constructed upon the noun, as in your saying: ʿAbd Allah, so strike him. You began with ʿAbd Allah and raised him by the inceptive (ibtida'), and you alerted the addressee to him so that he would know him by name, then you constructed the verb upon him, just as you do in the case of the predicate. But if you say: Zayd, so strike him, it is not right; you do not treat him as the inceptive. Do you not see that if you said: Zayd, so he is departing, it would not be right? This is evidence that it is not permissible for it to be an inceptive, meaning a topic about which a predicate is stated with an imperative verb preceded by the fa' that is permissible to enter upon the predicate." Then Sibawayh said: "If you wish, put it in the accusative governed by a verb which this explains." Since Sibawayh prohibited the nominative there as an inceptive with an imperative clause as its predicate because of the fa', he permitted its accusative by way of ishtighal (verbal preoccupation), not on the basis that the fa' is the particle entering upon the predicate of the topic.

The summary of what is understood from Sibawayh's words: an imperative clause without a fa' after a noun—the accusative is preferred there, and the nominative (inceptive) is permissible, with the imperative clause as its predicate. If the fa' enters upon it, then either you presume it to be the fa' entering upon the predicate, or it is a conjunctive fa'. If you presume it to be the fa' entering upon the predicate, then that noun cannot be an inceptive with the imperative clause as its predicate, except when the topic is treated as a conditional noun because of its resemblance to it, which has conditions mentioned in grammar. If it is conjunctive, that noun is nominative, either as an inceptive, as Sibawayh interpreted in his saying "al-sariq wa'l-sariqa" (p-480), or as the predicate of an omitted inceptive, as is said: "The moon, by God, so look at it." The accusative in this sense is less preferable than the nominative, because when you put it in the accusative you need a verbal clause to be conjoined to it with the fa', and an omission of the governing verb, and a displacement of the fa' from its proper position. When you say "Zayd, so strike him," the estimate is: "Be alert, so strike Zayd, strike him": "be alert" is omitted, "strike" is omitted, and the fa' is postponed until its entry upon the explained element. The nominative is preferable, because there is neither omission of an inceptive nor omission of a predicate. The omitted element is only one of the two components of the predication, and the fa' stands in its proper place, and the context and meaning of the speech indicate that omitted element.

Sibawayh said: As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿The adulteress and the adulterer, flog each one of them﴾ [an-Nur: 2] and ﴿The male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾ — this is not constructed upon the verb, but it came in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The parable of the Garden which the God-fearing are promised﴾ [Muhammad: 15], then after it He said: "in it are rivers..." and so on. The parable was set forth as a preface to the narrative that follows it, and it was mentioned after reports and narratives, as if He had said: "Among the stories is the parable of the Garden," or "what We relate to you is the parable of the Garden." So it is carried upon this supposition or the like, and God knows best. Likewise, the adulteress and the adulterer: when He said, exalted is He, ﴿A surah which We have sent down and imposed﴾ [an-Nur: 1], He said regarding the obligations: ﴿The adulteress and the adulterer﴾ [an-Nur: 2], or ﴿The adulteress and the adulterer﴾ among the obligations; then He said: "flog," so He brought the verb after the nominative had already passed in it, as he said. And as in the verse, "A speaker from Khawlan: so marry their young woman," where the verb came after the pronoun had governed it. Likewise "al-sariq wa'l-sariqa": as if he said: "Among what is imposed upon you is the male thief and the female thief," or "the male thief and the female thief concerning what is imposed upon you." These nouns came after stories and narratives. End of quotation.

So Sibawayh chose this analysis because it entails less burden than the accusative while the fa' is present; and the fa' is not the one entering upon the predicate of the topic, because Sibawayh does not permit that with the relative particle alif-lam. Thus, according to him, the two verses fall under the category of "Zayd, so strike him," and just as the preferred option there is the nominative, so likewise in the two verses.

* *

As for al-Razi's statement, "it would necessarily follow that among the readers there would be someone who read ﴿وَاللَّذَانِ يَأْتِيَانِهَا مِنكُمْ فَآذُوهُمَا﴾ with the accusative," etc., Sibawayh did not say that the accusative in this kind of construction is preferable, so it does not follow that among the readers someone would read "wa'lladhani ya'tiyanih" with the accusative. Rather, Sibawayh treated this verse in the same way as "al-sariq wa'l-sariqa," because the preceding context already indicates the omitted element, namely His saying: ﴿وَاللَّاتِي يَأْتِينَ الْفَاحِشَةَ مِن نِّسَائِكُمْ﴾ [an-Nisa: 15]. So Sibawayh construed the verse as involving an implied element. Sibawayh also said: this may apply to Zayd and ʿAmr in this manner when you are reporting matters or giving instructions, and then you say: "Zayd," i.e., Zayd is among those I instruct, so be kind to him and honor him. And in ﴿وَاللَّذَانِ يَأْتِيَانِهَا مِنكُمْ﴾ [an-Nisa: 16], it is permissible to be nominative as an inceptive, with the clause containing the fa' as its predicate, because it is a relative pronoun fulfilling the conditions of the relative that permits the fa' in its predicate, owing to its resemblance to the conditional noun. This is unlike His saying: ﴿وَالسَّارِقُ وَالسَّارِقَةُ﴾, for according to Sibawayh the fa' may not enter its predicate, because it does not function as a conditional noun and so is not made similar to it in the entry of the fa'.

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: The third [aspect], meaning among the flaws of Sibawayh's view: we only say that "al-sariq wa'l-sariqa" is the topic, and its predicate is what is implied, namely our saying: "in what is recited to you," and in something to which the fa' in His saying ﴿فَاقْطَعُوا أَيْدِيَهُمَا﴾ is connected. (I say): The wisdom of bringing the fa' and what it links has already been explained to us. Sibawayh estimated it as: "Among what is imposed upon you is the male thief and the female thief," and the meaning is: the ruling on the male thief and the female thief, because this verse came after mention of the punishment and rulings of those who wage war, so Sibawayh's estimate fits. The fa' is brought to link the second clause to the first, and the second came explaining the ruling left unspecified in what precedes it. Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: If [Sibawayh] says the fa' is connected to the verb indicated by His saying "al-sariq wa'l-sariqa," meaning: if he commits theft, cut off his hand, we say: when at the end of the matter you need to say "al-sariq wa'l-sariqa," its estimate is "whoever steals," so mention this first, so that the implied element you mentioned is not needed. (I say): Sibawayh does not say this, and we have already explained the ruling and function of the fa'.

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: The fourth [aspect], meaning among the flaws of Sibawayh's view: if we choose the accusative reading, it does not indicate that theft is the cause for the obligation of amputation; whereas if we choose the nominative reading, the verse conveys this meaning, and this meaning is reinforced by His saying: ﴿جَزَاءً بِمَا كَسَبَا﴾, so it is established that the nominative reading is preferable. (I say): This is strange from this man. He claims that the accusative does not indicate the causal ground that necessitates amputation, while the nominative conveys it. Is this anything other than causation by a descriptive attribute upon which the ruling is consequent? There is no difference in this respect between the nominative and the accusative: if you say "the thief, so that he be cut off," or "cut off the thief," there is no difference between them in terms of causation. Likewise "the adulterer, so that he be flogged," or "flog the adulterer." Then his claim that this meaning is reinforced by His saying: ﴿جَزَاءً بِمَا كَسَبَا﴾, the accusative can also be reinforced by something similar: if you say "cut off the thief as a recompense for what he committed," it is correct.

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: The fifth [aspect], meaning among the flaws of Sibawayh's view: Sibawayh said: "They give priority to what is more important, and what they are more concerned to explain." The nominative reading entails mentioning his being a thief before the obligation of amputation, and this requires that the greater concern be directed to explaining what pertains to the thief's state insofar as he is a thief; whereas the accusative reading entails that the concern be focused on explaining the amputation more than on his being a thief. It is known that this is not so, since the purpose of this verse is to express the ugliness of theft and to intensify the deterrent against it, so it is established that the nominative reading is definitively the required one. (I say): What Sibawayh stated, that they used to give priority to what is more important to them, and what they are more concerned to explain—these are the cases where the relation of predication differs, such as the agent and the object. Sibawayh said: If you place the object first and the agent after, the utterance proceeds as it did in the first case, i.e., in "ḍaraba ʿAbd Allāh Zaydan": he said: "that is, ḍaraba Zaydan ʿAbd Allāh, because you intended by the latter what you intended by the former, and you did not intend to occupy the verb with something before it, even though it is later in the wording. Hence the proper form of the wording is that it be first; this is a good and frequent Arabic usage, as if they give priority to what is more important to them, and what they are more concerned to explain, though both concern them and matter to them." End of quotation.

[p. 482] Al-Razi distorted the words of Sibawayh and applied them where no difference of relation can be conceived. The relation here is that of the subject (*mubtada'*) and predicate (*khabar*), and in it there is only one relation, unlike the agent (*fa'il*) and the object (*maf'ul*). The speaker may have a purpose in mentioning the one from whom the striking proceeds, so he puts the agent first, or in mentioning the one on whom the striking falls, so he puts the object first, because the relation of striking differs depending on which of the two is considered. As for the verse, it belongs to the category where the relation does not differ. It is simply the ruling concerning the thief, that his hand be cut off. What al-Razi mentioned does not derive from the words of Sibawayh in any way. It is strange that this man, with his boldness toward the sciences, wrote a book on grammar which he named *al-Muharrar*, and followed in it a strange and distant method, far from the terminology and aims of the grammarians. It is a slight book that contains some chapters of Arabic. I heard our shaykh Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr mention this work and say: "It does not follow the terminology of the people, and the confusion in the sciences that he followed in it is such that whoever is dominated by one discipline will show, in what he says on other subjects or ones close to it, this meaning." When I came upon this book in the land of Egypt, I saw what the master Abu Ja'far used to criticize in it, and that it leads the intellect of Fakhr al-Din astray in that he wrote in a science he did not belong to. Abu Ja'far used to say: "Every science has a limit at which it ends. When you see a speaker on one discipline who mixes it with another, know that this is either from his confusion and the muddling of his mind, or from the scantiness of his acquired knowledge and his deficiency in that science, so you will find him resting on what he knows of other things."

Al-Zamakhshari, after mentioning the view of Sibawayh on the i'rab (grammatical inflection) of *wa-al-sariqu wa-al-sariqatu*, said the following text: "Another possibility is that both are raised by the inchoative (*ibtida'*), and the predicate is *fa-aqta'u aydiyahuma*, and the entry of the *fa'* is because it contains the meaning of the conditional, because the meaning is: 'The man who stole and the woman who stole, cut off their hands,' and the relative noun has taken on the meaning of the conditional. Isa ibn Umar read it with the accusative, and Sibawayh preferred it over the reading of the common people because of the imperative, since *Zaydan fa-idribhu* is better than *Zaydun fa-idribhu*." End of quotation. This possibility that he permitted, although some have held it, is not allowed according to Sibawayh, because the relative pronoun has not been joined to a clause suitable for a conditional particle, nor to what takes its place of an adverbial phrase or a prepositional phrase. Rather, the relative here is *al* (the definite article as relative), and the clause of *al* is not suitable for a conditional particle. The relative has merged with its clause, so that the i'rab falls within the clause, unlike the adverbial and prepositional phrase, for the governing element in them is a clause that is not suitable for a conditional particle. As for his statement about the reading of Isa, that Sibawayh preferred it over the reading of the common people, this is not correct. What Sibawayh mentioned in his book is that there are two constructions: one is *zaydan idribhu*, and the second is *zaydun fa-idribhu*. In the first construction he chose the accusative, then they permitted the nominative by the inchoative. As for the second construction, he forbade that it be raised by the inchoative with the imperative clause as its predicate because of the *fa'*. He permitted its accusative by *ishtighal* (the verb being occupied with the pronoun), or by *igra'* (incitement). He mentioned that it is correct to raise it on the basis that there are two clauses, with *Zaydun* as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, *hadha Zaydun fa-idribhu* ("this is Zayd, so strike him"). Then he cited the verse and analyzed it on the basis of the omission of the predicate. His statement indicates that this construction can only be in two clauses: the first is inchoative. Then he mentioned the reading of some people with the accusative and did not prefer it over the reading of the common people. He only said: "It is, in Arabic, as I have told you, of great strength," that is, he put it in the accusative by *ishtighal* or *igra'*, and this is strong, not weak. Sibawayh has forbidden its raising by the inchoative with the imperative clause as predicate because of the *fa'*. We have mentioned the preference between its raising as a subject whose predicate is omitted, or a predicate whose subject is omitted, and he explained its accusative by *ishtighal*, since the nominative requires the omission of one predicate, whereas the accusative requires the omission of a clause and the supposing of another, and the shifting of the *fa'* from its place.

The apparent sense of his statement "*wa-al-sariqu*" is that no protected storage (*hirz*) is required for the stolen property. This was the view of Dawud and the Kharijites. The majority hold that a condition for the amputation is that the goods be removed from the protected storage, and that if he gathered clothes in a house but did not take them out, he is not amputated. Al-Hasan said: he is amputated. The apparent sense is that everyone who is called a thief falls under the generality of *wa-al-sariqu wa-al-sariqatu*. However, there is consensus (*ijma'*) that a father who steals from his son's property is not amputated, and the majority hold that a son is not amputated [for stealing from his father]. Abd Allah ibn al-Hasan said: if they (the parents) allow him to enter upon them, there is no amputation, but if they forbid him from entering, he is amputated. Those within the prohibited degrees (*dhawu al-mahram*) are not amputated according to Abu Hanifa, nor are grandparents on the father's or mother's side according to the majority and according to Ashhab. Abu Thawr said: every thief who steals what the hand is cut for is amputated, unless they agree on something, in which case it is submitted to the consensus. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said: a woman is not amputated if she steals from her husband's property, nor is a husband if he steals from his wife's property. Malik said: both are amputated. The apparent sense is that whoever confesses to theft once is amputated. This was said by Abu Hanifa, Zufar, Malik, al-Shafi'i, and al-Thawri. Ibn Shubruma, Abu Yusuf, and Ibn Abi Layla said: he is not amputated until he confesses twice. Abu Hanifa said: the thief of a copy of the Qur'an (*mushaf*) is not amputated. Al-Shafi'i, Abu Yusuf, Abu Thawr, and Ibn al-Qasim said: he is amputated if its value reaches the nisab (the minimum threshold). The apparent sense is the amputation for stealing a *tayyar* (a flying bird) if it reaches the nisab. This was said by Malik, al-Awza'i, Abu Thawr, and Ya'qub, and it is the view of al-Hasan. Abu Hanifa, Muhammad, and Ishaq held that if the dirhams were tied in his sleeve he is not amputated, but if they were inside [his garment], he is amputated. There is disagreement concerning the grave-robber (*nabbash*) who takes the shroud. Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, and Muhammad said: he is not amputated. This is also the view of Ibn Abbas and Makhul. Al-Zuhri said: the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ agreed, at a time when Marwan was governor of Medina, that the grave-robber is disciplined (*yu'azzaru*) and not amputated, and the Companions were numerous at that time. Abu al-Darda', Ibn Abi Layla, Rabi'a, Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Abu Yusuf said: he is amputated. This is also reported from Ibn al-Zubayr, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, al-Zuhri, Masruq, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, and Ata. The apparent sense is that if he repeats the theft of the same item after its amputation has been carried out for it, he is not amputated. This was said by the majority. Abu Hanifa said: he is not amputated, and if he steals a nisab from a thief, he is not amputated. This was said by al-Shafi'i. Malik said: he is amputated. The one addressed by His words *fa-aqta'u* ("so cut off") is the Messenger or those in authority such as the sultan, or whoever is authorized to carry out the prescribed punishments, or the judges and rulers, or the believers, so that they may cooperate in establishing the prescribed punishments. There are four views. Some scholars made a distinction, saying: if there is an imam in the city or a deputy of his, the address is directed to him; if there is none but there is a judge, the address is directed to him; if neither is there, it is directed to the general body of believers, and at that time it is a communal obligation (*fard al-kifaya*): when some of them carry it out, it is dropped from the rest.

The apparent sense of His words *fa-aqta'u aydiyahuma* ("so cut off their hands") is that two hands are cut from the thief. But consensus is against this apparent sense, and only the right hand is cut from the male thief, and the right hand of the female thief. Al-Zamakhshari said: *aydiyahuma* means their two hands. Similar to it is His words *faqad sagat qulubukuma* ("your hearts have inclined", 66:4), where the dual of the one added to is used in place of the dual of the one added, and by the two hands the two right hands are meant, based on the reading of Abd Allah: *wa-al-sariquna wa-al-sariqatu fa-aqta'u aymanahum* ("the male thieves and the female thieves, so cut off their right hands"). End of quotation. He equated *aydiyahuma* with *qulubukuma*, though they are not the same, because the pattern of *sagat qulubukuma* allows the plural to be placed in the position of the dual, which is when the two are two of two things, such as the heart, the nose, the face, and the back. But if each of the two has two (like the two hands, the two ears, the two thighs), the placement of the plural in the position of the dual is not regular; it is only preserved and not analogized from. This is because the mind only takes the plural in its apparent sense when it is used absolutely according to what its wording indicates. If one says *qutri'at adhanu al-Zaydayn* ("the ears of the two Zayds were cut off"), the apparent sense is the cutting of four ears, which is using the word in its denotation. Ibn Atiyya said: he used the plural *aydi* because each thief has one right hand that is exposed to amputation in theft, and the thieves have hands and the female thieves have hands, as if he said: "Cut off the right hands of the two kinds." So the dual is for the pronoun, which is for the two kinds. The apparent sense of His words *aydiyahuma* is that the foot is not cut. If he steals, his right hand is cut; if he steals again, his left hand is cut; if he steals again, he is disciplined and imprisoned. This is the view of Malik and the majority, and Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri said so too. Ali, al-Zuhri, Hammad ibn Abi Salama, and Ahmad said: his right hand is cut, then if he steals again his left foot is cut, then if he steals again he is disciplined and imprisoned. Ata narrated: in theft only the right hand is cut, then if he steals again he is disciplined and imprisoned. Al-Shafi'i said: if he steals the first time, his right hand is cut; the second time, his left foot; the third time, his left hand; the fourth time, his right foot. This was narrated from Umar. It was said that he then returned to the view of Ali. The apparent sense of cutting the hand is that it is from the shoulder joint, from the joint. It was narrated from Ali that for the hand it is from the fingers, and for the foot from the middle of the foot, which is the place where the strap is tied. The same was narrated from Ata and Abu Ja'far. Abu Salih al-Samman said: I saw the one whose hand Ali had cut off, and he was cut off from the tips of the fingers. It was said to him: "Who cut you?" He said: "The best of people."

The apparent sense is that what is required by the theft is only the cutting of the hand. If the property still exists in its own form, its owner takes it back; if the thief has consumed it, there is no liability upon him. This was said by Makhul, Ata, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Sirin, and al-Nakha'i, according to the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions. Al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, al-Nakha'i according to the view of Hammad, Uthman al-Battí, al-Layth, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Ishaq said: he must compensate and be fined. Malik said: if he is wealthy, he is liable; if he is poor, nothing is upon him.

*Jaza'an bima kasaba nakalan mina Allah* ("as a recompense for what they earned, an exemplary punishment from Allah"). Al-Kisa'i said: *jaza'an* is in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*). Qutrub said: it is in the accusative as an infinitive (*masdar*), meaning: "He recompensed them with a recompense." The majority said: it is an accusative of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*), *bima* is attached to *jaza'an*, and *ma* is a relative pronoun, meaning: "for that which they had earned." It is possible that it is a verbal noun (*masdariyya*), meaning: "a recompense for their earning." The accusative of *nakalan* is as an infinitive, or as an accusative of purpose. Al-adhab (the punishment) is the *nakal*, and *al-nakal* is the shackle. Its discussion was already given in His words: *fa-ja'alnaha nakalan* ("We made it an exemplary punishment", 2:66). Al-Zamakhshari said: *jaza'an* and *nakalan* are two objects of purpose. End of quotation. He followed in this al-Zajjaj. Al-Zajjaj said: it is an object of purpose; he means *jaza'an*. He said: and likewise *nakalan min Allah*. End of quotation. This is not good, unless the recompense is itself the punishment, in which case it is in the manner of apposition (*badal*). But if the two are different, they cannot both be objects of purpose without the mediation of a conjunction particle.

*Wa-Allahu 'azizun hakim* ("And Allah is Mighty, Wise"). It was said: the meaning is that He is mighty in the legislation of deterrence and wise in the ordaining of amputation. It was also said: He is mighty in His vengeance against the thief and others among the people of disobedience, and wise in His obligations and His prescribed punishments. It is reported that a Bedouin heard a reciter reading *wa-al-sariqu wa-al-sariqatu* to the end, and concluding it with His words *wa-Allahu ghafurun rahim* ("And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful"). He said: "This is not eloquent speech." It was said to him: "The recitation is not like that; it is: *wa-Allahu 'azizun hakim*." He said: "Bravo, bravo! He is mighty, so He ruled, and so He cut off."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 37–38 (part 1 of 3):

﴿They wish to come out of the Fire﴾. That is, they hope, or they desire, or they are about to, or they ask. These are close in meaning, and wishing is possible on their part, so it should not be taken out of its apparent sense. Al-Hasan said: When the Fire seethes with them, they flee from its violence, and at that point they wish to come out and hope for it. This is His saying: ﴿They wish to come out of the Fire﴾. It was said to Jabir ibn Abd Allah: "You, companions of Muhammad, say that a people will come out of the Fire, while Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and they will not come out of it﴾." Jabir replied: "This is only about the disbelievers specifically." Al-Tabari related from Nafi' ibn al-Azraq the Kharijite that he said to Ibn Abbas: "O you who are blind in sight, O you who are blind in heart, do you claim that a people will come out of the Fire when Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿and they will not come out of it﴾?" Ibn Abbas said to him: "Read what comes before it. This verse is about the disbelievers." Al-Zamakhshari said: As for what is related from Ikrimah, that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq said to Ibn Abbas, and he mentioned the account, then said: This is among what the Mujbira (the determinists, a group who deny human choice) fabricated, and it is not the first of their lies and inventions. It is enough to show its falsehood that it has Ibn al-Azraq confronting the cousin of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while he was in the midst of his supporters from Quraysh and his helpers from the Banu Abd al-Muttalib, and he was the scholar and sea of this community and its interpreter, with an address that no one among the people of this world would dare to use toward his like, and by its being traced back to Ikrimah, these are two clear proofs that the report is a fabrication beyond doubt. End of quote. He is in his usual manner and foolishness in abusing the people of the Sunnah, and his doctrine is that whoever enters the Fire does not come out of it.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿أنْ يَخْرُجُوا﴾ (an yakhrujū), in the active voice, and ﴿وما هم بِخارِجِينَ مِنها﴾ fits with this. Al-Nakha'i, Ibn Watthab, and Abu Waqid read ﴿أنْ يُخْرَجُوا﴾ (an yukhrajū), in the passive voice.

﴿And theirs is a lasting punishment﴾, that is, one that is perpetual and will not be changed.

﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands﴾. Al-Sa'ib said: It was revealed concerning Ta'mah ibn Ubayriq, and its story has passed in Surat al-Nisa'.

Its connection to what precedes it: when He mentioned the punishment of those who wage war (al-muharibun) with penalties that include cutting off hands and feet on opposite sides, and then commanded that one be cautious lest a person fall into any part of hirabah (armed robbery or brigandage), and then mentioned the state of the disbelievers, He mentioned the ruling on theft, because in it is the cutting of hands according to the Qur'an, and of feet according to the Sunnah, as will be mentioned. It is also a form of hirabah in meaning, because it involves seeking corruption, except that the one is done openly with force and power, while theft is done secretly and covertly. The apparent meaning is that cutting is obligatory for the mere name of theft, and this is the apparent sense of the text. If one steals an egg, his hand is cut off; if one steals a camel, his right hand is cut off; if one steals anything at all, little or much, his hand is cut off. This view was held by a group of the Companions and of the Successors, among them al-Hasan, and it is the doctrine of the Khawarij (an early sect) and of Dawud (al-Zahiri).

Dawud and those who agree with him said: The hand is not cut for stealing a single grain or a single date, but only for the least thing that is called property, and at the least thing that shows stinginess and niggardliness. It was said: The threshold (nisab) at which the hand is cut is ten dirhams or more, or its value in other goods. This was related from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Amr Ayman al-Habashi, Abu Ja'far, Ata', and Ibrahim, and it is the view of al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Zufar, and Muhammad (al-Shaybani). It was said: a quarter of a dinar or more. This was related from Umar, Uthman, Ali, Aisha, and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, and it is the view of al-Awza'i, al-Layth, al-Shafi'i, and Abu Thawr. It was said: five dirhams, and this is the view of Anas, Urwa, Sulayman ibn Yasar, and al-Zuhri. It was said: four dirhams, and this is related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Abu Hurayra. It was said: three dirhams, and this is the view of Ibn Umar. Malik, Ishaq, and Ahmad also said this, except that if the theft is of gold, the hand is not cut unless it is a quarter of a dinar. It was said: one dirham or more, and Uthman al-Battі held this. Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr cut a hand for one dirham. The theft for which the hand is cut has conditions mentioned in jurisprudence (fiqh).

The majority read ﴿والسّارِقُ والسّارِقَةُ﴾ (wa-l-sāriqu wa-l-sāriqatu) with the nominative (raf'). Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud) read ﴿والسّارِقُونَ والسّارِقاتُ فاقْطَعُوا أيْمانَهم﴾, "And the male thieves and the female thieves, cut off their right hands." Al-Khaffaf said: I found in the codex of Ubayy: "wa-l-suruqu wa-l-suruqatu," with a doubled sin vowelled with a damma in both, as Abu Amr vocalized it. Ibn Atiyya said: It seems that this is a scribal error by the one who vocalized it, because the reading of the community, when the word al-sariq is written without an alif, agrees with this in the script.

The nominative in ﴿والسّارِقُ والسّارِقَةُ﴾ is as a subject (mubtada', the topic of the sentence), and the predicate (khabar) is omitted. The estimate is: "What is recited to you" or "What has been made obligatory upon you" is the ruling on the male thief and the female thief. Sibawayh does not permit the predicate to be ﴿فاقْطَعُوا﴾, because the particle "fa" (fa') enters only into the predicate of a topic that is a relative construction (ism mawsul, a relative noun such as "the one who") joined to an adverb of place or time or to a prepositional phrase, that is, a clause suitable to follow a conditional particle. The relative here is "al" (the definite article used as a relative), and its complement is an active participle or passive participle, and according to Sibawayh the "fa" does not enter the predicate of such a construction. A group of the Basran grammarians permitted it, meaning that ﴿والسّارِقُ والسّارِقَةُ﴾ is the topic and the predicate is the imperative clause. They treated "al" and its complement as if it were the relative mentioned, because its meaning is general: that is, "the one who stole and the one who stole (feminine)." Since Sibawayh's view is that this is not permitted, he interpreted it by supposing an omitted predicate, so that his interpretation becomes: "In what is made obligatory upon you is the ruling on the male thief and the female thief," a clause whose apparent form would be independent, but the intended point is in His saying ﴿fa-qtaʿū (so cut off)﴾. The "fa" was brought as a linking particle for the second clause, so the first clause clarifies the ruling that was vague in the first clause.

Isa ibn Umar and Ibn Abi Abla read ﴿والسّارِقَ والسّارِقَةَ﴾ with the accusative (nasb) through what is called ishtighal (a construction in which the verb is occupied with a pronoun referring back to the noun). Sibawayh said: The preferred form in the speech of the Arabs is the accusative, as you say: "Zayd, strike him." But the common readers insisted on the nominative, meaning the majority of the readers. Since most of the readers are on the nominative, Sibawayh interpreted it in a way that is valid, namely that he made it a topic with an omitted predicate, because if he made it a topic and the predicate were ﴿fa-qtaʿū﴾, that would be a construction contrary to the usage of the Arabs, and the "fa" would enter the predicate of "al," which he does not permit.

Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Umar, known as Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, son of the preacher of al-Ray, presumed to criticize Sibawayh and attributed to him what he did not say. He said: What Sibawayh held is not valid, and several points show its corruption. The first: he criticized a reading transmitted by mass transmission (mutawatir) from the Messenger, and from the leading scholars of the community, and that is clearly false. (I say:) This is an invention against Sibawayh and a lack of understanding of him. Sibawayh did not criticize the reading in the nominative. Rather, he gave it the interpretation mentioned, and he made clear that the issue is not one of ishtighal built on the permissibility of making the noun a topic in it and the imperative clause being its predicate, nor of leaving the noun in the accusative. For if it were of that kind, the accusative would be preferable, as it is in "Zayd, strike him," according to what is established in the speech of the Arabs. So the fact that the majority of readers turned to the nominative is evidence that they did not make the nominative here a topic whose predicate is the imperative verb, because that is not permitted on account of the "fa." Therefore his statement "The common people insisted on the nominative" strengthens his interpretation and weakens the accusative as ishtighal in the presence of the "fa." For the accusative as ishtighal, preferred over the topic in such a structure, is not permitted, unless it is permissible for the noun to be a topic whose predicate is the verb that explains the governing element in the ishtighal, and here that is not permitted on account of the "fa" that enters the predicate. So the accusative should not be permitted. Thus the meaning of Sibawayh's speech supports the nominative as stated, so how could he be one who criticizes the nominative? Sibawayh also said: It is good and correct: "Abd Allah, strike him," when it is built on an implied or stated topic. As for the stated one, your saying: "This is Zayd, strike him." And if you wish, you do not state "this." It works in the same way when stated, as in your saying: "The crescent, by Allah, look at it," as if you said: "This is the crescent," then you brought the imperative. Among that is the verse of the poet:

"And a speaker said: 'Khawlan, marry their young women,' and the nobility of the two tribes is empty, just as it is."

Thus it was heard from the Arabs reciting it. End of quote. If Sibawayh says: "It is good and correct: Abd Allah, strike him," how could he be a critic of the nominative, when he says that it is good and correct? Rather, he allowed it on the basis that the nominative noun is a topic whose predicate is omitted, as he interpreted it in "the male thief and the female thief," or the predicate of an omitted topic, as in his saying: "The crescent, by Allah, look at it."

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: "If you say" — meaning Sibawayh — "I do not say that the reading with the nominative (raf') is impermissible, but I say that the reading with the accusative (nasb) is preferable," then we say to him: this is also poor, because preferring a reading that only ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read over the reading of the Messenger and of the entire community in the time of the Companions and the Successors is an abhorrent and rejected matter.

(I [Abu Hayyan] say): This objection was not raised by Sibawayh, nor is he one who would raise it. How could he say it, when he has already preferred the reading with the nominative, as we have made clear! Moreover, his statement, "because preferring a reading that only ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read over the reading of the Messenger and of the entire community in the time of the Companions and the Successors," is a disparagement and gives the false impression that ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read it on his own authority. That is not so. Rather, his reading is grounded in (p-478) the Companions and in the Messenger (ﷺ), so his reading is also the reading of the Messenger (ﷺ). And his statement, "and the entire community," this generalization is not valid, because ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, Ibrahim ibn Abi ʿAbla, those who agreed with them, and their teachers from whom they took this reading, are all part of the community.

Sibawayh said: "Some people have read: 'and the male thief and the female thief, and the adulteress and the adulterer,'" thereby informing us that it is the reading of some people. His statement "the entire community" is not a valid generalization.

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: The second of the aspects that indicate the corruption of Sibawayh's view: if the reading with the accusative were preferable, it would necessarily follow that among the readers there would be someone who read ﴿وَاللَّذَانِ يَأْتِيَانِهَا مِنكُمْ فَآذُوهُمَا﴾ [an-Nisa: 16] with the accusative. Since no reader is found to have read it that way, we know that this view is invalid.

(I say): Sibawayh did not claim that the accusative reading is preferable, so this objection does not apply to him. Rather, Sibawayh said: "Some people have read 'and the male thief and the female thief, and the adulteress and the adulterer,'" and it is, in Arabic, as I have mentioned to you, of considerable strength; but the general body of readers refused anything but the nominative reading. What Sibawayh means by "of strength" is: if it were stripped of the fa' (fa' al-jaza'/particle of consequence) that is presumed to enter upon the predicate of a nominative subject beginning a sentence, with the imperative clause as its predicate. But the general body of readers, i.e., the majority of readers, refused anything but the nominative, because of the reason for the entry of the fa', since it is not valid for the imperative clause to be the predicate of this subject. Thus, when the fa' entered, the majority preferred the nominative. For this reason, when Sibawayh mentioned the preference for the accusative in the imperative and prohibitive, he did not illustrate it with the fa' but with it stripped of it. Sibawayh said: "That is (p-479) your saying: Zayd, strike him; ʿAmr, pass by him; Khalid, strike his father; Zayd, buy him a garment." Then he said: "In the imperative and prohibitive, the verb may be constructed upon the noun, as in your saying: ʿAbd Allah, so strike him. You began with ʿAbd Allah and raised him by the inceptive (ibtida'), and you alerted the addressee to him so that he would know him by name, then you constructed the verb upon him, just as you do in the case of the predicate. But if you say: Zayd, so strike him, it is not right; you do not treat him as the inceptive. Do you not see that if you said: Zayd, so he is departing, it would not be right? This is evidence that it is not permissible for it to be an inceptive, meaning a topic about which a predicate is stated with an imperative verb preceded by the fa' that is permissible to enter upon the predicate." Then Sibawayh said: "If you wish, put it in the accusative governed by a verb which this explains." Since Sibawayh prohibited the nominative there as an inceptive with an imperative clause as its predicate because of the fa', he permitted its accusative by way of ishtighal (verbal preoccupation), not on the basis that the fa' is the particle entering upon the predicate of the topic.

The summary of what is understood from Sibawayh's words: an imperative clause without a fa' after a noun—the accusative is preferred there, and the nominative (inceptive) is permissible, with the imperative clause as its predicate. If the fa' enters upon it, then either you presume it to be the fa' entering upon the predicate, or it is a conjunctive fa'. If you presume it to be the fa' entering upon the predicate, then that noun cannot be an inceptive with the imperative clause as its predicate, except when the topic is treated as a conditional noun because of its resemblance to it, which has conditions mentioned in grammar. If it is conjunctive, that noun is nominative, either as an inceptive, as Sibawayh interpreted in his saying "al-sariq wa'l-sariqa" (p-480), or as the predicate of an omitted inceptive, as is said: "The moon, by God, so look at it." The accusative in this sense is less preferable than the nominative, because when you put it in the accusative you need a verbal clause to be conjoined to it with the fa', and an omission of the governing verb, and a displacement of the fa' from its proper position. When you say "Zayd, so strike him," the estimate is: "Be alert, so strike Zayd, strike him": "be alert" is omitted, "strike" is omitted, and the fa' is postponed until its entry upon the explained element. The nominative is preferable, because there is neither omission of an inceptive nor omission of a predicate. The omitted element is only one of the two components of the predication, and the fa' stands in its proper place, and the context and meaning of the speech indicate that omitted element.

Sibawayh said: As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿The adulteress and the adulterer, flog each one of them﴾ [an-Nur: 2] and ﴿The male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾ — this is not constructed upon the verb, but it came in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The parable of the Garden which the God-fearing are promised﴾ [Muhammad: 15], then after it He said: "in it are rivers..." and so on. The parable was set forth as a preface to the narrative that follows it, and it was mentioned after reports and narratives, as if He had said: "Among the stories is the parable of the Garden," or "what We relate to you is the parable of the Garden." So it is carried upon this supposition or the like, and God knows best. Likewise, the adulteress and the adulterer: when He said, exalted is He, ﴿A surah which We have sent down and imposed﴾ [an-Nur: 1], He said regarding the obligations: ﴿The adulteress and the adulterer﴾ [an-Nur: 2], or ﴿The adulteress and the adulterer﴾ among the obligations; then He said: "flog," so He brought the verb after the nominative had already passed in it, as he said. And as in the verse, "A speaker from Khawlan: so marry their young woman," where the verb came after the pronoun had governed it. Likewise "al-sariq wa'l-sariqa": as if he said: "Among what is imposed upon you is the male thief and the female thief," or "the male thief and the female thief concerning what is imposed upon you." These nouns came after stories and narratives. End of quotation.

So Sibawayh chose this analysis because it entails less burden than the accusative while the fa' is present; and the fa' is not the one entering upon the predicate of the topic, because Sibawayh does not permit that with the relative particle alif-lam. Thus, according to him, the two verses fall under the category of "Zayd, so strike him," and just as the preferred option there is the nominative, so likewise in the two verses.

* *

As for al-Razi's statement, "it would necessarily follow that among the readers there would be someone who read ﴿وَاللَّذَانِ يَأْتِيَانِهَا مِنكُمْ فَآذُوهُمَا﴾ with the accusative," etc., Sibawayh did not say that the accusative in this kind of construction is preferable, so it does not follow that among the readers someone would read "wa'lladhani ya'tiyanih" with the accusative. Rather, Sibawayh treated this verse in the same way as "al-sariq wa'l-sariqa," because the preceding context already indicates the omitted element, namely His saying: ﴿وَاللَّاتِي يَأْتِينَ الْفَاحِشَةَ مِن نِّسَائِكُمْ﴾ [an-Nisa: 15]. So Sibawayh construed the verse as involving an implied element. Sibawayh also said: this may apply to Zayd and ʿAmr in this manner when you are reporting matters or giving instructions, and then you say: "Zayd," i.e., Zayd is among those I instruct, so be kind to him and honor him. And in ﴿وَاللَّذَانِ يَأْتِيَانِهَا مِنكُمْ﴾ [an-Nisa: 16], it is permissible to be nominative as an inceptive, with the clause containing the fa' as its predicate, because it is a relative pronoun fulfilling the conditions of the relative that permits the fa' in its predicate, owing to its resemblance to the conditional noun. This is unlike His saying: ﴿وَالسَّارِقُ وَالسَّارِقَةُ﴾, for according to Sibawayh the fa' may not enter its predicate, because it does not function as a conditional noun and so is not made similar to it in the entry of the fa'.

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: The third [aspect], meaning among the flaws of Sibawayh's view: we only say that "al-sariq wa'l-sariqa" is the topic, and its predicate is what is implied, namely our saying: "in what is recited to you," and in something to which the fa' in His saying ﴿فَاقْطَعُوا أَيْدِيَهُمَا﴾ is connected. (I say): The wisdom of bringing the fa' and what it links has already been explained to us. Sibawayh estimated it as: "Among what is imposed upon you is the male thief and the female thief," and the meaning is: the ruling on the male thief and the female thief, because this verse came after mention of the punishment and rulings of those who wage war, so Sibawayh's estimate fits. The fa' is brought to link the second clause to the first, and the second came explaining the ruling left unspecified in what precedes it. Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: If [Sibawayh] says the fa' is connected to the verb indicated by His saying "al-sariq wa'l-sariqa," meaning: if he commits theft, cut off his hand, we say: when at the end of the matter you need to say "al-sariq wa'l-sariqa," its estimate is "whoever steals," so mention this first, so that the implied element you mentioned is not needed. (I say): Sibawayh does not say this, and we have already explained the ruling and function of the fa'.

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: The fourth [aspect], meaning among the flaws of Sibawayh's view: if we choose the accusative reading, it does not indicate that theft is the cause for the obligation of amputation; whereas if we choose the nominative reading, the verse conveys this meaning, and this meaning is reinforced by His saying: ﴿جَزَاءً بِمَا كَسَبَا﴾, so it is established that the nominative reading is preferable. (I say): This is strange from this man. He claims that the accusative does not indicate the causal ground that necessitates amputation, while the nominative conveys it. Is this anything other than causation by a descriptive attribute upon which the ruling is consequent? There is no difference in this respect between the nominative and the accusative: if you say "the thief, so that he be cut off," or "cut off the thief," there is no difference between them in terms of causation. Likewise "the adulterer, so that he be flogged," or "flog the adulterer." Then his claim that this meaning is reinforced by His saying: ﴿جَزَاءً بِمَا كَسَبَا﴾, the accusative can also be reinforced by something similar: if you say "cut off the thief as a recompense for what he committed," it is correct.

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: The fifth [aspect], meaning among the flaws of Sibawayh's view: Sibawayh said: "They give priority to what is more important, and what they are more concerned to explain." The nominative reading entails mentioning his being a thief before the obligation of amputation, and this requires that the greater concern be directed to explaining what pertains to the thief's state insofar as he is a thief; whereas the accusative reading entails that the concern be focused on explaining the amputation more than on his being a thief. It is known that this is not so, since the purpose of this verse is to express the ugliness of theft and to intensify the deterrent against it, so it is established that the nominative reading is definitively the required one. (I say): What Sibawayh stated, that they used to give priority to what is more important to them, and what they are more concerned to explain—these are the cases where the relation of predication differs, such as the agent and the object.
