Sibawayh said: If you place the object first and the agent after, the utterance proceeds as it did in the first case, i.e., in "ḍaraba ʿAbd Allāh Zaydan": he said: "that is, ḍaraba Zaydan ʿAbd Allāh, because you intended by the latter what you intended by the former, and you did not intend to occupy the verb with something before it, even though it is later in the wording. Hence the proper form of the wording is that it be first; this is a good and frequent Arabic usage, as if they give priority to what is more important to them, and what they are more concerned to explain, though both concern them and matter to them." End of quotation.

[p. 482] Al-Razi distorted the words of Sibawayh and applied them where no difference of relation can be conceived. The relation here is that of the subject (*mubtada'*) and predicate (*khabar*), and in it there is only one relation, unlike the agent (*fa'il*) and the object (*maf'ul*). The speaker may have a purpose in mentioning the one from whom the striking proceeds, so he puts the agent first, or in mentioning the one on whom the striking falls, so he puts the object first, because the relation of striking differs depending on which of the two is considered. As for the verse, it belongs to the category where the relation does not differ. It is simply the ruling concerning the thief, that his hand be cut off. What al-Razi mentioned does not derive from the words of Sibawayh in any way. It is strange that this man, with his boldness toward the sciences, wrote a book on grammar which he named *al-Muharrar*, and followed in it a strange and distant method, far from the terminology and aims of the grammarians. It is a slight book that contains some chapters of Arabic. I heard our shaykh Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr mention this work and say: "It does not follow the terminology of the people, and the confusion in the sciences that he followed in it is such that whoever is dominated by one discipline will show, in what he says on other subjects or ones close to it, this meaning." When I came upon this book in the land of Egypt, I saw what the master Abu Ja'far used to criticize in it, and that it leads the intellect of Fakhr al-Din astray in that he wrote in a science he did not belong to. Abu Ja'far used to say: "Every science has a limit at which it ends. When you see a speaker on one discipline who mixes it with another, know that this is either from his confusion and the muddling of his mind, or from the scantiness of his acquired knowledge and his deficiency in that science, so you will find him resting on what he knows of other things."

Al-Zamakhshari, after mentioning the view of Sibawayh on the i'rab (grammatical inflection) of *wa-al-sariqu wa-al-sariqatu*, said the following text: "Another possibility is that both are raised by the inchoative (*ibtida'*), and the predicate is *fa-aqta'u aydiyahuma*, and the entry of the *fa'* is because it contains the meaning of the conditional, because the meaning is: 'The man who stole and the woman who stole, cut off their hands,' and the relative noun has taken on the meaning of the conditional. Isa ibn Umar read it with the accusative, and Sibawayh preferred it over the reading of the common people because of the imperative, since *Zaydan fa-idribhu* is better than *Zaydun fa-idribhu*." End of quotation. This possibility that he permitted, although some have held it, is not allowed according to Sibawayh, because the relative pronoun has not been joined to a clause suitable for a conditional particle, nor to what takes its place of an adverbial phrase or a prepositional phrase. Rather, the relative here is *al* (the definite article as relative), and the clause of *al* is not suitable for a conditional particle. The relative has merged with its clause, so that the i'rab falls within the clause, unlike the adverbial and prepositional phrase, for the governing element in them is a clause that is not suitable for a conditional particle. As for his statement about the reading of Isa, that Sibawayh preferred it over the reading of the common people, this is not correct. What Sibawayh mentioned in his book is that there are two constructions: one is *zaydan idribhu*, and the second is *zaydun fa-idribhu*. In the first construction he chose the accusative, then they permitted the nominative by the inchoative. As for the second construction, he forbade that it be raised by the inchoative with the imperative clause as its predicate because of the *fa'*. He permitted its accusative by *ishtighal* (the verb being occupied with the pronoun), or by *igra'* (incitement). He mentioned that it is correct to raise it on the basis that there are two clauses, with *Zaydun* as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, *hadha Zaydun fa-idribhu* ("this is Zayd, so strike him"). Then he cited the verse and analyzed it on the basis of the omission of the predicate. His statement indicates that this construction can only be in two clauses: the first is inchoative. Then he mentioned the reading of some people with the accusative and did not prefer it over the reading of the common people. He only said: "It is, in Arabic, as I have told you, of great strength," that is, he put it in the accusative by *ishtighal* or *igra'*, and this is strong, not weak. Sibawayh has forbidden its raising by the inchoative with the imperative clause as predicate because of the *fa'*. We have mentioned the preference between its raising as a subject whose predicate is omitted, or a predicate whose subject is omitted, and he explained its accusative by *ishtighal*, since the nominative requires the omission of one predicate, whereas the accusative requires the omission of a clause and the supposing of another, and the shifting of the *fa'* from its place.

The apparent sense of his statement "*wa-al-sariqu*" is that no protected storage (*hirz*) is required for the stolen property. This was the view of Dawud and the Kharijites. The majority hold that a condition for the amputation is that the goods be removed from the protected storage, and that if he gathered clothes in a house but did not take them out, he is not amputated. Al-Hasan said: he is amputated. The apparent sense is that everyone who is called a thief falls under the generality of *wa-al-sariqu wa-al-sariqatu*. However, there is consensus (*ijma'*) that a father who steals from his son's property is not amputated, and the majority hold that a son is not amputated [for stealing from his father]. Abd Allah ibn al-Hasan said: if they (the parents) allow him to enter upon them, there is no amputation, but if they forbid him from entering, he is amputated. Those within the prohibited degrees (*dhawu al-mahram*) are not amputated according to Abu Hanifa, nor are grandparents on the father's or mother's side according to the majority and according to Ashhab. Abu Thawr said: every thief who steals what the hand is cut for is amputated, unless they agree on something, in which case it is submitted to the consensus. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said: a woman is not amputated if she steals from her husband's property, nor is a husband if he steals from his wife's property. Malik said: both are amputated. The apparent sense is that whoever confesses to theft once is amputated. This was said by Abu Hanifa, Zufar, Malik, al-Shafi'i, and al-Thawri. Ibn Shubruma, Abu Yusuf, and Ibn Abi Layla said: he is not amputated until he confesses twice. Abu Hanifa said: the thief of a copy of the Qur'an (*mushaf*) is not amputated. Al-Shafi'i, Abu Yusuf, Abu Thawr, and Ibn al-Qasim said: he is amputated if its value reaches the nisab (the minimum threshold). The apparent sense is the amputation for stealing a *tayyar* (a flying bird) if it reaches the nisab. This was said by Malik, al-Awza'i, Abu Thawr, and Ya'qub, and it is the view of al-Hasan. Abu Hanifa, Muhammad, and Ishaq held that if the dirhams were tied in his sleeve he is not amputated, but if they were inside [his garment], he is amputated. There is disagreement concerning the grave-robber (*nabbash*) who takes the shroud. Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, and Muhammad said: he is not amputated. This is also the view of Ibn Abbas and Makhul. Al-Zuhri said: the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ agreed, at a time when Marwan was governor of Medina, that the grave-robber is disciplined (*yu'azzaru*) and not amputated, and the Companions were numerous at that time. Abu al-Darda', Ibn Abi Layla, Rabi'a, Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Abu Yusuf said: he is amputated. This is also reported from Ibn al-Zubayr, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, al-Zuhri, Masruq, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, and Ata. The apparent sense is that if he repeats the theft of the same item after its amputation has been carried out for it, he is not amputated. This was said by the majority. Abu Hanifa said: he is not amputated, and if he steals a nisab from a thief, he is not amputated. This was said by al-Shafi'i. Malik said: he is amputated. The one addressed by His words *fa-aqta'u* ("so cut off") is the Messenger or those in authority such as the sultan, or whoever is authorized to carry out the prescribed punishments, or the judges and rulers, or the believers, so that they may cooperate in establishing the prescribed punishments. There are four views. Some scholars made a distinction, saying: if there is an imam in the city or a deputy of his, the address is directed to him; if there is none but there is a judge, the address is directed to him; if neither is there, it is directed to the general body of believers, and at that time it is a communal obligation (*fard al-kifaya*): when some of them carry it out, it is dropped from the rest.

The apparent sense of His words *fa-aqta'u aydiyahuma* ("so cut off their hands") is that two hands are cut from the thief. But consensus is against this apparent sense, and only the right hand is cut from the male thief, and the right hand of the female thief. Al-Zamakhshari said: *aydiyahuma* means their two hands. Similar to it is His words *faqad sagat qulubukuma* ("your hearts have inclined", 66:4), where the dual of the one added to is used in place of the dual of the one added, and by the two hands the two right hands are meant, based on the reading of Abd Allah: *wa-al-sariquna wa-al-sariqatu fa-aqta'u aymanahum* ("the male thieves and the female thieves, so cut off their right hands"). End of quotation. He equated *aydiyahuma* with *qulubukuma*, though they are not the same, because the pattern of *sagat qulubukuma* allows the plural to be placed in the position of the dual, which is when the two are two of two things, such as the heart, the nose, the face, and the back. But if each of the two has two (like the two hands, the two ears, the two thighs), the placement of the plural in the position of the dual is not regular; it is only preserved and not analogized from. This is because the mind only takes the plural in its apparent sense when it is used absolutely according to what its wording indicates. If one says *qutri'at adhanu al-Zaydayn* ("the ears of the two Zayds were cut off"), the apparent sense is the cutting of four ears, which is using the word in its denotation. Ibn Atiyya said: he used the plural *aydi* because each thief has one right hand that is exposed to amputation in theft, and the thieves have hands and the female thieves have hands, as if he said: "Cut off the right hands of the two kinds." So the dual is for the pronoun, which is for the two kinds. The apparent sense of His words *aydiyahuma* is that the foot is not cut. If he steals, his right hand is cut; if he steals again, his left hand is cut; if he steals again, he is disciplined and imprisoned. This is the view of Malik and the majority, and Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri said so too. Ali, al-Zuhri, Hammad ibn Abi Salama, and Ahmad said: his right hand is cut, then if he steals again his left foot is cut, then if he steals again he is disciplined and imprisoned. Ata narrated: in theft only the right hand is cut, then if he steals again he is disciplined and imprisoned. Al-Shafi'i said: if he steals the first time, his right hand is cut; the second time, his left foot; the third time, his left hand; the fourth time, his right foot. This was narrated from Umar. It was said that he then returned to the view of Ali. The apparent sense of cutting the hand is that it is from the shoulder joint, from the joint. It was narrated from Ali that for the hand it is from the fingers, and for the foot from the middle of the foot, which is the place where the strap is tied. The same was narrated from Ata and Abu Ja'far. Abu Salih al-Samman said: I saw the one whose hand Ali had cut off, and he was cut off from the tips of the fingers. It was said to him: "Who cut you?" He said: "The best of people."

The apparent sense is that what is required by the theft is only the cutting of the hand. If the property still exists in its own form, its owner takes it back; if the thief has consumed it, there is no liability upon him. This was said by Makhul, Ata, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Sirin, and al-Nakha'i, according to the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions. Al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, al-Nakha'i according to the view of Hammad, Uthman al-Battí, al-Layth, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Ishaq said: he must compensate and be fined. Malik said: if he is wealthy, he is liable; if he is poor, nothing is upon him.

*Jaza'an bima kasaba nakalan mina Allah* ("as a recompense for what they earned, an exemplary punishment from Allah"). Al-Kisa'i said: *jaza'an* is in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*). Qutrub said: it is in the accusative as an infinitive (*masdar*), meaning: "He recompensed them with a recompense." The majority said: it is an accusative of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*), *bima* is attached to *jaza'an*, and *ma* is a relative pronoun, meaning: "for that which they had earned." It is possible that it is a verbal noun (*masdariyya*), meaning: "a recompense for their earning." The accusative of *nakalan* is as an infinitive, or as an accusative of purpose. Al-adhab (the punishment) is the *nakal*, and *al-nakal* is the shackle. Its discussion was already given in His words: *fa-ja'alnaha nakalan* ("We made it an exemplary punishment", 2:66). Al-Zamakhshari said: *jaza'an* and *nakalan* are two objects of purpose. End of quotation. He followed in this al-Zajjaj. Al-Zajjaj said: it is an object of purpose; he means *jaza'an*. He said: and likewise *nakalan min Allah*. End of quotation. This is not good, unless the recompense is itself the punishment, in which case it is in the manner of apposition (*badal*). But if the two are different, they cannot both be objects of purpose without the mediation of a conjunction particle.

*Wa-Allahu 'azizun hakim* ("And Allah is Mighty, Wise"). It was said: the meaning is that He is mighty in the legislation of deterrence and wise in the ordaining of amputation. It was also said: He is mighty in His vengeance against the thief and others among the people of disobedience, and wise in His obligations and His prescribed punishments. It is reported that a Bedouin heard a reciter reading *wa-al-sariqu wa-al-sariqatu* to the end, and concluding it with His words *wa-Allahu ghafurun rahim* ("And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful"). He said: "This is not eloquent speech." It was said to him: "The recitation is not like that; it is: *wa-Allahu 'azizun hakim*." He said: "Bravo, bravo! He is mighty, so He ruled, and so He cut off."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 39:

﴿Then whoever repents after his wrongdoing and makes amends, indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ That is: whoever repents after his wrongdoing through theft. His "wrongdoing" (ẓulmihi) is an idafah (construct phrase) to the agent; that is, after he has wronged another by taking property or stealing. It has been said: or it is an idafah to the object; that is, after he has wronged himself. Yet the permissibility of this reading is open to question, since the sense would become: "after he has wronged him" (min ba'di an ẓalamahu). Had this been stated explicitly, it would not be permitted, because it would involve transferring a verb whose subject is an attached pronoun to an attached pronoun in the accusative, and this is not permitted except with verbs of the bāb ẓanna, faqada and ʿadima (the class of verbs of belief and lacking). The meaning of ﴿yatūbu ʿalayhi﴾ is: He will overlook his sin and accept his repentance. The apparent sense of the verse is that repentance alone is not accepted unless it is joined with making amends (iṣlāḥ), which is disengaging from the consequences (tabiʿāt) by returning the goods if possible, or otherwise by seeking the pardon of their owner, or by spending them in the way of Allah if the owner is unknown. Forgiveness and mercy are a metaphor for the removal of punishment from him in the Hereafter. The majority (al-Jumhur) recited it on the basis that the prescribed penalty (ḥadd) does not fall away through repentance. ʿAṭāʾ and a group said: it falls away through repentance before the thief is under the power of the authorities, and this is one of the two opinions of al-Shafiʿi. Mujahid said: repentance and making amends are that the prescribed penalty be carried out upon him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 40:

﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth? He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills.﴾ When He, exalted is He, mentioned His disposal of the rulings concerning those who wage war and the rulings concerning thieves, and did not spare the punishments He had mentioned for them, He drew attention to the fact that this is a disposal within His dominion and His possession, and that none can repel His judgment. So He punishes whom He wills, meaning those who oppose His command, and He forgives whom He wills, meaning those who repent. The address in "Do you not know" has been said to be to the Prophet (ﷺ) (p-485). It has also been said to be to every person who is legally responsible, and it has been said to be to the one who dares to steal or to commit other forbidden acts. The meaning then is: Do you not know that you are incapable of getting out of My dominion, of fleeing from Me and from My punishment? So why have you dared to do what I forbade you from? Far removed is the view of those who say that the address is to the Jews who were present in the presence of the Messenger. The meaning would be: Do you not know that to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that there is no kinship or lineage between Him and anyone that would make Him show favour to them, leaving aside those who say, "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved"? Al-Zamakhshari said: "Whom He wills" refers to whoever, in judgment, deserves punishment, and to whoever deserves forgiveness, among the persistent and the repentant. End of quote. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazilism (i'tizal). The prescribed penalty (hadd) for a warrior from the enemy camp may be dropped if he steals after repenting, so that he is more inclined to Islam and further from being repelled from it. But we do not drop it for a Muslim, because enforcing it brings benefit to the believers and life, as in ﴿And for you in retribution there is life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 179]. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: "He punishes whom He wills" means whoever dies in his disbelief, and "forgives whom He wills" means whoever repents of his disbelief. It has also been said that this refers to the present world: He punishes whom He wills in this world for their disobedience, by killing, sinking into the earth, taking captive, enslavement, the loss of wealth, drought, exile, humiliation, the poll tax, and other such things; and He forgives whom He wills among them in this world by turning to them in mercy from their disbelief and disobedience, so He rescues them from ruin and saves them from punishment.

﴿And Allah is over all things Powerful.﴾ This statement often follows what indicates complete disposal, ownership, creation and origination. It is most fitting after what they mentioned. An example of this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say that Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 17].

﴿O Messenger, let not those grieve you who race to disbelief, of those who say with their mouths, "We believe," but whose hearts have not believed; and of the Jews, who listen eagerly to falsehood, listening on behalf of another people who have not come to you. They distort words from their places, saying, "If you are given this, take it; but if you are not given it, beware." And whoever Allah intends to test, you cannot avail him anything against Allah. Those are the ones whose hearts Allah did not intend to purify. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.﴾ ﴿They listen eagerly to falsehood and consume what is unlawfully gained. So if they come to you, either judge between them or turn away from them. If you turn away from them, they cannot harm you at all. And if you judge, judge between them with justice. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 42] ﴿And how do they make you a judge while they have the Torah, in which is the judgement of Allah? Then they turn away after that. And those are not believers.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 43] ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light. By it the prophets who submitted judged for the Jews, and the rabbis and the scholars, by what they were entrusted with of the Book of Allah, and they were witnesses over it. So do not fear people, but fear Me, and do not sell My verses for a small price. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44] ﴿And We prescribed for them therein: a life for a life, an eye for an eye, a nose for a nose, an ear for an ear, a tooth for a tooth, and wounds in retaliation. But whoever forgoes it as charity, it is an expiation for him. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the wrongdoers.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45] ﴿And We followed them with Jesus, son of Mary, confirming what was before him of the Torah, and We gave him the Gospel, in which is guidance and light, confirming what was before it of the Torah, and as guidance and admonition for the righteous.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 46] ﴿Let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the defiantly disobedient.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 47] ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it of the Book and as a guardian over it. So judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires away from the truth that has come to you. For each of you We have made a law and a way. Had Allah willed, He would have made you one nation, but He tests you in what He has given you. So race to good deeds. To Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you about that in which you used to differ.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48]

As-suht (unlawful gain) and as-suht, with a sukun or a damma on the ha', mean what is forbidden. It is so called because it destroys (yushbitu) blessing, that is, it removes it. One says: sahatahu Allah, meaning He destroyed him, and it is said: ashtahu. Both are read in His words: ﴿fa-yushhitakum bi-'adhab﴾ [Ta-Ha: 61], meaning: He will uproot you, destroy you. From this is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"The bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left of wealth nothing but a destroyed or a stripped remnant."

The verbal noun of the triliteral is sahtun with two fathas, and sahtun with a sukun on the ha'. Al-Farra' said: the origin of as-suht is the hunger of a dog (kalb al-ju'). It is said: fulan is mashuh al-mi'dah (his stomach is consumed) when he is never met except in fear, and this returns to the meaning of destruction. (p. 486)

Al-habr: with a fatha or a kasra on the ha', means the scholar, and its plural is al-ahbar. Abu 'Ubayd used to deny this and say it is with a fatha. Al-Farra' said it is with a kasra, but Abu 'Ubayd preferred the fatha. This surah is called the Surah of the Rabbis, and it is said: Ka'b al-Ahbar. Al-hibr, with a kasra, is that with which one writes (ink), and the al-hibri (ink-maker) is attributed to it. It is said: kutub al-hibr, for the place of the ink with which one writes. It was called hibr for its beautifying of the script and its clarifying it. It is said: it was called hibr for its effect on the place where it is, from al-habar, which is the trace.

Al-'ayn: the faculty of sight, and it is feminine. Its plural in the paucity is a'yun and a'yan, and in the abundance 'uyun. The poet said:

"But I walk with upon me a wide coat of mail, smooth like the eyes of the ordered locusts."

It is said of the spy: dhu al-'aynayn (the one with two eyes). Al-'ayn is a homonym with many meanings, which the lexicographers have mentioned. Al-anf: is known; its plurals are anaf, anuf and unuf.

Al-muhaymin: the witness, the watchful guardian over a thing, the one who protects it, and it is an active participle from haymana. They said: no word came in this pattern except five: haymana, sayṭara, bayṭara, haymara, and bayqara. Al-Zajjaji mentioned this fifth in his commentary on the preface of Adab al-Katib. Its meaning is: he travelled from the Hijaz to Yemen, and from horizon to horizon. Haymana bina is a root. Some lexicographers held that muhaymin is an active participle from amman (to make safe) someone else from fear. He said: its origin is ma'man; the second hamzah was changed to a ya', disliking the meeting of two hamzahs, so it became mu'ayman, then the first hamzah was changed to a ha', as they said: ahraqa for araqa, and hiyyaka for iyyaka. This is a far-fetched reasoning which is not needed, and this pattern has been established in words, so this is one of them. Also, the hamzah in mu'min, the active participle of amana, has been dropped to avoid meeting two hamzahs, so it cannot be claimed that it was kept and replaced. As for what Ibn Qutaybah held, that it is the diminutive of mu'min, and its hamzah was changed to a ha', Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad wrote to him warning him against this view. Know that the names of Allah the Exalted are not diminutived.

Al-shir'ah: the sunnah (way) and the path. Shara'a yashra'u shar'an, meaning: he legislated. Al-sharii' is the broadest road, and manzil sharii' is when its door opens onto a passable road. Al-minhaj and al-manhaj: the clear path. Nahaja al-amr means it became clear, and nahajtu al-tariq means I made the path clear and manifest, and nahajtu al-tariq means I travelled it.

﴿O Messenger, let not those grieve you who race to disbelief, of those who say with their mouths, "We believe," but whose hearts have not believed﴾. It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah, Ibn 'Abbas and a group that the occasion of its revelation was: "A Jewish man committed adultery with a Jewish woman. It is said: in Medina, and it is said: in another land of the Hijaz. They asked the Messenger (ﷺ) and hoped that his judgement would be other than stoning, and in the Torah there was stoning. They denied that this was in the Torah, and were disgraced when they brought it. The Messenger (ﷺ) judged for the two of them with stoning and enforced it." Qatadah said: the occasion was that the Banu al-Nadir, when they raided the Banu Qurayzah, if a man of Qurayzah killed a man of al-Nadir, he would be killed in return; or if a man of al-Nadir killed a man of Qurayzah, he would pay the blood money. It is said: the blood money of the Qurayzi was half the blood money of the Nadiri. When the Messenger came to Medina, Qurayzah sought equality, because they were cousins, and they sought judgement from the Messenger (ﷺ). The Banu al-Nadir said: if he judges by what we follow, take it; otherwise beware. Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning a man from the Ansar, but this is far from the context of the verse. They mentioned that this man was Abu Lubabah ibn 'Abd al-Mundhir, whom Qurayzah indicated during their siege, asking what judgement they would be brought down to, and he pointed to his throat, meaning slaughter. Al-Sha'bi said: it was revealed concerning a group of Jews, one of whom killed another, so they charged a Muslim man to ask the Messenger. They said: if he rules for blood money we accept it, and if he rules for execution we will not accept it. This is similar to Qatadah's statement concerning Nadir and Qurayzah.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He, the Exalted, explained the rulings on banditry (hirabah) and theft, and in mentioning the fighters, that they wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive in the land to cause corruption, He commanded him not to grieve nor to be concerned about the matter of the hypocrites and the matter of the Jews, with their obstinacy, their waiting for misfortunes to befall him and those with him, their setting snares of harm for him, and the corruption that occurs among them in the land, and their setting up of war against Allah and His Messenger, and other vile acts issuing from them. His address to him: "O Messenger" here, and in ﴿O Messenger, convey﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67], and "O Prophet" in several places, is an honouring, exalting and magnifying of his rank. He addressed other prophets by their names, saying: ﴿O Adam, dwell﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35], ﴿O Noah, descend﴾ [Hud: 48], ﴿O Abraham﴾ [al-Saffat: 104] ﴿you have fulfilled the vision﴾ [al-Saffat: 105], ﴿O Moses, I have chosen you﴾ [al-A'raf: 144], ﴿O Jesus, I will take you [in death]﴾ [Al 'Imran: 55], ﴿O John, take the Book﴾ [Maryam: 12]. Mujahid and Abdullah ibn Kathir said: ﴿of those who say with their mouths, "We believe," but whose hearts have not believed﴾ refers to the hypocritical Jews, and "those who listen eagerly to falsehood" are the Jews. The meaning according to this is: do not be concerned with the hastening of the hypocrites into disbelief and of the Jews by openly showing what appears to them of the signs of disbelief, namely their scheming against Islam and its people, for Allah will surely help you against them. It is said: the cause hastened in it, and the corruption hastened in it, when it happened quickly. Their hastening into disbelief is their falling into it and their rushing into it, the swiftest of things, when they find an opportunity they do not miss. In this case, the first and second [phrases] are an alert and a division of those who race into disbelief. "Listen eagerly" (sammA'una) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are listeners, and the pronoun refers to both the hypocrites and the Jews. This meaning is supported by the reading of al-Dahhak: sammA'in, and its accusative is for censure, like the saying of the poet:

"I fight the Awf tribe and seek no other; faces of monkeys, seeking whom they deceive."

It is also permissible that ﴿and of the Jews who have judaized﴾ is a new sentence, and sammA'una is the subject, and they are the Jews. "With their mouths" is connected to "said", not to "believed". The meaning is that their speech did not go beyond their mouths; they only uttered belief, without conviction. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may also mean: do not let those who race to disbelief among the Jews grieve you; He described them as saying "We believe" with their mouths, but their hearts have not believed, as a reproach from Him for that, because they distorted their Torah and changed its rulings, so they say with their mouths: "We believe in the Torah and in Moses," while their hearts do not believe, since they changed and denied what it contains concerning the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and other things they deny. This interpretation is supported by His saying after this: ﴿and those are not believers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 43]. On this interpretation, His saying "of those who said" comes as if He said: "and of them." But He explicitly mentioned the Jews, since the group that listens eagerly is not the group that changes the Torah knowingly. End of quotation. This is a far-fetched and strained possibility. "Listen eagerly" is from the forms of intensive emphasis, and the literal meaning of hearing is not intended, unless "for falsehood" is an object of purpose, and the meaning is: they listen to your words in order to lie about you, relaying your speech, and adding to every word many times over in falsehood. If "for falsehood" is a direct object of "listen eagerly", and it is transitivised with the lam for the sake of strengthening the verb, then the meaning of hearing here is their acceptance of what their rabbis fabricate and invent of falsehood against Allah and the distortion of His Book, from their saying: "The king hears the words of so-and-so," and from it: "Allah hears whoever praises Him." The disagreement concerning the reading of "yahzunka" as triliteral and quadriliteral has been mentioned earlier. Al-Sulami read: yusri'una, without an alif, from asra'a. Al-Hasan and Isa ibn 'Umar read: lil-kidhb, with a kasra on the kaf and a sukun on the dhal. Zayd ibn 'Ali read: al-kudhub, with a damma on the kaf and the dhal, the plural of kadhub, like sabur and subur; meaning: listeners to the lies of the liars.

* *

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 41 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Listeners for other people who have not come to you﴾ It is possible that the meaning is: listeners to the lies of other people who have not come to you; that is, their lies. The ones who did not come to him were the Jews of Fadak. It was also said: the Jews of Khaybar. It was also said: the people of the two opinions (ahl al-ra'yayn). It was also said: the disputants concerning killing and blood-money (diyah). It is also possible that the meaning is: listeners on behalf of other people; that is, they are spies (ʿuyun) and informers (jawasis) for them, hearing from you and conveying to other people. This description may apply to the hypocrites and the Jews of Medina. It was also said: the listeners are the Banu Qurayza, and the other people are the Jews of Khaybar. It was said to Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna: "Has the mention of the spy (jasus) occurred in the Book of God?" He said: "Yes," and he recited this verse: "Listeners for other people who have not come to you." 

"Who have not come to you" is a description (sifah) of "other people." The meaning of "who have not come to you" is: they did not reach your assembly and kept away from you because of the intense enmity and hatred that had come from them. According to this, the apparent meaning is: they are rabbis who speak lies and fabrications, and among those who went to extremes in enmity, who cannot bring themselves to look at you.

﴿They distort words after their places﴾ It is read "al-kalim" with a kasra on the kaf and a sukun on the lam; that is, they remove it and turn it away from the places where God placed it. Ibn ʿAbbas and the majority said: these are the limits of God in the Torah, because they changed the stoning (rajm); that is, they put flogging in place of stoning. Al-Hasan said: they alter what they hear from the Messenger, peace be upon him, by lying about him. It was also said: by concealing the description of the Messenger. It was also said: by dropping retaliation (qawad) after it has become due. It was also said: by bad interpretation. Al-Tabari said: the meaning is "they distort the ruling of the speech," and the object was omitted because it is known. End. It is possible that this is a description of the Jews alone, and it is possible that it is a description of them and of the hypocrites regarding what they distort of statements when they lie, because the beginnings of their lies come from things that were said and done, and this is the lie that is readily accepted. As for the meaning of "after their places," al-Zajjaj said: after God had placed them in their places, so He made lawful what is lawful and unlawful what is unlawful.

* *

﴿They say: if you are given this, then take it﴾ The reference of "this" was said to be the tahmim and flogging for adultery. It was also said: to accepting blood-money in a matter of killing. It was also said: to preserving the dignity of the Nadir over Qurayza. This depends on the difference of opinion mentioned earlier regarding the occasion of revelation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you are given this," this distorted thing removed from its places, "then take it, and know that it is the truth, and act upon it." End. This returns to one of the things we have mentioned, and the omitted subject is the Messenger; that is, "if the Messenger comes to you with this."

﴿And if you are not given it, then beware﴾ That is: if Muhammad issues a ruling contrary to it, then beware and guard yourselves against accepting it, for it is falsehood and error. It was also said: "beware" that you inform him, according to al-Suddi's statement. It was also said: that you inform him of what is in the Torah, so that he makes you act upon it. It was also said: "beware" that you ask him after it. The apparent meaning is the first, because it is contrasted with his saying: "then take it." So the meaning is: if you are not given it, and another comes to you instead, then beware of accepting it.

﴿And whomever God intends to test, you will not be able to do anything for him against God﴾ Al-Hasan and Qatada said: "his testing" means his punishment by the Fire, and from it comes the verse "the day they will be tried upon the Fire"; that is, they will be punished. Al-Zajjaj said: his disgrace. It was also said: his examination by which his matter is made manifest. It was also said: his destruction. Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said: his disbelief and misguidance. It is said: "fatanahu ʿan dinihi" meaning he turned him away from his religion. Its origin is: you will not be able to avert what God wills for him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Whomever God intends to test" means leaving him bewildered and forsaken, so you cannot obtain for him anything of God's grace and success. End. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila. This sentence came as consolation to the Messenger and to lighten the weight of his grief over their hastening into disbelief, and to cut off his hope for their success.

﴿Those are the ones whose hearts God did not intend to purify﴾ That is: it was already decreed for them in God's knowledge, and that they would be defiled with disbelief. In this and what precedes it there is a refutation of the Qadariyya and the Mu'tazila. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Those are the ones whom God did not intend to grant of His favours that would purify their hearts, because they are not among its people, since He knows that it does not benefit them nor take effect in them. Indeed, those who do not believe in God's signs, God does not guide them. How would God guide a people who disbelieved after their belief?" End. This is according to his Mu'tazili doctrine.

﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾ That is: humiliation and disgrace. The disgrace of the hypocrites is the exposure of their concealment, and their fear of being killed if the Muslims discover their disbelief. The disgrace of the Jews is their subjugation, the imposition of the jizya upon them, and their being scattered across the lands under the protection (dhimma) of others and under their rule. Muqatil said: the disgrace of Qurayza was by their killing and enslavement, and the disgrace of the Banu al-Nadir was by their expulsion.

﴿And for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾ It is described as "great" because it is ever-increasing, so it has no end, or because of the increase of its pain, or both.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 42:

﴿Listeners to falsehood, devourers of unlawful gain.﴾ Al-Hasan said: They listen to speech from one who lies before them in his claim, and he brings them a bribe, so they take it. Abu Sulayman said: They are the Jews, and they listen to falsehood, which is the statement of some of them (p-489) to others: "Muhammad is a liar, he is not a prophet, and there is no stoning in the Torah," while they know their own lie. It was also said: "falsehood" here means false testimony. End of quote. If the phrase "listeners to falsehood" at the beginning is a description of the Children of Israel, then this description applies to them.

It has already been mentioned that suht (unlawful gain, i.e. ill-gotten wealth) is haram property. Its meaning here is disputed. From Ibn Mas'ud: it is the bribe in judgment, the wage of prostitution, the fee of the soothsayer (hulwan al-kahin), the price of a dog, of gambling, of wine, of swine, of carrion, of blood, and the stud fee of a stallion, the wage of the professional mourner and the singing girl, of the sorcerer, the wage of the image-maker, and the gift for intercession. They said: unlawful property is called suht because it destroys acts of obedience, or the blessing of wealth, or religion, or manliness (muru'a). From Ibn Mas'ud and Masruq: property taken in return for intercession is suht. From al-Hasan: what a man eats from the property of one who owes him a debt is suht. It was said to Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud): "We used to regard as suht what is taken for judgment," meaning bribery. He said: "That is kufr (disbelief)," citing the verse: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 44]. Abu Hanifa said: if a judge accepts a bribe, he is dismissed. In a hadith: "Every flesh that grew from suht, the Fire is more deserving of it." Ali and Abu Hurayra said: the earnings of the cupper (al-hajjam) are suht, meaning that it removes manliness. Whatever has been mentioned regarding the meaning of suht is among the examples of property whose earnings are not lawful.

Among the greatest forms of suht is the bribe in judgment, and it is what the verse refers to. The Jews used to take bribes for rulings and for making unlawful things lawful. From al-Hasan: when one of them came to the judge in the Children of Israel with a bribe, he would place it in his sleeve and show it to him, and then speak of his need. The judge would listen to him and not look at his opponent, thus eating the bribe and listening to falsehood. The two grammarians (al-Nahwiyyan) and Ibn Kathir read al-suhut with two damma (ḍammatayn). The rest of the seven readers read it with sukun on the ha' (al-suht). Zayd ibn Ali and Kharija ibn Mus'ab from Nafi' read it with fatha on the sin and sukun on the ha'. It was also read with two fathas. Ubayd ibn Umayr read it with kasra on the sin and sukun on the ha'. With damma, kasra, and the two fathas, it is a noun for the thing which is consumed (ism al-masḥut), like al-dahn (the oil), al-ra'y (the grazing), and al-nabḍ (the throbbing). With fatha and sukun it is a verbal noun used in the sense of the object (maf'ul), like al-ṣayd (the hunt) meaning the game caught; or the ha' was made sukun for the sake of lightness.

* *

﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them.﴾ That is: if they come to you for judgment between them, then you have the choice between judging or turning away. The apparent meaning is that this ruling of choice remains for the rulers of the Muslims. From Ata, al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, Qatada, al-Asamm, Abu Muslim, and Abu Thawr: when they resort to the rulers of the Muslims, if they wish they judge, and if they wish they turn away. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima, al-Hasan, Ata al-Khurasani, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, and al-Zuhri said: the choice is abrogated (mansukh) by His saying: ﴿and that you judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 49]. So when they come, the imam has no right to send them back to their own judgments. The meaning according to others is: "and that you judge between them by what Allah has revealed" if you choose to judge between them rather than turn away from them. From Abu Hanifa: if they seek judgment from us, they are compelled to the judgment of Islam, and the hadd (prescribed punishment) is enforced upon the adulterer who has relations with a Muslim woman and upon the thief who steals from a Muslim. As for the people of the Hijaz, they do not see the enforcement of the hudud (prescribed punishments) upon them; they hold that they have been reconciled upon their polytheism, which is greater than the hudud, and they say: the stoning of the two Jews occurred before the revelation of the jizya (poll tax). Ibn Atiyya said: the community is in consensus (ijma') that the ruler of the Muslims judges between the People of the Dhimma in cases of injustice (tazalum), and he has authority over them in changing [what is wrong], and among that is withholding goods that have been sold and seizing property. As for the matters of rulings in which there is no injustice, but are only supplication and are ambiguous, these are the ones in which the judge has the choice. End of quote. There is some abridgment in it. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that when the two disputants come to the judge, and their consent to his judgment is sufficient for him to proceed to judge between them. Ibn al-Qasim said: it is necessary along with that to have the consent of the bishops and monks; if the bishops consent without the two litigants, or the two litigants without the bishops, he has no right to judge. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, and others said: "if they come to you" refers to the people of the case of the adulterers, and then the verse includes all other cases. Some said: it was about the killing of Jews from Qurayza and al-Nadir. Some said: the choice is specific to the mu'ahidun (those with treaties) and is binding on them. The school of al-Shafi'i holds that it is obligatory upon the ruler of the Muslims to judge between the People of the Dhimma when they resort to him, because enforcing the judgment of Islam upon them is a humiliation for them. As for the mu'ahadun who have a covenant with the Muslims for a fixed term, it is not obligatory for him to judge between them; rather he has the choice in this, and this is the choice mentioned in the verse, and it is specific to the mu'ahadun. It is narrated from al-Shafi'i the same as the view of Ata and al-Nakha'i.

﴿And if you turn away from them, they will not harm you at all.﴾ That is: you are safe from their harm, and you are victorious over them in every state. They used to resort to him seeking what was easier and less burdensome for them, so flogging in place of stoning. When he turned away from them and refused to rule between them, it was hard for them, and they disliked his turning away from them, and they were fit to oppose him and harm him. So Allah protected him from them and informed him that they were not capable of any part of harming him.

* *

﴿And if you judge, judge between them with justice.﴾ That is: and if you wish to judge with justice (qist), with equity (adl), as you judge between the Muslims. Qist is what is explained in His saying: ﴿and that you judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 49], and he does not judge except with qist. So this is a command whose meaning is a report; that is: your judgment does not occur except with justice, because you are protected from following desire.

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.﴾ And you are their master, so His love for you is greater than His love for them. In this there is an exhortation to seek out justice and prefer it, since Allah mentioned that He loves whoever is characterized by it.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 43:**

﴿How would they make you judge, when they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at their seeking your judgment, although they do not believe in you or in your Book. In their own Book, which they claim to believe in, there is a clear text on the judgment of Allah the Exalted. So they do not truly intend the judgment of Allah. They intend only that there be with him a concession regarding what they bring before him, following their desires and indulging in their appetites. Whoever turns away from the judgment of Allah in the Book he claims to believe in, toward the judgment of one who believes neither in him nor in his Book, judges only out of desire for the violation of that Book. If they violate their own Book because it does not accord with their appetites, then it is all the more fitting and proper that they would violate you if you do not agree with them.

The waw in *wa-ʿindahum* (وعِنْدَهم) is for the state (*li-l-ḥāl*, the grammatical circumstantial clause). *Wa-ʿindahumu al-tawrātu* (وعِنْدَهُمُ التَّوْراةُ) is a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate). *Fīhā ḥukmu Allāh* (فِيها. حُكْمُ اللَّهِ) is a ḥāl (circumstantial complement) of al-Tawrah, and *ḥukmun* (حُكْمٌ) is in the nominative as a fāʿil (subject) through the prepositional phrase; that is, "with the judgment of Allah being in it." It is also permissible for *fīhā* to occupy a nominative position as the khabar about al-Tawrah, as when you say: *wa-ʿindahumu al-tawrātu nāṭiqatan bi-ḥukmi Allāh* (وعِنْدَهُمُ التَّوْراةُ ناطِقَةً بِحُكْمِ اللَّهِ), "and with them is the Torah speaking of the judgment of Allah." As for *wa* (وأوْ), it has no place in i'rab, and the clause is a mubayyina (explanatory clause), because "with them is what suffices them from seeking judgment," just as you say: "With you is Zayd, who advises you and points out to you what is right, so what do you do with anyone else?" These two grammatical analyses belong to al-Zamakhshari.

﴿Then they turn away after that﴾: that is, after your judgment, which accords with what is in their Book, because the wonder at their seeking judgment arose only after it had come from them. Then they turned away from it and were not pleased with it. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "*Min baʿdi dhālika* (مِن بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ), that is, after the judgment of Allah in the Torah and what resembles it of matters in which they opposed the command of Allah." End of quotation. This sentence is a fresh resumption (jumla mustaʾnafa, a new independent clause); that is, "then they turn away after this." It is information from Allah about their turning away, in keeping with their habit: when the truth becomes clear to them, they turn away from it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: To what does *thumma yatawallawna* (ثُمَّ يَتَوَلَّوْنَ) refer as a conjunction? I say: It refers to *yuḥakkimūnaka* (يُحَكِّمُونَكَ)." End of quotation. In that case it falls within the interrogative that is intended to express wonder; that is, "then how do they turn away after that?" So he has wondered at their seeking his judgment, and then at their turning away from it; that is, how they were pleased with it and then became angry with it.

﴿And those are not believers﴾: its apparent meaning is the negation of faith from them; that is, whoever makes the Messenger a judge, opposes his Book, and turns away from what he has ruled for him, although it accords with his Book, is a disbeliever. It has been said: it is information about them that they will never believe, so it is a report about the future, not the past. It has been said: it is the negation of faith in the Torah and in Musa (Moses) for them. It has been said: it is linked to his saying "How would they make you judge?"; that is, "Wonder at their making you judge, and they are not believers in you, nor do they hold the validity of your judgment to be true. This indicates that their intention is only to obtain the benefits of this world and their corrupt aims, not to follow the truth." (p-٤٩١)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 44 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which there is guidance and light.﴾ Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: it was revealed concerning those who denied the ruling of God, and it applies generally to everyone who denies the ruling of God. Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said: "O Messenger, do not grieve... then they are the disbelievers" (Q 5:41) was revealed specifically concerning the Jews, and he mentioned the story of the stoning of the two Jews. It was said to Hudhayfah: "And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, they are the disbelievers" (Q 5:44) was revealed concerning the Children of Israel? He said: Yes. Al-Hasan, Abu Mijlaz and Abu Ja'far said: it refers to the Jews. Al-Hasan said: it is obligatory upon us as well. Qatadah said: It was related to us that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to say when this verse was revealed: "We judge over the Jews and over those other than them among the people of religions." The verse contains an encouragement for the Jews to be like their earlier Muslim rabbis, and a reminder to those who deny the obligation of stoning. A group said: guidance and light are the same, and it was repeated for emphasis. Others said: they are not the same. Guidance is taken to refer to the explanation of the rulings, while light and clarity refer to monotheism, prophethood and the Return. Al-Zamakhshari said: it guides to justice and truth, and light clarifies what is ambiguous of the rulings. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: guidance is the instruction in belief and the laws, and light is that by which one is illuminated through its commands and prohibitions. It was also said: the meaning is that in it is the explanation of the matter of the Messenger, and what they came asking for a ruling about.

﴿By it the prophets who submitted judge for those who are Jews﴾. The apparent meaning of His words "the prophets" is plural. They said: they are from Moses to Jesus. 'Ikrimah said: Muhammad and those prophets before him. It was also said: the prophets are those who follow the religion of Abraham. Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: it is Muhammad (ﷺ), and that is when he judged the Jews by stoning, and He expressed it in the plural form, as in His words: "Or do they envy people?" (Q 4:54). "Who submitted" is a description praising the prophets, like the attributes that are applied to God the Exalted, and the purpose of applying it is an allusion to the Jews and Christians, since the Jews said that the prophets were Jews, and the Christians said that they were Christians. So He made clear that they were Muslims, as Abraham (peace be upon him) was. For this reason He said: "He named you Muslims before" (Q 22:78). By this description He indicated that the Jews and Christians are far removed from this attribute, which is Islam, and that it was the religion of all the prophets, past and present. The apparent meaning is that "for those who are Jews" is connected to His words "by it the prophets judge." It was also said: it is connected to "We sent down." It was also said the estimated sense is: guidance and light for those who are Jews, by which the prophets judge. In His words "for those who are Jews" there is a reminder that they are not Muslims, rather they are far from that. The lam in "for those who are Jews," when it is linked to "judge," indicates specification, so it includes both those for whom judgment is made and those against whom it is made. It was also said: there is an omitted element, meaning: for those who are Jews and against them. It was also said: the lam has the sense of "upon," meaning: upon those who are Jews.

* *

﴿And the rabbis and the scholars﴾. These two have one meaning, and they are the scholars. This was said by most of them, including Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj. Mujahid said: the rabbaniyyun are the jurists and scholars, and they are above the rabbis (ahbar). Al-Suddi said: the rabbaniyyun are the scholars, and the rabbis are the jurists. Ibn Zayd said: the rabbaniyyun are the rulers, and the rabbis are the scholars. It was also said: the rabbaniyyun are the scholars of the Christians, and the rabbis are the scholars of the Jews, and the explanation of the term rabbani has already been given. Al-Zamakhshari said: the rabbaniyyun and the rabbis are the ascetics and scholars from the descendants of Aaron, who adhered to the way of the prophets and kept away from the religion of the Jews. Al-Suddi said: what is meant here by the rabbaniyyun and the rabbis are those who judge by the Torah, the two sons of Suriya, one of whom was a rabbani and the other a habr. They had given the Prophet (ﷺ) a covenant that he should not ask them about anything in the matter of the Torah without them informing him of it. So he asked them about the matter of stoning, and they informed him of it accurately, and so the verse was revealed pointing to the two of them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: there is something to consider in this. The correct report is that the two sons of Suriya and others denied the matter of stoning, and 'Abd Allah ibn Salam exposed them regarding it. The word applies to every rabbi who was upright in past times, but in the period of Muhammad (ﷺ), if one had existed, he would have become a Muslim, and so he would not be called a rabbi or a rabbani. End of quotation.

﴿Because they were entrusted with the protection of the Book of God﴾. The bi in "bima" indicates cause, and it is connected to His words "judge." Istaf'ala here indicates request (talab), and the meaning is: because of what they were entrusted with (istaf'ala: to ask someone to do something). The pronoun in "were entrusted" refers to the prophets, the rabbaniyyun and the rabbis; that is, because of what God required of them, the preservation of the Book of God, which is the Torah. He charged them with preserving it and took His covenant from them to act upon it and to speak by it. God imposed upon the scholars the preservation of the Book in two ways: the first is preserving it in their hearts and reciting it with their tongues; the second is preserving it by acting upon its rulings and following its laws. These people neglected what they were entrusted with, until the Torah was altered. The passive form of the verb and the fact that the verb has the sense of request indicate that He, the Exalted, did not take on the preservation of the Torah Himself; rather He required them to preserve it and charged them with that, so they changed, altered and opposed the rulings of God. This is unlike our Book, for God the Exalted has taken on its preservation, so it is impossible that any alteration or change should occur in it. He, the Exalted, said: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians" (Q 15:9). It was also said: the pronoun in "were entrusted" refers only to the rabbaniyyun and the rabbis. Those whom He entrusted with the Torah were the prophets.

﴿And they were witnesses over it﴾. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to the Book of God; that is, they were watchers over it, lest it be altered. The meaning is: the prophets judge by the rulings of the Torah between Moses and Jesus, and there was between them a thousand prophets, judging those who are Jews by the rulings of the Torah, not letting them turn away from it, just as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did when he compelled them to the ruling of stoning and humbled their pride, and when they refused what they desired of flogging. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the ruling; that is, they were witnesses to the ruling. It was also said: it refers to the Messenger; that is, they were witnesses that he was a sent prophet.

* *

﴿So do not fear the people, but fear Me, and do not trade My signs for a small price﴾. This is a prohibition to the rulers against fearing other than God in their judgments, and against deviating in them and carrying them out contrary to what they were commanded regarding justice, out of fear of an oppressive ruler, or fear of harming someone among the creditors or friends. And do not seek with the signs of God a small price, which is bribery, seeking status and the approval of people, just as the rabbis of the Jews distorted the Book of God and changed its rulings, desiring the world and seeking leadership, and so they were ruined. This is a prohibition against all impure gains through knowledge and devising ways to obtain worldly things through religion. Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas that its meaning is: do not fear the people in making known the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and acting upon stoning, but fear Me in concealing that. Since the act of changing the rulings of God has two causes, fear and desire, and fear has a stronger effect than desire, He placed the prohibition against fear before the prohibition against desire and greed. The apparent meaning is that this address to the Jews is in the manner of narration and speech to the scholars of the Children of Israel. Muqatil said: the address is to the Jews of Medina; they were told: do not fear the Jews of Khaybar that you tell them about stoning, but fear Me in concealing it. End of quotation. Although this is an address to the scholars of the Children of Israel, it encompasses the scholars of this community. Ibn Juraij said: it is an address to this community; that is, do not fear the people as the Jews feared the people, so that they did not speak the truth.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 44 (part 2 of 3):

﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers.﴾ The apparent meaning of this is generality, so it includes this nation and others before them, although the apparent context is an address to the Jews. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibrahim, 'Ata' and a group held that it is general, covering the Jews and others, but it is "disbelief short of disbelief, injustice short of injustice, and sinfulness short of sinfulness" — meaning that the disbelief of a Muslim is not like the disbelief of an unbeliever, and likewise his injustice and sinfulness do not remove him from the religion (millah). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Tawus. Abu Mijlaz said: it is specific to the Jews, Christians and the people of polytheism, and it was revealed concerning them. Abu Salih said likewise, and said: there is nothing of it in Islam. A hadith has been narrated on this subject from al-Bara', from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "It refers to the three among the disbelievers." 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said: it is about the People of the Book. This was also said by 'Abdullah ibn 'Abdullah ibn 'Utbah ibn Mas'ud. Abu 'Ubaydah mentioned these opinions and said: some people interpret the verses in ways they were not revealed for; these verses were revealed only concerning two tribes of the Jews, Quraizah and al-Nadir, and he mentioned the account of the killing between them. Al-Hasan said: it was revealed concerning the Jews, (p-493) and it is obligatory upon us. It was said to Hudhayfah: "Was this verse revealed concerning the Children of Israel?" He said: "How excellent brothers the Children of Israel are for you — if you have every sweetness, they have every bitterness; you will certainly follow their path step for step." From Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Jarir preferred it: "The disbelievers, the wrongdoers and the sinners are the People of the Book." And from him: "What an excellent people you are; whatever is sweet is yours, and whatever is bitter belongs to the People of the Book." Whoever denies the ruling of Allah has disbelieved; whoever does not judge by it while acknowledging it is a wrongdoer and a sinner. From al-Sha'bi: "The disbelievers" refers to the People of Islam, "the wrongdoers" to the Jews, and "the sinners" to the Christians. It seems that he specified each general term by what follows it, since before the first there is: ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 42], and ﴿And if you judge, judge﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 42], and ﴿And how do they make you judge﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 43], and ﴿by which the prophets judged﴾; and before the second: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]; and before the third: ﴿And We sent after them in their footsteps Jesus son of Mary, confirming what was before him﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 46], to the end of the verse.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, scorning it" — this describes them as persisting in their disbelief when they wronged the signs of Allah by mockery and contempt, and rebelled by judging by other than them. End quote. Al-Suddi said: whoever opposes the ruling of Allah, abandons it deliberately, transgresses it while knowing, is truly among the disbelievers; and this is to be understood as denial (juhud), which is disbelief as the opposite of faith, as Ibn 'Abbas said.

The Kharijites argued by this verse that everyone who disobeys Allah is a disbeliever, and they said: it is a clear text regarding everyone who judges by other than what Allah has revealed, so he is a disbeliever; and everyone who sins has judged by other than what Allah has revealed, so he must be a disbeliever. It was answered: it was revealed concerning the Jews, so it is specific to them. This was weakened on the ground that the lesson is drawn from the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation. Some said: its implied sense is "and whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed among those previously mentioned," but this is weak, because "man" (من) is a general conditional, and adding what is supposed is an addition to what is apparent, which is not permissible. It was said: what is meant is the disbelief of ingratitude (kufr al-ni'mah), but this was weakened on the ground that when "disbelief" is used without qualification it refers to disbelief in religion. Ibn al-Anbari said: he did an act resembling the acts of the disbelievers; this was weakened on the ground that it is a departure from the apparent meaning. 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Yahya al-Kinani said: "what Allah has revealed" is a general expression, so the meaning is: whoever comes with the opposite of the ruling of Allah in all that Allah has revealed; and the sinner does not come with the opposite of the ruling of Allah except in a few matters, which are the actions, whereas in belief and affirmation he agrees. This was weakened on the ground that if it were so, this threat would not have included the Jews on account of their opposition to the ruling of Allah concerning stoning. The exegetes agreed that this threat includes the Jews on account of their opposition to the ruling of Allah in the incident of stoning, which indicates that this view falls. 'Ikrimah said: it applies only to one who denies in his heart and rejects with his tongue; but one who knows that it is the ruling of Allah and affirms with his tongue that it is the ruling of Allah, yet acts contrary to it, is a judge by what Allah has revealed but abandons it, so it does not necessarily follow that he enters under this verse.

﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life, and the eye for the eye, and the nose for the nose, and the ear for the ear, and the tooth for the tooth, and for wounds is retaliation﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]. The connection of this verse to what precedes it: Allah explained in the Torah that the ruling for the married adulterer is stoning, and the Jews changed it; and here He explained that in the Torah it is "life for life," and the Jews also changed that, favouring the Banu al-Nadir over the Banu Quraizah, and restricting the imposition of retaliation (qawad) to the Banu Quraizah rather than the Banu al-Nadir. The meaning of "We prescribed" (kataba) is "We obligated"; it was also said: "We said," with writing used in the sense of speaking. (p-494) It is also possible that writing is meant literally, namely writing on the tablets, since the Torah is written on the tablets. The pronoun in "therein" refers to the Torah, and in "for them" refers to those who became Jews.

Nafi', Hamzah and 'Asim read "the eye" and what follows it with the accusative, as coordinated with the operation of "anna" (that), the accusative. The predicate of "anna" is the prepositional phrase, and the predicate of "wounds is retaliation" is the same. Abu 'Ali held that the governing element in the prepositional phrase is "taken by the life" and so on through all the prepositional phrases. Al-Zamakhshari first estimated it as: "taken by the life, killed by it if he killed it without right"; likewise "the eye is put out by the eye," "the nose is cut off by the nose," "the ear is taken, cut off, by the ear," "the tooth is pulled out by the tooth." The statement of al-Zamakhshari — "killed," "put out," "cut off," "cut," "pulled out" — should be understood as an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of grammatical analysis, because when a prepositional phrase falls as a predicate it must have as its governing element a general (absolute) verb of being, not a restricted one. The "ba'" here is the ba' of equivalence and exchange, so one estimates what approximates the absolute being, which is "taken." When you say: "I sold the sheep, a ewe, for a dirham," the meaning is "taken for a dirham"; likewise "the free for the free, and the slave for the slave"; the estimate is: "the free is taken for the free, and the slave is taken for the slave"; and likewise "this garment for this dirham" means "taken for this dirham." Al-Hawfi said: "by the life" is connected to a deleted verb estimated as "must be," or "is established." Likewise "the eye for the eye" and what follows are of estimated absolute being; the meaning: its killing is established by the killing of the life.

Al-Kisa'i read "and the eye" and what follows with the nominative. Abu 'Ali allowed several explanations for the nominative reading. The first: the "wa" coordinates a sentence upon a sentence, just as it coordinates a single word upon a single word, so "and the eye for the eye" is a nominal sentence coordinated upon a verbal sentence, namely "and We prescribed"; those sentences are therefore not included under "We prescribed" in terms of wording, nor in terms of sharing the meaning of prescribing, but rather that is a new imposition and the beginning of legislation. The second: the "wa" coordinates a sentence upon the meaning in His saying "that the life is for the life," i.e., say to them: "the life for the life," and this coordination is one of coordination upon what is imagined (al-'atf 'ala al-tawahhum), since it gives the impression, in "that the life is for the life," that it is "the life for the life," and the sentences are included under the writing in terms of meaning, not in terms of wording. The third: that the "wa" coordinates a single word upon a single word, namely "and the eye" is coordinated upon the pronoun concealed in the prepositional phrase; that is, "by the life, it, and the eye," and likewise what follows. In this case the prepositional phrases are states clarifying the meaning, because the nominative here is the subject, since it is coordinated upon a subject.

These last two explanations are weak: the first of them is coordination upon what is imagined, which is not analogical and is only said where it has been heard. The second of them involves coordinating upon the attached nominative pronoun without separating it from the coordinating particle by anything, nor between the particle and the coordinated word by "la," and this is not permitted according to the Basrians (p-495) except in case of necessity; and it entails making these states obligatory, whereas the basic principle of a state is that it is not obligatory.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the nominative is for coordination upon the position of "anna al-nafs" (that the life), because the meaning is: "and there was prescribed upon them: the life for the life," either because "kataba" is treated as "qala," or because the sentence "the life for the life" is among the things that writing can take as its object, just as recitation takes it as its object; one says: "I wrote 'al-hamdu lillah' (praise be to Allah)," and "I recited a surah We have sent down." Likewise al-Zajjaj said: "If 'anna al-nafs' were read, it would be sound." End quote. This which al-Zamakhshari said is the second of Abu 'Ali's explanations, except that he departed from the technical term for it, for coordination upon the position is not called coordination upon the place in the technical sense, because coordination upon the place is restricted, and this is not of that kind; rather it is coordination upon what is imagined. Do you not see that we do not say that "that the life for the life" is in a nominative position, because the seeker of the nominative is absent; rather we say: the verbal noun formed from "anna" and its noun and predicate has a single wording and position, which is the accusative, and the estimate is: "and We prescribed upon them therein the life for the life," either because "kataba" is treated as "qala," so the sentence is related by it; or because both are among the things that can take writing as their object, since sentences are written just as single words are; and we do not say that the position of "anna al-nafs bi'l-nafs" occurs by this consideration.

Ubayy and the two Arabs (Ibn 'Amir? — the Syrians), and Ibn Kathir, read with the accusative "and the eye," "and the nose," "and the ear," "and the tooth," and with the nominative "and the wounds." This is related from Nafi'. Abu 'Ali explained the nominative of "and the wounds" according to the three possibilities he mentioned for the nominative of "and the eye and what follows." It is related that Anas reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) read "an al-nafs" with a lightened "anna" and nominative "al-'ayn" and what follows; this may have two aspects. One: that it be a verbal "anna" lightened from "anna," whose noun is the deleted pronoun of the matter, and the sentence is in the nominative position as the predicate of "an"; its meaning is the meaning of the heavy form that governs as the verbal "anna." The second aspect: that "an" be explanatory, the estimate being: "i.e., the life is for the life," because "kataba" is a sentence with the meaning of speech. Ubayy read "al-nafsa bi'l-nafs" with the accusative for the life and the four after it, and "wa an al-jurahu qisas" with the lightened "an" and the nominative "al-jurahu"; in this reading it must be that the "an" is the lightened form of the heavy "anna," and it is not permissible for it to be explanatory in terms of coordination, because "kataba" would be governing in one respect (as the heavy form) and not governing in another (as the explanatory form), and so it is not permissible; for coordination requires sharing, and if there is no governing there is no sharing.

Nafi' read "wa al-udhna bi'l-udhni" with the sukun on the dhal, definite, indefinite and dual wherever it occurs. The rest read with the damma. It is said: they are two dialects, like "nukur" and "nukr." It is said: the sukun is the original, and the damma was used by assimilation. It is said: the vowelled form is the original, and it was made sukun for lightness.

The meaning of this verse is that God prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul by way of a prescribed penalty (hadd), his own soul shall be taken; and likewise these organs (of the body). This ruling is binding in our religion by consensus (ijma')。 The majority hold that His saying ﴿that the soul is for the soul﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 45] is general, but is meant to be specific to equals. Some people said: a free man is killed for a slave, and a Muslim for a dhimmi (a non-Muslim protected under a covenant). This was the view of Abu Hanifa. They agreed that a Muslim is not killed for a musta'man (a non-Muslim granted temporary safe-conduct) or for a harbi (a non-Muslim from a hostile territory). A parent is not killed for his child, nor a master for his slave. A group may be killed for one person, contrary to 'Ali's view, and one person may be killed for a group by way of qisas (retaliation). When retaliation (qawad) is carried out, no property is owed. Al-Shafi'i said: he is killed for the first of them, and the blood-money (diyya) of the rest is owed. The discussion of this has already passed in al-Baqara in His saying ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾ [al-Baqara: 178], and so on.

Ibn 'Abbas said: they used not to kill a man for a woman, so this was revealed. He also said: God granted this community a concession and widened it through blood-money, and He did not give the Children of Israel blood-money in what was revealed to Musa and prescribed for them.

al-Thawri said: It has reached me from Ibn 'Abbas that he abrogated (naskh) ﴿the free for the free, and the slave for the slave﴾ [al-Baqara: 178] by His saying: that the soul is for the soul. The apparent meaning of His saying "the soul for the soul" is generality, and what is excluded from it is excluded by evidence, while the remainder stays general. The apparent meaning of His saying "the eye for the eye" is that the eye of one blind in one eye is put out for the eye of one who has two eyes. This was the view of Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i. It is related from 'Uthman and 'Umar, and others, that he owes the diyya.

Malik said: If (the victim) wishes, he may put out (the eye), and if he wishes, he may take the full diyya. This was also the view of 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, Qatada, al-Zuhri, al-Layth, Malik, Ahmad, and al-Nakha'i.

Half the diyya is related from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mughaffal, Masruq, and al-Nakha'i. This was the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri, and al-Shafi'i. Ibn al-Mundhir said: and we say this.

The right eye is put out for the left eye, and the incisor is extracted for the molar, and the reverse, because of the generality of the wording. This was the view of Ibn Shubruma. The majority said: this is specific to equality, so a right is not taken for a left when the (right) exists, except with consent.

If one puts out an eye that cannot see, then from Zayd ibn Thabit: in it are one hundred dinars; and from 'Umar: a third of its diyya. Masruq, al-Zuhri, Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, and Ibn al-Mundhir said: in it is a judgment of compensation (hukuma). If part of the light of the eye is removed and part remains, the position of Abu Hanifa is that in it there is arsh (assessed compensation). From 'Ali: his sight is tested, and he is given the amount by which the offender's property is reduced.

For all the eyelids together is the full diyya, and for each eyelid a quarter of the diyya. This was said by Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Qatada, Ibrahim, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa and his companions, and al-Shafi'i. al-Sha'bi said: for the upper eyelid a third of the diyya, and for the lower eyelid two-thirds.

There is a difference concerning one who cuts off a nose: does retaliation apply to it or not? Abu Hanifa said: if he cuts it off from its root, there is no retaliation in it, and there is only the diyya. It is related from Abu Yusuf that retaliation applies to it if the whole is taken. There is a difference concerning breaking the nose: Malik holds that there is retaliation for it when intentional, and ijtihad (judgment) when unintentional. It is related from Nafi': there is no diyya for it until it is entirely removed. It is related from 'Ali that he required retaliation for its breaking. al-Shafi'i said: if its break is set, then in it is a judgment, and what is cut from the cartilage (marin) is (compensated) in proportion. This is related from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz and al-Sha'bi, and al-Shafi'i held this. For the marin when it is cut and the nose is not entirely removed, the full diyya (is owed). This was said by Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and his companions. The marin is the soft part of the nose, and the arnaba and the rawtha are the tip of the marin.
