If he takes away the sense of smell or diminishes it, the majority hold that in it is a judgment of fair assessment.

The ear for the ear: this requires retaliation when it is entirely taken. If part of it is cut, then there is retaliation for it when its extent is known. al-Shafi'i said: for both ears the diyya, and for one of them half of it. Malik said: for both ears a judgment (hukuma), and the diyya is only for hearing, and its loss is measured as the loss of sight is measured. For nullifying (hearing) in one of them, half the diyya (is owed), even if he could not hear except with it.

The tooth for the tooth: this requires that extraction is retaliation, and there is no disagreement about this, even if part of it was broken. All teeth are equal: incisors, canines, molars, and the rubā'iyyāt (the teeth beside the incisors), each one (owing) five camels without excess. This was said by 'Urwa, Tawus, Qatada, al-Zuhri, al-Thawri, Rabi'a, al-Awza'i, 'Uthman al-Batti, Malik, Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Ishaq. It is related from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, and Mu'awiya. Ibn al-Musayyib related from 'Umar that he ruled, for what is in front of the mouth, five obligatory shares (fara'id), which is fifty dinars, each share ten dinars, and for the molars a camel each. Ibn al-Musayyib said: if the whole mouth were struck, under the judgment of 'Umar the diyya would decrease, or under the judgment of Mu'awiya it would increase. If I were (the judge), I would make it two camels for each molar. 'Umar said: the molars are twenty, and the teeth are twelve: four incisors, four rubā'iyyāt, and four canines. The disagreement concerns only the molars, not the teeth. Under the judgment of 'Umar the diyya is eighty, and under the judgment of Mu'awiya it is one hundred and sixty. According to Ibn al-Musayyib's view it is one hundred, which is the full diyya in camels.

'Ata' said, regarding the two incisors, the two rubā'iyyāt, and the two canines: five each, and for the rest two camels each; the upper and lower parts of the mouth are equal. If the tooth of a child who has not yet shed his teeth is extracted and then grows back, Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Shafi'i said: nothing is owed by the extractor. Except that Malik and al-Shafi'i said: if it grows back shorter than the tooth next to it, then something is taken from its compensation in proportion to its shortfall. A group said: in it is a judgment, and this is related from al-Sha'bi, and Abu Hanifa and his companions held this. If the tooth of an adult is extracted, and he takes its diyya, and then it grows back, Malik said: he does not return what he took. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: he returns it, and there are two opinions from al-Shafi'i. If a tooth is extracted as retaliation, and its owner returns it and it reattaches, then Abu Hanifa said extraction is not required, and this was said by 'Ata' al-Khurasani and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah. al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Ishaq said: he is compelled to extract it. This was said by Ibn al-Musayyib, and he repeats every prayer he prayed with it. Likewise if an ear is cut off and he reattaches it while the blood is still warm, and it sticks: this view is related from 'Ata', and Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: it is an error.

If one extracts an extra tooth, the majority said: in it is a judgment; and if part of it is broken, he gives in proportion to what was lost from it. This was said by Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad. al-Udfu'i said: I know of no disagreement about this. Zayd ibn Thabit said: for an extra tooth, a third of a tooth. If someone strikes a tooth and it turns black and then he treats it, this is related from Zayd and Ibn al-Musayyib, and this was said by al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, Shurayh, al-Nakha'i, 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Thawri. It is related from 'Imran: for it a third of its diyya, and this was said by Ahmad and Ishaq. al-Nakha'i, al-Shafi'i, and Abu Thawr said: in it is a judgment; if it falls out afterward, then in it is its diyya. This was said by al-Layth and 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Salama. If part of it turns black, it is (compensated) in proportion; this was said by al-Thawri.

Wounds (al-juruh) are subject to retaliation, meaning: those that admit of retaliation. The word "wounds" is general, and what is meant is specific: that which admits of retaliation. Equivalence is known and there is no fear of death from it. If there is fear, as with a wound reaching the brain (ma'muma), a broken thigh, and the like, then there is no retaliation for it. The meaning of "and wounds are subject to retaliation" requires that the wound be inflicted with a similar one; if it is not with a similar one, it is not retaliation. They differed concerning retaliation between men and women, and between slave and free. All that is other than the soul is among the injuries that He indicated by His saying "and wounds are subject to retaliation." But He detailed the beginning of the verse and summarized its end, so that it encompasses what was explicitly mentioned and what was not, and thus generality is achieved, meaning though not in wording. Among the wounds are the shijaj (head wounds) where retaliation is possible; there is no disagreement that it is obligatory there. Where it is not possible, there is no retaliation, as with the ma'mumah. Abu 'Ubayd said: there is no retaliation for any shijaj except the muwdiha (wound exposing the bone) specifically, because none of the others has a limit to which one can reach except it. As for the others among the shijaj, their diyya is owed. He finished. Others said: for the khari�sa (a deep wound) retaliation is by its measure, if no spread is feared from it. Ibn al-Zubayr exacted retaliation for a ma'mumah, and people disapproved of him. 'Ata' said: we know of no one who exacted retaliation for it before him. As for wounds in the flesh, some scholars mentioned that retaliation for them is possible by measuring by a similar (wound) and placing (the instrument) to the extent of that wound.

**Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 5, verse 45:**

﴿Whoever gives it as charity, it is an expiation for him.﴾ The one who gives charity (al-mutasaddiq) is the one who holds the right. The one who exacts retaliation (mustawfi al-qisas, *qisas* meaning legal retribution in kind) covers the soul, the limbs, and the wounds for which retaliation is due. The pronoun refers to the act of giving charity, meaning: the giving of charity is an expiation for the giving. The meaning is that whoever gives up his right to retaliation for his wound, it expiates for him. This is the view of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Abdullah ibn Umar, Abdullah ibn Amr, Jabir, Abu al-Darda, Qatadah, al-Hasan, and al-Sha'bi.

Abu al-Darda reported that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "No Muslim is afflicted with anything in his body and then forgives it, except that Allah raises him by it one degree and removes from him one sin." Makki also cited a hadith through al-Sha'bi: "He will have removed from him of his sins what he has pardoned of the blood money (*diyah*)." And from Abdullah ibn Umar: "He will erase his sins to the extent of what he has given in charity."

It was also said that the pronoun in *lahu* ("for him") refers to the offender, even though he has not been mentioned before, but he is understood from the context of the speech, and the meaning indicates it. The meaning is: that pardon and charity are an expiation for the offender, by which what was due from him of retaliation falls away. Just as retaliation is an expiation, so too pardon is an expiation, and the reward of the one who pardons is with Allah. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Subay'i, Mujahid, Ibrahim, al-Sha'bi, Zayd ibn Aslam, and Muqatil.

It was also said that the one who gives charity is the offender, and the pronoun in *lahu* returns to him. The meaning: if an offender commits an offence, it becomes unknown and its matter is hidden, and then he gives charity by making himself known and submitting himself, that act is an expiation for his sin. Mujahid said: if a man injures another man and the injured one does not know who injured him, and the one who caused the injury confesses to him, then it is an expiation for the one who caused the injury. Urwah, at the Corner (*al-Rukn*), injured a person while they were touching it (*yastalimun*), and the injured man did not know who had injured him. Urwah said to him: "I injured you, and I am Urwah ibn al-Zubayr. If any harm reaches you from it, then I am responsible for it." According to this view, *tasaddaqa* may be a verb of the form *tafa''ala* derived from *sadaqah* (charity), and it may also be derived from *sidq* (truthfulness).

Ubayy recited: *fa-huwa kaffaratun lahu* ("so it is an expiation for him"), meaning: then the giving of charity is his expiation, that is, the expiation that he deserves for himself, of which nothing is reduced. This is a magnification of what he has done, in accordance with the words: ﴿so his reward is upon Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 40], and an encouragement to pardon.

Some scholars interpreted the verse to mean: and wounds are subject to retaliation. So whoever is given the blood money (*diyah*) for the wound and gives it up as charity, it is an expiation for him, if it is accepted from him and received. In the Mushaf of Ubayy: ﴿And whoever gives it as charity, then indeed it is an expiation for him.﴾

* *

﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the wrongdoers.﴾ In the previous verses, mention of the disbelievers was appropriate, because this came after His words: ﴿Indeed, We revealed the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44], and so there is an indication in that that one does not judge by all of it, but opposes it outright. Therefore it came: ﴿and do not trade My verses for a small price﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44], and this is disbelief, so mention of the disbelievers was appropriate. Here, it came after specific matters concerning killing and wounds, so mention of wrongdoing (*zulm*) was appropriate, since it contradicts retaliation and the lack of equality, and as an indication of what they had established of the lack of equality between the Banu al-Nadir and the Banu Qurayzah.

﴿And We sent after them, following in their footsteps, Jesus son of Mary, confirming what was before him of the Torah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 46]. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that the Torah is judged by it by the prophets, He mentioned that He followed up after them with Jesus, as a reminder that he was among the prophets, an honouring of his name, and a declaration of his purity from what the Jews claim about him, and that he was among those who confirm the Torah.

The meaning of *qaffayna* ("We followed up") is: We brought him, following in their footsteps (*yaqfu athararahum*), that is, following them. The pronoun in *atharihim* ("their footsteps") refers to the prophets mentioned in His words: ﴿by which the prophets judged﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44]. It was also said: it refers to those upon whom these rulings were prescribed. *Ala atharihim* ("upon their footsteps") is connected to *qaffayna*, and *bi-Isa* ("with Jesus") is also connected to it. This is by way of *tadmin* (the verb being made to carry the sense of another verb), meaning: then We came upon their footsteps with Jesus son of Mary, following them. The doubling in *qaffayna* is not for making the verb transitive, since if it were for transitivity it would not have come with the *ba'* of transitivity, nor would it have been transitive with *ala*. This is because *qafa* is transitive to one object, as Allah says: ﴿and do not follow (*taqfu*) that of which you have no knowledge﴾ [al-Isra: 36], and one says: *qafa fulanun al-athara* ("so-and-so followed the trace") when he followed it. If the doubling were for transitivity, it would have been transitive to two objects in the accusative, and the construction would have been: *thumma qaffayna ala atharihim Isa ibna Maryam*, with Isa as the first object and *athārihim* as the second. But it was given the sense of *ja'a* ("came") and made transitive with *bi-*, and it was transitive to *athārihim* with *ala*. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*qaffaytuhu*" is like *'aqabtuhu* when you follow him, then one says *qaffaytuhu bi-fulan* and *'aqabtuhu bihi*, so you make it transitive to the second with the addition of the *ba'*.

(If you say): Where is the first object in the verse? (I say): It is omitted, and the adverbial phrase *ala athārihim* acts as its substitute, because when he was followed up with it upon its trace, he was followed up with it, that is, with it. End of quote. His speech needs interpretation, because he took *qaffaytu* with doubling to mean *qafawtu*, so that *fa''ala* has the sense of *fa'ala*, like *qaddara Allahu* and *qadara Allahu*, and this is one of the meanings for which *fa'ala* came. Then he made it transitive with *bi-*, and making a verb that is already transitive to an object transitive to a second object with *bi-* rarely occurs, to the point that some claimed it does not occur at all. It is not permitted to say, for example: *ta'ima Zayd al-lahm* ("Zayd ate the meat") becomes *at'amtu Zaydan bi-al-lahm* ("I fed Zayd with the meat"). Rather, the correct view is that it came rarely: you say *dafa'a Zayd Amran* ("Zayd repelled Amr"), then you make it transitive with *bi-* saying *dafa'tu Zaydan bi-Amrin*, meaning: I made Zayd repel Amr. Likewise, *sakka al-hajaru al-hajara* ("the stone struck the stone"), then you say *sakakttu al-hajara bi-al-hajari*, meaning: I made it strike it. As for his statement that the first object is an omitted adverbial phrase acting as its substitute, this is not sound, because the object is an explicit direct object, and an adverbial phrase does not substitute for it. His speech implies *tadmin* even though he does not state it explicitly. Do you not see his words: "because when he followed up with it upon his trace, he followed up with it him"? Al-Zamakhshari's statement "*faqad qaffa bihi iyyahu*" separates the pronoun, whereas it should be attached, and it is not a place for separation. If you say *Zayd darabtu bi-sawtin iyyahu*, it is not permitted except in poetic necessity; its correction is *Zayd darabtuhu bi-sawtin*.

*Musaddiqan* ("confirming") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) from Jesus. The meaning of *li-ma bayna yadayhi* ("of what was before him") is *li-ma taqaddamahu min al-Tawrah* ("of what preceded him from the Torah"), because it came before him, just as the Messenger is "between the hands" of the Hour. This discussion has already been covered. His confirmation of it consists in his affirming that it is a Book sent down from Allah in truth, whose action is obligatory before the arrival of abrogation (*naskh*), since his law differs from some of what is in it.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 46:**

﴿And We gave him the Gospel, in which there was guidance and light﴾. This clause is joined (ma'tuf) to his saying: "wa-qaffaynā" (and We caused to follow). In it is the exaltation of ʿĪsā (ʿalayhi al-salām), in that God gave him a divine Book. The reading of al-Ḥasan was mentioned earlier: "al-Injīl" with a fatḥa on the hamza, and what they mentioned about its derivation, if it is Arabic. His saying "fīhi hudan wa-nūr" is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause). The nominative of "hudan" is as the agent (fā'il) of the prepositional phrase (al-jārr wa-al-majrūr), since it depends on the preposition by having occurred as a ḥāl for a determined noun, meaning: "being, in it, guidance." Therefore he conjoined to it: ﴿and confirming what was before it of the Torah﴾. The pronoun in "yadayhi" refers to the Gospel. The meaning is that ʿĪsā and his Book which was sent down to him are both confirmers of what preceded them of the Torah. Thus the divine Book that was sent down and the prophet to whom that Book was sent down combined in confirming it. The meaning of its containing guidance is that it includes proofs of monotheism (tawḥīd), and the declaration of God's transcendence above having a son, a consort, a like, or an opposite, and guidance and calling to God the Exalted, and to reviving the rulings of the Torah. The "light" is what in it is illuminated by, since in it is the explanation of the rulings of the Sharīʿa and their details.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "Muṣaddiqan" is an emphatic ḥāl, conjoined to the position of the clause which is "fīhi hudan," for it is a clause in the position of a ḥāl. End of quotation.

He said that "muṣaddiqan" is an emphatic ḥāl in terms of meaning, because it follows from the Gospel being a divine Book that it confirms the divine Books. However, his saying that it is conjoined to the clause "fīhi hudan," being a clause in the position of a ḥāl, is a weaker opinion. For we have already explained that his saying "fīhi hudan wa-nūr" belongs to the category of the single word (mufrad), not to the category of the clause, since we estimated it as "being in it guidance and light." When it is a matter of choosing between the ḥāl being a single word or a clause, estimating it as a single word is better. If it were estimated as a clause, that would be rare, since it would be a nominal clause without the conjunction "wa," although the pronoun, which is the connecting element (rābiṭ), would suffice. Yet the more established and more common usage is to include the "wa," to the extent that al-Farrāʾ claimed that the absence of "wa" is anomalous even when there is a pronoun, and al-Zamakhsharī followed him in this.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: "Muṣaddiqan" is conjoined to the first "muṣaddiqan." End of quotation. In that case it would be a ḥāl from ʿĪsā, repeated for the sake of emphasis. This has distance in terms of the structure and the coherence of the meanings, and it is strained to make "wa-ātaynāhu al-Injīl" a circumstantial clause conjoined to "muṣaddiqan."

* *

﴿and guidance and admonition for the God-fearing﴾. al-Ḍaḥḥāk read "wa-hudan wa-mawʿiẓatun" with the nominative (rafʿ), meaning "and it is guidance and admonition." The majority read it with the accusative (naṣb) as a ḥāl conjoined to his saying "muṣaddiqan." He made it first "fīhi hudan wa-nūr," and he made it second "hudan wa-mawʿiẓatan." So it is in itself guidance, and it includes guidance. He made it guidance as an intensification of its description, since the Book of the Gospel gives good news of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the indication from it of his prophethood is clear. Since the strongest points of dispute between the Muslims, the Jews and the Christians were on this, God repeated the mention of guidance as a confirmation and clarification of the prophethood of Muḥammad (ﷺ). He described it as admonition, because it includes advice and powerful warnings. He restricted it to the God-fearing, because they are the ones who benefit from it, as the Exalted said: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqara: 2]. They are the ones intended in the knowledge of God the Exalted, although all are called and admonished. But for those other than the God-fearing it is blindness and regret.

al-Zamakhsharī permitted that "hudan wa-mawʿiẓatan" be in the accusative as objects of purpose (maf'ūl lahu) for his saying "wa-l-yaḥkum" (and that they may judge). He said: "It is as if it were said: 'And for guidance and admonition We gave him the Gospel, and for judging by what God sent down in it of the rulings.'" It is fitting that guidance and admonition be attributed in meaning to God, not to the Gospel, so that the object of purpose and the agent of the governing verb share the same subject. For this reason it came in the accusative. Since "wa-l-yaḥkum" has as its agent other than God, it was transitive to it by the preposition of cause (lām al-ʿilla). Also because of the difference of tense: the giving coincided with the guidance and the admonition in time, while the judging differs in that it is future in relation to the giving and past in its occurrence, so it was also transitive by the lām for that reason. What al-Zamakhsharī permitted is contrary to the apparent meaning.

al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you arrange 'hudan wa-mawʿiẓatan' in the thread of 'muṣaddiqan,' then what do you do with his saying 'wa-l-yaḥkum'?" (I say): "I treat it as I treated 'hudan wa-mawʿiẓatan,' when I made them objects of purpose. So I estimate: 'That the People of the Gospel may judge by what God sent down, We gave him the Gospel,' meaning 'We gave it to him.'" End of quotation. And that is a clear answer.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 47:

﴿Let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein.﴾ Allah, exalted is He, commanded the People of the Gospel to judge by the rulings that Allah revealed in it. This command is in the form of a report, and "We said to them: judge" means: at the time it was given to Isa, We commanded them to rule by what is in it, since it cannot be that this applies after the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), because his law abrogates all the laws. Or it means "by what Allah revealed therein" restricted to the proofs that indicate the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is the view of al-Asamm. Or it means restricted to the period until the mission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Or he expressed "judging by what Allah revealed therein" as a metaphor for not distorting or altering it. The meaning then is: let the People of the Gospel recite it in the form in which it was revealed, without changing or altering it. But this is far-fetched. The apparent sense of the command refutes the view of those who said that Isa was bound by the rulings of the Torah. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48]. The proponent of that view could say that "by what Allah revealed therein" refers to the obligation to act by the rulings of the Torah. What appears to be the case is that the legal rulings in the Gospel are few, and most of it consists of admonitions. Those rulings that contradict the rulings of the Torah were commanded to be acted upon, and for this reason it says: ﴿and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 50].

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) recited ﴿wa-liyahkum﴾ with a sukun on the lam of command, and some readers vocalize it with a kasra. Ubayy recited "wa-an liyahkama", with the addition of an before the lam of purpose (li-kay). The statement of al-Zamakhshari regarding this has already been mentioned. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the meaning is "We gave him the Gospel so that it would contain guidance, light and confirmation, and so that the People of the Gospel would judge by what Allah revealed therein." End of quotation. So he coordinated "wa-liyahkama" with an assumed cause, and for this reason he said "so that it would contain guidance." Al-Zamakhshari, however, made it coordinated with "guidance and admonition," on the assumption that the lam was pronounced with both of them, as if he had said: "and for guidance and admonition and for judgment." That is, he made it cut off from what precedes it, and the governing verb was delayed; that is: "and let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah revealed therein, We gave it to him." The statement of al-Zamakhshari is closer to the correct view, because the first "guidance," "light" and "confirmation" were not introduced as a cause. Rather, what was said, "therein is guidance and light," means being in it that and confirming, and this is the sense of a circumstantial state, and a circumstantial state cannot be a cause. Therefore Ibn 'Atiyyah's statement "so that it would contain such and such, and let them judge" is far-fetched.

﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah revealed, they are the defiantly disobedient.﴾ Mentioning "defiant disobedience" is appropriate here, because they went out from the command of Allah, exalted is He, since His words "and let them judge" came before, and that is a command. As Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Prostrate to Adam, and they prostrated, except Iblis; he was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 50]. That is, he went out from obedience to His command, exalted is He. Thus the correspondence has become clear: the first sentence ends with "the disbelievers," the second with "the wrongdoers," and the third with "the defiantly disobedient." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the repetition of these attributes for the one who does not judge by what Allah revealed is for emphasis, and the most correct thing said about them is that they encompass every believer and disbeliever. Thus all of that applies to the disbeliever in its fullest sense, and to the believer in the sense of the disbelief of sin, its wrongdoing and its defiant disobedience. Al-Qaffal said: they are attributes of one described person, as you say: "Whoever obeys Allah is the righteous one, and whoever obeys is the believer, and whoever obeys is the God-fearing one." It was also said: the first is about the one who denies, and the second and third about the one who acknowledges but abandons. Al-Asamm said: the first and second are about the Jews, and the third about the Christians. According to the view of Ibn 'Atiyyah, which encompasses every disbeliever and believer, the application of "the disbelievers," "the wrongdoers," and "the defiantly disobedient" to them is by way of sharing a common measure.

(p. 501)

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 48:**

﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it of the Book and as a guardian over it.﴾ When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that He sent down the Torah, in which there is guidance and light, He did not mention who it was sent down to, because all of them share the fact that it was sent down to Musa (Moses). So He left out his mention, since this was known from that. Then He mentioned ʿIsa (Jesus) and that He gave him the Injil (Gospel), and He mentioned him so that they would acknowledge that he is among the Prophets, since the Jews deny his prophethood, and when they deny him they deny his Book. So Allah explicitly named him and his Book. Then He mentioned the sending down of the Qur'an to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and He mentioned the Book and the One who sent it down, establishing his prophethood and his Book, because both groups deny his prophethood and his Book.

Here the mention of the one to whom it was sent down comes with the second-person address (kaf al-khitab), because it is more explicit regarding the intended meaning. Often this comes with the wording of direct address, because it does not cause any confusion at all.

(بِالحَقِّ): meaning accompanied by the truth and attached to it, never separated from it, since it contains the realities of matters, so it is as if it was sent down with them. It is possible that it is connected to "We sent down": that is, We sent it down in such a way that this is true, not that it was obligatory upon Allah, but it is true in itself.

The alif and lam in (al-Kitab) are for a specific known reference (lil-ʿahd), and it is the Qur'an without any disagreement. (مُصَدِّقًا) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) relative to (لِما بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ), meaning: confirming what came before it of the Book. The alif and lam in (al-Kitab) in that phrase are for the genus (lil-jins), because He intended by it the genus of the revealed books. It is also possible that they are for a specific reference, because He did not intend by it whatever is covered by the name "Book" in an unrestricted sense, but rather a specific known type of it, namely what was sent down from heaven other than the Qur'an. The difference between the two is that in the first case it requires supplying a qualifier, which has been omitted, and the intended meaning is: "of the divine Book." In the second case this supplying is not needed, because the definite reference in the noun includes, through the noun itself, all the attributes that belong to the noun, so there is no need to supply an omission.

(ومُهَيْمِنًا عَلَيْهِ): meaning trustworthy over it (أمِينًا عَلَيْهِ). Ibn ʿAbbas said this in the narration of al-Taymi, and Ibn Jubayr, Ikrima, ʿAta, al-Dahhak, and al-Hasan (said it too). Ibn Jurayj said: The Qur'an is a trustworthy guardian over the books before it, so whatever the People of the Book report about their Book, if it is in the Qur'an then confirm it, and if not, then deny it. Ibn ʿAbbas said in the narration of Abu Salih: "witness" (شاهِدًا). Al-Hasan also said this, and Qatada, al-Suddi, and Muqatil. Ibn Zayd said: confirming what it reports of the books. This is close to the first opinion. Al-Khalil said: al-Muhaymin is the watchful, protective guardian. From this is the saying of the poet:

*Indeed the Book is a guardian over our Prophet, and the truth is known to those of understanding.*

al-Zajjaj also reported this, and al-Zamakhshari explained it accordingly, saying: "Muhaymin (guardian) means a watchful overseer over all the other books, because it bears witness to their soundness and clarity." End of quote. The poet also said:

*A King over the throne of heaven, the Guardian; before His might the faces bow and prostrate.*

This was interpreted as "the Protector," and this is about the attributes of Allah. As for the Qur'an, its meaning is that it is a protector of the religion and the rulings. al-Dahhak also said its meaning is "judge," and Ikrima also said its meaning is "indicator." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: He mentioned several opinions that it means witness, that it means entrusted, that it means confirming, that it means trustworthy, and that it means watchful. He said: The word al-muhaymin is more specific than these expressions, because the one who is muhaymin over a thing is the one entrusted with its affair, the witness to its realities, and the protector of its bearer, so it does not admit into itself what is not part of it. Allah made the Qur'an a muhaymin over the books: it bears witness to the realities contained in them and to what the distorters have attributed to them. So it confirms the realities and nullifies the distortion.

Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin read (ومُهَيْمَنًا) with a fatha on the second mim, making it a passive participle (ism maful): meaning entrusted with it, i.e., preserved from alteration and change. The omitted agent is Allah or the protector in each land. If a letter, a vowel, or a sukun were removed from it, the one who knows would notice and reject it and refuse it. So in the reading of the active participle, the pronoun in (ʿalayhi) refers to the second Book, and in the reading of the passive participle it refers to the first Book. In both readings, it (muhaymanan) is a circumstantial state (hal) of the first Book, because it is conjoined to (مُصَدِّقًا), and what is conjoined to a hal is also a hal.

Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid his reading with the fatha, and said: its meaning is that Muhammad is entrusted with the Qur'an. al-Tabari said: On this view (muhaymanan) would be a hal from the kaf in (ilayka). This view was criticized because of the presence of the conjunction waw in (ومُهَيْمِنًا), since it is conjoined to (مُصَدِّقًا), and (مُصَدِّقًا) is a hal of the Book, not a hal of the kaf. For if it were a hal of the kaf, the construction would be (لِما بَيْنَ يَدَيْكَ) with the kaf of address. Interpreting it as an iltifat (shift from address to third person) is far from the arrangement of the Qur'an, and its supposed underlying meaning, "and We made you, O Muhammad, a guardian over it," is even further. Tha'lab rejected the view of al-Mubarrad and Ibn Qutayba that its original form is (mu'tamanun) (entrusted).

(فاحْكم بَيْنَهم بِما أنْزَلَ اللَّهُ) The apparent meaning is that he was commanded to judge by what Allah sent down. The statement of the one who said it abrogates His saying (أوْ أعْرِضْ عَنْهُمْ) [al-Ma'ida: 42] has already been mentioned, as has the view of the majority: "If you choose to judge between them by what Allah sent down." This is according to the view that the pronoun in (بينهم) refers to the Jews, and according to the view of the majority it would be a command of recommendation (amr nadb). If the pronoun refers to the litigants in general, then the address is for obligation, and there is no naskh (abrogation).

(ولا تَتَّبِعْ أهْواءَهُمْ) meaning: do not agree with them in their corrupt aims, such as distinguishing in retaliation between the noble and the lowly, and other such desires of theirs which are contrary to religion and the Law.

(عَمّا جاءَكَ مِنَ الحَقِّ) which is the Qur'an. The verb (تتبع) is taken to imply the meaning of (تنحرف) (deviate) or (تنصرف) (turn away), and therefore it takes (عن). That is: do not deviate or turn aside from what has come to you, following their desires, or because of their desires. Abu al-Baqa said: (عمّا جاءَكَ) is in the position of a circumstantial phrase, meaning "turning away from what has come to you." He did not take (تتبع) to imply the meaning of what takes (عن), and this is not good, because (عن) is a defective particle that cannot be a hal, just as it cannot be a predicate. When it is defective, it takes a restricted verb (kawn muqayyad), not an unrestricted one, and a restricted verb cannot be omitted.

(لِكُلٍّ جَعَلْنا مِنكم شِرْعَةً ومِنهاجًا) The apparent meaning is that the omitted noun governed by (كُلٍّ) is "a nation" (أُمَّةٌ), i.e., for every nation. The address in (مِنكم) is to humankind, meaning: O people. For the Jews there is a law and a path, and for the Christians likewise; this was said by ʿAli, Qatada, and the majority, and they mean in rulings. As for belief (al-muʿtaqad), it is one for the whole world: monotheism, faith in the Messengers and their Books, and what they contain regarding the Return and the otherworldly recompense. Allah mentioned a group of Prophets whose laws were different, then said: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-Anʿam: 90]. The meaning there is in beliefs.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is possible that the intended meaning is the Prophets, especially since their mention and the mention of what was sent down to them has already occurred. With this possibility, the verse is an admonition to Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: safeguard your law and your path, lest the Jews and others cause you to slip in any part of it. End of quote. So the omitted noun governed by (كُلٍّ) would be "every Prophet": that is, for every Prophet among you, O Prophets.

(الشِّرْعَةُ والمِنهاجُ) are two words with one meaning, that is: a way. The second is repeated for emphasis, as the poet said:

*And Hind — between her and us there came remoteness and distance.*

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and others said: a path and a sunna (way of life). Mujahid said: The shirʿa and the minhaj are the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ). Then the meaning would be: for every one of you, O people, We have made this pure religion, so follow it. The intended meaning is: We commanded you to follow the religion of Muhammad, since it abrogates all the religions. al-Mubarrad said: the shirʿa is the beginning of the way, and the minhaj is the way that continues. Ibn al-Anbari said: the shirʿa is the way which may be clear or unclear, while the minhaj is never anything but clear. It was also said: the shirʿa is the religion, and the minhaj is the indicator. It was also said: the shirʿa is the Prophet, and the minhaj is the Book. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: minhaj is an intensive form (bina' mubalagha) from al-nahj (the clear way). It is possible that by shirʿa is meant the rulings, and by minhaj the belief, i.e., it is one in all of you. But this possibility is far-fetched. End of quote.

It was said: In this there is evidence that we are not required to follow the laws of those before us.

al-Nakhaʿi and Ibn Wathhab read (شَرْعَةً) with a fatha on the shin. The apparent view is that (جَعَلْنا) means "made" (صَيَّرْنا), its second object is (لِكُلٍّ), and (مِنكم) is connected to an omitted verb whose sense is: "I mean, from among you." Abu al-Baqa said: It is not permissible for (مِنكم) to be an adjective of (كُلٍّ), because that would require separating the adjective from the noun it modifies with a foreign element that does not add emphasis to the sentence, and it would also require separating (جَعَلْنا) from its object (شِرْعَةٌ). End of quote. The construction would then be like your saying: "From every one I struck a Tamimi man," and that is not permissible.

(ولَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَعَلَكم أُمَّةً واحِدَةً) meaning: If Allah had willed to make you one nation, He would have made you one nation, i.e., a single congregation agreed upon one law, in error. It was also said: He would have made you one nation upon the truth.

(ولَكِنْ لِيَبْلُوَكم فِيما آتاكُمْ) meaning: But He did not will that, so that He might test you regarding what He gave you of the Books. al-Zamakhshari said: "Of the different laws; whether you act upon them, submitting and believing that they are benefits that vary according to circumstances and times, acknowledging that Allah, exalted is He, did not intend by their difference anything but what wisdom required; or whether you follow doubts and neglect action." End of quote. Ibn Jurayj and others said: But He did not will it, because He intended to test them and try them regarding the Books and laws He gave them, so they have nothing to do but strive in carrying out the commands.

(فاسْتَبِقُوا الخَيْراتِ) meaning: hasten to righteous deeds; this was said by Muqatil. They are the ones whose outcome is the best of things. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak said: the good deeds (الخَيْراتُ) are faith in the Messenger.

(إلى اللَّهِ مَرْجِعُكم جَمِيعًا) This is a resumptive clause (istinaf) with the sense of causation for His command to race toward good deeds, as if He is saying: it manifests the fruit of racing toward good deeds and hastening to them at the time of return to Allah, exalted is He, and His recompense.

(فَيُنَبِّئُكم بِما كُنْتُمْ فِيهِ تَخْتَلِفُونَ) meaning: so He will inform you of your deeds, and this is a metonymy (kinayah) for recompense with reward and punishment, and it is an informing of effecting (khabar iqa'). Ibn Jarir said: He has already made that clear in this world through proofs and evidences, and tomorrow He will make it clear through recompense. End of quote. By this admonition the difference becomes evident between the one who is right and the one who is wrong, and between the one who races ahead and the one who falls short in action.

(نَبَّأ) here came in its original form, transitive to one object by itself and to another by a preposition, and it was not made to imply the meaning of (أعْلَمَ) so as to take three objects.

And judge between them by what Allah has sent down. ﴿وأنِ احْكم بَيْنَهم بِما أنْزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: Some Jews said to others among them, Ibn Suriya, Shas ibn Qays, and Kaʿb ibn Usayd: "Come, let us go to Muhammad, perhaps we can seduce him away from his religion." So they came to him and said: "O Muhammad, you know that we are the rabbis and the nobles of the Jews, and if we follow you, all the Jews will follow you. Between us and a people there is a dispute, and we will bring it before you to judge, and you will decide in our favour against them, and we will believe in you." But the Messenger (ﷺ) refused that, (p-504) and so it was revealed. Muqatil said: A group of the Banu al-Nadir said to him: "Will you judge for us against our opponents, the Banu Qurayza, in the matter of blood-money, as we were accustomed to before, and we will pledge allegiance to you?" So it was revealed. Qadi Abu Yaʿla said: This verse is not a repetition of what preceded it; rather, it was revealed concerning two different matters: one of them is the matter of stoning, and the other is equal treatment. End of quotation. This verse is, according to some, abrogating (nasikha, from naskh, abrogation) the option (takhyir) expressed in His words: ﴿أوْ أعْرِضْ عَنْهُمْ﴾ "or turn away from them" [al-Ma'ida: 42], and this has already been mentioned. They permitted in ﴿وأنِ احْكم﴾ that it be in a position of nasb (accusative), in conjunction (ʿatf) with al-Kitab, meaning "and the judgment"; and in a position of jarr (genitive), in conjunction with bil-haqq; and in a position of raf (nominative), as an inchoative (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted and placed later, the sense being "and your judgment is by what Allah has sent down"; or placed earlier, the sense being "and it is obligatory that you judge by what Allah has sent down." It has been said that anna (أنْ) is explanatory (tafsiriyya), but this was deemed unlikely because of the waw (و), and it cannot be correct by supposing before the imperative verb an omitted verb carrying the sense of saying, i.e., "and We commanded you that you judge," because that would require omitting a clause explained by anna and what follows it, and that is not preserved in the speech of the Arabs. It was read with a damma on the nun in ﴿وأنِ احْكم﴾ by assimilation to the vowel of the kaf, and with a kasra on it according to the basic rule for meeting two sukun. The pronoun in ﴿بَيْنَهم﴾ refers to the Jews. It has been said that it refers to all the litigants.

﴿ولا تَتَّبِعْ أهْواءَهُمْ﴾ And do not follow their desires. The explanation of this clause has already been given.

﴿واحْذَرْهم أنْ يَفْتِنُوكَ عَنْ بَعْضِ ما أنْزَلَ اللَّهُ إلَيْكَ﴾ And beware of them, lest they seduce you away from some of what Allah has sent down to you. That is, lest they cause you to slip. He warned him against this, although he was hopeless of their seducing him, because they had given up their hopes; and He said "some of," because what they asked of him was a particular matter: they asked him to decide in their favour against their opponents in it, and he refused. The clause ﴿أنْ يَفْتِنُوكَ﴾ is in the accusative position as a substitute (badal), and it may also be an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi).

﴿فَإنْ تَوَلَّوْا فاعْلَمْ أنَّما يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ أنْ يُصِيبَهم بِبَعْضِ ذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾ Then if they turn away, know that Allah only intends to afflict them for some of their sins. That is: if they turn away from judgment by what Allah has sent down and desire other than it. The meaning of "to afflict them for some of their sins" is that He will punish them for some of their sins. Here He left "some" indefinite, and He means by it, Allah knows best, the turning away from the judgment of Allah and the desire for its opposite; so He placed "for some of their sins" in place of that, and intended that they are people of many great sins, not a counted number. This sin, despite its magnitude, and this indefiniteness, contains an exaltation of the act of turning away and of the excess of their transgression in committing it. Its parallel is the verse of Labid:

Or the soul is bound to its death (lit. "its death binds some souls")

He meant himself, and intended by this indefiniteness the magnification of its importance, as if he said: a great soul, or a soul of what a soul! This promise of calamity was fulfilled for him by the Exalted through the story of the Banu Qaynuqa', the story of Qurayza and al-Nadir, and the expulsion by ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, of the people of Khaybar, Fadak, and others. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: He specified their affliction as "for some of the sins" because this threat is only in this world; and their sins in this world are of two kinds: one kind that concerns them specifically, such as drinking wine, their fornication, and their bribery; and another kind that extends to the Prophet and the believers, such as their collusion with the disbelievers and their statements about the religion. This second kind is what Allah threatened them with in this world, while they are punished for all sins in the Hereafter. Ibn ʿAtiyya also said: The phrase "then if they turn away" has before it an omitted element of speech that the apparent text indicates, its sense being: "do not follow, and beware; then if they make you judge while remaining upright, that is good; and if they turn away, know." It would be good to suppose this omitted element as the counterpart to His words ﴿لَفاسِقُونَ﴾ "are indeed defiant." End of quotation. But this supposition is not needed.

﴿وإنَّ كَثِيرًا مِنَ النّاسِ لَفاسِقُونَ﴾ And indeed many of the people are defiant. That is: rebellious, going to extremes in leaving obedience to Allah. Ibn ʿAbbas said: What is meant by "defiance" here is disbelief (kufr). Muqatil said: sins (maʿasi). Ibn Zayd said: lying. The apparent sense of "the people" is generality, even though the context concerns the Jews, and it came in general wording to alert others besides them. It is possible that "the people" is for a specific reference (lil-ʿahd), namely the Jews mentioned earlier.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 50:

﴿Do they then desire the judgement of the Jahiliyyah?﴾ This is an interrogative whose meaning is disapproval of the Jews, since they are People of the Book and possess the lawful and the unlawful from Allah, the Exalted. Yet, despite this, they turn away from the judgement of Allah and choose over it the judgement of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance), which is based purely on desire, in consideration of what is most noble among them and in preferring the excellent over the inferior in worldly matters. In this there is the severest reproach of them, since they abandoned the divine judgement for a judgement based on desire and ignorance. Al-Hasan said: "It is general for everyone who seeks other than the judgement of Allah." (p-505)

Judgement is of two kinds: a judgement based on knowledge, which is the judgement of Allah, and a judgement based on ignorance, which is the judgement of Satan. He was asked about a man who favours some of his children over others, and he recited this verse.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿أفَحُكْمَ﴾ with a fatha on the mim, making it the object of yabghun (they desire). Al-Sulami, Ibn Wabbab, Abu Raja' and al-A'raj read "Afahukmu al-jahiliyyah" with a damma on the mim, making it the subject (mubtada'). The apparent reading is that the predicate (khabar) is his saying "yabghun" (they desire). The omission of the returning pronoun in this reading is made slightly more acceptable by the fact that the clause serves as a fasila (verse-ending). Ibn Mujahid said: "This is an error." Ibn Jinni said: "It is not so; other instances stronger than it have been found, and it has occurred in poetry." End of quote.

On this matter there is a difference among the grammarians. Some permit omitting this pronoun in speech, some restrict it to poetry, and some make a distinction. These positions and their evidences are mentioned in the science of grammar. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The omission of the returning pronoun from it is like its omission from the relative clause in: 'Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?' and from the qualifier in: 'The people are two men: a man you insulted and a man you honoured,' and from the circumstantial clause (hal) in: 'I passed by Hind, she beating Zayd.'" End of quote. If making the omission in it equal to the omission in these in permissibility and goodness, then it is not as he stated according to the Basrans. Rather, its omission from the relative clause under the conditions of omission is eloquent, its omission from the qualifier is rare, and its omission from the predicate is restricted to poetry or is rare. If the resemblance is in terms of omission in general, then it is correct.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The reading is only sound if the estimated meaning is: 'The judgement of the Jahiliyyah is a judgement you desire,' so yabghun is not made the predicate but is made a qualifier of an omitted predicate. Its parallel is: 'from those who distort (min alladhina yuharrifun),' estimated as: 'a people who distort.'" End of quote. This is a possible interpretation.

Qatada and al-A'mash read "Afahakama" with a fatha on the ha, the kaf and the mim, and this is a collective noun not intended to refer to one individual, as if it were said: "Ahukkama al-jahiliyyah" (the judges of the Jahiliyyah). This refers to the soothsayers who used to take al-hulwan, which is the bribe of soothsayers, and would judge in their favour according to it and according to their desires. In their foolishness, they wished that the Seal of the Prophets (ﷺ) would be a judge like those judges.

The majority read "yabghun" with a ya', in accordance with the preceding third-person pattern. Ibn 'Amir read it with a ta', in the second person, and in this there is a direct confrontation of them with disapproval, rebuke and reprimand, which is not present in the third person. This is the wisdom of the shift (iltifat) to address, directed at the Jews of Qurayzah and al-Nadir.

﴿And who is better than Allah in judgement for a people who are certain?﴾ That is: no one is better than Allah in judgement. It has preceded that "judge between them by what Allah has revealed," so this verse came pointing to this meaning. The meaning is that the judgement of Allah is the ultimate in goodness and in justice. This is an interrogative whose meaning is affirmation (taqrir), and it implies some measure of rebuke against them. The lam in "li-qawmin yuqinun" (for a people who are certain) is for clarification (lil-bayan), so it is connected to an omitted element, meaning: in "hayta laka" and "suqyan laka" (the lam is for clarification); that is, this address and this interrogative are for a people who are certain. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The suitability of the lam's entry in 'li-qawmin' from the perspective of meaning makes this clear to you, and 'for a people who are certain' becomes apparent." It has been said that the lam means "'inda" (with/at), that is: "with a people who are certain," and this is weak. It has been said that it is connected to the word "hukman" (judgement), meaning: that the judgement of Allah is for the believer over the disbeliever. The complement of "yuqinun" is omitted, and its estimate is: "they are certain of Allah," as said by Ibn 'Abbas. It has been said: "they are certain of Allah, the Exalted," as said by Muqatil. Al-Zajjaj said: "yuqinun means they affirm the covenant of Allah, the Exalted, in His judgement." They were specifically mentioned because of their quickness in submitting to the judgement of Allah, and because they are the ones who know that there is no judge more just than Him and none better in judgement.

(p. 506) ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies. They are allies of one another. Whoever among you allies with them is one of them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them, saying: "We fear that a misfortune may befall us." But perhaps Allah will bring victory or a decision from Him, and they will become regretful for what they concealed within themselves.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 52] ﴿And those who believe will say: "Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most solemn oaths that they were with you?" Their deeds have become void, and they have become losers.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 53] ﴿O you who believe, whoever of you apostatizes from his religion, Allah will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty toward the disbelievers, striving in the way of Allah, and not fearing the blame of any blamer. That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 54] ﴿Your ally is only Allah and His Messenger and those who believe, those who establish prayer, give zakat, and bow down in prayer.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 55] ﴿And whoever takes Allah and His Messenger and those who believe as allies, then indeed the party of Allah, they are the victorious.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 56] ﴿O you who believe, do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as mockery and play, from among those who were given the Scripture before you, nor the disbelievers. And fear Allah, if you are believers.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 57] ﴿And when you call to prayer, they take it as mockery and play. That is because they are a people who do not reason.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 58] ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, do you resent us only because we believed in Allah, and in what was revealed to us and what was revealed before, and because most of you are defiantly disobedient?"﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 59] ﴿Say: "Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah has cursed and with whom He was angry, and of whom He made apes and swine, and who worshipped the false deity. Those are worse in position and further astray from the right way."﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 60] ﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe," but they entered with disbelief and they left with it. And Allah knows best what they were concealing.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 61] ﴿And you see many of them hastening toward sin and transgression and consuming unlawful gain. Evil is what they have been doing.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 62] ﴿Why do the rabbis and scholars not forbid them from their saying of sin and their consuming of unlawful gain? Evil is what they have been producing.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 63] ﴿And the Jews say, "The hand of Allah is chained." Their hands are chained, and they are cursed for what they said. Rather, His hands are both extended; He spends however He wills. And what has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in defiance and disbelief. And We have cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection. Every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it, and they strive upon the earth in corruption, and Allah does not love the corrupters.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 64] ﴿And if the People of the Scripture had believed and been righteous, We would have removed from them their misdeeds and admitted them into Gardens of Bliss.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 65] ﴿And if they had established the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet. Among them is a moderate community, but many of them—evil is what they do.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 66] ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord. And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message. And Allah will protect you from the people. Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 67] ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, you are not upon anything until you establish the Torah and the Gospel and what has been revealed to you from your Lord." And what has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in defiance and disbelief. So do not grieve over the disbelieving people.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 68] ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians—whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds—no fear will there be for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 69] ﴿We had already taken the covenant of the Children of Israel and sent to them messengers. Every time a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, a group they denied and a group they killed.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 70] ﴿And they thought there would be no trial, so they became blind and deaf. Then Allah turned to them in forgiveness; then many of them became blind and deaf again. And Allah is Seeing of what they do.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 71] ﴿Certainly, those have disbelieved who say, "Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary." And the Messiah said, "O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord. Indeed, whoever associates others with Allah—Allah has forbidden him Paradise, and his refuge is the Fire. And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers."﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 72] ﴿Certainly, those have disbelieved who say, "Allah is the third of three," while there is no god except one God. And if they do not desist from what they say, a painful punishment will surely afflict those among them who disbelieve.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 73] ﴿Will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 74] ﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger; messengers had passed on before him. And his mother was a woman of truth; they both used to eat food. Look how We make the signs clear to them, then look how they are turned away.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 75]

al-Da'ira (الدّائرة): the singular of al-dawa'ir, which means the vicissitudes of time, its turns of fortune, and its calamities. The poet says:

*And he knows that the turning circumstances do turn.*

al-La'ib (اللعب): well known; it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that does not follow the regular pattern, and its verb is la'iba, yal'abu. al-Ifa' (الإطفاء): extinguishing, to put out completely so that no trace remains. al-Ifk (الأفك): with an open hamza, the verbal noun of afakahu, yafikuhu, meaning he turned it around and diverted it. From this comes the verse: ﴿Have you come to us to turn us away from what we worship?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 22], and: (He who is turned away from it is one who has been turned away). Urwa ibn Udhayna said:

*If you were turned away from the best of manliness, then among others who have been turned away.*

Abu Zayd said: al-ma'fuk is al-ma'fun, the one of weak intellect. Abu Ubayda said: a man who is ma'fuk is one who never attains any good. The town was ta'tafikat with its people, meaning it was overturned. al-Mu'tafikat (المؤتفكات) are the cities of the people of Lot, peace be upon him, which Allah overturned. Al-Mu'tafikat also refers to winds that change their directions.

* *

﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies; they are allies of one another.﴾ al-Zuhri and others said: the occasion of its revelation was the story of Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his clinging to the alliance with the Jews, and the disavowal of Ubada ibn al-Samit from their alliance when Badr ended. Ubada's story is long; this is its summary. Ikrima said: its cause was the command of Abu Lubaba ibn Abd al-Mundhir and his gesture to Qurayza that it meant slaughter, when they asked him about his opinion regarding their coming down from the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. al-Suddi said: when the matter of Uhud befell the Muslims, a group became frightened and some of them said to others: "Let us take a covenant from the Jews that they will support us if a calamity from Quraysh or from the rest of the Arabs strikes us." Others said: "Rather, let us join the Christians," and so it was revealed. It was also said: it is general regarding the hypocrites who displayed faith and sided with the Jews and the Christians.

Allah, exalted is He, forbade the believers from allying with the Jews and the Christians, supporting them and seeking their support, and associating with them as the believers associate with one another. The reading of Ubayy and Ibn Abbas was arbaban (lords) in place of awliya' (allies). The phrase "some of them are allies of others" is a conjoined sentence following the prohibition, indicating the reason for the prohibition of alliance, which is their gathering together in disbelief and their supporting one another against the believers. Apparently, the pronoun in "some of them" refers to the Jews and the Christians. It was also said that the meaning, with a deleted element, is: "Some of the Jews are allies of others, and some of the Christians are allies of others, because the Jews are not allies of the Christians, nor are the Christians allies of the Jews." It may be said that He gathered them in the pronoun in a general manner, and the enmity between them indicates the detail, and that some Jews only ally with their own kind, and likewise some Christians. al-Hawfi said: it is a nominal sentence in the place of a qualifier for awliya', and apparently it is a resumptive sentence with no grammatical position (i'rab).

﴿Whoever among you allies with them is one of them.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: "he is one of them" in the ruling of disbelief; that is, whoever allies with them in religion. Others said: whoever allies with them in this world, he is one of them in the Hereafter. It was also said: whoever among you allies with them in the covenant, he is one of them in opposing the command. This is a severe emphasis on dissociation from the people of disbelief, and on abandoning allying with them, and on distancing oneself from Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and whoever shares his characteristics. Entering into alliance with the Jews and the Christians without association is not included, while whoever allies with them through his actions only, without holding their belief and without harming his faith, is one of them in hatred and blame. Whoever allies with them in belief is one of them in disbelief. Ibn Abbas and others used this as evidence for the permissibility of eating the slaughtered animals of the Arab Christians, and he said: whoever enters the religion of a people is one of them. Ibn Sirin was asked about a man who sold his house to a Christian so that he would make it a church, and he recited this verse. In a hadith: "Let not their fires be within sight of each other." Umar said to Abu Musa regarding his Christian scribe: "Do not honor them since Allah has humiliated them, do not trust them since Allah has accused them of treachery, and do not bring them close since Allah has distanced them." Abu Musa said to him: "There is no stability for Basra except through him." Umar said: "The Christian has died, and peace be upon you."

﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ Its apparent meaning is general, while the intended meaning is specific: that is, whoever it has preceded in Allah's knowledge that he will not be guided. Ibn Atiyya said: or it may be intended as restricted to the duration of wrongdoing and the state of committing it, for there is no guidance in wrongdoing, and the wrongdoer, insofar as he is a wrongdoer, is not guided in his wrongdoing. Abu al-Aliya said: the wrongdoer is one who refuses to say: "There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner." Ibn Ishaq said: he meant the hypocrites. It was also said: the wrongdoer is one who places allegiance in other than its proper place. al-Zamakhshari said something similar to this, saying: He means those who wronged themselves by allying with disbelief; Allah withholds His kindness from them and forsakes them out of detestation for them. End. This follows the path of the i'tizal (the Mu'tazili doctrine).

(p-508) The address is to the Messenger, ﷺ. Those "in whose hearts is a disease" are ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and those who followed him among the hypocrites, or some of the believers of the Khazraj who followed out of ignorance and partisanship. This category therefore has a share of the disease of the heart. This is stated by Ibn ʿAṭiyya. The meaning of ﴿they hasten toward them﴾ is: they hasten toward their alliance and desire it. The discussion of "disease" (marad) has already been covered at the beginning of al-Baqara.

Ibrahim ibn Thabit recited ﴿fa-yara﴾ with the yāʾ from below (yaraa, "he sees"), and the subject is a pronoun referring to Allah or to the one who sees. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: It is also possible that ﴿alladhina﴾ is the subject of ﴿tara﴾ (you see); the meaning would then be "that they hasten," and "an" was omitted for brevity. End of quote. This is weak, because omitting "an" in this kind of construction is not a regular, analogical rule.

Qatada and al-Aʿmash recited ﴿yusriʿūna﴾ without alif, from asraʿa (to hasten). If ﴿tara﴾ is from seeing with the eye, then ﴿yusariʿūna﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). If it is from seeing with the heart, then it occupies the position of the second object. ﴿They say: "We fear that a misfortune may befall us"﴾. This is preserved as the words of ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy, and many hypocrites said it with him. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Its meaning is, "We fear that the affair of Muhammad will not be completed, and the matter will turn against us." It was also said: the "misfortune" is drought and famine, and that they would not be given provisions or loans. It was also said: it is a misfortune that would force them to seek the help of the Jews.

﴿So perhaps Allah will bring a conquest or a decision from Him﴾. This is good news for the Messenger and the believers, through His promise, exalted is He, of conquest and victory. Qatada said: By this He means the decree in these events, and al-Fattah (the Judge) is the one who decides. al-Suddi said: He means the conquest of Mecca. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The apparent meaning of "conquest" in this verse is the manifestation of the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, and the elevation of his word, so that they would have no need of the Jews. It was also said: it is the conquest of the lands of the polytheists. It was also said: it is the conquest of the villages of the Jews, meaning Qurayza, al-Nadir, Fadak, and what is similar to them. It was also said: "conquest" means relief, as stated by Ibn Qutayba. It was also said that His words, exalted is He, ﴿or a decision from Him﴾ refer to the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir and the seizure of their property, in which people had no action; rather, Allah cast terror into their hearts, so they surrendered by their own hands without any horse or riding camel being sent against them. They also refer to the killing of Qurayza and the taking of their children captive. This was stated by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil. It was also said: it is their humiliation until they pay the jizya. It was also said: it is abundance and ease, as stated by Ibn Qutayba. al-Zajjaj said: It is the manifestation of the affair of the hypocrites and their waiting for misfortunes. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: It appears that this division is only because the promised conquest is among the things that result from the striving of the Prophet and his companions, their earnest effort and their work. So Allah's promise is either a conquest that requires those deeds, or a decision from Him that destroys the enemies of the Law, which is also a conquest in which no human has any causative role. End of quote.

﴿Then they will become, over what they concealed within themselves, regretful﴾. That is: they will become regretful for what their souls had suggested to them, that the Prophet's affair would not be completed and that power would not belong to them when Allah brings the conquest or a decision from Him. It was also said: it refers to their alliance (with the Jews). Ibn al-Zubayr recited ﴿fa-tuṣbiḥu al-fussāq﴾ ("then the wicked will become"), placing "the wicked" (al-fussaq) in the place of the pronoun. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The word "becoming in the morning" (iṣbāḥ) was singled out for mention because a person thinks at night, so in the morning he sees the state that his thinking has produced. End of quote. Something similar to this has already been mentioned earlier, and we noted that aṣbaḥa can mean ṣāra (to become) without implying that the state occurs in the morning. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' agreed that the words ﴿fa-yuṣbiḥū﴾ (p-509) are conjoined to His words "that He bring," and this is the apparent reading. What permits this conjunction is the particle fa, because it carries the meaning of causation. It becomes like the example: "The fly that flies so Zayd becomes angry." If the conjunction were without fa, it would not be valid, because it would be conjoined to "that He bring" as the predicate of ʿasā, and that predicate is a statement about Allah, exalted is He. A conjoined element of a predicate is itself a predicate, so it would require a resumptive pronoun if it were the kind of clause that needs one, and there is no resumptive pronoun here. Therefore conjunction is not permitted. However, the particle fa is distinctive among all the conjunctive particles in permitting the sufficiency of a single pronoun for two clauses, whether in a relative clause, as in the example given, or in a descriptive clause, as in "I passed by a man who weeps so ʿAmr laughs," or in a predicate, as in "Zayd stands so Bishr sits." It was also permitted that it not be conjoined to "that He bring," but rather that it be in the subjunctive mood by the implied "an" after fa in answer to a wish, since ʿasā is a wish and hope regarding humans. This, however, is open to question.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 53:

﴿Those who believe will say, "Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most solemn oaths that they were with you?"﴾ The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: When Banu al-Nadir were expelled, the hypocrites (al-munafiqun) grieved over their departure. A hypocrite would say to his believing relative, when he saw him being zealous in opposing the Jews: "This is their reward from you! By Allah, how little they filled your belly!" When Banu Qurayza were killed, none of the hypocrites could contain what was in his soul, so they began to say: "Four hundred were reaped in a single night?" When the believers saw what had appeared from the hypocrites, they said: "Are these" — that is, the hypocrites — "the ones who swore by Allah with their most solemn oaths that they were with you?" The meaning is that some of them say to others, marvelling at their state, since they had been emphatic in their oaths to the believers that they were with them, and that they would support them against the Jews. Then, when what befell the Jews befell them, there appeared from the hypocrites what they had been concealing of their allegiance to the Jews and their collusion against the believers.

It is possible that the believers said this to the Jews, and that the address in His words ﴿they are with you﴾ is to the Jews, because the hypocrites had sworn to the Jews of alliance and support, as Almighty Allah said, relating about them: ﴿And if you are fought, we will surely support you﴾ [al-Hashr: 11]. So they said this to the Jews, emboldening them in their allegiance to the hypocrites, and that they would never avail them anything against Allah, and they rejoiced in what Allah had bestowed upon them of sincere faith and of not allying with the Jews.

The two Ibns (Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir) and Nafi' read without the conjunction waw (wa), as if it were the answer to someone asking: "What will the believers say at that time?" So it was said: "Those who believe will say," and likewise it is in the codices of the people of Mecca and Medina. The rest read with waw; Abu 'Amr read the lam with a fatha (naṣb), and the Kufans read it with a damma (raf'). 'Ali ibn Nasr narrated from Abu 'Amr both the raf' and the naṣb, and they said: it is in the codices of Kufa and the people of the East. The waw is conjunctive, joining one clause to another, this being when the lam is in the raf'. With the omission of the waw, connection is still present, since in the second clause there is a reference back to the preceding clause: the ones who "hasten" (yusari'un) and who say "we fear" (nakhsha) and who "will become" (yusbihu) — these are the ones of whom it was said: "Are these the ones who swore..." Sometimes connection is achieved by the pronoun alone, and sometimes it is emphasised by conjoining with waw. The apparent meaning is that this statement is issued by the believers upon seeing the conquest, as we have previously mentioned.

It is said: It is possible that it refers to the time when those in whose hearts is a disease were saying: ﴿We fear that a misfortune may befall us﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 52]. And when their questioning appeared concerning the matter of Banu Qaynuqa' and the questioning of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy concerning them, and the Messenger's (ﷺ) coming down to them, and 'Abd Allah's declaration that the fear of misfortunes was his fear for Medina and those in it among the believers, while every believer knew that he was lying in that, his action thus paved the way for the believers to say that.

As for the reading "wa yaqula" with naṣb (yaqulu in the subjunctive), it is construed on the basis that this statement was not made except at the time of the conquest, and that it is carried on the sense: it is conjoined to "an ya'tiya" (that He may bring), since the meaning of ﴿so perhaps Allah will bring﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 52] is "perhaps Allah will bring." This is what the grammarians call 'atf 'ala al-tawahhum (conjunction on the basis of a notional construction), where the speech is in one mould and is construed in another mould, since it is not correct that the pronoun of the name of Allah or anything of it be conjoined. Abu al-Baqa' permitted this on the assumption of a deleted pronoun, i.e., "wa yaqulu alladhina amanu bihi," meaning "by Him," that is, by Allah. This pronoun thus suffices for the connection. Or it is conjoined to "an ya'tiya" on the basis that "an ya'tiya" is a substitute (badal) for the name of Allah, not a predicate (khabar), so that 'asa at that point is complete (tammah), not incomplete (naqisah), as if you said: "perhaps [it is that] he [Allah] will bring, and [that] they [the believers] will say." Or it is conjoined to ﴿fa-yusbihu﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 52], on the basis that his statement ﴿fa-yusbihu﴾ is in the naṣb by the implied "an," as an answer to 'asa, since there is in it the sense of wishing (tamanni). We have mentioned that there is consideration in this aspect: namely, does 'asa operate in the sense of hope (tarajji) as laytа operates in wishing, or not? Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned this aspect from Abu Ya'la, and Ibn al-Hajib followed him, and Ibn al-Hajib did not mention any other. But 'asa from Allah is binding, so there is no hope in it. Both aspects before it are the derivation of Abu 'Ali. And al-Nahhas derived it on the basis that it is conjoined to his saying ﴿bi-al-fath﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 52], that He should bring a conquest and that they should say. This is not correct, because a separation has been made between them by his saying: "or a command from Him." The proper reading would be that it is a noun-phrase (lughah), since the verbal noun (masdar) resolves into "an" and the verb; the conjoined element is then part of the complement, so they are not separated. This holds if it is granted that al-fath is a verbal noun, which resolves into "an" and the verb. Apparently it is not meant that way; rather it is like your saying: "I am impressed by Zayd's intelligence and his understanding," not meaning that it resolves into "an" and the verb. And on the assumption of that, it is also incorrect, because the meaning is not "so perhaps Allah will bring" in such a way that "the believers say such-and-such." Also, it would entail separation between the two conjoined elements by his saying ﴿fa-yusbihu﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 52], which is extraneous to the two conjoined elements, since the apparent reading is that fa-yusbihu is conjoined to "an ya'tiya." An analogy is your saying: "Hind the wicked — Zayd intended to harm her by beating or imprisoning her, and to make her wake up humiliated," and the saying of his companions: "Is this the wicked one whom you claimed to be chaste?" so that "wa qawl" is conjoined to "bi-darb" (by beating). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "In my view, in the prohibition of the permissibility of 'asa Allah an yaqula al-mu'minun — there is consideration, since those whom He helped say: 'We support Him by displaying His religion,' so this should be permissible." End. What he said goes back to the point that it becomes a cause, because there is in the sentence a pronoun referring back to Allah, namely its implicit meaning: "by His help and the manifestation of His religion." If this is so, there is no disagreement about its permissibility; they only prohibited it where there is no linking element (rabit). The accusative of jahd is as an emphatic verbal noun (masdar muakkad). The meaning: "Are these the ones who swore by Allah, striving in their oaths, that they were with you?" Then it has now become apparent, from their allegiance to the Jews, what has exposed their oaths as false. It is permissible that it be in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), as they permitted in "fa'altahu juhdaka" (I did it with your utmost effort). His saying "innahum la-ma'akum" (that they are indeed with you) is a quotation of the meaning of the oath, not of their exact words, since had it been their words it would have been "inna la-ma'akum" (we are indeed with you).

﴿Their deeds have become void, and they have become losers﴾ Its apparent meaning is that it is among what the believers say, relying in reports on what has taken place in their belief; that is: their deeds have been nullified, if they were undertaking them according to outward appearance. Al-Zamakhshari said: There is in it the sense of wonder, as if it were said: "How He has nullified their deeds, and how they have lost!" It may be that it is a report from Almighty Allah, and it may be that it is not a report but a supplication, either from Almighty Allah or from the believers. The nullification (habt) of deeds here is in the sense of comparison, since in reality they have no deed that would be nullified. Al-Hawfi permitted that "habitat a'maluhum" be a second predicate about "hā'ulā'," the first predicate being "alladhina aqsamu," and that "alladhina" be an attribute of "hā'ulā'," and that "habitat" be the predicate. The reading of Abu Waqid and al-Jarrah "habatat," with a fatha on the ba', has been mentioned earlier, and that it is a dialectal form.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 54:

﴿O you who have believed, whoever among you reverts from his religion - Allah will bring forth a people He loves and who love Him﴾. Ibn Ka'b, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj and others said: it was revealed as an address to the believers in general, up to the Day of Resurrection. "Whoever reverts" is an independent conditional clause, and it is a report of the unseen.

The commentators have dealt here with those who apostatised (ridda), in a lengthy narrative which we shall summarise. We say: in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ), the tribe of Madhhij, led by their chief 'Abhalah ibn Ka'b, known as Dhu'l-Khimar, who was al-Aswad al-'Ansi, reverted. Fayruz killed him in his bed, and the Messenger (ﷺ) informed of his killing and named his killer on the night he was killed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died the following day, and news of his killing reached (Medina) at the end of Rabi' al-Awwal. The Banu Hanifah, led by Musaylimah, reverted; he was killed by Wahshi. The Banu Asad, led by Tulayhah ibn Khuwaylid, reverted; Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated him, and he escaped, then embraced Islam again and his Islam was good. These were three groups that apostatised during the lifetime of the Messenger (ﷺ), and their leaders claimed prophethood.

During the caliphate of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, seven groups apostatised: Fazarah, the people of 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn; Ghatafan, the people of Qurrah ibn Salamah al-Qushayri; Sulaym, the people of al-Fuja'ah ibn 'Abd Yalil; Yarbu', the people of Malik ibn Nuwayrah; and part of Tamim, the people of Sajah bint al-Mundhir, who claimed prophethood and was married by Musaylimah. The poet said:

*Our prophet has become a female, around whom we circle,*
*and the prophets of Allah have become males.*

And Abu al-'Ala' al-Ma'arri said:

*Sajah went to him, and Musaylimah befriended her;*
*a liar among the liars of this world.*

Then Kindah, the people of al-Ash'ath; and Bakr ibn Wa'il in Bahrain, the people of al-Hutam ibn Yazid. Allah sufficed them through the hands of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him.
