And one group apostatised in the time of 'Umar: Ghassan, the people of Jabalah ibn al-Ayham; the slap (of 'Umar) drove him away and he was sent to the land of the Romans after embracing Islam.

As for the people whom Allah will bring: they are Abu Bakr and his companions; or Abu Bakr and 'Umar and their companions; or the people of Abu Musa; or the people of Yemen - two thousand from the sea and five thousand from Kindah and Bajilah, and three thousand from mixed peoples, who fought on the days of al-Qadisiyyah in the days of 'Umar; or the Ansar; or the Muhajirun; or some tribes of Yemen, from Kindah, Bajilah and Ash'ar, who were not (in existence) at the time of the revelation, with whom Abu Bakr fought in the Ridda; or the kinsfolk (of the Prophet); or 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who fought the Kharijites. These are nine opinions.

In al-Mustadrak of Abu 'Abd Allah al-Hakim, with a chain of narration: when it was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pointed to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, and some said: "This one, and this is the most sound of the opinions." They had a great deal of merit in Islam during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and most of 'Umar's conquests were at their hands.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read *man yartadid* with two separate dals (*dalan*), and this is the dialect of the Hijaz. The rest read it with one doubled dal, and this is the dialect of Tamim. The pronoun referring back to the conditional particle in the apodosis is omitted because its meaning is understood; its implied form is: "then Allah will bring forth a people other than them, or in their place." *Wa-yuhibbunahu* is coordinated with his saying *yuhibbuhum*, so it is in the genitive position. Abu'l-Baqa' said: it may also be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the accusative, its implied form being: "and they love Him." He concluded. This is weak, and the like of it is not permissible in the Qur'an.

Allah described these people as those whom He loves and who love Him. Allah's love for them is His granting them success in faith, as He said: ﴿But Allah has made faith beloved to you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 7]; His rewarding them for this and for all other acts of obedience; His honouring them; His praise of them; their love for Him; their obedience to Him; their avoidance of His prohibitions; and their compliance with His commands. He placed His love before theirs because it is more noble and prior. Al-Zamakhshari said: as for what the most ignorant of people and the greatest enemies of knowledge and its people believe, those who are most hostile to the Sharia and worst in conduct - even if their way seems to foolish and ignorant people something - namely the excitable and the affected of the Sufis, and what they profess of love, passion and singing upon their chairs (may Allah ruin them), and in their dances (may Allah render them void), with love poems recited about beardless youths whom they call "martyrs of Allah", and their swoons, which resemble the swoon of Moses at the crumbling of the mountain - exalted is Allah far above that, supremely exalted. And among its words, just as He loves them in His essence, so they love His essence, for the pronoun refers to the Essence and not to the attributes and qualities. Among them is love, whose condition is that the intoxications of love overtake it; if that is not so, it is not love in reality. End of al-Zamakhshari's words, may Allah have mercy on him.

One of the contemporary scholars said: the matter of these excitable groups has grown great among the common people, and much is said about them concerning incarnation (hulul), unity (wahdah), the secrets of the letters, and interpreting the Qur'an in the manner of the Qaramita, the disbelieving Batiniyya. They claim the greatest miracles for the most wicked of sinners, and they harbour enmity towards knowledge and its people. Some of the hadith scholars intended to read hadith to a shaykh in their khawaniq (Sufi lodges), who narrated hadith; but as soon as they read anything of the hadith of the Messenger (ﷺ), the shaykh of shaykhs whom they follow came out, stopped the reading of hadith, expelled the reader and the hadith scholars, and said: "Go back to the madrasas; you have disturbed us." They do not allow anyone to recite the Qur'an aloud, nor to study knowledge. It is well established that one of them, who speaks of the era in their manner, heard people in a mosque reciting the Qur'an. He climbed his chair, upon which he thunders, and said: "O our companions, disturb them for us!" He rose shaking his garment, and his followers rose while he pointed them towards the Qur'an reciters; they beat them most severely, and swords were drawn against them by the followers of that roaring man, while he did not forbid them. He had taught his companions a saying which they had invented and attributed to some righteous people; he had them memorise it so that they recite it by heart like a surah of the Qur'an, yet he did not teach them the obligatory elements of ablution, nor its sunnas, let alone other obligations of Islam. The strange thing is that each of these leaders introduces a new saying which he teaches his companions until it becomes their slogan, and he abandons what is authentically reported from the Messenger (ﷺ) of supplications transmitted by tradition, which are commanded and found in the Book of Allah, despite the feebleness of their speech, its vulgarity, its lack of eloquence, and the paucity of its substance; yet they cling to it as though a revelation from Allah had come to them with it. You will not find the common people more obedient to anyone than to these men: they build for them the khawaniq and the ribats, and they endow for them the awqaf, while these men are the most hostile to knowledge and the scholars, and the most loved by these groups. The ignorant are enemies of the people of knowledge.

﴿humble towards the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾. It is the plural of *dhalil* (humble), not of *dhaluI* (docile), which is the opposite of weakness, because *dhalul* is not pluralised as *adhillah* but as *dhalal*. *Adhillah* is followed by *'ala* although the original construction is with *li*, because it implies the sense of compassion and kindness: as if he said, "inclining towards the believers in a manner of humility and modesty." It was said: or because it is an elided construction, the implied form being "in preference to the believers"; the meaning is that they humble themselves and submit to those over whom they are preferred, despite their nobility and lofty station. This is like His saying: ﴿harsh against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. This attribute came with the nominal form, which carries intensity, because *adhillah* is the plural of *dhalil* and *a'izzah* is the plural of *'aziz*, and both are intensive adjectives. The attribute before this came with the verb, in His saying: ﴿He loves them and they love Him﴾, because the noun denotes stability; since it is an intensive adjective and does not renew itself but is like an innate disposition, the attribute came in the noun form. And since the earlier attribute renews itself, because it refers to acts of obedience and the reward that follows them, it came with the verb which implies renewal. Since the attribute that relates to the believer is more emphatic, and because its subject was placed before the attribute relating to the disbeliever, and also because of the nobility of the believer, and since the attribute between the believer and his Lord is more noble than the attribute between the believer and the believer, His saying "He loves them and they love Him" was placed before His saying "humble towards the believers."

In this verse is evidence against the view of those who held that when an attribute is expressed by a noun and by a verb, the verbal attribute cannot precede the nominal attribute except in poetic necessity, such as the saying:

*And a plait that covers the back, jet-black,*

for here appeared what he claimed occurs only in poetic necessity: in this verse, the verbal "He loves them and they love Him" was placed before the nominal "humble." Likewise His saying: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed﴾ [al-An'am: 92]. *Adhillah* was read anomalously, and it is a noun; likewise *a'izzah* in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from an indefinite noun, which is made nearer to a definite noun by its description. 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud) read *ghulazaa'* ("harsh") against the disbelievers in place of *a'izzah*.

﴿They strive in the way of Allah﴾, that is, in support of His religion. The apparent sense of this clause is that it is a qualifier, and it is permissible for it to be a resumptive statement. Abu'l-Baqa' permitted that it be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *a'izzah*.

﴿and they do not fear the blame of any blamer﴾, that is, they are firm in their religion, not caring about whoever blames them for it. So whenever they undertake a matter of enjoining good or forbidding evil, they carry it through, and no objector's objection or any speaker's words prevent them. These two attributes, namely striving and firmness in religion, are the result of the preceding attributes: for whoever loves Allah fears none but Him, and whoever is mighty against the disbeliever strives to extinguish and uproot him. The placement of striving before the absence of fear of blamers is appropriate because of its proximity to ﴿mighty against the disbelievers﴾, and because fear is greater than striving, so this is an ascent from the lower to the higher. The waw in *wa-la yakhafuna* may be the waw of circumstance, meaning: they strive, and their state in striving is not the state of the hypocrites, for the hypocrites used to be allied with the Jews; when they went out with the army of the believers, they feared their Jewish allies and held back and caused others to hold back, so that no blame should fall upon them from them. As for the believers, they fought for the sake of Allah's face, not fearing the blame of any blamer. *Lawmah* (a single instance of blame) is indefinite in the context of negation, and so it is general: that is, they fear nothing at all of blame.

﴿That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills﴾. The apparent meaning is that "that" refers to the attributes already mentioned with which the believer is adorned. He mentioned that this is a bounty from Allah, which He gives to whom He wills; it is not by any prior merit of the recipient, but is a favour from Him, exalted be He, to whom He wills to show kindness. It was said: "that" refers to Allah's love for them and their love for Him. It was also said: it refers to His saying ﴿humble towards the believers﴾, which means gentleness of disposition and abandoning haughtiness towards a believer. Al-Zamakhshari said: He gives it to whom He wills of those whom He knows to have a hidden kindness (lutf). End of quotation. In this there is the subtle trace of Mu'tazilism (dasisat al-i'tizal). *Yu'tihi* is either a resumptive statement, or a predicate following a predicate, or a circumstantial clause.

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾, that is: abundant in bounty and favour, and knowing of whom to place it upon.

﴿Your only guardian is God, and His Messenger﴾. When He forbade them from taking the Jews and Christians as allies (awliya'), He made clear here who their guardian is: God and His Messenger. The word wali (guardian) is explained here in three ways: as the helper (al-nasir), as the one who takes charge of the matter (al-mutawalli al-amr), or as the one who loves (al-muhibb). The meaning is: you have no guardian except God. He said waliyyukum ("your guardian") in the singular and did not say awliya'ukum ("your guardians"), even though what is predicated is plural, because wali is a generic noun (ism jins). Alternatively, guardianship in its true sense belongs to God, in the sense of being original and independent, and then He included those who are mentioned in the same line, in the sense of being derivative. Had He used the plural, this meaning of primacy and derivation would not have been distinguished. ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) read it as mawlakum Allah ("your master is God"). The apparent meaning of His words ﴿and those who believe﴾ is the generality of all who believed among them, both those who had passed and those who remained, as al-Hasan said. Al-Baqir was asked about who this verse was revealed concerning, and whether it was ʿAli. He said: ʿAli is among the believers. It was also said that ﴿those who believe﴾ refers to ʿAli. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Muqatil also said it, and in that case it would be the use of the plural for the singular in a figurative sense (majaz). It was said (p-514) that it refers to Ibn Salam and his companions. It was said that it refers to ʿUbada, when he disassociated himself from his Jewish allies. It was said that it refers to Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, as ʿIkrimah said.

﴿Those who believe, who establish the prayer, pay the zakat, and bow down (in prayer)﴾. These are attributes by which the sincere believer is distinguished from the hypocrite, because the hypocrite does not persist in the prayer or in the zakat. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when they stand up for the prayer, they stand up lazily﴾ [al-Nisa: 142], and He said: ﴿Grudging towards good﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19]. Since the Companions, at the time this verse was revealed, were among those who established the prayer and paid the zakat, and in both states they were characterized by humility before God, exalted is He, and submission to Him, the verse was revealed with these sublime attributes. The bowing (ruku') here apparently means humility, not the bodily posture that is in the prayer. It was said that the intended meaning is the posture, and it was singled out for mention because it is among the greatest pillars of the prayer, so it was used to refer to the whole prayer. However, this view entails the repetition of the prayer, given His words ﴿they establish the prayer﴾. The repetition can be understood as emphasis, because of the nobility and greatness of the prayer among the Islamic obligations. It was said that by prayer here are meant the obligatory prayers, and by bowing the voluntary (tanafful) prayers. It is said: "So-and-so bows (yarka') when he performs voluntary prayer." It is narrated that ʿAli, may God be pleased with him, gave his ring in charity while he was bowing in prayer. The apparent sense of His words ﴿and they are bowing﴾ is that it is a nominal clause (jumla ismiyya) conjoined to the clauses before it, included in the same thread of the prayer. It was said that the waw is for the state (hal), meaning: they pay the zakat while they are humbled, not occupied with those to whom they give it. That is, they pay it and give charity while they are engaged in the prayer. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the position (mahall) of alladhina yuqimun (those who establish)? I say: it is in the nominative case, either as a substitute (badal) for alladhina amanu, or as the predicate of 'they are those who establish.'" End of quote. I do not know what prevented him from taking it as an attribute (sifa), since that is what comes to mind, because the substituted noun is in the position of being dropped, and it is not valid here to drop alladhina amanu, because it is the attribute upon which the validity of what follows of attributes depends.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 56:

﴿And whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe as allies—indeed, the party of Allah, they are the victorious.﴾ It is possible that the response to "whoever" (man) is omitted, because what follows indicates it; that is, "he is of the party of Allah and will prevail." It is also possible that the response is "indeed, the party of Allah," and that this is the placing of an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun; that is, "indeed, they are the victorious." The benefit of placing the apparent noun here in the position of the pronoun is the attribution to Allah the Exalted, by which they are honoured, and through it they became distinguished. The origin of *hizb* (party) is a people who gather for the matter of their party.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that he means the party of Allah, the Messenger, and the believers, and the meaning would be: whoever takes them as allies has taken the party of Allah and has strengthened himself with one who cannot be overcome." End of quotation. But it is awkward in its construction.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: That is, indeed He is the victor over everyone who opposes Him. The expression came general, that "the party of Allah, they are the victorious," for brevity, because this one who takes allies is of the party of Allah, and the party of Allah is victorious; so this one who has taken Allah and His Messenger as allies is victorious. And "whoever" is intended as a collective (genus), not a singular. "They" here may be a *fasl* (separating pronoun), and it may be a *mubtada'* (subject).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 57:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as a mockery and amusement, from among those who were given the Scripture before you, nor the disbelievers﴾ (p-٥١٥) Ibn Abbas said: Rifa'a ibn Zayd and Suwayd ibn al-Harith had professed Islam and then became hypocrites, and some of the Muslims used to befriend them, so this was revealed. When the Exalted commanded the believers not to take the disbelievers and the Christians as allies, He forbade taking as allies any disbelievers, whether Jews, Christians, or others. He repeated the mention of the Jews and Christians with His saying: ﴿from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾, even though they are included within the general meaning of "the disbelievers," by way of specifying some individuals of the general category, since they had been mentioned earlier in the preceding verses, and because their mockery is more extreme and their submission to Islam more remote, as they claim to follow a divine law. For this reason, the believers among the polytheists are very numerous, while the believers among the Jews and Christians are very few. It has also been said that by "the disbelievers" only the polytheists are meant, and this is supported by the recitation of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): "and from among those who associated partners." Ibn Atiyya said: The verse distinguishes between "the disbelievers" and "those who were given the Scripture," since the term "disbelief" (kufr) generally applies to those who associate partners with God by worshipping idols, as they are furthest in disbelief. He has also said: ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Tawba: 73], and so He distinguished between them for the sake of clarification. All of them are disbelievers, and although they were idol-worshippers, they are disbelievers in every respect. These other groups share with them the definition of disbelief, but differ from them in degrees: the People of the Scripture believe in God and in some of the prophets, while the hypocrites believe only with their tongues. End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari said: He singled out those who mock the People of the Scripture above the polytheists specifically. End of quotation. The meaning of the verse is that whoever takes your religion as a mockery and amusement is not fit to be taken as an ally, but rather is to be opposed, hated, and kept at a distance. As for their mockery, it has been said that it consisted of professing Islam while concealing disbelief. It has also been said that it consisted of their saying to the Muslims: "Guard your religion and persist in it, for it is the truth," and one of them saying to another: "We have played with their minds and laughed at them." Ibn Abbas said: They laughed at the Muslims at the time of their prostration. The discussion of the recitation of the word هُزُؤًا (huzu'an, "mockery") has already been mentioned. The two Basran/Kufan readers (al-Nahwiyyan) read والكُفّارِ ("and the disbelievers") in the genitive case; Ubayy read ومِنَ الكُفّارِ ("and from among the disbelievers") with the addition of مِن (min); and the rest read it in the accusative case. This last reading is the transmission of al-Husayn al-Ju'fi from Abu Amr. The grammatical analysis (i'rab) of the genitive and accusative readings is clear.

﴿And fear God, if you are believers﴾ When the believers were forbidden to take them as allies, they were commanded to fear God, for it is fear of God that moves one to carry out the commands and avoid the prohibitions. That is, fear God regarding allegiance to the disbelievers. Then He drew attention to the attribute that prompts fear of God, which is faith; that is, whoever is truly a believer refuses to ally himself with the enemies of the religion.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 58:

﴿When you call to prayer, they take it as a mockery and a game.﴾ Al-Kalbi said: Whenever the call to prayer (adhan) was made, the Muslims would stand up for it, and the Jews would say: "Stand up, may you not stand! Pray, may you not pray! Bow, may you not bow!" in a manner of mockery and laughter. So this was revealed. Al-Suddi said: A Christian in Medina, whenever he heard the muezzin say, "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," would say: "May the liar be burned." Then a spark flew into his house and he and his family were burned. So this was revealed. It has also been said: The Jews envied the Messenger (ﷺ) when they heard the adhan and said: "You have innovated something that was not [practised] by the prophets. Why do you shout like the shouting of the donkey? How ugly that sound is!" So Allah revealed this verse. And He revealed: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah﴾ [Fussilat: 33], and so on. End of quotation. The meaning is: when some of you call to prayer, because not all of them call. When He had mentioned that they are the ones who took their religion as a mockery and a game, all that the religion encompasses was included in that. Then He singled out from it the greatest of the pillars of religion (p-516) and specified it by name, which is the prayer, the bond between the servant and his Lord. Thus He drew attention to the fact that whoever mocks the prayer should not be taken as an ally and should be driven away. So this verse came as an emphasis on the verse before it. Some scholars said: In this verse there is evidence that the adhan is established by the text of the Book, not by dream alone. End of quotation. There is no evidence in this for its legislation, because He said "when you call" and did not say "call" as a command. Rather, this is a conditional clause which indicates that the legislation had already preceded, not that it was instituted by the condition. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "they took it" refers to the prayer, but it may also refer to the verbal noun understood from "you called," meaning: they took the calling, the mockery, the ridicule and the play, as a taking in a wrong way.

﴿That is because they are a people who do not understand.﴾ That is: that act from them. He negated understanding from them because they did not benefit from it in religion, and they took the religion of Allah as a mockery and a game, the act of one who has no understanding.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 59:**

﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, do you resent us for nothing except that we believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before, and that most of you are defiantly disobedient."﴾ Ibn Abbas said: A group of Jews came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him, "Who is it that you believe in among the messengers?" So he said, "I believe in Allah, and in what has been revealed to us" (Al-Baqarah 2:136), up to his words, "and to Him we are submitting" (Al-Baqarah 2:136). When they heard the mention of Jesus, they said, "We know of no people with less share in this world and the Hereafter than you, nor a religion more evil than your religion." Then this verse was revealed.

The meaning is: "Do you find fault with us, or disapprove of us, and consider it a sin or a defect, that which is neither disapproved of nor faulted, namely believing in all the revealed Books?" This is a subtle and concise rhetorical exchange which alerts the one who resents to the fact that he has resented nothing except what cannot be resented and is not counted as a fault. A parallel to it is the words of the poet:

*"There is no fault in them, except that their swords are notched by the clashing of the battalions."*

It is said that the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the particle *hal* here has the meaning of the negative *mā* (the negating *mā*, which denies rather than asks). The majority of readers recite *tanqimūna* with a kasra on the qāf, while the past tense is *naqama* with a fatha on it, which is the form that Tha'lab mentioned in *al-Faṣīḥ*. *Naqima* (with kasra) in the present *yanqamu* (with fatha) is a dialect form related by al-Kisa'i and others. Abu Haywa, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Abi 'Abla and Abu al-Birr Hushaym recited it with this form. *Tanqimūna* is explained as: you are displeased with, you dislike, you disapprove of, you find fault with; all of these are close in meaning.

*Illā an āmannā* is an exceptive construction in which the subject has been left empty (*mufarragh*), i.e., the exception stands alone without a stated subject. The majority recited *anzala* in the passive? No, they recited it with the active verb (*mabnīyan lil-fā'il*, built on the doer), in both places, and Abu Nahik recited both forms built on the doer as well. Nu'aym ibn Maysara recited *wa-inna akthara-kum fāsiqūn* with a kasra on the hamza, which is clear in meaning: Allah commanded him to say these two clauses to them, and they contain the announcement of the defiant disobedience and rebellion of most of them.

The majority recited *anna* with a fatha on the hamza, and this has been analysed as occupying a position of nominative case, or accusative case, or genitive case. In the nominative, it is in the position of the subject (*mubtada'*). Al-Zamakhshari estimated the predicate as a deleted, postponed predicate, meaning: "And the defiant disobedience of most of you is established and known to you, because you know that we are upon the truth and you are upon falsehood, except that love of leadership and bribery prevents you from acknowledging it." It is not appropriate for the predicate to be placed first unless it is preceded by *ammā* (as for), since the more correct view is that it is not begun with such a construction except after *ammā* alone. In the accusative case, there are several possibilities:

First: that it is conjoined to *an āmannā*, meaning: "You resent from us nothing except our faith and the defiant disobedience of most of you," so that the disobedience enters into what they resent. This is the view of most of the commentators. Its meaning is not coherent, because they do not believe that most of them are defiantly disobedient, so how could they resent it? But it may be understood to mean: "You resent from us nothing except this combined matter, that we are believers and most of you are defiantly disobedient," even though they do not concede that most of them are defiantly disobedient, just as you might say: "You resent nothing in me except that I spoke the truth and you lied," and "You dislike nothing in me except that I am loved by people and you are hated," even if he does not admit that he lied or that he is hated. It is as if it were said: "You resent from us nothing except your opposition, since we entered Islam while you remain outside it."

Second: that it is conjoined to *an āmannā*, but with a deleted noun (*muḍāf maḥdhūf*), its estimation being: "and our belief concerning you that most of you are defiantly disobedient." This meaning is clear, and it would then truly enter into what you resent.

Third: that the *wāw* is the *wāw* of accompaniment (*wāw ma'a*), so it is in the accusative position as an object of accompaniment (*maf'ūl ma'ahu*). The estimation is: "and the defiant disobedience of most of you," meaning: "you resent that together with the defiant disobedience of most of you." The meaning is: it is not fitting that you resent us while the defiant disobedience of most of you exists, just as you say: "You wrong me while I have done good to you."

Fourth: that it is in the accusative position as the object of a verb deleted and implied by the earlier *hal tanqimūna*, its estimation being: "and you do not resent that most of you are defiantly disobedient."

The genitive is on the basis that it is conjoined to his saying *bi-mā unzila ilaynā wa-mā unzila min qablu wa-bi-anna akthara-kum fāsiqūn* (in the sense of: "in what has been revealed to us, and what was revealed before, and in that most of you are defiantly disobedient"). The genitive is also on the basis that it is conjoined to a deleted cause (*'illah maḥdhūfah*). The estimation is: "You resent from us nothing except the faith, because of your lack of fairness and your defiant disobedience." Al-Hasan's explanation supports this: "for your defiant disobedience you resented that against us."

These are seven possibilities for the position of *anna* together with its clause. An eighth possibility appears, and it may be the most preferred: this is that *naqama* originally takes *'alā* (against), as you say: *naqamtu 'alā al-rajul anqimu* (I resented against the man). Then from it is formed the *if'alla* pattern, which then takes *min* (from), and it is given the meaning of striking someone with something disliked.

Allah, the Exalted, says: *"And whoever returns, Allah will take retribution from him, and Allah is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution"* (Al-Ma'idah 5:95). The reason for the implicit meaning here is that whoever finds fault with a person's action dislikes it without doubt, and strikes him with something disliked because of it, if he has the power. Here *fa'ala* is used in the sense of *if'alla*, due to their saying: "and they had seen him." For this reason it takes *min* rather than the preposition with which its original form is construed. So the meaning becomes: "and you do not inflict upon us, or strike us with, what we dislike, except that we believed," meaning: "because we believed." Then *an āmannā* is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl li-ajlihi*), and *wa-inna akthara-kum fāsiqūn* is conjoined to this cause. This, and Allah knows best, is the reason it is construed with *min* rather than *'alā*.

Most of them are singled out for defiant disobedience because among them are those who were guided to Islam, or because their defiant ones, who are the most extreme in leaving obedience, are those who say what they say and do what they do seeking closeness to kings and seeking status and leadership. They are defiantly disobedient in their religion and not upright. A disbeliever may be upright in his religion, but it is known that not all of them were upright in their religion, so the judgment of defiant disobedience was passed on most of them.

[p. 518] The address in this command is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and it includes the address to the People of the Scripture, whom he was commanded to call or address with the words of the Most High: ﴿O People of the Scripture, do you hold anything against us?﴾ This is the apparent meaning. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is also possible that the pronoun of address refers to the believers, meaning: Say, O Muhammad, to the believers: 'Shall I inform you of something worse than the condition of these deviators on the Day of Return to God? They are their forefathers, whom God cursed and with whom He was angry.' The demonstrative 'that' then refers to their condition." End of quotation. On this reading, the word *sharr* (worse) is an elative (*af'al al-tafdil*) that remains in its original sense, which indicates sharing in the attribute together with added excess over the one compared. So the misguidance and evil of those forefathers would be greater than the misguidance of these deviators. If the pronoun is an address to the People of the Scripture, then *sharr* is an elative in its usual sense according to the belief of the People of the Scripture, when they said: "We know of no religion worse than yours." In reality, there is no misguidance in the view of the believers, and they have no share in it with the People of the Scripture. As we have mentioned, this is a reference to the religion of the believers or the condition of the People of the Scripture, and so it requires the omission of a genitive-annexed element (*mudaf*), either before it or after it. Before it one would supply: "worse than the people of this condition," and after it: "the condition of him whom God cursed." Because of [the phrase] "whom God cursed," the demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishara*) in every case, whether feminine, dual, or plural, can be used just as it is for the singular masculine. So it is possible that *dhalikum* is from this usage, and thus it refers to individuals, as if he said: "worse than those [people]." Then there is no need to supply an annexed element either before or after the demonstrative, since "whom God cursed" becomes a specification of individuals by individuals. It is also possible that *dhalikum* refers to a specific entity, used in the sense of a kind, as if he said: "Say: Shall I inform you of something worse, in the category of the People of the Scripture, or in the category of the believer, according to the two suppositions mentioned above?" And "whom God cursed" would also be a specification of a person by a person.

Al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab recited *unbi'ukum* (from *anba'*), and Ibn Buraydah, al-A'raj, Nubayj, and Ibn 'Imran recited *mathwabatan* on the pattern of *ma'wurah*. The majority recited *nabba'* and *mathubatan* on the pattern of *ma'unah*. The explanation of the two readings was given in the verse ﴿Surely a reward from God is better﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:103]. *Mathubatan* is here in the accusative as a specifier (*tamyiz*). The more common and eloquent construction is to place the element compared-against (*mufaddal 'alayhi*) before the specifier, as in His saying: ﴿And who is more truthful in speech than God?﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:87]. Placing the specifier before the element compared is also eloquent, as in His saying: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to God?﴾ [Fussilat 41:33]. This reward is on the Day of Resurrection, in the gathering. If the original lexical sense is considered, then the meaning is "returned," which in that case does not indicate the sense of goodness. If the frequent use of the word for good and benefit is considered, then "reward" has been applied here in place of "punishment," in the manner of their saying: "Their greeting is a painful blow" and ﴿So give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:21]. *Man* (who) is in the nominative position, as if it were said: "Who is he?" and it was answered: "He is whom God cursed." Or it is in the genitive position as a substitute (*badal*) for *bi-sharr* (something worse). They also permitted that it be in the accusative position according to the place of *bi-sharr*, meaning: "I shall inform you of whom God cursed." It is possible that "whom God cursed" refers to the forefathers of the People of the Scripture, as has already been mentioned, or to both the forefathers and the descendants, so that those present are included among them. What eloquence requires is that the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, to draw attention to the attribute through which it became worse in reward, namely the curse and the anger. He also made the apes and the swine from among them, and the servants of the Taghut. It is as if it were said: "Say: Shall I inform you of something worse in reward with God than that? It is you"; that is, he is you. This meaning is supported by His saying afterward: ﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:61], so the pronoun is one.

Ubayy and Abdullah [Ibn Mas'ud] recited: *man ghadiba Allahu 'alayhim, wa-ja'alahum qiradatan wa-khanazir* ("whom God was angry with, and made them apes and swine"), and *ja'ala* here means "made/turned into" (*sayyara*). Al-Farisi said: it means "created," because after it comes *wa-'abada al-taghut*, and he was a Mu'tazilite who did not hold that God makes anyone a worshipper of the Taghut. The discussion of their transformation into apes was previously mentioned in al-Baqarah.

As for those who were transformed into swine, it is said they were the elders of the people of the Sabbath, since their young men had been transformed into apes; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. It is also said they were the companions of the table of 'Isa. A lengthy story has also been mentioned about the transformation of the Children of Israel into swine, the summary of which is: a believing woman among them fought the king of their city and those with him, and they had disbelieved in the one who gathered around her, of those whom she summoned to the jihad three times, and her followers were being killed while she escaped. After the third time she was taken captive and was tested in her religion, so God transformed the people of the city into swine during their night, to strengthen her in her religion. When she saw them, she said: "Today I know that God has made His religion mighty and established it." So the transformation into swine occurred at the hands of this woman. The explanation of *Taghut* has been given before.

The majority of the Seven [Readers] recited *wa-'abada al-taghut* ("and served the Taghut"). Ubayy recited *wa-'abadu al-taghut* ("and they served the Taghut"). Al-Hasan, in one transmission, recited *wa-'abda al-taghut* with a sukun on the *ba'*. Ibn 'Atiyyah explained this as meaning *wa-'abdan* with tanwin, and the tanwin was dropped as it was dropped in His saying: ﴿nor those who remember God much﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:35]. There is no basis for this explanation, because *'abdan* cannot govern *al-taghut* in the accusative, since it is neither a verbal noun nor an active participle. The correct explanation is that it is a lightening (*takhfif*) of *'abada* with a fatha on the *ba'*, like their saying: "in *salaf*, *salf*." Ibn Mas'ud, in one transmission, recited *'abuda* with a damma on the *ba'*, like *shariffa al-rajul* ("the man became noble"); that is, he came to have servants, like a habit or customary matter, as Ibn 'Atiyyah said. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, he became one worshipped besides God, like your saying *umira* when he became a commander. End of quotation. Al-Nakha'i, Ibn al-Qa'qa', al-A'mash in the transmission of Harun, recited *wa-'ubida al-taghut*, in the passive, like *durriba Zayd*. Abdullah, in one transmission, recited *wa-'ubidat al-taghut*, in the passive, like *durribat al-mar'ah*. These are six readings with the past verb, and their grammatical analysis is clear. The apparent view is that this object is conjoined to the relative clause (*silah*) of *man*, which is linked to *la'anahu*, *ghadiba*, *ja'ala*, and *'abada*. Al-Tabari weakened the passive reading, and it is valid only on the omission of the resumptive pronoun; that is, *wa-'ubida al-taghut fihim aw baynahum* ("and the Taghut was worshipped among them or between them"). It is possible that *wa-'abada* is not part of the relative clause, but is under the supposition of *man* (i.e., "and whoever served"). Ubayy and Abdullah recited it with the explicit pronoun: "and whoever served," so it is either conjoined to "the apes and the swine," or conjoined to *man* in His saying: *man la'anahu Allah* ("whom God cursed").

Abu Waqid al-A'rabi recited *wa-'ubbad al-taghut*, the plural of *'abid*, like *darrab Zayd*. Ibn 'Abbas in one transmission, and a group, Mujahid, and Ibn Wathhab recited *wa-'ubud al-taghut*, the plural of *'abd*, like *rahn* and *ruhun*. Tha'lab said: the plural of *'abid*, like *sharif* and *shurf*. Al-Zamakhshari, following al-Akhfash, said: the plural of *'abid*, so this is a plural of a plural. They cited:

"Attribute the slave to his forefathers, black-skinned, from a people of *'ubud*."

Al-A'mash and others recited *wa-'ubud al-taghut*, the plural of *'abid*, like *darib* and *durub*. Some Basran readers recited *wa-'ibad al-taghut*, the plural of *'abid*, like *qa'im* and *qiyam*, or the plural of *'abd*. Sibawayh cited:

"Do you threaten me with your people, O son of Hijl, *usabat* who think themselves *'ibad*?"

The Arabs of al-Hirah, from Iraq, were called *'ibad* because they entered into the obedience of Kisra.

Ibn 'Abbas in one transmission recited *wa-'abid al-taghut* ("and slaves of the Taghut"), the plural of *'abd*, like *kalb* and *kalib*. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr recited *wa-a'bud al-taghut*, the plural of *'abd*, like *fals* and *afluss*. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Abi Ablah recited *wa-'abada al-taghut*, meaning *wa-'abadah*, the plural of *'abid*, like *fajir* and *fajarah*, dropping the *ta'* for the annexation, or a collective noun (*ism jam'*), like *khadim* and *khadam*, and *ghA'ib* and *ghayab*. It was also read *wa-'abadat al-taghut* with the *ta'*, like *fajir* and *fajarah*. These are eight readings with the plural in the accusative, conjoined to "the apes and the swine," annexed to *al-taghut*. It was also read *wa-'abidi* [with a *ya'*]. Ibn 'Abbas in one transmission recited *wa-'abidu*. Awn al-'Uqayli recited *wa-'abidu*, which Abu 'Amr interpreted as *'a'abid*. These two are sound plurals annexed to *al-taghut*: with the *ta'* as conjoined to "the apes and the swine," and with the *waw* as conjoined to "whom God cursed," or to the implied pronoun of them. The reading of Awn may also allow *'abid* as a singular noun of the genus. Abu 'Ubaydah recited *wa-'abida*, on the pattern of *darib*, annexed to the word *al-shaytan* instead of *al-taghut*. Al-Hasan recited *wa-'abda al-taghut*, on the pattern of *kalb*. Abdullah in one transmission recited *wa-'abbada*, on the pattern of *hattama*, which is an intensive form. Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and Hamzah recited *wa-'abid*, on the pattern of *yaqid* and *nadis*. These are four readings with the singular intended as a genus, annexed to *al-taghut*. There is disagreement among scholars about the last of these. Nusayr the grammarian, a student of al-Kisa'i, said: "It is an error by the one who recited it. Let him ask the scholars about it until we know whether it is permissible." Al-Farra' said: "If it is a dialect like *hadhira* and *'ajila*, then it is a valid form; otherwise it is not permissible in recitation." Abu 'Ubayd said: "The meaning of *al-'ubud* among them is *al-a'bad*, meaning the servants of the Taghut, and we have not found that this is authentically attributed to any eloquent Arab, that *'abd* is said as *'abid*; rather it is *'abd* and *a'bud* with an alif." Abu 'Ali said: "There is nothing like it among the patterns of the plural, but it is a singular used to mean abundance, and it is a pattern used for intensification, so it is as if this one went far in the worship of the Taghut." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its meaning is excess in servitude, like their saying: 'a man who is *hadhir* and *fatin*,' meaning exceeding in caution and cleverness." The poet said:

"O sons of Lubayna, your mother is a slave-woman, and your father is *'abid*."

End of quotation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "*'Abid* is an intensive form, like *yaqiz* and *nadis*. It is a singular word intended to mean the genus, and it is patterned like adjectives, because *'abd* is originally an adjective, though it is used as a noun, and this does not remove it from the rule of an adjective. For this reason it was not impossible to form an intensive pattern from it." He cited "O sons of Lubayna..." and said: "al-Tabari and others mentioned it with a damma on the *ba'*." End of quotation. Ibn Malik counted *fu'ul* among the patterns of collective nouns, saying: "Among them is *fu'ul*, like *sumur* and *'ubud*."

Ibn 'Abbas, as transmitted by Ikrimah, recited *wa-'ubud al-taghut* as the plural of *'abid*, like *darib* and *durub*, and made *al-taghut* accusative, intending *'ubudan* with tanwin, and the tanwin was dropped because of the meeting of two unvoweled letters, as in His saying: ﴿nor those who remember God much﴾. So these are twenty-one readings with the reading of Buraydah, which become twenty-two readings.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, how could He make from them servants of the Taghut? I answer: there are two aspects. The first: He abandoned them until they served it. The second: He passed judgment upon them with that and described them with it, like their saying: ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:19]." End of quotation. This is according to the way of the Mu'tazilites. The explanation of *Taghut* has been given before. Al-Hasan recited *al-tawaghit* (the plural). It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, the Muslims used to reproach the Jews, saying: "O brothers of apes and swine!" and they would lower their heads.

This is the second part of the commentary, so I translate it as it stands.

﴿Those are worse in position﴾: the demonstrative refers to those described as cursed and what follows them, and "makanan" (in position) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). If this refers to the Hereafter, then "place" is meant literally, since it is Jahannam. If it refers to this world, then it is a kinaya (allusion) and isti'ara (metaphor) for rank in His saying ﴿those are worse﴾, because it falls under the category of kinaya, as in the expression "so-and-so has long neck-straps" (ṭawīl al-nijād), which is an indication of a thing by mentioning its accessories and attendants. The "outranked" party (al-mafḍūl) is the place of the believers, and there is no evil in their place. Al-Zajjaj said: "worse in position" is according to your claim and your assumption. Al-Naḥḥās said: the best thing said about "worse in position" is that it refers to the Hereafter, compared with your position in this world, because of the evil that will befall you. Ibn 'Abbas said: their place is Saqar, and there is no place worse in evil than it. What appears to be the case is that the outranked party is other than them, from among the disbelievers, because the Jews were brought clear proofs, messengers and miracles in a number that did not come to others, so they were the furthest of people from following the truth and affirming the messengers, and the most deeply immersed in disobedience. They disbelieved in various kinds of disbelief and toward the messengers, with absence following absence (i.e., repeated lapses). So God, exalted is He, informed about them that they are worse than the disbelievers.

[Qur'an 5:60] "And has strayed from the sound way of the path" — that is, from the middle of the path and its right course; that is, they are bewildered and do not find the straight way.

﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe," but they had entered with disbelief and they had left with it.﴾ The pronoun of absence in "jā'ūkum" (they come to you) refers to the Jews and to the contemporaries of the Messenger, especially the hypocrites among them; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and al-Suddi, and it is by omission of a modifier (ḥadhf muḍāf), since the apparent sense of the pronoun is that it returns to what precedes it; the estimate is: "And when they come to you, their people or their women." It has been mentioned from our statement that "those whom Allah has cursed..." to its end is an expression about the addressees in His saying: ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture"﴾ [5:59], and that it is of what the apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun, so it is as if it were said: "You," and so this does not need the omission of a modifier.

A group of the Jews used to enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), showing him faith out of hypocrisy, so Allah the Exalted informed about their affair and that they would leave as they entered, not having clung to anything (p-521) of what they heard of reminder and admonition. Según this, the address in "jā'ūkum" is to the Messenger (ﷺ). It was also said: it is to the believers who were in the presence of the Messenger. These two clauses are circumstantial (ḥāl) clauses, and "bil-kufr" and "bihi" are also circumstantial; that is, "while being entangled." For this reason "qad" entered, to bring it near to the time of the circumstance, and for another meaning, which is: that the signs of hypocrisy were manifest upon them, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was anticipating the disclosure of what they concealed, so the particle of anticipation entered and differed between the two circumstantial clauses for breadth in speech. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: His saying "wa-hum" is a clarification to remove the possibility of the expression that a people might enter with disbelief while they had left with it; so His saying "wa-hum qad kharajū bihi" removed the possibility; that is, they themselves. End.

The operator in the two circumstances is "āmannā"; that is, they said that, and this is their state. It was also said: "hum" is for emphasis in attributing disbelief to them, and it negates that there was from the Messenger anything that would necessitate their disbelief due to bad treatment from him toward them, rather he would be gentle with them and treat them in the best manner. So the meaning is: they are the ones who left with disbelief by their own choice, not that you are the one who caused their remaining in disbelief.

What we say is: the nominal clause occurring as a circumstance, introduced by a pronoun of the circumstance-holder and predicated by a verb or noun that bears the pronoun of the circumstance-holder, is more emphatic than the verbal clause, in that the subject is repeated within it, becoming like the example: "Zayd stood, Zayd." And since when they came to the Messenger or the believers they said "We believe" while being entangled with disbelief, it was fitting for them not to leave with disbelief, because seeing him (ﷺ) is sufficient for faith. Do you not see the saying of one of them when he saw the Messenger: "I knew that his face is not the face of a liar," along with what appears to them of extraordinary signs and dazzling proofs? So it was appropriate that, although they had entered with disbelief, they should not leave with it, but rather leave with the Messenger as believers outwardly and inwardly. So he emphasized their description with disbelief by repeating the subject to alert to their being established in disbelief and their persistence upon it, and that seeing the Messenger did not benefit them, and they were not affected by it. Likewise, if the pronoun of address in "wa-idhā jā'ūkum qālū āmannā" is intended, it was fitting for them to believe outwardly and inwardly, because of what they see of the believers' agreement and their affirmation of the Messenger, and reliance upon Allah the Exalted, and desire for the Hereafter, and asceticism in this world; and this is the state of one whose company is to be agreed with. And when they witnessed them, it was fitting that they follow them in their religion, and that their faith by speech accord with the belief of their hearts.

In the verse is evidence for the permissibility of two circumstances for one circumstance-holder, provided the "wāw" in "wa-hum" is the wāw of circumstance and not the wāw of conjunction, contrary to those who prohibit that except in the superlative form (af'al al-tafḍīl). The apparent meaning is that entering and leaving are literal. It was also said: they are figurative (isti'āra); the meaning: they fluctuated in disbelief; that is, they entered into their states concealing disbelief and left with it to other states concealing it too, and this is the fluctuation. The literal meaning of entering is separation of the body from outside a place into its inside, and of leaving is separation of the body from its inside to its outside.

﴿And Allah knows best what they were concealing﴾ — that is, of their disbelief and hypocrisy. It was also said it is a description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his attribute; in this is an emphasis on disclosing what they concealed of plotting against the Muslims, scheming, and enmity.

﴿And you see many of them hastening toward sin, transgression, and their consuming of what is forbidden. Evil indeed is what they have been doing.﴾

The verb ﴿تَرى﴾ (tará, "you see") may be basariyyah (used in the sense of sight), in which case ﴿يُسارِعُونَ﴾ (yusari'una, "they hasten") is a descriptive clause. It may also be ʿilmiyyah (used in the sense of knowing), in which case ﴿يُسارِعُونَ﴾ is the second object.

Al-Musara'ah (hastening) is starting something quickly. Al-Ithm (sin) is lying. Al-ʿUdwan (transgression) is injustice. The phrase "from their saying the sin" points to this meaning, but the literal meaning of al-ithm is not lying. Al-ithm is what pertains to the one who commits the disobedience, or al-ithm is what is specific to them, while al-ʿudwan is what extends from them to others. Or al-ithm is disbelief, and al-ʿudwan is aggression. Or al-ithm is what they concealed of faith, and al-ʿudwan is what transgresses in regard to it. It has been said that al-ʿudwan is their transgressing the limits of God. There are five opinions.

The majority hold that al-suht (forbidden gain) is bribery (al-rashaa). It has been said that it is usury (al-riba). It has also been said that it is bribery and all their other corrupt earnings.

He attached the seeing to "many of them" because some of them did not engage in all of that or in part of it. The use of al-musara'ah is most common for good deeds, so it is as if these acts of disobedience were among acts of obedience in their view, which is why they hasten to them. Al-ithm encompasses every act of disobedience that entails punishment. Al-ʿudwan and the consuming of al-suht were singled out from it and mentioned specifically, to magnify these two acts of disobedience: the injustice against others, and the corrupt food that causes the rejection of good deeds. Abu Haywah recited al-ʿIdwan (with a kasra on the ʿayn instead of a damma). The discussion of what follows bi'sa (how evil) was already covered in His words ﴿بِئْسَما اشْتَرَوْا بِهِ﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 90] (how evil is that for which they sold themselves).

(p-522)

﴿Why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them from their saying of sin and their consuming of the forbidden gain? Surely evil is what they have been doing.﴾

*Lawlā* (لَوْلا): a *taḥḍīḍ* (an urgent exhortation, a form of reproach). It contains a rebuke of the scholars and the worshippers for their silence about forbidding the disobedience of God Most High and for not enjoining good.

The scholars said: there is no verse in the Qur'an more severe in reproach against the scholars than this one. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: there is nothing in the Qur'an more frightening than it, and Ibn ʿAbbās said something similar.

*Al-ithm* (الإثْمَ) here apparently means disbelief, or it may be intended to mean all their sayings that entail sin.

Al-Jarrāḥ and Abū Wāqid read *al-Rabbiyyūn* (الرِّبِّيُّونَ) instead of *al-Rabbāniyyūn* (الرَّبّانِيُّونَ). Ibn ʿAbbās read *bi'sa mā kānū yaṣnaʿūn* (بِئْسَ ما كانُوا يَصْنَعُونَ) without the *lām* of oath.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in *kānū* (كانُوا) is to the rabbis and the scholars, since they are the ones being spoken of and reproached for not forbidding.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: every doer is not called *ṣāniʿ* (صانِع, a craftsman), and not every action is called *ṣināʿa* (صِناعَة, a craft) until one becomes proficient in it, trains in it, and is known for it. The meaning here is that one who commits a sin is driven by desire, which urges him to it and moves him to do it. As for one who forbids it, he has no desire in another's act. So if he goes to excess in denouncing it, his state is worse than that of the one who commits it. Thus the distinction becomes clear between censuring the one who engages in the sin and censuring the one who leaves off forbidding it: the former is described as *ʿamal* (عَمَل, action), and the latter as *ṣināʿa*. It may be said that he varied the wording for the sake of eloquent variety and to avoid repeating the same word.

In a hadith: "No man lives among a people, committing sins in their midst, and they do not take him by the hand, except that God is about to overtake them all with punishment because of him."

It was revealed to Yūshaʿ (Joshua) that forty thousand of the best of his people and sixty thousand of their worst would be destroyed. He said: "O Lord, what about the good ones?" He said: "They did not become angry at My anger, and they ate and drank with them."

Mālik ibn Dīnār said: God revealed to the angels that they should punish the town of such-and-such. The angels said: "Among them is Your servant, the worshipper." He said: "Let me hear his cries, for his face has not changed," i.e., it did not redden with anger.

Some scholars wrote to a worshipper who had become ascetic and withdrawn into the desert: "You have left Medina, the place of the emigration of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the descent of his revelation, and you have preferred the life of the desert." He replied: "How could I not leave a place whose leader is you? I never saw your face change for the sake of God, not even one day." Or words to this effect, or close to this meaning.

As for our own time, our scholars and our worshippers, their condition is well known. We have not seen in our ages anyone who comes close to the early generation (al-Salaf) in this, except one man, our teacher Abū Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr. He had standings in this matter with the kings and rulers of his lands, and his efforts were praised for them. In some of them he was beaten, his wealth was plundered, and his homes were ruined. In some of them his flight saved him from death, and in some of them prison became his lodging.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 64 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the Jews say, "The hand of Allah is chained up."﴾ It was revealed concerning Finhas; this is related from Ibn ʿAbbas. Muqatil said: it concerns him and Ibn Suriya and ʿAzir ibn Abi ʿAzir; they all said that. That statement is attributed to the Jews because these were their scholars and the people followed them in it. The word "yad" (hand) is literal when it refers to the organ, and figurative in other senses, so it is used to mean favour (niʿmah). The Arabs say: "I have a hand (yad) with so-and-so," meaning a favour owed to me; it is also used to mean power, dominion and ability. Say: ﴿Indeed, the bounty is in the hand of Allah﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 73]. The poet said:

"And you, over the burdens of your kingdom, are one who has a hand (yad)"

that is, one who has power. It also means support and aid: "the hand of Allah is with the judge when he judges, and with the divider when he divides." It also comes as a connective (silah) in ﴿of what Our hands have made, cattle﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71], that is, of what We have made; and in ﴿or the one in whose hand is the tie of marriage will pardon﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237], that is, the one who holds the tie of marriage. The apparent meaning of the Jews' statement that Allah has a hand, if they meant the organ, then it suits their doctrine, which is anthropomorphism (tajsim). They claimed that their Lord has white head and beard, sits on a throne, and that He finished creating the heavens and the earth on Friday, then lay on His back, placing one leg over the other, to rest. Allah rejected that in His saying: ﴿And He was not wearied by their creation﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 33] and ﴿And no fatigue touched Us﴾ [Qaf: 38]. The apparent context of the verse indicates (p-523) that by chaining and spreading the hand they meant figuratively stinginess and generosity. From this is ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it completely outstretched﴾ [al-Isra': 29]. The one who speaks this speech does not intend to affirm a hand, a chain, or an extension; for him there is no difference between this speech and what is used figuratively for it; they are two speeches following one another on one reality, to the extent that he uses it of a king who never gives a gift at all, and withholds only by his gesture, without using a hand, extending it or closing it. Habib said of al-Mutasim:

"He became accustomed to extending the palm, until if he folded it to grasp, his fingertips would not answer it."

By this he alluded to extravagant generosity. The cause of the Jews' statement, as Ibn ʿAbbas said, was that Allah used to extend provision to them; when they disobeyed the Messenger's command and disbelieved in him, He withheld from them what He had been extending, and so they said that. Qatadah said: when He borrowed from them, they said that, and He is stingy. It was said: when He sought their help for blood-money. These causes suit the context of the verse. Qatadah also said: when the Christians helped Bukhtnassar, the Magian, to ruin Bayt al-Maqdis, the Jews said: "If he were truthful, he would have prevented us from him; his hand is chained." Al-Hasan said: "chained" from punishing them, and so it has the meaning of ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved ones﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18]. These two sayings are refuted by His statement: ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched; He spends as He wills﴾. Al-Kalbi said: they were prosperous, and they said that out of obstinacy, mockery and derision. End. The apparent meaning is that their saying "The hand of Allah is chained up" is a report. Those who went further, holding it to be an interrogative ("Is the hand of Allah chained up, since He has restricted our livelihood?"), are mistaken. Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, al-Farra', Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj held that it means withheld from giving. Al-Hasan said it means withheld from punishing them, except as much as the dissolution of an oath, in proportion to their worship of the calf. Others held that it means until He returns our kingdom to us. al-Tabari said: "They were chained up" is a report and a threat that will certainly befall them in Hell. Al-Hasan also said: it is a report about them in this world, that Allah made them the most stingy of people; al-Zajjaj said this. Muqatil said: it held back from good. It was said: it is a supplication against them for stinginess and wretchedness, and for this reason they are the most stingy and wretched of Allah's creatures. al-Zamakhshari said: it may also be a supplication against them with the chaining of the hands literally, that they be chained as prisoners in this world, and in the Hereafter tormented with the shackles of Hell. The antithesis is in wording and in observing the original figurative sense, as when one says: "He cursed me, may Allah cut off his tail (dabir)," since cursing (sabb) originally means cutting. (If you say): how is it permissible for Allah to curse them with what is ugly, namely stinginess and wretchedness? (I say): what is meant is a supplication for abandonment (khidhlan) by which their hearts become hardened, so that they increase in stinginess upon their stinginess and in wretchedness upon their wretchedness; and what is caused by stinginess and wretchedness, namely the clinging of shame to them and the evil reputation that disgraces them and tears their honour. End of his words. He presented it in accordance with the Mu'tazilite method. What appears to be correct is that their saying "The hand of Allah is chained up" is a metaphor for withholding goodness by one who is subdued and constrained to withhold. For this reason they used the word "chained" (maghlulah), and only the subdued is chained. So His saying "their hands are chained" is a supplication against them with the chaining of their hands. They are, in every land and with every nation, subdued and overpowered; none of them can exert dominance or rise above others. This is a metaphor for their humiliation and subjugation, and that their hands do not extend to repel any harm that descends upon them. This is a counterpart to what their saying "The hand of Allah is chained up" contained. This statement is not novel from them, for they said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 181].

﴿Their hands are chained, and they are cursed for what they said﴾ may be a report or a supplication; and "for what they said" may mean this very statement of theirs, or it may be general, covering whatever they ascribed to Allah that is not permissible to ascribe to Him, so that this statement falls within the generality of what they said. Abu al-Sammal recited it with a sukun on the ʿayn, as in ʿusira for ʿusra (ʿusir → ʿusr); the poet said:

"If the ben-tree and musk were pressed from it, it would be pressed out."

What makes this reading good is that the kasrah lies between two dammahs, so lightening it is fitting.

﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched; He spends as He wills﴾: the belief of the People of Truth is that Allah, exalted is He, is not a body and has no organ, is not likened to anything of His creation, is not described as having a modality (takyif), is not confined in place, and is not the locus of accidents; all this is established in the science of the principles of religion (usul al-din). The majority hold that this is a metaphor for His abundant generosity and bounty, and He attributed it to the two hands following the Arab way of saying: "So-and-so spends with both his hands." From this is the poet's saying:

"Your hands are hands of glory: one palm is beneficial, and a palm which, when wealth is withheld, spends."

What supports that the two hands here mean bounty is the context of spending. Whoever considers the speech of the Arabs knows with certainty that extending and closing the hand is a metaphor for generosity and stinginess, and the Arabs use it even where there is no hand. The poet said:

"The hima' (pasture) extended both hands with downpour; its plains and valleys thanked its bounty."

Labid said:

"And on a morning of wind, and cold, I restrained them, when the north wind had already become holder of their reins."

It is said: "despair spread its palm in my chest," though despair is a meaning, not a body, and he gave it a palm. al-Zamakhshari said: whoever does not consider the science of rhetoric (bayan) will be blind to the clear path of correct interpretation of such verses, and will not escape the hand of the critic when it strikes him. Then he said: (If you say): why is "hand" dual in "Rather, both His hands are outstretched," when it is singular in "the hand of Allah is chained up"? (I say): so that the refutation of their claim and its denial may be more eloquent and more indicative of establishing His utmost generosity and negating stinginess from Him. The utmost a generous person gives is by his own self, and that he gives with both hands together; so the metaphor is built on that. End. His words are most excellent. It is said from Ibn ʿAbbas: "His two hands are His two blessings." It was said: they are two metaphors for the blessing of religion and the blessing of this world, or the blessing of soundness of limbs and senses and the blessing of provision and sufficiency, or the outward and the inward, or the blessing of rain and the blessing of plants. Similarly what occurs that gives the appearance of anthropomorphism, such as this. His saying: ﴿for what I created with My two hands﴾ [Sad: 75], ﴿of what Our hands have made﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71], ﴿the hand of Allah is above their hands﴾ [al-Fath: 10], ﴿so that you may be raised under My eye﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39], ﴿running under Our eyes﴾ [al-Qamar: 14], ﴿everything perishes except His face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88], and the like. The majority of the community holds that these are interpreted according to the rules of the language, the figure of metaphor, and the other varieties of speech.

Others, among them the judge Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib, said: all these are attributes additional to the essence, affirmed for Allah, exalted is He, without likeness and without renewal. Others, among them al-Sha'bi, Ibn al-Musayyab and al-Thawri, said: we believe in them and affirm them as they are stated, without specifying their interpretation, and without preceding reflection upon them. These two positions are the talk of one who has not deeply considered the language of the Arabs. This question has its proofs in the science of the principles of religion.

ʿAbd Allah (ibn Mas'ud) recited: basitani (spread out). It is said: "a hand that is basitah (outstretched), absolute, in the common usage." In the codex of ʿAbd Allah: bashtani; it is said: "his hand is bast (outstretched), in the common usage," and it is of the pattern fa'l, as one says: "a camel of sarh (lofty?) and a gait of sajh (easy)." ﴿He spends as He wills﴾: this is an emphasis of the description of generosity, and that He spends only in accordance with what His will requires. There is no place in the grammatical analysis for His saying "He spends" (tunfiq), since it is a resumed sentence. al-Hawfi said: it may be a predicate after a predicate, and it may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "outstretched." End. In these two analyses one needs the returning pronoun, referring either to the subject or to the one in circumstance, to be omitted; the estimate is: "He spends with them both." Al-Hawfi said: "kayfa" is a question about a circumstance and is in the accusative governed by "yashaʾ." End. It is not intelligible here that it is a question about a circumstance; rather it has the sense of a conditional, as when one says: "How will I be, I shall be" ("kayfa takunu akunu"). The object of "yashaʾ" is omitted, and the answer to "kayfa" is omitted, indicated by the preceding "yunfiqu," as the answer to a conditional is indicated in your saying: "I will stand if Zayd stands." The estimate is: "He spends however He wills to spend, He spends," as you say: "However you wish that I strike you, I strike you." It is not permissible for "kayfa yunfiq" to govern, because an interrogative particle of condition is not governed by what precedes it, unless it is a preposition; some conditional particles may be governed. A parallel to that is His saying: ﴿and He spreads it in the sky however He wills﴾ [al-Rum: 48].

﴿And much of them will surely increase in what has been revealed to you from your Lord in transgression and disbelief﴾: it is linked to "much" (kathir), because among them are those who believed, and those who increase only in transgression. This is an informing of the Messenger about the extreme of their obstinacy, since they should have hastened to faith because of what Allah informed them of through His Messenger of the secrets they conceal and which no one but they know; yet they arranged upon that something other than its proper consequence, and it increased them in transgression and disbelief, due to the extremity of their obstinacy and envy. al-Zajjaj said: whenever something is revealed to you, they disbelieve in it. Muqatil said: "And much of them will surely increase" refers to the Banu al-Nadir, in what has been revealed to you from your Lord concerning the matter of stoning and blood. It was said: what is meant by "much" is the scholars of the Jews. It was said: their persistence in disbelief is an increase by them in disbelief.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 64 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And We have cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection.﴾ It has been said: the pronoun in "among them" refers to the Jews and the Christians, because they were mentioned in His saying, ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51], and because His saying, ﴿O People of the Book﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 59], includes both groups. This is the view of al-Hasan and Mujahid. It has also been said that it refers only to the Jews, since they are divided into Jabriyya (determinists), Qadariyya (proponents of free will), Muwahhida (unitarians) and Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists). Likewise, the Christians are divided into Malkaniyya, Ya'qubiyya and Nestoriyya. What appears to be the meaning is that they will continue to hate one another and be hostile to one another, so their word cannot unite against you, they cannot harm you, and they cannot reach you or your followers, because the two groups have no mutual affection that would bring them together to fight you. In this there is a report of the unseen: that since Islam began until this time, a Jewish army and a Christian army have never combined to fight the Muslims. Al-Zamakhshari alluded to this meaning when he said: "They are always divided, their hearts are scattered, and no agreement or mutual support takes place among them." End of quotation. Enmity (al-'adawah) is more specific than hatred (al-baghda'), because every enemy is hated, but one may hate someone who is not an enemy. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It seems that enmity is something visible, from which action and war result, whereas hatred does not go beyond the souls." End of his words.

﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it.﴾ Some have said: this is to be taken literally and is not a metaphor (isti'arah). The Arabs used to set a time for fighting, and their sign was lighting a fire on a mountain or a hill. Then they would hasten to it while the army was marching by night, and whoever passed them at night would light a fire, which served as a warning. This is also a custom we have had with the Romans on the island of al-Andalus: a lookout (rabi'ah) would be stationed near their territory for the Muslims, hidden in a mountain cave. When the unbelievers went out to fight the Muslims, he would light a fire. When another lookout who had been posted for the Muslims near that mountain saw it, he would light a fire, and so on, until the news reached the Muslims in the shortest time, and they would know from which direction the enemy was approaching, so the Muslims would prepare to meet them. It has also been said: when the two hosts faced each other and the two armies drew close, they would light fires at night for fear of a night attack, and this is the origin of the fire of war. It has also been said: when they made a pact to be earnest in their war, they would light a fire and swear the oath. According to the view that the fire is literal, the meaning of extinguishing it is that God cast terror into their hearts, so they feared being attacked in their dwellings, and so they stopped; when they refrained from them, He extinguished the fire. God attributed the extinguishing to Himself as the attribution of the effect to its original cause.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) said: it is a metaphor. Kindling the fire is an expression for displaying spite, scheming, deception against the believers, plotting to assassinate them, and fighting them. Extinguishing it means God turning them away from that, dispersing their opinions, dissolving their resolve, scattering their word, and casting terror into their hearts. So they never intend to fight anyone without being defeated and overpowered, and no victory from God over anyone has stood for them, and Islam came to them while they were under the rule of the Magians. It has also been said: they opposed the Jews, so God sent Bukhtansar against them; then they corrupted, so God empowered Bitrik the Roman over them; then they corrupted, so God empowered the Magians over them; then they corrupted, so God empowered the Muslims over them. Others said: this is a parable coined for their exertion in war, the blazing of the sparks of their hearts, and the boiling of their chests. From this comes the saying "Now the oven (watis) has become hot," meaning the earnestness of war. And so one says, "So-and-so is a kindler of war (mus'ir harb)," who ignites it by his bravery. Extinguishing was used as a parable for humbling their noses and their defeat in every place. Mujahid said: it is good news to the Messenger that whenever they fight him, he will be victorious over them, and it is an allusion to the Jews present in his time. Al-Suddi, al-Rabi' and others said: it is a report about their predecessors, whom God destroyed their kingdom for ages, so no banner will be raised for them until the Day of Resurrection, and they will not fight together except in fortified villages. Qatadah said: you will not meet a Jew in any town without finding him among the most humiliated of people.

﴿and they strive throughout the land to cause corruption.﴾ It may be that by striving (al-sa'y) is meant the movement of feet, i.e., they do not suffice in displaying corruption except by moving their feet to one another, which would be more emphatic in exertion. The apparent meaning, however, is action and deed: they strive to plot against the people of Islam and to erase the mention of the Messenger from their books. The earth (al-ard) may be taken in a generic sense, or as the land of the Hijaz, in which case the "al-" is for a known reference. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: their corruption is by sins. Al-Zajjaj said: by repelling Islam and erasing the mention of the Messenger from their books. It has also been said: by shedding blood and making forbidden things lawful. It has also been said: by unbelief. It has also been said: by injustice. All these statements are close in meaning.

﴿And Allah does not love corrupters.﴾ The apparent sense of "the corrupters" is generality, so these people are included among them. It has also been said that "al-" is for a known reference, and they are these people. The negation of love is an allusion (kinayah) to His not bestowing His favor and kindness upon them. As for these, He will punish them; and if He does not reward them, then He is punishing them, since there is no intermediate state between punishment and reward.

(p-٥٢٦)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 65:

﴿Had the People of the Book believed and been mindful of God, We would have expiated their misdeeds and admitted them into the Gardens of Bliss.﴾ It is said: the intended people are their forefathers, though the contemporaries are included in meaning. The purpose is to inform about those whom God extinguished the fires of and humiliated through their sins, and what appears is that they are the contemporaries of the Messenger (ﷺ), and in this there is an encouragement for them to enter Islam. He mentioned two things, which are: faith (iman) and God-consciousness (taqwa). He attached two things to them: he matched faith with the expiation of misdeeds, since Islam erases what came before it, and God-consciousness, which is carrying out the commands and avoiding the prohibitions, is followed by entry into the Garden of Bliss. The attribution of the Garden to Bliss serves as an alert to what they would deserve of punishment had they not believed and been mindful. It is also said: "and been mindful" means: (mindful of) disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ) and in Jesus (peace be upon him). It is also said: the sins for which they were cursed. It is also said: polytheism (shirk).
