Al-Zamakhshari said: "Had they believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) and in what he brought, and joined their faith with God-consciousness, which is the condition for success through faith, We would have expiated those misdeeds from them, so We would not have held them accountable for them, and We would have admitted them into the Garden along with the Muslims." In it is an announcement of the magnitude of the sins of the Jews and Christians and the abundance of their misdeeds, and an indication of the vastness of God's mercy and His opening the door of repentance to every sinner, even if his sins are great and reach the extent of the misdeeds of the Jews and Christians, and that faith does not save nor bring happiness except when accompanied by God-consciousness; as al-Hasan said: "This is the pole, so where are the tent-ropes?" The end of his words. In it there is some of Mu'tazilism (i'tizal). And joining their faith with God-consciousness, which is the condition for success through faith, and his saying: faith does not save nor bring happiness except when accompanied by God-consciousness.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 66:

﴿If only they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel, and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet.﴾ This is an invitation to their belief, a reminder to them to follow what is in their books, and an encouragement for them toward the immediate benefits of this world and the expansion of provision for them in it. For most of what the Torah promises as a reward for obedience is kindness to them in this world. Since in the previous verse he had encouraged them with the promise of the Hereafter, namely the expiation of their misdeeds and their entry into Paradise, he encouraged them in this verse with the promise of this world, so that he would combine for them the two good things of this world and the Hereafter. Mentioning the promise of the Hereafter first was more important, because it is the lasting and enduring one, the one through which comes everlasting salvation and the bliss that never ends.

The meaning of "upholding the Torah and the Gospel" is to make manifest what they contain of rulings, of the good news of the Messenger, and of the command to follow him, like the saying of the Arabs: "they set up the market," meaning they got it moving and made it visible. This is a figure of speech (tashbih) likening it to a person standing upright, since standing is the most visible of a person's postures. In His saying "and the Gospel" there is evidence that the Christians are included in the term "People of the Book." The apparent meaning of His saying "and what was revealed to them from their Lord" is generality across the divine books, such as the Book of Isaiah (Ashiya'), the Book of Ezekiel (Hizqil), and the Book of Daniel (Daniyal), for these are full of good news of the sending of the Messenger. It has also been said that "what was revealed to them from their Lord" is the Qur'an.

The apparent meaning of His saying "they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet" is that it is a metaphor (isti'arah) for the abundance of blessings upon them and the widening of provision for them, as one says: "provision has covered him from his head to his foot," with neither above nor below. This was related by al-Tabari and al-Zajjaj. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Suddi said: "The sky would have given them its rain and its blessing, and the earth its plants," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And had We opened to them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾ [Al-A'raf: 96]. Al-Naqqash mentioned that "from above them" is the provision of Paradise, and "from beneath their feet" is the provision of this world, since it comes from the plants of the earth. It was also said: "from above them" is the abundance of fruit-bearing trees, and "from beneath their feet" is the productive crops. It was also said: "from above them" refers to gardens with ripe fruit, from which they pick what hangs down from the tops of the trees, and gather what falls from them to the ground; and "beneath their feet" [refers to...]. (p-528) Taj al-Qurra said: "from above them" is what comes to them from their nobles and kings, and "from beneath their feet" is what comes to them from their lowly and common people. He expressed "eating" as a figure for "taking," because it is the most excellent of its benefits and the most eloquent expression of what is needed for the continuance of life.

﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾ The pronoun in "among them" refers to the People of the Book. The word "community" (ummah) here is meant to denote a small group, in contrast to His saying "and many of them." Al-iqtisad (moderation) derives from al-qasd, which is balance and uprightness. It is of the form "ifta'ala," meaning "i'tamala" and "iktasaba" (to acquire); that is, they were first errant, then they became moderate. It was said: they are the believers of both groups, Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions, and forty-eight of the Christians. Their moderation is their belief in God, exalted is He. Mujahid said: "the moderate community" is the Muslims among the People of the Book, past and present. Ibn Zayd said something similar: they are the people of obedience to God among the People of the Book. Al-Zajjaj and others mentioned that they are the groups who did not oppose the prophets with the opposition of rebellious and fighting enemies. Al-Zamakhshari said: "moderate" means that their condition is that of communities in enmity toward the Messenger, ﷺ. Al-Tabari said: among the Children of Israel there are those who are moderate concerning Jesus, so they say: he is the servant of God, His messenger, and a spirit from Him; while most of them went to excess concerning him, and some of them said: he is God; and on this path went the Romans and whoever entered the religion of Jesus later. Others among them, and they are the majority of the Children of Israel, said: he is a human like any other, for his lack of rectitude. So it is clarified: is the moderation concerning the right of Jesus, or concerning opposition, or concerning belief? If it is concerning opposition, is it in relation to the Messenger alone, or in relation to the prophets? There are two opinions. If it is concerning belief, is it the belief of those who believed in the Messenger from both groups, or of those who believed in the past and the present? There are two opinions.

﴿And many of them, evil is what they do﴾ This is a variation in the detail. The first clause, "among them is a moderate community," has the prepositional phrase "among them" as its predicate, and the second clause, "and many of them, evil is what they do," has the predicate as the clause "evil is what they do." Between the two constructions there is a remarkable difference in meaning. This is because moderation was made a description, and a description is more inherent in the thing described than a predicate is, so he used the inherent description for the praised group, and reported about them with the words "among them," whereas a predicate is not necessarily inherent, especially here. He reported about them that they are of the People of the Book originally, and then this affiliation may be removed by Islam, so the expression about them and the report that they are "among them" is in regard to their former state. As for the second clause, they are "among them" in actuality, because they are unbelievers, so the description came as inherent and was not made a predicate, while the predicate of the clause "evil is what they do" was made so, because a predicate is not necessarily inherent. They are on the verge of some of them becoming Muslim, so the report of the content of this clause will cease for them. Al-Zamakhshari chose, regarding "sa'a" (evil/was evil), that it be the non-inflecting verb, because in it there is the sense of wonder, as if it were said: "how evil their deed is!" and he mentioned no other opinion than this. Ibn Atiyyah chose that it be the inflecting verb; you say "sa'a al-amr yasu'u" (the matter became evil), and he permitted that it be the non-inflecting verb, so that it is used like "ni'ma" and "bi'sa" (the verbs of praise and blame), as in His saying: ﴿sa'a mathalan﴾ [evil is the example]. The inflecting verb requires an implied object, that is: "evil is what they were doing to the believers," while the non-inflecting verb requires a specification (tamyiz), that is: "evil is their deed, what they were doing."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 67:

﴿O Messenger, proclaim what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. This is an address using the noble attribute which is the most honourable of the qualities of the human species, and it is a command to convey what was sent down to him, ﷺ. He had already conveyed what was sent down to him, so this is a command to continuity. Al-Zamakhshari said: "All of what has been sent down to you, and whatever was sent down, without being concerned in conveying it about anyone, nor fearing that some harm may befall you." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is a command from God to His Messenger to convey in full and completeness, for He has said 'proclaim,' so he was commanded in this verse not to hold back from anything out of fear of anyone, because his message, peace be upon him, included criticism of the various kinds of disbelievers and the corruption of their conditions, so he would meet hardship from them, and sometimes he feared them before the revelation of this verse." It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from him, peace be upon him: "When God sent me with His message, I was distressed by it, and I knew that among the people there are those who would deny me, so God sent down this verse." It was also said: this is a command to convey a specific matter, i.e., what was sent down to you concerning stoning and retaliation, which the Jews had altered in the Torah and the Christians in the Gospel. It was also said: a command to convey the matter of Zaynab bint Jahsh and her marriage. It was also said: to convey jihad and to urge it, and not to abandon it for the sake of anyone. It was also said: a command to convey the faults of their gods, since he had been silent, when the words ﴿And do not revile those who call upon other than God﴾ [al-An'am: 108] were revealed, about their defects. Each of these specific conveyances has been said to be the reason for the revelation of the verse. What appears is that God guaranteed him protection from the plotting of the Jews and the Christians, and commanded him to convey what was sent down to him concerning their affair and other matters without being concerned about anyone, because the discourse before and after this verse is with them, so it is far-fetched that this verse should be unrelated to what precedes and follows it.

﴿And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾. That is: and if you do not convey what was sent down to you. The apparent sense of this answer does not contradict the condition, since the meaning becomes: "If you do not do it, you do not do it," and the answer must differ from the condition in order for it to follow from it. Al-Zamakhshari said: there are two interpretations. The first: that if he does not carry out God's command to convey the message and conceals all of it, it is as if he had not been sent as a messenger, which would be a dreadful matter. It was also said: if you do not convey even a small part of it, even a single word, you are like one who has committed the dreadful act of concealing all of it, just as He magnified the killing of a soul with His words: ﴿it is as if he had slain all mankind﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 32]. The second: it is meant that if you do not do that, what the concealment of the whole revelation would entail of punishment will be upon you, so the cause is put in place of the effect; and this is supported by his, peace be upon him, saying: (God revealed to me: if you do not convey My messages, I will surely punish you). Ibn 'Atiyya said: that is, if you leave out something, it is as if you have left out the whole, and what you have conveyed is not counted as valid. So the meaning of "and if you do not" is "and if you do not complete." A similar statement is the words of the poet:

*You were asked, and you did not withhold, yet you gave no gift, so it is equal: there is no blame upon you nor praise.*

That is: if you do not give what counts as a gift... and that you do not lie. . . . the verse. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: The majority answered: "If you do not convey even one of them, you are like one who has conveyed nothing." This is weak, because one who conveys part and leaves out part... If it is said that he left out all of it, he would be lying; and if it is said that the magnitude of the offence in leaving out part is like the offence in leaving out all, this is the impossible and the forbidden, so this answer falls. End. What he used to weaken the majority's answer does not weaken it, because he said: "If it is said that he left out all of it, he would be lying," and they did not say that; they only said that no part of it is more deserving of being delivered than another, so if you do not deliver some of it, it is as if you have neglected delivering all of it. Just as one who does not believe in some of it is like one who does not believe in all of it, because each part of it conveys what the others convey, and their being in this respect one thing, and one thing cannot be conveyed and not conveyed, believed and not believed; so that conveyance of part is not counted as valid. As for what was mentioned, that the magnitude of the offence in leaving out part is like the offence in leaving out all is impossible and forbidden, there is no impossibility in it. God may attach a great punishment to a small sin, and He may pardon a great sin and call to account for a trivial one: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23]. This has appeared in the ordering of punishments in the legal rulings: for one who takes something by stealth and concealment, the hand is cut off along with returning what he took or its value; and for one who takes something by force, domination and usurpation, the return of that thing or its value if it is lost is ordered, without cutting off the hand. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: What is more correct in my view is to say that this came in the pattern of his saying: "I am Abu al-Najm and my poetry is my poetry," meaning: my poetry has reached such perfection, eloquence and solidity that whenever it is said of it that it is my poetry, its praise has reached the utmost limit that cannot be exceeded; and this statement conveys complete exaggeration in this respect, so likewise here. He said: "If you do not convey His message, then you have not conveyed His message"; meaning: it is not possible to describe the eloquent one as leaving off threatening with anything greater than that he has left off glorifying, so that was an alert to threat and warning. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read *risalatihi* (in the plural). The rest of the seven read it in the singular.

﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾. That is: do not be concerned in conveying, for God will protect you, so they have no power to kill you, neither by plotting, nor by assassination, nor by overpowering you by seizing and capturing. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it was revealed because of the Bedouin who drew the sword of the Prophet, ﷺ, to kill him. End. He was Ghawrath ibn al-Harith, and that was in the expedition of Dhat al-Riqa'.

The commentators narrate that Abu Talib used to send men from the Banu Hashim to guard him until the words ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾ were revealed; so he said: "Indeed God has protected me from jinn and men, so I have no need of anyone to guard me." Ibn Jurayj said: he used to fear the Quraysh, and when it was revealed he lay down and said: "Whoever wishes, let him forsake me," twice or three times. Abu Umamah narrated the hadith of "Rukana" ... a man of the sons of Hashim, a polytheist, the most treacherous and fiercest of people; he wrestled with the Messenger, and the Messenger threw him three times and called him to Islam, and he asked him for a sign, so he called the tree and it came to him, having split into two halves; then he asked him to return it to its place, and it joined together and returned. Abu Bakr and 'Umar sought him, and they were directed to him, that he had gone out to the valley of Udum, where Rukana was; so they went towards him and met him, and they mentioned that they had feared treachery from Rukana; so he informed them of his account with him and laughed, and he recited: ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾. This and what precedes it indicate that this was revealed in Makkah or at Dhat al-Riqa'. The correct view is that it "was revealed in Medina while the Messenger was residing there for a month, and Sa'd and Hudhayfah guarded him; he slept until he snored, and it was revealed, so he brought out his head to them from a leather tent and said: (Disperse, O people, for God has protected me; I do not care who helps me or who forsakes me)." The origin of this hadith is in Sahih Muslim. As for the wounding of his forehead and the breaking of his front tooth on the day of Uhud: it was said that the verse was revealed after Uhud. If it was before it, then the protection did not include this trial and the like, of the disbelievers' harm by words; rather, it included protection from killing and capture. As for such matters, there is in them a trial in which is the raising of ranks and the bearing of all harm short of the soul for the sake of God; and the trials of the prophets are more severe, and how great is their burden. He used the expression *ya'simuka* because the present tense indicates continuity and permanence; and "the people" is general, intended to mean the disbelievers, as what follows indicates. This clause contains the report of an unseen matter which occurred as he reported it, so no one reached him with killing or capture, despite the enemies' intent to overcome him and assassinate him. In this there is evidence for the validity of his prophethood, since his report of this could only be from God, the Exalted, and likewise all that he reported.

﴿Indeed God does not guide the disbelieving people﴾. That is: you are only responsible for conveying, not for guidance; whoever I have decreed to be a disbeliever and to die upon that will never be guided, so this is specific. Ibn 'Atiyya said: As for the general sense, that there is no guidance in disbelief, and God does not guide the disbeliever in his path of disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is that He does not enable them to do what they wish to bring down, rather to ruin. End. It is also the view of some that He does not help them to reach their aim against you. It was also said: the meaning is that He does not guide them to Paradise. The apparent meaning of guidance when it is used absolutely is what we explained it as at first.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 68:

﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, you are not upon anything until you establish the Torah and the Gospel and what has been revealed to you from your Lord."﴾ "Rafi' ibn Salam ibn Mishkam, Malik ibn al-Sayf and Rafi' ibn Huraymalah said: 'O Muhammad, do you not claim that you are upon the religion of Ibrahim, and that you believe in the Torah and the prophethood of Musa, and that this is true?' He said: 'Yes, but you have innovated, altered and concealed.' They said: 'We hold to what is in our hands, for it is the truth, and we do not believe you nor follow you.' So it was revealed." The discussion of establishing the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed has already preceded, so there is no need to repeat it. The negation that they are "upon anything" makes what they have into complete nothingness, due to its corruption and invalidity, so it is negated from its very root; or, "of value" is an omitted qualifier, meaning "upon anything that is considered valid," so that the negation is directed at the qualifier and not at the qualified.

﴿And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief.﴾ The explanation of this sentence has already preceded.

﴿So do not grieve over the disbelieving people.﴾ That is: do not be sorrowful over them. The apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun, to draw attention to the cause that necessitates the absence of grief; or it is general, so that they are included within it. It has also been said: in His saying ﴿until you establish the Torah﴾ the plural pronoun is used, and the intended meaning is distribution; that is, until the People of the Torah establish the Torah, and the People of the Gospel establish the Gospel. This is not needed if what is meant is the monotheism contained in the two Books, since the laws within them are equivalent.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 69:

﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabeans and the Christians, whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds, no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.﴾ The tafsir of the like of this verse has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. ʿUthman, Ubayy, ʿA'isha, Ibn Jubayr and al-Jahdari read *wa-l-ṣābiʾīna* (والصّابِئِينَ) with a genitive ending. Al-Zamakhshari said: Ibn Kathir also read it this way. Al-Hasan and al-Zuhri read *wa-l-ṣābiyūna* (والصّابِيُونَ), with a kasra on the bā' and a ḍamma on the yā', and this is from the lightening of the hamza, like the reading *yastahziʾūna* (يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ) [pronounced *yastahzūna*]. The seven readers read *wa-l-ṣābiʾūna* (والصّابِئُونَ) with a nominative ending, and this is what the mushafs of the regions and the majority follow.

There are several explanations for this reading. The first is the view of Sibawayh, al-Khalil and the grammarians of Basra: it is nominative by inception (*mubtada'*), with a delayed predicate intended. Its parallel is: *inna Zaydan wa-ʿAmrun qa'imun* (إنَّ زَيْدًا وعَمْرٌو قائِمٌ). The sense is: *wa-inna Zaydan qa'imun wa-ʿAmrun qa'imun*, so the predicate of ʿAmr is omitted because the predicate of *inna* indicates it. The intention of the phrase "wa-ʿAmrun" is the delay. ʿAmr's predicate, being this supposed predicate, is conjoined to the clause *inna Zaydan qa'imun*, and both have no place in i'rab (grammatical inflection).

The second explanation: it is conjoined to the position (*mawḍiʿ*) of the noun of *inna*, because before *inna* entered, it was in a position of nominative case. This is the view of al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'. As for al-Kisa'i, he permitted the conjunction to the position with a nominative ending whether the noun shows its i'rab or not. As for al-Farra', he permitted it on condition that the i'rab is hidden. The noun of *inna* here has hidden i'rab.

The third explanation: it is nominative, conjoined to the pronoun in *hadu* (هادُوا) [the wāw of the verb]. This was narrated from al-Kisa'i. It is rejected because conjoining to it requires that the Sabeans became Jews, and that is not the case.

The fourth explanation: *inna* is taken to mean *naʿam* (نَعَمْ, "yes"), a particle of answer, and what follows it is nominative by inception, so *wa-l-ṣābiʾūna* is conjoined to the nominative preceding it. This is weak, because whether *inna* can mean *naʿam* is disputed among the grammarians, and even if this is established from the Arabic language, it requires something preceding it that it confirms, and it does not come as an initial particle at the beginning of speech without being an answer to a preceding statement.

Al-Zamakhshari extended much in defending and supporting the view of Sibawayh, and that is mentioned in the science of grammar. He also raised questions and answers concerning the grammatical analysis of the verse, of which a similar example has already been discussed in al-Baqarah.

ʿAbdullah [Ibn Masʿud] read: ﴿O you who believe, and those who were Jews, and the Sabeans...﴾ (يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا والَّذِينَ هادَوْا والصّابِئُونَ).

We took the covenant of the Children of Israel and sent to them messengers. This is a report of what the forebears of the Jews did: breaking the covenant that God had taken from them, and the great crimes they committed, such as denying the prophets and killing some of them. Those who are present in the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ) are the successors of those people, so what comes from them toward the Messenger of harm and disobedience is no novelty, for it is a trait (shinshinah) inherited from their forebears.

﴿Whenever a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, a group they denied and a group they killed.﴾ The explanation of this has already been given in al-Baqarah. Al-Zamakhshari said here: "If you say, where is the answer (jawab) to the conditional? The phrase 'a group they denied and a group they killed' takes the place of the answer, because one single messenger cannot be two groups, and because it is not good to say: 'If you honour my brother, your brother I honour.'" I say: The answer is omitted, indicated by his saying 'a group they denied and a group they killed,' as if it were said: "Whenever a messenger came to them from among them, they opposed him." His saying "a group they denied" is a resumptive answer (jawab mustaʾnaf) in response to a questioner who asks: "How did they treat their messengers?" End of quotation.

As for his saying, "If you say, where is the answer to the conditional?" he called His saying "whenever a messenger came to them" a conditional, though it is not a conditional. Rather, kull (كُلَّ, "every") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), because it is annexed to the verbal noun (maṣdar) formed from the temporal mā (ما المصدرية الظرفية), and the governing element of it is what comes after the mentioned mā together with its relative clause (ṣilah), namely the verb, as in His saying: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We replace them﴾ [al-Nisa': 56] and ﴿Every time a group is cast into it﴾ [al-Mulk: 8]. The Arabs agree that kullamā is not used in the jussive (lā yujzam), and even if we grant that it is called a conditional, al-Zamakhshari's claim that his saying "a group they denied" turns away from the answer for two reasons is not correct. The first is his saying: "because one messenger cannot be two groups." This is not as he states, because in this construction "messenger" does not mean one individual; rather it means the category (jins), and whichever star rises. When it means the category, it divides into two groups: a group that was denied and a group that was killed. The second reason is his saying: "because it is not good to say: 'If you honour my brother, your brother I honour',"meaning that it is not permissible to place the object of the verb before the verb that serves as the answer. This is not as he states; rather, the view of the Basrans and al-Kisa'i is that this is permissible and good, and only al-Farra' alone prohibited it. All of this is on the assumption that kullamā is a conditional; otherwise there is no need to argue with this, and it is permissible to place the object of the verb that governs kullamā before it. So you say: "Every time you came to me, your brother I honoured." The general statements of the grammarians support this, for when they delimited what must have the object placed before the governing verb and what must have it placed after, they said: "Whatever is other than that, the object may be placed before the governing element or after it," and they did not exempt this form or mention any disagreement about it. Based on what we have established, the governing element of kullamā is His saying "denied" (kadhdhabū) and what is conjoined to it, and it is not omitted. Al-Hawfi and Ibn 'Atiyyah said: kullamā is an adverb of time, and its governing element is "denied." Abu al-Baqa' said: "denied" is the answer to kullamā. End of quotation.

He used the wording "killed" (yaqtulūn) to narrate the past state, to emphasise the gravity of killing and to bring that dreadful state to mind in order to express wonder at it; this was said by al-Zamakhshari. Its coming in this form is also made fitting by its being the end of the verse. The meaning is: they denied one group only, but they killed another group, and they did not kill them except along with denying them. So mention of killing has been sufficient instead of mention of denial; that is, some people were limited to denying one group, while others added killing to denial.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 71:

﴿And they thought there would be no trial, so they became blind and deaf; then Allah turned to them in forgiveness.﴾ Ibn al-Anbari said: It was revealed concerning a people who were upon disbelief before the mission (al-ba'tha), and when the Messenger was sent, they denied him out of rebellion (baghy) and envy (hasad), so they became blind and deaf by turning away from the truth. Then Allah turned to them, i.e., He gave them the opportunity to repent by sending the Messenger, ﷺ, even though they did not repent; then many of them became blind and deaf again, because they did not all unite in opposing him. End of quotation. The pronoun in "wa-hasibu" (and they thought) refers to the Children of Israel. The cause of their thinking was their being deceived by Allah's respite when they denied the messengers and killed them; or their belief in their own selves that they were the sons of Allah and His beloved, and that the Fire would not touch them except for the number of days in which they worshipped the calf; or Allah's granting them long lives and abundant provision; or their belief that Paradise would not be entered except by one who was a Jew or a Christian; and their conviction that abrogation (naskh) of the law of Moses was impossible, so that whenever a messenger came to them, they denied and killed him. These are five opinions. The word "fitnah" here means trial and testing. It is said: in this world, by famine, plague (ta'un), or killing, or enmity, or hardship of circumstances, or lice, frogs and blood, or wandering (in the desert), or fighting the giants, or all of what has been mentioned; these are eight opinions. It is said: in the Hereafter, by being disgraced before all witnesses, or it is the Day of Resurrection and its severity, or the punishment of the Fire and eternal abiding; these are three opinions. It is said: the fitnah is what befell them in this world and in the Hereafter. The verb-with-particle (an) and its complement (silah) stand in place of the two objects of "hasiba" according to the position of Sibawayh. The two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') and 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "takuna" with the nun in the accusative, with "an" as the governing particle for the imperfect verb; this is the original form, since "hasiba" is among the verbs which in their original usage are for what is not certain. Al-Nahwiyyan (Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i) and Hamzah read it with the nun in the nominative, where "an" is the lightened form of the heavy "anna", its noun being a omitted pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), and the negated clause is in the position of the predicate. Thinking (al-husban) has taken the place of knowledge in their breasts, and "hasiba" has been used in the sense of what is certain, though rarely; the poet said:

I thought piety and generosity the best trade, a profitable one, when a man becomes heavy (with burdens).

Here "takuna" is used as a complete verb (tammah).

﴿Then many of them became blind and deaf﴾ A group said: their repentance was their return to Jerusalem after the first expulsion, and their blindness and deafness. It was said: their plunging into their desires, so they did not see the truth and did not hear the call of Allah. Another group said: their repentance was by the sending of Jesus, peace be upon him. Another group said: the sending of Muhammad, ﷺ. It was said: the first (blindness and deafness) was in the time of Zechariah, John and Jesus, peace be upon them, and the granting of success to many of them for faith. The second was in the time of the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, when a group believed in him and many of them persisted in their disbelief. It was said: the first was the worship of the calf and then repentance from it; then the second was by seeking to see Allah, which is impossible and unintelligible regarding the attributes of Allah, said by al-Zamakhshari, following his Mu'tazili doctrine of denying the vision of Allah, Exalted. Al-Qaffal said, concerning Surat Bani Isra'il, what may be an explanation of this verse. It was said: the first was after Moses, then He turned to them by the sending of Jesus; the second was disbelief in the Messenger. What appears to be the meaning is that the Children of Israel thought, since they are the sons of the messengers and prophets, that they would not be tested if they disobeyed Allah; so they disobeyed Allah, Exalted, and He referred to disobedience with blindness and deafness. Then Allah turned to them when the trial befell them, by their return from disobedience to the obedience of Allah, Exalted. Blindness is mentioned first because it is the first thing that befalls one who turns away from the laws: he does not see the one who brings them from Allah; then even if he sees him, he does not hear his speech, so deafness to his speech befalls them. Since before that they were on the path of guidance, and then misguidance befell them, the act was attributed to them and ascribed to them, and it was not said: "Allah blinded them and deafened them," as came in His saying: "Those are the ones whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts, so He made them deaf and blinded their sight," because that applies to one for whom no guidance had preceded. The noble verb was ascribed to Allah, Exalted, in His saying: ﴿Then Allah turned to them﴾, and it was not said "then they repented," to show concern for them and His kindness toward them, Exalted. In the conjunction with "fa" (then) there is evidence that their disobedience and misguidance followed their thinking; and in the conjunction with "thumma" (then) there is evidence that they persisted in misguidance for a period until Allah turned to them. Al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab read "'umu" and "summu" with a damma on the ayn and sad and with a light mim, from "'amu", following the pattern of "zukima al-rajulu" and "azkamahu", and "humma" and "ahammahu". One does not say "zakamahu Allah" nor "hammahu Allah", just as one does not say "umituhu" nor "summitu-hu". These are verbs that came in the passive form whose subject is not named, and they are transitive triliteral; when they are made active they become intransitive; when you want to make them active and transitive you add the hamzah of transport (hamzat al-tanaqqul), which is a strange kind in verbs. Al-Zamakhshari said: "'Umu" and "summu", with a damma, on the assumption of "'amahum Allah" and "sammahum", i.e., He struck them with blindness and deafness, as one says "nazaktuhu" when you strike him with a spear (nayzak), and "rakibtuhu" when you strike him with your knee. End of quotation. The nominative "kathir" is in apposition (badal) to the pronoun. They permitted that it be nominative as the subject (fa'il), with the waw being a sign of the plural and not a pronoun, according to the dialect of "akaluni al-baragith" (the fleas ate me), but that is not appropriate because this dialect is rare. It was said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being "hum", i.e., the blindness and deafness are many of them. It was said: it is a subject, and the clause before it is in the position of the predicate. This was judged weak, because the verb has already occupied its place, so it is not intended to be delayed. The preferred reading is the first parsing. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "kathiran" with the accusative.

﴿And Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾ This contains a severe threat, and it is fitting to end the verse with this sentence containing "Basir" (Seeing), since before it came "fa-'amu" (they became blind).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 5, verses 72–73:**

﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary."﴾ The explanation of this sentence has already been given. Those who say this are the Ya'qubiyya (the Jacobites). They claim that Allah, exalted is He, manifested Himself in the person of ʿIsa (Jesus), peace be upon him.

﴿And the Messiah said, "O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord."﴾ Allah, exalted is He, refuted their statement by means of the words of the one whom they claim to be God, namely ʿIsa, that there is no difference between him and them, in that they are all sustained (marbubun). He commanded them to devote worship sincerely (to Allah), and He drew attention to the attribute that necessitates worship, which is lordship (al-rububiyya). In this there is a refutation of them regarding the corruption of their claim: the one whom they exalt and whose rank they raise above what is not fitting for him refutes their statement. What Allah, exalted is He, mentioned about him is also recorded in their Gospel, which they read but do not act upon, namely the words of the Messiah: "O assembly of the children of the baptism (al-maʿmudiyya)." In another narration: "O assembly of the peoples, arise, let us go to my Father and your Father, and my God and your God, and my Savior and your savior."

﴿Indeed, whoever associates others with Allah, Allah has forbidden him Paradise, and his refuge is the Fire.﴾ The apparent meaning is that this is from the words of the Messiah, so it falls under the (Messiah's) saying. In it is the greatest deterrent from worshipping (others besides Allah), for he informed that whoever worships other than Allah, Allah has barred him from the abode of those who devoted worship to Him alone, and made his refuge the Fire.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with.﴾ [an-Nisa 4:48] It has been said that this is a separate statement from the speech of Allah, exalted is He, informing of this by way of warning and threat. And in the authentic hadith from the narration of ʿItban ibn Malik, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Indeed, Allah has forbidden the Fire for whoever says 'There is no god but Allah,' seeking by that the Face of Allah."

﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.﴾ Its apparent meaning is that it is from the words of ʿIsa. He informed them that whoever transgresses and places a thing in other than its proper place, there is no helper for him and no one to assist him in what he has fabricated and invented. In this is a deterrent for them from what they have adopted concerning their claim that he is God, and that it is wrongdoing when they make what is impossible in reason a necessity that must occur; or (the meaning is) that there is no helper for him and no one to save him from the punishment of Allah in the Hereafter. It is also possible that this is from the speech of Allah, exalted is He, informing that they wronged and deviated from the truth regarding the matter of ʿIsa and their fabrication against him, so there is no helper for them in that.

﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three."﴾ These are the Malakiyya (the Melkites) among the Christians, who hold to the Trinity. The apparent meaning of His saying "the third of three" is "one of three gods." The exegetes said: they intended by this that Allah, exalted is He, ʿIsa and his mother are three gods, and this is reinforced by: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:116]; ﴿He has not taken a companion or a son﴾ [al-Jinn 72:3]; ﴿How can He have a son when He has no companion?﴾ [al-Anʿam 6:101]; ﴿Allah has not taken any son, and there was not with Him any god﴾ [al-Muʾminun 23:91]. The theologians (al-mutakallimun) related from the Christians that they say: one essence (jawhar), three hypostases (aqanim): Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (ruh qudus). These three are one God, just as the sun comprises the disc, the ray, and the heat. By "Father" they mean the essence (al-dhat), by "Son" the Word (al-kalima), and by "Spirit" the life (al-hayah). They affirmed the essence, the Word, and the life, and they said: the Word, which is the speech of Allah, mixed with the body of ʿIsa in the manner of water mixing with wine, or milk mixing with water. They claimed that the Father is God, the Son is God, the Spirit is God, and all of them are one God. This is clearly known to be false by the immediate judgment of reason: three cannot be one, and one cannot be three. In Arabic, in the phrase "thalith thalatha" (third of three), only the genitive construction (idafa) is permissible, because you do not say "thallathtu al-thalatha" (I made the three into a third). Ahmad ibn Yahya Thaʿlab (the grammarian) permitted the accusative (nasb) for the word that follows an active participle agreeing with it in form, and they refuted him by treating it like an active participle with a differing number, as in: "rabiʿu thalatha" (fourth of three), and this is not like it, for you say "rabbaʿtu al-thalatha," meaning: I made them four by means of you.

﴿And there is no god except one God.﴾ Its meaning is: there does not exist any god in existence except one characterized by oneness (al-wahdaniyya). He emphasized this by the addition of min (the particle "min," used for universal negation), and by restricting His divinity to the attribute of oneness. The word "ilah" (god) in "illa ilah wahid" is raised (marfuʿ) as a substitute (badal) in agreement with the place of the preceding "ilah." Al-Kisaʾi permitted agreeing with it in the form (of the word, i.e., genitive), because he permits the addition of min in an obligatory position. The sense is: "There is no god in existence except one God," that is, one described as unique, having no second, and He is Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And if they do not desist from what they say, a painful punishment will befall those among them who disbelieved.﴾ That is, from what they fabricate and believe concerning ʿIsa, that he is Allah, or that he is the third of three. He threatened them with the infliction of a painful punishment, in this world by captivity and killing, and in the Hereafter by eternal abiding in the Fire. He placed the threat before the argument from the marks of createdness (simat al-hudooth), for the sake of emphasis in deterrence; that is: this statement is at the extreme of corruption, such that intellects do not differ regarding its corruption, and therefore He first threatened punishment upon it, then followed the threat with an argument from the marks of createdness to demonstrate its falsity.

The lam in ﴿la-yamassanna﴾ is the answer (jawab) of an omitted oath that precedes the conditional particle. This construction most often occurs when in (the conditional particle) is accompanied by the lam that signals the omitted oath, as in His saying: ﴿If the hypocrites do not desist, and those in whose hearts is a disease, and the agitators in Madinah, We will surely incite you against them﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:60]. A parallel to this verse is: ﴿And if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-Aʿraf 7:23], and similar to it: ﴿And if you obey them, indeed you are associators﴾ [al-Anʿam 6:121]. The fact that in comes without a fa' (the particle of consequence) is evidence that there is an omitted oath before in, for were it not for the intention of an oath, he would have said: "fa-innakum la-mushrikun." (The phrase) "alladhina kafaru" means: those who persisted in this belief. He used the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, since the connection would have been achieved by "la-yamassanna-hum," in order to repeat the testimony against them of disbelief in His saying "Certainly they have disbelieved" (laqad kafara), and to inform that they were in a state of disbelief, since He placed the verb within the relative clause (silat alladhina), and this (construction) requires that it be known to the listener, settled, and established for them. The "min" in "minhum" is partitive (lil-tabʿid), that is: those among them. The connection is achieved by the pronoun, as if it were said: "those among them who disbelieved," and not all of them remained upon disbelief; rather, many of them repented from Christianity. Whoever holds that min can denote the kind (li-bayan al-jins) permits that here, and compares it with His saying: ﴿So avoid the filth of idols﴾ [al-Hajj 22:30].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 74:

﴿Will they not turn in repentance to Allah and seek His forgiveness?﴾ This is an act of gentleness toward them and an invitation to disavow that monstrous statement, after He had repeatedly declared to them the testimony of disbelief. The fa' in afa-la (afalā) is for conjunction (al-'atf); it has come between the interrogative hamza and the negating lā, and the underlying form is fa-a-lā. According to the method of al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH), it conjoins one verb to another, as if the intended sense were: "Will they remain upon disbelief, and so not repent?" The meaning is one of wonder at the absence of their repentance and their failure to seek forgiveness, though they are the most deserving of people of that, because their disbelief is the most reprehensible form of disbelief and the most scandalous in its corruption of belief, so He marvels that they do not repent of this grave sin. Al-Farra' (d. 207 AH) said: it is an interrogative whose meaning is a command, like His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91]. He said: it has the sense of a command because what is understood from the form is a request for repentance and an urging toward it, so its meaning is: "Repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness for your sin." Both of these views are untenable. End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the Majestic and Exalted showed gentleness toward them by urging them to repentance and to seeking forgiveness. End of quote. What they mentioned concerning urging and exhortation to repentance holds in terms of meaning, not in terms of the literal indication of the wording, because afa-la is not the same as alā, which is the particle of urging and exhortation.

﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ He, exalted is He, drew attention to these two attributes by which the acceptance of repentance and forgiveness of the sin are attained. The meaning is: how could repentance for this sin and the seeking of forgiveness fail to occur, when the One from whom it is sought is characterized by complete forgiveness and vast mercy toward these people and others?

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 5, verse 75:**

﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger; messengers had passed away before him.﴾ When he refuted the Christians' first claim with the words of the Messiah, ﴿Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord﴾ (Al-Ma'idah: 72), and their second claim with his words, ﴿There is no god except One God﴾ (Al-Ma'idah: 73), He established his messengerhood in the form of restriction (qasr). That is: the Messiah, son of Mary, is not anything of what the Christians claim, namely that he is God, or that he is one of three gods. Rather, he is a messenger of the same kind as the messengers who passed away and preceded him. He came with signs from Allah as they came. If he revived the dead and healed the blind and the leper by his hand, then Moses had already turned his staff into a moving serpent, split the sea, and obliterated (Pharaoh's) people by his hand. If he was created without a male, then Adam was created without a male or a female. In His saying, ﴿no more than a messenger﴾, there is a refutation of the Jews, who claimed that he was a liar in his claim to messengerhood, and who claimed that he was not of legitimate birth. Hattan read: "min qablihi rusulun" with indefinite nouns.

﴿And his mother was a siddiqah (a woman of great truthfulness)﴾. This form (fi'ilah) is one of the intensive patterns, and the more apparent view is that it derives from the bare triliteral root, since patterns of this kind derived from it include sikkit (very silent), sikkir (very drunk), shirrib (heavy drinker), and tibbikh (excellent cook), from the verbs sakata, sakira, shariba, and tabakha. A pattern built from a transitive triliteral verb does not govern an object in the way that fa'ul, fa''al, and mif'al do. So one does not say "Zayd shirrib al-ma'" (Zayd drinks much water), as one says "darrab Zayd" (Zayd strikes much) with an object. The meaning is the report about her as being very truthful. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may also be from taṣdiq (affirmation/believing), and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq was named by it. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention anything other than that it is from taṣdiq. This view contradicts the apparent meaning of this pattern. Al-Zamakhshari said: "And his mother was a siddiqah," meaning: his mother is no more than one of the women who affirmed the prophets, the believing women who believed in them. Their status is no more than the status of two humans, one of whom is a prophet and the other a companion, so how did the matter of the two of them become confused for you, so that you described them with what was not ascribed to any other prophets and their companions, when there is no distinction or difference between them and others in any respect? End of quotation. In this there is an imposition on the wording of the Qur'an of what is not in it. Among that is that His saying "and his mother was a siddiqah" contains only a report about her with the attribute of great truthfulness, but he made it a case of restriction, saying: "his mother is no more than one of the affirming women," and so on. This is his habit: he imposes on the words of the Qur'an what they do not indicate. Al-Hasan said: she affirmed Gabriel, peace be upon him, when he came to her, as Allah the Exalted related of her: ﴿And she affirmed the words of her Lord and His scriptures﴾ (At-Tahrim: 12). It was said: she affirmed the signs of her Lord and what her son reported. It was said: she was named thus for the extent of her truthfulness in her state with Allah, and her truthfulness in clearing herself of what the Jews accused her of. It was said: describing her as siddiqah does not indicate that she was a prophetess, since it is a rank that does not necessarily entail prophethood. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So those will be with those whom Allah has blessed, of the prophets and the siddiqun﴾ (An-Nisa': 69). Among that is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. And the angels speaking to a human does not necessarily entail that he is a prophet, since the angels spoke to people who were not prophets, as in the hadith of the three: the one with the bald head (al-Aqra'), the blind man, and the leper. Likewise Mary.

(﴿They both used to eat food﴾). This is an indication of the mark of createdness (huduth), and a distancing from what the Christians believed about them concerning divinity. Whoever needs food and what follows from it of accidents is only a composite body made of bone, flesh, veins, nerves, humors, and other things, and that indicates a created, composed, and governed thing like other bodies. There is no need to say, as the phrase "they both used to eat food" suggests, that it is a metaphor (kinayah) for their excretion, even if a group of exegetes said so. Rather, it is only an indication of the marks of createdness. The need for nourishment, which living beings require in their existence, is removed from God. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He feeds but is not fed﴾ (Al-An'am: 14). Although the need to eat food entails excretion, this is not what is intended by the wording, nor is it a metaphor for that. This sentence is a resumed report about the Messiah and his mother, indicating, as we mentioned, the marks of createdness, and that they both share this with people. This sentence has no place in grammatical analysis (i'rab, the grammatical parsing of words).

(﴿Look how We make the signs clear to them﴾) i.e., the clear proofs that show the falsity of what they believed. This is a command to the Prophet, ﷺ. Within that is also a command to his community, regarding the misguidance of these people and their distance from accepting what they were warned about.

(﴿Then look how they are turned away﴾). He repeated the command to look because the object of looking differs. The first is an observation of His, may He be exalted, making the signs clear to them and explaining them in such a way that no confusion arises with them. The second command is to look at how they are turned away from listening to the truth and reflecting upon it, or at how they reverse what has been made clear to them into its opposite. These are two matters of wonder. The particle "thumma" (then) is used to express the delay between the two wonders. It is as if it requires wonder at the clarifying and explaining of the signs, and then one looks at the state of the one to whom they were explained, and sees his turning away from the signs as more wondrous than their clarification. Since clarifying them entails that they become clear to them and that they return to them, their being turned away from them is more wondrous.

Say: "Do you worship, besides Allah, that which holds no power to harm you or to benefit you?" When He had shown, by the evidence of transmitted report and of reason, that divinity is not in Isa, and when He had threatened them and then invited them to repentance and seeking forgiveness, He rebuked them and denounced them from another angle: his inability and lack of power to repel harm or bring benefit. Whoever cannot defend himself is more deserving of being unable to defend you. The address is to the Christians: He forbids them from worshipping Isa and others, and states that what they worship besides Allah is equal to them in incapacity and lack of power. The meaning: that which does not possess for you the bringing of any good or benefit. It has been said: He expressed it with "ma" (what) as an alert to the earliest of his states, for there passed over him periods of the state of gestation in which he could not be described as rational, and one whose description is such, how could he be a god? Or because it is an ambiguous (mubham) term, as Sibawayh said. "Ma" is an ambiguous term that applies to everything, or it is intended to refer to what is worshipped besides Allah among those who have reason and those who do not. He expressed it with "ma," giving precedence to the non-rational, since most of what is worshipped besides Allah is non-rational, such as idols and images. Or the kind is intended: that is, the kind which does not possess for you harm or benefit, as in His saying: ﴿So marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [An-Nisa: 3], meaning the good kind. Since their associating partners with Allah involved both speech and belief, the verse closes with His saying: ﴿And Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, meaning: All-Hearing of your words, All-Knowing of your belief and what your intentions harbor. In reporting about Him with these two attributes there is a threat and a warning regarding what they say and believe. The verse includes a denunciation of them, in that they worshipped besides Him one who is characterized by incapacity to repel harm or bring benefit. It has been said: and one over whom periods have passed in which he neither hears nor knows; and they left the One who is capable absolutely, the All-Hearing of voices, the All-Knowing of intentions.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 77:

﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion beyond the truth."﴾ Its apparent meaning is an address to the People of the Scripture present at the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it also encompasses those who came after them. Since the discussion had already covered the falsehoods of the Jews and the falsehoods of the Christians, both groups were gathered together in the prohibition against exaggeration (ghuluw) in religion. The phrase "beyond the truth" (ghayr al-haqq) is in the accusative, and it refers to the false exaggeration. The religion meant here is not what they adhere to, but rather the true religion brought by Musa and Isa. Al-Zamakhshari said: Exaggeration in religion is of two kinds: true exaggeration, which is to investigate its realities, probe its remote meanings, and strive to obtain its proofs, as the theologians of the People of Justice and Monotheism (ahl al-'adl wa'l-tawhid) do; and false exaggeration, which is to go beyond the truth and transgress it by turning away from the evidences and following doubtful analogies, as the people of desires and innovations (ahl al-ahwa' wa'l-bida') do. End of quotation. The People of Justice and Monotheism are, in his view, the leaders of the Mu'tazilah, while the people of desires and innovations, according to him, are the People of the Sunnah and everyone other than the Mu'tazilah. Among the exaggeration of the Jews is their denial of the prophethood of Isa and their claim about him that he is God. Among the exaggeration of the Christians is what has already passed concerning the belief of some of them about him that he is God, and of others that he is one of three gods. The accusative of "ghayr" here is in the position of an attribute; that is, an exaggeration other than the truth. Whoever holds that it is an exception (istithna') of the connected type is far from the mark, and so is whoever holds that it is an exception and supposes the sentence to be: "But the truth, follow it."

﴿And do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before and led many astray and strayed from the sound way.﴾ These people are the forebears of the Jews and the Christians. They went astray themselves and led others astray in large numbers. Then he specified what they strayed from, which is the straight way that is the middle course in religion and its best, with neither excess nor deficiency, but a balanced, moderate, choice path. It has been said: the address is to the Christians, and this is the apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's words. He said: "They had gone astray before" refers to their leaders in Christianity, who were upon error before the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ); "and led many astray" refers to those who followed them in the doctrine of the Trinity; and "strayed from the sound way" refers to their going astray when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent, when they denied him, envied him, and rebelled against him. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this address is to the Christians who exaggerated concerning Isa, and the people are those whom the Christians were forbidden to follow in their desires. What led to this interpretation is that the Christians, in their exaggeration, were not following the desires of the Children of Israel; rather they were in opposition to them in statements, and they only came together in following a point of desire. So the verse is like your saying to one whom you blame for a crookedness: "This is the way of so-and-so," representing him by another who has become crooked in some kind of crookedness, even though their circumstances differ. God, exalted is He, described the Jews as having gone astray long ago and as having led many of their followers astray, then He emphasized the matter by repeating His words: "and strayed from the sound way." Some interpreters took the meaning to be: O People of the Scripture from among the Christians, do not follow the desires of these Jews who went astray before; that is, their forebears went astray before the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ), and they led many of the hypocrites astray, and they strayed from the sound way now after the truth has become clear. End of quotation. There is no need to take the speech away from its apparent sense, namely that it is an address to the People of the Scripture, both the two groups of Jews and Christians, and that His words "a people" refer to their forebears. The one who deviates from the truth often excuses himself by saying he is upon the religion and way of his father, as they said: "Indeed we found our fathers upon a community" (Az-Zukhruf: 22). So they were forbidden to follow their forebears. The indefinite form "a people" carries a sense of belittling them. What al-Zamakhshari went to is a restriction of a general statement without a reason calling for it. What Ibn 'Atiyyah went to is likewise a restriction and a remote interpretation in His words "do not follow the desires of a people," holding that the intended people are the Jews and that the meaning is: do not be upon desire as the Jews were upon desire, because the apparent sense is the prohibition against following the desires of those people. Whoever holds that the first going astray is from the religion and the second is from the path to Paradise is far from the mark.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 78–79:

﴿Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed upon the tongue of David and Jesus, son of Mary.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "They were cursed in every tongue. They were cursed in the time of Moses in the Tawrah (Torah), in the time of David in the Zabur (Psalms), in the time of Jesus in the Injil (Gospel), and in the time of Muhammad in the Qur'an." Ibn Jurayj related that their curse upon the tongue of David was accompanied by their being transformed into swine. This occurred because David passed by a group of people who were in a house, and he said: "Who is in the house?" They replied: "Swine," meaning that they were hidden. He said: "O Allah, (make them) swine," and they became swine. Then Jesus invoked a curse upon those who slandered him and his mother, and he cursed them. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that upon the tongue of David, the People of the Sabbath (Ashab al-Sabt) were cursed, and upon the tongue of Jesus, those who disbelieved after the Table (al-Ma'idah) were cursed.

Most of the exegetes said: When the people of Ayla (Eilat) transgressed on the Sabbath, David said: "O Allah, curse them and make them a sign," and they were transformed into apes. And when the companions of Jesus disbelieved after the Table, Jesus said: "O Allah, punish whoever disbelieved after eating from the Table with a punishment You have not inflicted upon anyone among the worlds, and curse them as You cursed the People of the Sabbath," so they became swine. They numbered five thousand men, among whom there was no woman and no child.

Al-Asamm and others said: David and Jesus gave glad tidings of Muhammad (ﷺ), and they cursed whoever denied him. It was also said: They invoked a curse upon whoever disobeyed them and cursed him. It is reported that David said: "O Allah, let them wear the curse like a cloak and like a belt around the loins. O Allah, make them a sign and an example for Your creation."

[p. 540] The apparent meaning of the verse, in its report about the forefathers of the Jews and the Christians, is that they are accursed. The passive construction of the verb allows that Allah, the Exalted, is the One Who curses them upon the tongues of David and Jesus, and it also allows that the two of them are the ones who curse them. Since they used to boast of their forefathers and that they were the children of the prophets, they were informed that the disbelievers among them are cursed upon the tongues of their prophets. Al-la'nah (the curse) is expulsion from the mercy of Allah. The verse does not indicate that the curse is accompanied by transformation (maskh).

The more eloquent usage is that when the two parts of a compound are separated, the singular form is preferred over both the dual and the plural forms. Accordingly, the phrase ﴿'ala lisan﴾ (upon the tongue) came in the singular, and it did not come as ﴿'ala lisanay﴾ (upon the two tongues) of David and Jesus, nor as ﴿'ala alsinat﴾ (upon the tongues) of David and Jesus. But if the two components were not separated, the plural form would be preferred over the dual and the singular, as in His saying: ﴿فَقَدْ صَغَتْ قُلُوبُكُما﴾ (your two hearts have indeed inclined) [al-Tahrim: 4]. The word lisan (tongue) here refers to the organ, not to language; that is, the one who utters their curse is David and Jesus.

﴿ذَلِكَ بِما عَصَوْا﴾ (That was because they disobeyed). That is, that curse was due to their disobedience. This was mentioned for emphasis, since the cause of the curse had already been understood by attributing it to those to whom the descriptive term indicating causation (al-'illiyyah) applies, namely "those who disbelieved." It is like saying: "The adulterer was stoned," whereby it is understood that the cause was fornication. Likewise, the cause of the curse is disbelief, but it was emphasized by mentioning it a second time in His saying: "That was because they disobeyed."

﴿وكانُوا يَعْتَدُونَ﴾ (and they used to transgress). This may be coordinated with "they disobeyed," so that it is interpreted as a verbal noun; that is, "and by their being transgressors," they exceed the limit in disobedience and disbelief and reach its furthest extent. It may also be a resumed statement from Allah that transgression was their habit and their condition. What follows supports this as an explanation, namely His saying: ﴿كانُوا لا يَتَناهَوْنَ عَنْ مُنْكَرٍ فَعَلُوهُ﴾ (They did not forbid one another from any wrong they committed). Its apparent meaning is the reciprocal form with the sense of mutual participation; that is, they did not forbid one another. This is because they combined committing wrong, openly displaying it, and not forbidding it. When disobedience is committed and within the servant's capacity, it is fitting that he conceal it. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever among you is afflicted with any of these filthy things, let him conceal it." But when it is committed openly and they agree not to denounce it, this becomes an incitement to commit it and a cause that stirs up its spread and multiplication.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: How did the abandonment of forbidding wrong come to be explained as disobedience?" I answer: Because Allah, the Exalted, commanded forbidding wrong, so neglecting it is disobedience, and that is transgression, since forbidding wrong closes the door to corruption.

In the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the first deficiency that entered the Children of Israel was that a man would meet another man and say: 'O such-and-such, fear Allah and leave off what you are doing, for it is not lawful for you.' Then he would meet him the next day, and he would still be in the same state, yet that would not prevent him from being his table companion, his drinking companion, and his sitting companion. When they did that, Allah struck their hearts, some against others. Then he recited: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed...﴾ up to ﴿...defiantly disobedient﴾. Then he said: 'By Allah, you must enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and you must seize the wrongdoer by the hand and force him back to the truth by force; otherwise Allah will strike the hearts of some of you against others, and He will curse you as He cursed them.'" Related by al-Tirmidhi. The meaning of "la-ta'tur-unnahu" is "you must turn him back."

It was also said that the reciprocal form here has the meaning of the reflexive form (al-iftial), as one says: "He desisted from the matter" (intaha 'an al-amr) and "he refrained from it" (tanaha 'anhu) when he restrained himself from it, just as one says: "They crossed over" (tajawazu) and "they crossed over" (ijtawazu). The meaning is: They did not refrain from any wrong. The apparent sense of "wrong" (munkar) is that it is not specified, so it may be applied to any wrong they committed. It was also said: It refers to hunting fish on the Sabbath. It was said: It refers to accepting bribes in judgment. It was said: It refers to usury and the sale of fats. The meaning of "refraining from what they did" is not valid as such; rather either the meaning is that they intended to do it, as you see the tools and signs of wickedness being prepared and made ready, and this is what is denounced, or it is elliptical, meaning: a repetition of a wrong, or the like of a wrong.

﴿لَبِئْسَ ما كانُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ (Surely evil is what they used to do). This is a censure of what proceeded from them of committing wrong and of their not forbidding one another from it. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is an expression of wonder at the evil of their deed, emphasized by an oath. So how grievous it is for the Muslims in their turning away from the door of forbidding wrong and their little concern for it, as if it were not part of the religion of Islam at all, despite what they recite from the Book of Allah and the emphases it contains on this matter. End of quotation.

The scholars of the discipline said: It is not a condition for the one who forbids that he be free of sin; rather, sinners forbid one another. Some of the jurists of principles (usul al-fiqh) said: It is an obligation upon those who indulge in drinking vessels (al-kuus) to forbid one another, and they took evidence from this verse, because His saying "they did not forbid one another" and "what they committed" requires their joint participation in the act, and He censured them for abandoning forbidding.

In the hadith: "The punishment will continue to be withheld from the servants so long as they conceal the disobediences of Allah. But when they display them openly and do not denounce them, they deserve the punishment of Allah, the Exalted."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 80–81:

﴿You see many of them take as allies those who disbelieve﴾ The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "minhum" (of them) refers to the Children of Israel. Muqatil said: "many of them" refers to those who were in the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ), who took the disbelievers and idol-worshippers as allies, and the intended ones are Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, who sought the aid of the polytheists against the Messenger (ﷺ). On this view, "tara" (you see) is visual (basariyyah). It may also be of the sight of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb), in which case what is meant may be their forefathers; that is, "you see now" when We have informed you. It was also said: "many of them" refers to the hypocrites among the People of the Book who took the polytheists as allies. It was also said: this is a discontinuous statement, unconnected to the mention of the Children of Israel, and it refers to the hypocrites who took the Jews as allies. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

﴿Evil indeed is what their souls have sent forward for them, that Allah has become wrathful toward them﴾ The discussion of the i'rab (grammatical analysis) has already passed. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding His words "an sakhita Allahu" (that Allah has become wrathful): that it is the object of dispraise (al-makhsus bi'l-dhamm), and its position is in the nominative, as if it were said: "Evil is their provision for the Hereafter: the wrath of Allah upon them," and the meaning is "what causes the wrath of Allah upon them." End of quote. This i'rab is valid only according to the view of al-Farra' and al-Farisi that "ma" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), or according to the view of those who take the pronoun in "bi'sa" (the verb of dispraise) and make "ma" a specifier (tamyiz) meaning "shay'an" (a thing), with "qaddamat" as an attribute of the specifier. As for the view of Sibawayh, this does not hold, because "ma" for him is a complete noun, definite, meaning "the thing," and the clause after it is an attribute of the omitted object of praise/dispraise; the estimate is: "Evil is the thing their souls have sent forward for them." Thus according to this, "an sakhita Allah" is in the position of nominative as a substitute (badal) for "ma." End of quote. This is not valid, whether "ma" is relative or complete, because the substitute takes the place of what it substitutes, and "an sakhita" cannot be the subject (fa'il) of "bi'sa," since the subject of "ni'ma" and "bi'sa" cannot be "an" with a verb. It was also said: "an sakhita" is in the accusative position as a substitute for the omitted pronoun in "qaddamat"; that is, "qaddamathu" (they sent it forward), as you say: "The one whom you struck Zayd, your brother," meaning "you struck him, Zayd." It was also said: it is on the dropping of the lam; that is, "li-an sakhita" (because He became wrathful).

﴿And in the punishment they will abide forever﴾ When He mentioned what they had sent forward to the Hereafter as provision, and dispraised it in the strongest terms, He mentioned what they had come to, which is the punishment, and that they would abide in it forever, and that it is the fruit of Allah's wrath, just as wrath is the fruit of disobedience. Had they believed in Allah, the Prophet, and what was sent down to him, they would not have taken them as allies—if what is meant by His words "you see many of them" is their forefathers; then the Prophet is Dawud and 'Isa; or if it refers to the contemporaries of the Messenger, then the Prophet is Muhammad (ﷺ) and "those who disbelieve" are the idol-worshippers. The meaning: had they believed with pure faith, without hypocrisy, since allying with the disbelievers is evidence of hypocrisy. The apparent reading of the pronoun in "kanu" (they were) and the subject pronoun in "ma attakhadhuhum" (they did not take them) is that it refers to "kathiran minhum" (many of them); and the object pronoun refers to "alladhina kafaru" (those who disbelieve). Al-Qaffal offered another view: that the meaning is: had these who turned to the polytheists believed in Allah and Muhammad (ﷺ), these Jews would not have taken them as allies. The first view is preferable, because the discourse is about "many of them," so keeping the pronouns in one consistent reference is preferable to varying them. The answer to "law" (if) is negated with "ma," without a lam, which is the most eloquent form; attaching the lam to it is rare, as in the verse of the poet:

"Had knowledge been a means of getting what sustains life, you would not have obtained from this world even a date-stone's worth."

﴿But many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ He specified the majority with defiant disobedience, since among them there is a minority who believed. The subject reported about them first is "the many," and the pronouns after it refer to it. The meaning is not "but many of that many," but when the phrase grew long it was repeated with its own wording; it is from placing the explicit noun in the position of the pronoun, since the context would have been: "they did not take them as allies, but they are defiantly disobedient." So the explicit noun was placed in the position of this pronoun.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 80–81:

﴿You see many of them take as allies those who disbelieve﴾ The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "minhum" (of them) refers to the Children of Israel. Muqatil said: "many of them" refers to those who were in the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ), who took the disbelievers and idol-worshippers as allies, and the intended ones are Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, who sought the aid of the polytheists against the Messenger (ﷺ). On this view, "tara" (you see) is visual (basariyyah). It may also be of the sight of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb), in which case what is meant may be their forefathers; that is, "you see now" when We have informed you. It was also said: "many of them" refers to the hypocrites among the People of the Book who took the polytheists as allies. It was also said: this is a discontinuous statement, unconnected to the mention of the Children of Israel, and it refers to the hypocrites who took the Jews as allies. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

﴿Evil indeed is what their souls have sent forward for them, that Allah has become wrathful toward them﴾ The discussion of the i'rab (grammatical analysis) has already passed. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding His words "an sakhita Allahu" (that Allah has become wrathful): that it is the object of dispraise (al-makhsus bi'l-dhamm), and its position is in the nominative, as if it were said: "Evil is their provision for the Hereafter: the wrath of Allah upon them," and the meaning is "what causes the wrath of Allah upon them." End of quote. This i'rab is valid only according to the view of al-Farra' and al-Farisi that "ma" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), or according to the view of those who take the pronoun in "bi'sa" (the verb of dispraise) and make "ma" a specifier (tamyiz) meaning "shay'an" (a thing), with "qaddamat" as an attribute of the specifier. As for the view of Sibawayh, this does not hold, because "ma" for him is a complete noun, definite, meaning "the thing," and the clause after it is an attribute of the omitted object of praise/dispraise; the estimate is: "Evil is the thing their souls have sent forward for them." Thus according to this, "an sakhita Allah" is in the position of nominative as a substitute (badal) for "ma." End of quote. This is not valid, whether "ma" is relative or complete, because the substitute takes the place of what it substitutes, and "an sakhita" cannot be the subject (fa'il) of "bi'sa," since the subject of "ni'ma" and "bi'sa" cannot be "an" with a verb. It was also said: "an sakhita" is in the accusative position as a substitute for the omitted pronoun in "qaddamat"; that is, "qaddamathu" (they sent it forward), as you say: "The one whom you struck Zayd, your brother," meaning "you struck him, Zayd." It was also said: it is on the dropping of the lam; that is, "li-an sakhita" (because He became wrathful).

﴿And in the punishment they will abide forever﴾ When He mentioned what they had sent forward to the Hereafter as provision, and dispraised it in the strongest terms, He mentioned what they had come to, which is the punishment, and that they would abide in it forever, and that it is the fruit of Allah's wrath, just as wrath is the fruit of disobedience. Had they believed in Allah, the Prophet, and what was sent down to him, they would not have taken them as allies—if what is meant by His words "you see many of them" is their forefathers; then the Prophet is Dawud and 'Isa; or if it refers to the contemporaries of the Messenger, then the Prophet is Muhammad (ﷺ) and "those who disbelieve" are the idol-worshippers. The meaning: had they believed with pure faith, without hypocrisy, since allying with the disbelievers is evidence of hypocrisy. The apparent reading of the pronoun in "kanu" (they were) and the subject pronoun in "ma attakhadhuhum" (they did not take them) is that it refers to "kathiran minhum" (many of them); and the object pronoun refers to "alladhina kafaru" (those who disbelieve). Al-Qaffal offered another view: that the meaning is: had these who turned to the polytheists believed in Allah and Muhammad (ﷺ), these Jews would not have taken them as allies. The first view is preferable, because the discourse is about "many of them," so keeping the pronouns in one consistent reference is preferable to varying them.
