The answer to "law" (if) is negated with "ma," without a lam, which is the most eloquent form; attaching the lam to it is rare, as in the verse of the poet:

"Had knowledge been a means of getting what sustains life, you would not have obtained from this world even a date-stone's worth."

﴿But many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ He specified the majority with defiant disobedience, since among them there is a minority who believed. The subject reported about them first is "the many," and the pronouns after it refer to it. The meaning is not "but many of that many," but when the phrase grew long it was repeated with its own wording; it is from placing the explicit noun in the position of the pronoun, since the context would have been: "they did not take them as allies, but they are defiantly disobedient." So the explicit noun was placed in the position of this pronoun.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 82–86 (part 1 of 2):

(p-2) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿You will surely find the most intense of the people in enmity toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate others with Allah. And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say, "We are Christians." That is because among them are priests (qissisin) and monks (ruhban), and because they are not arrogant.﴾ ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they recognize. They say, "Our Lord, we have believed, so register us among the witnesses."﴾ ﴿And why should we not believe in Allah and in what has come to us of the truth, while we aspire that our Lord will admit us among the righteous people?﴾ ﴿So Allah rewarded them, for what they said, with gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they abide forever. That is the reward of the doers of good.﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieved and denied Our signs — those are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 87] ﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you as lawful and good, and fear Allah, in whom you are believers.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 88] ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what you have intended in oaths. So its expiation is the feeding of ten needy people from the average of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. But whoever does not find [the means], then fasting for three days. That is the expiation for your oaths when you have sworn. And guard your oaths. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may be grateful.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 89] ﴿O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificial] stones, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 90] ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to occur among you through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 91] ﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger and beware. But if you turn away, then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only clear notification.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 92] ﴿There is no blame upon those who have believed and done righteous deeds for what they have eaten, if they fear Allah and believe and do righteous deeds, then fear Allah and believe, then fear Allah and do good. And Allah loves the doers of good.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 93] ﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of game that your hands and spears can reach, that Allah may make evident who fears Him unseen. And whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 94] ﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram. And whoever of you kills it intentionally, its penalty is an equivalent of what he has killed from livestock, as judged by two just men among you, as an offering brought to the Ka'bah, or an expiation of feeding needy people, or the equivalent of that in fasting, that he may taste the consequence of his action. Allah has pardoned what is past, but whoever returns to it, Allah will take retribution from him. And Allah is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 95] ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food as provision for you and for travelers, but forbidden to you is the game of the land as long as you are in the state of ihram. And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 96]

Al-qass, with a fatha on the qaf, is the tracking of a thing. Ru'bah said:
﴾They woke, heedless of the qass of harm, walking gently, averting, and fleeing.﴿
It is said: qassa al-athar, he tracked the trace, and also qassahu. Al-qass: the head of the Christians in religion and knowledge, and its plural is qusus. He was named by the verbal noun because he tracks knowledge and religion. Likewise al-qissis is of the pattern fi'il, like al-shirrib. Its plural is formed with the waw and nun, and it is also pluralized as qasawisah. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:
﴾Had there been a return, the qasawisah would have remained, while God revives them, and the scriptures are in their hands.﴿
Al-Farra' said: it is like mahalibah; the sins multiplied, so one of them was replaced with a waw, meaning that its analogy is qasasah. Ibn 'Atiyyah claimed that al-qass, with fatha or kasra on the qaf, and al-qissis, are non-Arabic words that were Arabicized.

Al-tama' is close to hope. It is said of it: tami'a yatma'u tama'an, wa tamā'atan, wa tamā'iyatan. The poet said:
﴾Greedy to be forgiven, that the forgiver forgives the sin.﴾
The active participle is tami'.

Al-rijs is a name for everything that is loathed of action. It is said: rajasa al-rajulu yarjusu rajsan, if he did a foul deed. Its origin is from al-rijs, which is the intensity of sound in thunder. The reciter said:
﴾From every rajjas who drives the rijs.﴾
Ibn Duraid said: al-rijz is evil, al-rijs is punishment, and al-rakas is filth and stench, and al-rijs is said of both matters.

Al-rumh is known; its plural in the paucity form is arma', and in the abundance form is rimah. Rama-hu means he stabbed him with a spear. A rajul rami' means one who has a spear, and there is no verbal form for the meaning of "one who has a spear"; rather it is like laban and tamir. A bull rami' has two horns. Dhu al-Rummah said:
﴾And many a time we startled from a wild cow and a horned one, the lands of the world are not their lands.﴾
Al-rammah is one who makes spears and practices the craft of spear-making. Al-wabal: the evil of consequence. Mar'an wabil: one who is harmed by it after eating it. Al-barr: the opposite of the sea. Al-Layth said: it is used indefinitely, one says: "I sat barran and went out barran." Al-Azhari said: it is from the speech of the muwallads. In the hadith of Salman: "Indeed for every matter there is an inner and an outer," meaning by that the secret and the public, and this is from a change of the relative form.

* *

﴿You will surely find the most intense of the people in enmity toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate others with Allah.﴾ Qatadah said: it was revealed concerning some people of the People of the Book who were upon a law of what 'Isa had brought; they believed in the Messenger, so Allah praised them. It was said: they were al-Najashi and his companions, when Ja'far ibn Abi Talib recited to them Surah Maryam when he emigrated to Abyssinia, and they believed and their eyes overflowed with tears. It was also said: they were the delegation of al-Najashi with Ja'far to the Messenger ﷺ, and they were seventy, whom he sent to the Messenger, wearing woolen garments: two and sixty from Abyssinia and eight from Syria, and they were Buhayra the monk, Idris, Ashraf, Thumamah, Qutham, Duraid, and Ayman. The Messenger ﷺ recited Ya-Sin to them, and they wept and believed, and said: "This is similar to what was sent down to 'Isa." So Allah revealed this verse concerning them. It is narrated from Muqatil and al-Kalbi that they were forty from the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b from Najran, and eighty-two from Abyssinia, and sixty-eight from Syria.

It is narrated from Ibn Jubayr something close to this. The apparent meaning of "the Jews" is general, including whoever was in the presence of the Messenger from the Jews of Madinah and others, because they were accustomed to denying and killing the prophets, and to rebelliousness and sins, and they sensed the curse and the imposition of humiliation and destitution; thus their enmity, their plotting, their envy, and their malice were intensified. In a hadith: "No two Jews were alone with a Muslim except that they intended to kill him." In Allah's description of them as "most intense in enmity" there is an indication of the difficulty of their accepting the truth; therefore the conversion of Jews is rare. It was said: "the Jews" here refers to the Jews of Madinah, because they were the ones who backed the polytheists against the Muslims. The conjunction of "those who associate others with Allah" upon "the Jews" makes them followers of them in that, since the Jews were more intense in enmity, as they differed with the Muslims in the law, not in kind, since between them there are connected ties of kinship and close lineage, so kinship inclines them toward the Muslims in every state; and because they are not upon a law from Allah, they are quicker to believe than any of the Jews and Christians. They are conjoined here as they were conjoined in His saying: ﴿And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life, and of those who associate others with Allah﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 96]. The lam in "la-tajidanna" is the lam of the oath that is implied, to which the oath is attached.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is the lam of the beginning, but this is not acceptable. And "al-nas" here means the disbelievers; that is, you will surely find the most intense of the disbelievers in enmity.

﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say, "We are Christians."﴾ That is, they are gentler in disposition and nearer in friendliness. He did not describe them with affection itself; rather He made them nearer than the Jews and the polytheists. They have fidelity, and the four traits which 'Amr ibn al-'As mentioned in Sahih Muslim: they honor from the people of Islam whoever they sense in him religion and faith, and they hate the people of wickedness; when they make peace their peace is pure, and when they fight their fighting is only defense, because their law does not command them otherwise. When the Romans overcame Persia, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was pleased, because the People of the Book had prevailed over the people of fire-worship, and because the greater enemy was destroyed by the lesser enemy, since it was feared for the people of Islam. The Jews have none of the characteristics of the Christians; rather their nature is treachery and twisting with the tongue. In the midst of your kindness to a Jew, he is watching for what will ensnare you with it. Do you not see what the Exalted related about them: ﴿That is because they said, "There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75]. In His saying, "Those who said, 'We are Christians'," there is an indication that they do not adhere to the reality of Christianity; rather that is a saying from them and a claim. The first "for those who believed" is connected to "enmity," and the second to "affection." It was said: both are in the position of a qualifier, and describing the enmity as "most intense" and the affection as "nearest" is evidence of the difference of the two kinds in relation to the believers: that enmity is the most intense and most manifest of enmities, and that affection is nearer and easier. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the Christians are in a better state than the Jews and nearer to the believers in affection; and upon this apparent meaning the verse was explained by those whose statements we have examined.

Some of them said: it is not upon its apparent meaning; rather what is intended is that they have more causes of affection than the Jews, and that is a reproach of them, for whoever has many causes of affection, his abandonment of affection is more shameful. For this reason Abu Bakr al-Razi said: among the ignorant are those who think that in this verse there is praise of the Christians and information that they are better than the Jews, and it is not so, because what is in the verse of that is only a description of a people who have believed in Allah and the Messenger ﷺ, as is indicated by what He mentioned in the sequence of recitation of their informing about themselves of belief in Allah and the Messenger. It is known to everyone of sound understanding who reflects on the two statements of the two groups that the statement of the Christians is uglier, more impossible, and more evidently corrupt than the statement of the Jews, because the Jews acknowledge monotheism in general, though among them is a resemblance to some of what they believe of tashbih (anthropomorphism) in general of monotheism. End of the words of Abu Bakr al-Razi;

(p-5) and the apparent meaning is what the exegetes and others said: that the Christians, on the whole, are in a better state than the Jews, and the exegetes have already mentioned, in what preceded, what the Christians were distinguished by over the Jews: nobility of character and swift entry into Islam. The discourse does not arise on account of doctrines; it arose on account of the reaction of the Muslims. As for his saying, "because what is in the verse of that is only a description of a people who have believed in Allah and the Messenger," it is not as he mentioned; rather the beginning of the verse requires generality, because He said: ﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say, "We are Christians"﴾, then He informed that among this group are scholars, ascetics, humble people, quick to respond to Islam, and many who weep upon hearing the Qur'an, whereas the Jews are the opposite. And existence confirms the nearness of the Christians to the Muslims and the distance of the Jews.

﴿That is because among them are priests (qissisin) and monks (ruhban), and because they are not arrogant.﴾ The indication of "that" refers to the nearest affection based on it; that is, among them are scholars and worshippers, and they are a people in whom there is humility and submissiveness, and they are not arrogant. The Jews are contrary to that; there were never among them people of monasteries, nor of cloisters, nor of withdrawal from the world; rather they are magnifiers, overreaching for its acquisition, as if they did not believe in an afterlife, and for this reason no ascetic is seen among them. Al-ruhban is the plural of rahib, like faris and fursan, and al-rahb and al-rahbah are fear, dread. It was said: al-ruhban is a singular in the pattern of sultan; and they recited:
﴾Had she beheld the monks of a monastery on the heights, the monks would have come down walking and slipping.﴿

It is also narrated as ﴿ونَزَلْ﴾ (wa-nazal, "and descended"). The word *qissis* (priest) has already been explained in the vocabulary section. Ibn Zayd said: it is the head of the monks. It was also said: it is the scholar. It was also said: it is one who raises his voice in recitation. It was also said: it is the *siddiq* (the truthful one). In this explanation there is evidence of the sublimity of knowledge, that it is a path to guidance, that withdrawal (from worldly pursuits) has a good outcome, that it is a way to reflect on the end result with humility, and that it is a cause for exalting the one who affirms God's oneness, since he witnesses in himself and in every created thing that it is in need of the One who brings it into being. Thus he is held in high esteem by the Originator of all things, the Creator, ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflow with tears because of the truth they have recognized﴾. This is a description of tender hearts and of being moved by hearing the Qur'an.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to priests and monks in general, so it is a general statement, and it reports about them what occurs among some of them. This is like what happened to the Negus when Ja'far recited to him Surat Maryam up to His words ﴿That is Jesus, son of Mary﴾ [Maryam 19:34], and Surat Ta-Ha up to His words ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:9], and he wept. Likewise were his people who came as a delegation to the Messenger (ﷺ), when he recited Surat Ya-Sin to them, and they wept.

Ibn 'Atiyya said, in substance: the beginning of the verse is general regarding the Christians, and ﴿when they hear﴾ is general regarding those among the arrivals from the land of Abyssinia who believed, since not all Christians act in this way. Rather, they were the ones whom the Negus sent to see the Prophet (ﷺ) and to hear what he had. When they saw him and he recited the Qur'an to them, their eyes overflowed from fear of God, the Exalted. End of quote.

As-Suddi said: when they returned to the Negus, he believed and emigrated with those who were with him, and then he died on the way. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) prayed over him, and the Muslims prayed for forgiveness for him.

﴿تَرى﴾ (you see) is from direct sight. The overflowing was attributed to the eyes, although in reality it belongs to the tears, as the poet said:

*So the tears of my eyes overflowed out of longing*

This is a case of attributing the effect to the cause's sphere (*iqamat al-musabbab maqam al-sabab*), since the overflowing is a result of being full. The underlying sense is: "you see their eyes filling with tears until they overflow," because overflowing over the sides of a vessel arises from its being full. The poet said:

*Biting words come to me and they belittle them, and water fills the vessel until it brims over*

It is also possible that he attributed the overflowing to the eyes as a form of hyperbole in describing weeping, since when they overflow with tears, the eyes themselves are described as overflowing, by way of metaphor and exaggeration.

As for ﴿مِن﴾ in ﴿مِنَ الدَّمْعِ﴾ (from the tears), Abu al-Baqa' said: it has two possibilities. The first is that ﴿مِن﴾ indicates the starting point, meaning its overflowing is from the abundance of tears. The second is that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and the meaning is "overflowing, filled with tears, because of what they recognized of the truth." The meaning of "because of what they recognized" is "on account of what they came to know." And ﴿مِنَ الحَقِّ﴾ (of the truth) is a circumstantial clause from the omitted returning pronoun, or a circumstantial clause from the subject pronoun in ﴿عَرَفُوا﴾ (they recognized).

It was also said that ﴿مِن﴾ in ﴿مِنَ الدَّمْعِ﴾ has the sense of *ba'* (by), meaning "with tears." Az-Zamakhshari said: ﴿مِنَ الدَّمْعِ﴾ means "on account of weeping," from your saying "his eye wept tears (damaʿat dam'an)." If you ask: what is the difference between the first ﴿مِن﴾ and the second ﴿مِن﴾ in His words ﴿مِمّا عَرَفُوا مِنَ الحَقِّ﴾? I say: the first indicates the starting point, in that the overflowing of tears began and arose from knowing the truth, and it was on account of it and because of it. The second is to specify the relative clause, which is *ma 'arafu* (what they recognized). It may also carry the sense of partition (*tab'id*), meaning that they recognized some of the truth and it made them weep. End of quote.

The clause beginning with ﴿وإذا سَمِعُوا﴾ (and when they hear) may be a new independent sentence, and it may also be conjoined to the predicate of ﴿إنَّهم﴾ (indeed they).

It was read as ﴿تَرى أعْيُنَهُمْ﴾ in the passive form (*al-bina' lima lam yusamma fa'iluhu*).

﴿يَقُولُونَ رَبَّنا آمَنّا فاكْتُبْنا مَعَ الشّاهِدِينَ﴾ (They say: Our Lord, we have believed, so record us among the witnesses). By ﴿آمَنّا﴾ (we have believed) is meant: we have brought into being the particular faith of this Islamic community. As for ﴿الشّاهِدِينَ﴾ (the witnesses), Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jurayj and others said: they are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and they said this because they are witnesses over the other nations, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:143]. Az-Zamakhshari said: they said this because they found their mention in the Gospel in this way. End of quote. At-Tabari said: its meaning, if it were said, "its meaning is: with those who bear witness to Your oneness from the whole of creation, those who came before and those who came after," would be correct. It was also said: its meaning is: with those who bear witness to the truth. Az-Zajjaj said: by ﴿الشّاهِدِينَ﴾ is meant the prophets, the believers, and the recording in the Preserved Tablet. It was also said: its meaning is "record us," from the saying "so-and-so was enrolled in the army," meaning he became established.

﴿يَقُولُونَ﴾ (they say) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, as Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Baqa' said, but they did not specify that circumstance or the element that governs it. It is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿أعْيُنَهم﴾ (their eyes), because it is in the genitive by annexation and has no place of either nominative or accusative, except according to the view of those who treat the predicate as if it were the annexed noun, and that is a mistaken view. We have explained this in our book *Manhaj al-Salik*. Nor is it permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from the subject pronoun in ﴿عَرَفُوا﴾ (they recognized), because then it would be a restriction on the recognition, while they recognized the truth in this state and in others. So the better option is that it be an independent sentence. He, the Exalted, informed about them that they were engaged in this statement, and the meaning is that they recognized the truth with their hearts, and their tongues uttered it and affirmed it.

﴿وما لَنا لا نُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وما جاءَنا مِنَ الحَقِّ﴾ (And why should we not believe in God and in the truth that has come to us?). This is a rebuke and an expression of astonishment at the absence of faith from them despite the presence of its cause, which is the recognition of the truth. Az-Zamakhshari and At-Tibrizi said: the motivating cause of faith is the hope of entering among the righteous. The apparent meaning is that this statement is one they make to themselves, as a conversation with the self, to repel whispers and fleeting thoughts, since leaving one way and adopting another to which one was not raised is difficult and hard. Or it is the statement of some believers to others, also as a form of reassurance. Or their saying is by way of argument against the disbelievers who opposed them when they returned to them and blamed them for their faith; the meaning is: "what prevents us from believing in God alone?" The right course has become clear to us and the luminous truth has appeared.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Jews (*p-7*) rebuked them and blamed them, and they answered them with this. The clause ﴿لا نُؤْمِنُ﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and it is the intended element, and its mention is the point of the statement. This is like your saying: "Zayd came riding," as an answer to someone who asked: "Did Zayd come walking or riding?" The element governing it is that which the prepositional phrase depends on; that is, "what is it that becomes settled for us and is set down as the absence of faith from us?"

In the Codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: ﴿وما لَنا لا نُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وما أنْزَلَ عَلَيْنا رَبُّنا ونَطْمَعُ﴾ (And why should we not believe in God and in what our Lord has sent down to us, and we hope...). This must be understood as an explanation of His words ﴿and the truth that has come to us﴾, because it contradicts what the Muslims agreed upon in the consonantal text of the Codex (*sawad al-mushaf*).

﴿ونَطْمَعُ أنْ يُدْخِلَنا رَبُّنا مَعَ القَوْمِ الصّالِحِينَ﴾ (and we hope that our Lord will admit us among the righteous people). The best and easiest reading is that it is a new statement of information from them, that they are hopeful of God's favor to them in admitting them among the righteous. So the conjunction ﴿و﴾ connects one sentence to another. ﴿ما لَنا لا نُؤْمِنُ﴾ is not conjoined to ﴿نُؤْمِنُ﴾, nor to ﴿لا نُؤْمِنُ﴾, nor is the ﴿و﴾ the *waw* of circumstance. Ibn 'Atiyya did not mention any view other than this one.

Az-Zamakhshari said: the ﴿و﴾ in ﴿ونَطْمَعُ﴾ is the *waw* of circumstance, and the element governing the circumstance is the sense of the verb governing ﴿لا نُؤْمِنُ﴾, but restricted by the first circumstance, because if you removed it and said "what is it for us that we hope," it would not be a complete statement. End of quote.

What he mentioned, that the two circumstances share one governing element, which is the sense of the verb within the preposition *li* (for us), as if it were said: "what has happened to us, not believing, hoping?", is not good. This is because the sounder view is that the governing element may not govern two circumstances for one owner of the circumstance without a conjunctive particle, except for the elative form (*af'al al-tafdil*); the sounder view is that this is permissible with it. The owner of the circumstance here is one, namely the pronoun governed by the preposition *li* in *lana* (for us). Moreover, the ﴿و﴾ has entered upon the imperfect verb, and the *waw* of circumstance does not enter upon the imperfect except through interpretation, so it would be necessary to supply: "and we are hoping."

Az-Zamakhshari also said: it is permissible for ﴿ونَطْمَعُ﴾ to be a circumstance of ﴿لا نُؤْمِنُ﴾, on the basis that they were condemning themselves, because they do not affirm God's oneness, and yet they hope to be companions of the righteous. End of quote.

This is not a good view, because it involves the *waw* of circumstance entering upon the imperfect verb, which requires interpretation.

Az-Zamakhshari also said: it is permissible for it to be conjoined to ﴿لا نُؤْمِنُ﴾ in meaning, as if it were: "what is it for us that we do not combine between the Trinity and hope for the companionship of the righteous?" Or in meaning: "what is it for us that we do not combine the two by entering Islam, since the disbeliever should not hope for the companionship of the righteous." End of quote.

What appears to me is a view other than what they mentioned: that it is conjoined to ﴿نُؤْمِنُ﴾, on the basis that it is negated just as ﴿نُؤْمِنُ﴾ is negated. The estimated meaning is: "what is it for us that we do not believe and do not hope," so that there is a rebuke for the absence of their faith and the absence of their hope, although they are able to attain both: faith and the hope of entering among the righteous. The word ﴿مَعَ﴾ (with) remains in its usual sense of accompaniment, although it was also said that it means *fi* (in). The righteous are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), as Ibn 'Abbas said, or the Messenger and his companions, as Ibn Zayd said, or the earliest emigrants, as Muqatil said. It was also said that the estimated meaning is: "that He admit us to Paradise."

﴿فَأثابَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِما قالُوا جَنّاتٍ تَجْرِي مِن تَحْتِها الأنْهارُ خالِدِينَ فِيها وذَلِكَ جَزاءُ المُحْسِنِينَ﴾ (So God rewarded them for what they said with gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the reward of the good-doers). The apparent meaning is that the reward with what was mentioned is consequent upon mere saying. But belief must accompany the saying, and what shows that it is accompanied by belief is that He said ﴿مِمّا عَرَفُوا مِنَ الحَقِّ﴾, describing them as those who recognize, which indicates that the saying is conjoined with knowledge. He also said ﴿ذَلِكَ جَزاءُ المُحْسِنِينَ﴾ (That is the reward of the good-doers). Either this is placing an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun, to draw attention to this attribute in them and to indicate that they were rewarded because this attribute, which is the rank of excellence (*ihsan*), was present in them. This is the rank that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) explained with his words: "That you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, He sees you." There is no sincerity nor knowledge higher than this rank. Or it means generality, so that they are included among the good-doers, on the basis that this reward was not consequent upon mere verbal utterance. For this reason Az-Zamakhshari explained ﴿بِما قالُوا﴾ (for what they said) as: "for what they uttered of belief and sincerity," from your saying "this is so-and-so's saying," meaning his belief and what he holds to. End of quote.

They explained this saying by their words ﴿وما لَنا لا نُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ﴾ (why should we not believe in God?). What appears is that by it He meant their saying ﴿يَقُولُونَ رَبَّنا آمَنّا فاكْتُبْنا مَعَ الشّاهِدِينَ﴾ (They say: Our Lord, we have believed, so record us among the witnesses), because it is the explicit statement of their faith. As for His words ﴿لا نُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ﴾ (we do not believe in God), there is no explicit affirmation of their faith in it; rather, it is a denunciation of the absence of faith from them despite the presence of its motivating cause, so the reward is not consequent upon it.

Al-Hasan read ﴿فَآتاهُمُ﴾ (so He gave them), from *iyta'* in the sense of giving, not from *ithaba* (reward). Reward is more emphatic than giving, since it necessarily results from an action, unlike giving, which does not necessarily result from an action. For this reason it came at the end with ﴿وذَلِكَ جَزاءُ المُحْسِنِينَ﴾ (That is the reward of the good-doers), drawing attention to the fact that this reward is a recompense, and a recompense is only for an action.

﴿والَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وكَذَّبُوا بِآياتِنا أُولَئِكَ أصْحابُ الجَحِيمِ﴾ (And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, those are the companions of Hellfire). The Jews, the Christians and others are included in ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وكَذَّبُوا﴾ (those who disbelieved and denied). When He mentioned what is for the believer, He mentioned what He has prepared for the disbeliever.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 82–86 (part 1 of 2):

(p-2) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿You will surely find the most intense of the people in enmity toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate others with Allah. And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say, "We are Christians." That is because among them are priests (qissisin) and monks (ruhban), and because they are not arrogant.﴾ ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they recognize. They say, "Our Lord, we have believed, so register us among the witnesses."﴾ ﴿And why should we not believe in Allah and in what has come to us of the truth, while we aspire that our Lord will admit us among the righteous people?﴾ ﴿So Allah rewarded them, for what they said, with gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they abide forever. That is the reward of the doers of good.﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieved and denied Our signs — those are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 87] ﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you as lawful and good, and fear Allah, in whom you are believers.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 88] ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what you have intended in oaths. So its expiation is the feeding of ten needy people from the average of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. But whoever does not find [the means], then fasting for three days. That is the expiation for your oaths when you have sworn. And guard your oaths. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may be grateful.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 89] ﴿O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificial] stones, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 90] ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to occur among you through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 91] ﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger and beware. But if you turn away, then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only clear notification.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 92] ﴿There is no blame upon those who have believed and done righteous deeds for what they have eaten, if they fear Allah and believe and do righteous deeds, then fear Allah and believe, then fear Allah and do good. And Allah loves the doers of good.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 93] ﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of game that your hands and spears can reach, that Allah may make evident who fears Him unseen. And whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 94] ﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram. And whoever of you kills it intentionally, its penalty is an equivalent of what he has killed from livestock, as judged by two just men among you, as an offering brought to the Ka'bah, or an expiation of feeding needy people, or the equivalent of that in fasting, that he may taste the consequence of his action. Allah has pardoned what is past, but whoever returns to it, Allah will take retribution from him. And Allah is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 95] ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food as provision for you and for travelers, but forbidden to you is the game of the land as long as you are in the state of ihram. And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 96]

Al-qass, with a fatha on the qaf, is the tracking of a thing. Ru'bah said:
﴾They woke, heedless of the qass of harm, walking gently, averting, and fleeing.﴿
It is said: qassa al-athar, he tracked the trace, and also qassahu. Al-qass: the head of the Christians in religion and knowledge, and its plural is qusus. He was named by the verbal noun because he tracks knowledge and religion. Likewise al-qissis is of the pattern fi'il, like al-shirrib. Its plural is formed with the waw and nun, and it is also pluralized as qasawisah. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:
﴾Had there been a return, the qasawisah would have remained, while God revives them, and the scriptures are in their hands.﴿
Al-Farra' said: it is like mahalibah; the sins multiplied, so one of them was replaced with a waw, meaning that its analogy is qasasah. Ibn 'Atiyyah claimed that al-qass, with fatha or kasra on the qaf, and al-qissis, are non-Arabic words that were Arabicized.

Al-tama' is close to hope. It is said of it: tami'a yatma'u tama'an, wa tamā'atan, wa tamā'iyatan. The poet said:
﴾Greedy to be forgiven, that the forgiver forgives the sin.﴾
The active participle is tami'.

Al-rijs is a name for everything that is loathed of action. It is said: rajasa al-rajulu yarjusu rajsan, if he did a foul deed. Its origin is from al-rijs, which is the intensity of sound in thunder. The reciter said:
﴾From every rajjas who drives the rijs.﴾
Ibn Duraid said: al-rijz is evil, al-rijs is punishment, and al-rakas is filth and stench, and al-rijs is said of both matters.

Al-rumh is known; its plural in the paucity form is arma', and in the abundance form is rimah. Rama-hu means he stabbed him with a spear. A rajul rami' means one who has a spear, and there is no verbal form for the meaning of "one who has a spear"; rather it is like laban and tamir. A bull rami' has two horns. Dhu al-Rummah said:
﴾And many a time we startled from a wild cow and a horned one, the lands of the world are not their lands.﴾
Al-rammah is one who makes spears and practices the craft of spear-making. Al-wabal: the evil of consequence. Mar'an wabil: one who is harmed by it after eating it. Al-barr: the opposite of the sea. Al-Layth said: it is used indefinitely, one says: "I sat barran and went out barran." Al-Azhari said: it is from the speech of the muwallads. In the hadith of Salman: "Indeed for every matter there is an inner and an outer," meaning by that the secret and the public, and this is from a change of the relative form.

* *

﴿You will surely find the most intense of the people in enmity toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate others with Allah.﴾ Qatadah said: it was revealed concerning some people of the People of the Book who were upon a law of what 'Isa had brought; they believed in the Messenger, so Allah praised them. It was said: they were al-Najashi and his companions, when Ja'far ibn Abi Talib recited to them Surah Maryam when he emigrated to Abyssinia, and they believed and their eyes overflowed with tears. It was also said: they were the delegation of al-Najashi with Ja'far to the Messenger ﷺ, and they were seventy, whom he sent to the Messenger, wearing woolen garments: two and sixty from Abyssinia and eight from Syria, and they were Buhayra the monk, Idris, Ashraf, Thumamah, Qutham, Duraid, and Ayman. The Messenger ﷺ recited Ya-Sin to them, and they wept and believed, and said: "This is similar to what was sent down to 'Isa." So Allah revealed this verse concerning them. It is narrated from Muqatil and al-Kalbi that they were forty from the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b from Najran, and eighty-two from Abyssinia, and sixty-eight from Syria.

It is narrated from Ibn Jubayr something close to this. The apparent meaning of "the Jews" is general, including whoever was in the presence of the Messenger from the Jews of Madinah and others, because they were accustomed to denying and killing the prophets, and to rebelliousness and sins, and they sensed the curse and the imposition of humiliation and destitution; thus their enmity, their plotting, their envy, and their malice were intensified. In a hadith: "No two Jews were alone with a Muslim except that they intended to kill him." In Allah's description of them as "most intense in enmity" there is an indication of the difficulty of their accepting the truth; therefore the conversion of Jews is rare. It was said: "the Jews" here refers to the Jews of Madinah, because they were the ones who backed the polytheists against the Muslims. The conjunction of "those who associate others with Allah" upon "the Jews" makes them followers of them in that, since the Jews were more intense in enmity, as they differed with the Muslims in the law, not in kind, since between them there are connected ties of kinship and close lineage, so kinship inclines them toward the Muslims in every state; and because they are not upon a law from Allah, they are quicker to believe than any of the Jews and Christians. They are conjoined here as they were conjoined in His saying: ﴿And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life, and of those who associate others with Allah﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 96]. The lam in "la-tajidanna" is the lam of the oath that is implied, to which the oath is attached.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is the lam of the beginning, but this is not acceptable. And "al-nas" here means the disbelievers; that is, you will surely find the most intense of the disbelievers in enmity.

﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say, "We are Christians."﴾ That is, they are gentler in disposition and nearer in friendliness. He did not describe them with affection itself; rather He made them nearer than the Jews and the polytheists. They have fidelity, and the four traits which 'Amr ibn al-'As mentioned in Sahih Muslim: they honor from the people of Islam whoever they sense in him religion and faith, and they hate the people of wickedness; when they make peace their peace is pure, and when they fight their fighting is only defense, because their law does not command them otherwise. When the Romans overcame Persia, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was pleased, because the People of the Book had prevailed over the people of fire-worship, and because the greater enemy was destroyed by the lesser enemy, since it was feared for the people of Islam. The Jews have none of the characteristics of the Christians; rather their nature is treachery and twisting with the tongue. In the midst of your kindness to a Jew, he is watching for what will ensnare you with it. Do you not see what the Exalted related about them: ﴿That is because they said, "There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75]. In His saying, "Those who said, 'We are Christians'," there is an indication that they do not adhere to the reality of Christianity; rather that is a saying from them and a claim. The first "for those who believed" is connected to "enmity," and the second to "affection." It was said: both are in the position of a qualifier, and describing the enmity as "most intense" and the affection as "nearest" is evidence of the difference of the two kinds in relation to the believers: that enmity is the most intense and most manifest of enmities, and that affection is nearer and easier. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the Christians are in a better state than the Jews and nearer to the believers in affection; and upon this apparent meaning the verse was explained by those whose statements we have examined.

Some of them said: it is not upon its apparent meaning; rather what is intended is that they have more causes of affection than the Jews, and that is a reproach of them, for whoever has many causes of affection, his abandonment of affection is more shameful. For this reason Abu Bakr al-Razi said: among the ignorant are those who think that in this verse there is praise of the Christians and information that they are better than the Jews, and it is not so, because what is in the verse of that is only a description of a people who have believed in Allah and the Messenger ﷺ, as is indicated by what He mentioned in the sequence of recitation of their informing about themselves of belief in Allah and the Messenger. It is known to everyone of sound understanding who reflects on the two statements of the two groups that the statement of the Christians is uglier, more impossible, and more evidently corrupt than the statement of the Jews, because the Jews acknowledge monotheism in general, though among them is a resemblance to some of what they believe of tashbih (anthropomorphism) in general of monotheism. End of the words of Abu Bakr al-Razi;

(p-5) and the apparent meaning is what the exegetes and others said: that the Christians, on the whole, are in a better state than the Jews, and the exegetes have already mentioned, in what preceded, what the Christians were distinguished by over the Jews: nobility of character and swift entry into Islam. The discourse does not arise on account of doctrines; it arose on account of the reaction of the Muslims. As for his saying, "because what is in the verse of that is only a description of a people who have believed in Allah and the Messenger," it is not as he mentioned; rather the beginning of the verse requires generality, because He said: ﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say, "We are Christians"﴾, then He informed that among this group are scholars, ascetics, humble people, quick to respond to Islam, and many who weep upon hearing the Qur'an, whereas the Jews are the opposite. And existence confirms the nearness of the Christians to the Muslims and the distance of the Jews.

﴿That is because among them are priests (qissisin) and monks (ruhban), and because they are not arrogant.﴾ The indication of "that" refers to the nearest affection based on it; that is, among them are scholars and worshippers, and they are a people in whom there is humility and submissiveness, and they are not arrogant. The Jews are contrary to that; there were never among them people of monasteries, nor of cloisters, nor of withdrawal from the world; rather they are magnifiers, overreaching for its acquisition, as if they did not believe in an afterlife, and for this reason no ascetic is seen among them. Al-ruhban is the plural of rahib, like faris and fursan, and al-rahb and al-rahbah are fear, dread. It was said: al-ruhban is a singular in the pattern of sultan; and they recited:
﴾Had she beheld the monks of a monastery on the heights, the monks would have come down walking and slipping.﴿

It is also narrated as ﴿ونَزَلْ﴾ (wa-nazal, "and descended"). The word *qissis* (priest) has already been explained in the vocabulary section. Ibn Zayd said: it is the head of the monks. It was also said: it is the scholar. It was also said: it is one who raises his voice in recitation. It was also said: it is the *siddiq* (the truthful one). In this explanation there is evidence of the sublimity of knowledge, that it is a path to guidance, that withdrawal (from worldly pursuits) has a good outcome, that it is a way to reflect on the end result with humility, and that it is a cause for exalting the one who affirms God's oneness, since he witnesses in himself and in every created thing that it is in need of the One who brings it into being. Thus he is held in high esteem by the Originator of all things, the Creator, ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflow with tears because of the truth they have recognized﴾. This is a description of tender hearts and of being moved by hearing the Qur'an.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to priests and monks in general, so it is a general statement, and it reports about them what occurs among some of them. This is like what happened to the Negus when Ja'far recited to him Surat Maryam up to His words ﴿That is Jesus, son of Mary﴾ [Maryam 19:34], and Surat Ta-Ha up to His words ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:9], and he wept. Likewise were his people who came as a delegation to the Messenger (ﷺ), when he recited Surat Ya-Sin to them, and they wept.

Ibn 'Atiyya said, in substance: the beginning of the verse is general regarding the Christians, and ﴿when they hear﴾ is general regarding those among the arrivals from the land of Abyssinia who believed, since not all Christians act in this way. Rather, they were the ones whom the Negus sent to see the Prophet (ﷺ) and to hear what he had. When they saw him and he recited the Qur'an to them, their eyes overflowed from fear of God, the Exalted. End of quote.

As-Suddi said: when they returned to the Negus, he believed and emigrated with those who were with him, and then he died on the way. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) prayed over him, and the Muslims prayed for forgiveness for him.

﴿تَرى﴾ (you see) is from direct sight. The overflowing was attributed to the eyes, although in reality it belongs to the tears, as the poet said:

*So the tears of my eyes overflowed out of longing*

This is a case of attributing the effect to the cause's sphere (*iqamat al-musabbab maqam al-sabab*), since the overflowing is a result of being full. The underlying sense is: "you see their eyes filling with tears until they overflow," because overflowing over the sides of a vessel arises from its being full. The poet said:

*Biting words come to me and they belittle them, and water fills the vessel until it brims over*

It is also possible that he attributed the overflowing to the eyes as a form of hyperbole in describing weeping, since when they overflow with tears, the eyes themselves are described as overflowing, by way of metaphor and exaggeration.

As for ﴿مِن﴾ in ﴿مِنَ الدَّمْعِ﴾ (from the tears), Abu al-Baqa' said: it has two possibilities. The first is that ﴿مِن﴾ indicates the starting point, meaning its overflowing is from the abundance of tears. The second is that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and the meaning is "overflowing, filled with tears, because of what they recognized of the truth." The meaning of "because of what they recognized" is "on account of what they came to know." And ﴿مِنَ الحَقِّ﴾ (of the truth) is a circumstantial clause from the omitted returning pronoun, or a circumstantial clause from the subject pronoun in ﴿عَرَفُوا﴾ (they recognized).

It was also said that ﴿مِن﴾ in ﴿مِنَ الدَّمْعِ﴾ has the sense of *ba'* (by), meaning "with tears." Az-Zamakhshari said: ﴿مِنَ الدَّمْعِ﴾ means "on account of weeping," from your saying "his eye wept tears (damaʿat dam'an)." If you ask: what is the difference between the first ﴿مِن﴾ and the second ﴿مِن﴾ in His words ﴿مِمّا عَرَفُوا مِنَ الحَقِّ﴾? I say: the first indicates the starting point, in that the overflowing of tears began and arose from knowing the truth, and it was on account of it and because of it. The second is to specify the relative clause, which is *ma 'arafu* (what they recognized). It may also carry the sense of partition (*tab'id*), meaning that they recognized some of the truth and it made them weep. End of quote.

The clause beginning with ﴿وإذا سَمِعُوا﴾ (and when they hear) may be a new independent sentence, and it may also be conjoined to the predicate of ﴿إنَّهم﴾ (indeed they).

It was read as ﴿تَرى أعْيُنَهُمْ﴾ in the passive form (*al-bina' lima lam yusamma fa'iluhu*).

﴿يَقُولُونَ رَبَّنا آمَنّا فاكْتُبْنا مَعَ الشّاهِدِينَ﴾ (They say: Our Lord, we have believed, so record us among the witnesses). By ﴿آمَنّا﴾ (we have believed) is meant: we have brought into being the particular faith of this Islamic community. As for ﴿الشّاهِدِينَ﴾ (the witnesses), Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jurayj and others said: they are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and they said this because they are witnesses over the other nations, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:143]. Az-Zamakhshari said: they said this because they found their mention in the Gospel in this way. End of quote. At-Tabari said: its meaning, if it were said, "its meaning is: with those who bear witness to Your oneness from the whole of creation, those who came before and those who came after," would be correct. It was also said: its meaning is: with those who bear witness to the truth. Az-Zajjaj said: by ﴿الشّاهِدِينَ﴾ is meant the prophets, the believers, and the recording in the Preserved Tablet. It was also said: its meaning is "record us," from the saying "so-and-so was enrolled in the army," meaning he became established.

﴿يَقُولُونَ﴾ (they say) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, as Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Baqa' said, but they did not specify that circumstance or the element that governs it. It is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿أعْيُنَهم﴾ (their eyes), because it is in the genitive by annexation and has no place of either nominative or accusative, except according to the view of those who treat the predicate as if it were the annexed noun, and that is a mistaken view. We have explained this in our book *Manhaj al-Salik*. Nor is it permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from the subject pronoun in ﴿عَرَفُوا﴾ (they recognized), because then it would be a restriction on the recognition, while they recognized the truth in this state and in others. So the better option is that it be an independent sentence. He, the Exalted, informed about them that they were engaged in this statement, and the meaning is that they recognized the truth with their hearts, and their tongues uttered it and affirmed it.

﴿وما لَنا لا نُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وما جاءَنا مِنَ الحَقِّ﴾ (And why should we not believe in God and in the truth that has come to us?). This is a rebuke and an expression of astonishment at the absence of faith from them despite the presence of its cause, which is the recognition of the truth. Az-Zamakhshari and At-Tibrizi said: the motivating cause of faith is the hope of entering among the righteous. The apparent meaning is that this statement is one they make to themselves, as a conversation with the self, to repel whispers and fleeting thoughts, since leaving one way and adopting another to which one was not raised is difficult and hard. Or it is the statement of some believers to others, also as a form of reassurance. Or their saying is by way of argument against the disbelievers who opposed them when they returned to them and blamed them for their faith; the meaning is: "what prevents us from believing in God alone?" The right course has become clear to us and the luminous truth has appeared.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Jews (*p-7*) rebuked them and blamed them, and they answered them with this. The clause ﴿لا نُؤْمِنُ﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and it is the intended element, and its mention is the point of the statement. This is like your saying: "Zayd came riding," as an answer to someone who asked: "Did Zayd come walking or riding?" The element governing it is that which the prepositional phrase depends on; that is, "what is it that becomes settled for us and is set down as the absence of faith from us?"

In the Codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: ﴿وما لَنا لا نُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وما أنْزَلَ عَلَيْنا رَبُّنا ونَطْمَعُ﴾ (And why should we not believe in God and in what our Lord has sent down to us, and we hope...). This must be understood as an explanation of His words ﴿and the truth that has come to us﴾, because it contradicts what the Muslims agreed upon in the consonantal text of the Codex (*sawad al-mushaf*).

﴿ونَطْمَعُ أنْ يُدْخِلَنا رَبُّنا مَعَ القَوْمِ الصّالِحِينَ﴾ (and we hope that our Lord will admit us among the righteous people). The best and easiest reading is that it is a new statement of information from them, that they are hopeful of God's favor to them in admitting them among the righteous. So the conjunction ﴿و﴾ connects one sentence to another. ﴿ما لَنا لا نُؤْمِنُ﴾ is not conjoined to ﴿نُؤْمِنُ﴾, nor to ﴿لا نُؤْمِنُ﴾, nor is the ﴿و﴾ the *waw* of circumstance. Ibn 'Atiyya did not mention any view other than this one.

Az-Zamakhshari said: the ﴿و﴾ in ﴿ونَطْمَعُ﴾ is the *waw* of circumstance, and the element governing the circumstance is the sense of the verb governing ﴿لا نُؤْمِنُ﴾, but restricted by the first circumstance, because if you removed it and said "what is it for us that we hope," it would not be a complete statement. End of quote.

What he mentioned, that the two circumstances share one governing element, which is the sense of the verb within the preposition *li* (for us), as if it were said: "what has happened to us, not believing, hoping?", is not good. This is because the sounder view is that the governing element may not govern two circumstances for one owner of the circumstance without a conjunctive particle, except for the elative form (*af'al al-tafdil*); the sounder view is that this is permissible with it. The owner of the circumstance here is one, namely the pronoun governed by the preposition *li* in *lana* (for us). Moreover, the ﴿و﴾ has entered upon the imperfect verb, and the *waw* of circumstance does not enter upon the imperfect except through interpretation, so it would be necessary to supply: "and we are hoping."

Az-Zamakhshari also said: it is permissible for ﴿ونَطْمَعُ﴾ to be a circumstance of ﴿لا نُؤْمِنُ﴾, on the basis that they were condemning themselves, because they do not affirm God's oneness, and yet they hope to be companions of the righteous. End of quote.

This is not a good view, because it involves the *waw* of circumstance entering upon the imperfect verb, which requires interpretation.

Az-Zamakhshari also said: it is permissible for it to be conjoined to ﴿لا نُؤْمِنُ﴾ in meaning, as if it were: "what is it for us that we do not combine between the Trinity and hope for the companionship of the righteous?" Or in meaning: "what is it for us that we do not combine the two by entering Islam, since the disbeliever should not hope for the companionship of the righteous." End of quote.

What appears to me is a view other than what they mentioned: that it is conjoined to ﴿نُؤْمِنُ﴾, on the basis that it is negated just as ﴿نُؤْمِنُ﴾ is negated. The estimated meaning is: "what is it for us that we do not believe and do not hope," so that there is a rebuke for the absence of their faith and the absence of their hope, although they are able to attain both: faith and the hope of entering among the righteous. The word ﴿مَعَ﴾ (with) remains in its usual sense of accompaniment, although it was also said that it means *fi* (in). The righteous are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), as Ibn 'Abbas said, or the Messenger and his companions, as Ibn Zayd said, or the earliest emigrants, as Muqatil said. It was also said that the estimated meaning is: "that He admit us to Paradise."

﴿فَأثابَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِما قالُوا جَنّاتٍ تَجْرِي مِن تَحْتِها الأنْهارُ خالِدِينَ فِيها وذَلِكَ جَزاءُ المُحْسِنِينَ﴾ (So God rewarded them for what they said with gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the reward of the good-doers). The apparent meaning is that the reward with what was mentioned is consequent upon mere saying. But belief must accompany the saying, and what shows that it is accompanied by belief is that He said ﴿مِمّا عَرَفُوا مِنَ الحَقِّ﴾, describing them as those who recognize, which indicates that the saying is conjoined with knowledge. He also said ﴿ذَلِكَ جَزاءُ المُحْسِنِينَ﴾ (That is the reward of the good-doers). Either this is placing an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun, to draw attention to this attribute in them and to indicate that they were rewarded because this attribute, which is the rank of excellence (*ihsan*), was present in them. This is the rank that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) explained with his words: "That you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, He sees you." There is no sincerity nor knowledge higher than this rank. Or it means generality, so that they are included among the good-doers, on the basis that this reward was not consequent upon mere verbal utterance. For this reason Az-Zamakhshari explained ﴿بِما قالُوا﴾ (for what they said) as: "for what they uttered of belief and sincerity," from your saying "this is so-and-so's saying," meaning his belief and what he holds to. End of quote.

They explained this saying by their words ﴿وما لَنا لا نُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ﴾ (why should we not believe in God?). What appears is that by it He meant their saying ﴿يَقُولُونَ رَبَّنا آمَنّا فاكْتُبْنا مَعَ الشّاهِدِينَ﴾ (They say: Our Lord, we have believed, so record us among the witnesses), because it is the explicit statement of their faith. As for His words ﴿لا نُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ﴾ (we do not believe in God), there is no explicit affirmation of their faith in it; rather, it is a denunciation of the absence of faith from them despite the presence of its motivating cause, so the reward is not consequent upon it.

Al-Hasan read ﴿فَآتاهُمُ﴾ (so He gave them), from *iyta'* in the sense of giving, not from *ithaba* (reward). Reward is more emphatic than giving, since it necessarily results from an action, unlike giving, which does not necessarily result from an action. For this reason it came at the end with ﴿وذَلِكَ جَزاءُ المُحْسِنِينَ﴾ (That is the reward of the good-doers), drawing attention to the fact that this reward is a recompense, and a recompense is only for an action.

﴿والَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وكَذَّبُوا بِآياتِنا أُولَئِكَ أصْحابُ الجَحِيمِ﴾ (And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, those are the companions of Hellfire). The Jews, the Christians and others are included in ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وكَذَّبُوا﴾ (those who disbelieved and denied). When He mentioned what is for the believer, He mentioned what He has prepared for the disbeliever.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 82–86 (part 1 of 2):

(p-2) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿You will surely find the most intense of the people in enmity toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate others with Allah. And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say, "We are Christians." That is because among them are priests (qissisin) and monks (ruhban), and because they are not arrogant.﴾ ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they recognize. They say, "Our Lord, we have believed, so register us among the witnesses."﴾ ﴿And why should we not believe in Allah and in what has come to us of the truth, while we aspire that our Lord will admit us among the righteous people?﴾ ﴿So Allah rewarded them, for what they said, with gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they abide forever. That is the reward of the doers of good.﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieved and denied Our signs — those are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 87] ﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you as lawful and good, and fear Allah, in whom you are believers.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 88] ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what you have intended in oaths. So its expiation is the feeding of ten needy people from the average of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. But whoever does not find [the means], then fasting for three days. That is the expiation for your oaths when you have sworn. And guard your oaths. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may be grateful.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 89] ﴿O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificial] stones, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 90] ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to occur among you through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 91] ﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger and beware. But if you turn away, then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only clear notification.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 92] ﴿There is no blame upon those who have believed and done righteous deeds for what they have eaten, if they fear Allah and believe and do righteous deeds, then fear Allah and believe, then fear Allah and do good. And Allah loves the doers of good.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 93] ﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of game that your hands and spears can reach, that Allah may make evident who fears Him unseen. And whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 94] ﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram. And whoever of you kills it intentionally, its penalty is an equivalent of what he has killed from livestock, as judged by two just men among you, as an offering brought to the Ka'bah, or an expiation of feeding needy people, or the equivalent of that in fasting, that he may taste the consequence of his action. Allah has pardoned what is past, but whoever returns to it, Allah will take retribution from him. And Allah is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 95] ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food as provision for you and for travelers, but forbidden to you is the game of the land as long as you are in the state of ihram. And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 96]

Al-qass, with a fatha on the qaf, is the tracking of a thing. Ru'bah said:
﴾They woke, heedless of the qass of harm, walking gently, averting, and fleeing.﴿
It is said: qassa al-athar, he tracked the trace, and also qassahu. Al-qass: the head of the Christians in religion and knowledge, and its plural is qusus. He was named by the verbal noun because he tracks knowledge and religion. Likewise al-qissis is of the pattern fi'il, like al-shirrib. Its plural is formed with the waw and nun, and it is also pluralized as qasawisah. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:
﴾Had there been a return, the qasawisah would have remained, while God revives them, and the scriptures are in their hands.﴿
Al-Farra' said: it is like mahalibah; the sins multiplied, so one of them was replaced with a waw, meaning that its analogy is qasasah. Ibn 'Atiyyah claimed that al-qass, with fatha or kasra on the qaf, and al-qissis, are non-Arabic words that were Arabicized.

Al-tama' is close to hope. It is said of it: tami'a yatma'u tama'an, wa tamā'atan, wa tamā'iyatan. The poet said:
﴾Greedy to be forgiven, that the forgiver forgives the sin.﴾
The active participle is tami'.

Al-rijs is a name for everything that is loathed of action. It is said: rajasa al-rajulu yarjusu rajsan, if he did a foul deed. Its origin is from al-rijs, which is the intensity of sound in thunder. The reciter said:
﴾From every rajjas who drives the rijs.﴾
Ibn Duraid said: al-rijz is evil, al-rijs is punishment, and al-rakas is filth and stench, and al-rijs is said of both matters.

Al-rumh is known; its plural in the paucity form is arma', and in the abundance form is rimah. Rama-hu means he stabbed him with a spear. A rajul rami' means one who has a spear, and there is no verbal form for the meaning of "one who has a spear"; rather it is like laban and tamir. A bull rami' has two horns. Dhu al-Rummah said:
﴾And many a time we startled from a wild cow and a horned one, the lands of the world are not their lands.﴾
Al-rammah is one who makes spears and practices the craft of spear-making. Al-wabal: the evil of consequence. Mar'an wabil: one who is harmed by it after eating it. Al-barr: the opposite of the sea. Al-Layth said: it is used indefinitely, one says: "I sat barran and went out barran." Al-Azhari said: it is from the speech of the muwallads. In the hadith of Salman: "Indeed for every matter there is an inner and an outer," meaning by that the secret and the public, and this is from a change of the relative form.

* *

﴿You will surely find the most intense of the people in enmity toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate others with Allah.﴾ Qatadah said: it was revealed concerning some people of the People of the Book who were upon a law of what 'Isa had brought; they believed in the Messenger, so Allah praised them. It was said: they were al-Najashi and his companions, when Ja'far ibn Abi Talib recited to them Surah Maryam when he emigrated to Abyssinia, and they believed and their eyes overflowed with tears. It was also said: they were the delegation of al-Najashi with Ja'far to the Messenger ﷺ, and they were seventy, whom he sent to the Messenger, wearing woolen garments: two and sixty from Abyssinia and eight from Syria, and they were Buhayra the monk, Idris, Ashraf, Thumamah, Qutham, Duraid, and Ayman. The Messenger ﷺ recited Ya-Sin to them, and they wept and believed, and said: "This is similar to what was sent down to 'Isa." So Allah revealed this verse concerning them. It is narrated from Muqatil and al-Kalbi that they were forty from the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b from Najran, and eighty-two from Abyssinia, and sixty-eight from Syria.

It is narrated from Ibn Jubayr something close to this. The apparent meaning of "the Jews" is general, including whoever was in the presence of the Messenger from the Jews of Madinah and others, because they were accustomed to denying and killing the prophets, and to rebelliousness and sins, and they sensed the curse and the imposition of humiliation and destitution; thus their enmity, their plotting, their envy, and their malice were intensified. In a hadith: "No two Jews were alone with a Muslim except that they intended to kill him." In Allah's description of them as "most intense in enmity" there is an indication of the difficulty of their accepting the truth; therefore the conversion of Jews is rare. It was said: "the Jews" here refers to the Jews of Madinah, because they were the ones who backed the polytheists against the Muslims. The conjunction of "those who associate others with Allah" upon "the Jews" makes them followers of them in that, since the Jews were more intense in enmity, as they differed with the Muslims in the law, not in kind, since between them there are connected ties of kinship and close lineage, so kinship inclines them toward the Muslims in every state; and because they are not upon a law from Allah, they are quicker to believe than any of the Jews and Christians. They are conjoined here as they were conjoined in His saying: ﴿And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life, and of those who associate others with Allah﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 96]. The lam in "la-tajidanna" is the lam of the oath that is implied, to which the oath is attached.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is the lam of the beginning, but this is not acceptable. And "al-nas" here means the disbelievers; that is, you will surely find the most intense of the disbelievers in enmity.

﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say, "We are Christians."﴾ That is, they are gentler in disposition and nearer in friendliness. He did not describe them with affection itself; rather He made them nearer than the Jews and the polytheists. They have fidelity, and the four traits which 'Amr ibn al-'As mentioned in Sahih Muslim: they honor from the people of Islam whoever they sense in him religion and faith, and they hate the people of wickedness; when they make peace their peace is pure, and when they fight their fighting is only defense, because their law does not command them otherwise. When the Romans overcame Persia, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was pleased, because the People of the Book had prevailed over the people of fire-worship, and because the greater enemy was destroyed by the lesser enemy, since it was feared for the people of Islam. The Jews have none of the characteristics of the Christians; rather their nature is treachery and twisting with the tongue. In the midst of your kindness to a Jew, he is watching for what will ensnare you with it. Do you not see what the Exalted related about them: ﴿That is because they said, "There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75]. In His saying, "Those who said, 'We are Christians'," there is an indication that they do not adhere to the reality of Christianity; rather that is a saying from them and a claim. The first "for those who believed" is connected to "enmity," and the second to "affection." It was said: both are in the position of a qualifier, and describing the enmity as "most intense" and the affection as "nearest" is evidence of the difference of the two kinds in relation to the believers: that enmity is the most intense and most manifest of enmities, and that affection is nearer and easier. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the Christians are in a better state than the Jews and nearer to the believers in affection; and upon this apparent meaning the verse was explained by those whose statements we have examined.

Some of them said: it is not upon its apparent meaning; rather what is intended is that they have more causes of affection than the Jews, and that is a reproach of them, for whoever has many causes of affection, his abandonment of affection is more shameful. For this reason Abu Bakr al-Razi said: among the ignorant are those who think that in this verse there is praise of the Christians and information that they are better than the Jews, and it is not so, because what is in the verse of that is only a description of a people who have believed in Allah and the Messenger ﷺ, as is indicated by what He mentioned in the sequence of recitation of their informing about themselves of belief in Allah and the Messenger. It is known to everyone of sound understanding who reflects on the two statements of the two groups that the statement of the Christians is uglier, more impossible, and more evidently corrupt than the statement of the Jews, because the Jews acknowledge monotheism in general, though among them is a resemblance to some of what they believe of tashbih (anthropomorphism) in general of monotheism. End of the words of Abu Bakr al-Razi;

(p-5) and the apparent meaning is what the exegetes and others said: that the Christians, on the whole, are in a better state than the Jews, and the exegetes have already mentioned, in what preceded, what the Christians were distinguished by over the Jews: nobility of character and swift entry into Islam. The discourse does not arise on account of doctrines; it arose on account of the reaction of the Muslims. As for his saying, "because what is in the verse of that is only a description of a people who have believed in Allah and the Messenger," it is not as he mentioned; rather the beginning of the verse requires generality, because He said: ﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say, "We are Christians"﴾, then He informed that among this group are scholars, ascetics, humble people, quick to respond to Islam, and many who weep upon hearing the Qur'an, whereas the Jews are the opposite. And existence confirms the nearness of the Christians to the Muslims and the distance of the Jews.

﴿That is because among them are priests (qissisin) and monks (ruhban), and because they are not arrogant.﴾ The indication of "that" refers to the nearest affection based on it; that is, among them are scholars and worshippers, and they are a people in whom there is humility and submissiveness, and they are not arrogant. The Jews are contrary to that; there were never among them people of monasteries, nor of cloisters, nor of withdrawal from the world; rather they are magnifiers, overreaching for its acquisition, as if they did not believe in an afterlife, and for this reason no ascetic is seen among them. Al-ruhban is the plural of rahib, like faris and fursan, and al-rahb and al-rahbah are fear, dread. It was said: al-ruhban is a singular in the pattern of sultan; and they recited:
﴾Had she beheld the monks of a monastery on the heights, the monks would have come down walking and slipping.﴿

It is also narrated as ﴿ونَزَلْ﴾ (wa-nazal, "and descended"). The word *qissis* (priest) has already been explained in the vocabulary section. Ibn Zayd said: it is the head of the monks. It was also said: it is the scholar. It was also said: it is one who raises his voice in recitation. It was also said: it is the *siddiq* (the truthful one). In this explanation there is evidence of the sublimity of knowledge, that it is a path to guidance, that withdrawal (from worldly pursuits) has a good outcome, that it is a way to reflect on the end result with humility, and that it is a cause for exalting the one who affirms God's oneness, since he witnesses in himself and in every created thing that it is in need of the One who brings it into being. Thus he is held in high esteem by the Originator of all things, the Creator, ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflow with tears because of the truth they have recognized﴾. This is a description of tender hearts and of being moved by hearing the Qur'an.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to priests and monks in general, so it is a general statement, and it reports about them what occurs among some of them. This is like what happened to the Negus when Ja'far recited to him Surat Maryam up to His words ﴿That is Jesus, son of Mary﴾ [Maryam 19:34], and Surat Ta-Ha up to His words ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:9], and he wept. Likewise were his people who came as a delegation to the Messenger (ﷺ), when he recited Surat Ya-Sin to them, and they wept.

Ibn 'Atiyya said, in substance: the beginning of the verse is general regarding the Christians, and ﴿when they hear﴾ is general regarding those among the arrivals from the land of Abyssinia who believed, since not all Christians act in this way. Rather, they were the ones whom the Negus sent to see the Prophet (ﷺ) and to hear what he had. When they saw him and he recited the Qur'an to them, their eyes overflowed from fear of God, the Exalted. End of quote.

As-Suddi said: when they returned to the Negus, he believed and emigrated with those who were with him, and then he died on the way. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) prayed over him, and the Muslims prayed for forgiveness for him.

﴿تَرى﴾ (you see) is from direct sight. The overflowing was attributed to the eyes, although in reality it belongs to the tears, as the poet said:

*So the tears of my eyes overflowed out of longing*

This is a case of attributing the effect to the cause's sphere (*iqamat al-musabbab maqam al-sabab*), since the overflowing is a result of being full. The underlying sense is: "you see their eyes filling with tears until they overflow," because overflowing over the sides of a vessel arises from its being full. The poet said:

*Biting words come to me and they belittle them, and water fills the vessel until it brims over*

It is also possible that he attributed the overflowing to the eyes as a form of hyperbole in describing weeping, since when they overflow with tears, the eyes themselves are described as overflowing, by way of metaphor and exaggeration.

As for ﴿مِن﴾ in ﴿مِنَ الدَّمْعِ﴾ (from the tears), Abu al-Baqa' said: it has two possibilities. The first is that ﴿مِن﴾ indicates the starting point, meaning its overflowing is from the abundance of tears. The second is that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and the meaning is "overflowing, filled with tears, because of what they recognized of the truth." The meaning of "because of what they recognized" is "on account of what they came to know." And ﴿مِنَ الحَقِّ﴾ (of the truth) is a circumstantial clause from the omitted returning pronoun, or a circumstantial clause from the subject pronoun in ﴿عَرَفُوا﴾ (they recognized).

It was also said that ﴿مِن﴾ in ﴿مِنَ الدَّمْعِ﴾ has the sense of *ba'* (by), meaning "with tears." Az-Zamakhshari said: ﴿مِنَ الدَّمْعِ﴾ means "on account of weeping," from your saying "his eye wept tears (damaʿat dam'an)." If you ask: what is the difference between the first ﴿مِن﴾ and the second ﴿مِن﴾ in His words ﴿مِمّا عَرَفُوا مِنَ الحَقِّ﴾? I say: the first indicates the starting point, in that the overflowing of tears began and arose from knowing the truth, and it was on account of it and because of it. The second is to specify the relative clause, which is *ma 'arafu* (what they recognized). It may also carry the sense of partition (*tab'id*), meaning that they recognized some of the truth and it made them weep. End of quote.

The clause beginning with ﴿وإذا سَمِعُوا﴾ (and when they hear) may be a new independent sentence, and it may also be conjoined to the predicate of ﴿إنَّهم﴾ (indeed they).

It was read as ﴿تَرى أعْيُنَهُمْ﴾ in the passive form (*al-bina' lima lam yusamma fa'iluhu*).

﴿يَقُولُونَ رَبَّنا آمَنّا فاكْتُبْنا مَعَ الشّاهِدِينَ﴾ (They say: Our Lord, we have believed, so record us among the witnesses). By ﴿آمَنّا﴾ (we have believed) is meant: we have brought into being the particular faith of this Islamic community.
