Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 89 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what you have intended in oaths.﴾ The discussion of the interpretation of a similar phrase has already preceded. The meaning of (ʿaqqadtum) is "you confirmed (wathaqtum) with intention and purpose." The two Ḥaramiyyān (Ibn Kathīr and Nāfiʿ) and Abū ʿAmr read it with a shaddah on the qāf; al-Akhawān (ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah) and Abū Bakr read it without the shaddah; and Ibn Dhakwān read it with an alif between the ʿayn and the qāf. Al-Aʿmash read it as (bimā ʿaqadati al-aymān), making the verb belong to the oaths. So the shaddah is either for intensification relative to the plural, or because it has the meaning of the unaugmented form, like qaddara and qadara. The unshaddah form is the basic one, and the form with the alif has the meaning of the unaugmented form, like jāwaztu al-shayʾ, juztuhu, qāṭaʿtuhu and qaṭaʿtuhu, meaning: I abandoned it (hajartuhu). Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: "ʿāqadtum may bear two meanings. One of them is that it is like ṭāraqtu al-naʿl (I struck the sandal) and ʿāqabtu al-liṣṣ (I pursued the thief)." End of quotation. But it is not like that, because you do not say ṭaraqtu al-naʿl nor ʿaqabtu al-liṣṣ without an alif, whereas here you say ʿāqadtu al-yamīn and ʿaqadtu al-yamīn. Al-Ḥuṭayʾah said:
"A people who, when they made a pact with their neighbour,"
So he took it to have the meaning of the unaugmented form, and this is the apparent meaning, as we have mentioned.
Abū ʿAlī said: "The other is that it may be intended as fāʿaltu, which requires two agents, as if the meaning were: bimā ʿāqadtum ʿalayhi al-aymān (by what you have made an oath-pact upon), it takes ʿalā because it has the meaning of ʿāhada. He said: ﴿bimā ʿāhada ʿalayhu Allāh﴾ [al-Fath: 10], just as ﴿nādaytum ilā al-ṣalāh﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 58] takes (bi-ilā), and its pattern is that you say nādaytu Zaydan, ﴿wa nādaynāhu min jānib al-ṭūr al-ayman﴾ [Maryam: 52], since it has the meaning of daʿawtu ilā kadhā. He said: ﴿mimman daʿā ilā Allāh﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 33]. Then it was extended, so the preposition was deleted, the verb was transferred to the object, then the pronoun returning from the relative clause to the relative pronoun, since it became bimā ʿāqadtumūhu al-aymān, as it was deleted from His saying ﴿fa-iṣdaʿ bimā tu'mar﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 94]." End of quotation. Making ʿāqada for the sharing of the agent and object role verbally, and sharing in both in meaning, is far-fetched, since the meaning becomes that the oath made a pact with him just as he made a pact with it when it is attributed to him, and he made it (ʿaqadahā) in the true sense, while attributing that to the oath is in the figurative sense, because it did not make a pact with him; rather, he is the one who made the pact with it. As for its estimation as bimā ʿāqadtum ʿalayhi, with the deletion of the preposition and then the pronoun in the gradual manner he mentioned, it is also far-fetched, and comparing it to His saying ﴿fa-iṣdaʿ bimā tu'mar﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 94] is not sound, because amara is transitive sometimes by a preposition and sometimes by itself to the second object; and though its original form has deletion, one says amartu Zaydan al-khayr and amartuhu bil-khayr. Also, in ﴿fa-iṣdaʿ bimā tu'mar﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 94] it is not necessarily the case that mā is a relative pronoun meaning "that which"; rather, it appears to be verbal (maṣdariyyah), so no returning pronoun is needed. Likewise here, the better view is that mā is verbal (maṣdariyyah), and this is strengthened and improved by the contrast with the oath-making in the verbal noun which is ﴿bi-al-laghw fī aymānikum﴾, since laghw is a verbal noun; so it is better to contrast it with a verbal noun, not a relative pronoun. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The meaning is: but He will hold you accountable for what you have made binding when you break them," so the time of accountability is deleted because it was known to them; or "for the breaking of what you have made binding," so the modified noun is deleted. End of quotation. The oath that is binding is one sworn by Allah, or by His names, or by His attributes.

Imam Aḥmad said: "If one swears by the Prophet ﷺ, his oath becomes binding, because he swore by something on which faith is not complete except by it." With some attributes there is detail, and there is a difference of opinion mentioned in jurisprudence.

﴿So its expiation is feeding ten needy persons from the middle of what you feed your families﴾. Kaffārah is the act which by its nature expiates the sin, i.e., covers it. The pronoun in (fa-kaffāratuhu) refers to mā if it is a relative noun phrase, and in that case there is an omitted modified noun, as mentioned before; if it is verbal (maṣdariyyah), the pronoun refers to what is understood from the meaning, which is the sin of breaking the oath, even though no explicit mention has preceded it, but the meaning requires it. Masākīn is more general, whether they are males, females, or both. The apparent meaning is the multiplicity of persons. So if one feeds one needy person for the expiation of ten days, it does not suffice; this is the view of Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī. Abū Ḥanīfah said it suffices. The verse addresses the kind of food from which one feeds, which is "from the middle of what you feed," and does not address the quantity each person is fed; this is the apparent meaning. Mālik and a group held that this middling is in quantity, and this was the view of ʿUmar, ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid. A group held that it is in kind, and this was the view of Ibn ʿUmar, al-Aswad, ʿUbaydah, al-Ḥasan and Ibn Sīrīn. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "The proper view is that he feeds, by the word 'middle,' both in quantity and in kind." End of quotation.

It is related from Zayd ibn Thābit, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ and Ibn al-Musayyab: one mudd for each needy person by the mudd of the Messenger, and this was the view of Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī. It is related from ʿUmar, ʿAlī and ʿĀʾishah: half a ṣāʿ of wheat, or a ṣāʿ of dates, and this was the view of Abū Ḥanīfah. The apparent meaning is that only feeding with what provides sufficiency at one time, by which one satisfies hunger, suffices; if he gives them lunch and dinner, it suffices. This was the view of ʿAlī, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, al-Qāsim, Sālim, al-Shaʿbī, Ibrāhīm, Qatādah, al-Awzāʿī, al-Thawrī, Abū Ḥanīfah and Mālik. Ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥakam and al-Shāfiʿī said: it is a condition of the validity of the expiation that food be transferred in ownership to the poor; if he gives them lunch and dinner, it does not suffice. The apparent meaning is that condiment is not a condition. Ibn ʿUmar said: the middle of what is fed is bread and dates, or bread and raisins, and the best of what we feed our families is bread and meat; and from others, bread and ghee, and the best of it is dates with bread. This was also related from Ibn Masʿūd. Ibn Ḥabīb said: bread alone without condiment does not suffice, but with olive oil, milk, meat or the like. The apparent meaning is that what is considered is what one feeds his own household, those who are specifically his; i.e., from the middle of what each person feeds the household of each person. It was said: what is considered is the living standard of the land, so the meaning is: from the middle of what you, O people, feed your families in general, from a city or a region. (min awsaṭ) is in the position of the second object of (iṭʿām), and the first is (ʿashrata masākīn), i.e., food from the middle. The returning pronoun of (mā) in (tuṭʿimūna) is in an omitted position, i.e., (tuṭʿimūnahu). The majority read (ahlīkum), the plural of ahl with the ending of ūn and nūn, which is anomalous in analogy. Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq read (ahālīkum), a broken plural, with a sukūn on the yāʾ. Ibn Jinnī said: ahālin is like layālin; its singular is ahlah and laylah, and the Arabs say ahl and ahlah, and from it is his saying:
"And households of love, I have travelled with their love"
Al-Zamakhsharī said: al-ahālī is a collective noun for ahl, like al-layālī for the plural of laylah, and al-arāḍī for the plural of arḍ. As for the sukūn of the yāʾ in ahālīkum, it is common in poetic necessity, and it was said that it is also in ordinary speech, as Zuhayr said:
"He obeys the spears, mounted every ... "
The yāʾ was likened to the alif, so all vowels were assumed in it.

﴿Or their clothing﴾. This is coordinated with his saying (iṭʿām). The apparent meaning is that kiswah is a verbal noun, although it is used for the garment that covers. Since the amount of food was not mentioned, the amount of clothing was not mentioned, and the apparent meaning is the unrestricted clothing. They agreed that a cap by itself does not suffice. Some said: clothing in expiation is a waist-wrap, a shirt and a cloak. It is related from Ibn ʿUmar: "or two garments for each needy person," said by Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, Ibn Sīrīn and al-Ḥasan. Some considered the custom and the commonly known clothing, and some said: a single garment does not suffice unless it comprehensively covers what one may adorn oneself with, such as a cloak or a blanket. al-Nakhaʿī said: a shirt, a coat of mail or a veil is not a comprehensive garment. al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥakam said: a turban with which one wraps his head suffices. Mujāhid said: anything suffices except the loincloth (tubbān). ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Jaʿfar and Manṣūr said: kiswah is a garment, a shirt, a cloak or a waist-wrap. Ibn ʿAbbās said: an ʿabāʾah or a shamlah suffices. Ṭāwūs and al-Ḥasan said: one garment for each needy person. From Ibn ʿUmar: a waist-wrap and a shirt, or a cloak. Whether giving the clothing of ten persons to one person within ten days suffices is a matter of disagreement, as with feeding. al-Nakhaʿī, Ibn al-Musayyab and Ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān read (kuswatuhum) with a ḍammah on the kāf. Ibn Jubayr and Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ read (aw ka-uswatihim) with a kāf of genitive on uswah. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the meaning is: or the like of what you feed your families, whether extravagantly or stingily, not diminishing them below the measure of their provision, but equalizing between them and yourselves. If you ask what the position of the kāf is, I say it is nominative. It was said: His saying ﴿or their clothing﴾ is coordinated with the position of ﴿min awsaṭ﴾, which shows that ﴿min awsaṭ﴾ is not in the position of a second object of the verbal noun; rather, the speech ends at His saying ﴿iṭʿām ʿashrata masākīn﴾, then he supposed an omitted subject which he predicated with the prepositional phrase, which is explained by what precedes it, its estimation being: their food is from the middle. According to what we have mentioned, that ﴿min awsaṭ﴾ is in the accusative position, the kāf in (ka-uswatihim) is in the accusative position, because it is coordinated with the position of ﴿min awsaṭ﴾, which we consider accusative. If (ka-uswatihim) is interpreted as referring to the food, the verse remains without mention of clothing. The scholars agreed that the one who breaks the oath has the choice between feeding, clothing and freeing a slave, and this is contrary to the consonantal text of the Muṣḥaf. Some said: (aw ka-uswatihim) refers to clothing. The apparent meaning is that it does not suffice to pay the value of the food and clothing; this is the view of al-Shāfiʿī. Abū Ḥanīfah said it suffices. The apparent meaning is that the needy are not restricted by a description, so it is permissible to give that to a dhimmī or a slave, and this is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah. Others said it does not suffice. They agreed that it does not suffice to give it to an apostate.

﴿Or the freeing of a neck﴾. Calling a person a "neck" is synecdoche, the naming of the whole by a part. It was specified in this way because the neck is generally the place of binding and holding, so it is the place of ownership; similarly, the head is used for it. Liberation (taḥrīr) is by removing someone from slavery, from captivity, from hardship, or from fatigue. al-Farazdaq said:
"O Banū Ghudānah, indeed I have freed you, so I gave you to ʿAṭiyyah ibn Jiʿāl"
i.e., I freed you from satire. The apparent meaning is that the expiation is achieved by freeing whatever is subject to being a neck, without consideration of any other matter, so the freeing of an unbeliever suffices; this was the view of Dāwūd and a group of the people of the apparent meaning. Abū Ḥanīfah said an unbeliever suffices, and one with a slight defect among those with afflictions. al-Ṭabarī chose the sufficiency of a female unbeliever. Mālik said: an unbeliever, a blind person, a leper or an insane person does not suffice. Ibn Shihāb and a group said... al-Nakhaʿī made a distinction: he permitted freeing one who does his tasks and serves, and prohibited freeing one who does not work, such as the blind, the paralysed or one with both hands useless.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 89 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿Then whoever does not find [the means], then [he must fast for] three days.﴾ That is: whoever does not find any of these three [options] of feeding, clothing, or freeing [a slave]. If his wealth is in another land and he finds someone who will lend to him, he does not move on to fasting. Or if he does not find anyone who will lend to him, it is said that he is not obliged to wait for his wealth from his own land, and he fasts. This is the apparent view, because he is not able [to pay] at present. It is also said that he should wait. The apparent view is that if he has a surplus beyond his own sustenance and the sustenance of those whose maintenance is obligatory upon him, for a day and a night, and beyond their clothing, in an amount sufficient to feed or clothe [the needy], then he is able [to pay]. This is the view of Ahmad, Ishaq, al-Shafi'i, and Malik. Malik said: unless he fears hunger, or he is in a land where no one will show him kindness. Ibn Jubayr said: if he has nothing except three dirhams, he feeds [the needy]. Qatadah said: if he has nothing except the amount with which he can make expiation, he fasts. Al-Hasan said: if he has two dirhams, he feeds [the needy]. Abu Hanifah said: if he does not have a nisab (the minimum threshold of wealth liable for zakat), then he is not able [to pay]. Others said: it is permissible for one who does not have a surplus over the capital with which he earns his livelihood, or he fasts. The apparent view is that consecutiveness is not a condition. This is the view of Malik and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibrahim, Qatadah, Tawus, and Abu Hanifah said: it is a condition. Ubayy, Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud], and al-Nakha'i recited (ayyāmin mutatābi‘āt) [i.e., "three consecutive days"]. They agreed that freeing a slave is the most excellent [option], then clothing, then feeding. Allah began with the easiest [option], then the next easiest, according to the circumstances. This expiation that Allah has stated explicitly is binding on a free Muslim. As for a slave who breaks an oath, Sufyan, Abu Hanifah, and al-Shafi'i said: he is obliged only to fast; nothing else suffices for him. Ibn Nafi' related from Malik: he does not expiate by freeing [a slave], because he has no wala' (the right of patronage over a freed slave), but he expiates by giving charity if his master permits him. Fasting is more correct. Ibn al-Qasim related from him that he said: if he feeds or clothes [others] with the permission of his master, that is not clear, and there is something in my heart about it. If someone swears by giving away his wealth in charity, al-Sha'bi, Ata', and Tawus said: nothing is obligatory upon him. Al-Shafi'i, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr said: he is obliged to make the expiation of an oath. Abu Hanifah said: [he gives] the amount of a nisab. Some said: [he gives] the amount of his zakat. Malik said: one third of his wealth. If someone swears by walking to Makkah, Ibn al-Musayyib and al-Qasim said: nothing is obligatory upon him. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Abu Thawr said: [he owes] the expiation of an oath. Abu Hanifah said: he is obliged to fulfil it; if he is unable to walk, he is obliged to perform the Hajj riding. If someone swears by freeing a slave, Ata' said: he gives something in charity. It is related from Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas, and Aishah: he is obliged to make the expiation of an oath, not [the obligation of] freeing [a slave]. The majority said: he is obliged to free [a slave]. As for one who says that divorce is binding upon him, al-Mahdawi said: all those whose statements are relied upon agree that divorce is binding upon one who swears by it and breaks the oath.

﴿That is the expiation of your oaths when you have sworn.﴾ That is: the aforementioned [expiation]. Al-Shafi'i used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of making expiation after the oath. It is also said [that the verse refers to] breaking the oath (al-hinth), and in it is an indication that expiation is only due after breaking the oath. So they assume an omitted element; that is: when you swear and break [your oath].

﴿And guard your oaths. Thus Allah makes His verses clear to you, so that you may be grateful.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, fulfil them and do not break them. He meant the oaths in which breaking them is a sin, because "oaths" is a generic noun which may be applied to part of the category and to all of it. It is also said: guard them by making expiation for them. It is also said: guard them by not forgetting them, as you swear by them, out of carelessness toward them. (Thus) that is, like that clarification, ﴿Allah makes His verses clear to you﴾ — the signs of His law and His rulings.

﴿so that you may be grateful﴾ for His blessing in what He teaches you, and makes the way out of it easy for you.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 90–92 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾ It was revealed concerning the incident of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, when a group of the Ansar and the Muhajirun drank wine and boasted to one another. Sa'd said, "The Muhajirun are better." An Ansari struck him with the jawbone of a camel, which split his nose. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the statement of Umar, "O Allah, make clear to us a satisfying explanation regarding wine." It was also said: it was revealed concerning the story of Hamzah and Ali, when Hamzah slaughtered the she-camel of Ali. He said, "Are you not but slaves of my father?" This is a lengthy story. It was also said: the matter of wine and the revelation of the verses occurred gradually, so there was revealed, "O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated" (Surah an-Nisa, 4:43). It was also said: it was revealed concerning the recitation of some of the Companions, who was intoxicated, during the Maghrib prayer, "Say, O disbelievers" (Surah al-Kafirun, 109:1) in other than the form in which it was revealed. Then what happened, happened, because of drinking it, from matters leading to its prohibition, until this verse was revealed.

Ibn Abbas said: it was revealed concerning two tribes of the Ansar who became intoxicated and acted riotously. When they became sober, each one saw a mark on his face and body and said, "This is the doing of so-and-so." Thus enmities arose among them.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it: when Allah, the Exalted, commanded them to eat of what He had provided for them, lawful and good, and forbade them from prohibiting what He had made lawful for them, which contains no sin, and what they considered pleasant and delightful were wine and gambling. They used to say, "Wine drives away worries, invigorates the soul, emboldens the coward, and incites to noble deeds. Gambling brings about the increase of wealth and the delight of winning." Allah, the Exalted, explained the prohibition of wine and gambling, because this delight is accompanied by great corruptions. In wine there is the destruction of the intellect and the squandering of wealth. For this reason some of the wise men of the Jahiliyyah censured squandering wealth on it, and made abstaining from it a praiseworthy quality, and said:

"My brother, trustworthy, wine does not squander his wealth,
but his gifts may ruin his wealth."

From it arise other corruptions: the killing of souls, intense hatred, and the committing of sins, because the root of all these is the intellect. When the intellect departs, these corruptions come. In gambling there is taking wealth by falsehood. This address is to the believers. What they were forbidden from in this verse are desires and habits. As for wine, it had not yet been prohibited; its prohibition was revealed only after the Battle of Uhud, in the third year of the Hijrah. As for gambling, there is in it delight and winning. As for the idolatrous altars, if they are the stones upon which they would slaughter and sacrifice, then they are judged as defilement, to repel what might remain in the heart of one of weak faith of venerating them. If they are the altars that are worshipped besides Allah, then the three are paired with them as an emphasis that they must be avoided, just as idols must be avoided. As for the divining arrows, which most of them used to make, with one marked (no), another marked (yes), and another blank (ghufl), and they used to venerate them, and some of them were with soothsayers, and some were with the Quraysh in the Ka'bah, and they had judgments by them. Of this category is the divining by birds and by wild animals, and taking omens from books and the like, which people do today.

Several forms of emphasis have gathered in the verse: among them, the opening with "innama" (indeed, only), the pairing of wine and gambling with idols if we interpret the altars as idols, the Hadith "The habitual drinker of wine is like a worshipper of an idol," and the description of them as defilement. Allah, the Exalted, said: "So avoid the defilement of idols" (Surah al-Hajj, 22:30). He described them as being from the work of Satan, and Satan brings nothing but pure evil. The command to avoid them and the hope of success, which is achieved by avoiding them, while failure is in committing them. It began with wine because the cause of revelation occurred through the corruption of it, and because it is the gathering point of sin.

The wine of Madinah at the time of the revelation was mostly made from honey, dates, raisins, wheat, and barley, and there was little made from grapes. The Muslims have agreed on the prohibition of both the small and the large amount of grape wine that has not been touched by fire and has not been mixed with anything. The majority of the Ummah holds that whatever intoxicates in large quantity is forbidden in small quantity as well. The disagreement regarding what does not intoxicate in small quantity but intoxicates in large quantity, from other than grape wine, is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence.

Ibn Atiyyah said: some people derived the prohibition of wine from describing it as defilement. Allah, the Exalted, has described carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine as defilement in another verse, so it follows that every defilement is forbidden. In this there is room for consideration. Avoidance means that you place a thing aside and in a corner, and it ends there.

Since Satan is the one who calls to engaging in these sins and incites to them, they were attributed to his work and doing, and were ascribed to him by way of metaphor and exaggeration in describing the extreme of their ugliness, just as in the verse, "So Moses struck him and killed him" (Surah al-Qasas, 28:15), he said, "This is from the work of Satan." The pronoun in "so avoid it" refers to the defilement mentioned about the four, so the command to avoid it encompasses them all. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, to what does the pronoun in "so avoid it" refer? I say it refers to an omitted noun that is added to, as if it were said: "The matter of wine and gambling is only their practice or the like of that," and for this reason it said "defilement from the work of Satan." There is no need to estimate this omitted addition, rather the ruling on these four themselves, that they are defilement, is more emphatic than estimating that addition, due to the words of Allah, the Exalted: "The polytheists are only impure" (Surah at-Tawbah, 9:28).

﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to occur among you through wine and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾ Allah, the Exalted, mentioned in wine and gambling two corruptions: one worldly and the other religious. As for the worldly, they stir up evils and grudges, and lead their drinker to severing of ties. Most often they are used in a group who intend to be sociable by gathering over them, and to show affection and love, but they reverse the matter upon them, and they come to mutual hatred, because it removes the intellect, which is the foundation of all things. A man may have something in his soul that he conceals by his intellect, and he reveals it when intoxicated, which leads to destruction. Do you not see what happened to Sa'd and Hamzah? How excellent is what was said by the chief judge of the community, Abu al-Qasim Ahmad ibn Yazid ibn Baqi, who was a scholar and jurist following the school of the People of Hadith, as I read it to the learned judge Abu al-Hasan ibn Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi al-Ahwas, from him, may Allah be pleased with them both, in his generosity:

"Behold, the world is only like an old wine,
whose cupbearers intended by it to bring about companionship.
When they passed it around, it kindled their grudges,
and what they had sought of companionship turned into its opposite."

As for gambling, a man does not cease gambling until he remains plundered, with nothing for himself, and the worst of its evil consequences is that he gambles even his family and children. This leads him to becoming the greatest enemy of the one who defeated him and beat him, because that is taken from him by way of compulsion and overpowering, and he cannot refrain from it. For this reason one of the Jahiliyyah said:

"If they were to gamble with a horse that I had gambled with,
and every gamble of people is a loss."

As for the religious corruption, it is in wine, due to the overwhelming joy in it, the exhilaration over souls, and the immersion in bodily pleasures, which distracts from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. As for gambling, if the gambler wins, his soul is gladdened, and the love of victory, domination, and gain prevents him from the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted. If he is defeated, then what he experiences of constriction, regret, and scheming to become the winner, leaves no room in his heart for the remembrance of Allah, because He, the Exalted, is not remembered except by a heart that has emptied itself for Him and occupied itself with Him above all else. We have witnessed people who play backgammon and chess, among whom there occurs such obstinacy, false oaths, and delaying prayer beyond its times, that a Muslim should be ashamed to be associated with. And this is while they play without placing any stake for the winner. So how would their state be if they played for something that the winner takes?

Here wine and gambling are mentioned separately, even though they were combined with the idolatrous altars and divining arrows, as an emphasis on the ugliness of wine and gambling and a distancing from engaging in them. Thus they were placed in the category of what the believers had already abandoned of the altars and arrows. Enmity relates to outward matters, and something more severe is joined to it, namely hatred, because its seat is the heart. For this reason, to the remembrance of Allah is joined what is more binding, more obligatory, and more emphatic, namely prayer. In what wine and gambling produce of enmity, hatred, and averting from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer, there is the strongest proof of their prohibition, and that the Muslim should desist from them. For this reason, after it came, "So will you not desist?" This interrogative is among the most forceful forms of prohibition, as if it were said: "What is in them of worldly and religious corruptions that necessitate desisting has already been recited to you. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the recitation of some of the Companions, who was intoxicated, during the Maghrib prayer, "Say, O disbelievers" (Surah al-Kafirun, 109:1) in other than the form in which it was revealed. Then what happened, happened, because of drinking it, from matters leading to its prohibition, until this verse was revealed.

"My brother, trustworthy, wine does not squander his wealth,
but his gifts may ruin his wealth."

As for describing the message as "clear" (mubin), this may be because it is manifest in itself, evident and plain, or because it makes clear to you the rulings of God Most High and His obligations in such a way that no doubt can afflict them; rather, they are plain, luminous and lucid. The majority (al-jumhur) hold that this verse indicates the prohibition of wine (khamr), and this is the apparent meaning. Umar swore an oath concerning it, and when it reached him that a people in Syria (al-Sham) had drunk it and said it was permissible, his opinion and that of Ali agreed that they should be asked to repent, and if they repented (well and good), otherwise they should be killed, because they had believed its permissibility.

The majority hold that wine is ritually impure in its substance, because it is called rijs (filth), and rijs means what is impure and abominable. Rabi'ah, al-Layth, al-Muzani and some of the later Baghdadi scholars held that it is pure (not impure); and they differed over whether intoxicating drink from it was permissible before its prohibition or not.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 93:

﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten, when they fear Allah, believe, and do righteous deeds, then fear Allah and believe, then fear Allah and do good, for Allah loves the good-doers.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, al-Bara' and Anas said: "When the prohibition of wine was revealed, some people said: 'What about one of us who died while drinking it and consuming gambling (maysir)?' So it was revealed." Thus Allah informed that blame and sin (al-janah) are attached only to committing acts of disobedience, and those who died before the prohibition were not disobedient. The apparent meaning of the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is that the wording is general but its meaning is specific. It was said: the verse is general, and the meaning is that there is no fault upon the believer for what he has eaten of pleasurable things, when he fears Allah regarding what Allah has forbidden of them. The case of one who drank it before the prohibition is among the forms covered by the generality. This verse is similar to the verse about the change of the qibla, when they asked about one who died facing the first qibla, and it was revealed: ﴿And Allah would not have caused your faith to be lost﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. As for ﴿for what they have eaten﴾, it was said: of wine. The word ta'm (eating/tasting) is literally used for food and figuratively for drink. In the verse of gambling it was said: of what they ate from gambling, so it is literal there. It was also said: of both, and by ta'm is meant dhawq (tasting), which is a common ground between them. These clauses are repeated for emphasis and affirmation of these attributes, and the affirmation does not conflict with the conjunction "then" (thumma), as it is like His saying: ﴿No! You will come to know﴾ [al-Takathur: 3], ﴿Then no! You will come to know﴾ [al-Takathur: 4]. Some scholars held that these clauses differ according to what they assumed to be the objects of the verbs. The meaning would then be: when they fear shirk and major sins, and believe with perfect faith, and do righteous deeds; then they fear Allah, meaning they remain steadfast and persist in the stated condition; then they fear Allah and do good, meaning they advance in piety to carrying out what is not obligatory of voluntary acts, such as prayer, charity, or other things; and this is ihsan (excellence in worship). Close to this is what al-Zamakhshari held. He said: "When they fear Allah regarding what was forbidden to them, and believe, and remain firm in faith and righteous deeds, and increase [in them]; ﴿then fear Allah and believe﴾ means they remain firm in piety and faith; ﴿then fear Allah and do good﴾ means they remain firm in avoiding sins and do their deeds well, and do good to people, comforting them with the good things Allah has provided," end of quote. It was said: the first stage refers to past time, the second to the present, and the third to the future. It was also said: the first fear of Allah concerns shirk and commitment to the Law; the second concerns major sins; and the third concerns minor sins. It was said: other than this, which the wording does not indicate. The meaning of the verse is praise of those who were in this state, and commendation of them for faith, piety, and excellence, since wine was not prohibited at that time. Therefore sin is lifted from one who engages in what is permissible, if he is a believer, pious, and a doer of good, even if that permissible thing would eventually lead to prohibition; its later prohibition does not harm the believing, pious, good-doing person. The explanation of ihsan has already been mentioned, and that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained it in the hadith of Jibril's question, so its explanation must not be exceeded.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 94–95 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of the game that your hands and your spears can reach﴾. It was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, when he (ﷺ) was staying at al-Tan'im. The wild animals and birds would come upon them in their camps while they were in the state of ihram (ritual consecration for pilgrimage). It was also said that some of them had entered ihram and some had not, so when game appeared, their circumstances differed and the rulings became confused. It was also said that Abu al-Yusr killed a wild ass with his spear, and it was said to him: "You killed game while you were in ihram," and so this was revealed. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He commanded them not to forbid the good things, and excluded from that the wine and the gambling, which are forbidden permanently, He then excluded from the good things that which is forbidden in one state but not in another, namely game. Game was something the Arabs lived on, and they took pleasure in hunting it, and they had poetry and fine descriptions about it. The apparent meaning is that the address in His words "O you who have believed" is general to the one who is not in ihram and to the one who is in ihram, but the test is only realized with ihram or in the sacred precinct (al-Haram). Ibn Abbas said: it is for those in ihram. Malik said: it is for those not in ihram, and the meaning is that Allah will test you, and He tested them with it while they were in ihram or in the Haram (the sacred precinct of Makkah).

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿with something of the game﴾ implies a limitation. It was said: so that it is known that it is not one of the great tests, like the test with one's self and one's wealth, but rather it is a comparison with what the people of Ayla were tested with, the fishing of fish, and they did not endure at this test, so how would they endure at what is harder than it? The "min" in ﴿of the game﴾ is partitive in the state of sanctity, since ihram may end and one may leave the Haram, so the game of some of these states is some of the game in general. Al-Tabari and others said: of land game, not sea game. Ibn Atiyya said: it is permissible that "min" be explanatory of the kind. Al-Zajjaj said: this is like your saying "He said: I will surely test you with something of the provision," and like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. The intended meaning of game is what is eaten, because "sayd" (game) applies to both the edible and the non-edible. The poet said:

*"The game of kings are hares and foxes, but when I ride, my game is the heroes."*

And Zuhayr said:

*"A lion of 'Atharr hunts men when the lion, among its peers, tells the truth."*

For this reason Abu Hanifa said: if the one in ihram kills a lion, or a fierce wolf, or what is similar to them, he is liable for its killing.

﴿that your hands and your spears can reach﴾: that is, some of it is taken by the hands because its approach is near, so that the hand can reach it, and some by spears because of its distance and dispersal, so it is not reached except by the spear. Ibn Abbas said: "your hands" means the young of birds and the young of wild animals. Mujahid said: "the hands" means the chicks and the eggs, and what cannot flee; and the spears reach the large game. It was said: what Mujahid said is not permissible, because "sayd" is the name for the wild and the one that resists, not for what does not resist, end of quote. He means that the term "sayd" is not applied to eggs. This does not prevent that as a naming of a thing by what it becomes. Ibn Atiyya said: the apparent meaning is that Allah singled out the hands for mention because they are the greatest means of action in hunting, and in them enter trained animals, snares and whatever is made by the hand of traps and nets, and He singled out the spears for mention because they are the greatest means by which game is wounded, and into them enters the arrow and the like. Some people argued from this verse that the game belongs to the one who takes it, not to the one who startles it, because the one who startled it did not have his hand or spear reach it yet.

Al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab read ﴿yanaluhu﴾ with a dotted "ya" below, and the clause ﴿tanaluhu﴾ is in the position of a description of ﴿bi-shay'in﴾, or in the position of a state of it, since it has been described. Whoever claims it is a state of "sayd" is far off the mark.

﴿That Allah may know who fears Him in the unseen﴾: this is a reason for His words ﴿will surely test you﴾. The meaning of "that He may know" is that the one who fears His punishment, exalted is He, who is absent and awaited in the Hereafter, may be distinguished, and then the game remains for the one who does not fear Him, so he advances upon it. So said al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Atiyya said: so that He may continue to observe it while it exists, since Allah has known that in eternity. Al-Kalbi said: Allah, exalted is He, has always been knowing, and He only expressed knowledge in terms of seeing. It was also said: it is by the omission of a noun: that is, "that the friends of Allah may know." It was said: the meaning is "that they may know that Allah knows who fears Him in the unseen," that is, in secret, where none of the people sees him. So the one who fears does not hunt, and the one who does not fear hunts. It was said: He deals with you as one who seeks to know. It was said: that the known may become manifest, which is the fear of the one who fears. "In the unseen" is in the position of an accusative as a state, and its meaning is that the one who fears is absent from seeing Allah, exalted is He. Similar to it are His words ﴿Whoever feared the Most Merciful in the unseen﴾ [Qaf: 33], and ﴿those who fear their Lord in the unseen﴾ [al-Anbiya': 49]. He, peace be upon him, said: "If you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." Al-Tabari said its meaning is in this world, where the servant does not see his Lord, so He is absent from him. Ibn Atiyya said: the apparent meaning is that "in the unseen" means from the people, that is, in seclusion, whoever fears Allah, end of quote, from the game in itself, end of quote. Al-Zuhri read ﴿liyu'lima Allahu﴾ from "a'lama." Ibn Atiyya said: that is, that He may let His servants know, end of quote. So it would be from "a'lama," the transitive form of "alima" (to know) transferred to one object, like the transfer of "arafa" (to know), so the first object is omitted, which is "His servants," because the meaning indicates it, and the second object remains, which is ﴿whoever fears Him﴾.

﴿So whoever transgresses after that﴾: the meaning is that whoever transgresses by opposing it and hunts. "That" is a reference to the prohibition implied in the meaning of the preceding speech, and its estimate is "so they should not hunt," which is indicated by His words ﴿that Allah may know who fears Him in the unseen﴾.

﴿For him there is a painful punishment﴾: it was said: in the Hereafter. It was said: in this world. Ibn Abbas said: his belly and back are stretched with lashes, and his garments are stripped off.

﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of sanctity﴾: "Those who have believed" is general, and here He explicitly prohibited the killing of game while they are in the state of being ones in sanctity. The word "ihrum" is the plural of "haram," and "haram" means the one made sacred, and the one who is in the Haram. The one who holds that the term is meant in its literal sense argues from His words ﴿while you are in the state of sanctity﴾ that the one in ihram and the one within the Haram are both prohibited from killing game. The one who does not hold this says: the meaning is those who enter ihram for Hajj or 'Umrah, which is the view of the majority. It was also said: the meaning is "while you are in the Haram." The apparent meaning is the prohibition of killing game, and the verse before this one indicated by its meaning the prohibition of hunting, so from the two verses together there is derived the prohibition of hunting and the prohibition of killing game. The apparent meaning is the generality of game. This generality has been specified for land game by His words ﴿Lawful to you is the game of the sea﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 96]. It was also said: and by the Sunnah, by the established hadith: "Five are harmful creatures that are killed both within the sanctuary and outside it: the crow, the kite, the mouse, and the rabid dog." The Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq limited themselves to these five. Malik analogized to the rabid dog every creature that attacks people and others, and considered it included in its wording: lion, leopard, panther, wolf, and every predator that attacks. He said: it is permissible for him to kill them, initiating the killing, but not the lion-like animal, the fox, or the hyena. If he kills them, he must pay a ransom. Mujahid and al-Nakha'i said: he may not kill any predator except one that attacks him, and something similar is narrated from Ibn Umar. The people of opinion said: if the predator attacks him first, he may kill it with no ransom, and if the one in ihram initiates and kills it, he must pay a ransom. Malik said about the young of predators before they prey: it is not appropriate for the one in ihram to kill them. It is established from Umar that he ordered those in ihram to kill snakes, and the people agreed on the permissibility of killing them. It is established from Umar the permissibility of killing the wasp, because it has the status of the scorpion, and venomous creatures have the status of the snake, like the viper and the tarantula. The position of Abu Hanifa and a group is that game is whatever is wild, whether edible or not. On this basis, if the one in ihram kills a predator whose meat is not eaten, he is liable, but the compensation does not exceed the value of a sheep. Zufar said: the compensation is whatever amount it reaches. A group said: game is what is eaten, and on this basis there is no liability for killing a predator, which is the view of al-Shafi'i, nor for killing the five harmful creatures, nor the wolf. If the game is of a kind that is lawful to eat, and the one in ihram kills it even by slaughter, the position of Abu Hanifa and Malik is that it is not slaughtered (dhakkah), so its meat is not eaten. This is the view of Ibn al-Musayyab and one of the two opinions of al-Hasan. The position of al-Shafi'i is that if the one in ihram slaughters the game, it is properly slaughtered. Al-Hakam, Amr ibn Dinar and Sufyan said: it is lawful for one who is not in ihram to eat it, and this is the other of the two opinions of al-Hasan.

(p-17)

(p-18)

﴿Whoever among you kills it intentionally, its penalty is an equivalent of what he killed from the livestock﴾. The apparent meaning restricts killing to the intentional act. So whoever kills by mistake, such as one who is forgetful of his state of ihram, or who shoots thinking it is not game and it turns out to be game, or who deflects an arrow he shot at something other than game so that it strikes game, bears no penalty. This was related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr, Tawus, ʿAta', and Salim, and Abu Thawr, Dawud, and al-Tabari said the same. It is also one of the two opinions of al-Hasan al-Basri, Mujahid, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Ibn ʿAbbas said, as transmitted by al-Daraqutni from him: "Expiation applies only to the intentional act, and they were made severe in the case of error so that they would not repeat it." It was also said that the verse came in the typical form, so the rare case is assimilated to it. It was also said that intention was mentioned because the context of the verse concerns one who killed intentionally, referring to the case of Abu al-Yasar, who killed a donkey intentionally while in ihram.

The position of Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafiʿi and their companions is that error, whether through forgetfulness or otherwise, is the same as intention. Intention means that he remembers his ihram and aims to kill. This was related from ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, Tawus, al-Hasan, Ibrahim, and al-Zuhri. Al-Zuhri said: "The penalty for intentional killing is in the Qur'an, and for error and forgetfulness it is in the Sunnah." The judge Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: "If by the Sunnah he means the reports that came from ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas, then how excellent they are, and how good they are as an example to follow."

Mujahid said: "Its meaning is that he killed intentionally while forgetting his ihram. But if he was remembering his ihram, then this is too grave and too great to be expiated, and he has exited the state, and he has no pilgrimage, because he committed what is forbidden in ihram, so it is nullified for him, just as if he spoke during prayer or broke his wudu' during it." He said: "As for the one who erred, he is the one upon whom the penalty falls." Ibn Jurayj said similarly. It was related from Mujahid that there is no penalty for one who killed intentionally, and he should seek forgiveness from Allah, and his pilgrimage remains complete.

The Kufans read ﴿فَجَزَاءٌ﴾ with tanwin, and ﴿مِثْلُ﴾ with damma. The nominative of jaza' is then the predicate of an omitted subject, whose predicate is estimated as: "Upon him is a penalty," and "mithl" is an adjective, meaning: "a penalty that is equivalent to what he killed." ʿAbd Allah read ﴿فَجَزَاؤُهُ مِثْلُ﴾, where the pronoun refers either to the slayer of the game or to the game. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah, ﴿فَجَزَاؤُهُ مِثْلُ﴾ is nominative as a subject and predicate. The rest of the seven readers read ﴿فَجَزَاءُ مِثْلُ﴾ with jaza' in the nominative and construct-state with mithl. It was said that mithl is inserted as in your saying "Mithlaka man yafʿalu kadha," meaning "you do such-and-such," so the estimate is "the penalty of what he killed." It was also said that this is the idafa of the verbal noun to its object. This estimate is supported by al-Sulami's reading ﴿فَجَزَاءٌ﴾ with damma and tanwin, and ﴿مِثْلَ مَا قَتَلَ﴾ with fatha. Muhammad ibn Muqatil read ﴿فَجَزَاءً مِثْلَ مَا قَتَلَ﴾ with fatha on both jaza' and mithl, and the estimate is: "Let him bring forth a penalty equivalent to what he killed," with mithl as an adjective of jaza'. Al-Hasan read ﴿مِنَ النَّعْمِ﴾ with the ʿayn sukun for lightness, as they say al-shaʿr. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "It is a dialect form." ﴿مِنَ النَّعَمِ﴾ is an adjective of jaza', whether jaza' is read nominative with mithl, or the idafa is made from jaza' to mithl, meaning "a penalty that is from the livestock." In the idafa reading, it is permissible for "min al-naʿam" to be connected to jaza', except in the first reading, because jaza' is a qualified verbal noun, and so it does not govern. Abu al-Baqa' erred in permitting "min al-naʿam" to be a circumstantial clause (hal) of the pronoun in "qatala," meaning the omitted object pronoun in "qatala" which refers to "ma" (what) said, because the killed one would be from the livestock. That is not the intended meaning, because what is from the livestock is what is the penalty, not what the muhrim kills. Also, livestock does not enter the category of game.

Regarding equivalence, the apparent meaning is that it is equivalence in form, creation, smallness, and size. This is the view of the majority. It was related from ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Jubayr, and Qatadah, and Malik, al-Shafiʿi, and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said the same. The details of what corresponds to each killed game have been lengthily discussed by a group of exegetes, but the wording of the Qur'an does not address them, and they are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence.

A group of the Successors held that equivalence is in value: one assesses the killed game, then with its value buys food from the livestock, then gives it in charity. This is the view of al-Nakhaʿi, ʿAta', and one of the two opinions of Mujahid. Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf said the same: he buys with the value an offering if he wishes, and if he wishes he buys food and gives each poor person half a sa', and if he wishes he fasts one day for every half sa'.

Some said: equivalence applies to what has a similar counterpart in form, and what has no counterpart, equivalence is in value. Abu Bakr al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari were strongly partisan for the school of Abu Hanifa, but the wording of the verse is at odds with his school, since the apparent meaning of the verse requires a choice between bringing an offering of livestock equivalent to what was killed, or expiating by feeding the poor, or fasting an equivalent number of days.

The apparent meaning is that penalty applies only to killing, not to capturing the game, nor to its kind, nor to eating it, in agreement with al-Shafiʿi, and against Abu Hanifa, who said that upon him is the penalty of what he ate, meaning its value. His two companions disagreed with him and said there is nothing upon him except seeking forgiveness, because he merely partook of it. The penalty also does not apply to pointing it out, contrary to Abu Hanifa and Ashhab, who said the one who points it out must pay the penalty. This was related from Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAwf. Al-Shafiʿi, Malik, and Abu Thawr said: the one who points does not pay, and the penalty falls on the killer. Nor is there a penalty for wounding it or for the reduction in its value because of that. Al-Muzani said there is something upon him. Some scholars said: if its value is reduced, for example by a tenth, then upon him is a tenth of its value. Dawud said there is nothing upon him.

The apparent meaning is that if a group of muhrims shared in hunting one game, only one penalty is due from them, because the killing is not attributed to each one of them. As for the one killed, it is one, so the equivalent must be one. This was said by al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, and Ishaq. Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Thawri said that each one of them must pay one penalty.

The apparent meaning, if His words ﴿وَأَنتُمْ حُرُمٌ﴾ [while you are in a state of ihram] are understood in both of their senses, namely being in ihram for hajj or ʿumrah, and being within the sacred precinct (ḥaram) even if they are not in ihram, is that if non-muhrims kill game within the haram, one penalty is due from them. This was said by Abu Hanifa. Malik said each one of them owes a full penalty.

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿مِنَ النَّعَمِ﴾ is that no specific age is required, so a young goat (jafr) or a female kid (ʿanaq) is sufficient according to the size of the game. This was said by Abu Yusuf and Muhammad. Abu Hanifa said it is not permissible to offer except what suffices for the sacrifice and the offering of qiran (combined pilgrimage).

The apparent meaning of restricting the prohibited ones from killing by His words ﴿وَأَنتُمْ حُرُمٌ﴾ is that if a non-muhrim hunts in a non-sacred area and then slaughters it inside the haram, there is no liability, and it is lawful. This was said by al-Shafiʿi. Abu Hanifa said upon him is the penalty.

﴿يَحْكُمُ بِهِ ذَوَا عَدْلٍ مِّنكُمْ هَدْيًا بَالِغَ الْكَعْبَةِ﴾ [Judged by it are two just men among you, as an offering reaching the Ka'bah]. That is, they judge by an equivalent of what was killed. Ibn Wahb said: "It is from the Sunnah that the two judges give the killer a choice, just as Allah gave him the choice between bringing an offering reaching the Ka'bah, or the expiation of feeding the poor, or the equivalent of that in fasting. If he chooses the offering, the two judges decide upon him what they consider fair in view of what he killed. The least offering is a sheep. If the value does not reach a sheep, they judge concerning it by food, and then he is given the choice between feeding them or fasting one day in place of each mudd (measure)." Malik said the same.

The apparent meaning is that two just men judge concerning it. So did ʿUmar in the hadith of Qabisah ibn Jabir: he summoned ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, and they judged concerning a gazelle with a sheep. Jarir and Ibn ʿUmar did the same. The apparent meaning is that the two just men must be male, so two just women do not judge in it.

Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad read ﴿يَحْكُمُ بِهِ ذُو عَدْلٍ﴾ in the singular, meaning: "judged by it is one who is just among you," and he did not intend the singular literally. It was also said he meant the imam (ruler).

The apparent meaning is that the two judges judge concerning the penalty for game by their own reasoning (ijtihad), and that is entrusted to them. This was said by Abu Hanifa, Malik, and a group of scholars. Al-Shafiʿi said: what has an equivalent among livestock, and what the Companions judged in with a ruling that is not to be departed from for another, is as they judged. What the Companions did not judge in is referred to the reasoning of the two judges, who look at the three categories of livestock, and whatever is closest in resemblance to it, they require that.

The apparent meaning is that one of the two judges must not be the killer of the game. This is the view of Malik. Al-Shafiʿi said: if the killing was by mistake, it is permissible for one of them to be the killer, but if it was intentional, then no, because he would be a sinner by it. He used as evidence the words of the Exalted, ﴿يَحْكُمُ بِهِ ذَوَا عَدْلٍ مِّنكُمْ﴾, as proof of the validity of analogical reasoning (qiyas), since He made the determination of the equivalent a matter for people's reasoning and assumptions.

Regarding the accusative of His words ﴿هَدْيًا﴾, they permitted it to be a circumstantial clause (hal) of "jaza'" for the one who described it by an equivalent, because the qualifier specified it and so it came close to a definite noun. It may also be an apposition (badal) of "mithl" in the reading of one who read mithl in the accusative, or of its place in the reading of one who read it in the genitive, or it may be in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). The apparent meaning is that it is a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in "bihi."

The meaning of ﴿بَالِغَ الْكَعْبَةِ﴾ [reaching the Ka'bah] is that it is slaughtered within the sacred precinct and given in charity wherever he wishes. This is according to Abu Hanifa. Al-Shafiʿi said: it must be within the haram.

Al-Aʿraj read ﴿هَدِيًّا﴾ with a kasra on the dal and shaddah on the ya'. The sentence "yahkumu" is in the place of a qualifier of ﴿جَزَاءٌ﴾, meaning: "judged by it are two just men."

His words ﴿مِّنكُمْ﴾ [among you] are evidence that the two judges are Muslims. He mentioned the Ka'bah because it is the mother of the sacred precinct. They said: the entire haram is a place of sacrifice for this offering. So what was brought to ʿArafah as an offering of penalty is slaughtered at Mina, and what was not brought there is slaughtered in Makkah and in the rest of the areas of the haram, on condition that he enters from outside the haram (ḥill), and he must combine within it both ḥill and haram, so that it reaches the Ka'bah.

﴿أَوْ كَفَّارَةٌ طَعَامُ مَسَاكِينَ﴾ [or an expiation of feeding poor people]. The two companions (Ibn ʿAmir and Ibn Kathir?) read it with the idafa (genitive). The idafa may be by the slightest connection, since expiation may be expiation of an offering, expiation of food, or expiation of fasting. No attention is paid to the saying of al-Farisi that he did not make "kaffarah" an idafa to "ta'am" because it is not for the food; it is for killing game. As for what al-Zamakhshari claimed, that the idafa is explanatory, as if it were said: "or an expiation of food for the poor," like your saying "khatam fiḍḍah" meaning "a ring of silver," that is not of this type, because "khatam fiḍḍah" is an idafa of a thing to its genus, whereas food is not a genus of expiation except by a very distant metaphor.

The rest of the seven read with tanwin and the nominative of ﴿طَعَامُ﴾. Al-Aʿraj and ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read the same, except that they used the singular ﴿مِسْكِينًا﴾ as a generic noun. Abu ʿAli said: "ṭaʿam" is an appositive (ʿaṭf bayan), because the food is the expiation itself. This is according to the school of the Basrans, for they stipulated that explanation applies to definite nouns, not indefinite ones, so it is better to parse it as an apposition (badal).

The amount of food and the number of the poor are not specified. The apparent meaning is that the least that applies to the plural "masakin" suffices. Ibrahim, ʿAta', Mujahid, and al-Qasim said: one assesses the game in dirhams, then with the dirhams buys food, and feeds each poor person half a sa'. This was related from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu Hanifa said it is by assessing the game. Mujahid, ʿAta', Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Shafiʿi, and Ahmad said: one assesses the offering, then with the value of the offering buys food. Malik said: the best I have heard is that one assesses the game, to see how much its price is in food, then feeds each poor person one mudd, and fasts one day in place of each mudd.

Or its equivalent in fasting (aw ʿadlu dhalika ṣiyāman). The more apparent view is that "dhalika" refers to the nearest thing mentioned, which is the food (ṭaʿām). The food mentioned in the verse is not specified either by measure (kayl) or by weight (wazn), so it follows that the fasting is likewise not specified in number of days. The fasting is based on the disagreement over the food: is it one mudd or two mudds? Ibn ʿAbbas and Malik said one mudd, al-Shafiʿi said two mudds, and from Ahmad there are two opinions. They also allowed that "dhalika" may refer to the hunted game killed. For a gazelle (ẓaby) it is three days; for a camel it is twenty days; for an ostrich (naʿāma) and a wild ass (ḥimār al-waḥsh) it is thirty days, as stated by Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn Jubayr said: three days up to ten days. The apparent view is that feeding and fasting are not restricted to a place, and a group of scholars held this view, so he may expiate with them wherever he wishes. ʿAtaʾ and others said: the offering (hady) and the feeding are in Mecca, and the fasting wherever he wishes.

The majority read ﴿ʿadl﴾ with a fatḥa on the ʿayn. Ibn ʿAbbas, Talha ibn Musarrif and al-Jahdari read it with a kasra on it, and its explanation was given at the beginning of al-Baqara. The apparent view is that "aw" (or) is for choice (lil-takhyīr), meaning that this is an act which suffices him whether he is wealthy or poor, and this is the view of the majority. Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibrahim and Hammad ibn Salama said: he does not move on to feeding unless he does not find an offering, and does not move on to fasting unless he does not find what to feed. The apparent view is that the choice returns to the one who killed the game, and this is the view of the majority. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: the choice belongs to the two judges. The apparent view is that the obligation is one of these three, so feeding and fasting are not combined, such that one feeds for a day and fasts in a single expiation; the companions of Abu Hanifa permitted that.

"Ṣiyāman" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz) of "ʿadl," like your saying "ʿalā al-tamrah mithluhā zubdan," because the meaning is: or that is assessed as fasting.

﴿Li-yadhuqa wabāla amrihi﴾ (that he may taste the consequence of his deed). Dhawq (tasting) is well known, and it is borrowed here for what affects one through penalty and the exhaustion of the self by fasting. Wabāl is the evil outcome of what he did, which is the violation of the sanctity of the state of ihram by killing game. Al-Zamakhshari said: "li-yadhuqa" is connected to his saying "fa-jazāʾun" (so a recompense), meaning: upon him is that he be recompensed or expiate "li-yadhuqa", end of quote. This is not permissible except on the reading of the one who made "jazāʾu" construct-annexed or who gave it tanwin and put "mithla" in the accusative. As for the reading of the one who gave tanwin and raised "mithlu", it is not permissible for the lam to be connected to it, because "mithlu" is an adjective of "jazāʾun", and when a verbal noun is described, its complement may not come after the adjective; if you said, "aʿjabanī ḍarbu Zaydin al-shadīdu ʿamran," it would not be permitted; but if the complement precedes the adjective, that is permitted. The correct view is that this reading is connected to a deleted verb, the estimate being: he was recompensed with that, "li-yadhuqa". It has occurred to some grammarians that it is connected to "ʿadlu dhalika", and this is an error.

﴿ʿAfā Allāhu ʿammā salafa﴾ (God has pardoned what has passed), i.e., in your jahiliyya, of your killing game in the sacred precinct.

Al-Zamakhshari said: because they were bound by the laws of those before them, and hunting was forbidden in them, end of quote. Ibn Zayd said: "ʿammā salafa" means for you, O believers, of killing game before this prohibition and forbiddance.

﴿Wa-man ʿāda fa-yantaqimu Allāhu minhu﴾ (and whoever returns, God will take vengeance upon him). I.e., whoever returns in Islam to killing game: if he regards it as lawful, God will take vengeance upon him in the Hereafter, and he disbelieves; or if he forgets his state of ihram, he expiates with one of the three options; or if he is disobedient, by returning deliberately and knowingly in his state of ihram, then there is no expiation for him, and God takes vengeance upon him by imposing expiation only. Whenever he returns, he expiates. Ibn ʿAbbas said: if he is deliberate and knowing of his ihram, there is no expiation for him, and God takes vengeance upon him. This is also the view of Shurayh, al-Nakhaʿi, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, and Dawud. The apparent meaning of "wa-man ʿāda" is general. Do you not see that "man" is conditional or relative, having taken on the meaning of the condition, so it is general? This is contrary to some people who claimed that it is specific to one particular individual, and they attributed to Zayd ibn al-ʿAlaʾ that a man hunted game while in ihram, and was then excused, then returned, so God sent a fire upon him which burned him; and that is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Wa-man ʿāda fa-yantaqimu Allāhu minhu﴾. Even if this report is authentic, this case does not restrict the generality of the verse, since this man is one individual of the general category upon whom God's vengeance was manifest. The fa' in "fa-yantaqimu" is the response of the condition, or it enters upon the relative clause that carries the meaning of the condition, and it is with a suppressed subject; i.e., "fa-huwa yantaqimu Allāhu minhu" (so He, God, takes vengeance upon him).

﴿Wa-Allāhu ʿazīzun dhū intiqām﴾ (And God is Mighty, Lord of retribution). I.e., He is Mighty and cannot be overcome; when He wishes to take vengeance, no one can overpower Him. In this clause there is a reminder of God's retributions and a warning.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 94–95 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of the game that your hands and your spears can reach﴾. It was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, when he (ﷺ) was staying at al-Tan'im. The wild animals and birds would come upon them in their camps while they were in the state of ihram (ritual consecration for pilgrimage). It was also said that some of them had entered ihram and some had not, so when game appeared, their circumstances differed and the rulings became confused. It was also said that Abu al-Yusr killed a wild ass with his spear, and it was said to him: "You killed game while you were in ihram," and so this was revealed. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He commanded them not to forbid the good things, and excluded from that the wine and the gambling, which are forbidden permanently, He then excluded from the good things that which is forbidden in one state but not in another, namely game. Game was something the Arabs lived on, and they took pleasure in hunting it, and they had poetry and fine descriptions about it. The apparent meaning is that the address in His words "O you who have believed" is general to the one who is not in ihram and to the one who is in ihram, but the test is only realized with ihram or in the sacred precinct (al-Haram). Ibn Abbas said: it is for those in ihram. Malik said: it is for those not in ihram, and the meaning is that Allah will test you, and He tested them with it while they were in ihram or in the Haram (the sacred precinct of Makkah).

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿with something of the game﴾ implies a limitation. It was said: so that it is known that it is not one of the great tests, like the test with one's self and one's wealth, but rather it is a comparison with what the people of Ayla were tested with, the fishing of fish, and they did not endure at this test, so how would they endure at what is harder than it? The "min" in ﴿of the game﴾ is partitive in the state of sanctity, since ihram may end and one may leave the Haram, so the game of some of these states is some of the game in general. Al-Tabari and others said: of land game, not sea game. Ibn Atiyya said: it is permissible that "min" be explanatory of the kind. Al-Zajjaj said: this is like your saying "He said: I will surely test you with something of the provision," and like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. The intended meaning of game is what is eaten, because "sayd" (game) applies to both the edible and the non-edible. The poet said:

*"The game of kings are hares and foxes, but when I ride, my game is the heroes."*

And Zuhayr said:

*"A lion of 'Atharr hunts men when the lion, among its peers, tells the truth."*

For this reason Abu Hanifa said: if the one in ihram kills a lion, or a fierce wolf, or what is similar to them, he is liable for its killing.

﴿that your hands and your spears can reach﴾: that is, some of it is taken by the hands because its approach is near, so that the hand can reach it, and some by spears because of its distance and dispersal, so it is not reached except by the spear. Ibn Abbas said: "your hands" means the young of birds and the young of wild animals. Mujahid said: "the hands" means the chicks and the eggs, and what cannot flee; and the spears reach the large game. It was said: what Mujahid said is not permissible, because "sayd" is the name for the wild and the one that resists, not for what does not resist, end of quote. He means that the term "sayd" is not applied to eggs. This does not prevent that as a naming of a thing by what it becomes. Ibn Atiyya said: the apparent meaning is that Allah singled out the hands for mention because they are the greatest means of action in hunting, and in them enter trained animals, snares and whatever is made by the hand of traps and nets, and He singled out the spears for mention because they are the greatest means by which game is wounded, and into them enters the arrow and the like. Some people argued from this verse that the game belongs to the one who takes it, not to the one who startles it, because the one who startled it did not have his hand or spear reach it yet.

Al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab read ﴿yanaluhu﴾ with a dotted "ya" below, and the clause ﴿tanaluhu﴾ is in the position of a description of ﴿bi-shay'in﴾, or in the position of a state of it, since it has been described. Whoever claims it is a state of "sayd" is far off the mark.

﴿That Allah may know who fears Him in the unseen﴾: this is a reason for His words ﴿will surely test you﴾. The meaning of "that He may know" is that the one who fears His punishment, exalted is He, who is absent and awaited in the Hereafter, may be distinguished, and then the game remains for the one who does not fear Him, so he advances upon it. So said al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Atiyya said: so that He may continue to observe it while it exists, since Allah has known that in eternity. Al-Kalbi said: Allah, exalted is He, has always been knowing, and He only expressed knowledge in terms of seeing. It was also said: it is by the omission of a noun: that is, "that the friends of Allah may know." It was said: the meaning is "that they may know that Allah knows who fears Him in the unseen," that is, in secret, where none of the people sees him. So the one who fears does not hunt, and the one who does not fear hunts. It was said: He deals with you as one who seeks to know. It was said: that the known may become manifest, which is the fear of the one who fears. "In the unseen" is in the position of an accusative as a state, and its meaning is that the one who fears is absent from seeing Allah, exalted is He. Similar to it are His words ﴿Whoever feared the Most Merciful in the unseen﴾ [Qaf: 33], and ﴿those who fear their Lord in the unseen﴾ [al-Anbiya': 49]. He, peace be upon him, said: "If you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." Al-Tabari said its meaning is in this world, where the servant does not see his Lord, so He is absent from him. Ibn Atiyya said: the apparent meaning is that "in the unseen" means from the people, that is, in seclusion, whoever fears Allah, end of quote, from the game in itself, end of quote. Al-Zuhri read ﴿liyu'lima Allahu﴾ from "a'lama." Ibn Atiyya said: that is, that He may let His servants know, end of quote. So it would be from "a'lama," the transitive form of "alima" (to know) transferred to one object, like the transfer of "arafa" (to know), so the first object is omitted, which is "His servants," because the meaning indicates it, and the second object remains, which is ﴿whoever fears Him﴾.

﴿So whoever transgresses after that﴾: the meaning is that whoever transgresses by opposing it and hunts. "That" is a reference to the prohibition implied in the meaning of the preceding speech, and its estimate is "so they should not hunt," which is indicated by His words ﴿that Allah may know who fears Him in the unseen﴾.

﴿For him there is a painful punishment﴾: it was said: in the Hereafter. It was said: in this world. Ibn Abbas said: his belly and back are stretched with lashes, and his garments are stripped off.

﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of sanctity﴾: "Those who have believed" is general, and here He explicitly prohibited the killing of game while they are in the state of being ones in sanctity. The word "ihrum" is the plural of "haram," and "haram" means the one made sacred, and the one who is in the Haram. The one who holds that the term is meant in its literal sense argues from His words ﴿while you are in the state of sanctity﴾ that the one in ihram and the one within the Haram are both prohibited from killing game. The one who does not hold this says: the meaning is those who enter ihram for Hajj or 'Umrah, which is the view of the majority. It was also said: the meaning is "while you are in the Haram." The apparent meaning is the prohibition of killing game, and the verse before this one indicated by its meaning the prohibition of hunting, so from the two verses together there is derived the prohibition of hunting and the prohibition of killing game. The apparent meaning is the generality of game. This generality has been specified for land game by His words ﴿Lawful to you is the game of the sea﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 96]. It was also said: and by the Sunnah, by the established hadith: "Five are harmful creatures that are killed both within the sanctuary and outside it: the crow, the kite, the mouse, and the rabid dog." The Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq limited themselves to these five. Malik analogized to the rabid dog every creature that attacks people and others, and considered it included in its wording: lion, leopard, panther, wolf, and every predator that attacks. He said: it is permissible for him to kill them, initiating the killing, but not the lion-like animal, the fox, or the hyena. If he kills them, he must pay a ransom. Mujahid and al-Nakha'i said: he may not kill any predator except one that attacks him, and something similar is narrated from Ibn Umar. The people of opinion said: if the predator attacks him first, he may kill it with no ransom, and if the one in ihram initiates and kills it, he must pay a ransom. Malik said about the young of predators before they prey: it is not appropriate for the one in ihram to kill them. It is established from Umar that he ordered those in ihram to kill snakes, and the people agreed on the permissibility of killing them. It is established from Umar the permissibility of killing the wasp, because it has the status of the scorpion, and venomous creatures have the status of the snake, like the viper and the tarantula. The position of Abu Hanifa and a group is that game is whatever is wild, whether edible or not. On this basis, if the one in ihram kills a predator whose meat is not eaten, he is liable, but the compensation does not exceed the value of a sheep. Zufar said: the compensation is whatever amount it reaches. A group said: game is what is eaten, and on this basis there is no liability for killing a predator, which is the view of al-Shafi'i, nor for killing the five harmful creatures, nor the wolf. If the game is of a kind that is lawful to eat, and the one in ihram kills it even by slaughter, the position of Abu Hanifa and Malik is that it is not slaughtered (dhakkah), so its meat is not eaten. This is the view of Ibn al-Musayyab and one of the two opinions of al-Hasan. The position of al-Shafi'i is that if the one in ihram slaughters the game, it is properly slaughtered. Al-Hakam, Amr ibn Dinar and Sufyan said: it is lawful for one who is not in ihram to eat it, and this is the other of the two opinions of al-Hasan.

(p-17)

(p-18)

﴿Whoever among you kills it intentionally, its penalty is an equivalent of what he killed from the livestock﴾. The apparent meaning restricts killing to the intentional act. So whoever kills by mistake, such as one who is forgetful of his state of ihram, or who shoots thinking it is not game and it turns out to be game, or who deflects an arrow he shot at something other than game so that it strikes game, bears no penalty. This was related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr, Tawus, ʿAta', and Salim, and Abu Thawr, Dawud, and al-Tabari said the same. It is also one of the two opinions of al-Hasan al-Basri, Mujahid, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Ibn ʿAbbas said, as transmitted by al-Daraqutni from him: "Expiation applies only to the intentional act, and they were made severe in the case of error so that they would not repeat it." It was also said that the verse came in the typical form, so the rare case is assimilated to it. It was also said that intention was mentioned because the context of the verse concerns one who killed intentionally, referring to the case of Abu al-Yasar, who killed a donkey intentionally while in ihram.

The position of Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafiʿi and their companions is that error, whether through forgetfulness or otherwise, is the same as intention. Intention means that he remembers his ihram and aims to kill. This was related from ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, Tawus, al-Hasan, Ibrahim, and al-Zuhri. Al-Zuhri said: "The penalty for intentional killing is in the Qur'an, and for error and forgetfulness it is in the Sunnah." The judge Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: "If by the Sunnah he means the reports that came from ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas, then how excellent they are, and how good they are as an example to follow."

Mujahid said: "Its meaning is that he killed intentionally while forgetting his ihram. But if he was remembering his ihram, then this is too grave and too great to be expiated, and he has exited the state, and he has no pilgrimage, because he committed what is forbidden in ihram, so it is nullified for him, just as if he spoke during prayer or broke his wudu' during it." He said: "As for the one who erred, he is the one upon whom the penalty falls." Ibn Jurayj said similarly. It was related from Mujahid that there is no penalty for one who killed intentionally, and he should seek forgiveness from Allah, and his pilgrimage remains complete.

The Kufans read ﴿فَجَزَاءٌ﴾ with tanwin, and ﴿مِثْلُ﴾ with damma. The nominative of jaza' is then the predicate of an omitted subject, whose predicate is estimated as: "Upon him is a penalty," and "mithl" is an adjective, meaning: "a penalty that is equivalent to what he killed." ʿAbd Allah read ﴿فَجَزَاؤُهُ مِثْلُ﴾, where the pronoun refers either to the slayer of the game or to the game. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah, ﴿فَجَزَاؤُهُ مِثْلُ﴾ is nominative as a subject and predicate. The rest of the seven readers read ﴿فَجَزَاءُ مِثْلُ﴾ with jaza' in the nominative and construct-state with mithl. It was said that mithl is inserted as in your saying "Mithlaka man yafʿalu kadha," meaning "you do such-and-such," so the estimate is "the penalty of what he killed." It was also said that this is the idafa of the verbal noun to its object. This estimate is supported by al-Sulami's reading ﴿فَجَزَاءٌ﴾ with damma and tanwin, and ﴿مِثْلَ مَا قَتَلَ﴾ with fatha. Muhammad ibn Muqatil read ﴿فَجَزَاءً مِثْلَ مَا قَتَلَ﴾ with fatha on both jaza' and mithl, and the estimate is: "Let him bring forth a penalty equivalent to what he killed," with mithl as an adjective of jaza'. Al-Hasan read ﴿مِنَ النَّعْمِ﴾ with the ʿayn sukun for lightness, as they say al-shaʿr. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "It is a dialect form." ﴿مِنَ النَّعَمِ﴾ is an adjective of jaza', whether jaza' is read nominative with mithl, or the idafa is made from jaza' to mithl, meaning "a penalty that is from the livestock." In the idafa reading, it is permissible for "min al-naʿam" to be connected to jaza', except in the first reading, because jaza' is a qualified verbal noun, and so it does not govern.
