Abu al-Baqa' erred in permitting "min al-naʿam" to be a circumstantial clause (hal) of the pronoun in "qatala," meaning the omitted object pronoun in "qatala" which refers to "ma" (what) said, because the killed one would be from the livestock. That is not the intended meaning, because what is from the livestock is what is the penalty, not what the muhrim kills. Also, livestock does not enter the category of game.

Regarding equivalence, the apparent meaning is that it is equivalence in form, creation, smallness, and size. This is the view of the majority. It was related from ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Jubayr, and Qatadah, and Malik, al-Shafiʿi, and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said the same. The details of what corresponds to each killed game have been lengthily discussed by a group of exegetes, but the wording of the Qur'an does not address them, and they are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence.

A group of the Successors held that equivalence is in value: one assesses the killed game, then with its value buys food from the livestock, then gives it in charity. This is the view of al-Nakhaʿi, ʿAta', and one of the two opinions of Mujahid. Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf said the same: he buys with the value an offering if he wishes, and if he wishes he buys food and gives each poor person half a sa', and if he wishes he fasts one day for every half sa'.

Some said: equivalence applies to what has a similar counterpart in form, and what has no counterpart, equivalence is in value. Abu Bakr al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari were strongly partisan for the school of Abu Hanifa, but the wording of the verse is at odds with his school, since the apparent meaning of the verse requires a choice between bringing an offering of livestock equivalent to what was killed, or expiating by feeding the poor, or fasting an equivalent number of days.

The apparent meaning is that penalty applies only to killing, not to capturing the game, nor to its kind, nor to eating it, in agreement with al-Shafiʿi, and against Abu Hanifa, who said that upon him is the penalty of what he ate, meaning its value. His two companions disagreed with him and said there is nothing upon him except seeking forgiveness, because he merely partook of it. The penalty also does not apply to pointing it out, contrary to Abu Hanifa and Ashhab, who said the one who points it out must pay the penalty. This was related from Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAwf. Al-Shafiʿi, Malik, and Abu Thawr said: the one who points does not pay, and the penalty falls on the killer. Nor is there a penalty for wounding it or for the reduction in its value because of that. Al-Muzani said there is something upon him. Some scholars said: if its value is reduced, for example by a tenth, then upon him is a tenth of its value. Dawud said there is nothing upon him.

The apparent meaning is that if a group of muhrims shared in hunting one game, only one penalty is due from them, because the killing is not attributed to each one of them. As for the one killed, it is one, so the equivalent must be one. This was said by al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, and Ishaq. Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Thawri said that each one of them must pay one penalty.

The apparent meaning, if His words ﴿وَأَنتُمْ حُرُمٌ﴾ [while you are in a state of ihram] are understood in both of their senses, namely being in ihram for hajj or ʿumrah, and being within the sacred precinct (ḥaram) even if they are not in ihram, is that if non-muhrims kill game within the haram, one penalty is due from them. This was said by Abu Hanifa. Malik said each one of them owes a full penalty.

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿مِنَ النَّعَمِ﴾ is that no specific age is required, so a young goat (jafr) or a female kid (ʿanaq) is sufficient according to the size of the game. This was said by Abu Yusuf and Muhammad. Abu Hanifa said it is not permissible to offer except what suffices for the sacrifice and the offering of qiran (combined pilgrimage).

The apparent meaning of restricting the prohibited ones from killing by His words ﴿وَأَنتُمْ حُرُمٌ﴾ is that if a non-muhrim hunts in a non-sacred area and then slaughters it inside the haram, there is no liability, and it is lawful. This was said by al-Shafiʿi. Abu Hanifa said upon him is the penalty.

﴿يَحْكُمُ بِهِ ذَوَا عَدْلٍ مِّنكُمْ هَدْيًا بَالِغَ الْكَعْبَةِ﴾ [Judged by it are two just men among you, as an offering reaching the Ka'bah]. That is, they judge by an equivalent of what was killed. Ibn Wahb said: "It is from the Sunnah that the two judges give the killer a choice, just as Allah gave him the choice between bringing an offering reaching the Ka'bah, or the expiation of feeding the poor, or the equivalent of that in fasting. If he chooses the offering, the two judges decide upon him what they consider fair in view of what he killed. The least offering is a sheep. If the value does not reach a sheep, they judge concerning it by food, and then he is given the choice between feeding them or fasting one day in place of each mudd (measure)." Malik said the same.

The apparent meaning is that two just men judge concerning it. So did ʿUmar in the hadith of Qabisah ibn Jabir: he summoned ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, and they judged concerning a gazelle with a sheep. Jarir and Ibn ʿUmar did the same. The apparent meaning is that the two just men must be male, so two just women do not judge in it.

Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad read ﴿يَحْكُمُ بِهِ ذُو عَدْلٍ﴾ in the singular, meaning: "judged by it is one who is just among you," and he did not intend the singular literally. It was also said he meant the imam (ruler).

The apparent meaning is that the two judges judge concerning the penalty for game by their own reasoning (ijtihad), and that is entrusted to them. This was said by Abu Hanifa, Malik, and a group of scholars. Al-Shafiʿi said: what has an equivalent among livestock, and what the Companions judged in with a ruling that is not to be departed from for another, is as they judged. What the Companions did not judge in is referred to the reasoning of the two judges, who look at the three categories of livestock, and whatever is closest in resemblance to it, they require that.

The apparent meaning is that one of the two judges must not be the killer of the game. This is the view of Malik. Al-Shafiʿi said: if the killing was by mistake, it is permissible for one of them to be the killer, but if it was intentional, then no, because he would be a sinner by it. He used as evidence the words of the Exalted, ﴿يَحْكُمُ بِهِ ذَوَا عَدْلٍ مِّنكُمْ﴾, as proof of the validity of analogical reasoning (qiyas), since He made the determination of the equivalent a matter for people's reasoning and assumptions.

Regarding the accusative of His words ﴿هَدْيًا﴾, they permitted it to be a circumstantial clause (hal) of "jaza'" for the one who described it by an equivalent, because the qualifier specified it and so it came close to a definite noun. It may also be an apposition (badal) of "mithl" in the reading of one who read mithl in the accusative, or of its place in the reading of one who read it in the genitive, or it may be in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). The apparent meaning is that it is a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in "bihi."

The meaning of ﴿بَالِغَ الْكَعْبَةِ﴾ [reaching the Ka'bah] is that it is slaughtered within the sacred precinct and given in charity wherever he wishes. This is according to Abu Hanifa. Al-Shafiʿi said: it must be within the haram.

Al-Aʿraj read ﴿هَدِيًّا﴾ with a kasra on the dal and shaddah on the ya'. The sentence "yahkumu" is in the place of a qualifier of ﴿جَزَاءٌ﴾, meaning: "judged by it are two just men."

His words ﴿مِّنكُمْ﴾ [among you] are evidence that the two judges are Muslims. He mentioned the Ka'bah because it is the mother of the sacred precinct. They said: the entire haram is a place of sacrifice for this offering. So what was brought to ʿArafah as an offering of penalty is slaughtered at Mina, and what was not brought there is slaughtered in Makkah and in the rest of the areas of the haram, on condition that he enters from outside the haram (ḥill), and he must combine within it both ḥill and haram, so that it reaches the Ka'bah.

﴿أَوْ كَفَّارَةٌ طَعَامُ مَسَاكِينَ﴾ [or an expiation of feeding poor people]. The two companions (Ibn ʿAmir and Ibn Kathir?) read it with the idafa (genitive). The idafa may be by the slightest connection, since expiation may be expiation of an offering, expiation of food, or expiation of fasting. No attention is paid to the saying of al-Farisi that he did not make "kaffarah" an idafa to "ta'am" because it is not for the food; it is for killing game. As for what al-Zamakhshari claimed, that the idafa is explanatory, as if it were said: "or an expiation of food for the poor," like your saying "khatam fiḍḍah" meaning "a ring of silver," that is not of this type, because "khatam fiḍḍah" is an idafa of a thing to its genus, whereas food is not a genus of expiation except by a very distant metaphor.

The rest of the seven read with tanwin and the nominative of ﴿طَعَامُ﴾. Al-Aʿraj and ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read the same, except that they used the singular ﴿مِسْكِينًا﴾ as a generic noun. Abu ʿAli said: "ṭaʿam" is an appositive (ʿaṭf bayan), because the food is the expiation itself. This is according to the school of the Basrans, for they stipulated that explanation applies to definite nouns, not indefinite ones, so it is better to parse it as an apposition (badal).

The amount of food and the number of the poor are not specified. The apparent meaning is that the least that applies to the plural "masakin" suffices. Ibrahim, ʿAta', Mujahid, and al-Qasim said: one assesses the game in dirhams, then with the dirhams buys food, and feeds each poor person half a sa'. This was related from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu Hanifa said it is by assessing the game. Mujahid, ʿAta', Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Shafiʿi, and Ahmad said: one assesses the offering, then with the value of the offering buys food. Malik said: the best I have heard is that one assesses the game, to see how much its price is in food, then feeds each poor person one mudd, and fasts one day in place of each mudd.

Or its equivalent in fasting (aw ʿadlu dhalika ṣiyāman). The more apparent view is that "dhalika" refers to the nearest thing mentioned, which is the food (ṭaʿām). The food mentioned in the verse is not specified either by measure (kayl) or by weight (wazn), so it follows that the fasting is likewise not specified in number of days. The fasting is based on the disagreement over the food: is it one mudd or two mudds? Ibn ʿAbbas and Malik said one mudd, al-Shafiʿi said two mudds, and from Ahmad there are two opinions. They also allowed that "dhalika" may refer to the hunted game killed. For a gazelle (ẓaby) it is three days; for a camel it is twenty days; for an ostrich (naʿāma) and a wild ass (ḥimār al-waḥsh) it is thirty days, as stated by Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn Jubayr said: three days up to ten days. The apparent view is that feeding and fasting are not restricted to a place, and a group of scholars held this view, so he may expiate with them wherever he wishes. ʿAtaʾ and others said: the offering (hady) and the feeding are in Mecca, and the fasting wherever he wishes.

The majority read ﴿ʿadl﴾ with a fatḥa on the ʿayn. Ibn ʿAbbas, Talha ibn Musarrif and al-Jahdari read it with a kasra on it, and its explanation was given at the beginning of al-Baqara. The apparent view is that "aw" (or) is for choice (lil-takhyīr), meaning that this is an act which suffices him whether he is wealthy or poor, and this is the view of the majority. Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibrahim and Hammad ibn Salama said: he does not move on to feeding unless he does not find an offering, and does not move on to fasting unless he does not find what to feed. The apparent view is that the choice returns to the one who killed the game, and this is the view of the majority. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: the choice belongs to the two judges. The apparent view is that the obligation is one of these three, so feeding and fasting are not combined, such that one feeds for a day and fasts in a single expiation; the companions of Abu Hanifa permitted that.

"Ṣiyāman" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz) of "ʿadl," like your saying "ʿalā al-tamrah mithluhā zubdan," because the meaning is: or that is assessed as fasting.

﴿Li-yadhuqa wabāla amrihi﴾ (that he may taste the consequence of his deed). Dhawq (tasting) is well known, and it is borrowed here for what affects one through penalty and the exhaustion of the self by fasting. Wabāl is the evil outcome of what he did, which is the violation of the sanctity of the state of ihram by killing game. Al-Zamakhshari said: "li-yadhuqa" is connected to his saying "fa-jazāʾun" (so a recompense), meaning: upon him is that he be recompensed or expiate "li-yadhuqa", end of quote. This is not permissible except on the reading of the one who made "jazāʾu" construct-annexed or who gave it tanwin and put "mithla" in the accusative. As for the reading of the one who gave tanwin and raised "mithlu", it is not permissible for the lam to be connected to it, because "mithlu" is an adjective of "jazāʾun", and when a verbal noun is described, its complement may not come after the adjective; if you said, "aʿjabanī ḍarbu Zaydin al-shadīdu ʿamran," it would not be permitted; but if the complement precedes the adjective, that is permitted. The correct view is that this reading is connected to a deleted verb, the estimate being: he was recompensed with that, "li-yadhuqa". It has occurred to some grammarians that it is connected to "ʿadlu dhalika", and this is an error.

﴿ʿAfā Allāhu ʿammā salafa﴾ (God has pardoned what has passed), i.e., in your jahiliyya, of your killing game in the sacred precinct.

Al-Zamakhshari said: because they were bound by the laws of those before them, and hunting was forbidden in them, end of quote. Ibn Zayd said: "ʿammā salafa" means for you, O believers, of killing game before this prohibition and forbiddance.

﴿Wa-man ʿāda fa-yantaqimu Allāhu minhu﴾ (and whoever returns, God will take vengeance upon him). I.e., whoever returns in Islam to killing game: if he regards it as lawful, God will take vengeance upon him in the Hereafter, and he disbelieves; or if he forgets his state of ihram, he expiates with one of the three options; or if he is disobedient, by returning deliberately and knowingly in his state of ihram, then there is no expiation for him, and God takes vengeance upon him by imposing expiation only. Whenever he returns, he expiates. Ibn ʿAbbas said: if he is deliberate and knowing of his ihram, there is no expiation for him, and God takes vengeance upon him. This is also the view of Shurayh, al-Nakhaʿi, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, and Dawud. The apparent meaning of "wa-man ʿāda" is general. Do you not see that "man" is conditional or relative, having taken on the meaning of the condition, so it is general? This is contrary to some people who claimed that it is specific to one particular individual, and they attributed to Zayd ibn al-ʿAlaʾ that a man hunted game while in ihram, and was then excused, then returned, so God sent a fire upon him which burned him; and that is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Wa-man ʿāda fa-yantaqimu Allāhu minhu﴾. Even if this report is authentic, this case does not restrict the generality of the verse, since this man is one individual of the general category upon whom God's vengeance was manifest. The fa' in "fa-yantaqimu" is the response of the condition, or it enters upon the relative clause that carries the meaning of the condition, and it is with a suppressed subject; i.e., "fa-huwa yantaqimu Allāhu minhu" (so He, God, takes vengeance upon him).

﴿Wa-Allāhu ʿazīzun dhū intiqām﴾ (And God is Mighty, Lord of retribution). I.e., He is Mighty and cannot be overcome; when He wishes to take vengeance, no one can overpower Him. In this clause there is a reminder of God's retributions and a warning.

﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travelers﴾. Al-Kalbi said: It was revealed concerning the Banu Mudlij, who used to dwell at the edges of the sea. They asked about the fish that the water had left behind (when it receded), and so this was revealed. Here "the sea" (al-bahr) means abundant, vast water, and the ruling is the same for a river, a valley, a pool, or a spring, with no difference. [p-23] It has also been said that what is meant by "the sea" here is the great sea, and the occasion of revelation points to this, while everything else is understood in its light. As for its food (ta'amuh), it is narrated from Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, and Ibn ʿUmar that it is what the sea casts up and what floats on it. Ibn ʿAbbas, a group of the Companions, the Successors, and those after them said that this is in accordance with his (ﷺ) saying: "Its dead is lawful." Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr, al-Nakhaʿi, Ibn al-Musayyab, Mujahid, and al-Suddi said: its game is its fresh (catch), and its food is what is salted from it. This is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and Zayd ibn Thabit. Abu ʿAbd Allah said: This is weak, because what has become salted was once fresh game at the beginning, so it would entail repetition. Others said: its food is the salt that forms from its water and whatever plants and the like are in it. Al-Hasan said: its food is what is cast up on the shore of its coast. It has also been said: its food is everything that the water waters and makes grow, because it grew from the water of the sea. It has also been said: the game of the sea is what is hunted for eating and for other purposes, such as the mussel for the sake of pearls, and some creatures for the sake of their bones and teeth. Its "food," meaning the edible part of it specifically, is a specific term following a general one. The absence of a restriction on lawfulness indicates permission for the one in ihram and for the one not in ihram. The "game" (al-sayd) is the thing hunted, and it is attributed to the place where it is found. The apparent meaning is that it is lawful to eat every kind of what is hunted from among its creatures, even what is called the sea-boar, the sea-dog, the sea-serpent, the crab, and the frog. This is the view of Ibn Abi Layla, Malik, and al-Awzaʿi. Al-Layth said: the sea-boar is not eaten, nor the sea-man, but its carrion, its dog, and its horse are eaten. Abu Hanifah and al-Thawri, as transmitted from him by Abu Ishaq al-Fazari, said: Of the creatures of the sea, only fish is eaten; its floating (carrion) is not eaten, nor the frog, nor its dog, nor its boar, and he said: these are among the vile things (khaba'ith). Al-Razi said: What is hunted from the sea includes fish, and all its kinds are lawful; frogs, and all their kinds, are unlawful; and they disagreed about what is other than these two. Al-Zamakhshari said: "the game of the sea" means what is caught from the sea, whether edible or not, and "its food" means what is eaten from its game. The meaning is: it is made lawful for you to benefit from everything hunted in the sea, and lawful for you to eat its edible part, which, according to Abu Hanifah, is fish alone. According to Ibn Abi Layla, it is all that is hunted from it, and the interpretation of the verse according to him is: lawful for you is the game of the sea's creatures, and that you feed it (to others). The interpretation of "and its food" as "and that you feed it" is contrary to the apparent meaning, and according to Ibn Abi Layla's view the pronoun returns to the game of the sea. The apparent meaning is that it returns to the sea, and that what is meant is the thing eaten, not the act of feeding. This is indicated by the apparent wording of "and its food" and by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Harith, who read "ṭuʿmuh" with a damma on the ṭa' and a sukun on the ʿayn. "Mataʿan" (as a provision) is in the accusative. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it is an infinitive (maṣdar), and the meaning is: He provided it for you as a provision from which you benefit and which you use as relish. Al-Zamakhshari said: "mataʿan lakum" is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: it is made lawful for you as a provision for you. In terms of the object of purpose, it stands in the same position as the verse: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift﴾ [al-Anbiya: 72] in the matter of the circumstantial accusative (hal), because His saying "mataʿan lakum" is an object of purpose specific to the food, just as "nafilah" (an additional gift) is a circumstantial accusative specific to Jacob. He means: its food was made lawful as a provision for you, to be eaten fresh, and for your travelers, who take it as dried provision, just as Moses, peace be upon him, took provision on his journey to al-Khidr. End of quotation. His restricting the object of purpose to "its food" accords with his school. The school of Abu Hanifah holds that the game of the sea includes what is edible and what is not, that "its food" is the edible part of it, and that provision (tamtiʿ) is achieved only through the edible part, whether fresh or dried. According to others' school, it is permissible for it to be an object of purpose with respect to both the game of the sea and its food. The address in "lakum" is to the residents of the sea and its cities, and "al-sayyarah" are the travelers. Mujahid said: the address is to the people of the villages, and "al-sayyarah" are the people of the cities. This disagreement concerns whether the resident and the traveler, the desert dweller and the town dweller, and the fresh and the salted are equal in this ruling.

﴿And forbidden to you is the game of the land as long as you are in the state of ihram﴾. God Most High forbade game to the one in ihram by His saying: ﴿not violating the game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1], ﴿but when you have left the state of ihram, then hunt﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2], and by His saying: ﴿Do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95], and by this verse; He repeated it to emphasize its ruling. The apparent meaning is that the hunting of land game is forbidden to the one in ihram in every respect: whether it was hunted, and for whoever it was hunted on his behalf, or not on his behalf. This is narrated from ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, Tawus, Ibn Jubayr, Abu al-Sha'tha', al-Thawri, and Ishaq. From Abu Hurayrah, ʿAta', and Ibn Jubayr it is narrated that they permitted the one in ihram to eat what a non-muhrim hunted for himself, or for a similar non-muhrim. Others said: it is forbidden for the one in ihram to hunt. As for if he buys it from its owner, slaughters it, and eats it, it is not forbidden; Abu Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman did this. Malik, al-Shafiʿi and his companions, and Ahmad said: he may eat what a non-muhrim hunted, if he did not hunt it on his behalf; but if it was hunted on his behalf, he may not eat it. If he eats it, Malik said: he owes a penalty (jaza'). This is also the view of al-Awzaʿi and al-Hasan ibn Salih. Al-Shafiʿi said: there is no penalty upon him. Abu Hanifah and his companions said: the eating of game by the one in ihram is permissible if a non-muhrim hunted it, and the muhrim did not order its hunting nor indicate it. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what does Abu Hanifah do with the generality of His saying "game of the land"? I say: Abu Hanifah took the implication (mafhum) from His saying: ﴿And forbidden to you is the game of the land as long as you are in the state of ihram﴾, because its apparent meaning is that it is the game of those in ihram, not the game of others. So it is as if it were said: "And forbidden to you is what you hunt in the sea," and thus excluded from it is the game of others and their game when they were not in ihram. This is indicated by His saying, Most High: ﴿O you who believe, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]. End of quotation. This is an overreach by al-Zamakhshari according to the apparent meaning; rather, the apparent meaning of "game of the land" is generality, whether the one in ihram or a non-muhrim hunted it. Ibn ʿAbbas read "ḥarrama" (with the verb active) and "ṣayda" (in the accusative), and "mā dumtum ḥurumā" with a fatha on the ḥa' and the rā'. Yahya read "mā dumtum" with a kasra on the dal, and this is a dialect in which one says "dimta tadāmu." There is no disagreement that what never leaves the sea is game of the sea, and what never leaves the land is game of the land. There is disagreement about what lives in one of them and may also live in the other. ʿAta', Ibn Jubayr, Abu Mijlaz, Malik, and others said: it is of the game of the land; if the one in ihram kills it, he must compensate. Abu Mijlaz mentioned among these the frog, the tortoise, and the crab. It is narrated from ʿAta' that one considers where most of its life is spent. He was asked about the water-bird (ibn al-ma'), whether it is game of the land or the sea, and he said: wherever it is found in greater number, it belongs to that place, and wherever it breeds, it belongs there; this is also the view of Abu Hanifah. The correct view regarding ibn al-ma' is that it is a bird that grazes and eats grain. The hafiz Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: The sound view is the prohibition concerning a creature that lives both on land and in the sea, because there is a conflict between an indication of prohibition and an indication of permission, and the indication of prohibition is given precedence as a precaution.

﴿And fear God, to whom you will be gathered﴾. This contains an admonition and a warning, coming after the permitting and the prohibiting. He mentioned the gathering (al-hashr) because it is on that day that the obedient and the disobedient become manifest.

(p-25) God made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of sustenance (qiyam) for the people, and the sacred month, and the offerings, and the garlanded animals.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is evident. He, exalted is He, mentioned the glorifying of the state of ihram by forbidding the hunting of game in it, to the extent that He legislated penalties for killing it. He also mentioned the glorifying of the Ka'bah in His saying: ﴿an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]. So in this verse He, exalted is He, mentioned that He made the Ka'bah a qiyam for the people, meaning He fixed in their hearts its glorification, such that no one would commit harm within it, and it became a restraint for them from harm. In the Jahiliyyah of ignorance, they did not hope for Paradise nor fear Hellfire, since they had no king to prevent some of them from harming others. So the sanctity of the Ka'bah took the place of the sanctity of a king, despite their rivalry, envy, enmity and pursuit of blood vengeance. For this reason He made the three things mentioned after the Ka'bah a qiyam for the people. So they would not molest anyone in the sacred month, nor anyone who had driven the offering, because it is not known whether he had come for war, nor anyone who set out intending the House for hajj or 'umrah, so that he wore garlands of the trees of the valley, nor anyone who had completed his rites, so that he wore garlands of the trees of the Haram.

When Quraysh sent al-Hulays to the believers during the time of al-Hudaybiyyah, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "This is a man who honours the sanctity, so meet him with the sacrificial camels marked (with garlands)." When al-Hulays saw them, that weighed heavily on him, and he said: "It is not fitting that these be barred." He returned from Quraysh's mission. Here jaʿala is used in the sense of ṣayyara (to make/render). It has also been said: jaʿala is in the sense of bayyana (to make clear), and this should be taken as an explanation of meaning, since jaʿala has not been transmitted as a synonym in this sense; but in terms of making (taṣyīr), it entails clarification and determination.

Since the word al-Ka'bah had been applied by some Arabs to other than the Sacred House, such as the house that was in Khath'am, called the Ka'bah of the Yemenis, God, exalted is He, made clear that what is meant here by al-Ka'bah is the Sacred House. It is either a badal (substitute) for al-Ka'bah or a ʿatf al-bayān (explicative apposition). Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-Bayt al-Haram is an ʿatf al-bayān for the purpose of praise, not for the purpose of clarification, just as an adjective comes in that way," and he finished. But this is not as he stated, because they mentioned in the condition for ʿatf al-bayān that it must be a non-derived noun (jumūd). If its condition is that it be non-derived, then there is no indication of praise in it, since it is not a derivative. Praise is only indicated by a derivative, unless it is said that when he described the ʿatf al-bayān with His saying (al-Haram), the whole conveys praise, and so that is possible.

Al-qiyam is a verbal noun like al-siyam (fasting), and it is said: "This is a qiyam for it" and "qiwam for it." It seems that some considered qiyam not to be a verbal noun but a noun like al-siwak (toothstick), and therefore the waw is sound. He said: "qiwam of this world and qiyam of religion." When the feminine ta' is attached it becomes obligatory: they said al-qiyamah.

They differed in interpreting His saying ﴿qiyaman lil-nas﴾ (a means of sustenance for the people). It was said: by the expansion of provision upon them, since He made it the destination of all regions, and Makkah had neither crops nor livestock. It was said: by the prohibition of raiding within the Haram. It was said: by the fact that they became the People of God, so everyone draws near to them. It was said: by the rites performed in it and the acts of worship; this is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. It was said: whoever turns toward it is safe, and this too is narrated from him. It was said: by the non-harm of those who were expelled from committing a crime and took refuge in it. It was said: by the continuance of the religion as long as it is visited on pilgrimage and faced in prayer. ʿAtaʾ said: "If they left it for one year, they would not be given respite nor delayed."

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: "It is not far-fetched to carry it on all these aspects, because the sustaining of livelihood is through abundance of benefits, through the repelling of harms, through the attainment of standing and leadership, and through the attainment of religion. The Ka'bah is a cause for the attainment of these categories," and he finished.

Ibn ʿAmir read qīman (without alif). If its origin is qiyaman with the alif deleted, it is said the ruling for this is that it occurs in poetry. If it is a verbal noun of the pattern (fiʿal), its analogy would be that the waw be sound, as in ʿiwaḍ. Al-Jahdari read qayyiman, with fatḥah on the qāf and a shaddah on the yāʾ with kasrah, and it is like sayyid: a noun that indicates the established attribute without restriction to a time. The word al-nas (the people) is general; it was said the meaning is the generality. It was said: the meaning is the Arabs. Abu ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi al-Fadl said: "The beauty of this metaphor is that the people of each town, when they say 'the people did such-and-such,' mean by it only the people of their own town; therefore they were addressed according to their custom," and he finished.

The sacred month, its apparent form is singular. It was said it is Dhu al-Hijjah alone, and al-Zamakhshari began with this, saying: "Because of its distinction among the sacred months by the mark of hajj, it has a status which God knows." It was said: the meaning is the category, which includes the four sacred months: the three by consensus of the Arabs, and the month of Mudar, which is Rajab, which many of the Arabs did not recognise; and for this reason it is called the month of God, since He, exalted is He, had attached it to the three in sanctity, so He attributed it to Himself and affirmed it. The meaning is the month of the family of God, and that is the month of Quraysh. To it ʿAwf ibn al-Ahwas says:

"And the month of the Banu Umayyah, and the offerings when they are held back, their blood smeared upon them."

Since the Ka'bah is a specific place that not every fearful person can reach, God made the sacred months, the offerings and the garlands a qiyam for the people, like the Ka'bah.

﴿That is so that you may know that God knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth﴾. The apparent reading is that the demonstrative refers to the implied verbal noun; that is, that making these things (a qiyam for the people and a security for them) is so that they may know that He, exalted is He, knows the details of the affairs that exist in the heavens and the earth, and your interests in your world and your religion. So look at His kindness to the servants despite their state of disbelief! Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the demonstrative refer to what was mentioned of preserving the sanctity of the state of ihram by abstaining from hunting and other things. Al-Zajjaj said: the demonstrative refers to what God, exalted is He, announced of the reports of unseen matters and the disclosing of secrets, like His saying ﴿listeners to falsehood, listeners to other people who have not come to you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41], and like His report of their distortion of the Scriptures; that is, that unseen knowledge which He informed you of through His Messenger indicates to you that He knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth. It was also said: the demonstrative refers to the turning of people's hearts toward Makkah in the known months, so its inhabitants live with them; and if not for that they would die of hunger; He knows what is in their interests, and so that they may infer that He knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth.

﴿And that God is Knower of all things﴾. This is a generality that includes the universals and the particulars, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Not a leaf falls but He knows it﴾ [al-An'am: 59].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 98:

﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾. This is a warning, as He informs that His punishment is severe for whoever violates His sanctity.

﴿And that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. This is an indication of forgiveness and mercy for whoever safeguards obedience to Allah, or repents from His disobediences.

﴿Upon the Messenger is only the conveying [of the message]﴾. When encouragement and warning had preceded, God, exalted is He, informed that He had charged His Messenger with conveying (al-tabligh), which is delivering the rulings to his community. This emphasizes the obligation to carry out what God has commanded. It also means the Messenger has completed what was incumbent upon him of conveying, the proof has been established against you, and obedience has become binding upon you, so you have no excuse for neglect. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is informative for the believers. It cannot be conceived that it is a truce (muwada'a) that has been abrogated (mansukha) by the verses of fighting. Rather, this is the state of one who believes in this and bears witness to the truth, for he has secured from the Messenger his property and his blood. So the Messenger has no obligation toward him beyond conveying." End of quote. Some exegetes mentioned the disagreement over whether it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) or abrogated by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf). The Messenger here is Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said that it may be a generic noun (ism jins), and the meaning would be: upon everyone who was sent is only the conveying. The words balagh and bulugh are both verbal nouns of balagha. When it is the verbal noun of balagha, the conveying of the laws entails the conveying by the one who was sent with them, so the necessary is expressed by what it necessitates. It is also possible that it is a verbal noun of ballagha (the intensive form), with the augmenting letters dropped, so the meaning of al-balagh is al-tabligh.

﴿And God knows what you disclose and what you conceal﴾. This sentence contains a warning, since God, exalted is He, has informed that He is aware of the servant's state, outwardly and inwardly, so He will recompense him for that with reward or punishment. It is also possible that the meaning is that God, exalted is He, obligated His Messenger to convey the law, and obligated you to convey it. He knows what you disclose of it and what you conceal, and He will recompense you for that. This is an address to his community, since disclosing and concealing can proceed from them, unlike the Messenger, for it is impossible for him to conceal anything of the laws of God, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 100:

﴿Say: The evil and the good are not equal, even though the abundance of the evil may impress you.﴾ Jabir narrated: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, wine was my trade. Will that wealth benefit me if I spend it in obedience to Allah the Exalted?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Verily Allah accepts only what is good.' So this verse was revealed confirming the words of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when Allah (exalted is He) warned against disobedience and encouraged repentance by saying: ﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 98], and the verse that follows, and He followed it with the obligation by saying: ﴿The duty of the Messenger is only to convey﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 99], then with encouragement to obedience and warning against disobedience by saying: ﴿And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 99], He followed it with another type of encouragement to obedience and warning against disobedience. So He said: "The evil and the good are not equal," and so on. Or it may be said: when He clarified that His punishment is severe for the one who disobeys, and that He is Forgiving and Merciful to the one who obeys, He clarified that the obedient and the disobedient are not equal, even if the disobedient and the disbelievers are many. Their multitude does not prevent Him from punishing them. The apparent meaning is that "the evil" (al-khabith) and "the good" (al-tayyib) are general terms, so they include lawful and unlawful wealth, sound and corrupt deeds, good and bad people, and sound and corrupt beliefs. The evil in all of this is not fit, is not loved, and does not have a good outcome, while the good, even if little, is beneficial and has a good outcome. Compare with this verse the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And the good land brings forth its vegetation﴾ [al-A'raf: 58], and so on. The evil is that which is corrupt within in things, to the point that it is thought to be sound, while the good is the opposite of that. Some of the earlier scholars specified "the evil" and "the good" here by some of what the generality of the wording requires. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: it is the lawful and the unlawful. As-Suddi said: it is the believer and the disbeliever. Al-Mawardi mentioned another view: that it is the obedient and the disobedient, and another view: that it is the good and the bad. It was also said: the good is knowledge and obedience, and the evil is ignorance and disobedience. The best approach is to take these views as examples of the good and the evil, not as restricting the wording to them. As for His saying: ﴿even though the abundance of the evil may impress you﴾, its apparent meaning is that it is part of what he was commanded to say. As for the address of the second person in His saying ﴿may impress you﴾, the meaning is: "may impress you, O listener, or O addressee." Alternatively, it is not part of what he was commanded to say, and is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ). Some have mentioned that this is possible, but the first view is preferable. Or it is understood as an address to him in outward form, while the intended meaning is someone else.

﴿So fear Allah, O people of understanding, that you may prosper﴾. That is: fear Him by preferring the good, even if it is little, over the evil, even if it is abundant. Az-Zamakhshari said: this verse should be used to rebuke the Mujbira (Determinists) when they boast of their numbers. Their poet said:

"Multiply yourself by Sa'd, for Sa'd is many, but do not expect from Sa'd fulfilment of promise or help."

Another said:

"Let not the number of their rabble overawe you, for most of them, indeed all of them, are cattle."

He does this in keeping with his habit of calling the People of the Sunnah "Mujbira" and disparaging them. Allah specified the address and the call to "people of understanding" because they are the foremost in distinguishing the good from the evil, so it is not fitting for them to neglect this. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It seems the reference is to the essence of experience, which exceeds the essence of obligation through innate disposition, acquired shrewdness, and far-reaching reflection. End.

(p-28) **Qur'an 5:101–103 (in the commentary):**

﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you. But if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you. Allah has pardoned that, and Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾ ﴿A people before you asked about such things, and then they became disbelievers because of them.﴾ ﴿Allah did not institute any bahira (a she-camel left unridden and unmilked for idols), nor sa'iba (a camel released freely), nor wasila (a sheep that gives birth to twins of alternating sexes), nor ham (a stallion let loose). But those who disbelieve invent lies against Allah, and most of them do not reason.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon." Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 104] ﴿O you who have believed, you are responsible for yourselves. Whoever has strayed will not harm you if you are guided. To Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 105] ﴿O you who have believed, the testimony between you when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest is two witnesses of justice from among you, or two others from outside your own people, if you are travelling through the land and the disaster of death befalls you. You shall detain them after the prayer, and they swear by Allah, "We will not exchange it for any price, even if it concerns a near relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of Allah; indeed, we would then be among the sinful."﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 106] ﴿But if it is discovered that the two have acquired sin, then two others will stand in their place from among those against whom the claim was made, the two nearest [in kinship], and they will swear by Allah, "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and we have not transgressed; indeed, we would then be among the wrongdoers."﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 107] ﴿That is more likely that they will give testimony in its correct form, or that they will fear that oaths will be repeated after their oaths. And fear Allah and listen. And Allah does not guide the defiant people.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 108] ﴿The Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, "What was your response?" They will say, "We have no knowledge. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen."﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 109] ﴿When Allah said, "O 'Isa, son of Maryam, remember My favour upon you and upon your mother, when I supported you with the Holy Spirit, you spoke to the people in the cradle and in maturity, and when I taught you the Book and wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel, and when you shaped from clay like the form of a bird by My permission, then you breathed into it and it became a bird by My permission, and you healed the blind and the leper by My permission, and when you brought forth the dead by My permission, and when I restrained the Children of Israel from you when you came to them with clear proofs, and those who disbelieved among them said, 'This is not but clear magic.'"﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 110] ﴿And when I inspired the disciples to believe in Me and My Messenger, they said, "We have believed, and bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 111] ﴿When the disciples said, "O 'Isa, son of Maryam, can your Lord send down to us a table spread from the sky?" He said, "Fear Allah, if you are believers."﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 112] ﴿They said, "We wish to eat from it, and that our hearts may be assured, and that we may know that you have told us the truth, and that we may be witnesses to it."﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 113] ﴿'Isa, son of Maryam, said, "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table from the sky, which will be a festival for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You. And provide for us, and You are the best of providers."﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 114]

(ism jam' (collective noun)) The view of Sibawayh and al-Khalil is that *ashya'* (أشياء) is *lafa'*, an inverted form of *fa'la'*, and that the original is *shay'an* from the root *shay'*, and that it is an ism jam' (collective noun), like *tura fa'* and *hulafa'*. The view of others is that it is a plural. They differed: al-Kisa'i and Abu Hatim said it is the plural of *shay'*, like *bayt* and *abyat*. Al-Kisa'i said *ashya'* is not declined (diptote), because its final part resembles the final part of *hamra'* and because it is used very frequently. The Arabs say *ashyawan*, just as they say *hamrawan*. Al-Farra' and al-Akhfash held that it is a plural on the pattern *af'ala'*. Al-Farra' said that *shay'* is a lightened form of *shay'*, just as they said *hunan* as the plural of *hayn*, the lightened form of *hayyin*. Al-Akhfash said: it is not a lightened form of *shay'*, but rather *fa'l* made plural as *af'ala'*. In these two views there are two hamzas: the radical of the word, and the hamza of feminine marking. So the hamza that is the radical was changed into a *ya'* because of the kasra before it, and then the *ya'* that is the middle radical was deleted for ease. Some held that the original pattern of *shay'* is *shayi'*, like *sadiq* and *asdiqa'*. Then the first hamza was deleted, and the vowel of the long vowel was opened, because what follows it is an alif. He said that in this view its pattern is *afya'*, and in the view before it, *aflaa'*. The exposition of these views, their soundness and invalidity, is mentioned in the science of morphology (ilm al-tasrif).

The *bahira* is *fa'ila* in the sense of *maf'ula*, like *nati'a* in the sense of *matnuha*. Abu 'Ubayda said: it is the she-camel when she has given birth to five offspring, and the last of them is a male. They split her ear, and let her go free. She is not ridden, not milked, and not driven away from water or pasture. Something similar is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, except that it is not mentioned from him that the last was a male. Qatada said: one looks at the fifth. If it is a male, they slaughter it and eat it. If it is a female, they split the ear of the female and say, "It is a bahira," so it is not ridden and not driven away from water or pasture. If an *alma'i* (a man of insight) meets her, he does not ride her out of scruple and reluctance. This is narrated from Ikrima, who added that her meat and milk are forbidden to women, and when she dies, they become lawful to women. Ibn Sida said: the bahira is the one released without a shepherd. Mujahid said: the bahira is the one born from a *sa'iba* female, whose ear was split and whose path was left free with its mother in the open, not ridden and not milked, as was done with its mother. Ibn al-Musayyib said: it is the one whose milk is withheld from the idols (taghut), so no one milks her. It was also said: it is the she-camel that gives birth to five or seven, and they split her ear. Ibn 'Atiyya said: when the she-camel gives birth to ten offspring, they split her ear lengthwise into two halves, and she is called *mabhura*. She is left to graze, to come to water, and nothing is benefited from her, and her meat is forbidden to women when she dies, but lawful to men. It was also said: the bahira is the young camel when it is born, whose ear they cut, and they say, "O Allah, if it lives, it is 'afiyy (free from restriction), and if it dies, it is dhakiyy (lawfully slaughtered)." When it dies, it is eaten. It is evident from the variation of these reports that the Arabs differed in their methods regarding the bahira, so each group had a method of its own, and all of them are misguidance.

The *sa'iba* is the active participle (fa'ila) from *saba*, when it moves over the face of the earth. It is said: the water flowed (*sab al-ma'*), and the snake moved (*sabat al-hayya*). It was also said: the *sa'iba* is *sayyiba*, an active participle in the sense of a passive, like their saying, "a pleasing life" (Qur'an 69:21), meaning "a pleasing one." Abu 'Ubayda said: when a man returned from a journey, or vowed a vow, or gave thanks for a blessing, he released a camel, and it had the same status as the bahira in all that was made lawful for it. Al-Farra' said: when the she-camel gives birth to ten female offspring, she is released, and she is not ridden, not milked, her wool is not shorn, and her milk is not drunk except by her offspring or a guest. Ibn 'Abbas said: the *sa'iba* is the one released for the idols, meaning freed. A man would release some of his property, bring it to the *sadana*, who were the servants of their gods, and they would feed travellers from its milk. Al-Shafi'i said: they used to vow to release a she-camel so that a person could perform a pilgrimage on it. It was also said: the *sa'iba* is a slave who is freed on condition that he has no *wala'* (right of patronage), no *'aql* (blood money obligation), and no inheritance.

The *wasila* is, according to most scholars, the sheep. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the ewe that gives birth to seven offspring. If the seventh is a female, women do not benefit from it at all, unless it dies, and then men and women both eat it. If it is a male or similar, they all eat it. If it is a male and a female, they say, "She has joined her brother," so she is left with her brother and is not slaughtered, and her benefits are for men, not women. When she dies, men and women share in her. Ibn Qutayba said: if the seventh is a male, it is slaughtered, and men eat from it, not women. They also said: it is exclusive to our males, and forbidden to our wives. If it is a female, it is left among the sheep. If it is a male and a female, it is as in Ibn 'Abbas's view. Ibn Ishaq said: it is the ewe that gives birth to ten offspring consecutively, in five births, and whatever she bears after that is for males, not females. Al-Farra' said: it is the ewe that gives birth to seven offspring, twins, two at a time. If in her seventh birth she bears a female kid and a male kid, it is said, "She has joined her brother," and so she takes the position of the *sa'iba*. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the ewe that bears a female, which belongs to them, or a male, which belongs to their gods. Abu 'Ubayda said something similar, and added: if she bears a male and a female together, they say, "She has joined her brother," so they do not slaughter him because of her. Al-Zuhri narrated from Ibn al-Musayyib that it is the first-born she-camel, who begins her first birth with a female, then gives birth to a second female, and they give her to their taghut, saying, "One has been joined to the other, with no male between them." It was also said: it is the ewe that gives birth to three or five offspring. If the last of them is a male kid, they slaughter it for their gods, or if it is a female kid, they keep her, and say, "This female kid has joined her brother," so it prevents him from slaughter.

The *ham* is the active participle from *hama*, and it is the stallion camel. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas said, and Abu 'Ubayda and al-Zajjaj preferred, that it is the stallion that sires ten offspring from his loins. They say, "He has protected his back," and they release him for their idols, so nothing is loaded on him. Ibn Abi Talha narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Farra' preferred, that it is the stallion that is born to the offspring of his offspring. 'Ata' said: it is the stallion that sires ten offspring from his loins, so that among his children ten females appear from his daughters and his daughters' daughters. Ibn Zayd said: it is the one to whom seven consecutive females are born. Al-Mawardi mentioned from al-Shafi'i that he would be used for stud among a man's camels for ten years.

*Al-habs* (restraint) is prevention from disposal. It is said: *habastu* (I detained), *ihtabastu faras fi sabil Allah* (I dedicated a horse for the cause of Allah), so it is *muhbas*, and *habis*, which I endowed for raiding.

*'Atar 'ala al-rajul* means he came upon him and became aware of him. It is derived from *al-'athra*, which is falling, because the one who stumbles only stumbles over something he did not see. When he stumbled over it, he became aware of it and looked at what it was. Therefore it is said of everyone who became aware of a matter that was hidden from him, "He came upon it" (*'atara 'alayhi*). It is also said "*'atara 'alayhi*" and "*a'thara 'alayhi*" when he made him aware of it. From this is the verse, "And thus We made them come upon [the truth]" (Qur'an 18:21), meaning, We made them aware. Al-Layth said: *'atara ya'tharu 'uthuran* means to fall upon a matter upon which no one else had fallen, and *'atara 'athratan* means to fall upon something.

*Al-ma'ida* is the table on which there is food. If there is no food on it, it is not a *ma'ida*. Abu 'Abd Allah said: it is the active participle in the sense of the passive, and it is from giving. *Al-mumtad* is the one from whom giving is requested; the root is *madda*, meaning "he gave," and *amtadda* means "he asked for giving." Al-Zajjaj said: it is the active participle from *mada yamid*, meaning "it moved," so it is as if it sways with what is on it. Ibn Qutayba said: *al-ma'ida* is food, from *madda yumiduhu*, meaning "he gave it," as if it gives the eaters, meaning it feeds them. It is the active participle in the sense of a passive, meaning the eaters are given by it. It was also said: it is from *al-mayd*, meaning inclination, and this is close to al-Zajjaj's view.

O Almighty (Allah) said: ﴿O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if they were made plain to you, would distress you﴾. Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated, and the wording is al-Bukhari's, from Anas, who said: A man said, "O Messenger of Allah, who is my father?" He (ﷺ) said, "Your father is so-and-so," and the verse was revealed. In another narration from Anas also: "A man said, 'Where will my place be, O Messenger of Allah?' He said, 'The Fire.'" The one who asked, "Who is my father?" was Abdullah ibn Hudhafa. In a narration other than that of Anas: "Another man stood up and said, 'Who is my father?' He said, 'Your father is Salim, the freedman of Shayba.'" It was also said that the verse was revealed because of their question about the pilgrimage (hajj): "Is it every year?" He was silent, and then they asked, "Is it every year?" He said, "No. Had I said yes, it would have become obligatory." This was narrated from Ali, Abu Hurayra, Abu Umama and Ibn Abbas. It was also said that the questioner was Suraqa ibn Malik. It was said that he was Ukkasha ibn Mihsan al-Asadi. It was said that he was Mihsan. It was said that he was a man from the Banu Asad. It was said that he was al-Aqra' ibn Habis.

Al-Hasan said: They asked about the matters of the Jahiliyya (the age of ignorance) that Allah has pardoned, and there is no point in asking about what Allah has pardoned. Ibn Jubayr said, and Mujahid narrated it from Ibn Abbas: They asked about the bahira (a she-camel whose ear was slit and released), the sa'iba (a camel released for free grazing), the wasila (a she-camel or sheep given special status) and the ham (a stallion camel released after a certain number of covering), and for this reason their mention came after it. It was narrated from Ikrima that they asked for signs and miracles. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi mentioned that it was revealed concerning the apportioning of the obligatory shares of inheritance (tasmih al-fara'id). It is also reported that when Allah, exalted is He, explained the matter of the Ka'ba, the hady (offering animals) and the qala'id (garlands), and informed that its sanctity was ordained by Him, since these were ancient matters going back to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, some Arabs went to ask about all the other rulings of the Jahiliyya, whether they were to be attached to this or not, for they had believed the whole of it to be a sunna, and did not distinguish between what came from Allah and what came from the devil. The apparent sense of the reports is that the bedouins pressed him with various kinds of questions, and so they were rebuked for this by this verse. It was also said that it was revealed concerning the pilgrims of Yamama, when the Muslims wanted to attack them, and they were forbidden from attacking them, even though they were polytheists.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it: when He said, ﴿The Messenger's duty is only to deliver (the message)﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 99], it was as if it were said: Accept what the Messenger has conveyed and submit to him, and what he has not conveyed, do not ask about it or delve into it, for perhaps a corrupt delving will bring upon you burdens that will be hard on you. This was said by Abu Abdullah al-Razi, with some abridgement. He also said: This is connected to His saying, ﴿Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 99]. So leave matters as they apparently are, and do not ask about varying conditions.

The conditional clause and what is conjoined to it in the conditional form occupy the position of a qualifier (sifa) for ashya' (things). The meaning is: do not multiply questions to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the point that you ask him about burdensome obligations which, if he gives you a ruling on them and imposes them upon you, will grieve you, distress you, and make you regret having asked about them. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, who built it upon what was reported as the occasion of revelation, that he was asked about the hajj.

The majority of readers read ﴿tubda lakum﴾ with a ta' and in the passive voice (mabni li-l-maf'ul). Ibn Abbas and Mujahid read it in the active voice. Al-Sha'bi read it with a ya' (yubda) with a fatha, with a damma on the dal in the sense of "yasu'kum" with ya' in both places, damma in the first and fatha in the second. Ibn Atiyya said: The correct reading is that Allah should make it manifest (yubdiha Allah) (p-31) exalted is He.

﴿And if you ask about them when the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be made plain to you﴾. Ibn Abbas said: its meaning is: do not ask about things which, within the telling of them, contain something that will grieve you, either because of a legal obligation that would bind you, or because of a report that would sadden you, like the one who said, "Who is my father?" But if the Qur'an is revealed concerning something, and your Lord begins with a command, then if you ask about its explanation, it will explain it to you and make it clear. End of quotation. Ibn Atiyya said: The pronoun in His saying "about them" (anha) refers to their kind, not to the first things about which He forbade asking. He said: It may also be in the sense of a warning, as if He said: do not ask, and if you ask, you will meet the consequence and the hardship of it, because you will be burdening yourselves and hastening what will grieve you, like the one who was told, "He is in the Fire." End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And if you ask about them when the Qur'an is being revealed﴾, that is, about these hard obligations during the time of revelation, which is as long as the Messenger is among you and revelation is coming to him, ﴿they will be made plain to you﴾: those obligations (which will grieve you) will be made plain and you will be commanded to bear them, so you will expose yourselves to the wrath of Allah by neglecting them. End of quotation. On this view, the pronoun in "about them" refers to the things themselves, not to their kind. What appears to be the case is that they were forbidden to ask about things that were described by two attributes: first, that if they asked about them, they would be made plain to them at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an, so that "when" (hina) is an adverbial complement of ﴿they will be made plain to you﴾, not of ﴿if you ask about them﴾. The second attribute is that if they were made plain to them, they would distress them. Although this second attribute is mentioned later, it is in fact dependent on the first, but it was placed first because it is a stronger deterrent from asking about those things: when they are told that such a question, if answered, would grieve them, they would be more repelled from asking afterwards. Since this attribute is more effective in restraining them from asking, it was placed first, and the attribute that contains no restraint or deterrence was mentioned later, relying on understanding of the meaning. Moreover, the conjunction of the second attribute with the letter waw (and) implies only association, not order. The saying "and if you ask about them" does not indicate the permissibility of asking, as some claimed, when they said: the pronoun refers to things, so how can the asking about the very same things be both forbidden and permitted at once? They answered with two points: first, that it is forbidden before the revelation of the Qur'an and commanded after its revelation; second, that although the two are not different, each of them concerns one and the same thing being asked about, and for this reason the unity of the pronoun is acceptable. End of quotation. This is not a second answer, because it assumes that asking about those very things is both forbidden and permitted, and if these are two different kinds, then the things themselves are not the same. The conditional clause, as we have explained, does not indicate permissibility. Do you not see that you say, "Do not commit adultery; and if you commit adultery, you will be punished"? The statement "and if you commit adultery, you will be punished" does not indicate permissibility. Rather, the conditional clause does not indicate occurrence, nor even possibility, since a conditional may be formed between two impossibilities, as in His saying: ﴿If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar: 65].

﴿Allah has pardoned them﴾. Its apparent meaning is that it is a new statement from Allah, exalted is He. Some held that it occupies the position of a genitive qualifier (sifa) for ashya', as if it were said: do not ask about things that are pardoned, and the meaning of "pardoned" (afa) would be: He left you without obligation concerning them and without hardship upon you through them, based on His saying, "Allah has pardoned you for the charity of horses," which is the first view. As for the view of it being a new statement, its meaning may be that Allah left them and did not make them known to you, and it may also mean that He overlooked your committing those questions and did not hold you accountable for them. The second meaning is supported by His saying: ﴿Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing﴾. Therefore al-Zamakhshari said: Allah has pardoned you for what passed of your asking, so do not return to the like of it.

﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 74]: He does not hold you accountable for what slips from you by punishing you. Al-Daraqutni narrated from Abu Tha'laba al-Khushani, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, exalted is He, has prescribed obligations, so do not neglect them; He has forbidden sanctities, so do not violate them; He has set limits, so do not transgress them; and He has been silent about things out of no forgetfulness, so do not search into them." Abu Salama narrated from Abu Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the greatest of people in crime is the one who asks about a matter that was not forbidden, so that it becomes forbidden because of his asking."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 101–103 (part 3 of 3):**

﴿Certainly a people before you asked such things, and then became disbelievers in them.﴾ The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (sa'alahā, "they asked it") refers to "things" (ashyā'). Al-Ḥawfī said: "It is not sound to take it in its apparent sense, neither from the standpoint of the Arabic wording nor from the standpoint of meaning. As for the wording, the verb would be construed with ʿan (about), so it would have to be 'they asked about them' (sa'ala 'anhā), as in ﴿Do not ask about things (ʿan ashyā')﴾, where the verb takes ʿan. As for meaning, the object of the question is definitely different in the two cases. The forbidden kind of question is like someone asking, 'Where is my place of entry? Who is my father? Who asked about the pilgrimage? Where is my she-camel? What is in the belly of my she-camel?' This is different from the question of the people who came before." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The pronoun in (sa'alahā) does not refer back to 'things', so that it would have to be construed with ʿan. Rather, it refers back to the question (al-mas'alah) indicated by ﴿do not ask﴾. The meaning is: a people of the earlier generations asked this question, and then they became (aṣbaḥū), that is, upon its return (bi-marji'ihā), disbelievers. The reason is that the Children of Israel used to seek rulings from their prophets about things, and when they were commanded to do them, they abandoned them, and so they perished." End of quote. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said, close to the view of al-Zamakhsharī: "The meaning of this verse is that these questions, which are provocations, demands for excess, proposals and disputations, were asked by the nations before you, and then they disbelieved in them." End of quote. What these two said cannot stand except by assuming an omitted governed noun (ḥadhf muḍāf, the dropping of a noun that a following noun depends on). Some exegetes have stated this explicitly: "They asked the like of them," that is, the like of this question, or the like of these questions.

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read sa'alahā with a fatḥah on the sīn and on the hamzah. Al-Nakha'ī read it with a kasrah on the sīn and without hamzah, meaning with the kasrah and imālah (vowel-raising), and he took the verb to be from the root s-w-l (not from the root s-'-l). Both are dialectal forms mentioned by Sībawayh. In the speech of the Arabs they are interchangeable (yatasāwalān), with the wāw form and the imālah. The imālah of al-Nakha'ī (sa'ala) is like the imālah of Ḥamzah in khāfa.

﴿a people﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās said: they are the people of Jesus, who asked for the table (al-mā'idah), and then disbelieved in it after it had been stipulated for them that they would receive a punishment that no one among the worlds would be punished with. Ibn Zayd also said: they are the people of Moses, who asked about the slaughter of the cow and its description. Ibn Zayd also said: they are those who said to a prophet of theirs ﴿Send us a king, that we may fight in the way of God﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:246]. It was also said: they are the people of Moses, who asked God to show Himself to them openly (jahratan), and that became a calamity for them. It was said: they are the people of Ṣāliḥ, who asked for the she-camel, and then slaughtered her after the condition had been made in God's words ﴿for her is a share of water and for you a share on a known day﴾ [al-Shuʿarā' 26:155], and after the punishment was made conditional on them if they touched her with harm. Muqātil said: the Children of Israel used to ask their prophets about things, and when the prophets informed them of them, they abandoned their statement and did not believe them, so they became disbelievers in those things. Al-Suddī said: like the Quraysh in their request that God make Ṣafā into gold for them. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the example of the Quraysh only fits their request for a sign, for when the moon was split, they disbelieved. End of quote. Some later scholars said: the people are the Quraysh, who asked for impossible things, as God has informed: ﴿They said: We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush for us from the earth﴾ [al-Isrā' 17:90]. This does not hold unless by "those before them" is meant their forefathers who died at the beginning of the revelation.

Abu al-Baqā' al-ʿUkbarī said: ﴿min qablikum (before you)﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:69] is connected to (sa'alahā). It cannot be a qualifier (ṣifah, attributive adjective) of "a people", nor a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), because a temporal adverbial (ẓarf al-zamān) cannot be a qualifier of a "people", nor a circumstantial clause of it, nor a predicate (khabar) about it. End of quote. What he mentioned is correct for a temporal adverbial stripped of description. But when it is described, they have mentioned that it can be a predicate, as you say: "We are in a good day." As for qabl and baʿd, in reality they are originally descriptive words. When you say, "Zayd came before ʿAmr," the meaning is "Zayd came at a time," that is, at a time earlier than the time of ʿAmr's coming. Therefore it is valid for it to occur as a relative clause (ṣilah) of a relative pronoun, and the description is not considered in it, even though it is a bare temporal adverbial. But if it is not valid for it to occur as a relative clause, as in God's words ﴿and those before you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:21], it is not valid to say "and those today." We have discussed this at the beginning of al-Baqarah. The meaning of ﴿then they became﴾ (thumma aṣbaḥū) is "then they became," and it is not meant that their disbelief was restricted to the morning.

﴿God did not institute any bahīrah, nor sā'ibah, nor waṣīlah, nor ḥām﴾. The connection of this to what precedes it: since God forbade asking about what He had not permitted and had not imposed on them, He forbade adopting matters that God had not legislated. When some people asked about these customs that existed in the pre-Islamic age, whether they were to be attached to the rulings of the Kaʿbah, God clarified that He had not legislated any of them. Or, when He mentioned the lawful and the unlawful in the law, He returned to speaking about the lawful and the unlawful without legislation.

It is related in a ḥadīth narrated from Abū Hurayrah, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "The first to change the religion of Ismāʿīl was ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy ibn Qamaʿah ibn Khindif. He set up the idols, let loose the sā'ibah, consecrated the baḥīrah, and protected the ḥāmī." And the Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw him dragging his intestines in the Fire. It is also reported that he was king of Mecca. Zayd ibn Aslam narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I know the first to consecrate the baḥīrah. He is a man from the Mudlij tribe, who had two she-camels. He slit their ears and forbade their milk and riding on their backs. He said: 'I have indeed seen him in the Fire, harming the people of the Fire with the stench of his intestines.'"

Al-Zamakhsharī said: the meaning of ﴿God did not institute﴾ is that He did not legislate that, nor command consecration (al-tabḥīr), letting loose (al-taysīb), or anything else. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "(ja'ala, did institute/make)" in this verse cannot mean "God created," because God created all these things, nor can it mean "made into" (ṣayyara), because of the absence of a second object. Rather, it means "legislated (sanna)" or "prescribed (shara'a)." The grammarians did not mention "prescribed" among the meanings of ja'ala. Rather, they mentioned that it comes in the sense of "created," in the sense of "cast," in the sense of "made into," and in the sense of "beginning an action," in which case it is among the verbs of approximation (afʿāl al-muqārabah). Some mentioned the meaning "named (sammā)." The omission of one of the two objects of ẓanna and its sisters has occurred, but it is rare. Taking the verb in a sense that has been heard is preferable to affirming a meaning that is not attested in the speech of the Arabs. So it is possible that the second object is omitted, meaning: God did not make a baḥīrah, sā'ibah, waṣīlah, or ḥāmī a legislated thing; rather these are from the legislation of other than God. ﴿And the livestock, He created them for you﴾ [al-Naḥl 16:5]: God created them as a kindness to His servants, a blessing He enumerated to them, and a far-reaching benefit. But the people of the Jāhiliyyah cut off the way of benefiting from them and removed God's blessing through them. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: Abū Ḥanīfah and his companions said: endowments and waqf (awqāf) are not permitted, and they made an analogy to the baḥīrah and sā'ibah. The difference is clear. If a man deliberately took a plot of land he owned and said, "This shall be a ḥabs (endowment held in perpetuity), its fruit not to be picked, its land not to be cultivated, and no benefit to be drawn from it," that would be comparable to the baḥīrah and sā'ibah. But a ḥabs whose way is defined and whose benefit continues is not of this kind. And it is enough that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb about a property he had: "Make it a ḥabs, its principal not to be sold." And the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) made endowments. End of quote.

﴿But those who disbelieved fabricate lies against God﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī said: by forbidding what they had forbidden.

﴿and most of them do not reason﴾. Thus they did not attribute the prohibition until they fabricated it, but they imitated their elders in forbidding it. End of quote. Al-Shaʿbī and others stated that the fabricators are the innovators, and that those who do not reason are the followers. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "those who disbelieved" means ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy and his companions. It was said: "do not reason" means they do not distinguish the lawful from the unlawful. Qatādah said: "do not reason" that this prohibition is from Satan, not from God. Muḥammad ibn Mūsā said: "those who disbelieved" here are the People of the Book, and "those who do not reason" are the people of the idols. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this is an interpretation that extracts the end of the verse from what precedes it, and connects it in meaning with what He informed about, in His words ﴿and when it is said to them﴾ [al-Mā'idah 5:104]. End of quote. Makkī said: mentioning the People of the Book here has no meaning, since there is no act or resemblance of this in them. Rather, this was mentioned about the polytheists of the Arabs, and they are the ones meant by it.

(p-28) **Qur'an 5:101–103 (in the commentary):**

﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you. But if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you. Allah has pardoned that, and Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾ ﴿A people before you asked about such things, and then they became disbelievers because of them.﴾ ﴿Allah did not institute any bahira (a she-camel left unridden and unmilked for idols), nor sa'iba (a camel released freely), nor wasila (a sheep that gives birth to twins of alternating sexes), nor ham (a stallion let loose). But those who disbelieve invent lies against Allah, and most of them do not reason.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon." Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 104] ﴿O you who have believed, you are responsible for yourselves. Whoever has strayed will not harm you if you are guided. To Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 105] ﴿O you who have believed, the testimony between you when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest is two witnesses of justice from among you, or two others from outside your own people, if you are travelling through the land and the disaster of death befalls you. You shall detain them after the prayer, and they swear by Allah, "We will not exchange it for any price, even if it concerns a near relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of Allah; indeed, we would then be among the sinful."﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 106] ﴿But if it is discovered that the two have acquired sin, then two others will stand in their place from among those against whom the claim was made, the two nearest [in kinship], and they will swear by Allah, "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and we have not transgressed; indeed, we would then be among the wrongdoers."﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 107] ﴿That is more likely that they will give testimony in its correct form, or that they will fear that oaths will be repeated after their oaths. And fear Allah and listen. And Allah does not guide the defiant people.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 108] ﴿The Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, "What was your response?" They will say, "We have no knowledge. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen."﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 109] ﴿When Allah said, "O 'Isa, son of Maryam, remember My favour upon you and upon your mother, when I supported you with the Holy Spirit, you spoke to the people in the cradle and in maturity, and when I taught you the Book and wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel, and when you shaped from clay like the form of a bird by My permission, then you breathed into it and it became a bird by My permission, and you healed the blind and the leper by My permission, and when you brought forth the dead by My permission, and when I restrained the Children of Israel from you when you came to them with clear proofs, and those who disbelieved among them said, 'This is not but clear magic.'"﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 110] ﴿And when I inspired the disciples to believe in Me and My Messenger, they said, "We have believed, and bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 111] ﴿When the disciples said, "O 'Isa, son of Maryam, can your Lord send down to us a table spread from the sky?" He said, "Fear Allah, if you are believers."﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 112] ﴿They said, "We wish to eat from it, and that our hearts may be assured, and that we may know that you have told us the truth, and that we may be witnesses to it."﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 113] ﴿'Isa, son of Maryam, said, "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table from the sky, which will be a festival for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You. And provide for us, and You are the best of providers."﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 114]

(ism jam' (collective noun)) The view of Sibawayh and al-Khalil is that *ashya'* (أشياء) is *lafa'*, an inverted form of *fa'la'*, and that the original is *shay'an* from the root *shay'*, and that it is an ism jam' (collective noun), like *tura fa'* and *hulafa'*. The view of others is that it is a plural. They differed: al-Kisa'i and Abu Hatim said it is the plural of *shay'*, like *bayt* and *abyat*. Al-Kisa'i said *ashya'* is not declined (diptote), because its final part resembles the final part of *hamra'* and because it is used very frequently. The Arabs say *ashyawan*, just as they say *hamrawan*. Al-Farra' and al-Akhfash held that it is a plural on the pattern *af'ala'*. Al-Farra' said that *shay'* is a lightened form of *shay'*, just as they said *hunan* as the plural of *hayn*, the lightened form of *hayyin*. Al-Akhfash said: it is not a lightened form of *shay'*, but rather *fa'l* made plural as *af'ala'*.
