The clause ﴿and we do not conceal the testimony of God﴾ is coordinated with his saying ﴿we do not sell thereby a price﴾, so it is part of what is sworn to. He ascribed the testimony to God because He, exalted is He, is the one who commands its establishment and forbids its concealment. It is possible that ﴿and we do not conceal﴾ is a statement from the two of them, reporting about themselves that they do not conceal the testimony of God, and it is not included in what is sworn to. Al-Hasan and al-Sha'bi read ﴿and we do not conceal﴾ with the mim jussed, as a prohibition (nahy) addressed by the two to themselves against concealing the testimony. The use of the prohibitive "la" with the first person is rare, as in the verse:

*"When we leave Damascus, let us not return to it ever, as long as the Jaradim are there."*

Ali, Nu'aym ibn Maysarah, and al-Sha'bi, in a variant reported from him, read ﴿the testimony of God﴾ with both words in the accusative, and "shahadatan" with tanwin, and they are governed by "naktum" ("we conceal"). The estimated sense is: "and we do not conceal God a testimony." Al-Zahrawi said: It is possible that the meaning is: "and we do not conceal a testimony, by God," then the waw was dropped and the verb put in the accusative for brevity. It is reported from Ali, al-Sulami, and al-Hasan al-Basri "shahadatan" with tanwin, and "a-llahi" with the madd on the hamzah of interrogation, which is a substitute for the particle of oath, entering for the sake of affirmation and making the souls of those swearing, or of those addressed, stand firm. It is reported from al-Sha'bi and others that he would pause on "shahadah" with a quiescent ha', and on "Allah" with the hamzat al-wasl cut off, without the madd of interrogation. Ibn Jinni said: Pausing on "shahadah" with a quiescent ha', and beginning the oath afresh, is good, because beginning it at the start of speech is more fitting for it and more awe-inspiring than that it should enter into the course of speech. It is reported from Yahya ibn Adam, from Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash, "shahadatan" with tanwin, "Allah" with the hamzah cut off and no madd, and the ha' of the divine name in the genitive; this reading is also reported from al-Sha'bi. Al-A'mash and Ibn Muhaysin read "lamina al-athimin" ("indeed of the sinners") with the nun of "min" assimilated (idgham) into the lam of "al-athimin," after the hamzah has been dropped and its vowel transferred to the lam.

﴿And if it is discovered that they two have incurred a sin﴾: that is, if after their oath it is discovered that they two have incurred a sin, namely a guilt, by their perjury in the oath, in that it does not correspond to the reality. ("Discovered," ʿuthira) is a metaphor (isti'arah) for what befalls one's knowledge after it has been hidden, and after one did not expect it nor intend it, as you say: "you fell upon the expert" and "you chanced upon such-and-such." Abu Ali said: "Sin" here is the thing taken, because taking it is a sin, so it is called a sin, just as what is taken without right is called an injustice (maẓlamah). Sibawayh said: "Maẓlamah" is the name of what is taken from you, and for this reason this taken thing is named by the verbal noun, end of quote. The apparent meaning is that "sin" here is not the thing taken, but the offence by which they incurred the state of being among the sinners, from which they disavowed themselves in their saying ﴿Indeed, then we would be among the sinners﴾. If "sin" were the thing taken, it would not be said of it "they incurred a sin," because they wronged and transgressed, and that is what necessitates the sin.

﴿Then two others shall stand in their place from among those against whom the rightful claim has been made, the two nearest﴾ (p. 45). The two Harameyn (Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr), the two Arabic-readers (Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim? in the sense of the Kufan and Basran readers), and al-Kisa'i read "istahagga" in the active voice, and "al-awlayani" as a dual in the nominative, the dual of "al-uwla" (the nearer). This reading is reported from Ubayy, Ali, Ibn Abbas, and from Ibn Kathir in the transmission of Qurrah from him. Hamzah and Abu Bakr read "istuhiqqa" in the passive voice, and "al-awwalina" as the plural of "al-awwal" (the first). Al-Hasan read "istahagga" in the active voice, with "al-awwalan" in the nominative, the dual of "awwal." Ibn Sirin read "al-awliyayn," the accusative dual of "al-awwal." As for the first reading, al-Zamakhshari said: "Two others" means two other witnesses, ﴿who shall stand in their place from among those against whom the rightful claim has been made﴾: that is, from among those against whom the sin was incurred, and its meaning is that they are those who were wronged, namely the family of the deceased and his kin. In the story of Budayl, when the treachery of the two men became evident, he made two men of his heirs swear that the vessel was the property of their companion, and that their testimony was more worthy than the testimony of the two. ("Al-awlayani") means the most worthy of testimony, by reason of their kinship, their knowledge, and their exalted status; it is as if it had been said: "Who are they?", so it was said, "the two nearest." It has been said: they are a substitution (badal) for the pronoun in "yaqumani" or for "akharani," and it is permissible that they be in the nominative by "istahagga," that is, "from among those against whom the rightful claim has been made, the two nearest of them began to testify, because of their awareness of the true state of affairs," end of quote. Abu Ali had preceded him in saying that the nominative of "al-awlayani" can be explained by positing "they two are the nearest," and as a substitution for the pronoun of "yaqumani," and Abu Ali added two other possibilities: one, that "al-awlayani" be a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), with the predicate being "akharani yaqumani maqamahuma," as if the sense were "the nearest by the deceased's command are two others who stand," so the speech runs like the saying: "I am a Tamimi"; the other possibility is that "al-awlayani" be the subject-agent of "istahagga." Abu Ali said there is another point concerning it, namely that "al-awlayani" be an attribute (sifah) of "akharani," since, when it was described, it was specified, so it was described because of the specification it had acquired. End of quote. This possibility is weak, because it entails demolishing what they had almost agreed upon, namely that an indefinite noun cannot be described by a definite one, nor the reverse. According to what Abu al-Hasan permitted, the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of His saying "fa-akharani" would be a subject (mubtada'), with the predicate "yaqumani," and it would have been described by His saying "min alladhina," or it would have been described by "yaqumani," with the predicate "min alladhina"; and the separation between the attribute and the described by the predicate does no harm. Or they may be two attributes of "fa-akharani," and "akharani" is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, "so the two witnesses are two others." It is permitted according to some of them that it be in the nominative as the agent: that is, "so let two others testify." As for the object of "istahagga," the earlier estimate of al-Zamakhshari was that it is "istahagga 'alayhim al-ithm" ("the sin was incurred against them"), and he means that it is a pronoun referring back to the sin, because the sin is omitted, since it is not permissible to omit the object of a verb whose subject is not named. Abu Ali and al-Huwfi preceded him to this estimate, and they permitted two other possibilities: one, that the estimate be "istahagga 'alayhim al-iyda'" ("the entrustment was incurred against them"), and the second, that it be "min alladhina istahagga 'alayhim al-wasiyyah" ("from among those against whom the bequest was incurred"). As for what al-Zamakhshari mentioned about "al-awlayani" being in the nominative by "istahagga," Abu Ali had permitted it, as already stated, then he forbade it, saying: because what is incurred is only the bequest or a part of it. As for "al-awlayani" by the deceased, it is not permissible that they should incur it, so that "istahagga" be attributed to them two; but al-Zamakhshari raised "al-awlayani" by "istahagga" on the estimate of an omitted modifier (mudaf) for which "al-awlayani" stands as substitute, so he estimated: "istahagga 'alayhim intidab al-awlayayni minhum lil-shahadah" ("the appointment of the two nearest of them to testify was incurred against them"), because of their awareness of the true state of affairs; so its interpretation is valid. Ibn Jarir permitted this, on the estimate: "min alladhina istahagga 'alayhim ithm al-awwalayn" ("from among those against whom the sin of the first two was incurred"). Ibn 'Atiyyah also permitted that "al-awlayani" be in the nominative by "istahagga," and he elaborated at length on establishing it. Its summary is that he understood "istahagga" here as a metaphor (isti'arah), since it is not literal entitlement, given the words "istahaqqa ithman" ("they two incurred a sin"); rather its meaning is that they overpowered the wealth, by virtue of this deceased man's being alone and lacking kin or co-religionists. So he made their seizure of him an entitlement in a metaphorical sense. The meaning is: "from among the group that was absent, and whose duty was to attend its guardian." He said: when it was absent and this bequeather was alone, that condition became its entitlement; and these two witnesses are from outside the religion, having the guardianship and the command over the two nearest against this group. Then the verb is built in the passive on this meaning, for brevity. This purpose is reinforced by the verb being construed with "'ala" when it denotes power, and here it is taken in the sense of the state of affairs; one does not say "istahagga minhu" or "fihi" except in genuine entitlement in its proper form, whereas "istahagga 'alayhi" is said of seizing, overpowering, and metaphorical entitlement, end of quote. The pronoun in "maqamahuma" refers back to the two false witnesses, and "min alladhina" are the guardians of the deceased. Al-Nahhas said regarding the view of those who estimated "alladhina istahagga 'alayhim al-wasiyyah": this is among the best of what has been said about it, because it did not make one particle a substitute for another, meaning that it did not make "'ala" mean "fi" or "min." It has been said that it means both, namely, "min alladhina istahagga minhum al-ithm," in accordance with His saying: ﴿when they take measure from people [al-mutaffifin: 2]﴾, that is, "from people, the sin was incurred against them." Ibn al-Arabi permitted the estimate of the bequest, and Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi and Ibn al-Fadl preferred that the estimate be "min alladhina istahagga 'alayhim al-mal" ("from among those against whom the property was incurred"). Abu 'Abd Allah said: People have said much about why the term "mawla" (guardian) was not described with this description, and they mentioned a view about it, but the most correct in my opinion is a single point: that they were described by this because, when he took their property, he incurred against them their property, for whoever takes another's property has tried to make his connection to that property like the connection of ownership, so it is sound to describe the owner as having incurred against you that property, end of quote. "Al-awlayani" may mean "the nearer to the deceased," or "the more entitled to the oath," because the two executors claimed that the deceased ancestor of these two witnesses had sold them the vessel, and they denied that; so the oath is their right, like a person who acknowledges a debt to another and claims that he paid it, so the oath is returned to the one who claimed first, because he has become the defendant. The possibilities for the i'rab of "al-awlayani" in this reading are summed up as: the subject (ibtida'), with the predicate for an omitted subject; the substitution for the pronoun of "yaqumani"; the substitution for "akharani"; the attribute of "akharani"; and the objective status of "istahagga," on an omitted modifier whose estimate is disputed.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 106–108 (part 4 of 4):

As for the second reading, which is the building of (istahagga) for the active voice with the first two (awliyan) in the nominative case, al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is "from among the heirs upon whom two of the nearest kin (awliyan) from among the (ones with a claim) by testimony have a right, that they should single them out for the standing of testimony and expose by them the lying of the liars," end of quote.

Ibn 'Atiyya said, in summary: "al-awliyan" is in the nominative, governed by (istahagga), and that is on the basis that the meaning is ﴿from those upon whom [the claim] has been seized﴾, meaning their property and their estate, and the two witnesses of falsehood, so they were called "awliyan" (the nearer ones); that is, the lack of people made them more entitled to this deceased and his estate, so they took from it. Or the meaning is "from those upon whom it became due that the two nearest be from among them," so (istahagga) carries the sense of (haqqa), like (istan'ajaba) and ('ajiba). Or (istahagga) carries the sense of striving and deserving, so the meaning is "from the folk among whom two nearest kin were present, so they strove for it (istahaqqa 'alayhim); that is, they strove for it on their behalf and made it due by their oaths and their closeness," end of quote. Some of them said: the object is elided; that is, "from those upon whom the two nearest kin took their bequest as due."

As for the third reading, which is the reading of (istuhiqqa) in the passive voice, and al-awwalina as the plural of al-awwal, it is analysed as: al-awwalina is an attribute of alladhina. Abu al-Baqa' said: or it is a substitute for the pronoun in the genitive governed by 'ala. Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is in the accusative by way of praise, and the sense of "awwaliyya" is precedence over outsiders in testimony, because they have more right to it, end of quote. This is according to the interpretation that His saying ﴿or two others from other than you﴾ refers to outsiders, not to disbelievers. Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is "from the folk upon whom their affair was seized," that is, they overcame it; then He described them as "awwalun," that is, as first in mention in this verse, and that is in His saying ﴿two men of justice from among you﴾, end of quote.

As for the fourth reading, which is the reading of al-Hasan, then al-awwalan is in the nominative governed by (istahagga). Al-Zamakhshari said: whoever holds that the oath is returned to the claimant, which is Abu Hanifa and his companions, may take proof from it; those who do not hold that, it is directed in their view that the heirs had claimed against the two Christians that they had betrayed them, so they swore; when their lying became apparent, they claimed the purchase regarding what they had concealed, so the heirs denied it, and the oath fell upon the heirs because of their denial of the purchase.

As for the fifth reading, which is the reading of Ibn Sirin, the accusative of the two (awliyan) is by way of praise.

﴿So the two will swear by God: "Our testimony is more truthful than their testimony, and we have not transgressed﴾; that is, the other two standing in place of the testimony of alteration swear that what they reported is true, and that what we have mentioned of the text of the story is more right than what they first related and altered, and that we have not exceeded the limit. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Our oath is more right than their oath." And whoever says that the testimony at the beginning of the story is not in the sense of the oath, here says "the testimony is an oath," and it was called testimony because the ruling is established by it just as a ruling is established by testimony. Ibn al-Jawzi said: "ahaqqu" is more correct, because of their disbelief and our belief, end of quote.

﴿Indeed, then we would be among the wrongdoers﴾: He concluded with this sentence to disown wrongdoing and to deem it repugnant. The word "wrongdoing" (zulm) is suited here by their saying ﴿and we have not transgressed﴾, and transgression (i'tida') and wrongdoing (zulm) are close in meaning. Concluding what the two witnesses of falsehood swore with His saying ﴿then we would be among the sinners﴾ is suitable, because the non-conformity of their oath with reality, and their concealing of the testimony, draw sin upon them.

﴿That is more suitable that they bring the testimony in its proper form, or fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths﴾; that is, that is the ruling mentioned earlier. Since the two witnesses have two states: a state in which doubt arises about them when they testify, in which case they are detained after the prayer and swear the oath prescribed in the verse; this state is answered by His saying ﴿That is more suitable that they bring the testimony in its proper form﴾, that is, in accordance with what they witnessed truthfully, without denial, alteration or lying. And a state in which it becomes known, when they testify, that they are guilty by the testimony and their lying in the oath; in that case their oaths are not regarded, and the oaths are returned to other witnesses, so their oaths are acted upon, and that is after their swearing and their exposure through the manifestation of their lying; this state is answered by His saying ﴿or fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths﴾. The conjunction used is (aw) because if the truthfulness of the two witnesses is not clear, they are necessarily in one of these two states: either doubt arises about their testimony, or their betrayal is discovered; therefore the conjunction is (aw), which is placed for one of two things or several things. So the meaning is: what has been mentioned of the rulings is closer to the establishment of testimony upon what is fitting, or to fear that oaths will be returned to other people, so their oaths fall and are not accepted. Ibn 'Abbas said: all of that brings closer the uprightness of this category in whatever calamities may befall, because they fear the stringent oath after the prayer, then they fear disgrace and the return of the oath, end of quote. It was said: that refers to the swearing of the two witnesses in the presence of a gathering of people. It was said: to the detention after the prayer only. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this appears from the words of al-Suddi, and it is interpreted on this interpretation as in the sense of your saying: "You love me, O Zayd, or you anger me," as if you said: "otherwise you anger me"; so likewise the meaning of the verse is: "That is more suitable that they bring the testimony in its proper form, otherwise they fear the return of oaths." As for according to the view of Ibn 'Abbas, the meaning is: that whole ruling is closer to their coming (with the testimony), or closer to their fearing, end of quote. Thus it is established that (aw) is either in its own sense, or in the sense of (wa). And (yakhafu) is conjoined in these two cases to (ya'tu), or it is in the sense of (ila an), like your saying: "I will surely stick to you, or you pay me my right," and this is what Ibn 'Atiyya expressed by that phrase earlier, of estimating it as a conditional with an elided verb and its response. When it is in the sense of (ila an), then according to the Basrans it remains in its own sense of being for one of two things. However, the conjunction with it does not occur upon the verb (ya'tu), but upon an implied verbal noun, and that is as established in the science of Arabic grammar. The pronoun in (ya'tu) and what follows is plural, though the antecedent is dual; it was said: it refers to the two witnesses in terms of category and type. It was said: it does not refer to both of them specifically, but to the witnessing people in general, and the sense is: that is more suitable that people avoid betrayal and therefore testify to the truth, out of fear of disgrace through the return of the oath to the claimant.

﴿And fear God and listen﴾; that is, beware of God's punishment, and take a shield from Him by not betraying, not swearing falsely by Him, rendering the trust to its owners, and listening with the listening of acceptance and compliance.

﴿And God does not guide the defiant people﴾: an indication that whoever altered the testimony is a defiant one, outside obedience to God; so God does not guide him unless he repents. The wording is general, and the meaning is the stipulation of the absence of repentance.

﴿O you who have believed, let there be [a witness] between you when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest: two [witnesses]﴾. Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Tamim al-Dari and ʿAdi used to travel to Mecca together. A young man from the Banu Sahm set out with them. He died in a land where there was no Muslim, [p-38] and he made them his executors. They handed over his estate to his family, but they withheld a silver cup decorated with gold. The Prophet ﷺ made them swear, [and in one narration: 'The Prophet ﷺ made them swear after the ʿasr prayer'], 'You have neither concealed nor appropriated [anything].' Then the cup was found in Mecca, and the people said: 'We bought it from ʿAdi and Tamim.' Two men from the heirs of the Sahmi came and swore that this cup belonged to the Sahmi, and that 'our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and we have not transgressed.' He said: 'So they took the cup.'" And concerning them the verse was revealed.

It is said that the Sahmi was a client (mawla) of the Banu Sahm, called Badil ibn Abi Maryam, and that the silver cup was what he intended to sell to the king, and it was his greatest merchandise, and that ʿAdi and Tamim sold it for a thousand dirhams and divided them.

It is also said: his name was Badil ibn Abi Mariyah, client of al-ʿAs ibn Wail al-Sahmi, and that he set out traveling by sea to the land of the Negus, and that the silver vessel weighed three hundred mithqal and was overlaid with gold. He said: "They came to Syria, and Badil fell ill, and he was a Muslim," and so on in the hadith.

Abu ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Fadl mentioned that the heirs of Budayl said to the two of them: "Did you not claim that our companion did not sell any of his goods? Then what is this vessel with you, which is among what our companion took out with him, and you have sworn concerning it?" They said: "We had bought it from him, and we had no proof of it, so we disliked acknowledging it to you, lest you take it from us and demand proof of it, which we cannot provide." So they brought them before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the verse was revealed. End of quotation.

In another narration, Tamim said: "When I embraced Islam after the Prophet ﷺ came to Medina, I felt guilty about that, so I went to his family and informed them of the matter, and I paid them five hundred dirhams, and I told them that my companion had an equal amount. They brought him to the Prophet ﷺ, and he asked them for proof, but they did not find what they had been commanded to produce. So he commanded them to have him swear by that which is binding upon the people of his religion, and he swore. Then Allah revealed this verse up to His words: ﴿after their oath﴾. Then ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs and another man from among them stood up and swore, and the five hundred were taken from the hand of ʿAdi ibn Zayd."

Al-Waqidi added in his account that Tamim and ʿAdi were brothers, and he means, Allah knows best, that they were brothers through the mother. He also mentioned that Budayl wrote his bequest with his own hand and placed it in his baggage, and bequeathed to Tamim and ʿAdi that they should deliver his belongings. The Messenger [ﷺ] made them swear after the ʿasr prayer, and he made ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs and al-Muttalib ibn Abi Wada'a swear.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned this occasion in brief and without detail. He said that Badil ibn Abi Maryam was one of the emigrants (muhajirun), and that he wrote a document containing what he had with him, and put it in his baggage, and did not inform his two companions of it. Then the people of Budayl found the document and demanded the vessel from the two of them. They denied it, so they were brought before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the verse was revealed.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "Nothing has been established to my knowledge regarding ʿAdi having companionship (suhba) with the Prophet, nor is his Islam confirmed, though some of the later scholars counted him among the Companions." Makki ibn Abi Talib said: "These verses are, according to the scholars of meanings, among the most difficult in the Qur'an, grammatically, semantically, and legally." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "This is the statement of one who was not struck by the snow (al-thalj) in its interpretation, and this is clear from his book." End of quotation. Abu al-Hasan al-Sakhawi said: "I have not seen any of the imams whose discussion of these [verses] was free from beginning to end." End of quotation.

The connection (munasaba) of this verse to what precedes it is that when He mentioned ﴿O you who have believed﴾, there was in that a warning against misguidance and a suggestion that one should not benefit from them in any matter of the affairs of the believers, such as testimony or otherwise. So Allah, exalted is He, informed that their testimony is legislated, or entrusting them with executorship during travel, as will be explained. Abu Nasr al-Qushayri said: "When the surah was revealed concerning fulfilling contracts and abandoning betrayals, the discussion extended to this."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿شَهادَةُ بَيْنِكُمْ﴾ with the nominative case (raf') and with the idafa of "shahadatu" to "baynikum". Al-Shaʿbi, al-Hasan, and al-Aʿraj read ﴿شَهادَةُ بَيْنِكُمْ﴾ with the nominative of "shahadatun" and its tanwin (nunation). Al-Sulami and al-Hasan also read "shahadatan" with the accusative and tanwin. This was also narrated from al-Aʿraj and Abu Haywa. [p-39] In these two readings, "baynakum" is in the accusative as an adverbial of place (zarf). So "shahadatu," according to the majority's reading, is a subject (mubtada') with an annexed noun, "bayn," after its extension (ittisaʿ), as in his saying: "hadhā firāqu bayni wa baynika" (this is the parting between me and you), and its predicate (khabar) is "ithnan" (two), its estimated form being: "the testimony of two." Or the estimate is: "those who possess the testimony between you are two." The deletion was needed so that the subject would agree with the predicate. The same explanation applies to the reading of al-Shaʿbi and al-Aʿraj.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that "ithnan" be nominative as the agent (fa'il) of "shahadatu," and that "shahadatu" be a subject with a deleted predicate, estimating it as: "in what has been imposed upon you, that two should bear witness."

It is also said: "shahadatu" is a subject, its predicate being ﴿إذا حَضَرَ أحَدَكُمُ المَوْتُ﴾ (when death approaches one of you). It is also said: its predicate is ﴿حِينَ الوَصِيَّةِ﴾ (at the time of bequest), and "ithnan" is nominative as the predicate of a deleted subject, the estimate being: "the witnesses are two, possessors of justice from among you," or as the agent, the estimate being: "two shall bear witness."

It is also said: "shahadatu" is a subject, and "ithnan" is nominative by it as agent, and the agent suffices in place of the predicate.

According to the first grammatical analysis (iʿrab), "idhā" is the object (maʿmul) of the testimony. As for "ḥīna," they mentioned that it is the object of "ḥaḍara" (approached), or a complement of time (ẓarf) for "al-mawt" (death), or a substitute (badal) for "idhā." Al-Zamakhshari mentioned none but the substitute. He said: "﴿ḥīna al-waṣiyya﴾ is a substitute from it, meaning from 'idhā'. In its substitution from it is evidence for the obligation of bequest, and that it is among the binding matters which a Muslim should not neglect or forget." "The approach of death" means its imminence, and the appearance of signs of the arrival of the term. End of quotation.

Al-Maturidi, followed by Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi, said: "The estimate is 'mā baynakum' (what is between you), so 'mā' was deleted." Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: "He means the testimony of what is between you, and 'baynakum' is a metaphor for dispute, because witnesses are only needed when a dispute occurs. The deletion of 'mā' in His saying 'mā baynakum' is permissible because it is evident. Its parallel is ﴿hādhā firāqu bayni wa baynika﴾ [al-Kahf 18:78], meaning 'mā bayni wa baynika,' and His saying ﴿laqad taqaṭṭaʿa baynakum﴾ [al-Anʿam 6:94] in the reading of the one who read it with the accusative." End of quotation.

The deletion of the relative "mā" is not permitted according to the Basrans, and with the idafa, it is not valid at all to estimate "mā." And His saying ﴿hādhā firāqu bayni wa baynika﴾ is not a parallel to ﴿laqad taqaṭṭaʿa baynakum﴾, because that is annexed to a pronoun, whereas this remains in its own form, so it is possible to imagine estimating "mā" in it, because the idafa removed it from the status of a complement of place and made it an object by way of expansion (saʿa). As for the explanation (takhrij) of the reading of al-Sulami and al-Hasan, "shahadatan" in the accusative with tanwin, and "baynakum" in the accusative, al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "li-yuqim shahadatan ithnan" (let two establish a testimony). He made "shahadatan" an object by implying this command, and "ithnan" nominative as agent of "li-yuqim." This which al-Zamakhshari estimated is exactly the estimate of Ibn Jinni. Ibn Jinni said: "The estimate is: 'li-yuqim shahadatan baynakumu ithnan' (let two establish the testimony between you)." End of quotation.

What Ibn Jinni mentioned contradicts what our companions (the Basran grammarians) have said. They said: "It is not permitted to delete the verb and retain its agent, unless the preceding context indicates the verb, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿yusabbiḥu lahu fīhā bil-ghuduwwi wal-āṣāl﴾ [al-Nur 24:36], according to the reading of the one who opened the bāʾ, reading it in the passive voice." They mentioned a disagreement regarding deriving this: that is, "yusabbiḥuhu rijāl" (men glorify Him), so "yusabbiḥu" indicates "yusabbiḥuhu." Or it is a response to a negation, such as when one is asked: "mā qāma aḥadun ʿindaka?" (Did no one stand by you?) and you answer: "balā Zayd" (Yes, Zayd), meaning: "qāma Zayd" (Zayd stood). Or it is a response to a question, as in the saying of the poet:

"Has there not come to Umm al-Huwayrith a messenger, rather Khalid, if the obstacles do not prevent him?"

The estimate is: "atā Khālid" (Khalid came), or "yaʾtīhā Khālid" (Khalid comes to her). The deletion of the verb which Ibn Jinni estimated, and which al-Zamakhshari followed, is not one of these three categories. What I hold is that this irregular reading (qirāʾa shādhdha) may be explained in two ways. One: "shahadatan" is accusative as an infinitive (maṣdar) that substitutes for the verb in the sense of a command, with "ithnan" nominative by it, and the estimate is "li-yashhad baynakumu ithnan" (let two bear witness among you). This would be of the type of your saying: "ḍarban zaydan" (striking Zayd), except that the agent in "ḍarban" is attributed to a pronoun of the addressee, because its meaning is "iḍrib" (strike!), whereas this is attributed to an apparent noun, because its meaning is "li-yashhad" (let him bear witness). The second way is that it is also an infinitive, not in the sense of a command, but as a predicate, substituting for the verb in the predicate, though this is rare, like your saying: "ifʿal wa karāmatan wa masarratan" (do, and with honour and joy), meaning "wa Ukrimuka wa Usarruka" (and I honour you and make you happy). "Karāmatun" and "masarratun" are substitutes for the verb in the predicate, as is the better reading in the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Standing there, my companions halted their mounts over me."

The nominative of "ṣaḥbī" and the accusative of "maṭiyyahum" are by "wuqūfan," because it is a substitute for the verb in the predicate; the estimate is "waqafa ṣaḥbī ʿalayya maṭiyyahum" (my companions halted their mounts over me). The estimate in the verse is: "yashhadu idhā ḥaḍara aḥadakumu al-mawtu ithnān" (two bear witness when death approaches one of you).

As for the testimony here, is it that by which rights are established before judges, or presence, or oath? Three opinions, the last of which is that of al-Tabari and al-Qaffal, like His saying: ﴿fashahādatu aḥadihim arbaʿu shahādāt﴾ (the testimony of one of them is four testimonies) [al-Nur 24:6]. It is also said that testimony (shahāda) comes in the sense of acknowledgment (iqrār), as in His saying: ﴿wal-malāʾikatu yashhadūn﴾ (and the angels bear witness) [al-Nisa 4:166]; and in the sense of knowledge (ʿilm), as in His saying: ﴿shahida Allahu annahu lā ilāha illā huwa﴾ (Allah bears witness that there is no god but Him) [Al ʿImran 3:18]; and in the sense of bequest (waṣiyya). This verse was interpreted in that sense, so there are four opinions regarding it.

*
﴿ownership of justice from among you, or two others from outside your [community]﴾.

﴿Dhawa 'adlin﴾ (two persons of justice) is a qualifier of the word *ithnan* (two), and *minkum* (from among you) is another qualifier. *Min ghayrikum* (from other than you) is a qualifier of *akharan* (two others). Al-Zamakhshari said: *minkum* means from your relatives, and *min ghayrikum* means from strangers, ﴿if you are travelling in the land﴾, meaning if death befalls you while travelling and none of your kinsmen is with you, then call upon two outsiders to witness the bequest. He made relatives the preferred choice because they know the condition of the deceased better, know what is most suitable, and are most sincere toward him. It has also been said that *minkum* means from among the Muslims, and that this was permitted at the beginning of Islam because Muslims were few and it was difficult to find them while travelling. Makhul reported that it was abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation) by His saying: ﴿And call to witness two persons of justice from among you﴾ [al-Talaq 65:2]. End of quotation.

What al-Zamakhshari chose and began with is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and al-Zuhri. They said: God commanded the calling of two just persons from among the kinsmen, since they have the greatest right to the matter of the bequest and are most knowledgeable about the justice required in it. If the matter occurs during travel and no kinsmen are present, he may entrust it to others from among the Muslim strangers. This view contradicts what al-Zamakhshari and other exegetes have mentioned. Even Ibn 'Atiyya said: "We know of no disagreement that the cause of revelation of this verse is that Tamim al-Dari and 'Adi ibn Zayd were Christians," and he related the aforementioned hadith. Thus this view contradicts the occasion of revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*).

As for the second view that al-Zamakhshari related, it is the position of Abu Musa, Ibn al-Musayyab, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Mijlaz, Ibrahim, Shurayh, 'Ubayda al-Salmani, Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Qatada [p. 41] and al-Suddi. This was also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Thawri said the same, Abu 'Ubayd leaned toward it, and Ahmad chose it. They said: The meaning of His saying *minkum* is from among the believers, and the meaning of ﴿from other than you﴾ is from among the disbelievers. Some of them said: this verse was revealed when there were no believers except in Medina, and they used to travel for trade in the company of People of the Book, idolaters, and various kinds of disbelievers.

The position of Abu Musa, Shurayh and others is that the verse is *muhkam* (not abrogated, in force). Ahmad said: the testimony of protected non-Muslims (*ahl al-dhimma*, people under the protection of the Muslim state) is valid against Muslims during travel when Muslims are not available. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi preferred this view and said: His saying ﴿O you who believe﴾ is addressed to all believers. So when He said ﴿or two others from other than you﴾, they are necessarily non-believers. Also, if the two others were Muslims, the permissibility of calling them as witnesses would not have been conditioned on travel, because a Muslim's testimony is valid both at home and while travelling. Also, the verse indicates the obligation of swearing an oath after the prayer, and the Muslims agreed that a witness is not required to take an oath; therefore we know that they are not Muslims. Also, the occasion of revelation is the testimony of the two Christians concerning Budayl, who was a Muslim. Also, Abu Musa ruled by the testimony of two Jews after having made them swear, and none of the Companions objected to it, so this constituted a consensus (*ijma'*). Also, most of the community agree that Surat al-Ma'ida is among the last parts of the Qur'an to be revealed, and there is nothing abrogated in it.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas, supporting the first view, said: "This rests on a subtle point in Arabic. In Arabic there is another meaning of the same kind as the first. You say: *marartu bi-karimin wa-karimin akhar* (I passed by a generous man and another generous man). The word *akhar* indicates that it is of the same kind as the first. According to the grammarians of Arabic, it is not permissible to say *marartu bi-karimin wa-khasisin akhar* (I passed by a generous man and another base man), nor *marartu bi-rajulin wa-himarin akhar* (I passed by a man and another donkey). Therefore it must follow that the meaning of His saying *aw akharani min ghayrikum* is: *'adlan* (two just persons), and disbelievers are not just." End of quotation.

What he mentioned in the example is correct, but what is in the verse differs from the example that al-Nahhas cited in its structure, because he gave an example with *akhar* and made it a qualifier of something not of the same kind as the first. As for the verse, it belongs to the category in which *akhar* is used as a qualifier, and it falls within the same kind as what precedes it, and the qualifying kind of the first is not considered. You say: *ja'anee rajulun muslimun wa-akharu kafirun* (a Muslim man came to me and another, a disbeliever), *marartu bi-rajulin qa'imin wa-akhara qa'idin* (I passed by a standing man and another seated man), *ishtaraytu farasan sabiqan wa-akhara, mub'iṭan* (I bought a swift horse and another, a slow one). If you had postponed *akhar* in these examples, the construction would not be permissible: if you said *ja'anee rajulun muslimun wa-kafirun akhar* (a Muslim man came to me and a disbeliever, another), *marartu bi-rajulin qa'imin wa-qa'idin akhar* (I passed by a standing man and a seated man, another), *ishtaraytu farasan sabiqan wa-mub'iṭan akhar* (I bought a swift horse and a slow one, another), it would not be permitted. The verse is not of this kind, except that its construction came as ﴿two persons, of justice, from among you, or two others from other than you﴾, so *akharani* is of the same kind as His saying *ithnani* (two). This is especially so if you parse it as *rajulani ithnani* (two men), then *akharani* are of the same kind as your saying *rajulani ithnani*. The qualifier in His saying ﴿of justice from among you﴾ is not considered, even though it differs from *min ghayrikum*, just as the qualifier of kind is not considered in your saying: *'indi rajulani ithnani muslimani wa-akharani kafirani* (I have two men, two Muslims, and two others, two disbelievers), since the condition for *akhar* when it precedes is not that it be of the same kind as the first with a distinct qualifier. This is the language of the Arabs. The poet said:

They were two groups, bending the glass goblets over the hollow shoulders, in whose jaws there is a large (vein)*.
And others upon the *mādhī* (fine silk) above them, of the weaving of Dawud, or what Iram bequeathed.

The estimated sense is: they were two groups, one group, or people who bend the goblets. Then he said: *wa-akharīna* (and others), so *akharina* is of the same kind as your saying *fariqan* (a group), and he did not separate it with its qualifier, which is his saying *yuṣghūna al-zujāja* (who bend the goblets), because the poet divided those mentioned into two distinct parts with two qualifiers of the same kind. This distinction is understood by few people, let alone those who know it.

As for the third view that al-Zamakhshari related, namely that it is abrogated, and he related it from Makhul, it is the view of Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Nakha'i, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and other jurists. However, Abu Hanifa differed from them and said: the testimony of disbelievers is valid against one another, but not against Muslims. The abrogating verses are His saying ﴿from among those whom you approve of as witnesses﴾ [al-Baqara 2:282], and His saying ﴿And call to witness two persons of justice from among you﴾ [al-Talaq 65:2]. They claimed that the verse of debt is among the last to be revealed. The apparent meaning is that *aw* (or) indicates choice (*takhyir*). Ibn 'Abbas said this. Whoever takes His saying ﴿from other than you﴾ to mean from among your clan may choose between calling upon his relatives or strangers from among the Muslims. Whoever holds that His saying ﴿from other than you﴾ means from among the disbelievers, they differed. Some said: "other than you" refers to the People of the Book, and this was reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Others said: the People of the Book and the idolaters, and this is the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿from other than you﴾. Others said: *aw* indicates sequence (*tartib*) if His saying ﴿from other than you﴾ means from outside your religious community, so the estimate is: if none is found from your community.

﴿If you are travelling in the land and death's disaster befalls you﴾. This is a shift (*iltifat*, shift of grammatical person) from third person to second person. Had it followed the wording ﴿when death approaches one of you﴾, the construction would have been: if he travels in the land and death's disaster befalls him. The shift came in the plural because His saying *ahadakum* (one of you) means that when death approaches each one of you, and the meaning is: if you travel in the land for your interests and livelihoods. The apparent meaning of the verse implies that calling upon two others from outside the Muslims is conditioned on travel in the land and the approach of the signs of death.

﴿You shall detain them after the prayer﴾. The address is to the believers, not to what the address in His saying ﴿If you are travelling in the land and death's disaster befalls you﴾ indicates, because the one who travels in the land and is struck by death is not the one who detains. The phrase ﴿you shall detain them﴾ is a qualifier of *akharan* (two others). An interjection (*i'tiraḍ*) was inserted between the qualified and the qualifier, namely His saying "if you are travelling … to death". The interjection conveys that the turning to two others from outside the religious community or from outside the kin, according to the disagreement of scholars on this matter, occurs only in the case of necessity of travel and the arrival of death during it. It dispensed with the response (*jawab*) of *in* (if), because of what preceded it in His saying ﴿or two others from other than you﴾. End of quotation.

Al-Hufi and Abu al-Baqa' held that ﴿you shall detain them﴾ is a qualifier, and this is the apparent meaning of Ibn 'Atiyya's words, since he did not mention any view other than the view of Abu 'Ali that we have already cited.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the position of ﴿you shall detain them﴾? I say: it is a resumptive new sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence beginning), as if it were said: after stipulating justice in both of them, what if we doubt them? So it was said: ﴿you shall detain them﴾. What al-Zamakhshari said about the new sentence is more apparent than the qualifier interpretation, because of the long separation by the conditional clause and the coordinated element between the qualified and its qualifier. Al-Zamakhshari said: "after stipulating justice in both of them," because he chose that His saying "or two others from other than you" means "or two other just persons from outside the kinsmen." It has already been mentioned in Abu 'Ali's words that the turning to two others from outside the religious community or kinship occurs only in the case of necessity of travel and the arrival of death during it, and so on to the end of his words. It is evident from this that the estimated response of the condition is: ﴿If you are travelling in the land and death's disaster befalls you﴾; then call upon two others from among other than you, or the two witnesses are two others from outside you. The apparent meaning is that the condition is a restriction on the testimony of two just persons from among the believers, or two others from outside the believers. Thus the legislation of the bequest for one travelling in the land who is near death is that he calls two persons to witness. The estimated response would be: if you travel in the land and death's disaster befalls you, then call two persons, either from among you or from other than you. In that case the condition is not a restriction on two others from outside us only, but a restriction on the one who travels in the land and approaches death: two from us or from outside us shall bear witness.

Ibn 'Abbas said: there is an omission in the speech. Its estimate is: ﴿and death's disaster befalls you﴾, and you have already called them to witness the bequest. Ibn Jubayr said its estimate is: and you have made the bequest. It was said: this is preferable, because the witness does not swear, but the testator swears.

The meaning of ﴿you shall detain them﴾ is that you shall secure them for the oath. The address is to those among the rulers of Islam who are responsible for this. The pronoun of the object refers, according to one view, to the two others from outside the believers; the apparent reference of it to two persons from among us or from outside us is the same, whether they are executors or witnesses.

The apparent meaning of ﴿after the prayer﴾ is that the definite article *al-* is generic, or it means after any prayer. This apparent meaning has been held, and Ibn 'Abbas specified it as the prayer of their religion, and that is an intensification of the oath. Al-Hasan said: after the afternoon prayer or the noon prayer, because the people of the Hijaz (*ahl al-Hijaz*, the Hijaz region of Arabia) used to sit for judgment after them. The majority said it is the afternoon prayer, because it is the time when people gather. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did likewise: he made 'Adi and Tamim swear after the afternoon prayer at the pulpit. This view was preferred on the basis of his action and his saying in the authentic collection: "Whoever swears a false oath after the afternoon prayer will meet God while He is angry with him." Also, the oath was known to be taken after these two prayers, so specifying by what is known dispenses with specifying by the wording. Also, all religions honour this time and mention God in it. Therefore, in this view the definite article is for a known reference (*al-'ahd*), and likewise in al-Hasan's view.

﴿They swear by God: "If you doubt, we will not sell it for any price, even if it were a relative, nor will we conceal the testimony of God; indeed we would then be among the sinners."﴾ The apparent meaning is that the swearing is restricted to the existence of doubt, so when no doubt exists, there is no oath. Abu Musa's having the two Jews swear, whom a Muslim had called upon as witnesses to his bequest when he died, should be understood as there having been doubt, even though this is not mentioned in the account of that Muslim. The *fa'* in His saying "they swear" (*fa-yuqsimani*) conjoins this sentence to His saying "you shall detain them." This is the apparent view. Abu 'Ali said: if you wish, you need not estimate the *fa'* as coordinating a sentence, but make it a response (*jaza'*), like the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

And the pupil of my eye sometimes dries up the water, so it appears; and sometimes it overflows, so it drowns.

Its estimated form is: "with them"; if he (the first witness) is found to have deceived, then likewise, if you detain both of them, let them swear. End of quote. There is no necessity to posit an omitted conditional clause while leaving its apodosis in place, which would make the fa' (fa of consequence) a fa' of the apodosis, nor to posit a pronoun hidden after the fa': that is, "so they two swear," and "so he appears." Our companions (the Basran grammarians) explained the verse of Dhu al-Rummah on another analysis, namely that his saying "yahsir al-ma' tara(tan)" ("he drains the water at times") is a clause in the place of the predicate (khabar), and it is unconnected to a linking pronoun (rabit). Analogically, it should not occur as the predicate of the subject (mubtada'). However, he coordinated with the fa' onto both of them a clause that contains the pronoun of the subject, so the connection was achieved thereby. And ﴿we do not sell﴾ is the response (jawab) to his saying "fa-yuqsimani billah" ("so they two swear by God"), and the oath has been separated from its response by the conditional clause. The meaning is: if you doubt their condition and accuse them, then make them swear. It has been said: if by "the two" (bihima) the witnesses are meant, then the oath of the two witnesses has been abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one); if the two executors (wasiyyan) are meant, then the oath of the two is not abrogated. It is reported from Ali that he would make the witness and the transmitter swear when he accused them. The pronoun in "bihi" ("by it") refers back to God, or to the oath, or to the distortion of the testimony; there are three opinions, and the third is that of Abu Ali. His saying ﴿we sell thereby a price﴾ is a metonymy (kinayah) for exchanging it for a worldly object, and it is by elision of a modifier (hadhf mudaf), that is, "one having a price," because the price itself is not what is bought. It is not valid for ﴿we do not sell﴾ to mean "we do not sell" here, even though that is the usage in the language. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, we do not swear by God falsely for the sake of wealth, even if the one for whose sake we swear is close to us; this is in accordance with their habit of truthfulness and trustworthiness always, for they are included in His saying: ﴿Be steadfast in justice, witnesses for God, even against yourselves or parents and near relatives﴾ [an-Nisa': 135]. He said "for they are included" to the end because the two and the other two (the witnesses) are, in his view, believers, so they fall under His saying: ﴿O you who believe, be steadfast for God﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8], and so on. Ibn Atiyyah said: He singled out near kin for mention because it is the custom that the self inclines toward its relatives and makes light of what would not be made light of for others' benefit. The clause ﴿and we do not conceal the testimony of God﴾ is coordinated with his saying ﴿we do not sell thereby a price﴾, so it is part of what is sworn to. He ascribed the testimony to God because He, exalted is He, is the one who commands its establishment and forbids its concealment. It is possible that ﴿and we do not conceal﴾ is a statement from the two of them, reporting about themselves that they do not conceal the testimony of God, and it is not included in what is sworn to. Al-Hasan and al-Sha'bi read ﴿and we do not conceal﴾ with the mim jussed, as a prohibition (nahy) addressed by the two to themselves against concealing the testimony. The use of the prohibitive "la" with the first person is rare, as in the verse:

*"When we leave Damascus, let us not return to it ever, as long as the Jaradim are there."*

Ali, Nu'aym ibn Maysarah, and al-Sha'bi, in a variant reported from him, read ﴿the testimony of God﴾ with both words in the accusative, and "shahadatan" with tanwin, and they are governed by "naktum" ("we conceal"). The estimated sense is: "and we do not conceal God a testimony." Al-Zahrawi said: It is possible that the meaning is: "and we do not conceal a testimony, by God," then the waw was dropped and the verb put in the accusative for brevity. It is reported from Ali, al-Sulami, and al-Hasan al-Basri "shahadatan" with tanwin, and "a-llahi" with the madd on the hamzah of interrogation, which is a substitute for the particle of oath, entering for the sake of affirmation and making the souls of those swearing, or of those addressed, stand firm. It is reported from al-Sha'bi and others that he would pause on "shahadah" with a quiescent ha', and on "Allah" with the hamzat al-wasl cut off, without the madd of interrogation. Ibn Jinni said: Pausing on "shahadah" with a quiescent ha', and beginning the oath afresh, is good, because beginning it at the start of speech is more fitting for it and more awe-inspiring than that it should enter into the course of speech. It is reported from Yahya ibn Adam, from Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash, "shahadatan" with tanwin, "Allah" with the hamzah cut off and no madd, and the ha' of the divine name in the genitive; this reading is also reported from al-Sha'bi. Al-A'mash and Ibn Muhaysin read "lamina al-athimin" ("indeed of the sinners") with the nun of "min" assimilated (idgham) into the lam of "al-athimin," after the hamzah has been dropped and its vowel transferred to the lam.

﴿And if it is discovered that they two have incurred a sin﴾: that is, if after their oath it is discovered that they two have incurred a sin, namely a guilt, by their perjury in the oath, in that it does not correspond to the reality. ("Discovered," ʿuthira) is a metaphor (isti'arah) for what befalls one's knowledge after it has been hidden, and after one did not expect it nor intend it, as you say: "you fell upon the expert" and "you chanced upon such-and-such." Abu Ali said: "Sin" here is the thing taken, because taking it is a sin, so it is called a sin, just as what is taken without right is called an injustice (maẓlamah). Sibawayh said: "Maẓlamah" is the name of what is taken from you, and for this reason this taken thing is named by the verbal noun, end of quote. The apparent meaning is that "sin" here is not the thing taken, but the offence by which they incurred the state of being among the sinners, from which they disavowed themselves in their saying ﴿Indeed, then we would be among the sinners﴾. If "sin" were the thing taken, it would not be said of it "they incurred a sin," because they wronged and transgressed, and that is what necessitates the sin.

﴿Then two others shall stand in their place from among those against whom the rightful claim has been made, the two nearest﴾ (p. 45). The two Harameyn (Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr), the two Arabic-readers (Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim? in the sense of the Kufan and Basran readers), and al-Kisa'i read "istahagga" in the active voice, and "al-awlayani" as a dual in the nominative, the dual of "al-uwla" (the nearer). This reading is reported from Ubayy, Ali, Ibn Abbas, and from Ibn Kathir in the transmission of Qurrah from him. Hamzah and Abu Bakr read "istuhiqqa" in the passive voice, and "al-awwalina" as the plural of "al-awwal" (the first). Al-Hasan read "istahagga" in the active voice, with "al-awwalan" in the nominative, the dual of "awwal." Ibn Sirin read "al-awliyayn," the accusative dual of "al-awwal." As for the first reading, al-Zamakhshari said: "Two others" means two other witnesses, ﴿who shall stand in their place from among those against whom the rightful claim has been made﴾: that is, from among those against whom the sin was incurred, and its meaning is that they are those who were wronged, namely the family of the deceased and his kin. In the story of Budayl, when the treachery of the two men became evident, he made two men of his heirs swear that the vessel was the property of their companion, and that their testimony was more worthy than the testimony of the two. ("Al-awlayani") means the most worthy of testimony, by reason of their kinship, their knowledge, and their exalted status; it is as if it had been said: "Who are they?", so it was said, "the two nearest." It has been said: they are a substitution (badal) for the pronoun in "yaqumani" or for "akharani," and it is permissible that they be in the nominative by "istahagga," that is, "from among those against whom the rightful claim has been made, the two nearest of them began to testify, because of their awareness of the true state of affairs," end of quote. Abu Ali had preceded him in saying that the nominative of "al-awlayani" can be explained by positing "they two are the nearest," and as a substitution for the pronoun of "yaqumani," and Abu Ali added two other possibilities: one, that "al-awlayani" be a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), with the predicate being "akharani yaqumani maqamahuma," as if the sense were "the nearest by the deceased's command are two others who stand," so the speech runs like the saying: "I am a Tamimi"; the other possibility is that "al-awlayani" be the subject-agent of "istahagga." Abu Ali said there is another point concerning it, namely that "al-awlayani" be an attribute (sifah) of "akharani," since, when it was described, it was specified, so it was described because of the specification it had acquired. End of quote. This possibility is weak, because it entails demolishing what they had almost agreed upon, namely that an indefinite noun cannot be described by a definite one, nor the reverse. According to what Abu al-Hasan permitted, the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of His saying "fa-akharani" would be a subject (mubtada'), with the predicate "yaqumani," and it would have been described by His saying "min alladhina," or it would have been described by "yaqumani," with the predicate "min alladhina"; and the separation between the attribute and the described by the predicate does no harm. Or they may be two attributes of "fa-akharani," and "akharani" is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, "so the two witnesses are two others." It is permitted according to some of them that it be in the nominative as the agent: that is, "so let two others testify." As for the object of "istahagga," the earlier estimate of al-Zamakhshari was that it is "istahagga 'alayhim al-ithm" ("the sin was incurred against them"), and he means that it is a pronoun referring back to the sin, because the sin is omitted, since it is not permissible to omit the object of a verb whose subject is not named. Abu Ali and al-Huwfi preceded him to this estimate, and they permitted two other possibilities: one, that the estimate be "istahagga 'alayhim al-iyda'" ("the entrustment was incurred against them"), and the second, that it be "min alladhina istahagga 'alayhim al-wasiyyah" ("from among those against whom the bequest was incurred"). As for what al-Zamakhshari mentioned about "al-awlayani" being in the nominative by "istahagga," Abu Ali had permitted it, as already stated, then he forbade it, saying: because what is incurred is only the bequest or a part of it. As for "al-awlayani" by the deceased, it is not permissible that they should incur it, so that "istahagga" be attributed to them two; but al-Zamakhshari raised "al-awlayani" by "istahagga" on the estimate of an omitted modifier (mudaf) for which "al-awlayani" stands as substitute, so he estimated: "istahagga 'alayhim intidab al-awlayayni minhum lil-shahadah" ("the appointment of the two nearest of them to testify was incurred against them"), because of their awareness of the true state of affairs; so its interpretation is valid. Ibn Jarir permitted this, on the estimate: "min alladhina istahagga 'alayhim ithm al-awwalayn" ("from among those against whom the sin of the first two was incurred"). Ibn 'Atiyyah also permitted that "al-awlayani" be in the nominative by "istahagga," and he elaborated at length on establishing it. Its summary is that he understood "istahagga" here as a metaphor (isti'arah), since it is not literal entitlement, given the words "istahaqqa ithman" ("they two incurred a sin"); rather its meaning is that they overpowered the wealth, by virtue of this deceased man's being alone and lacking kin or co-religionists. So he made their seizure of him an entitlement in a metaphorical sense. The meaning is: "from among the group that was absent, and whose duty was to attend its guardian." He said: when it was absent and this bequeather was alone, that condition became its entitlement; and these two witnesses are from outside the religion, having the guardianship and the command over the two nearest against this group. Then the verb is built in the passive on this meaning, for brevity. This purpose is reinforced by the verb being construed with "'ala" when it denotes power, and here it is taken in the sense of the state of affairs; one does not say "istahagga minhu" or "fihi" except in genuine entitlement in its proper form, whereas "istahagga 'alayhi" is said of seizing, overpowering, and metaphorical entitlement, end of quote. The pronoun in "maqamahuma" refers back to the two false witnesses, and "min alladhina" are the guardians of the deceased. Al-Nahhas said regarding the view of those who estimated "alladhina istahagga 'alayhim al-wasiyyah": this is among the best of what has been said about it, because it did not make one particle a substitute for another, meaning that it did not make "'ala" mean "fi" or "min." It has been said that it means both, namely, "min alladhina istahagga minhum al-ithm," in accordance with His saying: ﴿when they take measure from people [al-mutaffifin: 2]﴾, that is, "from people, the sin was incurred against them." Ibn al-Arabi permitted the estimate of the bequest, and Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi and Ibn al-Fadl preferred that the estimate be "min alladhina istahagga 'alayhim al-mal" ("from among those against whom the property was incurred"). Abu 'Abd Allah said: People have said much about why the term "mawla" (guardian) was not described with this description, and they mentioned a view about it, but the most correct in my opinion is a single point: that they were described by this because, when he took their property, he incurred against them their property, for whoever takes another's property has tried to make his connection to that property like the connection of ownership, so it is sound to describe the owner as having incurred against you that property, end of quote. "Al-awlayani" may mean "the nearer to the deceased," or "the more entitled to the oath," because the two executors claimed that the deceased ancestor of these two witnesses had sold them the vessel, and they denied that; so the oath is their right, like a person who acknowledges a debt to another and claims that he paid it, so the oath is returned to the one who claimed first, because he has become the defendant. The possibilities for the i'rab of "al-awlayani" in this reading are summed up as: the subject (ibtida'), with the predicate for an omitted subject; the substitution for the pronoun of "yaqumani"; the substitution for "akharani"; the attribute of "akharani"; and the objective status of "istahagga," on an omitted modifier whose estimate is disputed.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 106–108 (part 4 of 4):

As for the second reading, which is the building of (istahagga) for the active voice with the first two (awliyan) in the nominative case, al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is "from among the heirs upon whom two of the nearest kin (awliyan) from among the (ones with a claim) by testimony have a right, that they should single them out for the standing of testimony and expose by them the lying of the liars," end of quote.

Ibn 'Atiyya said, in summary: "al-awliyan" is in the nominative, governed by (istahagga), and that is on the basis that the meaning is ﴿from those upon whom [the claim] has been seized﴾, meaning their property and their estate, and the two witnesses of falsehood, so they were called "awliyan" (the nearer ones); that is, the lack of people made them more entitled to this deceased and his estate, so they took from it. Or the meaning is "from those upon whom it became due that the two nearest be from among them," so (istahagga) carries the sense of (haqqa), like (istan'ajaba) and ('ajiba). Or (istahagga) carries the sense of striving and deserving, so the meaning is "from the folk among whom two nearest kin were present, so they strove for it (istahaqqa 'alayhim); that is, they strove for it on their behalf and made it due by their oaths and their closeness," end of quote. Some of them said: the object is elided; that is, "from those upon whom the two nearest kin took their bequest as due."

As for the third reading, which is the reading of (istuhiqqa) in the passive voice, and al-awwalina as the plural of al-awwal, it is analysed as: al-awwalina is an attribute of alladhina. Abu al-Baqa' said: or it is a substitute for the pronoun in the genitive governed by 'ala. Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is in the accusative by way of praise, and the sense of "awwaliyya" is precedence over outsiders in testimony, because they have more right to it, end of quote. This is according to the interpretation that His saying ﴿or two others from other than you﴾ refers to outsiders, not to disbelievers. Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is "from the folk upon whom their affair was seized," that is, they overcame it; then He described them as "awwalun," that is, as first in mention in this verse, and that is in His saying ﴿two men of justice from among you﴾, end of quote.

As for the fourth reading, which is the reading of al-Hasan, then al-awwalan is in the nominative governed by (istahagga). Al-Zamakhshari said: whoever holds that the oath is returned to the claimant, which is Abu Hanifa and his companions, may take proof from it; those who do not hold that, it is directed in their view that the heirs had claimed against the two Christians that they had betrayed them, so they swore; when their lying became apparent, they claimed the purchase regarding what they had concealed, so the heirs denied it, and the oath fell upon the heirs because of their denial of the purchase.

As for the fifth reading, which is the reading of Ibn Sirin, the accusative of the two (awliyan) is by way of praise.

﴿So the two will swear by God: "Our testimony is more truthful than their testimony, and we have not transgressed﴾; that is, the other two standing in place of the testimony of alteration swear that what they reported is true, and that what we have mentioned of the text of the story is more right than what they first related and altered, and that we have not exceeded the limit. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Our oath is more right than their oath." And whoever says that the testimony at the beginning of the story is not in the sense of the oath, here says "the testimony is an oath," and it was called testimony because the ruling is established by it just as a ruling is established by testimony. Ibn al-Jawzi said: "ahaqqu" is more correct, because of their disbelief and our belief, end of quote.

﴿Indeed, then we would be among the wrongdoers﴾: He concluded with this sentence to disown wrongdoing and to deem it repugnant. The word "wrongdoing" (zulm) is suited here by their saying ﴿and we have not transgressed﴾, and transgression (i'tida') and wrongdoing (zulm) are close in meaning. Concluding what the two witnesses of falsehood swore with His saying ﴿then we would be among the sinners﴾ is suitable, because the non-conformity of their oath with reality, and their concealing of the testimony, draw sin upon them.

﴿That is more suitable that they bring the testimony in its proper form, or fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths﴾; that is, that is the ruling mentioned earlier. Since the two witnesses have two states: a state in which doubt arises about them when they testify, in which case they are detained after the prayer and swear the oath prescribed in the verse; this state is answered by His saying ﴿That is more suitable that they bring the testimony in its proper form﴾, that is, in accordance with what they witnessed truthfully, without denial, alteration or lying. And a state in which it becomes known, when they testify, that they are guilty by the testimony and their lying in the oath; in that case their oaths are not regarded, and the oaths are returned to other witnesses, so their oaths are acted upon, and that is after their swearing and their exposure through the manifestation of their lying; this state is answered by His saying ﴿or fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths﴾. The conjunction used is (aw) because if the truthfulness of the two witnesses is not clear, they are necessarily in one of these two states: either doubt arises about their testimony, or their betrayal is discovered; therefore the conjunction is (aw), which is placed for one of two things or several things. So the meaning is: what has been mentioned of the rulings is closer to the establishment of testimony upon what is fitting, or to fear that oaths will be returned to other people, so their oaths fall and are not accepted. Ibn 'Abbas said: all of that brings closer the uprightness of this category in whatever calamities may befall, because they fear the stringent oath after the prayer, then they fear disgrace and the return of the oath, end of quote. It was said: that refers to the swearing of the two witnesses in the presence of a gathering of people. It was said: to the detention after the prayer only. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this appears from the words of al-Suddi, and it is interpreted on this interpretation as in the sense of your saying: "You love me, O Zayd, or you anger me," as if you said: "otherwise you anger me"; so likewise the meaning of the verse is: "That is more suitable that they bring the testimony in its proper form, otherwise they fear the return of oaths." As for according to the view of Ibn 'Abbas, the meaning is: that whole ruling is closer to their coming (with the testimony), or closer to their fearing, end of quote. Thus it is established that (aw) is either in its own sense, or in the sense of (wa). And (yakhafu) is conjoined in these two cases to (ya'tu), or it is in the sense of (ila an), like your saying: "I will surely stick to you, or you pay me my right," and this is what Ibn 'Atiyya expressed by that phrase earlier, of estimating it as a conditional with an elided verb and its response. When it is in the sense of (ila an), then according to the Basrans it remains in its own sense of being for one of two things. However, the conjunction with it does not occur upon the verb (ya'tu), but upon an implied verbal noun, and that is as established in the science of Arabic grammar. The pronoun in (ya'tu) and what follows is plural, though the antecedent is dual; it was said: it refers to the two witnesses in terms of category and type. It was said: it does not refer to both of them specifically, but to the witnessing people in general, and the sense is: that is more suitable that people avoid betrayal and therefore testify to the truth, out of fear of disgrace through the return of the oath to the claimant.

﴿And fear God and listen﴾; that is, beware of God's punishment, and take a shield from Him by not betraying, not swearing falsely by Him, rendering the trust to its owners, and listening with the listening of acceptance and compliance.

﴿And God does not guide the defiant people﴾: an indication that whoever altered the testimony is a defiant one, outside obedience to God; so God does not guide him unless he repents. The wording is general, and the meaning is the stipulation of the absence of repentance.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 5, verse 109:**

﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the Messengers and say, "What response did you receive?" they will say, "We have no knowledge. Indeed, You are the Knower of the Unseen."﴾

The connection of this verse to what precedes it: when Allah, exalted is He, had informed of the ruling concerning the two witnesses of the bequest, and commanded taqwa (piety, fear of Allah) and listening and obedience, He reminded of this awesome and frightening Day, which is the Day of Resurrection. Thereby He combined the disgrace of this world with the punishment of the Hereafter for the one who distorted the testimony and for the one who did not fear Allah and did not listen.

The scholars have mentioned several possibilities concerning the grammatical case of (يَوْمَ, yawma, "Day"):

The first: it is in the accusative by an implied verb, *udhkuru* (remember).

The second: by an implied *uhdharu* (beware).

The third: by *ittaqu* (fear/be mindful of).

The fourth: by *isma'u* (listen), as stated by al-Hawfi.

The fifth: by *la yahdi* (He does not guide). Some, including al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa', said: He will not guide them on that Day to the path of Paradise. Abu al-Baqa' said: or, He will not guide them on that Day to the proof (argument).

The sixth: al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for the object in His saying ﴿wa-ittaqu Allah﴾ (and fear Allah), and this is the substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), as if it were said: "And fear Allah on the Day of His gathering." However, there is remoteness in this because of the long separation by the two sentences.

The seventh: that it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), and its governing element is postponed; its estimate being: ﴿On the Day when Allah gathers the Messengers﴾ such-and-such occurred. This was stated by al-Zamakhshari.

Ibn 'Atiyya, describing the verse and its eloquence, said: it is rather that this statement is resumptive (mustaʼnaf), and the governing element is *udhkuru* and *uhdharu*, from what is well-abbreviated because the hearer knows it. The reference of "this Day" is to the Day of Resurrection. He singled out the Messengers for mention because they are the leaders of creation, and within their gathering is the gathering of all creatures, and they are the first to be addressed. End of his words.

What we choose, other than what they mentioned, is that (يَوْمَ) be governed by His saying ﴿qalu la 'ilma lana﴾ (they say, "We have no knowledge"), meaning: the Messengers said at the time of their gathering and of Allah's saying to them ﴿ma dha ujibtum﴾ (what response you received). This is the parallel to what we have said regarding His saying ﴿wa-idh qala rabbuka lil-mala'ikati inni ja'ilun fi al-ardi khalifatan qalu ataj'alu﴾ (And when your Lord said to the angels, "I am going to place upon the earth a vicegerent," they said, "Will You place upon it...") [al-Baqarah: 30].

His, exalted is He, questioning them with His saying ﴿ma dha ujibtum﴾ is a question of reproach to their nations, so that the proof may be established against them, and their reckoning may begin, just as the buried infant girl (al-mawuda) was questioned, as a rebuke to her burier and a confrontation with him concerning the evil of his deed.

The accusative of ﴿ma dha ujibtum﴾: if the answer were intended, it would have been said *bi-madha ujibtum* (with what were you answered). This was stated by al-Zamakhshari. The standing of the interrogative *ma* in the place of the verbal noun (masdar) is permissible, and likewise *madha* when you make the whole of it an interrogative. They cited, as evidence for the coming of what has been mentioned as a verbal noun, the saying of the poet:

*"What do you lend my daughter of the lament of the two of them?
They neither sleep, nor is there misery for one who sleeps."*

Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is: "What did the nations respond with?" He did not make *ma* a verbal noun, but made it a metonym for the answer, that is, the thing with which one was answered, not for the verbal noun. This is what al-Zamakhshari meant by his saying: "If the answer were intended, it would have been said *bi-madha ujibtum*."

Al-Hawfi said: *ma* is interrogative, and it is a subject (mubtada') in the sense of *alladhi* (which), its predicate being *ujibtum* as its relative clause, and the estimate: "What were you answered with?" End of his words. The omission of this pronoun governed by the preposition is weak: if you say *ja'ani alladhi marartu* (the one whom I passed came to me), intending by it "who I passed by," it is weak, unless it is considered that the preposition was first omitted, so the pronoun became accusative, then it was omitted in the accusative position. And this is not far-fetched.

Abu al-Baqa' said: *madha* is in the place of the accusative with *ujibtum*, and the preposition is omitted; that is, *bi-madha ujibtum*, and *ma* and *dha* here are like a single noun. It is weak to make *dha* here in the sense of *alladhi*, because there is no returning pronoun here, and omitting the returning pronoun together with the preposition is weak. End of his words. What Abu al-Baqa' mentioned is weaker, because omitting the preposition is not analogical; it has been heard only in specific words, and they stated explicitly that it is not permissible to say *Zaydan marartu bihi* (intending "Zayd I passed by him") meaning "I passed by Zayd," nor *sirtu al-bayt* meaning "I went to the house," except in poetic necessity, like the saying of the poet:

*"She yearns, and displays what is in her of passion,
and I conceal that which, were it not for grief, would have decided me."*

He intends: "would have decided against me." So he omitted *ʿalayya* and made the verb reach the pronoun, putting it in the accusative.

Their denial of knowledge by His saying ﴿la 'ilma lana﴾ (we have no knowledge): Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is, "We have no knowledge except a knowledge which You know better than we do." It is as if the meaning were: "We have no knowledge that suffices and reaches the ultimate end."

Ibn Juraij said: the meaning of ﴿ma dha ujibtum﴾ is "what did they do after you, and what did they introduce?" Therefore they said, "We have no knowledge." This is supported by ﴿innaka anta 'Allamu al-ghuyub﴾ (indeed You are the Knower of the Unseen). However, the wording *ma dha ujibtum* recoils from being explained by "what did they do."

The exegetes mentioned, from al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Suddi and Sahl al-Tustari, sayings concerning the explanation of their words ﴿la 'ilma lana﴾ that are not appropriate to the Messengers, so we turn away from mentioning them altogether.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How can they say 'we have no knowledge' when they know what response they were given?" I answer: They know that the purpose of the question is the reproach of their enemies, so they leave the matter to His knowledge and His encompassing of what they were tested with from them. That is greater upon the disbelievers, more weakening to their resolve, more conducive to their regret and their collapse (suqut fi aydihim), when Allah's reproach and their prophets' complaint about them are combined.
