An example of this: one of the Kharijites rebukes the sultan, specifically one of his close companions, with a rebuke of which the sultan is aware, and he knows its reality and resolves to avenge himself upon him; so he brings the two together and says to him: "What did this Kharijite do to you?" while he knows what was done to him, intending his rebuke and humiliation. Then he says: "You know best what he did to me," delegating the matter to the knowledge of his sultan, relying upon him, displaying his complaint, and magnifying what befell him. End of his words.

The verse is not like this example he mentioned, because in the verse ﴿la 'ilma lana﴾ is a negation of all individual instances of knowledge from them with respect to the answer. In the example: "You know best what he did to me" does not negate knowledge from him; it only affirms for his sultan that he knows more about the Kharijite than he does.

Ibn Abi al-Fadl said concerning al-Zamakhshari's words: "It is not strong, because the question was addressed to the whole nation, and the whole nation were not all disbelievers, such that the Messenger would intend their reproach." It was said: its meaning is: "Our knowledge is fallen and submerged in Your knowledge, because You are the Knower of the Unseen, and whoever knows the hidden things, the apparent things by which the responses of the nations to their messengers are known are not concealed from Him. So it is as if we have no knowledge except beside Your knowledge." Al-Zamakhshari related this with this wording. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning in brief.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: the saying of Ibn 'Abbas is more correct, because it is preferred by submission to Allah, exalted is He, and returning the matter to Him, since they know only what they were witnessed in during their lifetimes, and what is in the hearts of those who witnessed them of hypocrisy and the like is hidden from them, as is what came after them of their nations; but Allah, exalted is He, knows all of that in full detail and completeness. So they saw fit to submit to Him and to humble themselves before His encompassing knowledge. End of his words.

It was also said: "We have no knowledge of what came after us, and the judgment belongs to the final outcome." Al-Zamakhshari said: "And how could their condition be hidden from them, when they saw them with black faces and blue eyes, rebuked?" End of his words.

Ibn Abi al-Fadl said: "The most correct is what Ibn 'Abbas chose; that is, You know what they displayed and what they concealed, while we know only what they displayed. So Your knowledge of them is more penetrating than our knowledge." With this meaning they negated knowledge from themselves, because their knowledge in the sight of Allah is as no knowledge. End of his words.

Thus, it would be among those in which the reality is negated apparently, while the intended meaning is the negation of perfection, as if he said: "We have no perfect knowledge," just as one says: "There is no man in the house," meaning: no man perfect in manhood in his strength and penetration.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: it is established in the science of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that knowledge is one thing, and conjecture (zann) is another, and what is attained by any person concerning others is only conjecture, not knowledge. For this reason the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "We judge by outward appearances, and Allah takes charge of the inner secrets." And he, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, you bring your disputes before me..." (the hadith). And the Prophets said, "We have no knowledge at all of their conditions; what is attained by us of their conditions is only conjecture." Conjecture was valid in this world, because the rulings in this world were based on conjectures. As for the Hereafter, there is no regard for conjecture in it, because the rulings are based on the realities of things and the inner truths of matters. For this reason they said, "We have no knowledge," and they did not mention at all what conjecture they had, because conjecture has no weight on the Day of Resurrection. End of his words.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "We have no knowledge of Your question, and no answer to it for us."

Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Haywa read ﴿ma dha ujibtum﴾ with the verb in the active voice (ajabtum). And he read ﴿'Allam﴾ in the accusative, and this is by omitting the predicate for understanding of the meaning, so the sentence is completed by what is estimated in His saying ﴿innaka anta﴾, that is: "Indeed You are the One described with Your well-known attributes, of knowledge and others."

Al-Zamakhshari said: Then ﴿'Allamu al-ghuyub﴾ was put in the accusative by specification (ikhtisas), or by vocative address (nida'), or as an adjective of the noun (inna). End of his words. This last possibility is not permissible, because they unanimously agreed that the pronoun of the speaker and the pronoun of the addressee cannot be described by an adjective. As for the third-person pronoun, there is an anomalous disagreement from al-Kisa'i.

Hamza and Abu Bakr read ﴿al-Ghiyub﴾ with a kasra on the ghayn wherever it occurs, as if whoever among the Arabs said this found the succession of two damma with the ya' heavy, so he fled to a vowel different from the damma, suitable to the adjacency of the ya', and that is the kasra.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 110–114 (part 1 of 3):

﴿When God said: "O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My favour upon you and upon your mother."﴾ It is possible that (idh) is a substitute (badal) for His saying: ﴿the Day when God will gather the Messengers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109]. The meaning is that on that Day He will rebuke the disbelievers by questioning the Messengers about their response, and by the multitude of great signs that were manifested at their hands; yet they denied them, called them sorcerers, and went beyond the bounds of belief to the point of taking them as gods, just as some of the Children of Israel said regarding the clear signs that appeared at the hand of Jesus: ﴿This is manifest sorcery﴾ [al-Naml: 13]. Some of them took him and his mother as two gods; this was said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that the governing element (al-'amil) in (idh) is an implied verb, its estimate being: "Remember, O Muhammad," and (qala) here means (yaqulu), because the apparent sense of this speech is that it takes place on the Resurrection, as a preface to His saying: ﴿Did you say to the people...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. It is also possible that (idh) is a substitute for His saying: ﴿the Day when God gathers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109], end of quotation. They also permitted that (idh) be in the position of the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "That is when God said..."

When the vocative is a single proper noun, with an apparent damma, qualified by "ibn" connected and idafa to a proper noun, it is permissible to make it fatha, following the fatha of "ibn"; this is the view of the majority (al-Jumhur). Al-Farra' permitted, and Abu al-Baqa' followed him, in the case where the damma and fatha cannot be shown; if you do not make ﴿Ibn Maryam﴾ a qualifier, but make it a substitute or a vocative, then for that proper noun only the damma is permissible. Some commentators and some of those who belong to grammar have confused the matter here: some commentators said: "It is permissible for (Isa) to be in the nominative position, since it is a definite vocative not in idafa, and it is permissible for it to be in the accusative position, since it is intended as an idafa, and then 'ibn' was made an emphatic (tawkid); everything like this may take either of the two forms, such as: O Zayd son of 'Amr." The grammarians recited:

> O Hakam son of al-Mundhir son of al-Jarud, you are the generous son of the generous, son of generosity.

Al-Tabrizi said: "The more evident to me is that the position of (Isa) is accusative, because you treat the name together with its qualifier, when you make it an idafa to a proper noun, as a single thing made idafa." The rule that the grammarians stated for such as "O Zayd son of Bakr," when you put a fatha on the final of the vocative, is that it is a vowel of following (harakat ittiba') for the vowel of the "n" of "ibn"; the quiescence of the "ba'" of "ibn" was not counted, since the quiescent letter is a weak barrier.

They said: the remembrance here may be intended as acknowledgment (al-iqrar), and it may be intended as informing (al-i'lam). The benefit of this remembrance is to make the nations hear what He specially bestowed upon him of honour, and to confirm His proof against his denier. It was said: he was commanded to remember in order to alert others to recognising the due of a favour and the obligation of thanking the benefactor. Al-Hasan said: "Remembering a favour is thanking for it." The favour here is a genus, and what supports this is what He enumerated after this verbal unity, of favours, and their being attributed to him, as an alert to their magnitude. His favours upon him He enumerated here, in al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran and Maryam, and in other places in the Qur'an. His favour upon his mother: her innocence of what was attributed to her, her being entrusted to Zakariyya, her being accepted with a good acceptance, and what is mentioned in Surat al-Tahrim (﴿and Maryam daughter of 'Imran﴾) to its end, and other things. He was commanded to remember the favour upon his mother because it is a favour that reaches him.

﴿when I supported you with the Holy Spirit﴾ Al-Jumhur read (ayyadtuka) with a shaddah on the ya'. Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin read (ayadtuka) on the pattern of (af'altuka). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "On the pattern of (fa'altuka)," then he said: "It appears that the original in both readings is (ayyadtuka), on the pattern of (af'altuka), then the i'lal (morphological alteration) differed; and the meaning in both is (ayyadtuka), from al-ayad (strength)." 'Abd al-Muttalib said:

> Praise be to God, the Mightiest, the Most Noble, who strengthened us on the day of the crowding of al-Ashram.

End of quotation. What appears is that (ayyada), in the reading of the majority, is not of the pattern af'ala, because its present tense comes as yu'ayyidu, so the pattern is fa''ala; if it were af'ala, its present would be yu'ayyidu like the present of amana, yu'minu. As for the one who reads (ayada), he needs to transmit its present from the speech of the Arabs: if it is yu'ayidu, then it is (fa'ala), and if it is (yu'ayyidu), then it is (af'ala). As for Ibn 'Atiyyah's statement that it appears in both readings that its pattern is af'altuka, then the i'lal differed, I do not understand what he meant. The explanation of the parallel of this clause has already been given in His saying ﴿and We supported him with the Holy Spirit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 87].

﴿you speak to people in the cradle and in maturity﴾ ﴿and when I taught you the Book and wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel, and when you create from clay the likeness of a bird by My leave, then you breathe into it and it becomes a bird by My leave, and you heal the blind and the leper by My leave, and when you bring forth the dead by My leave.﴾

The explanation of the parallel of these clauses and the readings in them, and the grammar, and what has not been mentioned earlier, we will mention, so we say: there it came as ﴿like the form of a bird by My leave, then you breathe into it and it becomes﴾ (Al 'Imran: 49). Ibn 'Abbas read ﴿fatanfukhuha fatakunu﴾ (you breathe into it). Al-Jumhur read (fatakunu) with a ta' from above. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read (fihi fayakunu), with a ya' from below, and the pronoun in (fihi). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The commentators have been confused about it." Makki said: "In Al 'Imran it refers to the bird, and here to the form," and he said: "The reverse is also valid." Others said: the pronoun mentioned refers to (clay). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is not valid for this pronoun to refer either to the clay or to the form, because the bird, or the bird whose form is like a bird's, has no breathing in it at all; likewise there is no breathing in its specific form; likewise the clay is general clay, and there is no breathing in that," end of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Part of the pronoun does not return to the form to which it is idafa, because it is not part of His creation, nor the breathing into anything; likewise the pronoun in (yakunu)," end of quotation. What should be taken as the meaning of Makki's words is that he does not intend what was understood from them; rather his saying "returns" refers to the bird, not the bird that is idafa to the form, but the bird that 'Isa fashioned, and the sense is: "And when you create from clay a bird, a form like the form of the real bird, and you breathe into it, and it becomes a real bird, by God's leave." And his saying "returns to the form" means not the form idafa to the bird, but the form in which the kaf is a qualifier, and the sense is: "And when you create from clay a form like the form of a bird, then you breathe into it," i.e., into the form described by the kaf, the creation of which is attributed to 'Isa. As for Makki's words, "and the reverse is valid," that is, the masculine pronoun referring to the form and the feminine pronoun referring to the bird, it may be explained as: the pronoun was masculinised though it refers to a feminine noun, because the sense of shape was observed in it, as if he had estimated a form like the form of a bird by his saying "a shape like the form of a bird." And the pronoun was feminised though it refers to a masculine noun, because the sense of form was observed in it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The proper course is that the feminine pronoun refers to what the verse necessarily requires, namely forms, or shapes, or bodies, and that the masculine pronoun refers to the created thing required by (you create)." Then he said: "You may also refer it to what the kaf indicates in the sense of likeness, because the meaning is: 'and when you create from clay the likeness of a form.' You may also refer the pronoun to the kaf itself, so that it is a noun outside poetry; this is the view of Abu al-Hasan alone among the Basrans." Likewise al-Zamakhshari said: the pronoun in (fihi) refers to the kaf, and said: "because it is the description of the form which 'Isa used to create and breathe into."

In Al 'Imran there is ﴿by God's leave﴾ (Al 'Imran: 49) twice, and here (bi-idhni) appears four times, after four clauses, because this is the place of mentioning the favour and bestowing it, so extended exposition is fitting; there is the place of informing the Children of Israel, so brevity is fitting. The estimate in ﴿and when you bring forth the dead﴾ is: "you give life to the dead," so he expressed giving life by bringing forth, like His saying: ﴿Thus is the coming forth﴾ [Qaf: 11] after His saying: ﴿and We revive therewith a dead land﴾ [Qaf: 11]; or the estimate is: "and when you bring forth the dead from their graves, living."

﴿And when I restrained the Children of Israel from you, when you came to them with the clear signs﴾ That is, I prevented them from killing you when they intended to harm you and surrounded the house in which you were. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: When God said to 'Isa: ﴿Remember My favour upon you﴾, he used to wear hair cloth, eat the leaves of trees, and did not store anything for the morrow, saying with each day "its sustenance"; he had no house to be ruined, nor a child to die; wherever night fell, he slept. This saying shows that 'Isa was addressed with that before the Raising. The clear signs here are the miracles already mentioned, which appeared at his hands. When He detailed His favour, He mentioned that attributed to 'Isa and not to his mother, because among these favours is the favour of prophethood and the manifestation of these extraordinary acts; so His favour upon him is greater than upon his mother, in that she bore such a noble prophet. A poet said regarding something like this:

> The worlds bear witness that she is precious, by the evidence of what she bore of noble ones.

﴿Then those of them who disbelieved said: "This is nothing but manifest sorcery."﴾ Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (sahir), with the alif, here, and in Hud and al-Saff; so "this" here refers to 'Isa. The rest of the seven read (sihr), so "this" refers to what 'Isa brought of the clear signs.

﴿And when I inspired the disciples: "Believe in Me and My Messenger."﴾ That is, I inspired them through the tongues of the messengers. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is either inspiration of inspiration (ilham) or inspiration of command. The Messenger here is 'Isa, and this inspiration to the disciples is among God's favours upon 'Isa, in that He made for him followers who affirm him and act upon what he brought. It is possible that it is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), since a clause having the sense of speech precedes it, and that it is verbal-masdar (masdariyyah).

﴿They said: "We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾ The explanation of the parallel of this clause has been given in Al 'Imran, except that there it is (amanna billah, "we believed in God"), because God alone had been mentioned in His saying: ﴿Who are my helpers in God? The disciples said: We are the helpers of God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 52]; here it came as (qalu amanna), without being restricted to the word of majesty, since it has already been mentioned (that they should believe in Me and My Messenger). There it came as ﴿and bear witness that we﴾ (Al 'Imran: 52), and here ﴿and bear witness that we﴾ (with the nun). This is the original, since the nun of (anna) is elided because of the gathering of like letters.

﴿Idh qāla al-ḥawāriyyūna yā ʿĪsā ibna Maryama hal yastaṭīʿu rabbuka an yunazzila ʿalaynā māʾidatan mina al-samāʾi qāla ittaqū Allāha in kuntum muʾminīn﴾ [When the disciples said, "O ʿIsa son of Maryam, can your Lord send down to us a table from the heaven?" He said, "Fear Allah, if you are believers."]. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: ﴿Idh qāla al-ḥawāriyyūna﴾ is an interjected clause (iʿtirāḍ) inserted into the description of the condition of the people of Allah's ʿIsa on the Day of Resurrection, and this interjection contains an announcement to Muhammad and his community about the incident of the disciples with the table, since it is a beneficial example for every community with its prophet, end quote. What the apparent wording requires is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Idh qāla Allāh yā ʿĪsā ibna Maryam udhkur niʿmatī ʿalayka﴾ [When Allah said, "O ʿIsa son of Maryam, remember My favour upon you"], up to the end of the story of the table, took place in this world. He reminded ʿIsa of His blessings and of the miracles He had brought about through his hands, and of the disagreement of the Children of Israel concerning him and their division into disbelievers and believers, and the believers were the disciples. Then it digressed to the story of the table, and then to His exalted question to ʿIsa, ﴿Did you say to the people﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 116]. Some scholars took it that this refers to the Hereafter because they believed that (idh) is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the Day when Allah will gather the messengers﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 109], and that at the end of the verses there is ﴿This is a day on which the truthful will benefit﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 119]. This interpretation is not required, as we will explain, Allah willing, in His saying ﴿This is a day on which will benefit﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 119]; rather, the apparent meaning is what we have mentioned.

Al-Jumhūr [the majority of reciters] read ﴿hal yastaṭīʿu rabbuka﴾ with the yāʾ and with a ḍammah on the bāʾ. The apparent meaning of this wording requires doubt about Allah's power to send down a table from the heaven, and this is what led al-Zamakhsharī to hold that the disciples were not believers. He said: If you ask, how could they say "Can your Lord?" after their faith and sincerity? I answer: Allah did not describe them as having faith and sincerity; rather, He related their claim to them, and then followed it with His saying (idh qālū), which indicates that their claim was false and that they were doubters. His saying ﴿hal yastaṭīʿu rabbuka﴾ is a statement that would not come from believers who revere their Lord. For this reason, ʿIsa's saying to them means: Fear Allah, and do not doubt His power and ability, and do not make demands upon Him, and do not prescribe for Him the signs you desire, lest you perish if you disobey Him after them.

﴿In kuntum muʾminīn﴾ means: if your claim of faith is sound, end quote. As for other than al-Zamakhsharī among the people of tafsīr (exegesis), they agreed that the disciples were believers, to the point that Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: I know of no disagreement that the disciples were believers. Some said: The disciples said this statement at the beginning of the matter, before they knew that he would heal the blind and the leper and bring the dead to life. The exegetes said: The disciples were the special companions of ʿIsa, and they were believers, and they did not doubt Allah's power over that. Ibn al-Anbārī said: It is not permissible for anyone to imagine that the disciples doubted Allah's power; rather, this is like a person saying to his companion, "Can you stand with me?" while he knows that the other is able to do so, but he means, "Is it easy for you?" end quote. Al-Fārisī said: Its meaning is, "Will He do that upon your request?" Al-Ḥasan said: They did not doubt Allah's power; rather, they asked him as an inquirer: Will He send it down or not? If He sends it down, then ask Him for us. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: Will He, exalted is He, do this, and will He grant them a response to it? Just as one says to ʿAbdullāh ibn Zayd: "Can you show me how the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed ablution?" So the meaning is, "Does He wish that, and will He do it?" end quote.

It was also said: The purpose of this statement is the question whether that is permissible or not. This is because His acts are contingent upon the aspects of wisdom; if none of the aspects of wisdom is realized, the act is impossible, since what contradicts the aspects of wisdom is like what contradicts the aspects of power. Abū ʿAbdullāh al-Rāzī said: This answer proceeds according to the view of the Muʿtazila. As for our school, it is taken to mean: Has He, exalted is He, decreed that? And has He known its occurrence? For if He has not decreed it and knows its occurrence, it would be impossible and not within the scope of power, since the opposite of what is known is not within the scope of power. He also said: The purpose of this statement is not that they were doubters concerning it; rather, the purpose is to establish that this matter is in the utmost clarity, like a person who takes the hand of a weak man and says, "Can the sultan provide for this one?" and his aim is that this is an evident matter about which a reasonable person may not doubt. Some were far off in saying: "Will your Lord send down a table from the heaven?" with (yastaṭīʿu) being a connective (ṣila). Others said: "The Lord" here is Jibrīl, because he used to nurture ʿIsa and favour him with various kinds of help, and for this reason, at the beginning of the verse, He said ﴿when I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 110].

It is related that what led them to this course of demand was that ʿIsa once said to them: "Would you like to fast thirty days for Allah, exalted is He, and then if you ask Him for a need, He will fulfil it?" When they had fasted them, they said: "O teacher of good! Indeed, it is the right of one who performs a deed to be fed, so can your Lord?" They wanted the table to be a feast (ʿīd) for that fast. Al-Kisāʾī read ﴿hal tastaṭīʿu rabbaka﴾ with a tāʾ at the beginning and a fatḥah on the bāʾ of (rabbaka), and this is the reading of ʿAlī, Muʿādh, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿĀʾishah and Ibn Jubayr. ʿĀʾishah said: The disciples were more knowledgeable of Allah than to say ﴿Can your Lord?﴾. She exonerated them from the offensiveness of the wording and from its apparent meaning. We have already mentioned the interpretations of this, and the meaning of this reading is: Are you able to ask your Lord? ﴿An yunazzila﴾ is an object of an omitted verb "ask" (suʾāl), since it is an omission without which the meaning is not complete. Abū ʿAlī said: It is possible to dispense with estimating a verb of asking, so that the meaning is: Are you able that your Lord send down by your supplication? Then the meaning becomes, but there must be an estimated element indicated by what is mentioned in the wording, end quote. What Abū ʿAlī said does not appear correct, because the act of Allah, exalted is He, even if its cause is supplication, is not within the power of ʿIsa.

Al-Kisāʾī assimilated the lām of (hal) into the yāʾ of (yastaṭīʿu). On this reading, ʿIsa's saying ﴿Fear Allah, if you are believers﴾ does not deny them the request for signs. In both readings, His saying ﴿if you are believers﴾ is an affirmation of faith, just as you say, "Do this and that, if you are a man."

Muqātil and a group said: Fear Him lest you ask Him for trial, because if it descends and you deny, you will be punished. Abū ʿUbayd and a group said: Lest you ask Him for what the nations before you did not ask. It was also said: Lest you doubt His power to send down the table. It was also said: Fear Allah regarding doubt about Him, and about His messengers and their signs. It was also said: Fear the disobedience of Allah. It was also said: He commanded them to piety so that it would be a cause for the attainment of this sought matter, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 2].

Al-Zamakhsharī said: Here, (ʿĪsā) is in the accusative position by following its vowel to the vowel of (ibn), as in your saying, "O Zayd son of ʿAmr!" and this is the prevalent dialect. It may also be in the nominative, as in your saying, "O Zayd son of ʿAmr!" and the proof of this is his saying: "Ḥār son of ʿUmar, it is as if I am wine," because truncation (tarkhīm) occurs only with the nominative, end quote. His saying "ʿĪsā is in the accusative position on this estimate" and on the estimate of its nominative, there is no exclusivity to its being in the accusative position on the estimate of following; so its corrected form, ʿĪsā, has an estimated fatḥah by following the vowel. His saying "it may also be nominative" is the view of al-Farrāʾ, and it is the estimate of fatḥah and ḍammah, and similar to it in what the ḍammah does not show, by analogy with the sound. He did not begin first with the ḍammah, which is agreed upon as an estimate. This is not a condition: do you not see the permissibility of truncating a man whose name is Muthannā, so that you say, "O Muthann, come!" and the permissibility of truncating Baʿlabakk, which is built on fatḥah, but it is in the estimate of the nominative noun. If he meant an estimated ḍammah, then this is fine; but if he meant an apparent ḍammah, this is not a condition. Do you not see the permissibility of truncating a man whose name is Muthannā, so that you say, "O Muthann"? For like "O Jaʿfar son of Zayd," that which has the final letter of the vocative pronounced with fatḥah for the sake of following is estimated with a ḍammah, because the letter is occupied by the vowel of following. Just as the Aʿrābī [the grammarian] estimated, in the reading of one who read (al-ḥamdi lillāh) with a kasrah on the dāl, for the sake of following the vowel of (lillāh), so your saying "O Ḥār!" is nominative by estimate, and even if the deleted thāʾ was originally occupied by the vowel of following, which is fatḥah, there is no contradiction between truncation and what was made fatḥah by following, while the ḍammah was estimated in it.

It was necessary for al-Zamakhsharī to speak on this question before this point, at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿When Allah said, "O ʿIsa son of Maryam, remember My favour upon you"﴾, where people spoke about it.

﴿They said: "We wish to eat from it, and that our hearts may be reassured, and that we may know that you have spoken the truth to us, and that we may be among its witnesses."﴾ When Jesus commanded them to fear God, disapproving of what they had said earlier, they stated the reason for asking for the table spread (al-ma'idah), namely that they wished to eat from it. This was for the sake of honour, not for satisfaction of hunger. Their hearts would be reassured, with thought at rest, once they witnessed this great miraculous sign descending from heaven, and once necessary knowledge and direct observation of its truth were established. Thus the doubts that arise in inferential reasoning would not trouble them. "Among its witnesses" means either that they would be among those who observe this sign, who transmit it to others and uphold this law, or among those who bear witness to God's oneness and to your prophethood. Some exegetes (mufassirun) elaborated at length on the objects of their wish, but in summary they wished to eat because of need and intense hunger. Ibn Abbas said: "When he went out, five thousand or more followed him, including a companion, one who was ill seeking cure, and a mocker. One day they found themselves in a desert without provisions. They became hungry, and they asked the disciples (al-hawariyyun) to ask Jesus to send down a table from heaven. Shim'un (Simon) told Jesus this, and he said: 'Tell them: fear God.' They wished to eat so that their faith would increase." Ibn al-Anbari said: "Or the honour of the table," as mentioned by al-Mawardi. Reassurance (al-itmi'nan) is either because God has sent you to us, or has chosen us as your helpers, or has answered you, or knowledge of the truth that if we fast for God thirty days, we will not ask God for anything without Him giving it to us, or [knowledge] that you are truly a Messenger, since a miracle is evidence of truth. Before that they had not seen signs. Or what is meant by knowledge is necessary knowledge and direct observation. End of quotation. These connected clauses are arranged in a subtle order. They would not eat from it except after witnessing its descent, so sight and taste combine to produce knowledge of it. Thereby the anxiety of disturbance leaves the heart, and it settles upon what a person has witnessed and tasted. With the reassurance of the heart, necessary knowledge of the truthfulness of the one through whose hands the miracle came is attained, since it came exactly as they asked. They asked for this great miracle, because its effect in the upper world through the supplication of one who is in the lower world is stronger and more wondrous than the effect of one who is in the lower world within his own lower world. Do you not see that among the greatest miracles of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) are the Qur'an and the splitting of the moon, both of which belong to the upper world? When necessary knowledge of Jesus's truthfulness was attained, they bore witness with certainty, with no doubt, suspicion or illusion stirring in it. By mentioning these causes that prompted the request for the table, the view of one who said is preferred: their request was made before they knew of Jesus's signs and miracles, and God's revelation to them to believe was at the beginning of the matter. At that point they said this statement, then they believed, saw the signs, persisted and were patient. Ibn Jubayr read (ونُعْلَمَ) with a damma on the nun, in the passive voice. This is likewise in the book al-Tahrir wa'l-Tahbir and in the book of Ibn Attiyah. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read (ويُعْلَمَ) with a damma on the ya', and the pronoun refers to the hearts. In the book of al-Zamakhshari, it is (ويُعْلَمَ) with ya' in the passive. Al-A'mash read (وتَعْلَمَ) with a ta', meaning "and the hearts will know it." The majority read (ونَكُونَ) with a nun. In the book al-Tahrir wa'l-Tahbir. Sinan and Isa read (وتَكُونَ عَلَيْها) with a ta'. In al-Zamakhshari. Their claim was made for the purpose of what they mentioned, like their claim to faith and sincerity. Jesus only asked, and was answered, so that they would be bound by the full proof, and so that punishment would be sent upon them if they disobeyed. End of quotation. He said this because the disciples were not believers in his view. When the light (mukhaffafah) form of (أنْ) is followed by a verb that is inflected for tense and not a supplication, if it is in the past tense, it is separated from it by (قَدْ), as in His saying (ونَعْلَمَ أنْ قَدْ صَدَقْتَنا). If it is in the present tense, it is separated by a future particle, as in His saying ﴿He knows that there will be among you those who are ill﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. It does not occur without a separator, though it is said: except rarely. It is also said: except out of necessity. As for what (عَلَيْها) is connected to, which was mentioned earlier in such expressions as ﴿Indeed, I am for you both among the sincere advisers﴾ [al-A'raf: 21]: al-Zamakhshari said: "devoted to it" (ʿakifina ʿalayha), on the basis that (عَلَيْها) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). This estimation is not good, because the governing verb of a prepositional phrase is not obligatorily omitted unless it is a general state of being, not a specific one, and devotion (al-ʿukuf) is a specific state. Also, when the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause, the governing word for it would be the implied (ʿakifina). We have already said that this is not good. Furthermore, al-Zamakhshari's statement is inconsistent, because if what (عَلَيْها) is connected to is ʿakifina, it would be in the accusative position as the object to which the verb extended by means of the preposition, but if it is in the circumstantial position, the governing word for it is a general state of being that must be omitted. So the contradiction between them is evident.

﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O God, our Lord, send down to us a table from heaven, which will be a festival for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You. And provide for us, for You are the best of providers."﴾ It is related that Jesus wore a garment of hair and a cloak of hair, and he stood praying, weeping and supplicating. The discussion of the word (اللَّهُمَّ) was given in Al ʿImran. He called upon his Lord first by the Name that no one shares, then secondly with the word (رَبَّنا), which is a correspondence to our reformer, nurturer and owner. The majority read ﴿will be for us﴾ as a clause describing "table." ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) and al-A'mash read (يَكُنْ) in the jussive, as a response to the imperative. The meaning is: "Let the day of its descent be a festival," and this is the day of Sunday, and for this reason the Christians took it as a festival. It was said that festival (ʿid) means joy and happiness, and for this reason one says "a day of festival." So the meaning is "it will be for us joy and happiness." A festival is a gathering on a day that is witnessed. Its customary usage is to say it of what recurs with the year, the month, the week, or similar. It was said: ʿid linguistically is whatever returns to you of something at a known time, whether it be joy or sorrow, and the customary usage overtook the linguistic meaning. Al-Khalil said: ʿid is every day that gathers people, because they return to it. Ibn Abbas said: "For the first of us" means for the people of our time, and "the last of us" means those who come after us. It was said: "the first of us" means our predecessors and leaders, and "the last of us" means the followers. The words "first" and "last" can carry the meanings of food, time or rank, but the apparent meaning is time. Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Jahdari read (لِأُولانا وأُخْرانا), with feminine forms, in the sense of the community and the group. The genitive noun is an apposition to "for us," and the governing preposition is repeated, as in His saying ﴿from it, from distress﴾ [al-Hajj: 22]. An apposition from a first- or second-person pronoun, when it is a partial apposition (badal al-ba'd) or an apposition of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), is permitted without disagreement. If it is an apposition of one thing from another where both refer to one entity, then if it conveys the sense of emphasis it is permitted for this apposition, since the meaning is "it will be a festival for all of us," like your saying: "I passed by you, your elders and your youngsters," because the meaning is "I passed by all of you." If it does not convey emphasis, then it is a matter of disagreement: al-Akhfash permits it, while other Basran grammarians prohibit it. The meaning of ﴿and a sign from You﴾ is a witnessing evidence of the truthfulness of Your servant. It was also said: a proof, and an indication of the perfection of Your power. Al-Yamani read (وأنَّهُ مِنكَ), and the pronoun in (وأنَّهُ) refers either to the festival or to the descent. (And provide for us) it was said: the table; it was also said: thankfulness for Your blessing. ﴿And You are the best of providers﴾, because You are the Rich, the Praiseworthy, who begins with provision. Abu Abd Allah al-Razi said: Reflect on this order. When the disciples asked for the table, they mentioned in their request several aims: they put mention of eating first and delayed the spiritual religious aims. Jesus requested the table and mentioned his aims: he put religious aims first and delayed the aims of eating, where he said (وارْزُقْنا). At this point there becomes apparent to you the levels of the ranks of souls, with some being spiritual and some corporeal. Then Jesus, peace be upon him, because of the intensity of the purity of his time and the illumination of his spirit, when he mentioned provision with the words (وارْزُقْنا), did not stop at it, but passed from the provision to the Provider, saying: ﴿And You are the best of providers﴾. His saying "Our Lord" is an opening from him with the call to the Truth, glorified and exalted be He. His saying ﴿send down to us a table﴾ is a transition from the Essence to the Attributes. His saying ﴿which will be a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾ is an indication of the spirit's joy in the blessing, not insofar as it is a blessing, but insofar as it proceeds from the Bestower. His saying ﴿and a sign from You﴾ is an indication of the portion of the soul. All of this descended from the presence of majesty. So observe how he began with the most noble, then the more noble, descending to the lower, then the lowest.

﴿And You are the best of providers﴾ is an ascent once more from the basest to the most noble. At this point there appears to you the aspiration concerning the manner of the ascent of luminous, divinely radiant spirits and their descent. O God, make us among its people. This is a discourse that lies between a philosophical term and a Sufi term, and both are far from the speech of the Arabs and their modes.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 110–114 (part 1 of 3):

﴿When God said: "O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My favour upon you and upon your mother."﴾ It is possible that (idh) is a substitute (badal) for His saying: ﴿the Day when God will gather the Messengers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109]. The meaning is that on that Day He will rebuke the disbelievers by questioning the Messengers about their response, and by the multitude of great signs that were manifested at their hands; yet they denied them, called them sorcerers, and went beyond the bounds of belief to the point of taking them as gods, just as some of the Children of Israel said regarding the clear signs that appeared at the hand of Jesus: ﴿This is manifest sorcery﴾ [al-Naml: 13]. Some of them took him and his mother as two gods; this was said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that the governing element (al-'amil) in (idh) is an implied verb, its estimate being: "Remember, O Muhammad," and (qala) here means (yaqulu), because the apparent sense of this speech is that it takes place on the Resurrection, as a preface to His saying: ﴿Did you say to the people...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. It is also possible that (idh) is a substitute for His saying: ﴿the Day when God gathers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109], end of quotation. They also permitted that (idh) be in the position of the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "That is when God said..."

When the vocative is a single proper noun, with an apparent damma, qualified by "ibn" connected and idafa to a proper noun, it is permissible to make it fatha, following the fatha of "ibn"; this is the view of the majority (al-Jumhur). Al-Farra' permitted, and Abu al-Baqa' followed him, in the case where the damma and fatha cannot be shown; if you do not make ﴿Ibn Maryam﴾ a qualifier, but make it a substitute or a vocative, then for that proper noun only the damma is permissible. Some commentators and some of those who belong to grammar have confused the matter here: some commentators said: "It is permissible for (Isa) to be in the nominative position, since it is a definite vocative not in idafa, and it is permissible for it to be in the accusative position, since it is intended as an idafa, and then 'ibn' was made an emphatic (tawkid); everything like this may take either of the two forms, such as: O Zayd son of 'Amr." The grammarians recited:

> O Hakam son of al-Mundhir son of al-Jarud, you are the generous son of the generous, son of generosity.

Al-Tabrizi said: "The more evident to me is that the position of (Isa) is accusative, because you treat the name together with its qualifier, when you make it an idafa to a proper noun, as a single thing made idafa." The rule that the grammarians stated for such as "O Zayd son of Bakr," when you put a fatha on the final of the vocative, is that it is a vowel of following (harakat ittiba') for the vowel of the "n" of "ibn"; the quiescence of the "ba'" of "ibn" was not counted, since the quiescent letter is a weak barrier.

They said: the remembrance here may be intended as acknowledgment (al-iqrar), and it may be intended as informing (al-i'lam). The benefit of this remembrance is to make the nations hear what He specially bestowed upon him of honour, and to confirm His proof against his denier. It was said: he was commanded to remember in order to alert others to recognising the due of a favour and the obligation of thanking the benefactor. Al-Hasan said: "Remembering a favour is thanking for it." The favour here is a genus, and what supports this is what He enumerated after this verbal unity, of favours, and their being attributed to him, as an alert to their magnitude. His favours upon him He enumerated here, in al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran and Maryam, and in other places in the Qur'an. His favour upon his mother: her innocence of what was attributed to her, her being entrusted to Zakariyya, her being accepted with a good acceptance, and what is mentioned in Surat al-Tahrim (﴿and Maryam daughter of 'Imran﴾) to its end, and other things. He was commanded to remember the favour upon his mother because it is a favour that reaches him.

﴿when I supported you with the Holy Spirit﴾ Al-Jumhur read (ayyadtuka) with a shaddah on the ya'. Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin read (ayadtuka) on the pattern of (af'altuka). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "On the pattern of (fa'altuka)," then he said: "It appears that the original in both readings is (ayyadtuka), on the pattern of (af'altuka), then the i'lal (morphological alteration) differed; and the meaning in both is (ayyadtuka), from al-ayad (strength)." 'Abd al-Muttalib said:

> Praise be to God, the Mightiest, the Most Noble, who strengthened us on the day of the crowding of al-Ashram.

End of quotation. What appears is that (ayyada), in the reading of the majority, is not of the pattern af'ala, because its present tense comes as yu'ayyidu, so the pattern is fa''ala; if it were af'ala, its present would be yu'ayyidu like the present of amana, yu'minu. As for the one who reads (ayada), he needs to transmit its present from the speech of the Arabs: if it is yu'ayidu, then it is (fa'ala), and if it is (yu'ayyidu), then it is (af'ala). As for Ibn 'Atiyyah's statement that it appears in both readings that its pattern is af'altuka, then the i'lal differed, I do not understand what he meant. The explanation of the parallel of this clause has already been given in His saying ﴿and We supported him with the Holy Spirit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 87].

﴿you speak to people in the cradle and in maturity﴾ ﴿and when I taught you the Book and wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel, and when you create from clay the likeness of a bird by My leave, then you breathe into it and it becomes a bird by My leave, and you heal the blind and the leper by My leave, and when you bring forth the dead by My leave.﴾

The explanation of the parallel of these clauses and the readings in them, and the grammar, and what has not been mentioned earlier, we will mention, so we say: there it came as ﴿like the form of a bird by My leave, then you breathe into it and it becomes﴾ (Al 'Imran: 49). Ibn 'Abbas read ﴿fatanfukhuha fatakunu﴾ (you breathe into it). Al-Jumhur read (fatakunu) with a ta' from above. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read (fihi fayakunu), with a ya' from below, and the pronoun in (fihi). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The commentators have been confused about it." Makki said: "In Al 'Imran it refers to the bird, and here to the form," and he said: "The reverse is also valid." Others said: the pronoun mentioned refers to (clay). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is not valid for this pronoun to refer either to the clay or to the form, because the bird, or the bird whose form is like a bird's, has no breathing in it at all; likewise there is no breathing in its specific form; likewise the clay is general clay, and there is no breathing in that," end of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Part of the pronoun does not return to the form to which it is idafa, because it is not part of His creation, nor the breathing into anything; likewise the pronoun in (yakunu)," end of quotation. What should be taken as the meaning of Makki's words is that he does not intend what was understood from them; rather his saying "returns" refers to the bird, not the bird that is idafa to the form, but the bird that 'Isa fashioned, and the sense is: "And when you create from clay a bird, a form like the form of the real bird, and you breathe into it, and it becomes a real bird, by God's leave." And his saying "returns to the form" means not the form idafa to the bird, but the form in which the kaf is a qualifier, and the sense is: "And when you create from clay a form like the form of a bird, then you breathe into it," i.e., into the form described by the kaf, the creation of which is attributed to 'Isa. As for Makki's words, "and the reverse is valid," that is, the masculine pronoun referring to the form and the feminine pronoun referring to the bird, it may be explained as: the pronoun was masculinised though it refers to a feminine noun, because the sense of shape was observed in it, as if he had estimated a form like the form of a bird by his saying "a shape like the form of a bird." And the pronoun was feminised though it refers to a masculine noun, because the sense of form was observed in it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The proper course is that the feminine pronoun refers to what the verse necessarily requires, namely forms, or shapes, or bodies, and that the masculine pronoun refers to the created thing required by (you create)." Then he said: "You may also refer it to what the kaf indicates in the sense of likeness, because the meaning is: 'and when you create from clay the likeness of a form.' You may also refer the pronoun to the kaf itself, so that it is a noun outside poetry; this is the view of Abu al-Hasan alone among the Basrans." Likewise al-Zamakhshari said: the pronoun in (fihi) refers to the kaf, and said: "because it is the description of the form which 'Isa used to create and breathe into."

In Al 'Imran there is ﴿by God's leave﴾ (Al 'Imran: 49) twice, and here (bi-idhni) appears four times, after four clauses, because this is the place of mentioning the favour and bestowing it, so extended exposition is fitting; there is the place of informing the Children of Israel, so brevity is fitting. The estimate in ﴿and when you bring forth the dead﴾ is: "you give life to the dead," so he expressed giving life by bringing forth, like His saying: ﴿Thus is the coming forth﴾ [Qaf: 11] after His saying: ﴿and We revive therewith a dead land﴾ [Qaf: 11]; or the estimate is: "and when you bring forth the dead from their graves, living."

﴿And when I restrained the Children of Israel from you, when you came to them with the clear signs﴾ That is, I prevented them from killing you when they intended to harm you and surrounded the house in which you were. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: When God said to 'Isa: ﴿Remember My favour upon you﴾, he used to wear hair cloth, eat the leaves of trees, and did not store anything for the morrow, saying with each day "its sustenance"; he had no house to be ruined, nor a child to die; wherever night fell, he slept. This saying shows that 'Isa was addressed with that before the Raising. The clear signs here are the miracles already mentioned, which appeared at his hands. When He detailed His favour, He mentioned that attributed to 'Isa and not to his mother, because among these favours is the favour of prophethood and the manifestation of these extraordinary acts; so His favour upon him is greater than upon his mother, in that she bore such a noble prophet. A poet said regarding something like this:

> The worlds bear witness that she is precious, by the evidence of what she bore of noble ones.

﴿Then those of them who disbelieved said: "This is nothing but manifest sorcery."﴾ Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (sahir), with the alif, here, and in Hud and al-Saff; so "this" here refers to 'Isa. The rest of the seven read (sihr), so "this" refers to what 'Isa brought of the clear signs.

﴿And when I inspired the disciples: "Believe in Me and My Messenger."﴾ That is, I inspired them through the tongues of the messengers. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is either inspiration of inspiration (ilham) or inspiration of command. The Messenger here is 'Isa, and this inspiration to the disciples is among God's favours upon 'Isa, in that He made for him followers who affirm him and act upon what he brought. It is possible that it is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), since a clause having the sense of speech precedes it, and that it is verbal-masdar (masdariyyah).

﴿They said: "We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾ The explanation of the parallel of this clause has been given in Al 'Imran, except that there it is (amanna billah, "we believed in God"), because God alone had been mentioned in His saying: ﴿Who are my helpers in God? The disciples said: We are the helpers of God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 52]; here it came as (qalu amanna), without being restricted to the word of majesty, since it has already been mentioned (that they should believe in Me and My Messenger). There it came as ﴿and bear witness that we﴾ (Al 'Imran: 52), and here ﴿and bear witness that we﴾ (with the nun). This is the original, since the nun of (anna) is elided because of the gathering of like letters.

﴿Idh qāla al-ḥawāriyyūna yā ʿĪsā ibna Maryama hal yastaṭīʿu rabbuka an yunazzila ʿalaynā māʾidatan mina al-samāʾi qāla ittaqū Allāha in kuntum muʾminīn﴾ [When the disciples said, "O ʿIsa son of Maryam, can your Lord send down to us a table from the heaven?" He said, "Fear Allah, if you are believers."]. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: ﴿Idh qāla al-ḥawāriyyūna﴾ is an interjected clause (iʿtirāḍ) inserted into the description of the condition of the people of Allah's ʿIsa on the Day of Resurrection, and this interjection contains an announcement to Muhammad and his community about the incident of the disciples with the table, since it is a beneficial example for every community with its prophet, end quote. What the apparent wording requires is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Idh qāla Allāh yā ʿĪsā ibna Maryam udhkur niʿmatī ʿalayka﴾ [When Allah said, "O ʿIsa son of Maryam, remember My favour upon you"], up to the end of the story of the table, took place in this world. He reminded ʿIsa of His blessings and of the miracles He had brought about through his hands, and of the disagreement of the Children of Israel concerning him and their division into disbelievers and believers, and the believers were the disciples. Then it digressed to the story of the table, and then to His exalted question to ʿIsa, ﴿Did you say to the people﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 116]. Some scholars took it that this refers to the Hereafter because they believed that (idh) is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the Day when Allah will gather the messengers﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 109], and that at the end of the verses there is ﴿This is a day on which the truthful will benefit﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 119]. This interpretation is not required, as we will explain, Allah willing, in His saying ﴿This is a day on which will benefit﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 119]; rather, the apparent meaning is what we have mentioned.

Al-Jumhūr [the majority of reciters] read ﴿hal yastaṭīʿu rabbuka﴾ with the yāʾ and with a ḍammah on the bāʾ. The apparent meaning of this wording requires doubt about Allah's power to send down a table from the heaven, and this is what led al-Zamakhsharī to hold that the disciples were not believers. He said: If you ask, how could they say "Can your Lord?" after their faith and sincerity? I answer: Allah did not describe them as having faith and sincerity; rather, He related their claim to them, and then followed it with His saying (idh qālū), which indicates that their claim was false and that they were doubters. His saying ﴿hal yastaṭīʿu rabbuka﴾ is a statement that would not come from believers who revere their Lord. For this reason, ʿIsa's saying to them means: Fear Allah, and do not doubt His power and ability, and do not make demands upon Him, and do not prescribe for Him the signs you desire, lest you perish if you disobey Him after them.

﴿In kuntum muʾminīn﴾ means: if your claim of faith is sound, end quote. As for other than al-Zamakhsharī among the people of tafsīr (exegesis), they agreed that the disciples were believers, to the point that Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: I know of no disagreement that the disciples were believers. Some said: The disciples said this statement at the beginning of the matter, before they knew that he would heal the blind and the leper and bring the dead to life. The exegetes said: The disciples were the special companions of ʿIsa, and they were believers, and they did not doubt Allah's power over that. Ibn al-Anbārī said: It is not permissible for anyone to imagine that the disciples doubted Allah's power; rather, this is like a person saying to his companion, "Can you stand with me?" while he knows that the other is able to do so, but he means, "Is it easy for you?" end quote. Al-Fārisī said: Its meaning is, "Will He do that upon your request?" Al-Ḥasan said: They did not doubt Allah's power; rather, they asked him as an inquirer: Will He send it down or not? If He sends it down, then ask Him for us. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: Will He, exalted is He, do this, and will He grant them a response to it? Just as one says to ʿAbdullāh ibn Zayd: "Can you show me how the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed ablution?" So the meaning is, "Does He wish that, and will He do it?" end quote.

It was also said: The purpose of this statement is the question whether that is permissible or not. This is because His acts are contingent upon the aspects of wisdom; if none of the aspects of wisdom is realized, the act is impossible, since what contradicts the aspects of wisdom is like what contradicts the aspects of power. Abū ʿAbdullāh al-Rāzī said: This answer proceeds according to the view of the Muʿtazila. As for our school, it is taken to mean: Has He, exalted is He, decreed that? And has He known its occurrence? For if He has not decreed it and knows its occurrence, it would be impossible and not within the scope of power, since the opposite of what is known is not within the scope of power. He also said: The purpose of this statement is not that they were doubters concerning it; rather, the purpose is to establish that this matter is in the utmost clarity, like a person who takes the hand of a weak man and says, "Can the sultan provide for this one?" and his aim is that this is an evident matter about which a reasonable person may not doubt. Some were far off in saying: "Will your Lord send down a table from the heaven?" with (yastaṭīʿu) being a connective (ṣila). Others said: "The Lord" here is Jibrīl, because he used to nurture ʿIsa and favour him with various kinds of help, and for this reason, at the beginning of the verse, He said ﴿when I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 110].

It is related that what led them to this course of demand was that ʿIsa once said to them: "Would you like to fast thirty days for Allah, exalted is He, and then if you ask Him for a need, He will fulfil it?" When they had fasted them, they said: "O teacher of good! Indeed, it is the right of one who performs a deed to be fed, so can your Lord?" They wanted the table to be a feast (ʿīd) for that fast. Al-Kisāʾī read ﴿hal tastaṭīʿu rabbaka﴾ with a tāʾ at the beginning and a fatḥah on the bāʾ of (rabbaka), and this is the reading of ʿAlī, Muʿādh, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿĀʾishah and Ibn Jubayr. ʿĀʾishah said: The disciples were more knowledgeable of Allah than to say ﴿Can your Lord?﴾. She exonerated them from the offensiveness of the wording and from its apparent meaning. We have already mentioned the interpretations of this, and the meaning of this reading is: Are you able to ask your Lord? ﴿An yunazzila﴾ is an object of an omitted verb "ask" (suʾāl), since it is an omission without which the meaning is not complete. Abū ʿAlī said: It is possible to dispense with estimating a verb of asking, so that the meaning is: Are you able that your Lord send down by your supplication? Then the meaning becomes, but there must be an estimated element indicated by what is mentioned in the wording, end quote. What Abū ʿAlī said does not appear correct, because the act of Allah, exalted is He, even if its cause is supplication, is not within the power of ʿIsa.

Al-Kisāʾī assimilated the lām of (hal) into the yāʾ of (yastaṭīʿu). On this reading, ʿIsa's saying ﴿Fear Allah, if you are believers﴾ does not deny them the request for signs. In both readings, His saying ﴿if you are believers﴾ is an affirmation of faith, just as you say, "Do this and that, if you are a man."

Muqātil and a group said: Fear Him lest you ask Him for trial, because if it descends and you deny, you will be punished. Abū ʿUbayd and a group said: Lest you ask Him for what the nations before you did not ask. It was also said: Lest you doubt His power to send down the table. It was also said: Fear Allah regarding doubt about Him, and about His messengers and their signs. It was also said: Fear the disobedience of Allah. It was also said: He commanded them to piety so that it would be a cause for the attainment of this sought matter, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 2].

Al-Zamakhsharī said: Here, (ʿĪsā) is in the accusative position by following its vowel to the vowel of (ibn), as in your saying, "O Zayd son of ʿAmr!" and this is the prevalent dialect. It may also be in the nominative, as in your saying, "O Zayd son of ʿAmr!" and the proof of this is his saying: "Ḥār son of ʿUmar, it is as if I am wine," because truncation (tarkhīm) occurs only with the nominative, end quote. His saying "ʿĪsā is in the accusative position on this estimate" and on the estimate of its nominative, there is no exclusivity to its being in the accusative position on the estimate of following; so its corrected form, ʿĪsā, has an estimated fatḥah by following the vowel. His saying "it may also be nominative" is the view of al-Farrāʾ, and it is the estimate of fatḥah and ḍammah, and similar to it in what the ḍammah does not show, by analogy with the sound. He did not begin first with the ḍammah, which is agreed upon as an estimate. This is not a condition: do you not see the permissibility of truncating a man whose name is Muthannā, so that you say, "O Muthann, come!" and the permissibility of truncating Baʿlabakk, which is built on fatḥah, but it is in the estimate of the nominative noun. If he meant an estimated ḍammah, then this is fine; but if he meant an apparent ḍammah, this is not a condition. Do you not see the permissibility of truncating a man whose name is Muthannā, so that you say, "O Muthann"? For like "O Jaʿfar son of Zayd," that which has the final letter of the vocative pronounced with fatḥah for the sake of following is estimated with a ḍammah, because the letter is occupied by the vowel of following. Just as the Aʿrābī [the grammarian] estimated, in the reading of one who read (al-ḥamdi lillāh) with a kasrah on the dāl, for the sake of following the vowel of (lillāh), so your saying "O Ḥār!" is nominative by estimate, and even if the deleted thāʾ was originally occupied by the vowel of following, which is fatḥah, there is no contradiction between truncation and what was made fatḥah by following, while the ḍammah was estimated in it.

It was necessary for al-Zamakhsharī to speak on this question before this point, at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿When Allah said, "O ʿIsa son of Maryam, remember My favour upon you"﴾, where people spoke about it.

﴿They said: "We wish to eat from it, and that our hearts may be reassured, and that we may know that you have spoken the truth to us, and that we may be among its witnesses."﴾ When Jesus commanded them to fear God, disapproving of what they had said earlier, they stated the reason for asking for the table spread (al-ma'idah), namely that they wished to eat from it. This was for the sake of honour, not for satisfaction of hunger. Their hearts would be reassured, with thought at rest, once they witnessed this great miraculous sign descending from heaven, and once necessary knowledge and direct observation of its truth were established. Thus the doubts that arise in inferential reasoning would not trouble them. "Among its witnesses" means either that they would be among those who observe this sign, who transmit it to others and uphold this law, or among those who bear witness to God's oneness and to your prophethood. Some exegetes (mufassirun) elaborated at length on the objects of their wish, but in summary they wished to eat because of need and intense hunger. Ibn Abbas said: "When he went out, five thousand or more followed him, including a companion, one who was ill seeking cure, and a mocker. One day they found themselves in a desert without provisions. They became hungry, and they asked the disciples (al-hawariyyun) to ask Jesus to send down a table from heaven. Shim'un (Simon) told Jesus this, and he said: 'Tell them: fear God.' They wished to eat so that their faith would increase." Ibn al-Anbari said: "Or the honour of the table," as mentioned by al-Mawardi. Reassurance (al-itmi'nan) is either because God has sent you to us, or has chosen us as your helpers, or has answered you, or knowledge of the truth that if we fast for God thirty days, we will not ask God for anything without Him giving it to us, or [knowledge] that you are truly a Messenger, since a miracle is evidence of truth. Before that they had not seen signs. Or what is meant by knowledge is necessary knowledge and direct observation. End of quotation. These connected clauses are arranged in a subtle order. They would not eat from it except after witnessing its descent, so sight and taste combine to produce knowledge of it. Thereby the anxiety of disturbance leaves the heart, and it settles upon what a person has witnessed and tasted. With the reassurance of the heart, necessary knowledge of the truthfulness of the one through whose hands the miracle came is attained, since it came exactly as they asked. They asked for this great miracle, because its effect in the upper world through the supplication of one who is in the lower world is stronger and more wondrous than the effect of one who is in the lower world within his own lower world. Do you not see that among the greatest miracles of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) are the Qur'an and the splitting of the moon, both of which belong to the upper world? When necessary knowledge of Jesus's truthfulness was attained, they bore witness with certainty, with no doubt, suspicion or illusion stirring in it. By mentioning these causes that prompted the request for the table, the view of one who said is preferred: their request was made before they knew of Jesus's signs and miracles, and God's revelation to them to believe was at the beginning of the matter. At that point they said this statement, then they believed, saw the signs, persisted and were patient. Ibn Jubayr read (ونُعْلَمَ) with a damma on the nun, in the passive voice. This is likewise in the book al-Tahrir wa'l-Tahbir and in the book of Ibn Attiyah. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read (ويُعْلَمَ) with a damma on the ya', and the pronoun refers to the hearts. In the book of al-Zamakhshari, it is (ويُعْلَمَ) with ya' in the passive. Al-A'mash read (وتَعْلَمَ) with a ta', meaning "and the hearts will know it." The majority read (ونَكُونَ) with a nun. In the book al-Tahrir wa'l-Tahbir. Sinan and Isa read (وتَكُونَ عَلَيْها) with a ta'. In al-Zamakhshari. Their claim was made for the purpose of what they mentioned, like their claim to faith and sincerity. Jesus only asked, and was answered, so that they would be bound by the full proof, and so that punishment would be sent upon them if they disobeyed. End of quotation. He said this because the disciples were not believers in his view. When the light (mukhaffafah) form of (أنْ) is followed by a verb that is inflected for tense and not a supplication, if it is in the past tense, it is separated from it by (قَدْ), as in His saying (ونَعْلَمَ أنْ قَدْ صَدَقْتَنا). If it is in the present tense, it is separated by a future particle, as in His saying ﴿He knows that there will be among you those who are ill﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. It does not occur without a separator, though it is said: except rarely. It is also said: except out of necessity. As for what (عَلَيْها) is connected to, which was mentioned earlier in such expressions as ﴿Indeed, I am for you both among the sincere advisers﴾ [al-A'raf: 21]: al-Zamakhshari said: "devoted to it" (ʿakifina ʿalayha), on the basis that (عَلَيْها) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). This estimation is not good, because the governing verb of a prepositional phrase is not obligatorily omitted unless it is a general state of being, not a specific one, and devotion (al-ʿukuf) is a specific state. Also, when the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause, the governing word for it would be the implied (ʿakifina). We have already said that this is not good. Furthermore, al-Zamakhshari's statement is inconsistent, because if what (عَلَيْها) is connected to is ʿakifina, it would be in the accusative position as the object to which the verb extended by means of the preposition, but if it is in the circumstantial position, the governing word for it is a general state of being that must be omitted. So the contradiction between them is evident.

﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O God, our Lord, send down to us a table from heaven, which will be a festival for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You. And provide for us, for You are the best of providers."﴾ It is related that Jesus wore a garment of hair and a cloak of hair, and he stood praying, weeping and supplicating. The discussion of the word (اللَّهُمَّ) was given in Al ʿImran. He called upon his Lord first by the Name that no one shares, then secondly with the word (رَبَّنا), which is a correspondence to our reformer, nurturer and owner. The majority read ﴿will be for us﴾ as a clause describing "table." ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) and al-A'mash read (يَكُنْ) in the jussive, as a response to the imperative. The meaning is: "Let the day of its descent be a festival," and this is the day of Sunday, and for this reason the Christians took it as a festival. It was said that festival (ʿid) means joy and happiness, and for this reason one says "a day of festival." So the meaning is "it will be for us joy and happiness." A festival is a gathering on a day that is witnessed. Its customary usage is to say it of what recurs with the year, the month, the week, or similar. It was said: ʿid linguistically is whatever returns to you of something at a known time, whether it be joy or sorrow, and the customary usage overtook the linguistic meaning. Al-Khalil said: ʿid is every day that gathers people, because they return to it. Ibn Abbas said: "For the first of us" means for the people of our time, and "the last of us" means those who come after us. It was said: "the first of us" means our predecessors and leaders, and "the last of us" means the followers. The words "first" and "last" can carry the meanings of food, time or rank, but the apparent meaning is time. Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Jahdari read (لِأُولانا وأُخْرانا), with feminine forms, in the sense of the community and the group. The genitive noun is an apposition to "for us," and the governing preposition is repeated, as in His saying ﴿from it, from distress﴾ [al-Hajj: 22]. An apposition from a first- or second-person pronoun, when it is a partial apposition (badal al-ba'd) or an apposition of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), is permitted without disagreement. If it is an apposition of one thing from another where both refer to one entity, then if it conveys the sense of emphasis it is permitted for this apposition, since the meaning is "it will be a festival for all of us," like your saying: "I passed by you, your elders and your youngsters," because the meaning is "I passed by all of you." If it does not convey emphasis, then it is a matter of disagreement: al-Akhfash permits it, while other Basran grammarians prohibit it. The meaning of ﴿and a sign from You﴾ is a witnessing evidence of the truthfulness of Your servant. It was also said: a proof, and an indication of the perfection of Your power. Al-Yamani read (وأنَّهُ مِنكَ), and the pronoun in (وأنَّهُ) refers either to the festival or to the descent. (And provide for us) it was said: the table; it was also said: thankfulness for Your blessing. ﴿And You are the best of providers﴾, because You are the Rich, the Praiseworthy, who begins with provision. Abu Abd Allah al-Razi said: Reflect on this order. When the disciples asked for the table, they mentioned in their request several aims: they put mention of eating first and delayed the spiritual religious aims. Jesus requested the table and mentioned his aims: he put religious aims first and delayed the aims of eating, where he said (وارْزُقْنا). At this point there becomes apparent to you the levels of the ranks of souls, with some being spiritual and some corporeal. Then Jesus, peace be upon him, because of the intensity of the purity of his time and the illumination of his spirit, when he mentioned provision with the words (وارْزُقْنا), did not stop at it, but passed from the provision to the Provider, saying: ﴿And You are the best of providers﴾. His saying "Our Lord" is an opening from him with the call to the Truth, glorified and exalted be He. His saying ﴿send down to us a table﴾ is a transition from the Essence to the Attributes. His saying ﴿which will be a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾ is an indication of the spirit's joy in the blessing, not insofar as it is a blessing, but insofar as it proceeds from the Bestower. His saying ﴿and a sign from You﴾ is an indication of the portion of the soul. All of this descended from the presence of majesty. So observe how he began with the most noble, then the more noble, descending to the lower, then the lowest.

﴿And You are the best of providers﴾ is an ascent once more from the basest to the most noble. At this point there appears to you the aspiration concerning the manner of the ascent of luminous, divinely radiant spirits and their descent. O God, make us among its people. This is a discourse that lies between a philosophical term and a Sufi term, and both are far from the speech of the Arabs and their modes.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verses 110–114 (part 1 of 3):

﴿When God said: "O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My favour upon you and upon your mother."﴾ It is possible that (idh) is a substitute (badal) for His saying: ﴿the Day when God will gather the Messengers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109]. The meaning is that on that Day He will rebuke the disbelievers by questioning the Messengers about their response, and by the multitude of great signs that were manifested at their hands; yet they denied them, called them sorcerers, and went beyond the bounds of belief to the point of taking them as gods, just as some of the Children of Israel said regarding the clear signs that appeared at the hand of Jesus: ﴿This is manifest sorcery﴾ [al-Naml: 13]. Some of them took him and his mother as two gods; this was said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that the governing element (al-'amil) in (idh) is an implied verb, its estimate being: "Remember, O Muhammad," and (qala) here means (yaqulu), because the apparent sense of this speech is that it takes place on the Resurrection, as a preface to His saying: ﴿Did you say to the people...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. It is also possible that (idh) is a substitute for His saying: ﴿the Day when God gathers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109], end of quotation. They also permitted that (idh) be in the position of the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "That is when God said..."

When the vocative is a single proper noun, with an apparent damma, qualified by "ibn" connected and idafa to a proper noun, it is permissible to make it fatha, following the fatha of "ibn"; this is the view of the majority (al-Jumhur). Al-Farra' permitted, and Abu al-Baqa' followed him, in the case where the damma and fatha cannot be shown; if you do not make ﴿Ibn Maryam﴾ a qualifier, but make it a substitute or a vocative, then for that proper noun only the damma is permissible. Some commentators and some of those who belong to grammar have confused the matter here: some commentators said: "It is permissible for (Isa) to be in the nominative position, since it is a definite vocative not in idafa, and it is permissible for it to be in the accusative position, since it is intended as an idafa, and then 'ibn' was made an emphatic (tawkid); everything like this may take either of the two forms, such as: O Zayd son of 'Amr." The grammarians recited:

> O Hakam son of al-Mundhir son of al-Jarud, you are the generous son of the generous, son of generosity.

Al-Tabrizi said: "The more evident to me is that the position of (Isa) is accusative, because you treat the name together with its qualifier, when you make it an idafa to a proper noun, as a single thing made idafa." The rule that the grammarians stated for such as "O Zayd son of Bakr," when you put a fatha on the final of the vocative, is that it is a vowel of following (harakat ittiba') for the vowel of the "n" of "ibn"; the quiescence of the "ba'" of "ibn" was not counted, since the quiescent letter is a weak barrier.

They said: the remembrance here may be intended as acknowledgment (al-iqrar), and it may be intended as informing (al-i'lam). The benefit of this remembrance is to make the nations hear what He specially bestowed upon him of honour, and to confirm His proof against his denier. It was said: he was commanded to remember in order to alert others to recognising the due of a favour and the obligation of thanking the benefactor. Al-Hasan said: "Remembering a favour is thanking for it." The favour here is a genus, and what supports this is what He enumerated after this verbal unity, of favours, and their being attributed to him, as an alert to their magnitude. His favours upon him He enumerated here, in al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran and Maryam, and in other places in the Qur'an. His favour upon his mother: her innocence of what was attributed to her, her being entrusted to Zakariyya, her being accepted with a good acceptance, and what is mentioned in Surat al-Tahrim (﴿and Maryam daughter of 'Imran﴾) to its end, and other things. He was commanded to remember the favour upon his mother because it is a favour that reaches him.

﴿when I supported you with the Holy Spirit﴾ Al-Jumhur read (ayyadtuka) with a shaddah on the ya'. Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin read (ayadtuka) on the pattern of (af'altuka). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "On the pattern of (fa'altuka)," then he said: "It appears that the original in both readings is (ayyadtuka), on the pattern of (af'altuka), then the i'lal (morphological alteration) differed; and the meaning in both is (ayyadtuka), from al-ayad (strength)." 'Abd al-Muttalib said:

> Praise be to God, the Mightiest, the Most Noble, who strengthened us on the day of the crowding of al-Ashram.

End of quotation. What appears is that (ayyada), in the reading of the majority, is not of the pattern af'ala, because its present tense comes as yu'ayyidu, so the pattern is fa''ala; if it were af'ala, its present would be yu'ayyidu like the present of amana, yu'minu. As for the one who reads (ayada), he needs to transmit its present from the speech of the Arabs: if it is yu'ayidu, then it is (fa'ala), and if it is (yu'ayyidu), then it is (af'ala). As for Ibn 'Atiyyah's statement that it appears in both readings that its pattern is af'altuka, then the i'lal differed, I do not understand what he meant. The explanation of the parallel of this clause has already been given in His saying ﴿and We supported him with the Holy Spirit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 87].

﴿you speak to people in the cradle and in maturity﴾ ﴿and when I taught you the Book and wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel, and when you create from clay the likeness of a bird by My leave, then you breathe into it and it becomes a bird by My leave, and you heal the blind and the leper by My leave, and when you bring forth the dead by My leave.﴾

The explanation of the parallel of these clauses and the readings in them, and the grammar, and what has not been mentioned earlier, we will mention, so we say: there it came as ﴿like the form of a bird by My leave, then you breathe into it and it becomes﴾ (Al 'Imran: 49). Ibn 'Abbas read ﴿fatanfukhuha fatakunu﴾ (you breathe into it). Al-Jumhur read (fatakunu) with a ta' from above. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read (fihi fayakunu), with a ya' from below, and the pronoun in (fihi). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The commentators have been confused about it." Makki said: "In Al 'Imran it refers to the bird, and here to the form," and he said: "The reverse is also valid." Others said: the pronoun mentioned refers to (clay). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is not valid for this pronoun to refer either to the clay or to the form, because the bird, or the bird whose form is like a bird's, has no breathing in it at all; likewise there is no breathing in its specific form; likewise the clay is general clay, and there is no breathing in that," end of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Part of the pronoun does not return to the form to which it is idafa, because it is not part of His creation, nor the breathing into anything; likewise the pronoun in (yakunu)," end of quotation.
