In both readings, His saying ﴿if you are believers﴾ is an affirmation of faith, just as you say, "Do this and that, if you are a man."

Muqātil and a group said: Fear Him lest you ask Him for trial, because if it descends and you deny, you will be punished. Abū ʿUbayd and a group said: Lest you ask Him for what the nations before you did not ask. It was also said: Lest you doubt His power to send down the table. It was also said: Fear Allah regarding doubt about Him, and about His messengers and their signs. It was also said: Fear the disobedience of Allah. It was also said: He commanded them to piety so that it would be a cause for the attainment of this sought matter, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 2].

Al-Zamakhsharī said: Here, (ʿĪsā) is in the accusative position by following its vowel to the vowel of (ibn), as in your saying, "O Zayd son of ʿAmr!" and this is the prevalent dialect. It may also be in the nominative, as in your saying, "O Zayd son of ʿAmr!" and the proof of this is his saying: "Ḥār son of ʿUmar, it is as if I am wine," because truncation (tarkhīm) occurs only with the nominative, end quote. His saying "ʿĪsā is in the accusative position on this estimate" and on the estimate of its nominative, there is no exclusivity to its being in the accusative position on the estimate of following; so its corrected form, ʿĪsā, has an estimated fatḥah by following the vowel. His saying "it may also be nominative" is the view of al-Farrāʾ, and it is the estimate of fatḥah and ḍammah, and similar to it in what the ḍammah does not show, by analogy with the sound. He did not begin first with the ḍammah, which is agreed upon as an estimate. This is not a condition: do you not see the permissibility of truncating a man whose name is Muthannā, so that you say, "O Muthann, come!" and the permissibility of truncating Baʿlabakk, which is built on fatḥah, but it is in the estimate of the nominative noun. If he meant an estimated ḍammah, then this is fine; but if he meant an apparent ḍammah, this is not a condition. Do you not see the permissibility of truncating a man whose name is Muthannā, so that you say, "O Muthann"? For like "O Jaʿfar son of Zayd," that which has the final letter of the vocative pronounced with fatḥah for the sake of following is estimated with a ḍammah, because the letter is occupied by the vowel of following. Just as the Aʿrābī [the grammarian] estimated, in the reading of one who read (al-ḥamdi lillāh) with a kasrah on the dāl, for the sake of following the vowel of (lillāh), so your saying "O Ḥār!" is nominative by estimate, and even if the deleted thāʾ was originally occupied by the vowel of following, which is fatḥah, there is no contradiction between truncation and what was made fatḥah by following, while the ḍammah was estimated in it.

It was necessary for al-Zamakhsharī to speak on this question before this point, at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿When Allah said, "O ʿIsa son of Maryam, remember My favour upon you"﴾, where people spoke about it.

﴿They said: "We wish to eat from it, and that our hearts may be reassured, and that we may know that you have spoken the truth to us, and that we may be among its witnesses."﴾ When Jesus commanded them to fear God, disapproving of what they had said earlier, they stated the reason for asking for the table spread (al-ma'idah), namely that they wished to eat from it. This was for the sake of honour, not for satisfaction of hunger. Their hearts would be reassured, with thought at rest, once they witnessed this great miraculous sign descending from heaven, and once necessary knowledge and direct observation of its truth were established. Thus the doubts that arise in inferential reasoning would not trouble them. "Among its witnesses" means either that they would be among those who observe this sign, who transmit it to others and uphold this law, or among those who bear witness to God's oneness and to your prophethood. Some exegetes (mufassirun) elaborated at length on the objects of their wish, but in summary they wished to eat because of need and intense hunger. Ibn Abbas said: "When he went out, five thousand or more followed him, including a companion, one who was ill seeking cure, and a mocker. One day they found themselves in a desert without provisions. They became hungry, and they asked the disciples (al-hawariyyun) to ask Jesus to send down a table from heaven. Shim'un (Simon) told Jesus this, and he said: 'Tell them: fear God.' They wished to eat so that their faith would increase." Ibn al-Anbari said: "Or the honour of the table," as mentioned by al-Mawardi. Reassurance (al-itmi'nan) is either because God has sent you to us, or has chosen us as your helpers, or has answered you, or knowledge of the truth that if we fast for God thirty days, we will not ask God for anything without Him giving it to us, or [knowledge] that you are truly a Messenger, since a miracle is evidence of truth. Before that they had not seen signs. Or what is meant by knowledge is necessary knowledge and direct observation. End of quotation. These connected clauses are arranged in a subtle order. They would not eat from it except after witnessing its descent, so sight and taste combine to produce knowledge of it. Thereby the anxiety of disturbance leaves the heart, and it settles upon what a person has witnessed and tasted. With the reassurance of the heart, necessary knowledge of the truthfulness of the one through whose hands the miracle came is attained, since it came exactly as they asked. They asked for this great miracle, because its effect in the upper world through the supplication of one who is in the lower world is stronger and more wondrous than the effect of one who is in the lower world within his own lower world. Do you not see that among the greatest miracles of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) are the Qur'an and the splitting of the moon, both of which belong to the upper world? When necessary knowledge of Jesus's truthfulness was attained, they bore witness with certainty, with no doubt, suspicion or illusion stirring in it. By mentioning these causes that prompted the request for the table, the view of one who said is preferred: their request was made before they knew of Jesus's signs and miracles, and God's revelation to them to believe was at the beginning of the matter. At that point they said this statement, then they believed, saw the signs, persisted and were patient. Ibn Jubayr read (ونُعْلَمَ) with a damma on the nun, in the passive voice. This is likewise in the book al-Tahrir wa'l-Tahbir and in the book of Ibn Attiyah. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read (ويُعْلَمَ) with a damma on the ya', and the pronoun refers to the hearts. In the book of al-Zamakhshari, it is (ويُعْلَمَ) with ya' in the passive. Al-A'mash read (وتَعْلَمَ) with a ta', meaning "and the hearts will know it." The majority read (ونَكُونَ) with a nun. In the book al-Tahrir wa'l-Tahbir. Sinan and Isa read (وتَكُونَ عَلَيْها) with a ta'. In al-Zamakhshari. Their claim was made for the purpose of what they mentioned, like their claim to faith and sincerity. Jesus only asked, and was answered, so that they would be bound by the full proof, and so that punishment would be sent upon them if they disobeyed. End of quotation. He said this because the disciples were not believers in his view. When the light (mukhaffafah) form of (أنْ) is followed by a verb that is inflected for tense and not a supplication, if it is in the past tense, it is separated from it by (قَدْ), as in His saying (ونَعْلَمَ أنْ قَدْ صَدَقْتَنا). If it is in the present tense, it is separated by a future particle, as in His saying ﴿He knows that there will be among you those who are ill﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. It does not occur without a separator, though it is said: except rarely. It is also said: except out of necessity. As for what (عَلَيْها) is connected to, which was mentioned earlier in such expressions as ﴿Indeed, I am for you both among the sincere advisers﴾ [al-A'raf: 21]: al-Zamakhshari said: "devoted to it" (ʿakifina ʿalayha), on the basis that (عَلَيْها) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). This estimation is not good, because the governing verb of a prepositional phrase is not obligatorily omitted unless it is a general state of being, not a specific one, and devotion (al-ʿukuf) is a specific state. Also, when the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause, the governing word for it would be the implied (ʿakifina). We have already said that this is not good. Furthermore, al-Zamakhshari's statement is inconsistent, because if what (عَلَيْها) is connected to is ʿakifina, it would be in the accusative position as the object to which the verb extended by means of the preposition, but if it is in the circumstantial position, the governing word for it is a general state of being that must be omitted. So the contradiction between them is evident.

﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O God, our Lord, send down to us a table from heaven, which will be a festival for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You. And provide for us, for You are the best of providers."﴾ It is related that Jesus wore a garment of hair and a cloak of hair, and he stood praying, weeping and supplicating. The discussion of the word (اللَّهُمَّ) was given in Al ʿImran. He called upon his Lord first by the Name that no one shares, then secondly with the word (رَبَّنا), which is a correspondence to our reformer, nurturer and owner. The majority read ﴿will be for us﴾ as a clause describing "table." ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) and al-A'mash read (يَكُنْ) in the jussive, as a response to the imperative. The meaning is: "Let the day of its descent be a festival," and this is the day of Sunday, and for this reason the Christians took it as a festival. It was said that festival (ʿid) means joy and happiness, and for this reason one says "a day of festival." So the meaning is "it will be for us joy and happiness." A festival is a gathering on a day that is witnessed. Its customary usage is to say it of what recurs with the year, the month, the week, or similar. It was said: ʿid linguistically is whatever returns to you of something at a known time, whether it be joy or sorrow, and the customary usage overtook the linguistic meaning. Al-Khalil said: ʿid is every day that gathers people, because they return to it. Ibn Abbas said: "For the first of us" means for the people of our time, and "the last of us" means those who come after us. It was said: "the first of us" means our predecessors and leaders, and "the last of us" means the followers. The words "first" and "last" can carry the meanings of food, time or rank, but the apparent meaning is time. Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Jahdari read (لِأُولانا وأُخْرانا), with feminine forms, in the sense of the community and the group. The genitive noun is an apposition to "for us," and the governing preposition is repeated, as in His saying ﴿from it, from distress﴾ [al-Hajj: 22]. An apposition from a first- or second-person pronoun, when it is a partial apposition (badal al-ba'd) or an apposition of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), is permitted without disagreement. If it is an apposition of one thing from another where both refer to one entity, then if it conveys the sense of emphasis it is permitted for this apposition, since the meaning is "it will be a festival for all of us," like your saying: "I passed by you, your elders and your youngsters," because the meaning is "I passed by all of you." If it does not convey emphasis, then it is a matter of disagreement: al-Akhfash permits it, while other Basran grammarians prohibit it. The meaning of ﴿and a sign from You﴾ is a witnessing evidence of the truthfulness of Your servant. It was also said: a proof, and an indication of the perfection of Your power. Al-Yamani read (وأنَّهُ مِنكَ), and the pronoun in (وأنَّهُ) refers either to the festival or to the descent. (And provide for us) it was said: the table; it was also said: thankfulness for Your blessing. ﴿And You are the best of providers﴾, because You are the Rich, the Praiseworthy, who begins with provision. Abu Abd Allah al-Razi said: Reflect on this order. When the disciples asked for the table, they mentioned in their request several aims: they put mention of eating first and delayed the spiritual religious aims. Jesus requested the table and mentioned his aims: he put religious aims first and delayed the aims of eating, where he said (وارْزُقْنا). At this point there becomes apparent to you the levels of the ranks of souls, with some being spiritual and some corporeal. Then Jesus, peace be upon him, because of the intensity of the purity of his time and the illumination of his spirit, when he mentioned provision with the words (وارْزُقْنا), did not stop at it, but passed from the provision to the Provider, saying: ﴿And You are the best of providers﴾. His saying "Our Lord" is an opening from him with the call to the Truth, glorified and exalted be He. His saying ﴿send down to us a table﴾ is a transition from the Essence to the Attributes. His saying ﴿which will be a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾ is an indication of the spirit's joy in the blessing, not insofar as it is a blessing, but insofar as it proceeds from the Bestower. His saying ﴿and a sign from You﴾ is an indication of the portion of the soul. All of this descended from the presence of majesty. So observe how he began with the most noble, then the more noble, descending to the lower, then the lowest.

﴿And You are the best of providers﴾ is an ascent once more from the basest to the most noble. At this point there appears to you the aspiration concerning the manner of the ascent of luminous, divinely radiant spirits and their descent. O God, make us among its people. This is a discourse that lies between a philosophical term and a Sufi term, and both are far from the speech of the Arabs and their modes.

The Qur'an quotations are rendered in English within ﴿ ﴾, and the bracketed page marker from the source is kept as it appears.

﴿God said, "Indeed, I will send it down to you. Whoever among you disbelieves after that, I will punish him with a punishment with which I shall not punish anyone among the worlds."﴾ The apparent meaning is that the table (al-ma'ida) was sent down, since God said, "I will send it down," and the majority (al-jumhur) held that it was sent down.

Ibn Atiyya said: He stipulated for them the condition customary among nations: whoever disbelieves after the sign they asked for is punished with the most severe punishment. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: When they heard the condition, they became apprehensive, so it was not sent down. Mujahid said: It is a parable that God set forth for people, so that they would not ask for such signs. Those who said it was sent down differed over whether it was lifted because of an innovation they introduced, or was not lifted. Most said: They ate from it for forty days, morning and evening. Ishaq ibn Abd Allah said: They ate from it whenever they wished. It was also said: They became insolent, so it kept descending upon them day after day. The historians said: It used to descend at the height of the morning (al-duha), they ate from it, and then it rose to the sky while they watched its shadow on the earth.

They differed over the manner of its descent, what it consisted of, the number of those who ate from it, and what became of those who ate from it. The exegetes mentioned a confused, contradictory disagreement, and I have turned away from mentioning it (darabtu 'an dhikrihi safhan), since none of it is indicated by the wording of the verse. The best thing said about it is what al-Tirmidhi transmitted in the chapters on tafsir from Ammar ibn Yasir, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The table was sent down from heaven as bread and meat, and they were commanded not to store it for the next day, nor to betray, but they betrayed, stored it, and kept it for the next day, so they were transformed into monkeys and swine." Abu Isa said: This is a hadith narrated by Asim and others from Sa'id ibn Urwa, from Qatada, from Khilas, from Ammar ibn Yasir, as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet). We do not know it to be marfu' except from the hadith of al-Hasan ibn Qaza'a: Humayd ibn Mas'ada narrated to us, he said: Sufyan ibn Habib narrated to us from Sa'id ibn Urwa, similar to it, but he did not trace it to the Prophet. This is more authentic than the hadith of al-Hasan ibn Qaza'a, and we do not know the hadith to be marfu' at all.

Nafi', Ibn Amir and Asim read (munazziluha) with shadda (intensive form). The rest of the seven read it without shadda. Al-A'mash and Talha ibn Musarrif read: inni sa-unziluha, with the sin of the future (sin al-istiqbal) indicating "later," i.e., after its sending down.

Here al-adhab (punishment) carries the meaning of ta'dhib (punishing), so its case-ending is that of the verbal noun (masdar). Abu al-Baqa' allowed that it could be an object (maf'ul bihi) by extension (ala al-si'a), and this is a permissible construction (i'rab sa'ig).

It is not permissible that by "punishment" is meant the means by which one is punished, for then the verb would have to reach it through a preposition, and the construction would be: "I punish him with a punishment." One cannot say that the preposition was deleted, so that the verb reached it and put it in the accusative, because deleting the preposition in such a case is restricted to poetic necessity (darura).

The apparent reference of the pronoun in la u'adhdhibuhu is to al-adhab in the sense of ta'dhib, and the meaning is: "I will not punish anyone with a punishment like this punishment." Abu al-Baqa' allowed that the sense could be: "I will not punish anyone with it," that it could be an object by extension, and that it could be the pronoun of the emphatic verbal noun, as in your saying: "I thought him to be Zayd, going away," in which case it does not refer back to al-adhab. The clause that is a qualifier (sifa) of adhaban is linked to it by the generality inherent in the emphatic verbal noun, as in your saying: "He is a kind," and (adhaban) is indefinite, so the verbal noun encompasses it, just as the generic noun Zayd is encompassed in: "Zayd is the excellent man." He also allowed that it could be the pronoun of (min) with an ellipsis, meaning: "I will not punish with the punishment of the disbeliever." These are strained constructions, from which the Qur'an should be declared free.

Ibn Abbas said: He transformed them into swine. Others said: into monkeys and swine, and this occurred in this world. The disbelief referred to, which necessitated their punishment, was said to be their apostasy. It was also said: their doubt about Jesus and their casting doubt upon people. It was also said: their opposition to the command not to betray, not to conceal, and not to store, as Qatada said. Ammar ibn Yasir said: Their day had not ended before they betrayed, stored, and kept it.

The apparent meaning of al-alamin (the worlds) is generality. It was also said: the worlds of their own time.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 116:

﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah'?"﴾ Abu 'Ubayda said: "*idh*" (when) is superfluous (*za'ida*). Others said it has the meaning of "*idha*" (whenever). The apparent meaning is that it retains its original usage, and that the past tense verb following it has already occurred, and no interpretation (*ta'wil*) is needed. al-Suddi and others said: this statement was from Allah, the Exalted, when He raised Jesus to Himself, and the Christians said what they said and claimed that Jesus had commanded them to do so. al-Tabari chose this view.

Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and the majority said: this statement is from Allah, the Exalted, and it will be on the Day of Resurrection, when He says it to him in front of all creation, so that the disbelievers will know that what they were upon was false. In this case there is a figurative usage (*tajawwuz*) in using "*idh*" to mean "*idha*," and the past tense verb after it carries the meaning of the future. Also, [in this view] there is the placing of the interrogative (*istifham*) before the noun, and the verb coming after it indicates that the act has actually occurred in existence. However, the interrogation concerns the attribution: was this act, which has occurred, issued by the one addressed or not issued by him? The explanation of this is that you say: "*Adrabta Zaydan*" (did you strike Zayd?), which is an interrogation asking whether a striking of Zayd proceeded from you or not, with no indication in it that the striking of Zayd has taken place. But when you say: "*Anta darabta Zaydan*" (you struck Zayd?), the striking has taken place upon Zayd, but you are asking about its attribution to the one addressed. This is a matter of rhetoric (*bayaniyya*), as Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash stated.

The commentators mentioned that none of the Christians claimed the divinity of Mary, so how is it said "*ilahayn*" (two gods)? They answered that when they said she did not give birth to a human but gave birth to a god, it became necessary for them to say, in terms of partiality (*al-ba'diyya*), that the one she bore is divine, so they became like one who says [such a thing]. End. The apparent meaning is that this statement is issued in existence, not from Jesus, and the issuing of the statement does not necessarily entail the existence of the taking [of such gods].

﴿He said, "Glory be to You"﴾: that is, exaltation of You (*tanzihan laka*). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "[Glory be to You] from saying this and uttering it." al-Zamakhshari said: "from there being a partner for You." The apparent meaning is the first, due to His saying afterwards: ﴿It is not for me to say what I have no right to say﴾. Abu Rawq said: When Jesus heard this statement, his joints trembled, and from the root of every hair a spring of blood burst forth. Then, at that point, he responded to Allah, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Glory be to You﴾, exalting and magnifying You, and declaring You free from every imperfection.

﴿It is not for me to say what I have no right to say﴾: this is a negation supported by the proof of reason. It is rationally impossible for a created human to claim divinity. "*Bi-haqq*" (with right) is the predicate of "*laysa*" (is not), meaning "it is not deserved." They permitted that "*li*" (for me) be an explanatory element (*tabyin*), or that it be a descriptive complement to "*bi-haqq*" which came before it, so it becomes a circumstantial (*hal*); meaning, "with a right for me." It appears that it is connected to "*bi-haqq*," because the "*ba*" is superfluous, and "*haqq*" means "*mustahiqq*" (deserved); i.e., what is not deserved. Some permitted that the speech is complete at His saying: ﴿what I have no right to﴾, and that "*bi-haqq*" is connected to its knowing (*'ilmiyyatihi*), which is the answer to the condition (*jawab al-shart*). This was refuted by claiming anteriority and posteriority (*taqdim wa ta'khir*) in what apparently contradicts it, and one does not resort to anteriority and posteriority except for a meaning that requires it, or by a stipulation, or where nothing else is possible. End of this view and its refutation. It is impossible for it to be connected to its knowing, because nothing of the objects (*ma'mulat*) of the verb of the condition may precede the condition, nor of the objects of its answer. Nafi' and other readers paused at His saying: ﴿bi-haqq﴾, and this was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿If I had said it, You would have known it﴾: Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: This is a station of submission and humility. So he put forward the negation of the statement from himself, and did not say "what I said," but entrusted that to His all-encompassing knowledge of everything. This is an exaggeration in courtesy, and in displaying humility and lowliness in the presence of majesty, and entrusting the matter entirely to the Truth, glorified is He. End. There is some abridgment in it.

﴿You know what is in my self, and I do not know what is in Your self﴾: He specified "*nafs*" (self) because it is the place of concealment and of keeping knowledge hidden. It was said: the meaning is: You know what I conceal, and I do not know what You conceal. It was also said: You know what is with me, and I do not know what is with You. It was said: You know my secret, and I do not know Your secret. al-Zamakhshari said: You know what I know, and I do not know what You know. He used the phrase ﴿what is in Your self﴾ by way of opposition (*muqabala*) and parallelism (*tashakkul*) with His saying ﴿what is in my self﴾; so it resembles His saying: ﴿And they plotted, and Allah plotted﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54], and His saying: ﴿We are only mockers﴾ [al-Baqara: 14], ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqara: 15]. As for one who claims that "*nafs*" is applied to the essence and reality of a thing, the meaning according to him is: You know the true nature of my essence, and I do not know the true nature of Your essence. The anthropomorphists (*al-mujassima*) have used as evidence His saying: ﴿You know what is in my self, and I do not know what is in Your self﴾. They said: "*nafs*" is the person, and that requires that He be a body. Exalted is Allah far above that, a great exaltation.

﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen [of all things]﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 109]: This is a confirmation of both sentences together, because what souls conceal is among the unseen matters; and because what ﴿the Knower of the unseen﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 109] knows does not end with anyone. So if You are the one specialized in knowledge of the unseen, then I have no knowledge of the unseen, so how could divinity be mine? al-Tirmidhi transmitted from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that He recited to him ﴿Glory be to You, it is not for me to say what I have no right to say﴾, the whole verse. Abu 'Isa said: This is a hasan sahih hadith.

﴿I said to them nothing except what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord"﴾. He informed that he did not exceed God's command when He commanded him to worship Him, and he acknowledged His lordship. In His saying ﴿my Lord and your Lord﴾ there is a disavowal of what they claimed about him. In the Gospel he said: "O children of the baptism (al-Ma'mudiyya)! Rise, let us go to my Father and your Father, and my God and your God, and my Savior and your Savior." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: The original form would have been: "I did not command them except what You commanded me," but he placed the verb "say" in the position of "command," out of regard for good manners. Al-Hasan said: He only changed the wording so as not to make himself and his Lord both commanders together, and it indicates that the original form is what was mentioned. The interpretive "an" (an-mufassira). Al-Hawfi and Ibn 'Atiyya said: The "an" in "an i'budu" (﴿an i'budu﴾) is interpretive (mufassira), having no place in the grammatical analysis (i'rab, the study of case endings and sentence structure), and it is valid for it to be a substitute (badal) for "ma" (what), and it is valid for it to be a substitute for the pronoun in "bihi" (by it). Ibn 'Atiyya added that it is also valid for it to be in the genitive position, under the assumption of: ﴿an i'budu﴾. Abu al-Baqa' permitted the genitive (jarr) as a substitute for the pronoun "ha'" (the ha of bihi), the nominative (raf') by supposing "huwa" (he), and the accusative (nasb) by supposing "a'ni" (I mean), or as a substitute for the position of "bihi." He said: It is not permissible for it to have the meaning of the interpretive "an," because the saying has been explicitly stated, and "an" does not occur with an explicit "say." Al-Zamakhshari said: The "an" in His saying ﴿an i'budu Allah﴾ — if you make it interpretive, it must have something it explains, and the thing explained is either the verb of saying or the verb of commanding, and both have no justification. As for the verb of saying, the speech following it is quoted without the interpretive particle being placed between them; you do not say: "I did not say to them except ﴿an i'budu Allah rabbi wa rabbakum﴾," but rather "I did not say to them except: Worship Allah." As for the verb of commanding, it is attributed to the pronoun of God, Exalted, so if you explained it with "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord," it would not be right, because God does not say: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord." And if you make it a relative clause (mawsula) linked to the verb, it must be either a substitute for "ma amartani bihi" (what You commanded me with), or for the "ha'" in "bihi," and both are unsound, because the substitute is what takes the place of the thing substituted, and one does not say "I did not say to them except that worship Allah," meaning "I did not say to them except His worship," because worship is not said. Likewise if you make it a substitute for the "ha'," for if you were to put ﴿an i'budu Allah﴾ in its place, the relative would be left without a return-pronoun referring back to it from its clause. If you say: "Then how do you handle it?" I say: The verb of saying is taken in its meaning, because the meaning of ﴿I said to them nothing except what You commanded me with﴾ is: "I did not command them except with what You commanded me," so that its explanation by ﴿an i'budu Allah rabbi wa rabbakum﴾ becomes sound. It is also permissible for it to be a relative (mawsula) in apposition (ʿatf) to the explanation of the "ha'," not as a substitute. End of quotation, with some abridgement. As for his saying "as for the verb of commanding" up to the end of the objection, and his saying "because God, Exalted, does not say: Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord," it is not sound because he joined the sentence and what follows it to the verb of commanding, whereas it is correct that the verb of commanding is explained by His saying ﴿Worship Allah﴾, and ﴿my Lord and your Lord﴾ is from the speech of Jesus, under the assumption of "a'ni" (I mean), that is: "I mean my Lord and your Lord," not as the attribute which al-Zamakhshari understood, and so it was not right in his view. As for his saying "because worship is not said," this is correct, but that is valid by omitting a modifier (mudaf): that is, "I did not say to them except the word which You commanded me, the word of worshipping Allah," that is, the word including the worship of God. As for his saying "because the relative is left without a return-pronoun referring back to it from its clause," it does not necessarily follow in every substitute that it must take the place of the thing substituted. Do you not see the grammarians' permission of: "Zayd, I passed by him, Abu 'Abd Allah," and if you said: "Zayd, I passed by Abu 'Abd Allah," it would not be permitted by them, except according to the opinion of al-Akhfash. As for his saying "as an apposition to the explanation of the ha'," this is far-fetched, because the explicative apposition (ʿatf al-bayan) is mostly with fixed proper nouns, and what al-Zamakhshari chose and others permitted, that "an" is interpretive, is not sound, because it came after "illa" (except), and everything that comes after the exception particle "illa" must have a place in the grammatical analysis, while the interpretive "an" has no place in the grammatical analysis. Consider what the dialogue of Jesus contained, and his response with God, Exalted: when there struck his hearing what could not possibly be, he glorified God, Exalted, and declared Him free of evil, and of having any partner with Him. Then he informed about himself that he could not say what is not his right, so he used a general negative term, namely the word "ma" (what), under which every saying that is not true is included, even this specific saying. Then he disavowed it a third time, by referring that to God's knowledge and entrusting it to Him, while Jesus knows that he did not say it. Then, when he referred it to knowledge, he affirmed God's knowledge of it and denied his own knowledge of what belongs to God. In this is an indication that it is impossible for that to occur to his mind, let alone that he would utter it or say it. The totality of this became a negation of this saying and a negation that it would occur to the soul. Then he gave as the reason that He, Exalted, has exclusive knowledge of the unseen. Then, when he had glorified God, Exalted, and been cleared of saying that and of its occurring to his soul, he moved on to what he had told them, presenting it restricted by "illa" (except), bound to the fact that it is what God commanded him to convey to them from Him.

﴿And I was a witness over them while I remained among them﴾: that is, a watcher, like a witness over the one witnessed against, preventing them from saying that and from adopting it as a religion. He used the form "fa'il" (fa'eel) for intensity: one who greatly guards over them and constantly accompanies them. "Ma" is temporal, and "dama" (remain) is complete, that is: "as long as I remained among them," that is, a witness during the worldly life.

﴿So when You took me back﴾: It was said: This indicates that He caused him to die a death before raising him. This is not right, because reports have been widely transmitted about his being raised alive, that he is alive in heaven, that he will descend and kill the Dajjal (the Antichrist). The meaning of ﴿tawaffaytani﴾ is "You took me to Yourself," by raising. Al-Hasan said: "Tawaffi" is the death of death, the death of sleep, and the death of raising. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿You were the watcher over them, and You are a witness over everything﴾ — You prevent them from saying it by the proofs You set up for them, the clear signs You sent down upon them, and the messengers You sent to them. End of quotation. In it is the subtle hint of Mu'tazilism (dasisat al-i'tizal).

﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Indeed they are Your servants﴾, and those whom You punish are deniers of Your signs and deniers of Your prophets. ﴿And if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty﴾, the Powerful over reward and punishment, ﴿the Wise﴾, who does not reward or punish except for wisdom and rightness. If you say: forgiveness does not apply to disbelievers, so how does He say ﴿and if You forgive them﴾? I say: He did not say "You forgive them." Rather, He structured the speech on the basis that it be said: if You punish them, You are just, for they deserve punishment; and if You forgive them despite their disbelief, You have not lost, in forgiving, the aspect of wisdom, because forgiveness is good for every criminal in reason. Indeed, whenever the criminal is greater in crime, pardoning him is better. This is from al-Zamakhshari an inclination toward the positions of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah), for forgiveness of disbelief is permissible according to them, and according to the majority of the Basran scholars among the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) by reason. They said: because punishment is a right of God over the sin, and in its removal there is a benefit, and there is no harm to God in removing it; therefore it must be good. The revealed proof in our law indicates that it does not occur; so perhaps this revealed proof did not exist in the law of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. The words of the majority of the Basran Mu'tazilah end here. The People of the Sunnah said: the intent of ʿĪsā is the complete entrusting of all matters to God, Exalted, and the total abandonment of objection. For this reason he concluded the speech with his words ﴿indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾, meaning: You are capable of what You will, in all that You do, and there is no objection against You. It was also said: when God said to ʿĪsā ﴿Did you say to the people...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], it became known that a group of Christians related this statement from him, and the one who relates this disbelief is not a disbeliever but a sinner, since he lied; and forgiveness of sin is permissible. Therefore he said ﴿and if You forgive them﴾. It was also said: ʿĪsā knew that they had introduced sins and acted after him in ways he had not commanded, though they were still upon the pillar of his religion; so he said ﴿and if You forgive them﴾ for what they introduced of sins after me. This applies to the view of one who says that God's statement to him ﴿Did you say to the people...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116] was at the time of the raising (to heaven), because he said that while they were alive and he did not know what they would die upon. It was also said: the pronoun in (You punish them) refers to those who died as disbelievers, and in ﴿and if You forgive them﴾ it refers to those among them who repented before death. It was also said: he said that in the manner of seeking their favor and showing compassion toward them, while knowing that disbelievers are not forgiven; for this reason he did not say "because they disobeyed You." The words of al-Zamakhshari end here. This has some remoteness, because seeking favor is only fitting for one for whom pardon and lightening are hoped; and disbelievers are not hoped to receive that. What I choose from these views is that God's statement, Exalted, ﴿And when God said, "O ʿĪsā son of Maryam, did you say to the people..."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116] is a statement that has already occurred, and a meaning that connects it to what has occurred and passed. Its coming with (idh), which is an adverb of time for the past, and it is said that it is literally in the past, so all that came in these verses with (idh) "said" is to be understood according to its original usage. If that is so, then ʿĪsā's statement ﴿and if You forgive them﴾ uses the cause to express the effect, because it is known that forgiveness is dependent on repentance. And if this statement was at a time other than the Hereafter, they were in a position where either punishment or forgiveness resulting from repentance could apply to them. The apparent meaning of his words ﴿indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾ is that it is the answer to the condition, and the meaning is: indeed You are the Mighty, whom nothing that You desire can resist, the Wise in what You do, You misguide whom You will and guide whom You will. A group recited ﴿indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾, in accordance with what his statement ﴿and if You forgive them﴾ requires. ʿIyad ibn Musa said: it is not part of the Mushaf. Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said: the Qur'an has been criticized by one who said that His statement ﴿indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾ does not fit with His statement "and if You forgive them", because the fitting would be ﴿indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾. The answer: this cannot bear anything except what God, Exalted, revealed, and when it is changed to what this critic said, its meaning becomes weak, for "the Forgiving, the Merciful" would stand alone with the second condition and would have no connection to the first condition, which is what God revealed. The Muslims have unanimously agreed on its recitation, and it is tied to both conditions, the first and the last, since its summary is: if You punish them, then You are Mighty and Wise; and if You forgive them, then You are the Mighty, the Wise, in both matters, punishment and forgiveness. Therefore "the Mighty, the Wise" is more fitting in this place, due to its generality, and because it joins both conditions; "the Forgiving, the Merciful" could not bear what "the Mighty, the Wise" bears. The words of Ibn al-Anbari end here. As for the view of one who holds that there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, its supposed form being: if You punish them, then indeed You are the Mighty; and if You forgive them, then indeed they are Your servants, then it is nothing, and it is the statement of one who has dared to speak about the Book of God without knowledge. Al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Dharr, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) stood (in prayer) until morning with this verse: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise.﴾"

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 119:**

﴿Allah said, "This is a Day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness."﴾ The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿هَذا يَوْمُ﴾ with a *damma* (*raf*) on *yawm*, taking *hadha* (هَذا) as a *mubtada'* (subject) and *yawmu* (يَوْمُ) as its *khabar* (predicate) (*mubtada'* means the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence, and *khabar* means its predicate). The clause is reported speech after *qala* (قالَ), and it stands in the position of the object of *qala*, meaning: "this time is a time when the truthful benefit." This contains an indication of the truthfulness of Jesus, peace be upon him.

Nafi' read ﴿هَذا يَوْمَ﴾ with a *fatha* on the *mim*. The Kufans interpreted it as *mabni* (indeclinable, fixed in form) and as the *khabar* of *hadha*, and it is *mabni* because it is attached to a verbal clause (*ila al-jumla al-fi'liyya*). They do not require that the verb in the clause be *mabni* for the time-noun to be *mabni* when it is attached to a clause; according to their view, the two readings have the same meaning. The Basrans said: the condition for this *bina'* (fixed form) when the time-noun is attached to a verbal clause is that the clause begin with a *mabni* verb, because the fixity does not extend to it except from a *mabni* element to which it is attached. The matter is established in the science of grammar (*'ilm al-nahw*). According to the Basrans, the word is *mu'rab* (inflected), not *mabni*, and its *nasb* (accusative) is explained in two ways mentioned by al-Zamakhshari and others:

First, that it is an adverbial complement (*zarf*) of *qala*, and *hadha* refers to the utterance (*masdar*), so it is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning: Allah said this statement. Or *hadha* refers to the report, or the narrative, as in your saying: "Zayd said a poem" or "Zayd said a sermon," so it refers to the content of the clause.

It has been disputed whether it is in the accusative as a verbal noun or as an object (*maf'ul bihi*). On this disagreement, when it refers to the report or narrative, it is in the accusative either as a verbal noun or as a direct object.

Ibn Atiyya said: its accusative is as an adverbial complement, and its sense is: Allah said, "This," meaning the narrative or the report, "is a Day when..." This meaning removes the eloquence of the verse and the splendor of its wording and meaning.

The second way: it is an adverbial complement serving as the predicate of *hadha*, and *hadha* is in the nominative as the subject. The sense is: "This which we have mentioned of the words of Jesus takes place on the Day when..." and *hadha yawma yanfa'u* forms a reported clause after *qala*.

Al-Zamakhshari said: al-A'mash read ﴿يَوْمًا يَنْفَعُ﴾ with tanwin, like His saying: ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another﴾ (al-Baqarah 48).

Ibn Atiyya said: al-Hasan ibn 'Ayyash al-Shami read ﴿هَذا يَوْمُ﴾ with *raf'* and tanwin.

The majority read ﴿صِدْقُهُمْ﴾ with *raf'* as the subject (*fa'il*) of *yanfa'u*. It was also read with *nasb* and was explained as: an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), meaning "because of their truthfulness"; or with the preposition elided, meaning "by their truthfulness"; or as an emphatic verbal noun (*masdar mu'akkid*), meaning "those who speak the truth, the truthfulness"; or as a direct object, meaning "they speak the truth," as you say: "I fought him in battle," and the sense is: they realize truthfulness.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: if their truthfulness is meant in the Hereafter, then it is not a place of action; and if it is meant in this world, then it does not correspond to what is reported in it, because it carries the sense of testimony for Jesus, peace be upon him, for his truthfulness in what he answers on the Day of Resurrection. I say: its meaning is the continuous truthfulness of the truthful in their worldly life and their Hereafter. End of quote. This is based on the view of those who say that this statement comes from Allah the Exalted in the Hereafter. Al-Zajjaj followed al-Zamakhshari in his view that the reality of this is the report, and the meaning of ﴿the truthfulness that they had in this world will benefit them on the Day of Resurrection, because the Hereafter is not a place of action, and whatever one says there, however good, benefits no one; even if the unbeliever were truthful and confessed to what he had done, saying "I disbelieved and did wrong," it would not benefit him; and only the truthful one benefits from the truthfulness that he had in this world and the Hereafter﴾. End of quote. The apparent meaning is that it is the beginning of a speech from Allah the Exalted.

Al-Suddi said: this is a separate part of the speech of Jesus, peace be upon him, meaning that Jesus says on the Day of Resurrection: "Allah the Exalted said."

The scholars differed about this Day. It was said: it is the Day of Resurrection, as we have mentioned, and it was specifically mentioned because it is the Day of recompense, in which the lasting, complete fruits of truthfulness are gathered; otherwise truthfulness benefits on every day and at every time. It was also said: it is a day of the days of this world, since action benefits only when it is done in this world.

Here "the truthful" (*al-sadiqun*) may mean the prophets, and their truthfulness is their conveying of the message; or it may mean the believers, and their truthfulness is their sincerity in their faith; or the truthfulness of their covenants; or their truthfulness in acting for Allah the Exalted; or their truthfulness in refraining from lying about Allah and His messengers; or their truthfulness in the Hereafter in testifying (p-64) for their prophets that they conveyed the message, or in bearing witness against themselves concerning their deeds. The way it benefits them would be that they are spared punishment for having withheld testimony, and they are forgiven by their confession to their prophets and against themselves. There are six opinions on this. The apparent meaning is general, so every truthful person is benefited by his truthfulness.

﴿For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. This is as if it were the answer to a questioner who asks: "What is their reward for truthfulness?" So it is said: "For them are gardens."

﴿Abiding therein forever﴾: an indication of the everlasting permanence of their dwelling in Paradise.

﴿Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him﴾. It was said: He is pleased with their good deeds being accepted, and they are pleased with Him for what He has given them of honor. It was also said: He is pleased with their obedience, and they are pleased with Him in the Hereafter for His reward. Al-Tirmidhi said: He is pleased with their truthfulness, and they are pleased with Him for fulfilling their right. It was also said: this is in this world, and they are pleased with Him in the Hereafter. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: in His saying ﴿Allah is pleased with them﴾ there is an indication of exaltation (*ta'zim*); this is according to the apparent view of the theologians (*mutakallimun*). As for the people of illuminated spirits, lit by the lights of the majesty of Allah the Exalted, there are wondrous secrets beneath His saying ﴿Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him﴾ which pens do not permit to be recorded like them; may Allah make us among their people. End of quote. This is a wondrous statement, resembling the statements of the philosophers and the Sufis.

﴿That is the great success﴾. *Dhalika* (that) refers to what preceded: the eternal abiding of the gardens for them, and the good pleasure of Allah with them; because the Garden with all that is in it is as nothing in comparison with the good pleasure of Allah. It is established in the authentic (*sahih*) collection that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah will look upon the people of Paradise and say: 'O people of Paradise, are you pleased?' They will say: 'O our Lord, how could we not be pleased, when You have distanced us from Your Fire and admitted us into Your Garden?' Allah the Exalted will say: 'And I have for you something better than that.' They will say: 'And what is better than that?' Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will say: 'I will let My pleasure descend upon you, and I shall never be displeased with you after it, ever.'"

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 5, verse 120:

﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is over all things competent.﴾ When the Christians claimed divinity for Jesus and his mother, the claim required that they be owners and capable, so God refuted them. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that this is among what will be said on the Day of Resurrection, and it is possible that it is a separate statement addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community." End of quote. It was also said: this is the answer to a questioner who asks, regarding the verse ﴿That is the great achievement﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 119], "To whom does [this reward] belong?" So it was said: "To the One to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: the heavens and the earth contain rational and non-rational beings, so did [the word] 'what' (ما) prevail for the rational ones, such that it says 'and whoever is in them' (ومن فيهن)? I say: (ما) encompasses all kinds in a general way. Do you not see that when you see a figure from afar, you say 'ما هو' before you know whether it is rational or not? So it is more fitting for the meaning of generality." End of his words. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "The non-rational were given precedence (غُلِّب) to indicate that all created beings are subjugated within the grip of His dominance, His decree, His judgment and His power. In that subjugation they are like inanimate objects that have no power and like beasts that have no intellect. So the knowledge of all, in comparison to His knowledge, is as no knowledge, and the power of all, in comparison to His power, is as no power." He also said: "The opening of the surah (p-65) was with the mention of the covenant established between lordship and servanthood, so the servant begins in servanthood and arrives at complete annihilation of himself entirely. The first is the Shari'a (the revealed religious law), and it is the beginning; the other is the Haqiqa (the inner reality), and it is the end. So the opening of the surah is of the Shari'a, and its closing is with the mention of God, the Mighty and Majestic, His greatness, His might, His dominance and His exaltation, and that is the arrival at the station of Haqiqa. How excellent is the correspondence between that opening and this closing." End of his words. The Haqiqa, the Shari'a and the distinction between them are not from the words of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, nor from the words of the Successors. Rather, these are among the terminology and technical expressions of the Sufis, and they have lengthy discourse on this. And Allah knows best what is correct.
